video_details.title: COVID-19 Therapy Session Managing Fear and Anxiety: A Therapist's Advice With Monica Blume
video_details.description:

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, and I don't think you should say boss.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You don't want me to say boss?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Colleague, maybe? Okay. I knew you wouldn't like that, but I'm going to talk about you for a second, and you're going to be flattered.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, and again, I'm used to it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi everyone, Emma McAdam here. I'm a Licensed Marriage and Family Therapist, and today I have my colleague, best friend, and clinical director Monica Bloom here. I've been trying to get you on my channel for years, right?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yes, it's exciting to be here finally.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Monica has been helping people through the stress and anxiety of the coronavirus pandemic. She's been a therapist for over 20 years, specializes in difficult cases, and is also a marathon runner. How many have you done, Monica?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I just completed 78 full marathons.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Only 78? Rollerblading is another thing she does. Do you have a life analogy from that?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I love rollerblading. One analogy is about fearlessness. I decided to go down a big hill even though I couldn't use the brakes. Instead of flailing out of fear, I decided to enjoy it and yell 'Woo-hoo!' We cannot live in fear, so we do what we can, like wearing a helmet, but we still make the decision to enjoy it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's an excellent story. We probably all feel like we are flying down a hill on rollerblades without brakes right now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And we didn't choose this hill. Monica, what are some common concerns you're seeing from clients right now?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Anxiousness and fear. People who have anxiety have more of it, and those who don't are feeling it now. I see people worried about their ability to handle this as healthy coping resources are wiped away. Secondary effects, like marriage struggles and lack of schedule, are affecting people as much as the virus itself.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Every person's coping resource is kind of wiped away. What do you tell people who are feeling so much worry?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It is normal to have feelings about this. It doesn't mean you're weak or not coping. Being completely without feeling about this would feel less natural. Taking a break is normal.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Like the only people not feeling anxiety are psychopaths. We find ways to laugh and honestly face something scary. It's a sign that you're human, not broken. Emotional intelligence is the ability to feel multiple emotions at once.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Absolutely. We aren't going to die from feeling anxious. We assess what we need to do and use our strength to manage. We can have depth in our emotions, not just anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How do you help people use their strength to manage what's going on?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: People are often already handling it in unique ways. I think it's important to recognize the strengths you already have. We build knowledge of our strength by doing hard things. Whether it's sitting with an emotion or solving a problem, doing hard things helps us realize we are strong.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Clients might feel they can't handle it, but deep inside they are capable. What are some specific examples of strength you've seen?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm seeing survival at its finest. People are problem-solving, networking, and searching for hopefulness. They are looking for ways to use their specific skills to help, even while they have enough to deal with personally.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's cool to see people connect and show generosity, like stores opening early for the elderly. People are finding ways to serve in interesting ways through this experience.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So many people are checking in on each other. When we find ourselves drawn into the scary stuff, we have to pull back and connect with the actual world. We don't just have the negative; we have the positive too.

diarization.speaker: Ther therapist
diarization.text: What's the difference between noticing the positive and burying your head in the sand?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Burying your head in the sand is pretending everything is normal. Taking a break is an intentional choice to step away from the news for a bit to read a book or talk to a friend about something else.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you letting fear run the show, or are you making an intentional choice about your time and energy? Fear happens, but I'm going to choose my actions.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Bad things happen, but we can still choose when we can how to handle it. When we can't, we're going to get through it. When you have a moment that you can, do something that is helpful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We have to look at this once-in-a-lifetime situation actively. The entire world has joined together facing a crisis. We embrace our experiences as valuable, even those we didn't choose. BUILDING strength and realizing our capability could be one piece of this.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So sitting with this and trying to see the good that can come from it. How else do we take in this experience?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Communicate with friends, family, and neighbors. Sometimes you'll buoy up that person, and sometimes they'll buoy you up. It's awesome to hear how people are coping.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What are some practical steps people should be taking?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do what you need to be prepared, like wearing a helmet, but then get out of your own head and do something. When you can't control a situation, move to something else you can work on. Mulling over helplessness draws you into anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We should look at what's in our control, even simple things like doing the dishes. Physical movement and exercise are also essential to help the body calm down and think clearly.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We have to sleep, eat, and keep moving. We have to do those basic things so that we can rationally think clearly and problem-solve. Redirecting your thinking is vital when you feel emotionally flooded.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When you're overwhelmed, use movement or nature to lower that physiological response. Then you can think more clearly. It's okay if you're not starting a monumental service project; just do something that feels healthier for you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Take time to look at what's in your control. When you're calmed down, look at what you value and who you can help. What you look for is what you're going to find.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The entire world is united in this cause, which might lead to better global action on mental health. I'm seeing teenagers finding safe ways to connect and women doing girls' nights out online. People are being so creative.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: People are having to be really intentional about how they find moments of hope and connect with others. You do a great job at helping people discover that strength inside of them, Monica.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're also a wonderful therapist. I have such a huge respect for you as a clinician. Thank you for having me here to talk a bit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Appreciate you taking the time. Hopefully, as we move forward, people keep looking for resources and seeing the beauty around them. Learn from this experience. Thank you all for watching, and take care.

video_details.title: Trouble Staying Organized—High Support: Several Weeks Later
video_details.description:
These fictional scenes are based on Cognitive Adaptation Training – CAT for short — an organized approach that uses “environmental supports” that are integrated into the routines and living spaces of people with schizophrenia and other similar mental health challenges.

The Supporting a Family Member with Schizophrenia manual and website offers tools and resources that help people with schizophrenia and their families develop customized strategies that support an independent and fulfilling life

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I noticed the sign's gone. How's the smoking situation?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I didn't need it anymore. Three weeks, no smoking.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh my goodness, that's wonderful! You must feel fabulous.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I do. I can taste again, I can breathe again. It's kind of amazing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Nice. And imagine all the money you've saved.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's a start. It's good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's good. It's good. It's excellent. And how is the job situation?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I went to check out a drop-in for this one gig at a restaurant on King Street. I didn't think it through and went during dinner time, so that didn't exactly impress them. It was a short-sighted thing to do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Because you went at the wrong time. I'm sorry to hear that. Well, now you know you've got to do research to go at the right time. Did you check the list on the door before you left?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Which list?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The list on the door, remember? Of what you're supposed to do before you leave the house?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I do. When I remember to, yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I've got another helpful hint. I'm putting these bells on the door. Every time you hear them, it'll remind you to look at the list and make sure you have everything you need for your outing. It'll trigger the habit.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Lovely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's another tool to help you be successful. How's the research going for your schooling?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's good. This option looks like it would make the most sense to do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, when's the application date?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I didn't even check. Hold on. It says it right here at the end... wait, what's today?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, it's today. Before I go, we'll get into that and make sure your application is in. What do you think?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I can't not do it if it's right in front of me. I'll leave it right there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you'll make sure you do it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'll set a timer for that. How long until you want me to do it?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Great. How's your list been going?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not bad. I'm mostly remembering to do it. Checking some of these off feels good. Yoga mat, check.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Nice. Have you been writing on your calendar? Wow, it's filled up! My goodness. Hey, why don't we celebrate three weeks of not smoking? How's that sound?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe part of the celebration is me treating you to this, because I think that would be nice for a change.

video_details.title: Trouble Staying Organized—High Support: One week later
video_details.description:
These fictional scenes are based on Cognitive Adaptation Training – CAT for short — an organized approach that uses “environmental supports” that are integrated into the routines and living spaces of people with schizophrenia and other similar mental health challenges.

The Supporting a Family Member with Schizophrenia manual and website offers tools and resources that help people with schizophrenia and their families develop customized strategies that support an independent and fulfilling life

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I saw the smoking sign outside and I like this. How are the signs working for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You know, when I print them out properly, they're working pretty well but whatever. Yeah, it's really making me feel guilty about smoking, so I have been smoking less.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good. That's really, really good. So how's the job situation coming along?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. It kind of sucks to be honest. I was late last shift and my boss was like giving me that, you know, stare of like death and I'm like, you know, thinking why do I keep doing this?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Why? Why were you late?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just I keep missing the bus and that's a stupid excuse, but that's, you know...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: First, why don't we put a list on the door to tell you, you know, what you need to go to work, you know, don't forget any of your paraphernalia. So you're making your lists, are you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, and I'm checking them twice. Like, more like 10 times, because...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But are they working for you? And I noticed your yoga mats here. Have you been using it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's it's in my face, but it's not in my way. It's kind of good in that little corner there, so it's been pretty good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's good to see. And your desk is so organized! I'm loving this. This is great.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It is, right? But I mean, mostly. I really need to... these pens and stuff are not where they should be, so...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, look what I have for you. I brought you some trays to put all your files in. So what do you think of that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Looks good. I like the black. It's nice and simple.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's your color. I know it's your color.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, black's not a color, though. It's a shade.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, yeah, you would know, you're the artist. Okay, we got a pen for you and we have a... you can put all your pencils over there. You can put them right in here. And how about your school search? How's that been coming along?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh, I missed my deadlines. Like you can imagine, so I have to wait until next round.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Did you put them on the calendar? The date?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I did. I put them on the calendar. I saw them and I'm like, okay, there you are.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good. Why'd you miss the deadline?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Why didn't I miss the deadline? Surfing? Well, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I know, I know. Remember we talked about that last week. It's a timer. That's cool. So we give you two hours a day. That's more than enough time for you to play Warcraft and whatever you do on the internet. How does that sound? It will help you, it'll help you focus. Just little bits at a time, one step at a time. That's why we have the lists, that's why we have the calendar, that's why we have the notebook. These are all helpful hints, they're tools in your toolbox. And things are looking rosy, looking better, more exciting, right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, yeah, I mean pragmatically, I think I've got some, you know, I've got some anchors to kind of work around, so to speak.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Absolutely. Great anchors. I'm so proud of you. You are getting there, but we are seeing changes. So maybe we should check on some of the veterinarian what you need for school.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: All right, because I'm on that page, let me show you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, great.

video_details.title: Trouble Getting Started—High Support: A first meeting between a brother and sister
video_details.description:
These fictional scenes are based on Cognitive Adaptation Training – CAT for short — an organized approach that uses “environmental supports” that are integrated into the routines and living spaces of people with schizophrenia and other similar mental health challenges.

The Supporting a Family Member with Schizophrenia manual and website offers tools and resources that help people with schizophrenia and their families develop customized strategies that support an independent and fulfilling life

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I stopped for coffee because I wasn't sure if you had any coffee. How are you doing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm sick of thinking about how I am.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I hear you. Now you remember that thing I was telling you about that I found online?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: What thing?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I was telling you about it, how it helps you break down your goals into smaller steps. I thought maybe we could try it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We've tried all this kind of stuff before.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I understand. You know, I've always loved this picture of you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I haven't felt like this in a long time. That was like my old life. I don't even know who that person is anymore or how to be her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, what do you miss about your old life?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, having friends and going out, but I just can't seem to get started, though.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about we start at the beginning? How do you start your day?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I sleep late and I know I should clean up around here, but it's so intimidating, so I just do nothing like a loser.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like you're pretty hard on yourself. Maybe if you start feeling a little bit better you'd be more apt to want to go out and see your friends.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I notice your alarm clock is broken.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, yeah. It needs batteries.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I got you this alarm clock that doesn't need batteries. What time would you like to get up?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, why don't we start with 11 o'clock? You said you've been getting up in the afternoon. We could try 11 and then you can move it up in a couple of days.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I thought maybe a calendar would help. How about we write stuff on it and then we could put it up where you'll see it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like what?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, how about wake up at 11 a.m. and have a shower, maybe pick up clothes?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, but I have nowhere to put the dirty ones.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's a good point. I can bring something next time, maybe.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'll give it a try.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's great, Jules. Now what should we think about for next time?

video_details.title: Trouble Getting Started—High Support: One week later
video_details.description:
These fictional scenes are based on Cognitive Adaptation Training – CAT for short — an organized approach that uses “environmental supports” that are integrated into the routines and living spaces of people with schizophrenia and other similar mental health challenges.

The Supporting a Family Member with Schizophrenia manual and website offers tools and resources that help people with schizophrenia and their families develop customized strategies that support an independent and fulfilling life

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I see you made your bed. That's great. It really makes a difference. How did waking up earlier go?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it worked for like a day or two, but then the power went out so then my alarm clock stopped working and then I kind of started sleeping in again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I thought that might happen, so I made this sign for you. It'll help you remember to set the alarm.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, um, I did get out to the park.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How did that go?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It didn't go so well. I don't have enough clean clothes and I felt really uncomfortable. This thing is really hard, man. Like, why bother?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, that's why I bought you these. We can put your dirty clothes in the hamper and your clean clothes we can fold them up and put them into this bin.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's cool.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Well, last time we talked about how you forget to take a shower. So I brought you this hygiene basket because I remembered you become overwhelmed. If you keep it here by the bed, it'll remind you to take a shower and you can carry it with you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think I could use a shower.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well why don't you go have one? I'll put the calendar up for you and I'll also put this picture I love up here by the bed. Oh, guess what? I got you a container so you can put all your meds in. If you fill it up for each day and keep it by your bed with a glass of water it'll remind you to take your pills.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm gonna go take that shower now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sounds good. I'll put up your calendar.

video_details.title: Donate a kidney to a stranger and parachute jump at 80: How to live better for longer
video_details.description: Jane donated a kidney to a stranger in her 70s, has promised her body to science and plans to jump out a plane in a parachute to celebrate her 80th birthday. Here, she advises Dr Rachel Coats on how to live better, for longer.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I'd like to talk about being cognitively active. So you're retired now. What did you used to do?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was a nurse for 44 years.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And presumably that kept you very busy?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It did, it did. It wasn't just that. I had five children and I helped my husband run a sub-post office. So I was working a 70-hour week in those days because I did two nights' night duty, they were 12-hour shifts separated, and then I worked in the shop.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Several jobs.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So for five years I did that. So that was, you know, and looked after the children and the house and that. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Wow. And do you do any, now that you're retired, do you do any voluntary work or anything else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I've got involved with things around the church, with visiting the housebound and taking them out and things like that. And I still, and one of my daughters decided to get me a job as a transport passenger assistant for special needs on the minibuses that go around Leeds. So they were desperate for them and she said, you'd be good at that, Mum.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Signed you up?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: She signed me up because she was the manager. So I did that until I was 77. And I also did the 11 weeks of the stewarding for the ABRSM music exams.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would you say that keeping busy is important to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I'm just a busy person. So it just comes natural to me. I can't sit really for long.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. And have you always been like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have a lot of social support?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I do. Yeah. Well, even more so now, now that the children have press-ganged me into Facebook and WhatsApp. Wow. I mean, it's just full-on around the world now, you know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, international friends.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And I believe that you are an Airbnb host?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I do. So the world comes to me that way. And then I'm Facebook friends when they go home apparently in China and Brazil and Rome.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any invitations to visit?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, Brazil. Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Wow. And you said you've got grandchildren and great-grandchildren.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: And great-grandchildren.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you think that intergenerational contact is important?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Very important.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Why?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Because when you're busy bringing up children, you haven't time to see the world through their eyes or even really listen to them because you're too busy and preoccupied. But then grandchildren come along and more importantly now great-grandchildren, and seeing the world fresh through these new eyes is just, it's quite mind-blowing actually. So I've learned a lot. In the old days, grandchildren used to learn at their grandparents' knee, but nowadays it's the grandparents learning at the grandchildren's knees now, definitely. Oh, yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And do you think that it also benefits them to spend time with people of different generations, different ages?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, as I said, they don't see it as age, you see, which is very releasing because, well, it just is, you know, after my generation, the way I was brought up to be seen and not heard and to sit in the parlor with all these old people. And now, well, you're going round flipping parks, you know, the adventure things and they're saying, come on the slide with us and all this, you know, which I do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Which I do. I don't turn anything down. That's the secret. Not turn anything down. Just say yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good philosophy.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Except drugs. Try everything once. Try everything once.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's your view on nutrition and kind of having a so-called healthy diet?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think the younger generation stress on it too much, far too much. When you think that if my generation are living to be 100 and we were brought up with dripping sandwiches, meat with marbling in, etc., etc., full cream milk, all the rest of it, why get stressed out? Just eat everything in moderation and enjoy life, for goodness sake.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I like that philosophy. How do you minimize the effects of stress? Do you have any techniques or if something stressful happens, is there anything particular that you do?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Gin and tonic or wine. I've got a very good thing, if I'm really cross with somebody and I'd really like to speak my mind to them, I'm very good at writing letters. I don't send the letter to them, but I do write it down and get it out of my system and I keep it in a drawer in case one day I might need to plonk it down in front of them.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: But it's out of my head. And if I need to go to the doctor about anything, I will write down what I want to say to him because I don't believe they listen to you all the time, especially a woman if it's a man doctor. Well, you know, bitter, they think, oh God, it's her again, you know. So I think, put this down and smile at him and he's got to read it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think you're in your 70s now. Do you enjoy being in your 70s? What was your favorite period in life, if there's an answer to that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, there isn't. You should just enjoy every day as it comes and not get hung up about age because I'm surrounded by 90-year-olds now and honestly they're like 9-year-olds. We have the biggest laughs and they do the silliest things and you know, we feel as if we've been set free from your age, you know, you're a mother, set an example to the children.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So do you think it makes a difference, kind of moving on from those responsibility kind of times of life, so when you are looking after your children, is that what you mean by you feel a sense of relief later?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, because you're not, no one's judging you except that you're hanging around too long. But apart from that, no, it's good. I mean, I was brought up by a Victorian father who was a bank manager and it was always, just remember who I am in this town, you know, they were somebody in those days. You're my children. And then I went to a convent grammar, just remember who you are girls, you're convent grammar school girls. You know, so it didn't leave much to sin, did it? It didn't leave much to...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Suppress.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. So, yeah, there's all these pressures as you're going through life. So it's nice to be... and my husband died in his 50s, so I had to reinvent myself, which was scary, very scary after being a wife and mother all those years. But my goodness me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think it was either earlier this year or last year you did something quite big for a stranger.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, the kidney donation, yes, in February. In February this year.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In February this year? You donated a kidney to a stranger.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, a gentleman I believe, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Wow. How did you decide to do that or find out about that and then decide to?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I found out on Facebook. Don't ask me what the heading was, but I'm already like most people donated after death, you know, everything. I mean, I'm leaving my body to Leeds Medical School as well, which hasn't pleased one of my daughters, but there you go. How can we grieve if you're still hanging around, she said. So, yeah, so some of them were for it and some of them weren't.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And going through the transplant operation is quite a big thing to go through.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I think all last year I was doing tests, you know, everything from psychological tests to all the physical tests and brain scans and everything scanned. It was better than a thousand mile service and I thought, well, I'm doing this for the right reasons, I know that. But who knows, they might find something totally wrong with me and that's the way I found out. So it's a win-win situation, I believe. And you know that if they do accept you, and I was the oldest one that they've ever had they said, and it'll last 20 years apparently, a kidney can last 20 years. That was good.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So it's a win-win.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think I've asked most things on my list that I wanted to talk about. Is there anything that you think that I've missed that is worth covering in terms of the theme of living well for longer?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I think if you can do something for somebody else for whatever reason, however tiny, the come back to yourself is just huge. But as long as you don't look for that come back, but it just is. And it also consolidates the reason why you're still alive, that you're not just taking up space on the planet and that, you know, you should do something. Like in January, hopefully tandem parachute jump for Alzheimer's.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, is that the plan? To raise money for Alzheimer's? Tandem jump out of a plane.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's the plan when I'm 80. Yeah, yeah. That should be good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there any advice that you would give to yourself aged 20 or any of our students?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not to take life so seriously. For one, you don't know how long you're here for and two, nobody's that important, you know, you're not the center of the universe for goodness sake. So just get on with things and it's like, I feel sorry with Facebook, you know, if they don't get enough likes, it must ruin their day, some people. Well, this is all false, it's all smoke and mirrors. One thing a friend did say to me that was very important and I very proudly was saying that I now owned my own house, you see. And she just laughed and she said, do you think you really? I went, yes, you know. Oh, you're taking it with you are you? She said, you don't own anything, she said, it's smoke and mirrors, all of it. And it's true, isn't it? So just laugh and get on with it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you.

video_details.title: Chest Pain - OSCE history taking for Medical Students | Drs Manual
video_details.description:
https://www.drsmanual.com

In this video we take you through a basic structure for taking a history from someone presenting with a chest pain. It includes a pain history using SOCRATES and how to take a cardiovascular history. 

Follow us on instagram @Drsmanual 
for daily MCQ content and to stay up to date with developments


Please note, that this video should be used for learning purposes only and should not be used as the sole resource for clinical practice. Adhere to the protocols and guide

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good afternoon. My name is Anas Ali, I'm one of the final year medical students. Before we start, can I check your name and age?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's Zain Hassan and I'm 55 years old.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how would you like me to address you today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Zain's fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I've been asked by one of the doctors to have a conversation with you about what brought you into hospital. Anything we discuss remains confidential. Are you happy to go ahead?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, absolutely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Great. So tell me a bit about what's been going on.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: This morning, as I was leaving my house around 8:00 AM, I experienced some pretty bad chest pain. My wife called an ambulance and they brought me in.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I see. Would you say you've been quite worried about it or not so much?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was quite worrying, actually. I've never had anything like this happen before.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is this the first time you've had pain like this? Can you tell me a bit more about it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was in my chest. The episode lasted about 40 minutes, and the ambulance gave me some painkillers which helped quite a bit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Where exactly was the pain? Can you point specifically?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was in the center of my chest, but it moved down my arm and up my neck.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Did it move anywhere else, like to the back?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I don't think so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you describe the pain for me?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It felt like a pressure, like someone was sitting on my chest.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Did the pain come on gradually or suddenly?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It came on quite suddenly just as I was leaving the house.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Did it last the whole 40 minutes or did it come and go?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was there the whole 40 minutes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Did anything help apart from painkillers? Changing position, leaning, or taking deep breaths?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, nothing changed it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Anything made it worse?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, it was just bad the whole time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: On a scale of 0 to 10, how would you rate the pain?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Quite high, an 8 or a 9.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how is it at the moment? Do you have any thoughts on what could be going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm a bit worried that this is a heart attack.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Why are you worried about that specifically?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My dad had something similar happen when he was about 65. He had a major operation and was off work for ages.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That must have been tough. Did he recover well? Do you have other concerns or expectations?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He recovered reasonably well. My main concern is finding out what's happening and what the next steps are.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We've ruled out a few things, but I have more questions. Any recent fever, weight loss, or nausea?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was feeling a bit nauseous about 10 minutes into it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Did you vomit or feel like your heart was racing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I didn't vomit, but my heart was racing the whole time during the pain.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any sweating, cough, calf swelling, or recent surgery?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, none of that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any breathlessness or heartburn?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No breathlessness, but I do get reflux. This pain felt different though, like pressure instead of burning.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you take for heartburn? Did you try it for this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I take Gaviscon, but I didn't try it because it felt so different.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any recent injuries? How is your general health? Do you have high blood pressure?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I have high blood pressure. I take Ramipril, but my last readings were a bit high, about 160.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any high cholesterol, diabetes, or strokes?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have high cholesterol and take a statin. No diabetes or stroke.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any other medications, over-the-counter herbs, or allergies?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, that's it. No allergies.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any other conditions in your family?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My mom has diabetes, but no other heart problems.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you working? How is that going?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm working and enjoying it. My colleagues have been very understanding about the situation.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you smoke or drink alcohol?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've smoked half a pack a day for 25 years. I drink a few glasses of wine on weekends.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any recreational drugs?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, none at all.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'll talk to the doctors and then we'll do an examination. How does that sound?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That sounds okay. Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good, we'll proceed with the plan then.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

video_details.title: MRCP Paces Communication & Ethics
video_details.description: This video is about MRCP Paces Communication & Ethics

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Welcome to this communication skills and ethics station for the MRCP PACES examination. I'm just going to read out the scenario for you. For this scenario, you get 14 minutes with the patient, a minute to collect your thoughts, and then five minutes with the examiner. The patient scenario for today: you've been called to the emergency department to see a patient who is 12 weeks pregnant and she's 20 years old herself. Two weeks ago she has had a long uninterrupted car journey and two days ago she has had an episode of shortness of breath which again happened today. She has been reading a pregnancy magazine and has been concerned about clots on her lungs. Her oxygen saturations are 91% but the rest of the examination and her chest x-ray are normal. Current guidelines suggest that if the clinical probability of a PE is high, you organize a Doppler ultrasound of the legs first, and once you exclude a DVT, you consider either a VQ scan or a CTPA to confirm or exclude the diagnosis of a PE. She's currently only on folic acid supplementation. Your task is to explain what can be done to establish the diagnosis and what treatment is appropriate.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello. Hi. My name is Dr. Puneker. Is that Dr. Agarwal?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yes, that's me. So this is Station 4, communication skills and ethics for the MRCP PACES examination. You have read the scenario outside. You get 14 minutes with the patient, a minute to collect your thoughts, and then five minutes with the examiner. I'm going to give you a warning when two minutes are left with the patient. Okay, would you like to proceed?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Hi, is it Lauren?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It is, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, my name's Sunil Agarwal, I'm one of the doctors that's just come down here just to have a chat with you to see what we can do to help you. What's your last name, sorry?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Bradley.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And is it okay if I call you Lauren? Can you just confirm your date of birth for me?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's 15th of the 6th, '98.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So that makes you 20 years old today? So this is the first time I've met you, so are you able to give me a bit of a talk to me about what's brought you in here and if you have any particular concerns or worries at all?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: This morning I was just walking, I'd been at the supermarket and I was walking and I got really, really short of breath really quickly. Yeah, it was just a bit scary really.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And did that just happen today or have you been feeling out of breath over the past few days at all?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It happened I'd probably say about two or three days ago, something like that. Sort of similar, really short of breath, quite...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. And any other symptoms, like any pain in your chest or any cough at all or anything?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, no.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And I was told by having a look at your notes before that you're pregnant, is that right? How many weeks pregnant are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: 12 weeks, okay. And has there been any concerns at all with the pregnancy up until now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, it's been going really well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, okay. And other than the shortness of breath, any other symptoms you've noticed?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, no, not that I can... No. They get a bit sore at the end of the day if I've been doing a lot of walking round, but...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, okay. And have you been any long-distance journey at all recently or have you...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We went down to see family in Somerset a few weeks ago. The car ride back from there was quite a long time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: About how long was the car ride about?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We didn't really stop so I'd probably say about 6 or 7 hours, something like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And do you take any medications or anything?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I'm just on the folic acid at the minute.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The folic acid, okay. So you said over the past few days you've been getting a bit more out of breath and you're 12 weeks pregnant at the moment and you're taking folic acid. You also mentioned this long distance journey that you had. Is there anything else you think I've missed in terms of your symptoms or any other episode?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, no. Another reason why I was quite frightened this morning just before it happened, I was actually reading... I'm subscribed to this pregnancy magazine and I was flicking through that probably about 20 minutes or so before it happened. I was reading about sometimes a bit of shortness of breath can be caused by like clots and things like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So that's something you think that you've read about and you think it could be that? It's made me panic a little bit. Right. And we'll talk a bit about that afterwards, but other than that do you have any other concerns or any specific questions you have? Okay. What I'd like to do now is just have a bit of a chat about what I think could be causing this and about some of the investigations we might need to do and some of the treatments involved. Is that okay? So as you were saying about in pregnancy, the magazine you were reading, sometimes you can get clots in your body. Because of what happens to your body during pregnancy, it can make your blood a lot more likely to clot. So sometimes people can get things like clots in their legs or sometimes clots in their chest, and that can give them symptoms like shortness of breath if you get a clot in your chest. Now don't worry, it doesn't sound obviously doesn't sound very nice to have a clot in your body. However, they are relatively common things and they're very treatable as well, which we'll go on to talk a bit about afterwards. Also, as you said you've been being pregnant you're more at risk of that and people have had a long time where they've not been moving around, such as the long car journey, that can make people more at risk of these clots, which is why I think this is something we need to look into and we probably need to do a few further tests to see if this is something like a clot in your body.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Will those tests need to be done today? Just because I've got quite a young boy at home and he's with my partner and I'm a little bit worried about him not...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, okay. So the tests that we do, I'll talk in a second. Now the issue with this condition is, as I said, it's relatively common. It's something that can be treated if you do have something like a clot. However, they can sometimes be severe and if they're not treated or investigated promptly, they can develop and can make people quite unwell. And obviously that could affect your child as well, your pregnancy, if it was to make you quite unwell. Also your oxygen levels are quite low. Because of that we'd need to give you oxygen to get your oxygen levels to a way that to a level that is acceptable and obviously that would be beneficial to your pregnancy. So I think it would be unsafe for you to leave until we get this sorted, because if we were to delay the treatment or the investigation that could affect you and your pregnancy as well, and not giving you oxygen as well could affect things. Does that sound reasonable or is that going to be a problem if you were to stay with us in hospital for the next day or so?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We could sort something out. I'm not going to die, am I?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So again, obviously it's good that you came to us early. This is something that is very treatable if it is a clot in the lung and we can give you treatment for it and the treatment is successful. It's usually you obviously don't know what's going to happen in the future but this if it is a clot in the lung that's a very successful the treatment's very successful. However the main thing is if treatment is delayed or if the diagnosis is delayed, that could affect you and your and your baby. And that's obviously part of the reason why we would take this seriously, why we would want to keep you in hospital to monitor to check for, you know, any complications or any signs that things could be getting worse. Okay. Is there any other specific questions or concerns you have for me?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I don't think so. Just any risk that the test might have towards the baby.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what I'd like to do now is talk a bit about the tests that we do. What we would do initially is a scan of your legs. As I said, these clots in your lungs, if you do have a clot in your lung, they usually develop because you first developed a clot in your legs, in one of the veins in your legs, and that can travel to your lungs. So the first test we would do is a jelly-type scan called an ultrasound of your legs to see if there is a clot there. If there is a clot, then we give you the treatment for the clot and there's no further tests we need we need to do. However, if we don't discover the clot there, we then need to do tests on your lungs to see if there is a clot on your lungs. The two tests that we might need to do, one is called a... they've both got fancy names... one is called a CTPA. Basically means you go into a scanner, we cover your baby so your baby's not affected by the CTPA, and you go into a scanner and they give you x-rays to see if you do have a clot in your lung. That's one of the tests. The concern or the issue with that is that if someone's pregnant, because of the changes to a woman's breasts when they're pregnant, it can give a very, very, very small increase of breast cancer several years later on. But I emphasize that's a very, very small increased chance in the future with a with a CTPA, okay? The number is about 0.7% increased risk, so it's a very, very, very small increased risk. The alternative to a CTPA is something called a VQ scan. Now a VQ scan, they give you an injection and it looks... it does various things to see if there is a clot in your lung. The downside to a VQ scan is that again it's a very, very, very small risk, but if you're pregnant there can be a tiny increased risk of childhood types of cancers with a VQ scan. And as I say that sounds very horrible, it doesn't sound very nice, but these risks, the increased risks to your baby of childhood cancers is very small with a VQ scan, or of the CTPA the increased risk to you of breast cancer later on in life is a very, very small increased risk. I know that's a lot of information I've given you. Is there any questions you have or anything that's not made sense or anything you're concerned from what I've told you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just other than obviously with the VQ scan, with the CTPA there's no risk to my baby is there at all?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No, no risk to the baby. They cover your baby, so they put, I don't know exactly what it is but it's sort of a board, I think it's a lead board they put over your tummy when they do the scan so that your baby's not affected during it. Yeah. Okay.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. And how do they treat it? Is the treatment different because I'm...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the treatment that we give, for someone who's pregnant, if you do have, if one of these tests does discover you have a clot, we give you injections called Heparin, or low molecular weight heparin. And they're these small injections that people usually give in their tummy. They're not too uncomfortable, lots of people manage it very, very well. And you usually have them maybe once or twice in the day, and you have that throughout your pregnancy and up to six weeks after, six weeks afterwards. Sometimes people need to continue longer but usually it's up to six weeks afterwards. Okay.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Would I be able to go home with that or do you need to be in hospital more?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No, so again this is something if you do have the clot we would give you the treatment here and then we can train you, or if you're not happy, some people have concerns about injections with something we can train maybe someone who's close to you to give you the injections. But the injections that we give you, as I say, every injection has mild side effects, but it's to help the clot from progressing and obviously to have no negative effects on your on your baby. Okay. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Are there any other treatment options or is that the only one?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So with pregnancy this is the one we choose. If you weren't pregnant we usually start patients on a medication called Warfarin. I don't know if you've heard of Warfarin before at all. So it's just another type of medication that we give for clots and the reason we don't give Warfarin during pregnancy is because Warfarin can be harmful to your baby. Okay. So that's why we don't give Warfarin to treat clots during pregnancy. We give you these injections because they won't harm they won't harm your baby. Okay. Do you have any other questions for me or anything that's not been clear at all or any concerns from what I've said?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, just a bit scared about the whole thing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, and as I say, it's understandable. I've given you a lot of information about various things. I can give you some leaflets about some of the tests that we've talked about and obviously whilst you're here if you have any concerns or worries you can write them down or ask any of the nursing staff or any other doctors that you see whilst you're whilst you're here. But as I say, the main thing is that what we think you may have, the clot in your lung, that's a relatively common thing, it is treatable, and we're keeping you in hospital and doing the tests, we'll find out what's going on to do the best that we can for you and your and your developing baby. Okay.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Will the test be done today or do you think I'll be in a couple of days?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It depends on we'll request the test and it depends on what you choose. So you don't have to decide today about the CTPA or the VQ scan. We can give you some information about that and depend on what you want to do if that's needed, because we do the jelly scan first. But it's likely that you will have to wait for a few days or so until we can do the tests, as there's usually a queue for the tests and only people who are very, very, very unwell, as in they need it very, very urgently, will get the test first. So you will likely end up staying for a day or so in hospital, I'm afraid.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Which one would you recommend?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So again, I wouldn't want to because you're your own person, I wouldn't want to tell you what to do, and you don't need to make a decision today about the test that you want to have. We can give you some information about that, about the risks to your baby of the VQ scan and about the risks to you of the CT scan and help you to make the decision. Usually the CTPA scan has a bit better at detecting the clots than the VQ scan. So if you had the CTPA, it is slightly a bit more better at detecting a clot if there is one there than the VQ scan, because a VQ scan can very rarely sometimes miss a clot that's there. But you have to consider that the CTPA you might not want that because of the small increased risk to yourself later in life, and again with the VQ scan you might not want that because of the small increased risk of childhood cancers with having that. Which isn't an easy decision to make, but we can help you with that. Okay. Any other questions for me?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I think that was it. Just I'm really grateful for your reassurance.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, okay. Well we've talked a lot today and as I say, if you have any further questions ask us and we'll start with the treatment and get these scans organized for you. Okay. Nice to meet you Lauren, thank you. Right, okay. So you've seen the patient, you've spoken to her about this suspected diagnosis of a PE. Would you like to tell me what principles guided your discussion, your conversation with the patient please?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So my discussion was mainly guided by the four main principles of core principles of medical ethics. The main one with this that was relevant was autonomy, which was the patient's choice and her right to choose what investigation she had and what treatment she had. The other principle is beneficence, and doing the right thing for your patients and making sure that everything that we're doing is really in the best interests for the patient and the baby as well. And also non-maleficence is another important principle and that goes about not doing any harm. And that can be tricky sometimes, beneficence and non-maleficence, they can contradict one another in a situation. For example with this, a CTPA would be beneficial, or a VQ scan would be beneficial to the mother in seeing if there was a PE, but it could harm the baby in some way. So there is a balance sometimes between beneficence and non-maleficence. And the final principle, justice, is about treating people equally, which may not be as relevant in this situation but that's another principle to keep in mind.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, good. Let's just come to your first principle you mentioned, autonomy. Are there any situations you can think where you wouldn't give that autonomy to your patient?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So autonomy, the only time you wouldn't is if the patient doesn't have capacity. And if someone you don't believe they have capacity, there's various reasons for that, you as a doctor would have to do what is in the best interest of the patient. And that may mean involving relatives or carers or close family friends or maybe other healthcare professionals who have known the patient for a long time to try and see what is the best thing to do for that patient.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Let me just ask you a couple of questions on capacity. Can you think of the principles of how you would assess capacity?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so there are four things that... Number one is that you should always assume that a patient has capacity. Only when you feel they don't have capacity, then you go and assess. So you should assume that every patient you see has capacity. There are four ways in which someone needs to have to say they do have capacity. Number one is that they understand what you're saying and they accept that as the truth. Number two is they can retain that information, they can remember that information for a reasonable period of time. The third one is that they can weigh that information up to make a decision. That decision may not be what you think is appropriate but it's that they can weigh that information up to make a balanced decision. And the fourth thing is that they communicate that decision in some way. And if they have all those four then a patient has capacity.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Can you think of any examples where a patient might lack capacity?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So one example is a patient who may have cognitive impairment such as Alzheimer's dementia. Because of the Alzheimer's dementia, their short-term memory may be impaired. So they may not be able to retain the information you're giving them for a long enough period of time to weigh that information up. So that's one example where someone may lack capacity.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you think of an example where they may have a lack of an ability to communicate?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So patients who have strokes. Sometimes if their speech is affected or their writing is affected, sometimes it may be difficult to communicate. In that situation, you as a healthcare professional should do everything you can to enhance how they can communicate. So there are visual aids where people can point to things, or sometimes with locked-in syndrome people blink to try to communicate. Yeah, yeah. Good, good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Let me just move on from your principles of assessment of capacity onto the treatment and the investigations that you were offering to the patient. You mentioned about the risk of breast cancer to the mother. How much did you say was the increased risk?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I believe from the literature the increased risk for breast cancer is just about 0.7%, so seven out of a thousand increase.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that the increased risk? Yes. Okay, okay. Good. And you said you're going to treat her for the entire duration of her pregnancy, which is going to be about seven, seven and a half months from now, possibly seven months. And also for six weeks after. Yes. Okay. So for example you sorry you decided not to give Warfarin. Can you think of a reason why we don't use Warfarin in such patients?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Because Warfarin is teratogenic, it will pass the placenta and can give fetal warfarin syndrome. Thank you. Thank you.

video_details.title: Therapy Session: Really Bad Counseling Skills 1
video_details.description: Therapy Done poorly. Demonstration of how NOT to do therapy that is a useful teaching tool. This is the second or third session with this client, Eva, a successful professional woman who struggles with hoarding disorder. You will see almost no empathy, few if any open-ended questions, no collaborative goal setting, no sensitivity to the client, and no processing of deeper issues. You will see blurring of boundaries, manipulating of the client to obtain a gift, and inappropriate interruptions. Ev

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So comfortable?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Never mind the water.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No, I have a water too, yeah, so we can both drink our waters.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you had a good day today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I love work. It was great. It was just... I'm just the buzz still from the project meeting. It's a really exciting project and I can really relate to it. Can I tell you what it is, the project?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, what is it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, it's a video game. Non-violent, which I'm so glad because I hate it if I have to manage a team with that. And it's for autistic kids for comprehension of words and understanding. They have a really hard time with word association when they take things so literally. Trying to cross that bridge with visuals and an actual game.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, that sounds pretty interesting.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, we had a pretty excited team today about that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, so you had a busy day at work.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, so you know all the aspects of project management. It keeps me going, I love it. I have a good team, good people.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well why, you know, since you like your job so much, I don't understand why you'd ever get depressed.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You know?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I mean it seems like you could just go to work and feel so much better.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well I do at work. But home is so depressing compared to work. I can't stay at work all day.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, maybe you could work a little more.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I already do 50 hours a week.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: 50? Okay, I guess that is a lot.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My marriage isn't holding out too well with that as it is because I'm gone so much, pretty much 10 hours a day. I leave at seven and I'm home at seven if I'm lucky.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, that's a long day.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's always in my head. I wish I could be who I am at work. It's kind of like this adrenaline and high...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, you seem like a really happy person right now. It's actually hard for me to believe that you get depressed.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe my depression is hidden because I can be like a chameleon. I get excited before I come to therapy too. I mean look at this place, it's beautiful. Home is where I'm being crucified right now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, I just had some lunch before we met and I think I've got something in my teeth. Excuse me just a second because I hate it when I have stuff in my teeth and don't want you looking at that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I probably wouldn't tell you if I saw something because I can never do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, I know. Maybe I have one... do you want one of these?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, here, try one.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, thanks! Damn, I like this. This is fun.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, I just get them at Bartell's.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Stimy-dents! Oh my god, my mom used those!

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Really, your mom used these?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes!

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Uh-oh, is that good or not good?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's just a memory flash. How do I get this off? I don't want to get them all dirty.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's not hard. You just kind of put your finger in here and pull one off.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I didn't know they made Stimy-dents anymore. I can remember my mom talking and doing this.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I hope you liked your mom because in therapy, you know, the therapist might be kind of like your parent or something.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, you dress stylishly like she did. She was such a perfectionist. If I caught her using a Stimy-dent, it was kind of like seeing her do something really human. She usually didn't want us to see that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Then what happened?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, she would... I mean, especially if you told her. I'd never tell anyone if they had something in their teeth. Never.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, I know. That's the worst. I've had that where I go and look in the mirror after a whole session and I have a piece of lettuce in my teeth. It's terrible.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Would you want... do you call us patients or clients?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, either one. Patients, clients, all the same, you know.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Would you want a patient to tell you if you had something in your teeth?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, yeah, I would, because I don't like to go and look in the mirror and then see it there after.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well maybe if that happens I'll try to get the courage to tell you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, please, yeah, tell me.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, this is really special. I never expected something like this in therapy. I'll keep this.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're going to keep that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think I want to. Don't worry, I won't hoard Stimy-dents.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, okay. So you don't think that...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't hoard. I don't like that word.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, but I think you do, Eva. I mean I think you do hoard because we've talked about how you collect all that stuff.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, but I'm not a hoarder. Look at me, do I look like a hoarder?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well what does a hoarder look like?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Some homeless tramp that smells. That's a hoarder.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No, no. No, you're not that. But you've got a lot of stuff in your home. I think it sounds like you hoard stuff.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: John called me that the other night. Oh my god.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: He was probably right, you know. Maybe someone needed to tell you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I'm here. I get... maybe, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, well we'll work on it, you know.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh man. Such a stigma. They have a TV show about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, they do. Yeah, have you ever watched it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can't. I mean, that's... it's just filth.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, it's unbelievable, those people on that show.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: And they can't part with stuff? I mean, I understand that. But I mean to the point where they're hysterical and it's just junk. I'm neat. I collect shoes and beautiful clothes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you collect really nice things, it sounds like. I mean, what makes you get the impression you're a hoarder? Did I say that?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, you know, I was reading in the DSM-5 and I read the diagnostic criteria and I thought 'Wow, that really sounds a lot like Eva.' They call it Hoarding Disorder, you know?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Disorder? Hoarding Disorder? Oh my god.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, be careful there. It just means that you tend to collect... What's... excuse me, it's my phone. Oh, I've got to get this, I'm sorry.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe I should check mine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello? 7 o'clock? Okay, do you want to meet at my office? Okay, great. Bye. I'm sorry about that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm embarrassed I don't have an iPhone.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, you don't have an iPhone? What do you have?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I work at Microsoft and I don't have an iPhone. Apple, who wants that?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, yeah, that's definitely true. I don't know, I just kind of can't let go of it. It does what it's supposed to. They're harassing me at work to get up to speed because they can't get ahold of me on that one, but, you know... I just rely on my computer.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well maybe we can work on you getting a phone. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't want to change. But I suppose that's something else, that's not hoarding, is it?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, part of hoarding is not being able to let go of things. Maybe you'd feel bad if you let go of the phone? Something like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Things get tied up in memories.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But I'm interested in the shoes. You mentioned the shoes.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, the shoes, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, you have beautiful shoes. I've been noticing them every time you come in. You always have a different pair.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh thanks. It's kind of my trademark and they're always red.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Always red?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Always red shoes. At work they gave me a flower vase that was ceramic red shoes. So it's kind of fun.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Wow, that's kind of... yeah, kind of classy.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I think every day of my life I wear red shoes and I have since I was 17.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Wow, you know I had one pair of patent leather red shoes about 10 years ago and every time I wore them I got so many compliments.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Because do you think it was because they were red or were they high heels?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think it's because they were red. They weren't really that special except they were red.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I love red high heels. I like to wear my red tennis shoes to work, take them off and then they see my red tennis shoes when I come in. Then I change into the high heels.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Where do you shop?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, all over. I can afford any shoe I want, so I sometimes can really spend a lot. And my husband, John, he doesn't keep the books, so he doesn't...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So he doesn't know.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, except he sees them eventually in the closet. I put them in special hangers with pockets and now they're filling closets. We have three bedrooms with no kids.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Got lots of space.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Lots of space. He doesn't hang his clothes in there, but there's probably about four hangers with shoes in our bedroom. So I think he's starting to feel a little bit moved out.
