diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What did you just say?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think he's feeling moved out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I just lost track for a minute. It was kind of intense for a second.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's all right! I love that you're so human. Therapists always seem so together, and you seem really human.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well thanks! That's nice of you to say. It makes me feel better, almost like I want to talk to you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh wow. Yeah, I've really enjoyed the last couple sessions. I can let down my hair. I can stop being so on.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I'm glad that you can do that. That's good.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, because I mean... but then again I don't know what to say.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, why don't we just talk about where to go buy shoes? I mean, I would like some ideas about that because look at these. These are just plain black shoes.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, they're gorgeous.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, but they're classic. But I would love to have something like you wear. Your shoes are really pretty.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh thanks. Those are gorgeous, the shape.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, thanks. Yeah, they're very comfortable actually.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, you know, it's all about sculpting the foot. Ballet was my original love. See how that classes up your foot? You still got the price tag on your shoe!

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh my god! Oh my gosh, that's so embarrassing! I'll have to take care of that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Those are great though. I'd like those in red. Where did you get them?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I got them online, actually. They were Clarks, actually.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Clarks? Okay. Oh, I'll have to check that out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But, you know, I like shopping on Nordstrom online too. You don't have to go to the really high-end places.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Have you ever ordered any shoes from France?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No. Actually, it reminds me, I saw Mary Stuart Masterson in Paris at a cafe wearing red, super stacked high heels.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh my gosh! Wow!

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And it was her, I swear. I almost went over and talked to her about it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, that's really cool. Yeah. I wonder if she has a thing for red shoes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Maybe so, yeah, maybe she does.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. So maybe it's not that big of a deal to collect red shoes. But I mean it's not just red shoes that I collect, it's the newspapers and magazines too. It is becoming oppressive. I walk in the door at home and it is depressing. But I still don't want it to go away.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I just think you just need to go to work. When you're at work you feel pretty good.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just go to work? What do you think it is about work that makes me feel so normal? My desk is really neat.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I don't even know if it matters why. I just think it seems to help. When you're at work you seem better.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, but I have to go home. I can't live there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, what if you guys just bought a new house?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, that's what I think about, but so many memories at our house. My one son, Fred, I think he has his eyes on our house to have it someday.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, like he'd like to have it someday?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I kind of think that's where he is. I do feel bad that I don't have a bedroom for his kids to sleep in because I have things collected in each room. And he's mentioned it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But they're adults now, right? They've got their own places and stuff?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They do, but it's getting tight with his two kids. Do you have any... have you bought any new things lately or do you have anything in that bag?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's funny because they're so cute but I always feel kind of ashamed and try to hide my stuff when I go home. I went to a little boutique and these I just thought would be so cute for summer. And they look like ballet shoes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: They do! Wow, those are really cool. Can I see? I mean, they're unusual, very well made. Unbelievably expensive. Italian? Real leather.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, no, it's probably leather. Quite beautiful shoes. Really unusual style, classic.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Those are really nice, yeah. Do you think... would you want them?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would I want them? Oh.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well maybe I need to do something like... I mean, I don't know how I'm going to ever stop buying shoes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, really as therapists we're not supposed to take gifts, but if it would help you let go of something... maybe it could kind of be part of the therapy, you know? If you think you'd wear them.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think they're my size. Well, I don't know, this is going to be weird but maybe I should try it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, it might be kind of a first step, you know, in letting go of something.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It might. I mean... okay. You sure?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Mhmm. I'll try it. I mean, I can just pretend I'm giving a Christmas present today.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well yeah! Thank you so much. I hope I see them on you here. One night going home without shoes. I mean, I have shoes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, how's it feel?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Weird. It's kind of weird.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, you know, I'm noticing the time and I actually have to end a little bit early tonight because I have something I have to do.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, okay. Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But maybe next time I'll add a few minutes on at the end if that's okay. So we probably should stop.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Can I have a Kleenex? Thank you. Yeah, that's fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, I usually don't end early but I just need to today. Thank you so much for the shoes.

diarization.speaker: Patient

video_details.description: Therapy Done Effectively. This video demonstrates good therapy and is a useful teaching tool. This is the second or third session with this client, Eva, a successful professional woman who struggles with hoarding disorder. You will see good attending throughout the session, effective listening, validating of the clients thoughts and feelings, deepening questions, summarizing, and communication of hope. This is not a perfect therapy session; no such thing exists. So it has strengths and weaknesse

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Kind of think of some I just don't know what to do. It's just I don't want to be left alone in the house with the piles of my collections, I want to call them now but because I don't want John if John goes and I'm left alone then I just that to me would be really scary.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Well I hear that. I hear that you're really scared of being left alone with all this these objects... even though it comforts me when he's there but if he was gone and I was... right then it feels like it'd be a whole different story. Okay so I'll remember that and I'll make sure that we work on that. Okay.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Well thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. You're welcome. All right, thank you. Yeah, thank you. I appreciate it. And I'll see you next week.

video_details.title: CBT Demo Socratic Questioning
video_details.description:
A demonstration of Socratic Questioning in a Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) counselling setting.

⭐ Info about our CBT Training Services: http://qualiacounselling.com/

𝗦𝗢𝗖𝗜𝗔𝗟 𝗠𝗘𝗗𝗜𝗔

❤️️ Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/qualiacbt/
❤️️ Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/qualiacounsellingservices
❤️️ Twitter: https://twitter.com/qualiacbt
❤️️ Blog: http://qualiacounselling.com/blog/

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay Brett, so we've got this situation where you were walking down the street the other day and you saw a friend of yours across the street and they didn't acknowledge you. They didn't wave or even look at you from across the street, right? And we've kind of identified this thought or this assumption here that they don't like me. All right. So, I thought we'd maybe do a little bit of kind of a dialogue back and forth. I could ask you some questions about wondering about this a little bit, and this is called Socratic questioning. Is that okay if we move into this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure. Sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So, kind of in relation to this idea here, this situation, and we kind of named this already, that you think the other person's point of view is they don't like you. Is that right? Do you want to round that out anymore? What else they might be thinking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, well, I'm just, you know, I waved. I thought they saw me and just kind of looked away, or, you know, so I'm thinking, yeah, they don't like me. They're kind of a jerk, you know, that kind of stuff.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, right. So, kind of one about you, they don't like me, and another one about them, they're kind of a jerk. Yeah. Right. Which one feels a little bit stronger? Should we think about right now or both?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They don't like me. Kind of focus on that one. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. All right. So, if you think about that idea in your mind, they don't like me, are you making any assumptions, or are there any assumptions kind of running in the background of that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I'm assuming because they didn't acknowledge me that they don't like me. I guess that's an assumption.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, so kind of a link that acknowledging you would mean they like you and not acknowledging you would mean they don't like you. Right, right. Okay. Anything else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I'm assuming they saw me. Yeah. Even though I think they did, you know, I guess I can't be 100% sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Big assumption there that they actually saw you. Yeah, yeah. And could there even be an assumption that, or maybe this has happened to you, you see someone across the street but you don't really know who they are. Maybe they saw you but even didn't recognize you fully. Could that have been the case?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I'm assuming that wasn't the case. Right, right. Yeah, yeah. Good point.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Okay. So, a couple of assumptions here. One assumption that you named, that acknowledgement means liking and vice versa. The assumption that they saw you in the first place. The assumption also that they recognized you. Right. Right. Yeah, a couple of things there. Okay. So, and based on those assumptions we've got this conclusion they don't like you. Do you have any kind of proof or evidence that would suggest they don't like you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh, well, I think the evidence would be the lack of acknowledgement. I think that would be evidence that they don't like me. I don't know, I guess other times, you mean like, set other points where they have, um, I don't know, I think sometimes they can be a little cold towards me, I think. So I guess that makes me think they don't like me. Sure, yeah. They don't go out of their way to include me in things.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So, there's a couple of pieces there, right? And so, you know, you're walking down the street, they didn't see you, these things happened, and you just think, you know, oh yeah, they don't like me. Yeah, yeah. Why do you think that's the conclusion you settled on? Is that the best one?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I hope, I mean, I hope it's not true, but I, it just seems the evidence points to that. Right, I would think.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, but given kind of what we've talked about, our assumptions and this, these pieces of evidence, are there other viewpoints or other conclusions that you could have settled on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Got to change the way I look at it, huh? Yeah, you got to change the way you look at it. Right. Um, I guess they could have been distracted, busy, sure, stressed out. Yeah, yeah. Those could be other conclusions I suppose. Stressed, distracted, busy. Right. Um, I don't know. I don't know other explanations for that. Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, and so those are, you know, we kind of talk about hypotheses or these thoughts we've got, right? One thought is they don't like me based on these things. Um, and that's the one you hung onto. Yeah. Why do you suppose you rejected these other ones? They were busy, they didn't see me, they're stressed out.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I didn't think of them. You didn't think of them? No. Hmm, okay. But now you're thinking of them now. What do you think now? I guess it's possible. It's possible. You know, I can't say it's not possible. Right, right. Okay. Yeah, I mean it takes looking at it in an entirely different way, I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And let's go back to that first one, they don't like me. When that goes through your mind or you kind of hang onto that one, what's the result?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, depression. Yeah. Yeah, I feel sad. Sadness. Fear, anxiety. Yeah, all those things. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sure. Okay. And then we've got these other possibilities, right? They were stressed, they didn't see me, they didn't recognize that. What would be the implications of latching onto those or, or taking those on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, if that were true, then I would not be depressed. I would just say, whatever, you know, they were busy. They were busy. Right. Hmm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's it like to kind of have a conversation like this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh, it's, yeah, it's different. It's forcing me to look at things differently. You know, for sure. Yeah, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And now that we are looking at things differently, how does that make you feel emotionally?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Intrigued a little bit. Intrigued. And a little bit like surprised. Hmm, how, you know, how come I didn't think of these things? You know what I mean? Like I just immediately took for granted this, the belief that they rejected me. You know, and I still kind of think, I still think that's true, but this is causing me to doubt it a little bit. You know, doubt the certainty of that conclusion.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. Well, and that's kind of the intention of this, to start wondering about different things and considering different possibilities, thinking about thinking and seeing if it changes the way we feel. Okay.

video_details.title: multicultural counseling

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: People your age, it's very different for this generation who they do have a lot of it figured out. So, if I ask you, how would you describe yourself? And it can be on any dimensions. How would you describe yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would describe myself... are you asking as far as...?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any way that's important to you about knowing who you are.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would say I'm a biracial woman in my middle 20s, and that's about it. Nothing to be specific or anything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But it seems like those three pieces—being biracial, being a woman, and age-wise—those are pieces of just locating yourself in space and time at this point in time. How long have you thought of yourself as a biracial woman? Or biracial?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, to be honest... maybe like third grade I knew that I was different... yeah I would say that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How'd you know that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When my dad came to pick up my report card from school... and everyone was looking and pointing and everything. It wasn't a problem for the students, it was a problem for the faculty and the teachers.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Were you treated differently after that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Maybe it would be good for me just to stop and ask you, what is your ethnic and racial background?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My father is of Latino descent and my mother's African-American.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, after that encounter in that third grade, your dad goes... he's Latino? Goes to pick up your report card and pick you up. How were you treated differently after that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, the next day I went to school, I had a note, and back then they stapled it to your shirt. So, when I got home, of course my mother read the note and they wanted a parent-teacher conference.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: And when we got there, I was asked to leave the room. From what I got the gist of it, they told my parents how me being a mixed race or having two different parents at the time could be a bad thing for me because I went to a predominantly African-American school.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Teasing would be something sort of like 'apples and oranges don't mix,' or 'you're not black.' When Black History Month came around, I picked Harriet Tubman, and it was like, 'Oh, you're not black enough to be her.' They asked if I was going to put black paint on my face and said I didn't know what it was like to be a slave.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So it became a... I didn't understand, right?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you're sure none of it hurt at that point?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't think it was a hurt. I just didn't understand, you know?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But at times would it just sort of get to you over the years? Because there's an age where the kids get sort of meaner about the teasing and aren't really even thinking.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: High school. High school the same thing came up. I participated in a Cinco de Mayo event and both the African-American and Latino students had a problem with it, and then I'm caught in the middle. So it's just like what do you do?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And do you think she's guarded?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yes, I do. I think she's emotionally guarded. I think there have been injuries related to the race pieces where she has felt judged, under scrutiny, and it just keeps repeating itself. So there is a guardedness and a sensitivity, which is her way of protecting some of her vulnerability.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Let's move on to...

video_details.title: Family Counseling Role-Play - Couple Struggling with Independence vs. Security
video_details.description: This video features session one of a family counseling session role-play in which counseling techniques are used to help resolve a disagreement between a couple. In this session, the disagreement is related to the desire for independence in one spouse versus the desire for security in the other. Techniques from several different counseling theories are used including person-centered, existential, and cognitive-behavioral therapy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, this is Dr. Grande. I hope you find this video useful. If that's the case, please like it and subscribe to my channel. And as always, thanks for watching.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello Frank, hello Sarah. How you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Doing well. Doing well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I understand that you've come in because you're having a little difficulty in your relationship. Can you tell me about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So basically, it's been getting a little bit worse since we got married. I thought we were both kind of independent people, but it's kind of gotten to the point now where I just want my own personal space and I want to be left alone sometimes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so you're looking for independence in your relationship. And how long have you been together?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We just got married a year and a half ago, but we've been dating for about four or five years total.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so total of four or five years, married for a year and a half. And Frank, when did you notice the lack of independence?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess once we got married. After that, it seemed like we were spending all of our time together. About six months to a year in, it progressed to becoming a burden. I just want my own personal space and freedom.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sarah, does this resonate with you, what Frank is saying?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just feel like we're newlyweds and I want to spend time with him. I feel like he doesn't want that, he wants to be with his friends. I sometimes don't feel wanted and I can tell he's so angry at me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, can you tell him that? What you just told me.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just want to feel wanted and I don't feel that way. I feel like you're so angry with me, but the truth is I just want to spend time with you and do everything with you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So Frank, what's it like to hear that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It reminds me of how it used to be. Back then independence wasn't a problem, but now we're spending every moment together and we're always worried about each other. It feels like I have pressure on me and I feel guilty trying to go do things by myself.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You feel guilty?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sarah, do you sense that in Frank, that he feels guilty about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I just feel like he's pushing me away and I feel rejected.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has this been happening right from the beginning of the marriage or a little bit after?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was a little bit after. The first six months were really good, but then it became a burden spending so much time together trying not to get into fights.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has it been the same for you, Sarah? Was the beginning of the marriage different than what you have now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I thought everything was great during the honeymoon and a couple months after, and then that's when it started later on.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Around the same time you started experiencing this difficulty. So it sounds like you want more space, Frank, and Sarah, you feel like this desire for space is a rejection.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just feel like he wants space all the time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you okay with some space?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think so. Maybe it's something we could try and work on.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You don't seem real certain.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, I just get anxiety a little bit when he's gone and feel like I need to be with him.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So maybe this idea of space isn't really something you feel will work for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I want to try to make our marriage work, so I want to try.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so you want to try to address Frank's concerns, but you seem apprehensive. How could this play out?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe next week he could go out with his friends some night and I can see how it makes me feel. I know it's something I can work on.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so an experiment. In the year and a half you've been married, has there ever been a night when you've gone out by yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: There's been a couple times where I've gone out for a guys' night or to see old college friends.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what happened between you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Getting out of the house is the hardest part. I try to ensure her it'll be okay, but she gets upset and doesn't want me to go. I don't want to be the only guy there who shows up with his wife, and I feel guilty leaving her alone.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there any reason to believe it'll be different next week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess not. Every time we do it, it's the same result with her getting worried. I really want my space but sometimes I can't get out of her grip.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sarah, what do you think about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Lately on the weekends he wants to be with his friends, and that's when I want to go on a date or go to the movies with him.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would it have to be on the weekend? Could it happen during the week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, absolutely. A lot of my friends go out during the week, so I could definitely go out then.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you could agree to an experiment where you spend the weekends together, and Frank goes out during the week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think we could try that. It would feel like more of a balance. I respond better to that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Something you could try next week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Walk me through what happens when you're getting ready to leave.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'll let her know where I'm going and give her phone numbers to reach me, but then she doesn't want me to leave. That makes me feel guilty because I want her to be more independent and have her own social circle.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So ultimately you do go, but you feel guilty. Do you have a good time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes I can't get over the fact that my wife is at home upset at me, so I'm trying to find a balance between my independence and her doing her own thing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about when you come home?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Usually things go back to normal. We've had exchanges of words, but we're an affectionate couple. Sometimes it's just overbearing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that how you see it, Sarah?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Things go back to normal, but inside I'm worrying about the next time it'll happen. I get nervous and think of all the bad things that could happen when he's gone.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What are you thinking while he's out?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I wonder what he's doing or if he's talking to someone else. I get anxious that something bad is going to happen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there any basis for thinking something bad's going to happen?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Absolutely not. I love Sarah, but I would like some independence. We have to work on these issues, and that's why we came to you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What could we change to increase the chances of the experiment working next week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Don't give me someone else's phone number, and don't stay out later than you say you will. Just be available when I call.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that something that's normally possible, Frank?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, most of the time I'm very good at responding to her and making sure she knows I'm okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So that's a compromise you're willing to make. Any other reassurances needed?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I think he means what he says and we can try this again under different circumstances.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sarah, do you have a plan to call Frank or would you just do it if you felt the need?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've called before just to make sure everything was okay, just for reassurance.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does that seem reasonable to you, Frank?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess, but I want privacy and to be in the moment with my friends. Getting phone calls during the night gets a little frustrating. A text would be better.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would a text or two be a good compromise? It might decrease her anxiety and work toward more freedom.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does that sound like an experiment you both can buy into?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We can try it. I think so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Try it out. Track your thoughts and experiences independently while you're apart, and we'll compare next time. Does that sound like a plan?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It does. It does.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, try that out and I'll see you in a week.

video_details.title: SOWK 647 - Emotionally Focused Couple Therapy (EFT) Session
video_details.description:
Starring:
Katelyn as Therapist
Michael as Jack
Julia as Linda
Filmed/edited by Jeff

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's so good to see you both this week. I know that the past couple of weeks there have been a lot of really hard conversations in this room, and I think it's so brave that you're both back here today. I'm wondering how this week has gone.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's gone pretty good, but we had a pretty bad fight about the dishes. I just really need them done, but he completely ignores it. It's hard to ignore you, but do this, do the dishes, wake up—that's all I hear every time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it seems like you're hesitant and resistant to doing the dishes because that's the only thing that you're hearing Linda say to you right now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, every time I've done the dishes in the past, she tells me what I did wrong. She's trying to discipline me like a child, and I don't need another mother.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So even when you do do the dishes, you're feeling like you aren't measuring up basically.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, she's treating me like I'm a child.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So she's telling you what to do and you're feeling like a little kid. It's not an equal relationship then, right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes I feel that way.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So sometimes you're feeling like Linda might be the one with the power in the relationship.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Whenever you have these fights, what happens?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We argue for hours and he just ignores me. I think he would be shocked to see how disconnected he looks.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you mean? What would shock him?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just how disconnected he is. If he saw himself, he would be shocked at how he treats his wife. It's pretty intense.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Help me, is that scary for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's really scary. What else is he going to stop talking to me about or disconnect from me about?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what about you, Jack? Are you a little afraid in that situation?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I can see that it's scary to disappoint my wife and be able to block her out like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's go back to the fight. How does it normally end?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He usually leaves for about 15 minutes and then comes back. He just leaves the situation.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you leave, Jack?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I walk out of the house just to leave the scene of the situation.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what do you do?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just leave the scene. When I come back, he gets really defensive and it's like nothing gets resolved. It doesn't go anywhere.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think I understand what you're both saying. But whenever Jack does come back, are you guys able to talk about it then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, it's like nothing happens. We never get to anything and we just can't get on the same page.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This must be so hard for you, Linda. You're trying to communicate and you feel like he's shutting you out.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right, like just tell me what's happening and what's going on.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Not knowing what's happening must be scary.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it is.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what about you, Jack? Are you feeling a little bit of fear in the unknown of this situation?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel like she doesn't want me around her at all. I just withdraw because I'm angry and sad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In this situation, it seems like it would be super hard to be close and supportive to one another.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just can't. He keeps apologizing, but then I don't want to be close. I need him to say it with actions, not just words.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm hearing that you're feeling some distance with Jack. Is it hard to be held by him?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, there are really few instances of intimacy now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you withdraw a lot when this happens?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, a lot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So Jack, you get the feeling that Linda doesn't really want to be around you, and when you try to connect, you feel rejected and like you're not enough.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, pretty much. It's like I blew it up and now she doesn't want to be around me anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How do you handle that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't like it. I don't like that at all.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You feel like you've screwed up, and then what do you do?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just leave it alone, but eventually I feel a disconnect and a postponement of our connection.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Even though you get caught in this pattern, you both disconnect into two different islands. Is that right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's me trying to struggle with the situation, and then I feel some kind of disconnect in that area.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Like there's some distance, right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there anything you're feeling about yourself that might cause this distance? Do you blame yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't really know, but yeah, kind of.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Jack, what is a word that you'd describe yourself as?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Generally a mean kind of guy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that right? You think you're a mean type of guy?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't think so, but it looks like that's what she sees me as.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, so you feel that Linda sees you as a mean guy. I didn't hear Linda say that. Linda?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's not what I mean at all. It's just the way that you go about things, that's all.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Jack, that must be so hard to carry with you every day, thinking that your wife thinks you're a mean guy.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes I just feel she doesn't want to be around me because of my behaviors and attitude.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Feeling that much pain around an everyday task like the dishes must be exhausting.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, sometimes it is.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You value the relationship, and feeling like you aren't meeting expectations must leave you feeling raw. Do you feel a little rejected by her?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It is really hard. When I try to apologize or give her a kiss and she rejects me, I feel rejected because I know I messed up.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It seems like there is a pattern where Linda asks Jack to do something, Jack feels like he'll fail, and you both end up disconnected. Is that right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, and it's just super, super frustrating. That's why we're here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're here to become connected again. Jack, after you argue, you expect to make up, but Linda isn't connecting in that way, and that brings up rejection.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Exactly, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Jack, it sounds like you think Linda doesn't care, but she's here working this out.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think she doesn't care how I feel. That wouldn't be true, though, because I'm here working this out. I'm here, and that should count.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Linda cares so much that she's here. If she didn't care, she would have left a long time ago.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would have just left. I would have been gone.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But for whatever reason, Jack's not feeling that the relationship is valuable.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think he does, I just think what I'm trying to say isn't coming out right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Jack, hearing Linda say that, how does it make you feel?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just don't like telling people my feelings anymore. I've messed up in the past and don't want to mess up anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Jack feels he's messed up so much and wants to be a perfectionist. Linda, turn to Jack and tell him how that makes you feel.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It makes me sad. I can tell you care because you don't want to mess up anymore. Your feelings are important to me, and I want to change by sharing emotions. I'll also do the dishes this weekend.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You both came in frustrated but were able to be honest and share your emotions. Through this, you connected in a new way. It was about a lot more than just the dishes.

video_details.title: Motivational Interviewing Role-Play - Precontemplative Client Who Reports Being in Action Stage
video_details.description: This video features a motivational interviewing (MI) counseling role-play session in which MI techniques are used to identify and explore ambivalence. In this role-play, the client (played by an actress) is in the precontemplation stage of change, but reports attitudes and plans consistent with the preparation and action stages.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, this is Dr. Grande. I hope you find this video useful. If that's the case, please like it and subscribe to my channel. And as always, thanks for watching.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello Brittany, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm doing alright, how are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. I understand that you had a little difficulty with drinking this week and you want to talk about that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, yeah. I was a little upset, I didn't get to go out this weekend and I ended up drinking quite a lot this weekend.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Quite a lot?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, really a lot. But I stopped on Sunday. On Sunday, yeah, I did, I stopped on Sunday.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So Brittany, I've been seeing you for a while now and during the last session we talked about that during this session we would look at some strategies for helping you beat this alcohol addiction. Are you still ready to do that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh yeah, most definitely. Yeah, I definitely want to stop drinking and and really get my life on track like it was before. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so you're ready to stop drinking. You've been drinking now for five or six years?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's about six.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: About six years. And more or less, it seems like always the same pattern on the weekend binge drinking and then waking up at a different point, sometimes Sunday, like this last time, sometimes during the week, Wednesday or Thursday.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What makes you think that you're ready to take this step and and be done with alcohol?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I'm trying to get this promotion at my job and I think that in order for me to really do well, I will need to get past this drinking problem.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you have a potential promotion at work. And my guess is this promotion wouldn't mix well with drinking.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, because I'll I'll be the manager so I'll have to you know make sure everybody's on top of their game and make sure the restaurant is moving smoothly. So it's just a lot of pressure and I know that the drinking is not gonna help it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so I've talked about a lot of these strategies before, uh, but you're telling me you're you're more interested now in taking a look at this. So let's try anything you got.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'm ready to try anything you got.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so let's talk about some of the environmental suggestions that we've talked about before. Uh, I know you live in an apartment and you mentioned that you store some alcohol there, right, quite a bit?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah, quite a bit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So we talked about setting up an environment where you take that alcohol out and dispose of it. Don't have any inside the apartment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I could, but I can't right now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, why is that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, because they're they're doing some construction in my apartment, so to get out of my apartment and, you know, cross over and all that and carrying those bottles, it just it'd be a lot. It'd be too hard to do right now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. What about enlisting some of your friends to come over and help you? You could take a few bottles, make several trips.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. Yeah. That... Well, that wouldn't work because, you know, all of our schedules for work are all different, so that wouldn't really work. Oh, it's hard to get everybody on the same page. Yeah, everybody works crazy hours, so that wouldn't work.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so that would be... That would be tough. Uh, you mentioned that with the particular job you have, we've talked about before how some of the social influences seem to be motivating you towards... towards the drinking.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I have to try to stay clear of that, but definitely a lot at work. Um, well everybody drinks that I'm around. Everybody drinks, yeah. It's like, oh of course not the managers, and they've got a few people who are a little uptight, but just about everybody else drinks. Take breaks and sometimes we'll take breaks and take shots and yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So could you see yourself working in a different environment, working in a different place?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, probably. Maybe. Um, right now because again I'm trying to get the promotion it wouldn't really look... I mean I would want a recommendation and things like that and I wouldn't want to go to another job as a hostess. I would want to you know be able to move up so I think that I should stay here and you know try to get the manager position and then you know work the manager position for a little bit and then go ahead and and find a different environment to work in.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so... So maybe a good idea just not a good idea right now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, something maybe like maybe a year or two from now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So we've talked about before how the initial drinking is one problem and then kind of the binge drinking evolves, in part because when you go to work you're carrying a lot of cash so you're able to buy the alcohol as you go. How about not bringing that cash into work?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I could, yeah that... See the only thing about that is I have to you know sometimes help give out change to the you know waitresses and waiters and um they really sometimes depend on me to have that change because I'm the hostess and I'm always there and interacting with everyone and so that would kind of kind of interfere with my job a little bit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, you mentioned you carry a lot of twenties and fifties. Is that a popular bill denomination for change?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, no, but sometimes I might you know need to stop and get gas on the way so I might get change and then I'll have extra change in my pocket for when I go to to work.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so... So going to work with a couple hundred dollars in cash, that's something you... it's really hard for you to avoid doing.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, because you know we have a lot of you know waiters and waitresses and they need a lot of change so I need to make sure I have enough. Definitely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so that... that strategy might not work. Um, you usually give the money to your friends to go out and purchase the alcohol, especially when you get more or less incapacitated from it. Could you talk to them and ask them not to purchase that alcohol for you, even if you hand them the money?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I could be willing to do that. I mean I don't think they'll listen but I think I could probably try to do that. The only issue is you know my friends you know we all like to drink together so likelihood of them saying no is kind of less likely but I could try.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You could try, but I don't sense like that... that you think that's going to be too successful.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't think so, but I'm willing to try. I'm willing... I definitely am willing to try. I want to definitely make a change.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. So today is Monday. Um, when do you think you could... could talk to... When do you work next?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, well I have to work Friday. Definitely Friday. Um, maybe Thursday.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, do you know who you're going to talk to, like how you're going to approach them, what you're going to say?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah, I think I could probably talk to my closest friend, T. Um, don't really know what I would say to be honest.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Um, how about another strategy we talked about. You mentioned that especially on Saturday, you seem vulnerable to the drinking after work. And you talked about a few times how when the shift ends, you have to do a little bit of work after everybody leaves the restaurant, but the socializing really doesn't start till a few minutes later in the parking lot. So you could park your car on the other side of the parking lot and just go directly out, get in it and drive home. How about that strategy? Is that possible?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I mean that... that does sound um possible. But you know I don't want to seem like you know mean to people when they ever want to you know socialize and I'm just walking past them, not speaking and just going straight to my car and you know taking off. That's kind of mean and I don't want people to you know think I'm mean or that I don't like them or that I don't want to talk to them so...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, you're afraid that might send the wrong message to them. Even if you told them this is to avoid the binge drinking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think they'll still take it that way.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so that... that might not really work as a possibility. So Brittany, we've been talking today and and really over the last few years, we've had a lot of ideas of things that may help reduce the chances of the binge drinking. Uh, but there... there seems to be a lot of barriers, right? It just seems to be a bad time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And it makes me wonder, is this a goal that you're really committed to? The... the stopping the drinking? Is this... is this really important to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, definitely. It's really important. Um, I see myself, you know, definitely living a a happier life and more being more comfortable and less worries and less stress and I think that, you know, being able to get past this part will allow me to move forward in life and get the promotion that I want, you know. So I definitely definitely definitely want to make this change. I definitely want to stop binge drinking. It's getting out of hand.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, you want to stop the binge drinking. It's just right now the kind of ideas that that I've had and we've discussed before and the timing just doesn't seem to be working.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, it just seems... I mean they were good suggestions, but they just don't seem to fit with my life right now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. Do you have any suggestions of things you could do to stop drinking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just try to not... No, not really besides just try to avoid it. I really can't... Just try to avoid it. Yeah, can't really think of anything. Yeah, not really.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you want to continue next session working on other ideas of how to stop?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh definitely. I definitely would like to come back and hopefully we can brainstorm something that'll fit. Just right now you know with the promotion and the stress and trying to get through you know this whole manager test and things that we have to do to try to even get the position, it's just a lot of stress right now. Just yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, just a tough time for you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right Brittany, so um thanks for spending this time today. I'm sorry that none of those suggestions seemed to be um something that could work for you. When we pick up next session we'll we'll start talking about this again and kind of see if we can figure things out. Maybe uh during this week if you can I would ask you to take a look at some of the things, some of the reasons that are motivating you to stop and maybe some of the things that are working in the other direction like keeping you drinking. Maybe write some of those down, we could talk about kind of the the pros and cons of of discontinuing alcohol and and what's motivating you uh toward it and away from it. We could talk about those things.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. I'll definitely think about that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that something you think you can take some time this week and write down?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, definitely can, you know, take some time to do that. You know I have to work but I can try to find some time to do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You could try to fit that in. All right. All right Brittany, I appreciate this time and working with me today. I will see you next week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

video_details.title: Video 4. Difficulty Setting an Agenda: Dr. Brown and Eric. Wright/APA Publishing
video_details.description:
https://www.appi.org/Learning_Cognitive-Behavior_Therapy_Second_Edition
Learning Cognitive-Behavior Therapy: An Illustrated Guide, Second Edition

Building on its successful “read-see-do” approach, this second edition of Learning Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy: An Illustrated Guide seamlessly combines videos with informative text and figures, charts, worksheets, checklists, and tables to help readers not only learn the essential skills of CBT but achieve competence in this important evidence-based

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So Eric, what's on the agenda for today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Definitely my dad. He's just been on my case all week, being a real jerk. He barges into my room when I'm playing video games or talking to friends, getting on me at dinner, about getting a job and getting my life together. Even first thing in the morning there's an email from him telling me to do stuff I don't want to do. He doesn't get that I'm not feeling good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let me interrupt for a second to make sure I understand. You're upset about your father getting on you this past week and want to talk about it today. Is there something we could do to help the situation out?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We've got to figure out a way to get him to back off. Maybe we can bring him in here, or write him a letter, or something to get him to leave me alone.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Bringing him in here to get him to back off is an idea, but he's not here now. Maybe there's something you can do to help him calm down or back off the situation?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He's the one being a jerk.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That may be, but maybe you could be more assertive to let him know how you're feeling, or to calm things down?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, if you've got ideas I'll listen, I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, maybe we can put our heads together and come up with strategies to deal with your dad better. Does that sound alright?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that something we could put down in the agenda then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I definitely want to talk about that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How should I describe that then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Dealing with my dad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, dealing with dad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there anything else you'd like to put on the agenda?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've been really tired lately, just sleeping a lot the last week or two.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so I'll put down tired and sleep. We have dealing with dad and tired/sleep. Which do you want to talk about first?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Definitely my dad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We don't want to forget about the homework, so let's put that on the agenda too.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, you want to talk about dealing with your dad or do the homework first?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Definitely my dad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Definitely with your dad. We want to make sure we allow enough time for homework since that's important. So tell me what happened this past week with your dad.

video_details.title: Video 2. Modifying Automatic Thoughts: Dr. Wright and Kate. Wright/APA Publishing
video_details.description:
https://www.appi.org/Learning_Cognitive-Behavior_Therapy_Second_Edition
Learning Cognitive-Behavior Therapy: An Illustrated Guide, Second Edition

Building on its successful “read-see-do” approach, this second edition of Learning Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy: An Illustrated Guide seamlessly combines videos with informative text and figures, charts, worksheets, checklists, and tables to help readers not only learn the essential skills of CBT but achieve competence in this important evidence-based

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Kate, it's great that you brought in that log of some of the thoughts that you had. Can you explain what happened?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah. I... they asked me at work to go, we needed some file folders. And so they needed somebody to go pick them up. And I just felt really panicky. So I wrote it down.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Did you actually go to get the folders?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I did.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So is this log of the thoughts that you were having before you went or during or what is it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, sort of before and during.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, good. Well, why don't you explain it to me so I can understand what happened?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, so like before I was thinking, well, I can't do it. Okay, and then I was thinking, well, could I get somebody else to do it? You know, could I make somebody else do it?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, they're very similar to thoughts that you had for some other things that triggered the anxiety. I think we talked about that in another session, right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, they sort of are. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the 'I can't do it' is a familiar thing then, isn't it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, very much so. And so then when I got in the car and I was driving there, I started feeling like I was going to pass out and I started feeling really anxious and I kept thinking, you know, like somebody's going to slam into my car. You know, like I'm going to be going through an intersection and somebody's just going to broadside me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what was the anxiety rating that was associated there? Oh, I see 100%? Way up to the top of the scale.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, it was like 100%.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So let's take a look at some of those thoughts if it's okay today. We really haven't gone into detail on the thoughts before and tried to take a look at them to check them out. And that's what I'd like to do now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So let's see, which one of those would you like to start working with? You have 'I'll pass out', 'someone will slam into me'.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think these two. The one 'someone will slam into me' and 'I'll pass out'.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, the 'I'll pass out' one seems to have been particularly difficult for you from what I gather.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I don't want to drive if I'm afraid I'm going to pass out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that a recurrent thought that you have?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Pretty much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. Now let's just take a look at that and check out to see whether it would come true or not, how accurate it is. So let's see, you've driven probably lots of times in your life already, haven't you? Even though you've been anxious sometimes.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So how old are you now? You're early 50s? 52, I think it was. And you started driving at about what age?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like 16, 17.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And so you've been driving for what, 36 years? And as you were having this thought, what was it, earlier this week? What day was it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it was Wednesday.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Wednesday. What do you think the likelihood, at that time you were having that thought, the likelihood was in your mind that you actually would pass out?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, I'd say... the likelihood? I'd say about 90%.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, 90% sure that you were going to have a... you were going to pass out? Or that you could pass out?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, that I could, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Uh-huh. And then going back to this number of years you've been driving, 36 years, and you know, there are a lot of days in the year, and we think of roughly how many times would you have driven daily over those years? Just to give us an average.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, probably one or two every day.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: At least one or two. Yeah. I suspect maybe there would have been days you'd have driven more. So we add all that up and I wonder about how many times that you've actually driven a car since you've been 16?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it's got to be in the thousands.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. Well, at least 10,000, maybe if we did twice a day it'd be up 20,000 or more. And have you ever passed out in those 20,000 or so times of driving?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. Never passed out, but I feel like I'm going to.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, you feel like it, but it hasn't happened. And so we have this 90% estimate that it's going to happen, and yet we have 0% actually happening. So what do you think, is there another estimate that you could make that would be more on target?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I mean, you're right. You're right. I've driven for a long time. I've often felt like I was going to pass out, but I haven't done it. So maybe like 5%?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: 5%. Yeah. So we went from 90 to 5 by thinking it through, which is great. But it's still way over 5, and we have the actual experience of zero. I think what we're seeing here is something that happens with lots of people that have anxiety just like you. And that is that for one reason or another, they get to the point where they overestimate the risk of something bad happening.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're still giving a 5%. Now the point here is not to say there's no risk ever of things happening that are bad, but that if we can be realistic about it, it helps us manage the anxiety. So why don't we do the same thing with that thought about someone slamming into your car. So what do you think the probability of that was in your mind at the time the thought popped into your mind, right when it occurred?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd say the probability was about an 80.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: 80, so that one was pretty high too. And again, we look at all these days of driving and the 10 or 20,000 or more times you've driven. How many times has someone hit you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: None.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: None. Well, that's fortunate. Some people do get into accidents. I mean, in my life I've had a couple that people have run into me. Fortunately, none of them have harmed me. They've been what they call fender benders. But it looks like for both you and for me the risk is way lower than what did you say, 80% or something like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So as you look at these two estimates of risk, could you mark a different level on that for now? What do you think?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'll put the 5% down. It might be lower, but 5% still seems the way it is.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, that's what we have to deal with, the way you see things. How about for someone running into you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd say maybe 2% for that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So that's gone down a fair amount. Yeah. Now, I have a hunch that having experienced panic attacks influences the way you see things like fear of passing out. When you're having a panic attack, you get that feeling like you're dizzy...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm pretty convinced that it's going to happen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So that's something that we're going to be working on to try to help you with managing these panic attacks. And I don't think we'll have the time this session, but in a session before too long, we're going to work on some ways to manage your breathing and some other things that can help you calm down your emotions. So I think that'll give you an extra advantage and hopefully it'll move it down even below the 5%. So that'll be a project for the future, okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So for homework, perhaps you could continue to do some of this logging and you could even add a column here for checking it out. We could call that the 'realistic thoughts' column.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. I'll do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So we have a good project ahead of us.

video_details.title: AFTER WINTER a family's account of life after Schizophrenia
video_details.description:
When a promising young student is suddenly afflicted with a disturbing psychotic episode, his parents rally to diagnose and support their son’s recovery. Diagnosed with schizophrenia, Quentin takes us deep behind the delusions and depression, the relapses, and his remarkable recovery that sees him continue to chart his impressive academic achievements.

Directed by Nimisha Mukerji

For educators and healthcare providers,  please contact us about how to access our films ad-free.

#schizophrenia #

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: There is a science behind everything. We grow up learning how to rationalize and reason. Our minds allow us to imagine, create, form connections and solve problems. But what if suddenly your thoughts became irrational? What if you were lost but inside your own head? As a survivor of mental illness, I'm living proof that there's life with schizophrenia.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My name is Quinton and I'm 23. I live in Halifax, Nova Scotia. I was born here, but my parents are from France. Quinton was an amazing baby, it was probably his easiest delivery. He was a regular baby, very happy and healthy. Mostly he was a very curious child, loves playing with Legos and building and drawing.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was always playing different sports, but I think the one sport I stuck with till now is soccer. I was always like an outdoorsy kid. This is me trying to do a backflip. It didn't end so well. He actually presented a couple of science fair projects and then he was selected to go to the national level, so he went to Ottawa.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was in grade 8 at the time. I won a bronze medal in science and mathematics and then an award in astronomy. I like math because I like to problem-solve and I think having a set of conditions and trying to find a solution to those conditions is pretty cool. By grade 11, everything was on track. I had really good grades and I had great friends.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My dad decided to take a sabbatical for seven months, so our family was living in Mexico. We were having a great time, I was learning about the culture, the history and the land. I was enrolled in a high school there and learning Spanish. I was also doing courses from Canada, in an International Baccalaureate program.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's really a higher level than just regular high school, so that actually put pressure on any kid who does that program. But I think what really pushed it over the edge is that I was actually doing two high school programs at the same time, one in Mexico and one back in Halifax. I could feel a bit of the tension building.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I had this big essay that was on my plate and I wasn't moving along, I was really struggling with it. And I think I just cracked. I just couldn't take the stress anymore, and that's probably where the psychotic episode came from. It was very gradual at first. I noticed very small changes in my environment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: For example, I would see a red car outside just going down the street. And then for some reason I would see a red flower and I would try to connect the dots. I thought that seeing the color red twice represented red blood, and that meant someone in my family was going to die. Over the course of several weeks, it really got worse.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A lot of people would describe it as a really bad trip. I can't compare it with drugs, but it's probably worse than any trip you can have. You think the aliens are there, you think the police is out to get you. All these thoughts are very scary and they don't make a lot of sense to other people, but for me they made sense.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My parents did the most they could, but they had no idea what was going on. Quinton was making less and less sense. He was a different person. He was completely restless, up and down, up and down. He must have been 16 or 17. There is also the possibility that maybe this is just a phase, sort of a teenage phase.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was completely living inside my own head. I was walking down a beach and my father was walking and I thought I had to walk in his footsteps in order to avoid the sun to protect him. The number one feeling I went through was fear. The diving trip was what caused my parents to realize I needed help.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My mother was my diving partner. This photo was the last photo taken before I had a complete breakdown. I remember being underwater and seeing all these fish and the way they moved was very hypnotic. I wanted to touch them because I thought maybe I would get some kind of superpower from them.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: This is probably the most vivid part of my memories. I went straight to the surface, which is something you shouldn't do. All of a sudden he went up. You need to tell everybody there's something wrong. I got in the ship and I wasn't even talking to anyone, I was just in my own world.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Complete silence on the boat. He didn't talk to me. I tried to engage him. He was looking up, looking down, completely no Quinton. I kind of started to cry. You don't know if you've lost him forever. When this happened, we went back in town and I managed to get an appointment with a psychiatrist pretty quickly.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When I saw the psychiatrist, they very quickly realized I was having a psychotic episode. They gave me medication immediately.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Quinton is a patient of the Nova Scotia Early Psychosis Program. Early intervention in psychosis and schizophrenia is very important, not only to get control of the symptoms, but really trying to maximize those long-term outcomes for that person with as minimal disruption as possible.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They told my parents that it would take time to start working. We had to keep an eye on him, keep the window closed. The doctor said, don't let him approach any window. In this state, he might just walk out and jump because maybe he thinks that he can fly. Disoriented, very paranoid, very delusional. I could have done something really bad.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I received my diagnosis of schizophrenia in Canada. Schizophrenia was constantly on my mind. Understanding that schizophrenia is now with me for the rest of my life was difficult to process. When I went back to school, grade 12, I had a relapse. I had missed my medication dose for four or five days because I didn't get my refill on time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Symptoms were returning. I couldn't control it. I was walking down the hallway and I was very afraid and shivering all over. I knew I needed to get out of there and just be by myself. After the relapse, the depression started. I just wanted to lie in my bed and just shut off the world.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Three things that were crucial in my recovery were medication, family and friend support, and having a good medical team.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How are you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm good, how are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The goal when you treat someone with schizophrenia is one, for recovery, and two, to prevent relapse. In that first year things can happen. Especially when you're a young person who's had such an interruption to their life. So how are you doing overall with the medication?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Pretty good. Apart from the little fatigue I've been feeling, but it's been really good.
