diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think taking a medication orally every day does give you that reminder that you have an illness. So Quinton, since he's been switched to the injection, has been doing really well. As a physician, I don't have to worry about that compliance issue. It gives me a sense of safety because there's less chance of relapse.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My parents never gave up on me. They continued to support me and encourage me. I kept taking my medication. Coming to accept what I had gone through and learning to live with the condition was key. I graduated with honors and went to prom. I was determined not to let schizophrenia hold me back.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I applied to university and got into Dalhousie. I'm currently doing a concurrent degree in science and engineering. I want to make a difference in the world through helping the planet. Renewable energy and sustainable living is very important for my family. I want to work in the green building industry, making buildings more energy efficient.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He's getting more confident about himself. Most of my close friends know, and they've seen the transformation. Six years ago, I would probably be still home in my bed. It feels really good to be out playing soccer with my friends. Exercise is probably pretty important in recovery as well.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm fortunate to have the friends I have, for them to be able to see beyond my schizophrenia and see me as a person. Everyone should have friends like that. Seeing Quinton go through it was really hard, but seeing him coming out is powerful. Some people never get over it, but I was able to with a lot of help.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm not afraid of schizophrenia anymore. I've been able to live through it and it can get better. I'm living proof that there's life with schizophrenia.

video_details.title: Motivational Interviewing Role-Play - Doubts about Substance Use after DUI
video_details.description: This video features a motivational interviewing (MI) counseling role-play session in which MI techniques are used to identify and explore ambivalence. In this role-play, the client (played be an actress) appears to be in the contemplation stage of change.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello, Penelope. How are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm okay. How are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm good, thanks for asking. I understand you've come here today because you've had a recent arrest.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I got a DUI for being under the influence of alcohol and marijuana about a week ago.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alcohol and marijuana? And how recent was this DUI?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: About a week ago.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So what's been going on since that happened?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I have to go to court soon and I'll probably need treatment, but I really don't want to. I'm just coming here to see if I can get out of it by being in some type of treatment.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Get out of it? You mean get out of the charge?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I feel like they're probably going to make me go to rehab and I don't want to do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you feel like you can get out of the rehab part too?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm not sure. The DUI made me realize I need to change, but I'm not ready to stop drinking or using marijuana. They are the only things that really help me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So with this recent arrest, you realize it may be a good idea to stop using, but you really don't want to.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mm-hm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're stuck there.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, kind of. Drinking and using marijuana haven't got me anywhere positive, but it's all I know and the only thing that makes me feel better.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When you drink, do you ever socialize at the same time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes at bars, but most of the time just at my house.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alone? And same thing with the marijuana?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I have a few people I smoke with, but usually it's by myself since I do it every day.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it doesn't sound like you're really worried about losing your social support if you stop using.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, not really.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what are you losing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I use it to cope with pain from an old brain injury. It's the only thing that's ever helped with it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The alcohol and marijuana. All right. So you take it for pain relief. Any other reasons?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's just easier. The marijuana relaxes me and makes it easier to forget about things when I'm using.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Like forget about problems? So it affects your mood in a positive way?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I like the feeling once I'm drunk, and the marijuana helps with anxiety. I don't feel anything, so I don't have to deal with negative feelings.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you used since you had the DUI?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I haven't drank, but I've still been smoking a bit, though I've cut back.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So the use takes away pain and anxiety, but then you have these legal consequences. How do you figure those two things out?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know if there's a way. I just couldn't imagine not drinking or using marijuana.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you can't imagine that. Can you imagine having further incidents with law enforcement, like more charges?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I hadn't really considered that. I want this to go smoothly and not be in this situation again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you can picture an outcome where you beat these charges and you're more careful in the future?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess I just wouldn't drive if I was drinking right before and try to avoid that situation again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So with that thinking, you could continue to use but take out the part that got you in trouble.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But first you have to get out of trouble this time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yep.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If you could have the pain and anxiety go away without the alcohol and marijuana, would you continue using it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can't imagine anything else helping. Plus, I couldn't imagine not drinking with my friends if they called me to go out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so there is a social component here.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A little bit. Most of my friends work nine-to-five jobs and only drink on the weekends, but when we do go out, they all drink.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So even if you had no anxiety or pain, you'd have to give up those interactions with your friends.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mm-hm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How would they respond if you went out with them and didn't drink?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They probably wouldn't understand, and I would feel out of place.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it'd be socially awkward and strain the relationships with your friends.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mm-hm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So quitting usage doesn't seem like a good route for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, not at all.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But this recent situation is making you second-guess some of it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's making me think that maybe I need to make a change, just not that change.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you need to make some change, but not with the alcohol and drugs.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I don't know what, but...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have any theories?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe just cutting back and not drinking and driving, but I haven't really thought of what else I could do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you could reduce usage and avoid driving. Would that be enough to stop the anxiety and the pain?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. I might not drive as often, but I'm not sure if I can cut back drinking enough to still feel okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hm, so that strategy might not work.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess not.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It seems like all your options here are kind of grim.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that just me or does it seem that way to you too?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Now that I'm talking through it, yeah. I don't think I have any choice really.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You don't have any choice? What's going to happen is going to happen?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. I don't really know what to think.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Let's start with what we know. You don't want to make a bad impression in court. What do you think you could do that would make a bad impression?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Going to court drunk, testing positive on a drug test, or getting another DUI in the meantime.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So you know for sure you want to avoid those behaviors.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mm-hm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would it be acceptable to do those things in your mind?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really. I can avoid drunk driving and maybe not drink on the court date, but the marijuana part is tougher.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's tougher. So would you appreciate those as goals, like avoiding going into court drunk?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Goals that you could get behind?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can try, but I'll be stressed on my court date, so it'll be hard not to drink that day.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're not striking me as overly enthusiastic about this idea.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I'm not.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This is really tough for you. The substances are important to you and the DUI has encroached on that. Is this an inconvenience or a major life event that will change things?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know because I have to deal with it or there'll be a warrant for me. I can't avoid this situation.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What if the judge says no more drinking or marijuana period, or else you go to jail?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was hoping it wouldn't get to that. It possibly could, but I don't know what I'll do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I would think it almost certainly would at some point.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can't imagine not drinking or using drugs. I might say I would at court, but I don't know what would happen once I got home.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How long have you been using alcohol and marijuana?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: For about six years.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Six years. Had you ever envisioned stopping until now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What was your plan before the DUI?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I didn't really have a plan. Marijuana never affected my life too much, but the drinking has gotten worse recently.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So without this, you would have continued using for years to come.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I never thought I wanted to stop until now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Could this be, in a strange way, an opportunity?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess if I wanted to stop, this would be a reason for me to stop.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If you really wanted to stop, could you stop?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I could try, but I've never tried before so I don't know. It's an unknown.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So where do you want to go from here? What can I do to help you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Help me figure out if I actually want to stop because I might have to. If I actually want to stop, it'd be easier to do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Like a place in terms of your thinking and your mentality?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, you want to work on that? Any hearings coming up in the next week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, they're not for a few more weeks.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. I'll see you in a week and we'll pick up with that. Let me know if anything changes. Thanks, Penelope.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Thank you.

video_details.title: Video 5. Eliciting Automatic Thoughts: Dr. Sudak and Brian. Wright/APA Publishing
video_details.description:

Learning Cognitive-Behavior Therapy: An Illustrated Guide, Second Edition

Building on its successful “read-see-do” approach, this second edition of Learning Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy: An Illustrated Guide seamlessly combines videos with informative text and figures, charts, worksheets, checklists, and tables to help readers not only learn the essential skills of CBT but achieve competence in this important evidence-based

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So why don't we move on to agenda item number two, because it sounds like you had a really rough weekend. And what might help me is if you would kind of describe what happened. I know we had made some plans that you were going to try out. What went on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I made plans to go to happy hour with some friends from work. I told everyone I was going to be there. I got my stuff together and headed towards the restaurant, but I couldn't go. I ended up just going back to my apartment and sat there all weekend.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like you had some thoughts and feelings in the car that were really pretty strong and changed your plan. I think it would be helpful to try and capture some of those so we can see how your thinking affects your mood. If we could go back to Friday, you're approaching the restaurant, what happens next?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I got to the restaurant and I parked. I saw a group of people from work there, and I just couldn't get out of the car. I sat there for what felt like an eternity, but then I just had to leave. I turned around and drove away.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what were the feelings that you were having right then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just felt like I'm never going to fit in with these people, I'm never going to be one of them. I don't even understand why they would want me there. I'm nobody to them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Those are really the thoughts you were having right then: "Never going to fit in," "I'm never going to be one of them," "Why would they want me there?" It sounds like you had some painful emotion associated with that too. So then you drove home?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I just drove home as fast as I could.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what happened next?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When I got home, I felt a sigh of relief. But then I realized there's nothing there, just me. I just sat down in my chair and turned the television on and that was my weekend.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you spent the whole weekend in front of the TV. When you were sitting there, what kind of thoughts were going through your mind then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just felt so alone. I'm never going to fit in or be able to make a life here in this city.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I can understand that this was another painful weekend. I'm wondering if we could try a little something different and take a look at some of these thoughts. We've talked about how thoughts, emotions, and behaviors are connected. This is a "thought record" to help us organize information about these situations. Situation one was driving to happy hour; situation two was sitting in front of the TV at home. My guess is these are pretty typical for you lately.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, definitely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Great, because we're working on the stuff that has promise in making a dent here. Here are the thoughts you had: "I'm never going to fit in," "I'm never going to be one of them," "Why would they want me here?"

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And when you were at home sitting in front of the TV: "I'm never going to fit in," "I'm so alone," and "I'll never make a life here." These are pretty common things you think to yourself.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, most of the time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And when you have thoughts like this, they generate a fair amount of emotion. What emotion?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just sadness. Alone. Feeling I'm so lonely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: On a scale of 0 to 100, how strong was that sadness on Friday night?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was up there. It was probably like 100%.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: 100% in the parking lot. How about when you were at home?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, it wasn't quite at that point, but I would probably say it was up there around 95%.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Which one of these thoughts was associated with the sadness the most?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd probably say that "I'm never going to fit in."

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And if I were to rate the percentage that you believe that thought, 0 to 100, what would that be?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Really strongly believe that. So when we look at the thoughts you had at home, which of those is most associated with the sadness?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When I'm back at home, it's just that I'm just so alone.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how much do you believe that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably about 95%.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So we have some really strongly held thoughts associated with strong emotion. We should find things you can do besides watch TV, but first I wonder if we could look at the thought "I'm never going to fit in." It seems like an extreme perspective. Examining it might provide some relief. Would you be willing to do that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure.

diarization.text: So, Eric, how'd the homework go this week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I didn't really do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, last week was kind of helpful in session but then I got home and I felt kind of worse and then it just sort of seemed like what's the point of writing down how bad I'm feeling. diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So, remember it was somewhat helpful last week when we did it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, but then I felt worse when I was doing it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, let's go over the rationale for doing the homework and maybe I didn't explain it well enough last week so maybe I'll just review it again. Okay? So, the purpose of the homework was for you to notice that shift in your mood when something upsetting happens, and then to write down what your mood is and then to ask yourself the question 'what's going through my mind' so you can identify those automatic thoughts that you're having.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess it just feels like when I write my mood down I'm just like sitting in it and it just feels uncomfortable.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, I understand that and I can see how you could feel worse when you write your mood and your thoughts down. And we're going to work on those thoughts and maybe come up with some ways to challenge them to help you feel better. But before we get to that, the first step is just knowing that you're having them to start with. But we'll get there. So, what I'd like to do is kind of break this task down into a simpler part first and help you to identify when you're having those automatic thoughts during a mood shift. Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think I got it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So, what I'd like to do since you didn't do it this past week is maybe do a thought change record in session. Would that be okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, I have one right here, maybe we could fill it out together. Okay. Was there a situation that happened this past week that was upsetting to you, caused you distress?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, there was this thing, one of my buddies from college called me up and he knows this girl that he wanted to maybe set me up with and he thought I'd really like her and we might be a good fit but I don't know, I just told him no. And I felt pretty bad after that phone call.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Just bad, or were you feeling a particular emotion there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Kind of sad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sad. And did you notice your thought right at that point that you started feeling sad?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just thought that she's not going to like me. There's just no way. I mean, I'm living at home, I don't have a job, there's no way this person's going to be interested in me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, well this sounds like a good situation for a thought change record. So what I'd like you to do is maybe write this down. Do you want me to write it or are you willing to write it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'll write it. Thanks.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So just write down what happened.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So, write my buddy called to set me up with a girl? That okay?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sounds good. Okay. And then in the emotion column write the emotion you were feeling. You said sad.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sad, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And maybe we could rate that emotion so on a scale of 0 to 100, 100 being the most sad you've ever felt, how sad did you feel?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was pretty strong, maybe like an 80.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, 80. And did you have any other emotions?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Kind of lonely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Lonely, okay. And how intense was the loneliness?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not as much as the sadness, but like a 60 I think.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Sounds good. And what was the thought you were having?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That she's not going to like me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Were there any other thoughts that you were having?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I just think about how's anybody going to like me. You know, it feels like I'm never going to be in a relationship.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, well that's an important thought, let's put that one down.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any other thoughts?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think that was it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That was it? Okay. Um, and of those two thoughts, which thought is kind of grabbing you the most, which one's the most upsetting to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Really I guess this 'I'm never going to be in a relationship'.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, why don't you put a star next to that one? Okay. So that's a great job. So what do you think of that? What do you think of this exercise?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, as long as we get to that point where you think we can change these, but it feels okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Mhmm. So review for me again the reason for doing this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: To pay attention to these thoughts, right, when my moods change?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Exactly. And the reason that we're highlighting the thoughts for you is for what reason?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That the thoughts are making me feel bad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Exactly. And if you notice that the thoughts are making you feel bad, then what do we want to do eventually?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Change the thoughts.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Change the thoughts, exactly. Great job. So maybe we can talk a little bit more about how to change those thoughts. Great.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So when your dad asked you about that job opportunity, what was going through your mind right then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was pretty pissed off. Just angry with him and wanting him to get out of my room and just stop hassling me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Were you having any other thoughts at that point?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, how do I get him out of the room.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I want to help you identify some of the thoughts that you were having when you were upset. Right. How are you feeling right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A little angry, I guess, but not like when I was at that point.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I have an idea. Maybe this is something we can do to help you feel a little more angry and notice that change in your mood.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You want me to feel worse?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, I think so. Just for purposes of helping you to identify the specific thoughts that you were having at that moment in time. And so one thing I'd like to do is what's called an imagery exercise, where I get you to close your eyes and kind of set the stage, describe the room that was going on and walk me through scene by scene what was happening with your father and kind of get into it a little bit more.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now do you understand the reason why we'd want to do that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: What's the point? You just want me to know how I'm feeling?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Exactly. Exactly. So I want you to know how you're feeling and when you have that change in mood, then you'd ask yourself what?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thoughts? What am I thinking?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What you're thinking. Exactly. That sounds great. So if you agree, I'd like you to close your eyes and kind of describe what was going on. Where were you when this happened?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was in my room, sitting on my bed, just playing video games like I usually do and it was in the evening and I heard my dad come home from work. I heard the door open. It wasn't like three minutes later, four minutes later, he barges into my room and he's getting on me, you know, 'you didn't follow up on that lead I gave you, did you?' You know he knows I've been in there playing games all day and sleeping. So I don't know why he's on me about it. Just angry and tense and just want him to get out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And so what was going through your mind right at that moment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You know, what does he want from me? Why is he on my case?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Anything else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know what he wants from me. There's nothing I can do to get him to back off. There's nothing I can say that'll make him happy or not angry with me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you any other thoughts?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just don't feel like I'm good enough. He wants me to get a job, nobody's going to hire me. I'm not going to follow up on his leads and then deal with getting rejected. And it just feels like I'm going to feel like this forever. It's never going to go away and he's just yelling at me about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, that sounds really good. Let's open your eyes and I wrote down some of the thoughts you were having here. Why is he on my case? There's nothing I can do to make him not angry with me. I don't feel I'm good enough. I'll feel like this forever. So of those four thoughts...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: More than I thought, right?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: More than you thought, right? So of those four thoughts, which is the one that's most upsetting to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think right now there's nothing I can do about it. There's nothing I can say. I mean, it just feels helpless.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I'm going to put a star next to that thought. And maybe this is something we could talk about in more detail today. We call this identifying the hot thought. So you had a bunch and pick out the one that's most upsetting to you and then focus in on that particular thought. Okay. How does that sound?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That sounds good. So you think there's something we can do about that?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think so. Yeah. Before we get into talking about that particular thought, let me ask you what you thought of this exercise in general.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was good. I guess kind of surprising.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In what way?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When I was talking about it before, it felt like it happened really fast, and it helped me slow it down a little.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the exercise helped you slow it down. Yeah. Anything else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was having more thoughts than I thought I had.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Anything else that was helpful?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess, you know, I said I was like pissed off, but I was also feeling kind of sad when we went through it, when I started talking about that stuff.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So you were more angry and more sad than you thought. Yeah. Right. Remember the purpose of doing the exercise to start with, which was what?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: To get these thoughts.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: To get the thoughts. Yeah. And how do you know when to ask yourself the question of what's going through your mind?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When my mood's changed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Exactly. Perfect. Okay, so let's talk about this particular thought here, okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So why don't we take a look at this thought, "I'll never fit in," and spend some time looking at the evidence that supports it and the evidence that wouldn't support it, now and over your lifetime.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just am so different from everybody. Everyone is just so different from how I have always been. They go to happy hours and they drink a lot, that's just never been me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Mhm, so you're different from the people at work. Some of that is because they drink a lot and appearance is really important and people get pretty dressed up where you work.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess the fact that it's been three months since I've been here and nothing's changing. It just seems like it's getting worse.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So in the three months you've been in Philadelphia, you haven't made much headway in making relationships. If we were looking at evidence against, is there any relationship that you've been able to make?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, there is somebody at work, Jack. We've worked together on a couple of projects. At work we get along pretty well, we work well together.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So not only have you felt like you've been in sync at work with him, but other people have noticed that you work well together. What about interpersonally?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, we do have some things in common, but outside of work, he has his family, he's married and has a child.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so he has some differences, but still you've had a lot of conversations about work things that you felt good about. Anybody else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: There's some people here and there like at my apartment complex that I've casually said hi to, but nothing substantial, I would say.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What about before? Before you came to Philly?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, before I came to Philly, life was just so much different. I ran cross country and I sang in the choir, so I had those groups of people.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So all the way up to when you moved here, you had connections and friends there. Any other relationships, friends that you've kept in touch with since you've moved?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure, I still keep in touch with some of my friends from choir and cross country from time to time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have any of them moved away?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A couple, a couple have, living in other cities. From time to time we catch up.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How are they doing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They all seem to be doing pretty well, judging on the things that they post online. They seem to be pretty happy and their lives are all put together pretty well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But they're looking like they've established things a little more than you felt like you have?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They post pictures of, you know, with their new friends, they're making friends, they're networking, and I've been doing some comparing, it sounds like.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Looking at all of this evidence together, how much do you believe "I'll never fit in" when you look at all of this on a scale of zero to 100?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, looking at it like this, I guess it seems like it's not as intense as it was before. I'd say probably about like a 70.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's come down a little bit. It seems to me that some of the issue here is that you just haven't had much experience with moving away and beginning to establish a life for yourself.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's right, this is my first time moving away from home.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Being lonely is actually something we think about now as being something that happens to people biologically, and it's actually a pretty painful experience. This depression has really kept you from reaching out.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, absolutely, and I kind of don't want to put myself out there because I don't want to let them know that I'm not doing so well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think those walls that you're putting up might be getting in the way too. In this next week, I was hoping that we would start to collect some more thoughts using this thought record.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The other thing I'm going to give you is this list of the kinds of common ways that all humans really think about things that get them into trouble. Which one do you see?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Overgeneralizing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And that is a negative event seen as a never-ending pattern of defeat. So does that seem like a plan for the week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure, absolutely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, great. I think this will give us a handle on things a little more and we'll get to how to change these thoughts when you come back in next week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sounds good.

diarization.text: Well, I think I at least need to go to the grocery.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, is that something that you haven't been doing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, not lately. I've just been grabbing food at work or going through fast food on the way home.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Well, going to the grocery, I think, is a more doable goal, something that you can hopefully work toward more easily than just eating healthy all at once. What are some possible barriers or obstacles that could make it difficult for you to get to the grocery, do you think?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Lately, I just haven't had the energy or desire to go. And I've also been working a lot trying to save up money for the baby. So, finding the time might be hard.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so finding time and finding energy could be some difficulties there. Okay. Well, what sorts of things have you done in the past to help yourself find time and energy to do things?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I used to go every week on Sunday, and I used to already have a list in mind before I went.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so maybe setting aside a specific day would be helpful. Okay. What about in addition to setting aside a specific day, would setting aside a specific time to go to the grocery make it easier as well?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That would probably make it more likely for me to go. I don't have to be at work until the afternoon that day, so I could maybe go, if I sleep in a little, maybe at like 10:00 on Sunday.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, I like that you're setting a specific time for yourself, that helps give you something concrete to work with. So maybe going at 10:00 on Sunday would be helpful. Now as far as finding energy, what do you think you could do to help with that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, lately when I haven't felt like doing things that I really need to do, I'll give myself a reward. And I know that there's this great bakery on the way. So if I tell myself if I go to the grocery, then I can stop by the bakery on the way home, then I may be more likely to go.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, very good idea. These are great ideas, Meredith, and I think that what you will find is when you make efforts to become more active and to eat healthier, hopefully that'll give you more energy for other activities as well. So, I really like these ideas, and I'd like to take a moment to write some of these down on a card so that you have an action plan to take with you today. Does that sound like a good idea?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay.

video_details.title: Video 9. Developing Rational Alternatives: Dr. Sudak and Brian. Wright/APA Publishing
video_details.description:

Learning Cognitive-Behavior Therapy: An Illustrated Guide, Second Edition

Building on its successful “read-see-do” approach, this second edition of Learning Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy: An Illustrated Guide seamlessly combines videos with informative text and figures, charts, worksheets, checklists, and tables to help readers not only learn the essential skills of CBT but achieve competence in this important evidence-based

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So this is terrific. You were able to really come up with a number of different thoughts that happened for you this week. And it really looks to me like the one that's the most common is this idea, 'I'll never fit in.' And that's really associated with lots of, lots of distress.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's my main, the main thought that seems like it keeps coming up and popping up in my head.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. I'm hoping that it would be okay with you if we could go back to the evidence that we had last week about that thought and maybe start to think about generating some different kind of perspective. See what we could come up with in terms of that, and whether or not that change in perspective might help you to feel a lot better and potentially start doing some different things. Is that alright?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, great. So this is the sheet we came up with last time. I'm just going to put this under here, and you had come up with a fair amount of evidence. You came up with the evidence for this as being 'everybody's different,' 'I spend my time alone, so I'll never be able to make a life here for myself.' And then you had a fair amount of different evidence about having had relationships before you came to Philadelphia, having a relationship with a coworker that felt pretty good, and still having some attachment to friends. I'm kind of wondering as we look at the quality of this evidence if there are any things about those thinking errors that you read about that you see in some of these things that we wrote down from last time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, looking back, 'I'll never fit in' is pretty much kind of like black and white. It's like either all or nothing, basically. It's either you're going to fit in or you're not.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, right, right. All or nothing.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: And 'everyone is different from me' is kind of, I guess that's more like overgeneralizing the fact that there's not going to be anybody else out there that I'm going to be able to have a connection with.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. Both in terms of overgeneralizing that everybody is like the people that are at work, and also it seems to me you don't have a lot of information about the people at work really when it comes right down to it. You just know that they go to happy hours and they dress a little differently, but you haven't gotten to know too many of them from what you've told me.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what about, 'I'll always be alone, I'll never make a life for myself because of the way I spent this Friday night'?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's pretty much all or nothing also, pretty like overgeneralizing things.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you're taking that overgeneralization there.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And when we look at the whole picture, how does that relate to 'I'll never fit in'?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess it's kind of ignoring the evidence also that, you know, there are some things in the past that have worked out in the past and I'm not taking that into account when I say that I'll never fit in.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, that certainly wasn't taken into account the amount of people that have been in your life before. So with all of this in mind, if we are to think about this particular thought, 'I'll never fit in,' can you come up with maybe another way to think about the struggle that you've been having with making new connections here?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it's hard to think about that, like with the way I've been feeling, but I guess maybe I might be able to fit in.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, that's a somewhat different perspective for sure, but I'm not sure that it's enough to fortify you to really make a dent in getting out there and taking the risk to be with other people. So I want to get just a little bit more information if that's okay with you. One of the jobs I had given you was to get back in touch with some of your old friends, see if their move had been anything like yours, and I'm wondering what you found out about.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. I did. I was able to contact one of my old friends from back home who had moved recently around the same time I had. And I was kind of surprised because he also had gone through a similar situation where he did feel alone and he did feel isolated. He moved to a somewhat also smaller town, but at the same time he had a hard time meeting people, felt lonely, and even though he had just posted everything positive online, it was kind of surprised to find that he also felt the same way that I had and also had a hard time at first.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Huh. And he was able to do some things eventually that made a dent?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, he got to know some people at work and joined a gym outside of work, after work he would go and work out and met some friends there. He would go to the happy hours at work and he would engage with the people there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so he kind of pushed himself a little bit. And it sounds like he, like many people, puts up the successful end of the story when it comes to online posting and leaves out some of that other part. So it's easier to draw those kind of conclusions that you drew and not know that maybe he had a little bit of a struggle too.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You know, I kind of wonder if he was in the position that you're in and he was really struggling with this thought 'I'll never fit in' and had this same evidence, what might you tell him about his situation that might be more accurate?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would probably tell him just to give it some time. You know, moving to a new area takes time to meet new people. It's not something that happens automatically or overnight. And that, you know, just point out to the fact, remind him of all the good times that we had in the past and that, you know, you had people and friends around him and that it's probably possible in the future to be like that again, I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. I'm going to try to get this down in a couple of lines. So moving to a new area takes time to meet new people, and it doesn't mean it will always be like this, and remember that you've made connections before. Okay. Now, if last Friday night you had a piece of paper or something in your pocket that said, when you were sitting in the parking lot, 'moving to a new area takes time to meet new people, it doesn't mean that you'll always be alone, remember you've made good connections before.' How believable would that have seemed to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: At that time, it wouldn't have been all that believable.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how believable is it sitting here?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right now it's, I mean, it's more believable than it was back then. Let's say 0 to 100, I'd say about maybe 50%.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And if you had this in your car on Friday and you were feeling a little bit of trepidation about doing the happy hour, even if you believed it less than 50%, do you think it would have made any difference in whether or not you would go?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I might have.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Because I mean, it looks like what was really different about your friend is that he pushed himself to do some of the things that felt a little less than comfortable for him in order to start to make connections with people. And sometimes what we need is the facts and encouragement to help us in that circumstance.
