Learning Cognitive-Behavior Therapy: An Illustrated Guide, Second Edition

Building on its successful “read-see-do” approach, this second edition of Learning Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy: An Illustrated Guide seamlessly combines videos with informative text and figures, charts, worksheets, checklists, and tables to help readers not only learn the essential skills of CBT but achieve competence in this important evidence-based

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So Meredith, last time we met we talked about an assignment where you were going to be logging some of your activities for a day, and I see that looks like you brought that with you. Do you mind if we take a look at that together? Okay. Well very good. Can you share with me some of the things that you may have noticed from doing this activity?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I did the activity we planned last time, going to the grocery. Um, and when I, I looked at it, for one, I was, I was glad I went. And, um, you asked me also to rate how it made me feel, how much I think mastery and pleasure I got from the activity. And I was really surprised at how good actually getting that activity done made me feel. Um, it seems sort of like a 'have-to' and it was hard to just muster up the energy and the desire to go, um, but once I got there I noticed that my mood was better.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Very good. It sounds like you found it to be helpful. And I found that a lot of times when patients struggle with motivation, um, trying to get in these activities that they are having a difficult time doing, sometimes it's just getting over that first step, that hurdle of doing it and then realizing how much pleasure you do get from it. And so I hope that this will continue to be something that is helpful for you. Any other things that you've noticed or learned from doing this activity?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well we talked about eating healthier and when I got home from the grocery, you know my mood was better and I actually sat down and made lunch, and I enjoyed that meal more than any meal I have the rest of the week. Um, so that was, that was a surprise.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Very good. Very good. And I also noticed that you have on here that you had a visit from your brother and his children. Could you tell me about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, my brother and I are, are pretty close, and he's been calling for weeks and I just didn't feel like answering the phone. Um, so he just ended up popping in. He stopped over with the kids and when they first got there I was like 'Oh, I really didn't feel like interacting with them, I didn't think I was going to have the energy to play with the kids.' Um, but once they were there for just a few minutes, having them there was really nice. I really was able to enjoy the time that they were there and even after they left, I noticed that I felt a little bit better.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, great. So again, it sounds like just kind of getting over that first hurdle of doing the activity um is difficult but then once doing it you realize how helpful it is. Um, and I know that this could you also mentioned before that feeling of being alone um and not being as active, including being with others and being with family. Um, so this kind of sounds like getting back to your old self again. Um, do you think that visits with your brother or other family or friends could be something you may implement more into your schedule?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think so. Um, having him stop by I really didn't have to plan it so that was, that was nice. Um, but I did feel so much better so I think adding some of that back in may, may be helpful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good. Good. I would agree. Now I did also notice here that you had watching television down here as one of the activities, and it has a pretty low pleasure rating. Could you talk to me about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Having to write down what I was doing during the day, I was really surprised at how much TV I was watching. And when I had to rate, you know, how good I felt doing that, I was surprised that it was, it was pretty, pretty low like you can see. Um, it always seems like the easiest thing to do and I thought it was something I at least liked doing, um, but when I really had to sit down and write it out, I noticed that I really felt worse when I spent a lot of time in front of the TV.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So again, kind of tying this back to that energy piece, you've been feeling like you've had less energy lately, not doing as much, less active, and so I can see that it can be easy to kind of fall back into watching television and so much time passes by. But hopefully when you take a look at what you have written down that it doesn't really bring you much pleasure or make you feel much better, I hope that this can help you organize kind of where you want to put more effort into what activities. So, I hope that this has been helpful for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It has. You know it makes me wonder why am I spending so much time doing this if it's really makes me feel worse, it doesn't make sense.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, right. Well very good. I think you did an excellent job there. I wonder if you know, talking about some of these activities, do you have any other ideas about maybe new activities or other activities you might want to implement into your schedule?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I was thinking you know in trying to get back to the way I used to be, one of the things I used to enjoy doing was swimming. I used to be on the swim team in high school and then after high school, um, I would go with a friend and um I used to really enjoy that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Okay. So are you saying that it's something you might want to get back into again?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I do. I do want to start swimming again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Well why don't we kind of break that down a little bit. If you were to get back into swimming, when do you think you would do that and how often?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I used to swim every day. Um, so I think a good place to start would be maybe going three times a week.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And I'm glad to hear you be very enthusiastic in wanting to get back into swimming. I just wonder again if that would be a lot to do all at once. Three times a week um is a lot. What percent likelihood do you think um you would put on if you would swim three times per week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess that does kind of sound like a lot. Um, maybe 30 or 40 percent.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So that's kind of low. What do you think might be more reasonable or might be more doable for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think going that very first time is going to be the toughest, actually getting over that hurdle and getting started. Um, so maybe if I can set the goal to just go that one time and get the first time out of the way, that may be more doable.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. I agree with you. I think that's something more doable, more reasonable. Maybe if we take a look at just getting over that first hurdle like you said and do that very first time then we can look later at maybe how often you want to do it after that. Um, so that's great. If you were to put a percent likelihood to that of doing it just that one time in the next coming week or so, what would you say?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just doing it once? That would be more about 70 or 80 percent.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So that's a lot higher. So very good. Now I'm sure there's maybe some other things that you would need to do to prepare if you were going to start swimming again. Can we kind of brainstorm what that would be?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. Um, well, I have a place to go but um, you know it's been a while since I've gone so I'd have to think about where I put my swimsuit, where I put my goggles, that sort of thing. Um, so I may have to work on finding those things and getting them organized.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. I agree. And I think that maybe if you plan that out beforehand and not just trying to find those things the day that you're going to swim but actually get those things out beforehand, it might make it a lot easier for you to actually um then swim on that day that you're deciding to do that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. I know that with the grocery having the list done the night before was really helpful when it came to the day to go, so maybe having those things already set aside before I'm planning to go might be helpful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I agree. Good. Very good. Now the one thing, we've talked about these activities. There was something else that I wanted to touch base with you on and that was, you had mentioned to me that there were times when people would call, friends would call, and you didn't really feel like answering the phone. How has that been lately?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I I still haven't been answering the phone when they call. Like my brother just sort of stopped by because he couldn't get a hold of me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So when people call, help me understand your thought process. What's going on that you generally don't answer?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just don't feel like talking to anyone. Okay. Okay. And then afterwards when I don't answer the phone, I kind of feel bad that I didn't answer their call.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Well like you mentioned with your brother, it was something that maybe initially um you didn't have a lot of motivation to do but once he dropped by it made you feel better. I wonder if something um could be similar with answering a phone call, or maybe you have any other idea with how to deal with that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well when we we when we mentioned swimming, um I used to swim with a friend of mine and she's one of the people who've actually been calling and I've not been answering the phone. And I think it would be nice to to reconnect with her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. That would be good. Um, so what do you think you would do? Would you then answer a call if she were to call or do you think you may take the initiative to give her a call?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think at this point I probably need to give her a call.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Well again, you've come up with some really great ideas as far as some activities. One thing we haven't done yet is talk more specifically about when you would actually do those. Right. Can we talk about that a little bit? Do you think there are maybe some um times where you could fit the phone call with your friend in or the swimming?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. Like when we set a date for the grocery, it really helped me to get that done instead of just saying one day I'm going to go to the grocery. So I think that setting a time would be helpful. Um, with my friend, I think I just need to go ahead and call her today and and get that done. I think if I delay it any longer then I'm going to be less likely to call her. So I think that's something I can do later today.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, very good. And as far as the swimming, is there a specific day of the week that you want to plan to do that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Let's see. Looking at my schedule I think that Wednesday morning would be a good day for me to do that. I have that that morning off.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you have some free time then. Okay. Very good. Well it sounds like we have our activities that we can see have been helpful, maybe others that have been less helpful. We also have some new activities that you want to put into your schedule. So it sounds like we have a pretty good plan in place, what do you think?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay.

video_details.title: Video 14. Difficulty Completing an Activity Schedule: Dr. Chapman and Charles. Wright/APA Publishing
video_details.description:
https://www.appi.org/Learning_Cognitive-Behavior_Therapy_Second_Edition
Learning Cognitive-Behavior Therapy: An Illustrated Guide, Second Edition

Building on its successful “read-see-do” approach, this second edition of Learning Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy: An Illustrated Guide seamlessly combines videos with informative text and figures, charts, worksheets, checklists, and tables to help readers not only learn the essential skills of CBT but achieve competence in this important evidence-based

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay Charles, let's take a look at your homework from last week, the activity schedule.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not very much on it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'll take a look at it. You did complete most of it. I don't see mastery ratings, but you have pleasure ratings for everything. You woke up at 8, drank coffee, read the paper, rated that as a 2. Went to the grocery store, rated that as a 3. Ate a sandwich, watched TV, rated that as a 2. Nap, then mail/bills, rated that as a 2. Dinner at a Chinese place, rated that as a 3. More TV, rated that as a 2. Tell me about the mastery ratings Charles, what made it difficult to complete those?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't see the point. How do you master watching TV or eating a meal? If I had used chopsticks, maybe some mastery involved in that, but I didn't. Food was okay, but not great.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It was tough. I want to be clear that this is very typical for many people we work with. It's difficult to complete homework worksheets because things happen, you don't feel well, things get in the way. Our job together is to figure out the barriers. What would you say were some barriers to completing your mastery ratings?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't enjoy anything. I used to enjoy a lot of things. I don't look forward to breakfast particularly. A cup of coffee. The news is mostly bad. The paper doesn't carry much national news anymore. I have to eat, but I really don't see the point of a lot of things.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think something useful for both of us is to collaboratively work together and figure out how we can look at the perceived benefit of doing some of these things versus the cons. There's a worksheet called a decisional balance worksheet. It takes two separate decisions: one to engage in activities (benefits and costs) and another to not engage (benefits and costs). One objective way for us to look at this worksheet would be to determine what things you could do and whether there's more benefit or cost. What do you think?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, sure. That sounds okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's take a look at this decisional analysis. Here's a pen. There are four boxes. At the top, one decision is to change - engage in activities. If we're honest, there are benefits to doing that, but also costs. At the bottom, the other decision is to stay the same. There are benefits to staying the same, but also costs. Let's start with the most obvious one: engaging in activities. What would be some perceived benefit of engaging in certain activities to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That would depend on the activity. I could get in touch with somebody. I could call a friend maybe, try to meet somebody for lunch.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's a great idea. So what would be a benefit of calling a friend or meeting someone for lunch?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would enjoy the company and I wouldn't be as lonely, I suppose.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That sounds great. One benefit would be you'd enjoy the company and you wouldn't be as lonely. I'll write that down.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Company. Not lonely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you think of a downside to potentially doing that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, one downside might be that he wouldn't be interested in having lunch with me. I haven't been a whole lot of fun lately. Or he might be busy and not be able to have lunch. Or he might want to talk about what's going on in my life and I really don't want to talk about that with somebody. I'll talk about it with you, of course.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like the most practical one of those would be that he may be busy. That could be the downside.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Great job with the top two boxes with the first decision. Let's move to the second decision, which would be to stay the same. There's some benefit and some cost.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay Charles, so we completed the worksheet. What's your overall impression about the benefits of changing versus the cons and staying the same?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it makes sure that the benefits outweigh the cons if I make the change. If I don't make the change, I'll be doing just what I've been doing and I'll be getting up wondering what's the point and still be lonely. And if I do call somebody and if they do say sure, then I'd have at least some time with somebody else whose company I enjoy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Those are good observations, Charles. So which activity does it make the most sense to try for homework this week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I'd call somebody, I think.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, let's say for homework then you try to call someone to get together with a friend, and how about also trying to complete a full day of the activity schedule and completing both the mastery and the pleasure ratings. What do you think about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure, okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And if it gets difficult, which again is pretty normal for that to take place, we can talk about it next time and we can problem solve together and figure out how to remove those barriers. Does that sound good?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure, okay.

video_details.title: Video 10. Difficulty Finding Rational Alternatives: Dr. Brown and Eric. Wright/APA Publishing
video_details.description:
https://www.appi.org/Learning_Cognitive-Behavior_Therapy_Second_Edition
Learning Cognitive-Behavior Therapy: An Illustrated Guide, Second Edition

Building on its successful “read-see-do” approach, this second edition of Learning Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy: An Illustrated Guide seamlessly combines videos with informative text and figures, charts, worksheets, checklists, and tables to help readers not only learn the essential skills of CBT but achieve competence in this important evidence-based

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Eric, I see you did the homework this week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I did, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's great. Let me take a look at it. Why don't you walk me through this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. So the thing I wrote about, I heard about this job opening for a line cook at this noodle place close to my house. I thought it was something I could actually do. I ended up driving to the place and sitting in the parking lot in my car for a while trying to talk myself into going in, and I ended up just driving back home. When I got back home, I was feeling pretty sad and kind of depressed. I know you said to do these things when my mood changed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Exactly.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So I started trying to get some of those thought things that you wanted. I just don't think I'm going to get the job. There's no way. Why are they going to hire me? So I don't know why I should try. What's the point? It feels like everyone else is going to be more qualified than me. I haven't worked in years, I didn't graduate college. I don't want to just get rejected again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I hear you. So I think you did a great job filling out the three columns. What I'd like to do today is move on to the fourth column, which is the rational response. We want to take an alternative point of view here. To help you do that, there are a couple of questions you can ask yourself. One is, what's the evidence for the thought, and the other is, what's the evidence against the thought?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So which of those thoughts do you want to focus on? Because you had several there.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think the 'what's the point in trying'.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's the point in trying? That sounds good. So what's the evidence for the thought?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's where all the evidence is. I'm unemployed, I'm depressed...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, let's get this down.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Unemployed, I'm depressed. I just quit anyway. That's what's happened in all my other jobs. I'd probably stop showing up. I don't think I'd do a very good job even if I went. They're just going to pick somebody else. I don't have the energy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, it sounds like you have a lot of evidence supporting the thought. Anything else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think that's it. It feels like a pretty solid case to me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So let's tackle the other question. What's the evidence against the thought?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Evidence that there is a point?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, the evidence against 'what's the point.' It's kind of tough coming up with something. A lot of people when they get depressed have difficulty coming up with evidence opposing that particular thought. It seems like you were able to come up with a lot of evidence supporting the thought. Let's see if we can put our heads together and maybe come up with some evidence against the thought. I can ask you a couple of questions that might help you. Is there a time when you weren't depressed when you went and started working?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's been a while, but I had this job at a burrito place that went pretty well for the first couple of months. I ended up not showing up and getting fired, but at the beginning, it went pretty well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And so what went well about it? Can you be more specific?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was a good worker. I showed up on time and I worked hard while I was there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That sounds like good evidence to me. Why don't you put that down?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Alright. Good worker...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what did you write down?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That I'm a good worker and that I showed up on time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Is there any other time when you weren't depressed that you felt good about yourself and what you were doing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When I started college, that felt pretty good. I dropped out, but that first year was really good actually.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what was that like?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I had a lot of friends. I was a really hard worker. I studied a lot and got really good grades.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sounds important to me. Hard worker, had a lot of friends. Anything else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, when I'm not depressed I feel like I'm a pretty reliable person. It just feels like all these things are when I'm not depressed and now I am depressed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. But I think it's important to look at the evidence for and the evidence against. So that's clearly evidence against the thought, right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So why don't you read through both the evidence for and the evidence against and tell me what you think?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The evidence for is that I'm unemployed and depressed and I'd probably just quit and I wouldn't do a good job anyway and they'd just pick somebody else. The evidence against, I guess in the past I've been a good worker, I show up on time, I work hard, and I've been reliable.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So let's come back to that original thought that you had, 'what's the point.' How much did you believe that on a scale of 0 to 100?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: 100 percent.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. How much do you believe that now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess it's gone down some. Maybe 70 percent now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, why don't you write 70 percent. Anything else about this that you noticed changed?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I haven't really thought about those times when I wasn't depressed in a while. It feels good reminding myself that I had those times.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In what way does it feel good?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm less sad, less depressed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Less depressed, less sad? Okay, why don't you jot a note down there that reminds you of that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I think about if I can get back to that place again, maybe my life will get better, that maybe I could get a job at some point.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So maybe feel a little more hopeful?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sounds good. So do you think that you could do that this week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think so. I mean I think it's still going to be pretty tough to kind of come up with the other side of the argument.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. What would help to remind you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, I guess having this on here was good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So maybe you could review that before you did another thought record?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think that might help.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, that would be helpful. I noticed you had some other thoughts there. What was the other thought that you had on there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That I'm not going to get the job and that everyone else is more qualified.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let me see that. Notice there's what we call a cognitive error or thinking style. I'm thinking that this type of thought is an 'all-or-none' thinking because you said 'everyone'.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: But I've been unemployed for a while...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. But you said here 'everyone is more qualified.' Everyone in the world.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh, well maybe not everyone I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So we call that all-or-none thinking. Do you see that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So sometimes what we write in this column would be 'all-or-none thinking' for that thought. I'm going to give this sheet to you. Maybe you could review it for homework and see if you have any other types of thinking errors.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So you want me to read that?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, just read it for homework and then maybe if you notice any types of thinking errors in your thought record you could write them down. Sound good?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, great.

video_details.title: Video 15. Developing a Graded Task Assignment: Dr. Chapman and Charles. Wright/APA Publishing
video_details.description:

Learning Cognitive-Behavior Therapy: An Illustrated Guide, Second Edition

Building on its successful “read-see-do” approach, this second edition of Learning Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy: An Illustrated Guide seamlessly combines videos with informative text and figures, charts, worksheets, checklists, and tables to help readers not only learn the essential skills of CBT but achieve competence in this important evidence-based

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So Charles, it sounds like things have been going pretty well recently.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, they've been going better. I did call a friend and we had lunch. I hadn't seen this guy in two or three years and it was good to see him. And I got back in the kitchen. I made this pretty good asparagus potato soup. I'm feeling some better, I think.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's good. I'm proud of you for taking the initiative. One thing you did mention was the woodworking shop that we've talked about in the past. How's that been?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, that's still a mess. It's such a mess that I really can't get in there and do any work. Every surface is covered with tools, scraps of wood, and paper plans.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's really difficult to get started on things we've avoided for quite some time. Let's brainstorm and try to figure out how we can get some movement in the woodworking shop. What are your thoughts when you are looking at it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, when I stand there, I feel helpless. It's hopeless, it seems to me, just to get it back in shape again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's explore that. What's the evidence that it's hopeless to do some work in the shop?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just the mess that it is. Sometimes if I need a tool for the house, I can't find it. It takes longer to find than it's worth taking the time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it sounds like you're saying then, it's disorganized and it's a mess.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How do you feel when you think about the woodworking shop that way?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hopeless, I think. I just give up on it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It prevents you from actually getting things done. If I viewed it as overwhelming, then I probably wouldn't do anything either. What's an alternative way to view the shop that would actually be helpful?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, if I could get one workbench cleaned off, I would have some space to work on.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's a really good start. What would that lead to?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I could make some things I've been thinking about for some time, like a small medieval catapult for my grandson or a boomerang.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That would be cool.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I could get one or both of those built, perhaps.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What would that lead to if you got those things built?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would drive four hours to where my grandkids are to give them the toys, show them how they work, and spend time with them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like there's a lot of benefit to clearing out a bench, which would lead to you spending time with your grandkids. You'd also feel better about the woodworking shop in general. Is that basically what you're saying?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would, yeah. Sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It still takes steps to get there. I think one useful strategy is for us to work on a step-by-step plan. How about we talk about the first step, which sounds like moving things off one bench?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd have to start by moving one thing off of that bench. The paper is no problem; I've got a shelf where I could put plans and instructions. I could also pick one place in the shop for wood scraps.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's sketch out what each day would look like so that we won't feel overwhelmed. Does that sound good?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure.

video_details.description:

Learning Cognitive-Behavior Therapy: An Illustrated Guide, Second Edition

Building on its successful “read-see-do” approach, this second edition of Learning Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy: An Illustrated Guide seamlessly combines videos with informative text and figures, charts, worksheets, checklists, and tables to help readers not only learn the essential skills of CBT but achieve competence in this important evidence-based

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So thank you David for telling me your story. As you noticed that crisis got more intense and then it came back down. And one of the things I like to do is identify some of the warning signs or triggers of that crisis. And so I want to record this on your safety plan so that you know when to use the safety plan. So what were some of the warning signs that you had?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess, like I said, when I heard about the test score and not being able to make the grade, I just felt like a complete failure, you know, and it just was so overwhelming because I put out my best and the fact that I didn't get the results I was looking for, it's like what good am I? And the first thing I thought was like my parents are going to be so disappointed, I can't tell them. So I was feeling overwhelmed and anxious about that and just so ashamed that this was the way things turned out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, that's a good summary. So let's list down specifically what they were. What do I put on the first line here?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess when I start to feel overwhelmed or anxious or ashamed, even.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Great. So you had those feelings. What else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not being able to tell my parents. I'm usually very open and can talk to them about anything, but I feel like whenever I feel like I can't, when I need to shut down and I feel like I can't share those things with them, I think...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I can't tell my parents. And what else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just overall feeling like a failure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Feeling like a failure. Okay. So whenever you have any of these warning signs, you'll know to look at your safety plan. That's a cue to you to use it. So the first thing I want to talk about is when you go to that dark place, you're feeling overwhelmed, anxious, ashamed, having these other thoughts and maybe feeling like giving up. That's when you use some strategies to help you get through the crisis or keep it from escalating. So I'd like you to think about some things, see if we can brainstorm some ways that you can identify some strategies that's going to take your mind off your problems, kind of get away from that crisis for even a little while. What have you done in the past that's helped you deal with a crisis like this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I guess in high school whenever I was feeling kind of down and dealing with this kind of stuff, I used to sing in a choir. So I'd like to just go off and sing by myself. Top 40s stuff, classic rock, that kind of stuff.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So singing top 40. Sounds good. So what other strategies could you use to take your mind off your problems?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Something that I think I've started since coming to college, I've started cooking more by myself and I like making some of the foods that remind me of home. A lot of stir-frys, rice stuff, things like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So cooking stir-fry. Sounds like a good strategy. And you have a kitchen that you can cook in? Yeah, okay. So what other strategies could you use to distract yourself from the crisis, you think?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: This is sort of new. I discovered it freshman year in a class, but there's a pottery studio just down the street from my apartment that I can go down and throw pots for hours and it feels good making something.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And is that something that you could do at any point or is available? That sounds very good. So let's put down pottery. Now you have singing, cooking, and pottery. If none of those strategies are helpful for you getting outside yourself and feeling better, then go to the next step, which is to socialize with people or go to places where there are people who are actually very good distractors. So is there somebody in your life that you can go to who's available that you like to hang out with?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure, yeah. Charlie, my roommate. He's a good guy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, let's put down Charlie. And I guess he lives with you, so you know how to get in touch with him and you have his phone number.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the next step on your safety plan is learning to make the environment safe. And I have to ask you this question, and I ask this of everybody I do safety plans with. Do you have access to a firearm?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No, okay, that's good to hear. I know you've taken medicine in the past and had an overdose several years ago, and I don't want anything like that to happen again. So I want to make sure the medication you're taking is secure, or that it's safe for you. What do you think we can do about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess it would be helpful if there was somebody that kind of knew how much I was taking and made sure I was taking exactly what was prescribed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, that sounds good. Somebody to dispense the medication. Who do you think could do that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I could ask my roommate, Charlie. He's a good guy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does he know you're taking medication? Yeah. So I'll write down give the medication to Charlie. So the next step on the safety plan is coming up with reasons for living. This is important so that it gives you a sense of hope and meaning in your life and something to go to when you're feeling in crisis. So can we come up with some reasons for living?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My family, I think.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, anybody in particular that...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure, I've got a little sister. I think I'm the world to her and she looks up to me and I just don't want to lose that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, your sister. Anybody or anything else that gives you meaning in your life?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have a best friend back home that we're kind of miles apart right now, but anytime we call, it's like we pick up like we just were where we left off. Her name's Vanessa.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Vanessa. Okay, and how will you remember both your sister and Vanessa? How would you remind you of a reason for living?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just would think back to all of the times that even before school and all this mess, that I'm not like the perfect person but they don't care, you know, we hang out and enjoy each other's company. Just recall memory maybe. Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So David, what other reasons do you have for living?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: There's a lot of things I haven't gotten to do yet. I have some family in China that I haven't seen and met before and I'm really looking forward to going out there at some point, taking a trip out there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Taking a trip to China. That sounds like fun. Other reasons for living?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I find a lot of meaning and joy out of just singing in general and I wouldn't want to give that up.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'll put singing and then I'll put joy.

video_details.title: Video 19. In Vivo Exposure Therapy for OCD: Dr. Hembree and Mia. Wright/APA Publishing
video_details.description:

Learning Cognitive-Behavior Therapy: An Illustrated Guide, Second Edition

Building on its successful “read-see-do” approach, this second edition of Learning Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy: An Illustrated Guide seamlessly combines videos with informative text and figures, charts, worksheets, checklists, and tables to help readers not only learn the essential skills of CBT but achieve competence in this important evidence-based

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, you did it. That was a really good job. How do you feel?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A little better.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A little better. Okay. What's your level right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I would say like 60.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: 60. Okay, down a bit. Okay. So now we move into the in vivo exposure, right? Okay. Remember, we're going to just for the next 40 minutes or so handle that leash. Allow yourself to have whatever thoughts come up or worries you have about it. You can verbalize them. Talk about whatever's in your head. Okay? Why don't you pull it out of the bag.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Did you put it in that bag?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I asked my husband to.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. What's your level right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would say 65.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: 65. Okay. All right. What are you thinking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That it's disgusting and I don't want to touch it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Hold it a little closer to your body. Maybe hold it with two hands.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you notice about it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's a lot of hair and stains.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you think the stains are?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't want to think about it. I don't know. Saliva, dog poop. It smells so bad. I'm starting to get sick.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. That's all right. Just let it happen. It's okay. What's that spot on it? Looks almost like it's breaking or chewed or something. Is that...?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. He chews on it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Why don't you touch that spot?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're doing good. I know it's hard. That's good. What's your level?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like 90.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: 90. Okay. What jumped? What are you thinking? What made it jump? What's going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm just thinking I'm going to get sick. I really want to vomit right now and what if that part I touched has saliva? And what if the dog has... like they have all sorts of things in their mouth.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, they even lick their own butts, don't they?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. And then he chewed on that leash and you're holding that leash. Wow. You're brave. Good for you. Okay. You're also noticing you're kind of holding it away from yourself. Let me show you something. Can I hold it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Ah, yeah. That is quite a leash. It's old and it has been chewed on, hasn't it? So watch this. Okay.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So I have to do that now?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. I'm not going to make you do anything, you know that. But I think that the more kind of full-body contact you can have with that leash, the better the exposure we're doing. Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good. All right. What's going through your mind?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That I'm getting all the bacteria in my skin and I want to take a shower right now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So your urge to wash is coming up. How strong is it? Give me a rating on that zero-to-100 scale for your urge to wash right now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like 80.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: 80. Okay. That means you're doing good exposure. Oh, good for you! On your face! Mia, that's great!

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. What else are you thinking? Just keep telling me what's on your mind.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I'm just thinking of all the times I saw the dog biting on it and licking on it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So saliva is worse than other things? The dog's saliva anyway?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's just... Yeah. I can feel it in my hands.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is it that makes saliva worse? What's so bad?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The smell, the consistency. And I know they have bacteria there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So it's a bigger source of the bacteria. Okay. That's all right. Just keep thinking that, then. That's okay. Good.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm scared I'm going to make myself sick and then I touch my baby and I make him sick.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. You're realizing things that I don't think you've described to me before. Just handling that thing. How long has it been since you've touched that leash without gloves?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like five years.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Wow. Okay. Good for you. Good.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I used to get the gloves even bleached because I don't want to touch the gloves.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You mean after you used them, if you had to walk the dog, you would bleach them? Okay. Where are those gloves now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I threw them away because you asked me to.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good. Good for you. Good. Okay. Well, after doing this, you can take him for a walk anyway without them, right? Maybe.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's your level now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like 60.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: 60. Okay. All right. Ha, it's going down a bit.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you make of that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I think it's what we talked about, that at the beginning, just the fear of thinking of getting the leash makes me more anxious, so I get that anticipatory anxiety. And then the more I touch it and the more I get used to it, I guess I habituate.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So one other thing that helps... one of the things that helps in a moment like this is to try to sort of up the exposure a little bit. Can you put it around your neck? Sort of let it touch the upper part of your body.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How's that feel?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Disgusting.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Disgusting. What's your level?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like 70.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. It's okay.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So we're going to do this the whole session?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. You've been at it for like about eight minutes or so, seven minutes. We're going to do it longer.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You want to touch it to your face again? That was really good when you did that before.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Could even touch it to your lips.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You're killing me. It smells so bad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Smells bad, yeah. You're doing great, though. I know this is hard. Mia, it's tough, but you're doing a really, really good job. And this is going to help. It's also going to make it a little bit easier to do what I'm going to ask you to do for homework, which is to take it home again and to touch it every day. So part of your homework will be not only to listen to that imaginal exposure recording that we made, but also to spend about an hour just holding onto that thing, touching your body with it, using it to kind of contaminate other things in the house—furniture, other surfaces, your clothing. You could tie it around your waist while you do things at home.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play – Complete Session – Depression and Alcohol Use – Part 1
video_details.description: This video features part one of a complete cognitive-behavior therapy (CBT) counseling role-play session in which CBT techniques are used to address depression and alcohol use. Part one includes a check-in, scaling, and setting the agenda.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, this is Dr. Grande. I hope you find this video useful. If that's the case, please like it and subscribe to my channel. And as always, thanks for watching.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello, Sophia. How are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm good, how are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. I saw you last time a week ago, and I know you had some concerns with employment. But first, before we get into that, I wanted to check in to see how you're doing emotionally. I know from last week, on a scale of one to ten, you said your depression was about seven. How is it today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's been up and down. I think today it's probably a seven again, but I've been back down to a nine lately. I guess maybe I feel a little better because I'm coming here and I know I'll get to talk about it. But last time we were talking about me trying to get a full-time job, and I think I just realized last week that it's really hard for me to work full-time. Right now I'm doing the part-time thing with the work program and they want us to do volunteer work in the afternoon if we haven't found a full-time job by a certain week. Just thinking about it, I don't think I can do that. I just don't think I can work a full eight hours every day. It's just too much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so you're having some concerns about full-time work and that level of energy you'd have to exert and that commitment.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so would it be okay today if we kind of structured what we're going to do for the session? If it's okay with you, I'd like to talk about that and get some more details about what's going on this week and your feelings surrounding that. I'd like to talk about your core beliefs that might be contributing to some of these feelings of depression. And then for the last part, we'll work on some interventions to try to help you with what's going on at work and with your depressed mood. We can make changes to this as needed, but I just want to start with an outline.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I mean, that makes sense.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, great. So tell me a little bit more about what's going on with the work.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I mean, I don't really know why it is. I know I'm always tired because I just have so much trouble sleeping, as I've told you before. It doesn't matter how tired I am, I can't sleep. But I go in the morning, eight to noon, but then in the afternoon it's just so hard to keep going on. It's just such a long amount of time and I just feel like I don't know if I can really do it. And especially in the winter, if you work eight hours, by the time you get out of work, it's dark out and it just makes my depression so much worse.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the latter part of the day is more of a struggle for you, the latter part of the work day.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So getting up in the morning, getting to work on time, you do okay with that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's hard, but I feel like I'm better at that. I'm already up anyway, so I know I've got to get up and do what I have to do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the work program you're in now, you work in the morning?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What hours are you there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Eight to noon.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And there's some work you have to do in the afternoon?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, yeah, since I've been there for eight weeks and I haven't found a job yet, they want us to volunteer in the afternoon. They find us our own place to volunteer, so that's good. I guess they want to get you used to doing something for eight hours a day and maybe have something to put on your resume. Having a big gap on your resume doesn't look good either. But just thinking about it, it's so exhausting. I get out of the work program and I think if I had to go to another place, I can barely make it home. All I want to do is go home.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thinking about it's exhausting. Can you tell me what type of thoughts you're having as you...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just don't think I can do it. I just don't think I'm the kind of person that can work eight hours a day. And it just makes me feel like what's the point? I'm going to work eight hours a day? I don't think I can. It's just too many hours.

video_details.title: Video 18. Imaginal Exposure for OCD: Dr. Hembree and Mia. Wright/APA Publishing
video_details.description:
https://www.appi.org/Learning_Cognitive-Behavior_Therapy_Second_Edition
Learning Cognitive-Behavior Therapy: An Illustrated Guide, Second Edition

Building on its successful “read-see-do” approach, this second edition of Learning Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy: An Illustrated Guide seamlessly combines videos with informative text and figures, charts, worksheets, checklists, and tables to help readers not only learn the essential skills of CBT but achieve competence in this important evidence-based

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, Mia, great job on your homework. That was really excellent. You listened to the imaginal exposure recording about six times. Is that right? And you did the in vivo exposure of walking around and touching things like door knobs and other surfaces and objects you normally wouldn't touch, both at your house and at other places you went. And you sat down on the floor and you even ate lunch off the floor at your house and at your mom's house. And no hand washing, no extra washing. Perfect. Good for you. So what'd you learn from all that, do you think, over the course of the time you've done that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It just got easier. At the beginning it was really hard and I feel like my SUDS were much higher than at the end. So I guess that was what we talked about, the habituation.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Habituation, right. The fact that when you do something like that that initially makes you anxious and you do it repeatedly, especially for prolonged periods of time, your anxiety comes down. We're just not built to stay indefinitely anxious. You notice any other changes or anything else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I noticed that before doing the exposures I was really, really anxious and then it kind of went down, like the anticipatory anxiety that we've also discussed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. Did that change by say yesterday?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, the SUDS were initially really high before the exposure and then they went down the more I did them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're saying you not only noticed that it went down during the exposure, but you started feeling less anxious even approaching it. Good. All right, so you're doing so well, we're gonna take another step up the hierarchy today like we planned. So this is the dog leash day, right? Did you bring it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, good. We'll get to that later in the session. First, we're gonna do some imaginal exposure. You remember what the purpose of that is? Why are we gonna do imaginal?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That way I can kind of relive a story or a situation that would make me really anxious and eventually deal with the feared consequence of getting sick, in my case.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Exactly. The idea is this is how we are able to have you have exposure to or sort of a confrontation in imagination with the consequences you fear of touching things that are contaminated and not doing your rituals. Perfect. So did you write the story?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, let me see. All right, good. All about taking the dog for a walk with that leash and what happens because of that. Excellent. In a minute when we start, I'm going to ask you to close your eyes and to narrate or describe this scene where you're handling the dog leash and very aware of the way it's contaminated. I want you to describe in the story not just what you're doing, but also what you're kind of feeling and what you're thinking as you do this, leading to the consequences you fear. Any questions before you start? Okay, so what's your level right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would say like a 70.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: 70. Okay. Go ahead and start when you're ready.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Should we press play?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, thank you for reminding me. Yep, we'll start the recording so you have that for homework. Okay.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So I'm in my house and the dog starts barking and I know that that means that I have to take him out. I really don't want to, so I'm thinking maybe I should wait until Joe gets home. But I know if the dog keeps barking he's gonna wake up the baby. So I decide to go to the front door and get the leash. I'm not gonna wear the gloves I usually wear so I fully experience touching the leash. I'm already feeling really anxious. I look at the leash and I see that it's gross and it's full of hair and the dog has been biting on it and it probably has saliva and other things. I see stains and I start thinking what if that's dog poop and I get sick? I just feel myself shaking and really sweaty and my heart is beating really fast. I'm feeling really, really anxious but I push myself and I grab the leash. I get the dog, open the door, go out and grab the leash.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's your level now, Mia?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like 90.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: 90. Okay. You're doing great. Just keep going.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So I grab the leash and the dog is pulling and I feel the leash kind of pushing through my skin and I'm thinking all the bacteria that's getting there and I'm gonna get sick. I walk the dog, came back home and I just leave the leash in the front door. I really want to wash my hands, really want to take a shower. But I try not to and I stop myself. I'm feeling really, really anxious. I can't stop thinking about washing. So I try to go to bed, decide to fall asleep. The next morning I wake up and I already feel sick. I know I'm sick. I'm shivering and I feel like I have a fever and I'm really nauseated. So I go to the bathroom, start vomiting and I know I'm sick. I already got something. I should have washed. I start thinking about that. I'm gonna get the baby sick and I feel really, really sick.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, great job. What's your level now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like 80.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: 80. Okay. All right, so just keep visualizing this. I'm going to describe it now and you just stay with that image as much as you can. You're in the house and the baby's sleeping. Suddenly you hear the dog at the front door barking and your heart rate jumps up and you get anxious because you know that means he needs to go out. It makes you scared because you're not going to use the gloves that you always use. So you go toward the leash and it makes you even more anxious to see it. It's dirty and gross and you see stains on it and you think about what those are from and maybe they're from dog poop and that's going to get on you. You pick it up anyway and as you go out the door, he pulls that leash into your hand and you feel the contamination from the leash entering your body through the pores of your skin. You feel like it's just running up your arm through your bloodstream. You keep thinking, 'Oh my God, what if I get sick from this?' but you keep walking him. You bring him back inside the house, take the leash off and the urge to wash is so powerful. You want to go scrub your hands and get in the shower and get all these germs off from the leash, but you don't do that. You make yourself not do the ritual. Then you go back in and keep doing things, but that sense of feeling sick is staying with you. That night you go to sleep still anxious and wake up in the morning and before you have your eyes open even a couple minutes, you know that you're sick. You rush to the bathroom and vomit. You're sick and you know it's because you handled that leash and didn't wash. And now you're sick and the baby will probably get sick. And if only you had done the washing. Okay. What's your level now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like 80.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: 80. Okay. Okay, you take it back and you do it again, okay? Good job.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, okay. So I'm home and the dog starts barking.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play – Complete Session – Low Self-Confidence at Work – Part 11
video_details.description: This video features part eleven of a complete cognitive-behavior therapy (CBT) counseling role-play session in which CBT techniques are used to address low self-confidence at work. Part eleven includes evaluating evidence, creating self-talk and evaluating reactions.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, this is Dr. Grande. I hope you find this video useful. If that's the case, please like it and subscribe to my channel. And as always, thanks for watching.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How many times have you gone to work and made a mistake?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, I mean, I guess none technically, none that have been something I've gotten in trouble for or anything like that. Sometimes it's hard to tell because you know, you don't always hear from people afterwards. You can't really tell, was it a mistake or not? But I guess none that have had like any major consequences.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. So none, but there might be a few small ones that you just haven't found out about. So less than a tenth of a percent of the days you go in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Very small.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, really, really small.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the probability of the statement that you're making being true is pretty low. The thought rather, that 'I'm going to make a mistake' is probably not supported by the evidence. So the automatic thought is not accurate and not useful. Alright, so it's got a couple strikes against it. But it is the thought you're having, so let's deal with it. 'I'm going to make a mistake'. So what could you tell yourself as the first part of that adaptive response, which acknowledges that fear of making a mistake?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I guess like, everybody makes mistakes?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Everybody makes mistakes. I could make a mistake today, but it's unlikely. So 'everybody makes mistakes, I could make a mistake but it's probably not going to happen', rather than 'I'm going to make a mistake'. You're going to have that automatic thought either way, until you start to apply these adaptive responses. So what could be a next part which is realistic but also positive that can help get you past the reaction of being late and worrying?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm a good caseworker and I need to do my job so I can help other people and it's going to be okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so there's a few elements in there. 'It's going to be okay', 'I need to do my job', 'I help people'. All those are true. So applying as you now even as you say this here with me, what reaction are you having right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, it feels a little better. It's hard to, you know, I still feel like it's dangerous, I might make a mistake, but I guess it helps a little bit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you see yourself being able to in the moment of having that automatic thought and having that worry come in, can you see yourself applying this self-talk?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think I probably will because now it'll be hard to have those thoughts and not think of you and think okay, I need to calm myself down a little bit since we've been talking about it for so long.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you've already used self-talk on your own before you even knew about these strategies.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yep, that's true. And it did help in the past, so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A lot of the effectiveness of this is based on your ability in that moment to take a step back and follow the training. Just like many professionals depend on their training to help them make the correct decision. So think of this like something you learned in a training. This self-talk is pre-packaged, it's ready to go. You can even have it written down. It's a matter of following the protocol. You're just looking to grab a moment in there and apply this strategy. Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that makes a lot of sense.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sometimes, it's likely you probably won't. And it's important in those moments to not get discouraged. You could have a self-talk for that too. Something like 'Dr. Grande said it was likely that once in a while I wouldn't be able to do this'.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's not going to work every time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah, that makes a lot of sense.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's the chaos of life and the chaos of emotions that sometimes interfere. The more times you have success, that seems to be tied with better chance of improving and reduction of symptoms, but allow yourself failures as well. There's not going to be a perfect connection between an automatic thought and applied self-talk.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that makes sense because like if you could just flip a switch, I would only have to have one therapy session.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You'd be in good shape, right. Yeah, so it's a bit more difficult than that. But overall, these strategies are fairly straightforward and you can definitely learn them. I want you to have that confidence. It's normal to have mistakes occur, but overall you should be able to... it'll get easier in the future to develop your self-talk for different thoughts.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play – Complete Session – Low Self-Confidence at Work – Part 10
video_details.description: This video features part ten of a complete cognitive-behavior therapy (CBT) counseling role-play session in which CBT techniques are used to address low self-confidence at work. Part ten includes psychoeducation and encouraging.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, this is Dr. Grande. I hope you find this video useful. If that's the case, please like it and subscribe to my channel. And as always, thanks for watching.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So when you have those type of thoughts, like "I can't make a mistake," we call those automatic thoughts. We'll have plenty of time to talk about the different structures in CBT over the course of several sessions. Let's just take pieces of it for now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We believe that your beliefs combine with the situation to create these thoughts. For instance, if you're laying in bed before work and you believe you're not competent, the stress of it being time to actually get up creates an automatic thought tied to dread and fear. What is the thought in that moment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: If I go to work, I'm going to make a mistake.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the thought is, "I'm going to make a mistake," which leads to worry and anxiety. When we identify an automatic thought like that, we use what's called self-talk. At first, it may seem a little odd, but it is a rehearsed statement that you literally say to yourself.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Over time, applying self-talk will eventually change the outcome, the reaction, and the underlying belief. At first, it's going to seem quite foreign to you. Tell me how you're processing this now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So I mean, what am I supposed to say to myself, I guess?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's a good question. Let's look at building some adaptive responses. The thought, "I'm going to make a mistake," leads to feelings of dread and being late. Have there ever been times when you've had that thought but still went to work on time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I guess I tell myself I have to get to work on time because if I don't, it's going to be even worse if I make a mistake and I'm late. I tell myself it's going to be okay and I just have to get through the day.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When you do that, you are applying self-talk. You just didn't have a label for it, and it seems to work. The message you're sending yourself includes a mix of positive and negative thoughts. Self-talk needs to be realistic, but I'd rather focus on more positive elements as we refine it.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play – Complete Session – Low Self-Confidence at Work – Part 9
video_details.description: This video features part nine of a complete cognitive-behavior therapy (CBT) counseling role-play session in which CBT techniques are used to address low self-confidence at work. Part nine includes exploring the worst-case scenario and creating self-talk.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, this is Dr. Grande. I hope you find this video useful. If that's the case, please like it and subscribe to my channel. And as always, thanks for watching.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So let's say you go into a house, you go into the community with your job. You go into a house and you're having an off day, maybe worried about making mistakes, maybe stressed about that, maybe tired. And there's some evidence there that you should be able to pick up, but you just don't. Somebody lies to you about what the conditions there are and you kind of realize that they might not be telling the truth, but you're ready to go home, so you leave and then somebody's hurt. Would that be a kind of a worst case?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's the type of mistake you're afraid of making. And what would that feel like to make that mistake?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Terrible. It would feel like I had a role in that kind of thing happening to somebody. Like I'm partially to blame for somebody being harmed, and that is like the exact opposite of what my job is supposed to be.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So that would be a worst case outcome. You'd be extremely upset. You're extremely upset now, but you were an eight when you were in bed in the morning.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is it reasonable that a professional makes a mistake like that? Is it reasonable that they continue on in the field and try to learn from that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. I mean, I'd like to think that it's not possible to make that kind of mistake, but I think that that's naive. I think it is possible and I would like to learn from that, but I don't know what other people would do, like if I would lose my job.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, there might be consequences for that type of error. It's not intentional, it's something that would happen due to a confluence of circumstances. After making a mistake like that, what would your thought be? What would you be thinking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would be thinking I don't know how this will ever be better. I don't know how I'm ever going to feel okay about what I did.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So by extension, I'll never feel okay about what I did?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what do you think you would do then in terms of your reaction to that thought?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. I mean, I guess ideally I would say to myself it's going to get better and this will pass, but it's just hard.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you think it would do to your work performance?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think I would probably have to take some time off. I would be so stressed afterwards and worried I would make another mistake because I'm so stressed out and having trouble focusing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So in a strange way, the anxiety and the thoughts you're having now are leaving you more at risk to make a mistake.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean, I guess I never thought about it like that, although that makes a lot of sense. If I just calm down and try to let it go, then I'll do my job better and I won't have that risk as much. But if I keep feeling like this, I'm not focusing and then I could make a bigger mistake because of it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So one of the thoughts you're having now is 'I can't make a mistake because it would be too devastating'. And that thought is leaving you emotionally less prepared and probably at increased risk of making a mistake.
