video_details.title: CBT Role-Play – Complete Session – Low Self-Confidence at Work – Part 8
video_details.description: This video features part eight of a complete cognitive-behavior therapy (CBT) counseling role-play session in which CBT techniques are used to address low self-confidence at work. Part eight includes reframing and exploring beliefs.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yes, you really get where they're coming from. You really understand the suffering involved.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess maybe that's part of where it's so hard for me is like, I know that I'm causing a lot of suffering for people.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, let's talk about that. So you're in a position where you have to make some decisions about people's lives. And sometimes those decisions result in people being separated from their family, sometimes they don't.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you really the cause? In the larger picture, are you really the cause of these families being broken up?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess not, like it's their actions. If they were doing the right things, even if I did come in, their kids wouldn't be removed. But it is still hard to be the one that pulls that trigger, you know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, you're the immediate cause, kind of at the end of the whole process. But the true cause happened years or months before you got there as people made decisions that maybe weren't the best for their children or for themselves.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're really coming in, to some extent, at the tail end of a long series of behavioral choices.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah, that's true.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Ultimately, for this family that you're worried about, looking at it with a long-term lens, do you think the children are better off because they're not with that family right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably. I mean, if they get with a good family, which usually they do, it's good for them. You know, maybe it could be a wake-up call for the parents, or if not, at least the kids are getting their needs met. It's probably really hard for the kids, but overall we wouldn't be doing this if we didn't think it would be best for them to go to a place where they're going to be taken care of.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So immediately there's some pain because you have to break up the family, but in the long run, maybe there's a better result.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Even with that though, let's talk about the concern you have about making a poor decision. Based on what you're describing, do you believe this was actually a poor decision?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess not. It just feels like it is.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, it feels like it is, and it was a tough decision.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mm-hmm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But looking at it in the way that the evidence suggests, maybe you can appreciate that you might have had to do the same thing even if you went back in time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah, I think so. And I'm not sure anybody else would have made a different decision either.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you really did what you had to do.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mm-hmm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But because there's still a pain component there for them, you're feeling torn.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you don't want to go through this again.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I mean, not this feeling, but I do want to keep doing my job.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But doing your job in a world where you could make a mistake, that's not as appealing.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean, I guess I always knew I could make mistakes, but it just feels really real now, I guess is the difference.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So in this particular instance, based on what you're saying, it doesn't seem like a mistake. Let's consider a situation where you did make a mistake.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now that would be the worst case, right? We're just taking things to the worst-case scenario. Your fear here is that, regardless of what already happened, going forward you'd be mortified to make an error.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mm-hmm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Because this pain you're feeling right now is just unbearable, and it's thrown everything into chaos for you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So looking around where you work and the history of your profession, what's a mistake you see people make from time to time that you would be frightened of?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess the biggest mistake you can really make is to miss some form of abuse or something like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And then someone's hurt.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mm-hmm.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play – Complete Session – Low Self-Confidence at Work – Part 7
video_details.description: This video features part seven of a complete cognitive-behavior therapy (CBT) counseling role-play session in which CBT techniques are used to address low self-confidence at work. Part seven includes encouragement and offering alternative ways of thinking.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, this is Dr. Grande. I hope you find this video useful. If that's the case, please like it and subscribe to my channel. And as always, thanks for watching.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I could see these types of decisions where you're talking about potentially breaking families up and having real consequences to families. I could see how these decisions could be, I'm sure there's guidelines you're supposed to follow that you really don't have a whole lot of choice in, but you could also really agonize and over-analyze a decision like that because the consequences are so great. Do you feel like that could be happening?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think so. I mean, you're right to a certain extent we have guidelines and everything like that, but I also feel like certain things, it just isn't black and white and I have to make a judgment call. And I used to trust my judgment, but now I feel like how do I know that I'm making the right decisions?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, well and this is really one of the key parts of what may be causing this distress is that you talked about this insecurity. You're unsure. And so, you know, one question may be, did you make an efficient or less than efficient decision with this particular family? But the larger question is, you as a person, can you do this job? And if you do it and make a mistake, what do you do then? Could you go through this again?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think that's where the fear is, is that if 99 times out of 100 I do it right, there's still going to be that one that I messed up. And I'm starting to feel like that one mistake could be like life-changing for somebody.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And it could be. Yeah, you're certainly in a job where, like most jobs where mistakes have consequences. You also do a lot of good for a lot of people. So by you not being in the field, they're not getting the benefit of the skills you have.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess that's true. Like, yeah maybe somebody else could come in and replace me, but do I think that they would be better at it? I don't know. I feel like I was pretty good at it before I started to have all these doubts.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So mostly this was good until this incident. Well, alright. Let's look at this from another point of view. You really seem like you can empathize with these families. You really, to me, it seems like you really know what they're feeling.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I care about them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And appreciating their perspective, take a moment and try to walk in their shoes. Okay? If a professional like yourself came to you and your family situation and maybe you're engaged in the activities where it was warranted that your family be broken up temporarily, what would you want? How would you want them to process that? Like, so thinking about the caseworker from the point of view of the family, how would you want them to feel about it? How would you want them to process that decision?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. That's a hard question. I mean, if they took my kids away, even if it was the right thing, I would want them to be at least a little bit, you know, feel a little bit bad about having to make such a hard decision. But I guess if they fell apart every time that they made that kind of decision, they wouldn't be able to help other people.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, so from the family's point of view, if you're in that situation, you can appreciate what the caseworker has to do, but you'd like them to have some compassion for you. Okay. That seems reasonable. So now flip back into the role you're in. You made a decision you had to make, although you're second-guessing it. That's separate. Do you have compassion for them?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: For the families that I took? Yeah, I mean, I think that might be the problem is I have too much of it, you know? I worry about how they feel even if maybe taking the kids away was the right thing. It's just like so devastating to lose your kids whether you're doing the right things or not, you know? You want your kids with you. You want to be able to take care of them even if you're not doing a really good job at it.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play – Complete Session – Low Self-Confidence at Work – Part 12
video_details.description: This video features part twelve of a complete cognitive-behavior therapy (CBT) counseling role-play session in which CBT techniques are used to address low self-confidence at work. Part twelve includes scaling, assigning homework, and assessing client strengths.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So now as you kind of take an emotional inventory of your stress and worry and anxiety and you scale it, where would you put yourself now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think it's probably closer to a three now. I'm feeling more hopeful and kind of not feeling, I guess maybe feeling like it's a little bit less of a big deal than I felt like when I came in.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So some of the intimidation of this concern has been relaxed a bit, it's backed off. It's still there. Three's still suffering, but not as much as before and not nearly as much as at the peak.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you think going forward you can apply this self-talk in the morning when that automatic thought comes up? Can we make that kind of the plan?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think that'll be good because then also in the morning I'll remember it's the morning, I'm having these thoughts, I need to do this.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: There are a lot of places we're going to go as we talk about CBT and how it relates to what you're going through. And I don't want to put too much on you at one time, so I'm kind of deliberately not going into a long explanation of the theory and not assigning a lot of homework, but homework is an important part of it. And one that I feel is in the best interest of clients to really take seriously and make a best effort to do. So I'd like that to be one of the, you know if you're okay with it, that'd be one of the homework steps. And the other one, so it'll just be two things for this week, so that self-talk in the morning and the other one was really just starting to cultivate an awareness in the day of when you're having these automatic thoughts. So these automatic thoughts precede feelings and behaviors that you don't like, like feeling worried. So they're a little hard to pick up at first because you're already having the feeling before you even think to think about the thought, if that makes sense. I know there's a few steps in there, but you're already having the feeling of worry, and now I'm asking you to stop in that moment and try to recover the thought that led to that. So that's not an easy request, so that's why I'm starting out with just trying to bring up an awareness of that. If you can, and I think this would be very helpful, the best way is to write it down, if it's safe to do so and you can. So perhaps sometime in the day you find yourself extra worried, and then you think back to what was going through your mind and you find it was worrying about the welfare of that family. Like a thought like 'Oh, they're not doing so well'. Just don't judge the thought, just write it down: 'I was thinking the family might not be doing so well'.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: What should I do with it? Should I like write it on a sticky note and then get rid of it? Should I keep it in a journal or...?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good question. I would say keep it in a journal and bring it in, and to the extent you're comfortable talking about it, we can go over it and we'll try to together develop self-talk to address that thought. So we're going to build an inventory of adaptive responses. Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have any questions or concerns about today and kind of what we talked about?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I mean I think it was really helpful. I just had to remember to, you know, kind of combat things in the morning and then as the day goes by if I notice any other thoughts just write them down and everything. I can do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. I think that would be a great start and we'll set up a time when we're done here for another appointment for next week, we'll get that all situated. But I want to close just by letting you know kind of my impressions from this first session. I know you have worries and I am working on understanding them, with the family and the decision you made and I can certainly appreciate it's a struggle for you. At the same time I see somebody very conscientious, I know you're very concerned about the work you do, you're concerned about the people you interact with, compassionate, empathetic. I see a lot of strength in terms of your ability to understand these concepts I'm talking about and apply them in your life. So I want you to take away from this, I hope you take away from this, that you should be hopeful. I feel like you have a lot of positive characteristics and strengths that you can bring to overcome this struggle and I think you'll be stronger as a result of working to overcome it. Does that resonate with who you, how you think of yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean I think you know I've worked a lot to help other people so I think I probably do have the ability to help myself as well and I also believe that you know if I do the work then in the future when stuff makes me stressed out I might be a little better at handling it, so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, so I hope that you'll be able to overcome what's going on now but also build a skill set that you can use to overcome new challenges because you'll face new ones and I want you to be the most prepared you can be and I feel like even though you have these worries and anxieties I want you to remember you have a lot of strengths and I feel like you can do pretty well with this. All right, so we'll stop there if you're good and we'll set you up for an appointment next week. Thank you Sarah.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thanks.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play – Complete Session – Low Self-Confidence at Work – Part 6
video_details.description: This video features part six of a complete cognitive-behavior therapy (CBT) counseling role-play session in which CBT techniques are used to address low self-confidence at work. Part six includes reframing, exploring logic, and clarifying evidence.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, alright, let's take a step back and talk about competency. What education did you need for the job you have now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have my bachelor's degree. And we got a little bit of training, you know, every so often we get some training at work and stuff like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you evaluated at work by anybody to see if you're doing the job you should be?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I have a supervisor, so they check up on stuff. And also, like, if I feel like I have questions and stuff like that, I can go to them as well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you been found in that system to be somebody who's satisfying requirements in terms of competency? Satisfying the requirements of an employee?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean I haven't been fired, so that's a good sign, I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's a good sign. Yeah, you haven't been fired. Have you ever had any type of write-up or somebody discussing something with you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I just kind of feel like maybe the climate has changed a little bit at the office after this happened. Like maybe other people think I didn't make the right decision. I guess maybe that's part of where all my doubts are coming from. Like no one has said to me, and I haven't... you know, my supervisor hasn't called me in and said, 'I'm concerned about this,' but I just feel like maybe other people think that I did something wrong.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so there's no evidence supporting that in a kind of direct fashion, like a supervisor coming to you, but there's other evidence supporting it based on what you're feeling and how you're maybe perceiving things. You're getting this feeling that by the way they're interacting with you, by the way they're relating to you, that...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, which I guess maybe I shouldn't be that freaked out about because there have been other people who have made mistakes and the supervisors have talked to them, and you know, even then they didn't lose their jobs. So it's not like I have... you know, I don't know, I guess it's not like just hearing them or thinking that they're judging me is an indication that something terrible is gonna happen or that I made this huge mistake.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so you can see that from talking this through, you can see that some of this could be feelings, thoughts you're having combined with what you're actually observing. So you're filtering your observations in a way that's maybe making them seem a little more destructive, a little more negative.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's kind of like I know it's not that big of a deal because like I said, my supervisor hasn't talked to me and it's not like I've heard anything terrible about anything happening to the kids or anything like that, but I just feel like, you know, I have those thoughts like 'Oh, is she saying something? When she said that, was she referring to what happened?' and stuff like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you provide an example of an interaction with a coworker where they said something that you thought maybe was referring back to this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, so like we were having like our regular work meeting and we kind of discuss how things are going, and it's been kind of a big deal, more so than usual, that the kids were removed from this family. So one of my coworkers kind of nudged me and said like, 'Oh, you're the bulldozer, you plowed right through that family and took those kids away.' And I think she meant it kind of like as a joke and just, you know, maybe to say like you did what you needed to do, but it kind of made me feel like does she think that I'm just callous? Like does she think that I just didn't care and... you get what I'm saying?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah, so she referred to you as a bulldozer. And one way to take that would be powerful, efficient, but another way to take that would be kind of destructive, callous, mechanical. They don't have a lot of feeling. So you don't know exactly how she meant it, but you're thinking maybe it was connected that way.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, and I guess it kind of like it goes back to like my fear that I didn't think it through, that I kind of just made the report and that was that. And you know, it makes me feel like was I being mechanical? Did I just... was I just nonchalant about it? Should I have put more thought into it? And it really, you know, it hit me where it hurt, I guess, you know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So her saying that really kind of brought up this thought that maybe you are... maybe you are not empathetic enough or compassionate enough.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, or even just thoughtful. I guess maybe I was just being, you know, just going about my job without putting a lot of thought into what I was doing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Automatic?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Exactly.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So maybe one thing you would have done differently in light of that comment at the time of making the decision, you would have thought through the steps more?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, maybe taken a little bit more time. But at the same time, I mean, I don't have a ton of time, like I've been good at my job, I've been doing things that way, but then it just kind of made me think, have I been missing stuff all along? I don't know.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play – Complete Session – Low Self-Confidence at Work – Part 5
video_details.description: This video features part five of a complete cognitive-behavior therapy (CBT) counseling role-play session in which CBT techniques are used to address low self-confidence at work. Part five includes encouraging, clarifying, eliciting beliefs, and discussing cognitive distortions.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, this is Dr. Grande. I hope you find this video useful. If that's the case, please like it and subscribe to my channel. And as always, thanks for watching.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So can you think of another case you're working on, another family, different than the one that we've initially talked about, where you've made a decision that seemed like it was fairly clear-cut, like one you would have made before, and yet you're thinking about it, replaying it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I have this case recently where it's a single dad, the mom passed away, and I go in and check on him and his son and things are going well. But I think the dad has a hard time, so it's not like it was before when the mom was there. Not that I wasn't there before that, but you can just tell that things are a little different. But obviously my decision is that things are going well for the kid, he's going to stay there, dad is stable, but I just worry, like, is the dad under too much stress? Is he really taking care of the kid as good as, you know, what if he's just cleaning up the house and doing the right things while I'm there? And while I'm not there, does he have the energy to take care of his kid? Is everything really the way it appears, or is there more going on? I just don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so you're handling it to the best of your ability, but there's still these thoughts that are coming up kind of encouraging you to second-guess your judgment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, and it's like I can't let it go. Like I saw them like two weeks ago and I still wonder. And I have other cases like that, it's like they're all running through my head and I have these thoughts, like, did I do the right thing? Can I do the right thing?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And maybe what if the worst happens?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: And I didn't see it? Like what if something terrible happens and I should have known better?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it speaks back to your competency as a professional again. So that seems to be kind of core to this. Several things you talk about seem to connect back to 'Are you capable of being in this field? Should you be trusted?'

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, definitely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So kind of moving back to thinking, there are errors in thinking that all people make. And when these errors become repetitive and you can kind of see them applied in more than one area of somebody's life, we refer to that as a cognitive distortion. It's not bad or good, it's just how people think, it's just patterns that people fall into. And there are several different cognitive distortions, there's several patterns that we kind of see come up often in this work as a counselor. I'm wondering in the situation where you're thinking the worst possible outcome is unbearable or likely or both, if you may be really focusing and emphasizing on that to the exclusion of other evidence that suggests you've made a good decision. So you're really focused on the negative outcome, the worst possible and maybe even unlikely outcome, and maybe not weighing all the evidence with the same weight, like you're putting more weight on the negative. Does that kind of make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean, I think that that's probably true because before I felt fine and now I just feel like everything's falling apart and not that much has changed. And so it kind of makes me think that that's probably what's going on, but I don't know how to change that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This is frustrating for you. This self-doubt and this worry.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play – Complete Session – Low Self-Confidence at Work – Part 4
video_details.description: This video features part four of a complete cognitive-behavior therapy (CBT) counseling role-play session in which CBT techniques are used to address low self-confidence at work. Part four includes creating distance between thoughts and feelings, analysis of thinking, and reframing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would you be okay now kind of taking a look at some of your thinking and look at the situation from that point of view? Some things kind of stand out for me in hearing you talk about what's been happening and your feelings. I can appreciate it's really painful and I would say to the degree that you can step back and try to look at the thoughts, I think that you'll see it's helpful. Although I know it's a little difficult or unusual to separate feelings from thoughts sometimes. But I'd like to try to kind of distinguish between the two.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You said that you've been at your job for about five years. You really like your job.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm. I used to, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me about your job, like kind of how you felt about it, but frame it in a time before this ever happened.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I like my job because I felt like I was helping people, so it was meaningful. And, you know, when I went there, the time went by fast, so it was kind of like I was enjoying myself, you know, not super fast, I wasn't having the best time of my life, but it was something where I would go and, you know, I felt like I was doing something important and the day didn't drag on and, you know, I got along with my coworkers and that kind of thing. So it felt meaningful to me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Meaningful. So do you remember accomplishing things at that job that you felt benefited society, the people you help?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I feel like, you know, doing my job, I got to know people, you know, help people out with things that they needed. You know, when things were bad, I could, you know, get kids out of situations that were really dangerous for them and, you know, no one else was going to do that for them. So I felt like I was the kind of person that was making, keeping people safe, I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You kept people safe. And you had a lot of satisfaction from the work you did. And now, doesn't feel that way?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, not at all.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The way you described it, it almost sounds like you're—well, you did, you talked about how you're afraid of making that mistake. You're thinking about yourself in a way where you're almost a risk to—

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I was just about to say, it feels dangerous to be there, like to do my job, it feels dangerous.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Your work right now, even though you have this one situation that's extremely stressful and hard on you, you have other families that you interact with now, too, right? Can you tell me about those interactions?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, I guess it's like quantitatively the same as before. I do the same things with families, but now I kind of feel like I can't trust my own judgment. Like everything—before everything just kind of felt a little more black and white, and now it just feels like everything is so much a shade of grey that I just can't tell, you know, what's right and what's wrong anymore. And every time I feel like I have a good instinct, I doubt it, I question it. I have all these ideas of, well, you know, if I remove the kids from this family, what if they're not really doing the things I think they're doing? Like what if the parents are actually good parents? What if the kids get put into a home that's bad for them?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So before, so this is maybe what's different based on what you're saying from before till now, is decisions seemed clear-cut.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, sometimes it was tougher than others, but it just seemed more like I could make a decision and kind of wipe my hands of it and, you know, move on to the next thing. And now I just feel like there's all these doubts in my head and all these questions about if I'm doing the right thing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So you're looking inward, you're looking at yourself, a lot of self-doubt, right? You're looking at decisions as much more difficult. It's much more difficult to come to the right decision. And second-guessing—it sounds like maybe you're second-guessing a bit when you do make a decision, like playing over and over in your mind what could go wrong here. Is that the thought you're having?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah, definitely. I feel like I'm second-guessing everything.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play – Complete Session – Low Self-Confidence at Work – Part 3
video_details.description: This video features part three of a complete cognitive-behavior therapy (CBT) counseling role-play session in which CBT techniques are used to address low self-confidence at work. Part three includes identifying automatic thoughts and scaling.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, this is Dr. Grande. I hope you find this video useful. If that's the case, please like it and subscribe to my channel. And as always, thanks for watching.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you mentioned before that when you wake up in the morning, you don't want to go to work. What's going through your mind?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm going to have to hear what my coworkers have to say about what's going on, I might make another mistake, who knows if I'm going to find out that something terrible happened to these kids when I go back to work. I guess a lot of stuff like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, so looking at the one 'I'm going to make a mistake,' this kind of connects to what we were talking about before. This is the uncertainty, you're not sure of your own skills. And you're afraid of an error that's going to be costly. So when you think that thought, 'I'm going to make a mistake,' this is when you're in bed before you start your day and you have that thought, what happens right then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel more anxious. I think about what could happen to somebody else if I make a mistake, like kids going to the wrong home or not being with their parents when their parents weren't doing anything wrong. I just feel really overwhelmed and it gets hard to breathe, and I just want to go back to sleep and not have to face anything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, so there's the emotional consequence and then the behavior is you don't want to get out of bed.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've been late a lot more lately because I have trouble getting out of bed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now when you're staying in bed, are there more thoughts coming up?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean if I don't go back to sleep then I have more thoughts like, well I need to go to work, if I don't go to work then I'm going to be late, then people are going to notice me and they're going to be thinking about what happened and thinking there's something wrong with me and that she's not good enough to do her job. I don't want people to know how stressed out I am because then they're going to doubt my abilities just like I do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, so this is really weighing on you. And you've identified these thoughts that seem to be connected with feelings that are unpleasant and behaviors that are unpleasant but also maybe not useful, right? They're impeding...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, they're keeping me from getting to work and stuff like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So we have a reference point for later on as we continue counseling, I'd like to scale this problem, like maybe on a scale of one to ten, where ten represents feelings that are nearly unbearable, and one not really a problem. How do you feel on that scale? Where do you rate yourself right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right now in this moment probably like a five.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's right around the middle.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, like I'm really stressed out but I'm not like when I'm in bed, like I can't get out of bed that kind of thing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How would you rate yourself when you're in bed before you go to work?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably like an eight.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And is that as bad as it gets?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: With this feeling, it's about as bad as it gets, maybe sometimes it gets to a nine. You know, I still feel like I can function, but it's really, really difficult.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, so an eight, sometimes a nine, and right now a five. So still not feeling great. And if you had to pick an emotion that was standing out above the rest in the anxiety, sadness, sense of dread, what would be the worst right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right now probably anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So a five on a scale of one to ten, and anxiety is really standing out more.

video_details.title: Conducting a Quick Screen for Trauma - Child Interview
video_details.description:
These videos are meant for educational purposes, and the scenarios are played by actors, and developed by CAMH staff.

For more information on trauma and children, as well as screening and assessment visit the toolkit website: https://www.camh.ca/en/science-and-research/institutes-and-centres/cundill-centre-for-child-and-youth-depression/childhood-trauma-toolkit

You can see the video on conducting a quick screening interview with a parent at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bxbSsK5D_PY

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Asking children about potential traumas is essential as adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) significantly impact lifelong health. Dr. Lawson previously assessed 10-year-old Sam's ACE score as three based on his mother's report. Now, she interviews Sam alone to confirm these findings.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Sam, thanks for waiting. I talked to your mom about things at home and school. Now I'm going to ask you some screening questions I ask all kids. Feel free to ask me anything as we talk, okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: First, how have things been going at home?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How's your mom doing? Is there ever a time where she isn't able to get out of bed or do what she needs to do?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, she's looking after me most of the time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What does most of the time mean? Is there anything she could do better?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe getting dinner, because sometimes I just have to get a bowl of Cheerios for myself.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How many times a week are you having Cheerios for dinner? Is your mom with you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Pretty much every day, and I'm mainly by myself.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there enough food in the fridge? Have you been worried about it, or about having a winter coat and boots?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. My mom says we'll go shopping, but we never do because she's too busy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are there times your mom seems down or upset for days at a time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: She might be a little stressed because of Grandma. They've been arguing and yelling a lot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me more about that. Have you ever been afraid someone might get hurt?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They argue about things. I just go to my room. Once, maybe, I was afraid because they were getting really mean.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How intense does it get? Has anybody been physical, used fists, or thrown objects? Where are you during this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I just go to my room and try to ignore it. Afterwards, they just stay away from each other for a while.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has anyone ever said mean or hurtful things to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes my grandma criticizes me and won't help me with what I'm doing wrong.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What about your mom? Also, has anyone ever touched your body in an inappropriate or sexual way?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not that I know. And no to the other thing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does anyone hit or spank you, or hurt your body physically?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there any drug or alcohol use in your home that worries you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How do you feel in your close relationships? Do you feel loved and cared about?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My mom pays more attention to my little brother. When I want something, she doesn't really listen and won't really ask me later.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there any adult you feel loved by or would go to for help?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I like to be in my room. I wouldn't have anybody. I just go to my room and think.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has anyone been in jail? What are the main stressors at home?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. The stressors are the fighting with Grandma and my dad moving away because they got divorced.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you see your dad? When was the last time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, not since a year ago. There's no plan to see him.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I hear that there are stressors like the arguing, your dad moving away, and not always feeling loved. Do you think that makes school hard?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think so. I'm thinking about that instead of what I'm doing, so I don't get a lot done.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That makes sense. When things are stressful at home, kids have trouble concentrating. I'll talk to your mom and figure out how to help you both. Thanks for coming in.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sam's interview confirms his ACE score is three due to parental loss, physical neglect, and emotional deprivation. Dr. Lawson can now collaboratively develop an evidence-based intervention plan to help change Sam's lifetime health trajectory.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play – Complete Session – Low Self-Confidence at Work – Part 2
video_details.description: This video features part two of a complete cognitive-behavior therapy (CBT) counseling role-play session in which CBT techniques are used to address low self-confidence at work. Part two includes reflection, clarification, evaluating evidence, and eliciting automatic thoughts.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi this is Dr. Grande. I hope you find this video useful. If that's the case, please like it and subscribe to my channel. And as always, thanks for watching.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has it made you rethink your entire job and the profession you're in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean, it's making me think like, you know, if I just had some desk job, like if I just crunched numbers or something, I would never have to have this responsibility. Why would they trust me with a job like this? I'm just a human being who doesn't know any better than any other person and I just don't know if I can do this. Before I felt like I could handle it and now I just feel like it's so much responsibility for one person. I don't want to change jobs because I've been here for so long and I liked it before, but I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're fearful of this happening again, and how you may handle it, and what may happen.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I feel like it's just around the corner. And this isn't even resolved. I'm still afraid of the consequences of this. What if these kids are out of their parents' home and something bad happens to them where they are now? That's going to fall on me. My coworkers know that I'm the one that did this. So if something happens to the kids, I'm going to be the one they blame for it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So just to make sure I understand, they were engaging in these behaviors and your report is what precipitated them being broken up?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, because before that, probably nobody else would have known about it. So I made the report about what was going on and I think yeah, it was a direct result.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, let's take a look at the evidence. In CBT we like to evaluate evidence and look at the facts as we understand them. We want to scrutinize and carefully review the facts and hold a light to it to figure out what's going on. What would have happened with this family if no one intervened?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. It wasn't going great for the kids, it wasn't a great environment, but I just feel like if I had left it alone, the kids would be with their parents.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, so they'd all be together and you feel like right now them being apart is not as good as if they were together.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean, I guess I feel like it probably wasn't great for them to be there, that's why I made the report, that's my job. But it just feels like I'm playing God. That I'm just coming in here and spending five, ten minutes with a family and then turning their whole world upside down.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you have a tremendous amount of power. And if you misuse that power you could devastate families. And that's maybe what you think happened here.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, mhm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so going back to what would have happened to them. They would still be together without your intervention and that could be a positive. What about consequences that may be more negative?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, like I said, I thought they were using drugs in the home, so that's a really dangerous situation for kids. You don't know what kind of people are coming in and out of the home, if the parents are going to be coherent enough to help them if there's an emergency, or if the parents are even making them food and taking care of their needs. In that sense that's really concerning and that's a big part of why I made the report.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you made the report because it's your responsibility, but also you had concerns about their welfare. If you could go back and do it again, would you change anything?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, I guess that's just the hardest part for me is I feel like I can't make the right decision. I just don't know if I'm equipped to be the person to make that kind of decision.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you don't know if you made a good decision or not, and further you question your ability going forward to make decisions. And that's the uncertainty and anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, definitely. Mhm.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play – Complete Session – Low Self-Confidence at Work – Part 1
video_details.description: This video features part one of a complete cognitive-behavior therapy (CBT) counseling role-play session in which CBT techniques are used to address low self-confidence at work. Part one includes discussion of the problem and setting the agenda.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, this is Dr. Grande. I hope you find this video useful. If that's the case, please like it and subscribe to my channel. And as always, thanks for watching.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello Sarah, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm alright.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Doing alright? I understand that you've come to counseling because you have a particular issue that's been bothering you recently.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I've been really stressed out at work. I'm getting to the point where it's really hard to handle things that are going on.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So work-related problems? Are you okay talking about that today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm. I think I need to, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. I'd like to set a plan for our meeting today to give us some structure. I want to co-create this with you, so your input is valuable. I want you to be an active part of this.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'd like to start by having you explain in depth what you're going through at work. Then I'll look for patterns in your thinking. Finally, we can discuss things you can do between sessions to feel better. Does that seem straightforward?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Mhm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any changes or anything you'd like to make to that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I think as long as you think I can tell my whole story in enough time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me what's going on as you feel comfortable, and don't worry about the agenda. But just know that overall that's the structure. Let's get started. Tell me about your job.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm a caseworker and I usually go into homes to talk to families and do inspections. I've been doing it for about five years and I like it, but something happened recently that makes me feel out of control.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I made a report about a family where I felt the children were malnourished and the house was unclean. I suspected drug use and it was not a good environment. The kids were taken away and I'm really freaked out.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Even though it wasn't a great environment, I know those kids love their parents, and it's really weighing on me. It's become a big issue at work, and I feel like I tore that family apart. I'm second-guessing everything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This is really stressful on you. So, you like your job, but this situation has really thrown you for a loop?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's making me not like my job. I wake up wanting to pretend I'm sick, I'm more stressed at night, and I feel on edge all the time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's drastically changed your work experience?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I used to enjoy going to work and feel fulfilled, and now I just feel like I do not want to go at all.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there's a sense of dread and anxiety. Do you feel down at all?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, definitely. On weekends I want to stay in bed. I'll be having a good time and then remember what happened and it brings me back to that place. I don't like it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's not a good feeling.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

video_details.title: Linehan DBT with Suicidal Clients Video
video_details.description:
For the full video, go to: http://www.psychotherapy.net/video/dbt-suicidal-clients-linehan

Watch Dialectical Behavior Therapy creator, Marsha Linehan, do DBT therapy with a suicidal and self-harming client

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Between here and there, obviously if it were easy you wouldn't need me. You wouldn't have had 13 therapists. If this were easy, you would have been to a life you wanted a long time ago. So it's obvious that if it were easy, it'd already be done, because it sounds like you're a person with a lot of motivation who works really hard because there are very few people who wouldn't have quit before 13 therapists. So that's a very good quality. The very fact that you've gone through all these therapists is a good sign for us. Nonetheless, it is difficult. Between here and there, there's going to be hell.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Exactly.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So I figure our number one priority has to be to get you to stay alive through hell so that we can get to the life you want. And that's where we're at now. So we gotta have some sort of agreement. Not by writing a contract or because I'll fire you if you try to kill yourself, but because we both sort of have to face the fact that to get there you've gotta go through there, and to go through there you've gotta stay alive.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, I'll make you a deal.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, what?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You guarantee that you can help me and I'll guarantee I won't kill myself.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What are you going to do if I fail? If I break my promise?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, then all bets are off. Okay, that's... I mean that can be the deal.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So if I don't help you, you'll kill yourself.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, but if I do help you, you won't.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think so. Yeah, I mean yes, if you can help me, no, I won't kill myself.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, and how long you gonna give me to try?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I don't know.

video_details.title: Marsha Linehan DBT with Suicidal Clients Video
video_details.description:
To see the full video go to: http://www.psychotherapy.net/video/dbt-suicidal-clients-linehan

Watch Dialectical Behavior Therapy creator, Marsha Linehan, do DBT therapy with a suicidal client.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, let's talk about then how you ended up cutting yourself.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's pretty obvious.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what happened? First of all, tell me what you did exactly.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: What do you mean what I did?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I mean where'd you cut yourself? I know you said you cut yourself, but I mean where?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Same as always. Same as always.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: On your arm?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What'd you cut yourself with?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A razor.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How deep?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Do you want to see it?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. Let me see. You know, those look to me like they did - did you go to the - it doesn't look like you went and got any stitches, but that looks to me like you could have used them. What do you think?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think if you've ever been to an ER when you cut yourself, you'll know why I don't go.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, but part of the problem is those look deep and like you're going to have significant scars. So my suggestion is in the future if you do it, is that you put some sort of band-aid on it to keep it closed. But let's talk about how - how this happened. First of all, tell me, you were telling me on the phone that you wanted to die, but did you - was this a suicide attempt or do you think it was just a cutting? Were you thinking about killing yourself or wanting to die when you did it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was thinking about killing myself. I thought you would help me and you didn't. That's what I want to talk about. I want to talk about how it is that my life is not going better and you are not helping me and you are not available to me when I need help.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so let's - okay. So it sounds like me not being available - was me not being available to you related to you cutting yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I cut myself the first time. I called you thinking you would help me. You wouldn't help me, so then I figured what the hell, I might as well just go all the way, and so that's why I cut myself that deep.

video_details.title: Conducting a Quick Screen for Trauma - Parent Interview
video_details.description:
These videos are meant for educational purposes, and the scenarios are played by actors, and developed by CAMH staff.

For more information on trauma and children, as well as screening and assessment visit the toolkit website: https://www.camh.ca/en/science-and-research/institutes-and-centres/cundill-centre-for-child-and-youth-depression/childhood-trauma-toolkit

To see the video about interviewing a child, please visit https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rKTYOAI65zE&t=4s

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Many clinicians can have a lot of uncertainty about the best way to ask about and screen for childhood traumas or adverse childhood experiences. This video models how a clinician can ask about these things in a structured and evidence-based way, even in the context of a routine clinical appointment. The questionnaire being used is called the ACE, or the Adverse Childhood Experiences Questionnaire. It's a 10-item tool that asks about childhood experiences such as sexual, physical, or verbal abuse, physical neglect, and emotional deprivation. It also asks if a child has experienced parent loss due to incarceration or divorce, major mental illness or substance use in a parent, and domestic violence. For each endorsed item, the child gets one point, called their ACE score. We screen for these because a large body of literature links these events with long-term serious physical and mental health outcomes. Higher scores increase the risk of cardiovascular disease, stroke, diabetes, depression, substance use, and suicide. In the following scenario, Dr. Lawson meets with 10-year-old Sam and his mom, Dana. She's about to wrap up a routine checkup when Sam's mom raises concerns about his behavior at school and home. So, Sam's healthy other than some seasonal allergies, and everything else okay then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Actually, not quite. Between last school year and this year, I'm suddenly getting phone calls from his teacher saying he's not paying attention. They think he has ADHD all of a sudden. This is not the same kid I had a year ago.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like there's more going on. Perhaps we can take a few minutes to chat, and then I'll spend a few minutes with Sam. Sam, do you want to hang out in the waiting room for a bit?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Go ahead, honey.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So tell me about Sam and the issues he's having at school.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He's like a totally different kid. I'm getting calls multiple times a week about him acting out, having angry spurts, and not doing homework. His grades are slipping from 90s to 60s.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This feels like a real change from last year.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh totally, like night and day.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like there have been some problems at home. I'm going to ask you some screening questions I ask all parents. It'll take about five minutes. Why don't we start with how you're doing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm getting by. Daryl and I got divorced last year. He's somewhere out in BC, only knows where.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is Sam seeing him at all?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They Skype maybe once every couple months, but he's not really in contact or sending the child support he promised. So, I'm not thrilled with him right now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has that meant that finances have been tight?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, things are tight. My mother also moved in with me recently. She's starting to get dementia. I decided to take her in rather than put her in a home.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Lots of changes going on. How do you feel like you're managing with all of that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Some days are better than others. I'm not getting enough sleep and things are tight financially.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Emotionally, how have you been doing and managing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's very stressful when my mother has an episode or I get a call from school, but I don't think I'm depressed or anything. It's just a day-to-day thing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are there ever times where you're not able to get out of bed or do the things you need to do?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I sleep in some mornings, but I still get everything done that I need to. I don't feel like it's going to be hopeless forever.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you ever cope with using drugs or alcohol?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. My mother used to drink, so I try to be very aware of not using that as a crutch.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So then no drinking or drugs at home at all?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: None of either.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What about making sure the children have what they need, like winter coats or food?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm doing the best I can. We haven't gone winter coat shopping yet. Sam's from last year still kind of fits, so that's the solution for now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have a sense if that's hard because of finances or other reasons?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mostly finances, but time too. It's a big ordeal to get everyone out to go shopping. We didn't pick up everything he wanted for back to school either. It would be easier if I had more money and hours.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So Sam is not always having the things he needs right now. What about food?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess not exactly, no. But we have a bulk food store membership, so I let Sam pick out things he likes, like macaroni, sandwiches, or cereal. There is always something for him to eat.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what kinds of things does Sam have for dinner?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He'll do macaroni, or sometimes snack food, or more comprehensive meals.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is he cooking, or are you cooking, or both?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's a mix. I can get dinner together a couple nights a week, or we'll order pizza, but I just don't have time to cook.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: With all this stress, has anyone gotten really upset with Sam, yelled, or said mean things to him?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really. My mother has always been judgmental, and she gets mouthy with her dementia. She'll sort of go off on him, but I do the best I can to let him know he's loved and it's not his fault.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how is discipline handled? Has anybody ever spanked or hit Sam?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, never. I used to give him time-outs, but I don't actually have time to discipline him now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What about sexual abuse? Has anyone touched Sam in an inappropriate way?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Excuse me?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I ask everybody that question, as it's hard to hear. Has it ever happened?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, never. I would never let that happen to my child.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. How do you think Sam's doing in his family relationships? Does he feel loved and supported?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I haven't been around for him as much as I'd like. I've heard him mouth off and say I love the baby more, but that's obviously not true.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you think he would say if I asked him if he felt loved?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd hope he'd say yes. But I guess sometimes I'm not doing enough for him.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You mentioned difficulties with your mom. Can you tell me more about what's happening with her in the home?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: She has good days and bad days with her dementia. She is very judgmental and opinionated.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has she ever become physically aggressive in the home?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, never.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how are you managing together?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I try to check her behavior when she gets too mouthy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has it ever come to physical blows between you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, just arguments here and there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How intense do those arguments get?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We raise our voices. I'm doing the best I can here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And it's never come to physical blows?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, never. I'd have to take other action if that happened.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is the intensity yelling, screaming, or throwing objects?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We've gotten pretty loud. She'll slam things in her room. I'd never let her hurt the kids.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Where are Sam and the baby when these things are happening?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sam usually goes and hides in his room with his music up. To be honest, I do lose my patience and scream more than I'd like.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How often would you say this yelling and arguing happens?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess like a few times a week.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has anyone in your family ever been in prison or jail?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, never.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you for sharing all of that. To recap, there have been a lot of stressors over the last year. Sam's dad moving away created financial changes, meaning Sam hasn't always had the food or clothing needed. Your mom moving in has caused stress and tension. These factors may have contributed to Sam not feeling as loved or cared for. On the other hand, you're managing emotionally, not using drugs or alcohol, and there are no concerns about physical or sexual abuse or incarceration. I think there is likely a connection between Sam's difficulties at school and these changes at home. I'm going to book a follow-up appointment for you and Sam to develop a plan together.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sounds good, thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Make sure to make an appointment on your way out.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: And you said you wanted to see Sam for a bit as well?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yes, I'm going to see Sam right now. When I'm done, just talk to reception.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: All right. Thanks, Dr. Lawson.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Based on this interview, Sam's ACE score is three, due to parent loss, physical neglect, and emotional deprivation. His score might even be higher if we investigate verbal abuse or domestic violence further. If abuse was reported, I would have to contact child protective services. Even with a score of three, Sam is at an elevated risk for physical and mental health issues. This screen is an effective first step to assess childhood trauma and develop an evidence-based plan of care.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play - The Premack Principle with Weight Loss
video_details.description: This video features a cognitive-behavioral therapy counseling role-play in which the Premack principle is applied to address a weight loss goal. The Premack principle states that a high probability behavior can be used to increase participation in a low probability behavior.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well Kathy, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You okay? I know when we spoke last time, you had some goals that you wanted to talk about this time. You ready to do that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I need to, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you have in mind?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just keep thinking about losing this weight and I just, I really want to do it and I just can't get there and I don't know why.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're frustrated.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's so ridiculous. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Frustrated trying to lose the weight. Now you had said before that you had a specific number of pounds in mind. Do you still have that in mind?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would like 20 pounds. I've tried to do more in the past and I don't even get past a couple of days, so if I can do 20, that would be great.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. And you've tried before, and what do you think got in the way?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. I guess it wasn't convenient. I want to do it and it means a lot for me and my family. I think I'd be a lot healthier.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's important to you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. But just like something always gets in the way, and then I lose focus. I'm not very good at staying focused on stuff like that anyway.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Loss of focus. So you start trying to lose the weight and your focus gets disrupted.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: And I forget and then I make spaghetti casserole for six people and then I eat a lot of it. I'll eat what my kids don't eat and then it's just like I forget that I'm supposed to be making healthy choices.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so you know how to lose weight and you know you can lose weight, but your focus is a little off when you're trying and that's causing the problem.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think so. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Could we break that goal of losing 20 pounds down into smaller units? Like say five pounds.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe. I always just keep the chunk of weight ahead of me. I don't break it into smaller increments. That might work. I don't know how I'd have to stay on top of it though, weighing myself every day.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that something you could do?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm so busy, I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Or once a week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I could probably do once a week. Put a sticky note somewhere or something. I'm going to say yes because I want to try it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you mentioned the loss of focus is one problem. How about motivation? Do you feel motivated to move through all those steps, like five pounds at a time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right now, yes. I think I would need something to keep me going week to week.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A little bit of something extra to help you stay motivated.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, like when you give a kid a special treat for dessert when they do their homework early. That helps keep it going.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So some sort of activity or item that you enjoy that you could reserve for when you reach that goal, say the first five pounds.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. I've been so embarrassed lately, so if I can find something that keeps me motivated, that would be great.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Do you have an activity or item in mind that we could put in place as a reward for yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like after the first five pounds?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, we could do that, or it could be for something you do every day if that day you're successful. What do you think would motivate you more?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe something every day? So I remember. I get so distracted, so if there was a goal at the end of the day or something if I made the right choices.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, so each day you're aware when the day comes to a close if you had a successful day or a less than successful day.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And if you have a successful day, then you could engage in an activity or receive an item that we work out in advance.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. That could be watching a favorite TV show. I don't watch TV at night because I'm so busy, so maybe I could just take some time for myself and watch a show.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So let's do that. By what time would you know in the evening if the day was successful?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably as I'm preparing dinner. If I prepare a good dinner or avoid eating the fun food I make for my kids, I would know maybe by six or seven.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, let's say seven. By 7:00 PM you're aware if you met your goal, and at that point you would have a TV show that you would watch.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And if you're not as successful, you wouldn't. It'd be like something to keep you motivated throughout the day.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. It'd be a lot of fun.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you think that behavioral strategy would give you enough motivation to have successful days through this process?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, but it would probably beat the way I feel right now. I'm willing to try anything. I'll write it down and have a note in the kitchen to check in at 7:00 PM.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, and you could also track it. We can look at those different patterns and add levels to this plan. But for now, we'll go with the TV show after 7:00.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. So that's leading up to the five pounds.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. We take this in five pound increments four times to get to your goal of 20 pounds.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does that sound good?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So far so good, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We'll give that a shot. Record everything around seven each day and bring that in. I'll see you again in a week and we'll reevaluate.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So I could start tonight.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Start tonight. We'll give that a shot and I'll see you in a week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Thanks.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks Kathy.

video_details.title: Demonstration of Beginning a Counselling Session

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now I will show you a video in which the initial contact with a client is being made.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Neha, good morning. Are you comfortable? Please sit down. Did you want to speak with me about something?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. About my school.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: About school? Tell me, how are your studies going?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's going well. I like the school and I like studying.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You like studying? Do you like all your subjects? Which ones do you study?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I like Social Studies more, and also Hindi.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you like those two. Are there any subjects you don't like as much, or like less?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Math and Science.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Math and Science? Why is that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't understand them well and they feel very strange to me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: They feel strange and you don't understand them. In what way? Tell me more.

diarization.speaker: Patient
