diarization.text: The formulas... I don't understand why they are what they are.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You don't understand the formulas? What else? What about Science?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: In Science, it's about why and how things are made. It's difficult for me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But you like Social Studies and Hindi. How are your grades in those?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They are good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good grades? Do you remember the material easily? Have you tried getting help with Science?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I go to my teachers during my free time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do they help clear things up? Why is it that you don't remember it later?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I forget. I try to recall what the teacher said, but I can't seem to bring it back to mind.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It doesn't come back. Have you mentioned this struggle to your teacher?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You haven't? Would you like to learn how to remember things better? What have you tried so far?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I try reading and understanding, but it just doesn't sink into my mind.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It doesn't sink in. Why do you think that happens?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What exactly is your approach when you try?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I try to study when I have time, trying to understand why and how, but it's still not working.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: On your own? Do you feel like you simply won't be able to do it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You feel that 'I can't do this'? Have you discussed this with other students?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Never discussed it? But you get great marks in Hindi and Social Science. Do you participate in class?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How much time do you spend on each subject, including the ones you find difficult?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I spend about four hours daily, one hour for each subject. If I miss a day, I catch up the next.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I see. And what do you do during that hour for Math? Tell me.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I try to understand the questions the teacher solved, then I try new ones.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I see.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I manage some, but for others, I ask the teacher. I practice, but clarity still doesn't come.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you think? Do you feel other girls in your class can do it while you can't?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Some are like me and struggle as well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And the ones who are good at it? Have you talked to them about how they understand it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They take tuitions and they just seem to understand things much faster.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Did they tell you that, or is it just your observation?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's what I've seen with my friend.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Why do you think you don't understand as quickly? Do you think you lack a 'math brain'?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you really think that? Has anyone else ever told you that you aren't capable?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, never.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Teachers haven't discouraged you? So you feel they're better because of tuitions and you aren't?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, that's it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You saw that the counselor was comforting and welcoming. This initial rapport formation helps the client reflect on their problems clearly.

video_details.title: Appraisal Role-Play - Communicating Assessment Results to a Client with Paranoia - SCL-90-R
video_details.description: This video features a counseling appraisal role-play in which communicating the results of an assessment to a client with paranoia is demonstrated. The assessment in this example is the Symptom Checklist 90 Revised (SCL-90-R).

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, this is Dr. Grande. I hope you find this video useful. If that's the case, please like it and subscribe to my channel. And as always, thanks for watching.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello Peggy, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hi Dr. Grande, I'm okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm glad to hear that. Yesterday when you were here, you took a few different tests. One was the Symptom Checklist 90, or SCL-90. Do you remember that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think so. True and false questions?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: They're numbers that you select. I have the results and I want to review some of those findings with you. Is that all right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This instrument measures areas like depression or anxiety. I'm going to review sub-scales where you scored higher than expected and we can talk about it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, are you recording this?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm not. Are you worried about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I think you probably are, because it happens to me a lot. I think I was recorded while taking the test yesterday.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That sounds worrisome. You're certain that's happening? You're not being recorded now, though I know it feels like it. I appreciate you bringing up that concern.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I need to explain the concept of percentile rank. If you have a rank of 65, your score is equal to or higher than 65 percent of people who took the test. Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think so, in school.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: On the phobic anxiety scale, you were at the 64th percentile, which is higher than what we normally see in outpatient mental health treatment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So I have more phobic anxiety than most people.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It seems that way. This measures fears of crowds or going out. Does that seem like a fear you have?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I don't like crowds or public transportation; they make me nervous. If I have to speak in public, I feel like I'm going to pass out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That score makes sense then. On the paranoia sub-scale, you were at the 84th percentile, which is quite a bit higher.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Is that where you were recording me? Are you going to share those results? If the government asked, you'd have to give them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Nothing was recorded here. Results are only shared with the treatment team or if you sign a release. I wouldn't share this with the government. Are you worried about results getting to others?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm worried that I know people are recording me, and the test makes it look like I have a problem when I'm just reporting what I know is true. It says I'm wrong to think that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you feel the test makes you look paranoid for something you believe is true? That would explain the elevated score. Do you think the test could be measuring something that is actually there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I don't think so. I'm higher than 84 percent of the population because those people just think it's happening, while I know it is.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The last sub-scale is psychoticism, where you were at the 93rd percentile. This is when people hear or see things others don't, or have outside-the-norm beliefs. Does that feel like you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Are you going to put me away?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No, this is just to inform our treatment. We'll provide care based on these results.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes I hear things other people don't hear. Maybe that part is true.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Finally, the Global Severity Index gives a big picture of how you're doing. You were at the 68th percentile. Do you feel like you're dealing with symptoms okay overall?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't like to go out much, and it frustrates me when I hear things others don't. But if the paranoia score shouldn't be high, I might be closer to normal than you think.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So if adjusted for your view on paranoia, your global severity might be lower, closer to the 50th percentile. We still want to deliver treatment to address the symptoms. Is that okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It is. The counselor isn't going to record our session, is she?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: She won't. I'll explain your feedback to her and she'll have your results. Does this all make sense? I appreciate you going over this with me.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It does. Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks, Peggy. We'll get you assigned and move forward with treatment.

video_details.title: Appraisal Role-Play - Communicating Assessment Results to a Client - SASSI
video_details.description: This video features a counseling appraisal role-play in which communicating the results of an assessment is demonstrated. The assessment in this example is the Substance Abuse Subtle Screening Inventory (SASSI).

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, this is Dr. Grande. I hope you find this video useful. If that's the case, please like it and subscribe to my channel.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Kathy, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm okay. How are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing fine. I have the results of one of your assessments and I wanted to share those with you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, okay. I didn't know it would be that fast, but go ahead.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The instrument, the SASSI, is designed to assess the probability that you may have some difficulty with substances.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Looking at the results, there are a few areas where I'm a little concerned. Does this surprise you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just feel you can never trust tests, but I'm willing to hear what you have to say.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You scored higher than expected for alcohol and drug concerns. Do you understand the concept of a percentile?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A 75th percentile means your score is greater than or equal to 75% of the population.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like growth charts for kids? Okay, got it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: With that in mind, you were in the 99th percentile for alcohol and drug concerns.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess we have to talk about it. That number is pretty high and embarrassing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You also scored in the 98th percentile for putting other people's needs in front of your own.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, every day. I'm divorced and exhausted, but I make it work for my kids.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That sacrifice is reflected in the score. It's a wonderful attribute but can hold you back when coping with substance issues.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: There's also an area indicating a higher potential for random answering. Did you just randomly select true or false?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I think I was pretty honest.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You responded true to 'Nearly everyone enjoys being picked on' and false to 'Most people laugh at jokes.'

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think I just misread them. I was frustrated and don't like taking tests.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you think was going on there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm embarrassed to be here and missing time with my family. If the test says something is wrong, how can I still be there for them?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Putting the results aside, do you feel like you have a problem with alcohol or drugs?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. It started with the divorce. Alcohol helps me calm down and sleep, but I've even forgotten to pick the kids up a couple times.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about the drug use?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I take my son's Adderall throughout the day to stay elevated when I have low energy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you prescribed Adderall or using any other substances?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. Sometimes we'll use cocaine socially with friends, but that's just for fun.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We treat these problems here. Would you like to receive treatment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, but what does that entail? Does it mean I can't go home?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It would likely be an intensive outpatient program for several hours a day. It matches the symptoms you're presenting with.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Does this mean I lose custody of my kids?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I don't have a say in that. We'll discuss confidentiality before we finalize the schedule. Do you feel comfortable moving forward?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess it's time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'll go get the schedules for the program and we can discuss the next steps.

video_details.title: Suicide Assessment Role-Play - Relationship Stressors
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play session that demonstrates a suicide assessment of a client (played by an actress) who presents with recent relationship stressors.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello Ashley.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hey.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I understand you've been having some difficulties today.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'm just having a really hard time right now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I am. What's going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's just a lot of stuff. I just found out that my husband has cancer, and it's really hard to deal with because our relationship has not been very good, and everybody's expecting me to just keep everything together. I already have my own stuff to deal with my depression, and I don't know how I'm going to do it. I don't know how I'm supposed to pick us up and bring us through this.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you just found this out?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. It's horrible.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So this whole situation has you overwhelmed?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'm just feeling like I don't even know which way to go. It's like, what's the point? You know what I mean? It's too much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's the point of...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just any of it. It's just hard to imagine trying to make any sense of this, trying to live life when I'm supposed to be taking care of him. I'm not even sure if I love him, and now he's dying, so I'm a horrible person for thinking that. And I'm just stuck. I'm stuck with him and I feel horrible for saying that, but that's just how I feel. I don't know what else to say.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So he's not doing well, you don't love him, and you feel badly for saying that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I mean, it just makes me wonder what I'm even doing. What is the point of me even being a human being if I can't love the one person I'm supposed to love and take care of him when he's dying? I'm just not worth it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You feel like you're not worth being a person?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I don't know, what do you think? Isn't that horrible? That's a horrible thing to say.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's how you feel, right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, but it's a really terrible way to feel. I mean, what does that say about me as a person?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, how do you feel about it? What do you think it says about you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can't even put it into words. I just... it's not good. I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it doesn't point to you being a good person in your estimation.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, obviously not. I mean, it's not like I want him to die, and that's the worst part. It would be so easy if he would just be okay and then we could take our relationship wherever it needs to go. But with things being the way they are, I just feel stuck. And like I said, it's not like I want him to die. It's just that I don't know if I can be the person that takes care of him for the next however long.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you feel like you need to fulfill a role now, taking care of him, a caretaker, and you don't want to fill that role, and you're trapped in that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like, what are people going to say if I leave my dying husband? Like, that is a terrible person. That is a person that your friends whisper to you about. Like, did you hear about Ashley? She left her husband when he's dying of cancer. What a terrible person. And so I am stuck because I can't leave him. That would make me a terrible person. But at the same time, I know it's not right to be with somebody and to lie to them while they're dying. And I just don't want to tell him I don't love him when he's dying either. And it just makes me feel like there's no point in going on. It's just...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You feel like there's no point in you going on.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So where does that leave you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. I feel like I can't even think straight. It's all too much. It's too much to deal with. It just doesn't even feel real.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When did you find out?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Last week.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So all this is very new for you. Has the way you've been feeling changed since the moment you found out till now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really, no. Still the same intensity.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean there's moments where it feels a little better and there's moments where it feels even worse than it does right now. But overall, it's not getting better if that's what you're asking.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what do you see as your options with all this? You mentioned a few. You mentioned you could leave, however you're afraid of how people would see you, so that's not an option. You could stick it out, you could stay and take care of him. What do you think about that option?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. I wish I would just not wake up, you know? It would make everything a lot easier. You know, I would just die and people would say, you know, she was a good wife. It's such a shame she's not here to take care of her sick husband. She was a good person, you know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you having thoughts of ending your life?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're not sure?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that idea of ending your life something that's occurred to you in the last week, like a thought?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, I just think sometimes things would be better off without me. I guess it always kind of pops into my mind just all the time. I'm not sure if that means anything. I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Who would be better off without you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Everybody probably. I mean, my husband wouldn't have me to take care of him, but like, I'm sure there would be other people. You know, his mom's old but she's still alive, and I think she would probably just take him in. He'd probably get a girlfriend or something to take care of him, you know? And it's not like we have any kids, so...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you think he would be better off if you were gone. Anyone else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know if I think he would be better off without me, but I think that he would be okay without me. I think I would be better off without me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You think you would be better off if you were gone. What would happen to you if you were gone?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just be over. I wouldn't have to feel this way anymore. I wouldn't have to worry about anything. I wouldn't have to feel this burden. I wouldn't have to do anything. I could just... it would just be a relief.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you imagine a time in the future if you remained alive where you might be glad that you're alive?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. I mean, what am I going to be glad for, when my husband's dead and I'm free? That's horrible. Why would I be glad, ever? Why? I don't know. I don't think so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No, there'll never be a time when you might want to be alive again.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, maybe one where I would want to be alive, I guess. Like, I don't know. I don't want to be dead, I just don't want to have to go through all this. I don't know what to do. What do I do? Like, is there an answer to this? There's... I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, you've mentioned some of the options, and they don't seem like options you're really connecting with. And then you have this option of suicide, which I don't feel that's a good option either. As you said before, you're really in a place where you're stuck.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has there ever been a time before all this with your husband when you felt this same way, where it was something you wanted to avoid and you'd be better off if you weren't here?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: With him?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Just in your entire life.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean, there have been times where, like, I've thought about killing myself before.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And clearly you didn't, so was there a time after that where you were glad that you didn't?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess so. It just seems like, like, yeah, there's times when it gets better, but then it gets worse again, and it's just seems so pointless to keep going through this, you know? It's exhausting.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So going through this cycle where things are good sometimes and not as good other times, it's just wearing you out, and you feel like it'd be better if you weren't here.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It'll be easier.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What are some reasons you might have to want to stay alive?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think my friends would be upset.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me about their reactions, what would they do?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They'd cry. I think it would be hard for them. I know what it's like when you lose somebody and, you know, that never goes away. It would be hard to hurt them like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And that's what you'd be doing, you'd be hurting them.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: But I can't really think about anybody else that would care.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it would hurt your friends, your husband might be okay, and no one else would be affected that you could think of, and you feel like you'd be better off.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about your other family members?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We don't really talk. I don't think they would care, I really don't. I mean, maybe they would, but I don't really care if they care, honestly.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're not really worried about their feelings in this, but you are somewhat worried about how your friends would feel.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have a plan to hurt yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I mean, I think about a lot of different things, nothing specific, you know? Like, I could cut myself, I could get some pills, I could jump off a bridge. But nothing like sticks in my mind.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So you have some ideas but you don't have anything specific you've planned out. Do you intend to?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. I mean, I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're not sure. Do you feel like you're at risk to do it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. I mean, you're not going to put me in the hospital or something, are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you worried about that, that I would put you in the hospital?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean, I don't want to go to the hospital. It's embarrassing. I don't want to go to the hospital.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well what would happen if you did end up in the hospital? You mentioned it would be embarrassing, what else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, that's about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you think you'd feel better if you were there for a period of time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know if I'll ever feel better. I don't know, I don't want to go to the hospital.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you been there before?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I mean, I've been to the hospital but not for that. I don't want you to put me in there with those crazy people. Like, I'm not... I'm not going. I'm not... I'm not doing that, you know? I have to take care of my husband, I'm not going to the hospital where he has to get his chemo and go in there in the loony bin. Like, I'm not doing that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're not doing that, but at the same time you're having these thoughts of suicide and you're not really sure if you're going to carry out the suicide.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, I don't think... I don't think I'm going to hurt myself. I'm just feeling really overwhelmed. But I don't want you to put me in there. I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you telling me that you're not going to hurt yourself because you're worried about the hospital?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, like what does it even matter? Like, what difference does it make?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Whether you're alive or not?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, like what do you care? I mean, what difference does it make if I go to the hospital or not? What difference does it make?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well I care, I don't want you to hurt yourself. And we've talked about this when you first came into treatment, that if there was ever a time when I felt like you were going to hurt yourself, I would stop you. I would do my best to stop you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Why would you care? Like why? Why does it make a difference to you? You see a thousand other people, I bet you've had a bunch of people kill themselves. What difference does it make to you? You don't go home and, you know, think about all your clients. Like I'm just another person to you. What difference does it make to you if I hurt myself?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well I believe that life is valuable, I believe your life is valuable. I have a responsibility to do my best to protect you in this relationship. I think you have value as a person.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: How? How do I have value as a person? I want to leave my husband who's dying. How do I have value as a person? That doesn't even make any sense.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And I understand you feel that way, that you're taking that situation where you don't love him and you feel stuck with him to mean that you're a bad person.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I am a bad person.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, you feel like a bad person, and there's a difference between those two constructs, right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess so, but I don't know. I don't know. It's just frustrating.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you need to be convinced that you're not a bad person to continue living?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't think that you can convince me that I'm not a bad person, you know? If I thought I was a good person, yeah, I probably would want to continue living, but I think the evidence is clear. I don't know what more I need to know to show me that I'm not a bad person, like...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does it work that way, though, or are people good or bad?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. I guess, like, if you feel the way I feel, then you are a bad person. Like, if you have the thoughts that I'm having, that's a bad way to think. That's... you're being a bad person. Like, that's not good. Good people don't think like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But could somebody do things that other people consider good and other people consider bad at the same time? Could both of those coexist in the same person?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean, that... yes, but I don't think that's what's happening in this situation. Like, you could do something and some people like it and some people don't, that happens all the time. But this is pretty cut and dried. It's not a good thing to want to get a divorce from your husband who's dying. That's not the way good people feel.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. You feel that's bad, wrong, morally wrong. Are there other things you do that are good, morally right? I mean, the way you make it sound is that you're irredeemable. Is that the case, that you're all bad and no good?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, I guess I'm not all bad, but...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So right now we're still at a point where you're having these thoughts, and you told me before that you weren't sure if you're going to carry it out. And then the subject of the hospital came up and you kind of backed off that a little bit. Is that about right? Can you appreciate where I'm in a position where I can't really be certain what you're going to do?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is it also possible that making a decision like suicide, that type of decision should not be made when you're frustrated, anxious, depressed? Like, there's just certain moods that aren't conducive to good decision-making of any type. Do you feel like you're in one of those moods now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel like I'm in a lifetime of that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A lifetime of that mood? Maybe a little bit worse now with recent events?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would you be okay voluntarily going to the hospital?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, I guess. I mean, I don't even know where to go. Like, I just go in and tell them like I'm going to kill myself and walk into the emergency room? I don't...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I could have one of the case managers take you over there. They're familiar with the procedure for admitting. Would that be something you could do voluntarily? And we'll see how long they keep you. It's up to them once you go in there, but say a week or two, and then we could meet again and kind of see where you are, state of mind. Does that sound like an okay plan? You'd be okay with that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Tired.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. Maybe you just need a little bit of a break. You've had a lot put on you recently. All right, Ashley, let's do this. Let me get that arranged, we'll get you over there. And then when you're there and we coordinate with them, when you're there they're going to contact me and we'll get you an appointment for the day that you get released. That work? All right, I'll get that arranged and I guess as you'll feel at least somewhat better when I see you again. We'll work through it, okay?

video_details.title: Getting Started: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy in Action

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now, one thing I thought we might do today is to get an example of one of these situations in which you get really anxious and try to see if we can understand more about how you think and how you feel when you're in the middle of one of those situations. So can you think of an example of something that's happened recently?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. My daughter has been... she's actually been sick. And so she had a fever yesterday and they started her on an antibiotic and I had to go pick it up from the drugstore and that's like, I don't usually go there. It's hard to get there. It's not right in the neighborhood.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any expressways or bridges to get there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not expressways, but it's busy. It's busier and it's like in a mall, so there's four lanes. So it just... it's not some place I usually would go. And if I was going to go, usually I would either have her go with me or my husband go with me, but she was sick and he was at work.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So to try to understand what goes through your mind, let's try to take you back. And now you know that the prescription's there and your daughter's sick and I guess you don't want to ask her to drive over there. Probably not the wisest idea. So you're thinking about doing the drive. And what's going through your mind? What are the thoughts that are turning inside?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm just, you know, I'm sort of thinking about going there and I'm already starting to think, well, you know, what if... what if I'm driving and somebody crashes into me? What if I'm driving and I can't do it? You know, what if I just have to stop because I can't do it anymore? And it was raining and I'm sort of like, I've got this picture of myself out in the middle of the road.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's the picture look like? You're out in the middle of the road and it's raining?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm stranded and it's dark and my shoes are gone... I'm just like, it would be a million miles to get back home.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Pretty miserable? Yeah, pretty scary.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, terrifying. And I just... it's so hard to get there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And Kate, as you put yourself back into that situation and have those thoughts going through your mind, what kinds of feelings go along with it? And by feelings I mean things that are inside, like fear, anxiety, physical things that are going on.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, fear and anxiety, and I just feel really shaky and I feel really like lightheaded and dizzy and I just don't feel like I can breathe very well and I feel like I'm going to like fall over.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is this a panic attack now? You've told me about having some panic attacks.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've had worse ones, but it's getting there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Not quite to a panic, but you know, it's brewing.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah. It feels like it might.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What I think we might do to try to move things along toward getting a plan of attack on this is to actually sketch this out and see if we can figure out some things we might be able to start doing to give you a better handle on it than you have right now. So let's put some boxes here and one of them is going to be 'event'. These are the things that trigger your anxiety. And in this case, the event was...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The drive... having to drive to the pharmacy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Drive to pharmacy. And then this next box I'm going to label something we call automatic thoughts. And by automatic I mean that they occur relatively automatically, they just sort of pop into your mind and you don't stop to check them out. And we all have these kinds of automatic thoughts. I suspect that you have lots of those thoughts and you just gave me some examples of them. So that's why we call them automatic.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So the... like the 'what ifs'?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, so let's put a couple of those down in this box. In the automatic thoughts box. And they are...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: What if someone runs into me? What if I get stranded?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Get stranded. What else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can't do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I can't do it. And then there was this image about the rainstorm and you don't have your shoes on and so forth. What should we put down for that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think 'what if I can't get back home?'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I can't get back home. Sort of lost? Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. What if I end up on this road forever?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And then we're going to put another box. There's sort of a chain of events here. The event can make you think in ways that stir up feelings of anxiety and so forth. So if you're thinking like this, it makes sense that you'd be feeling pretty nervous inside and you might have some of these physical reactions. So let's put those in here. This is the 'emotions' box. And they are... shaky you said? A lot of fear. If we're going to rate that fear on a zero to 100 scale, where would you be at this point?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, I'd say about an 80.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: 80, pretty high. It's gone higher though, I suspect.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, yeah. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But at this point it's an 80. Okay, and then you had some other feelings inside?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, yeah, I sort of felt like I might fall over and my heart was pounding and I didn't feel like I could breathe very well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Heart pounding. How about your stomach? Any flip-flops in your stomach or anything like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So a lot going on here and a pretty high level of distress.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And then we're going to complete this loop by putting a box we're going to call 'behavior'. This is how you actually acted when you were in the situation. So what did you do after you had these thoughts and you had these feelings?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I went to the pharmacy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You did do it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I had to.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, and what was it like for you when you were going to the pharmacy and driving there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was so bad. I just, you know, I think I left permanent marks on the steering wheel because I was holding on to it so tight.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you were gripping tightly. Okay. So in this case you actually did go to the pharmacy, but you maybe did some damage to the steering wheel.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. But I really had no choice. I mean, I think usually I wouldn't go to the pharmacy. Usually I would call my husband and say, can you pick it up on your way home?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Get an escape route if you would. Yeah. So usually you would avoid this. The usual behavior would be to try to get out of it or avoid it. Is that right? Okay. And so if you do avoid it, then what happens?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I feel better. It's like such a relief.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Better, relief. The emotions calm down now, right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, yeah, because I don't have to worry about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So that's what happens for a single episode of this anxiety. I'm wondering though, if we look at the impact of avoiding and getting relief overall as far as managing driving, what do you think it does there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I feel like I don't really have much confidence when it comes to this, to being able to do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so in a way it decreases your confidence over time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I suspect that not doing it repeatedly gives you this belief about your capacity to do these driving things. And what's that belief?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I don't feel like I can do it. I can't do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it really comes back to this thought 'I can't do it'. And you can't do it and you don't do it. Right. So here's this chain of events. Events trigger thoughts, we call them automatic thoughts, and then they influence your emotions, these feelings you have, and then that influences how you handle the situation. Okay. Now let's think together for a moment of how we might proceed. Do you know anybody else that drives regularly that might think differently than you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I mean, I think almost everybody. I think most people drive without too much problem, but like my sister loves to drive. I mean, she just... she drives every opportunity she can.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But you do have some differences in the way you think about driving that might be something that we could begin to work on in our sessions. We might, for example, check it out, you know, what's the chances of someone slamming into you? Or what's the chances of you being stranded out there on the highway? And even if you were stranded, is there a way you could cope with that? So I'm going to mark here: we could work on these thoughts. And then by working on the thoughts, we might be able to help you reduce the emotions. But there are also some things that I might be able to teach you that you could use to reduce this level of distress that you have.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, that would be really nice.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: To be able to calm yourself down in situations. So we'll try to build some skills to manage your emotions. And then on this behavior side, one thing that we might begin to work on is helping you gradually begin to take on some of these driving things so that you can build your confidence back up. And I can see that that causes a little bit of edginess here. What were you thinking when I mentioned that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was thinking that I hope that this doesn't like make me worse, you know, like trying to do some of these things.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I'm glad you gave me that feedback. I certainly wouldn't want to do anything to make you worse or to cause you too much anxiety. And what we'll try to do is pace it at just the level that's right for you so that you can make some progress and get to the place you want to be, which is to be able to drive to your new office, cross that big bridge, and maybe even drive those couple hours to visit your son. Right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Well, I think that that would, if I could do those things, it would be really nice.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, I think it'd be really nice too. So that'll be our goal.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

video_details.title: Suicide Assessment Role-Play - Divorce Stressor
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play session that demonstrates a suicide assessment of a client (played by an actress) who presents with stressors related to an upcoming divorce.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello Ashley, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm doing alright.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I understand that you've been going through a bit of a rough time, you want to tell me what's going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, me and my husband separated and it's just it's really hard because this is my second divorce, I guess we're getting a divorce and...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you just separated? When was that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably about a month ago.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: About a month ago. And you know from that time you know it's going to end up in a divorce?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah I think it's where we're ready for that obviously, you have to wait and everything, but it's up.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So this has been a tough time for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's just a lot. I mean I've already been through this once and it's just really hard to have two failed marriages.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So this would be your second divorce. When was the first divorce?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: About 10 years ago.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A painful memory?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it got really nasty and it's just so sad to see something with someone you cared about so much just end so badly and there's just it's so difficult. It kind of I don't know it just makes me feel like I don't know I've just been having thoughts about hurting myself I guess because it's just a lot to deal with.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This idea of having to go through all this again, kind of overwhelming.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean there's just there's so much to deal with. You know going to court, the kids' custody, all the money, dividing up everything we own, all the drama and the fights and you know having to tell people that I'm getting another divorce... it's just embarrassing and it's sad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And all this has led to thoughts of hurting yourself. When did those thoughts start?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. I mean I think I've always had them on and off but it obviously got worse when things started getting bad in our relationship.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How strong are the thoughts?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, I don't know how to answer that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you know about how much of the day they take up? Is it something that's happening all the time, occasional?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would say it's occasional. I think it kind of pops into my head and I think about it for a little while and then I kind of get distracted and go onto other stuff. So I don't think it's all the time, luckily. I think that would be really hard.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So occasionally you've been having thoughts of harming yourself. Do you have a plan of how you'd harm yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I mean no not really.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you plan on carrying it out? Do you intend to hurt yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't think so, I don't know. I don't think so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So mostly just these painful thoughts of wanting to hurt yourself. This has happened before, these thoughts have happened before. And this situation in a manner of speaking has happened before, you were divorced before.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you're thinking about what it's going to be like to get divorced again and all the different circumstances that that brings along with it. Like you mentioned family court and dividing up assets.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's just it's a lot, it's really overwhelming to think about having to go through that all again. I mean I know how extremely painful it was the first time and the second time I thought this is really going to work... it just feels like I have no control over like what happens to me, I have no control over whether I'm going to be happy or not.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's the uncertainty, part of it's the uncertainty, lack of control over the situation.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, especially the lack of control. It's just like the court comes in and they make all these decisions about your life. He wants to do one thing, I want to do something different, so then the court comes in and screws everything up, nobody's happy, and it's just it's so difficult. Like I don't know what's going to happen with my kids... it just feels so outside of my control, just feels like everything, I'm powerless, I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're just being kind of pushed through all these different situations with no ability to slow down, stop it, change course, this lack of power.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean yeah, that's how it feels.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And sometimes when contemplating that lack of control you have these thoughts that it might be better to not be here.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Did you have those thoughts after the first divorce?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I did. I mean I don't think it was as bad back then. You know maybe it's just a way for me to try to take back control, you know me deciding whether I live or not. At least I have control over that if I can't control anything else.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the comfort you take in those thoughts is the idea that you can have power in the situation.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess, I mean I'm not sure it's like conscious that that's why but I think maybe that's why.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That might be part of it. Just wanting to have control over something. In the end of all this, like when the divorce is over and you've recovered from all the things that come with divorce, do you think that you could enjoy life and be productive, have purpose?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think so. It's just it's kind of hard to see the light at the end of the tunnel but I know it's there. You know I love my kids, I don't want to die. It's just it's hard sometimes to see the light at the end of the tunnel.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You don't want to die, but you don't want to face going through this again.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I really don't. It's too much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: At the same time you can kind of picture getting through it even though it's tough and you can picture yourself being happy again.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I can. It's hard to believe it but I think it's true.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, I'd like you to work with me on a safety plan if you'd be okay with that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: What does that mean?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, you have some suicidal thoughts that have been bothering you and this significant stressor in your life. And I think it would be a good idea to have a plan in place so that if those thoughts become more powerful, if your feelings become worse in terms of sadness, that you have some steps that you can follow to make sure you're safe.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Are you worried I might hurt myself?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, it's certainly a concern based on what you're going through and what you've said. And I just want to make sure we take every precaution to prevent that. To have a plan in place so that if things do escalate with you, we can respond in a way that prevents anything bad from happening. Does that seem reasonable?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have any family supports as you're going through all this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'm staying with my sister right now. She's great, she helps with the kids and everything, she's my best friend.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so your sister, a major positive figure in your life. Any friends you can rely on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really. I mean I have friends but none that I'm that close with that I would want to talk about these things with. I can talk about the divorce but I don't want to tell people about my thoughts.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so they can support you to a degree. You just wouldn't want to tell them everything that's going on. But your sister you feel like you can talk to.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think so. It'll probably be hard but I think I could.

diarization.speaker: Ther therapist
diarization.text: All right, so should that be in your plan, maybe the first line of defense if these suicidal thoughts get stronger, talking to your sister?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean I think that makes sense. That's probably what I would do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, and that would probably help most of the time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: At the same time, if you could, call in to me and we'll make sure to get you in quickly for an appointment. Right? Kind of at that same level if you talk to your sister and you're still a little worried, make sure you call in.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What if it gets past that? What if you talk to your sister, you still don't feel too much better, you call in to me, make an appointment, but things still are not going well? Would you be okay contacting a crisis line if I gave you a number for that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: What's a crisis line?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: There's a number set up here where you can call and they can kind of talk you through the crisis that's going on in terms of suicidal thoughts, something like that, and they can respond accordingly. Sometimes you just talk to them. Certainly as I mentioned you'd be coming in to see me as soon as we get that scheduled. They could also in extreme cases send out emergency personnel.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean I think I could do that. I don't think I would need that but if I did, I could call them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So if the thoughts get stronger, get worrisome, talk to your sister. At the same time call in here, of course I'm only around the day, so I want to make sure we have a plan that covers when I'm not here. If it gets worse, call crisis.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how about if things get really bad, to where you really feel like you're going to go through with it? Would you be okay calling 911 as that last part of the plan?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: What would they do if I called 911?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, it depends on how bad things are in terms of how strong the suicidal thoughts are and what's going on, but in all likelihood probably send somebody out to transport you to a hospital.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Yeah, I mean I could do that. Like I said earlier, I don't think that I'll need that but if I needed to, I could do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so we'll put that as part of the plan even though it doesn't seem likely you'll need that, but it's there. I guess you never know what you're going to need. I just don't want you to be worried or anything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well I am worried about you, but I feel like you are taking the right steps with me now to help protect yourself. So I'd like to take a moment and kind of write that plan down and make sure you have a copy and get to read through it before you leave.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I know that what you're going through must be terrible and you wish you could avoid it. Try to keep in mind that you have survived this before and that you can picture a time when this is over and you'll be glad you're alive.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. I mean yeah, I do, I don't want to die. I have my family and everything, it's just hard sometimes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, this is a tough experience and you've been through this before, you know it's painful, so it's understandable you wouldn't want to go through it again. I just don't want suicide to be the end result.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, me neither, me neither.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so it sounds like you understand the plan and you're kind of looking at things a little bit more positively, is that accurate?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, would you be okay, I know I see you every week, would you be okay this week coming in two days just to check in with me?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think that would be fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so I'll get that safety plan together and I'll find a time on the schedule so I can see you in a couple days. And if anything happens between then, of course we talked about the plan: talking to your sister, calling in, crisis and then if need be 911. Okay? I'll get that together for you and we'll get you on the schedule for a couple days from now. I know this has been tough to talk about, I really appreciate you being open with me and discussing this.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah well I thank you because you know I want to stay safe too and I appreciate you helping me and caring so thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Absolutely.

video_details.title: The Standardised Mini-Mental State Examination (SMMSE) - Performance Impairment
video_details.description: This video demonstrates an administration of the Standardised Mini-Mental State Examination (SMMSE) with an actor playing the role of a client with a cognitive performance impairment.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, this is Dr. Grande. I hope you find this video useful. If that's the case, please like it and subscribe to my channel. And as always, thanks for watching.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hi, how are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing okay. Thanks for asking. What's your name?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Tom Bancroft.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tom Bancroft. And which hand do you normally write with?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right hand.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Your right hand. Would it be alright if I ask you some questions about your memory?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm going to ask you some questions and give you some problems to solve. Please try to answer them as best you can. What year is this?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What season of the year is this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Winter.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is the date today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh, the 16th.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What day of the week is this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Tuesday.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What month is this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: January.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me what country we are in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: United States.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What county are we in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh, Wilmington?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What city are we in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Wilmington.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is the name of this building?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The Graduate Center.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What floor of the building are we on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: First floor.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I am going to name three objects. After I have said them, I want you to repeat them back to me. Apple, table, penny.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Apple, table, penny.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Remember what they are, because I'm going to ask you to name them again in a few minutes.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now I'm going to give you a word and ask you to spell it forward and backward. The word is world. First, can you spell it forward?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: W-O-R-L-D.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now, spell it backward.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: D-L-O-R-W.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What were the three objects I asked you to remember?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Apple, table, penny.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is this called?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A watch.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is this called?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A pen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I would like you to repeat a phrase after me. The phrase is, no ifs, ands, or buts.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh, no ifs, buts, or ands.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Read the words on this page, then do what it says.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Close your eyes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Take this paper in your right hand, fold the paper once with both hands, and put the paper down on your lap.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Take this. Write any complete sentence on that piece of paper for me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Here is a drawing. Please copy the drawing on the same piece of paper.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you. You did well.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

video_details.title: The Folstein Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) - Memory Loss
video_details.description: This video demonstrates a cognitive assessment using the Folstein Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) with an actor playing the role of a client with indications of memory loss.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Sue, it's good to see you again.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You too.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I was hoping today I could give you a test of your memory. Are you okay with that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. All right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that all right? Okay. So I'm going to read a series of questions and ask you to do some different things and this will just take a few minutes. All right? Sue, what is today's date?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think it's the 10th. I think it's the 10th.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is today's year?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is the month?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's January. It's 2017. It's January.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What day is today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's the 10th.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you also tell me what season it is?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Christmas.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you also tell me the name of this clinic?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh God, what was it? I saw it when I came in. Oh, I don't remember.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What floor are we on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Red. It's a red floor. Red carpet.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What city are we in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Dover.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What county are we in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Dover County?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What state are we in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Delaware.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I'm going to test your memory. I want to read these three words and I want you to repeat them back to me. Ball, flag, tree. Can you repeat those back?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Ball, frog...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Let me do that again. Ball, flag, and tree.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Ball, flag, and tree.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. I want you to remember those because I'm going to ask you to repeat them again later on. Okay. Can you begin with the number 100 and count backwards by seven? 100...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Continue.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, that's good. Thank you. Can you spell the word world backwards?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: World. L, R... no. D-R-L-W.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. I want you to name the three words that I asked you to remember a few moments ago.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Ball, frog. I think that was it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me what this is?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A watch.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me what this is?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A pen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm going to say a phrase and I'd like you to repeat it back to me exactly as I say it. The phrase is: No ifs, ands, or buts.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No ifs and buts.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you right-handed or left-handed?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right-handed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'd like you to take this piece of paper from me in your right hand, fold the paper in half, and put the paper on the floor.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Can only fold it with my right hand?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You can use both hands.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, you're done?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mm-hmm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm going to hold up a piece of paper with instructions and I'd like you to follow those instructions. Okay, thank you. With the blank sheet of paper that I gave you a moment ago, can you write on that a complete sentence?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just anything? Any complete sentence?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, thank you. I'm going to show you a drawing and I'd like you to copy the drawing on that same piece of paper.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: This is kind of hard.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, thank you. So I want to thank you for participating in this memory test. It's been very helpful.

video_details.title: MRCP Paces Station 3 - Abdominal
video_details.uploader: Blackpool Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: My name is Dr. Punekar and this is an MRCP PACES station 3, abdominal examination.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello Dr. Punekar. My name is Dr. Patata and this is station 3 of the MRCP PACES exam. We've got an abdominal examination.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This is Luke, a 21-year-old university student referred by his GP with abdominal pain and being unwell. Would you like to examine his abdominal system, please?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello, is it Luke? Nice to meet you. I'm Dr. Patata. Is it okay if I examine your abdomen and a few other parts of your body?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, that's fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, okay. Can I ask you to just take your gown down? I'm having a look for any scars or significant signs. I'll check your hands for clubbing, muscle wasting, or tremors. I'd check the pulse and feel for lymph nodes in the neck. Do you have any pain anywhere?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A little bit of pain up there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you. I'll check your eyes for anemia or jaundice. Please lie down flat. I'm checking for scars and organomegaly, and I'll palpate, percuss, and auscultate the abdomen. No signs of pedal edema. Thank you, you can dress now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, have you finished?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yes. To complete my examination I'd like to perform a shifting dullness test, check his urine dip, perform a full lymphadenopathy screen, and check his observations.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, good. Would you like to present your case now, please?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I examined a 21-year-old student with abdominal pain. The only positive findings were jaundice and a two-finger breadth hepatomegaly, with no other signs of chronic liver disease.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, that's good. You mentioned jaundice. Are you sure the patient was jaundiced?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: He had a very faint hint of jaundice in the sclera, though it wasn't overt.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you mentioned hepatomegaly. Was the patient tender in his abdomen?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yes, he had tender hepatomegaly on palpation.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would you like to think of a few causes of tender hepatomegaly in a young patient like Luke?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Top differentials would be infectious or alcoholic hepatitis. Other possibilities include malignancies, infiltrative disorders, or Budd-Chiari syndrome.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Looking at this case, what would be the top of your list for this 21-year-old student?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I would consider hepatitis as the top differential, probably viral or alcoholic hepatitis.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What if I add that he returned two weeks ago from the Central African Republic? What would you think then?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'd consider viral hepatitis A through E, though hepatitis B is less likely given the two-week history of return.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you come across any blood tests that would confirm or rule out viral hepatitis?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I would perform serological tests. For hepatitis A, I'd check IgM antibodies. For hepatitis B, I'd check surface antigens, core antibodies, and e antigens.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Which antigen goes up first in hepatitis B?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That would be the hepatitis B surface antigen and core antibody.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In hepatitis A, what type of antibodies are you expecting to rise initially?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Within the first four-week period, I'd expect a rise in IgM, followed by an IgG rise afterwards.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, that's good. Thank you.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play – Complete Session – Social Anxiety Disorder – Part 2
video_details.description: This video features part two of a complete cognitive-behavior therapy (CBT) counseling role-play session in which CBT techniques are used to treat social anxiety disorder. Part two includes identifying automatic thoughts, understanding the symptoms, and imagery.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does the feeling itself, the worry about not being prepared, interfere with preparing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. It's really hard. So like when I'm in the middle of being worried, it's really hard for me to focus. So I can't focus on what I need to do because I feel like my mind is on a lot of different things and I can't focus on, you know, exactly what I should be doing. It's just like I'm worried about, you know, all the different aspects.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so your ability to concentrate to do the hard work of preparing...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, to like focus my energy on the right things. I'm just like wasting time worrying.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so this excessive worrying and this interference of preparing, all this goes on right up until you're getting ready to present?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, and then like while I'm presenting.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
