diarization.text: Alright, so let's talk about that. Let's go into the actual day of presenting. So we have this excessive worry coming in, it's interfered with your ability to prepare, it's distressing for you. Now it's, what, in class? These presentations are in class?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, mm-hmm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're in the classroom. Are you the only one to present during that class or does it rotate through several people?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It depends on the presentation. Sometimes there's like one or two other people that have to present that night, depending on like how long the topic is.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, well let's use the last time you presented in that class as a template. What was the order? Like what order did you go in there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The one... well the one that I really messed up, I think I was first. But usually like I'm second maybe.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so for this example let's say you're the second. So you're sitting in the classroom and another student is presenting. What's going through your mind then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel like I am totally zoned out, like I'm not even paying attention to what that person's saying because I'm so worried about how I'm going to mess it up. I'm starting to like be sweaty, like my hands are clammy, my heart's starting to race a little bit, and I'm just totally zoned out on what they're doing. I'm just worrying about what's going to happen when I get up there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so in that moment as you're seated, you're not really watching their presentation as much because you have these somewhat strong physical symptoms. You have your heart racing a bit, you said, sweaty palms, you're zoned out. Have you ever felt the need, desire to like run out of the room?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, it's funny you should say that. I was a little bit hesitant to mention that but I kind of, I do. I feel like I need to find an excuse to like use the bathroom or I just need to get out of there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, so what do you feel is most pressuring you to leave the room? Like what symptom?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would say that just like my anxiety and my heart rate are starting to increase and I feel like I just need to get out of there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what thoughts go through your mind right then? So let's take that kind of most severe moment when you're still before the presentation. So you're sitting at the desk and your heart rate's elevated and you're not focusing on what they're doing, you're zoned out, your anxiety's high. What thought is going through your mind right then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think I'm thinking like I'm going to bomb this anyway so I might as well just not go through the stress of having to do it. Like I've already in my head, I know that it's going to end badly.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, 'I've already, I've already failed'?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. So there's no sense in getting up there and maybe if I don't get up there, I guess it couldn't be any worse so I might as well just leave.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you embarrassed that the professor or other students will see that you were really anxious?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I figure if I leave then people will just maybe think I was sick or whatever and it'll be a better situation if I just left than having to see me up there sweating and all these other symptoms that I have when I actually get up there. It would be better just to leave before that starts.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So better to be thought ill, that you just had to leave because you were sick?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, or have them wonder what happened than to just be up in front of everybody. That severe anxiety in front of everybody and then they can see... it's very embarrassing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, that would be a very undesirable outcome for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. So as you're debating that thought, like as that's coming into your head and you're thinking 'I just need to flee'...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I've just gotta get out of here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What happens there? So we're maybe what, 15 minutes before you present?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So tell me about that. So you have that thought, you want to flee...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right, and I'm looking at the clock and saying you know like, 'how much more time in this presentation before I have to go?', 'should I go, should I not go?', 'what are the consequences of running out?', you know, and kind of playing out which would be worse.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever had to run out?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, once I went to the bathroom to try to like calm myself down or talk to myself or you know like cool off my face. But I came back.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you presented?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, and then I presented.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so you survived one of the more stressful...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I almost felt like I was going to be ill, I was so stressed that day.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That was very, very tough on you, that particular day.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But you did survive it, which was very unpleasant.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So now we're right about to where it's time to get up and present. Let's say in this scenario you haven't fled but you had those thoughts. You're anxious and you have some physical symptoms going on. You get up and it's time to present. What's the sequence from this point on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So typically like I go to load my presentation. At this point I have my note cards or whatever in front of me. I am like shaking at this point. I don't know if it's scared or worried or maybe a combination of everything and I'm just like sweating, my heart is racing, like I almost feel dizzy. I'm just so stressed out about what's going to happen and then you know I'm starting to speak and then the presentations are usually like 20 minutes or so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So I have to stay up there for the duration and I'm just like you know sweating and then I'm wondering like are people looking at me? Are people... can people see it? You know, am I going to forget something?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the thoughts are: 'I wonder if they can see how anxious I am', 'I wonder if I'm going to do poorly on the presentation'...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right, or are they thinking I'm lazy and I didn't prepare? Are they going to think that you know I'm dumb or I don't know you know what I'm doing? What are they going to think about me?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so they might think less of you as a person.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right, or like be judging me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there's a number of concerns that kind of go through your mind in that moment. So when does it start to turn around? So you start presenting, it's 20 minutes, you initially get up there and get your presentation up on the projection monitor, something like that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When does it start to turn the corner?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, it depends. Sometimes I settle down a little bit but then usually I get some sort of rhythm I think and then, but then it gets anxiety again until I get my grades. Do you know what I mean? And I'm like until that happens because I feel like I'm going to do poorly until that happens.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And when do you receive the grades?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes... she usually doesn't give them that day but like often like the next day or the day after.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So does that intense anxiety that you're having while you're presenting last all the way to...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. It's... it definitely like dissipates once I can like go sit down.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so the next big drop off for symptoms would be when you're done with the presentation.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, when eyes are maybe no longer on me, they've moved on to somebody else, so I figure like, 'okay they forgot about me, I'm safe' for right then.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But then there's this other worry of: now we have to see what the grade's going to be.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. And I convince myself that I did poorly.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the thought that's going through your mind is 'I'm going to receive a bad grade'?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. And that everyone saw me you know sweating and all these symptoms that I have, everyone is judging me.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play – Complete Session – Social Anxiety Disorder – Part 5
video_details.description: This video features part five of a complete cognitive-behavior therapy (CBT) counseling role-play session in which CBT techniques are used to treat social anxiety disorder. Part five includes identifying cognitive distortions, understanding the effects of beliefs, and exploring reactions.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, this is Dr. Grande. I hope you find this video useful. If that's the case, please like it and subscribe to my channel. And as always, thanks for watching.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so let's, if we could, let's talk about the moment in the presentation again. I want to try to help you develop some strategies to bring those anxiety symptoms down.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's actually go right before the moment. So you're still sitting down and you're getting ready to present, let's just say you're second to present like we've talked about, and you're thinking they're going to see me as anxious, they're going to think I don't belong here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So these thoughts occur because you have an expectation, a rule, an attitude that you've brought into that class. It's perfectly natural, everyone has these beliefs. They combine with the stressor of the presentation and classmates watching, and result in these automatic thoughts.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And just like the beliefs, they're not good or bad, they're just thoughts. Actually, they're fairly understandable and natural thoughts.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The problem is that they lead to symptoms. You're sitting there and thinking, 'They're going to see that I'm anxious. They're going to think I'm not good enough.' What reaction do you have when you have that thought?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I'm very observant, I start looking around, I'm sweating. I'm having physical responses and looking around to see if anyone's already looking at me, like hyper-vigilance.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so distressing symptoms.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's something that you could say to yourself in that moment that would maybe get in between that thought and that reaction?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I think in that moment most people are looking at the person who's presenting and not at me. I could maybe take some deep breaths or try to calm myself down, maybe look over my notes one more time, because they're all watching the person presenting, not me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So some deep breathing, looking over your notes, kind of focusing on that and realizing they're not really looking at you anyway at that moment. You bring your notes with you to class?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, like usually I have index cards or maybe some stats on something that I want to look over, like some numbers or something I don't want to forget.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you always have those with you. And it's just a matter of can you focus your attention on them?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right, exactly, enough to not forget them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And if you're focusing on that and thinking about that, you're not thinking about whatever they might be thinking about. And how about the deep breathing? Is that a strategy you've tried before?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A little bit, but with not much success because usually when I think to remember it, I'm in panic mode and then it's really hard.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you've been able to do it sometimes, just not often.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not consistently.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play – Complete Session – Social Anxiety Disorder – Part 6
video_details.description: This video features part six of a complete cognitive-behavior therapy (CBT) counseling role-play session in which CBT techniques are used to treat social anxiety disorder. Part six includes behavior experiments, goal setting, and self-talk.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, this is Dr. Grande. I hope you find this video useful. If that's the case, please like it and subscribe to my channel. And as always, thanks for watching.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have on your presentation, do you have so many bullet points you want to cover? Like an outline?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, like an outline sort of thing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would it help to time the deep breathing with reviewing each one of those bullet points?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I never thought about that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I don't know how many bullet points you'd have in your presentation. Maybe you'd have 10 or 20, depending on how long it is.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Something like that, yeah. Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So maybe as you start to review a certain bullet point, as you're trying to get it into your memory and think about it, you breathe in really deeply and then as you continue on, you just let out that breath really slowly.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like a rhythm sort of. Yeah, I could do that. I've never thought about it that way.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm just thinking it'd be some way to structure so you would get in so many breaths, so many good breaths. Yeah, something that kind of becomes a habit.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Just make sure you keep your bullet points at a length that will work. Not a few paragraphs, but just a few seconds each so you can get a good deep breath in. Just some rhythm that you could kind of grab onto, something concrete.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, because I know that in that moment things are probably, like you mentioned, zoning out, and it becomes very easy to lose your anchors and just get really foggy, almost dizzy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, so if you can remember for a particular bullet point that you want to take three deep breaths, you know, that might be something you can really grab onto and would kind of cut through that fogginess. When's the next presentation in that class?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The next one I believe is next Friday.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that the next presentation you have in all the classes?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And that's next Friday. Do you know where you are in the order for presenting?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think I'm actually third in this one. So not first.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Not first. And this one's how many minutes?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like 15 or so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so a little shorter than the 20-minute mark. So 15 minutes. So you'll have about a half hour, maybe a little more if there's time to switch out, of kind of sitting there and potential time when you could be anxious.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But also potential time when you could be reviewing the notes, your bullet points, and breathing. And saying to yourself that self-talk, that they're not really paying attention to me anyway.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Because that might help reduce that anxiety. What's one thing you could say to yourself when you're up there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I could say that, you know, in general I do pretty well. One bad grade isn't going to make me—doesn't mean that I don't deserve to be here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so the self-talk up there could be 'I deserve to be here.'

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe I've prepared enough, you know, that I know that I've prepared and I'm a good student.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. 'I've prepared enough. I'm a good student. I deserve to be here.'

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that something it would be helpful to write down and have as part of your notes that you can recite internally as you're up there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think it would actually, because it's not long. I think it would be easy to remember and I could just maybe put it down on one of my note cards in front of me or something.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how much do you believe that those statements are true?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think, you know, sitting here now, I believe them. In the moment sometimes it's a little hard to believe because I convince myself otherwise, but I think I actually believe that that's true, that I do deserve to be in the program.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so those self-talk items, you believe them to be true. But you recognize in the moment—and I want you to be aware of this—you might not believe them as much. But remember that we worked on them, you came up with them, and you believe them now. So try to keep that in your mind as you start to doubt yourself and be ready to recite them.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's easy, I realize it's easy to form these plans, but in the chaos of the anxiety and the worry it's harder. So the more tasks you can make concrete and that you can write down and you can rehearse, I think the better off you'll be.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I would like to see you—your presentation's next Friday—I would like to see you right before that, so it'd be about a week. Do you have any questions? These are items you can rehearse still: the self-talk and the breathing and of course preparing.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't think so. I think it makes sense.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You understand kind of the plan to attack that anxiety symptom?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. And I think, you know, what you kind of suggested before, like maybe practicing my deep breathing like maybe now when I'm calm and getting into a habit of deep breathing, like I'm more apt to also remember it then.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so good. So you have some behavioral pieces, the studying, the focus on studying, the breathing, and some cognitive pieces, the self-talk we talked about that you use when you're seated and that you use when you're at the podium and actually presenting. All right, good. So I'm glad we have a plan going forward. I think that you did a really good job today helping kind of untangle all this and figure out what's going on. And I appreciate that you were able to really connect with the symptoms and the thoughts and kind of realize how they're related. I feel like this is something that's going to serve you well as you move through this. I'll see you in a week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you. Okay, thanks.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks, Hazel.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play – Complete Session – Social Anxiety Disorder – Part 4
video_details.description: This video features part four of a complete cognitive-behavior therapy (CBT) counseling role-play session in which CBT techniques are used to treat social anxiety disorder. Part four includes evaluating evidence, challenging beliefs, and identifying the effects of emotions.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, this is Dr. Grande. I hope you find this video useful. If that's the case, please like it and subscribe to my channel. And as always, thanks for watching.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any other evidence that points toward you being an imposter?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Besides my bad grade that I got that one time, yeah, not a whole lot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So it'd be safe to say that a lot of that thought of 'I'm not good enough' is kind of based on these feelings of anxiety?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, which are really intense, like panic almost in the moment.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, so in a way, you're believing what the anxiety would lead you to believe. But in the bright light of scrutiny, there aren't a lot of facts to support the worst case, which is you don't deserve it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. How about evidence that refutes that you're not good enough?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would say that, you know, I was accepted into the program, like there's kind of like a pretty rigorous sort of testing and stuff which I passed to get an interview and such to get into the program. So I did that. Like I said, I'm a pretty good student all considering, you know, before this kind of was happening.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you got through a rigorous process to become a student, you're doing well, you mentioned before just the one bad grade, right? Okay. So if you have friends in this program, right? If one of them came to you with this imbalance of, you know, one bad grade and some anxiety versus passing rigorous standards and doing well otherwise, what advice would you give them?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, now that you're kind of like talking about it like a this or that sort of thing, it makes sense. I would probably say that well, you seem to be doing pretty well so far, you know, that anyone evaluating would look at all of the cumulative how you're doing, your performance, rather than that of late.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would you feel comfortable giving that advice to yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think I try to sometimes, but my anxiety symptoms kind of like really, like you were saying, your anxiety tells you sort of. I think I can think that, but I think my anxiety symptoms are such in the moment that it's really hard, you know, and I'm replaying what happened before in my head, anticipation, predicting that'll happen again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so let's look at the thought and the feeling. If you had to rate the percent that you believed this thought, this belief that you are not good enough to be in the program, like right now, here with me, how much of your mind believes that that's true?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would say like, you know, a two or a three, like not very, I don't believe it very much right now because, you know, I'm not presenting and it's just you and I, not like a group full of people. So that pressure is not there here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So right now you're really not buying the idea that you're not good enough to be in the program. So now let's move to let's say right near the end of like a presentation when that anxiety is there and the classmates, they could be looking at you, they could be negatively evaluating you, like that's what you're worried about. How much do you believe that thought then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, I feel really confident in that moment. It feels very real, like at any moment they're going to kick me out. Like I'm just not doing well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's that bad? Yeah. Really intense. So would you think that you're a more accurate evaluator of what's true or not now, or when you're in that state of anxiety?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Definitely now. Now when that anxiety and that, you know, heart rate and the sweating is not there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So this evaluation, the percent that you believe that thought is true, this evaluation is more accurate?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I think so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how much time in any given day would you spend kind of in a mood you're in now where you can evaluate accurately?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would say, you know, when I'm not at risk of presenting, like I feel like I spend the majority of my time, like it's not something I worry about all the time, just leading up to and then mostly that day.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So you're able to evaluate the way you are now the vast majority of the time. There's a limited amount of time when you're not, when there's a lot of emotions going through. And at those times, you're maybe a little less reliable?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right, like my judgment is clouded.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: However, in that moment, you still those beliefs are strong, right? Very. And troubling. Even though it's a small percentage, it's intense and you kind of carry that around with you a little bit. Exactly. So I can see how this is frustrating for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play – Complete Session – Social Anxiety Disorder – Part 3
video_details.description: This video features part three of a complete cognitive-behavior therapy (CBT) counseling role-play session in which CBT techniques are used to treat social anxiety disorder. Part three includes ranking automatic thoughts, the downward arrow technique, and identifying beliefs.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, this is Dr. Grande. I hope you find this video useful. If that's the case, please like it and subscribe to my channel. And as always, thanks for watching.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so let's, if we could, let's rank those two things. Right? So one is everyone's judging me if they saw how I was, and the other is a poor grade. Which one is a larger fear for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I would say maybe like judging.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So the grade's a concern...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, but I figure I could do better on a subsequent one, but when people have this opinion of you, I feel like that doesn't go away as quickly.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Um, and what, what would it mean if they, they thought you were anxious during that presentation?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I guess I worry that, that they would think I'm anxious because I don't know what I'm doing or I don't belong there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. I don't belong there. All right, so if they notice your anxiety, then they think you don't belong at that, at that level?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, like I don't deserve to be in that program.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I don't deserve to be in that program. Okay. If they don't recognize those symptoms, they wouldn't think that, but if they do, that's what they might think.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right, like that maybe they think that that's why I'm anxious or that's why I'm not doing well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, how do you feel about your abilities and status in the program you're in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think, you know, typically I'm one of the top students in my program and I seem to get the concepts pretty well. It's just when I have to demonstrate those concepts or demonstrate via like a presentation or something that I'm worried that, you know, maybe I'm an imposter or something. But so I start to question myself. But I think in general that, you know, I'm a pretty good student before this and that I'm doing pretty well in the program.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so you're a good student, you recognize that. You have this one area where you don't feel like you do a great job, and that's presentations. But in terms of grade, you've really only had one bad presentation grade. But grades aside, you're anxious and you're worried your classmates are going to pick up on that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, exactly.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So if they thought you were, you used the word imposter. So if they thought you were an imposter, let's just say that that was something they actually believed because of what's been happening. What would that mean? What would it mean to you if your classmates thought you were an imposter?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I don't know. Maybe I am. Maybe I don't deserve to be there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I don't deserve to be there.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, like maybe I shouldn't be in this program. Like maybe I should just drop out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So if they believe, if they believe you're an imposter based on these physical symptoms and this anxiety, maybe that means to you, anyway, that maybe that means you shouldn't, or you are an imposter, you shouldn't be there. What's it feel like to say that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Depressing. Yeah, I feel like I've worked really hard, you know, to get through, you know, the at least halfway through my program and it really hurts to think that that would be true.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: To think that this whole time you've really been, you've been faking it, you don't really belong there.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I'd like to move a little bit into evaluating evidence, if that's okay. Right. So in cognitive therapy, we like to look at what's, you know, what we're feeling and what we're thinking and what's, what we can see, what's observable around us and, you know, that becomes evidence and then we, we analyze it, we evaluate it. You're worried at some level, you're worried that you don't deserve to be where you are right now, that you're not good enough to be a student in this program, in the program you're in. What evidence supports that belief that you're not good enough?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Now that I'm thinking about it here, I mean, there's not a ton to support it. But in, on that day, I can think of all sorts of, you know, things to tell myself.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, let's go there then on that day.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, so maybe like, um, I'm not because I'm not prepared or because I'm messing up on the presentation that I'm going to get a bad grade and, you know, if I can't, if I can't speak in front of people, how am I going to speak in front of kids as a teacher, you know, one day, that it will translate to something else, like if I can't get past this.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So even if I survive the program somehow, I might be bad at my job.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play - Challenging Relationship with Family Member
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which cognitive-behavioral therapy techniques, including evaluating evidence, identifying strengths, and exploring beliefs, are used to treat frustration and sadness related to a challenging relationship with a family member.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, this is Dr. Grande. I hope you find this video useful. If that's the case, please like it and subscribe to my channel. And as always, thanks for watching.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Susan, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're okay. I know that when you saw me last time you were going through a bit of a struggle. How are things going with that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's still a struggle. I'm planning a surprise party for my husband and his mother doesn't talk to me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're planning a surprise party for your husband, his mom doesn't talk to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. So she doesn't really try to interact with her grandkids or me. And the way I was raised is the matriarch is going to, you know, make all attempts to, you know, keep the family connected. So I try to call her and let the kids talk to her, but she won't answer her phone. And now with the party coming up, I would like her to be there, but she's not responding.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Just so I can get a little bit of background, is this relationship new or this dynamic new? Or you've been part of this family for a while?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, we've been married for five years and dating for about 11, but we dated in the past and, you know, lost parted ways and then came back together later.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And this dynamic with his mother not talking to you, that's been the whole time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. When I got pregnant with my first daughter before we got married and he was away at school, she felt that I was trying to interrupt his studies and trap him. So she's been she disapproved of the relationship from the beginning. During the wedding, she had insight and she kind of just took over my wedding.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So she you're saying she disapproves and that she felt as though you were trying to trap her son. How did you come by this information?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, when I was pregnant, she told me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: She told you, okay. So it's not something that you were reading into it or guessing, it was fairly direct? And in kind of those words?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. She kind of said that he's in school, he's not ready for a kid, and suggested that I have an abortion.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So she made that suggestion to you and made it clear that she disapproved of the whole relationship or just the timing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think it's the whole relationship because now he's graduated, he has a great job, we have three kids, and she still behaves the same way. So I would think it's the whole relationship.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you feel as though your relationship with him has been productive for you, for him, for the children? Like it's been a success?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No? You don't feel that way? You feel it's been a failure?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Some aspects, I guess. I really believe in family, my family's not here. So I think it's really important that the family I'm a part of is together. So if I'm the cause that this family is not together, it's really hurtful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're really hurt by all this and you feel like all these relationships, none of them have been productive and successful. This has been anxiety-provoking, frustrating, sad. How long have you been with these emotions?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'll say like maybe the last three years. Because we tend to end up in like the same mix of people and activities and she treats me like I'm not even there. And then there's the kids that's just, I don't know what to say to them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So she treats you poorly, like you're not there. She doesn't interact much with the kids or at all? And how about with your husband, with her son?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I guess they still need him for stuff, so he can talk to them, they'll talk to him. He still pays for his little sister's phone bill, and she's an adult and she lives with her mom. So they still depend on him for certain things.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you feel as though that's why there's still communication? Otherwise, what would happen?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think he's also kind of dependent on them. It goes both ways. I kind of feel like there's no way he doesn't see how she behaves, and I don't feel that he is receptive to my pain.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you've conveyed to him that you have pain in this, or you haven't? So he doesn't know what's going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well no, so she at one point in time I think said something to him about when I was pregnant the first time. I think he kind of just brushed it off. But he has to be aware of his kids don't go over there, she doesn't call them. On Grandparents' Day, I suggested that he take the kids over there and call her, and he came back and said his mom said, 'Oh this must have been Susan's idea.'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're sensing a lot of hostility, but there haven't been lately anyway a lot of direct conversations.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I tried to call her regarding the party every day for like maybe a week. And when she finally answered the phone, she just said, 'Susan, stop calling me' and hung up the phone.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well that's fairly direct. Do you have any evidence that suggests that her behavior is going to change?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, I would want to. I think if I was to hang in there and be the best parent I can be, maybe eventually she'll want to have a relationship with her grandkids. I'm not really worried about her liking me as much as the children.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So even with that, you hang in there and it's your hope that she'll come around, that her attitude will change. But so far it doesn't sound like she's given you a lot of evidence that that's a likely outcome.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But you can be hopeful, of course. How about your emotions, you know the sadness, the anxiety? Is that something you want to work on to resolve those absent of a change in her?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, because I think it's important to have family and right now all I want to do is, I think it'd be best if we moved away to another state. So I'm wondering if that's just because I'm sad, you know? So maybe if I was to work on my sadness, then maybe I'll feel more okay with being here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: With all of this disapproval and all these stressors which sound really tough, do you feel as though you can move through all this if nothing in her changes? So let's just assume for a second that her behavior will never change. Can you at some level be okay with all this in terms of frustration and sadness?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think so. I can try.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I mean, is that a goal?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, because I really can't control her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's not ideal though. The ideal would be if she would warm up to you and engage in the family in a more inviting, friendlier and accepting role. There hasn't been much in our discussion here in the way of evidence that leads to that conclusion. Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So that leaves you not on your own, but it leaves you without her as a support to work through all these emotions. What do you think about when I say that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I think that it's going to be hard because I do consider how her behavior affects my kids. But I know I probably will have to like let go of wanting her approval in order to be a better, more involved parent instead of just allowing myself to stress over that relationship. If she the invite has always been there, she can always engage with the kids.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what you're saying is that that desire for approval, that's what's causing these symptoms, that's what's maintaining them. And that's what you want to be able to let go of is that desire.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you have a belief at some level that she must give you approval. There's a belief in there somewhere that reads something like that: she should give me approval.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think I'm a pretty likable person.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, you're a likable person and I would agree. And it would make sense she should give you approval. That's kind of the belief. And the consequence of that belief when it meets the reality that she doesn't seem to be giving you approval is that sadness and frustration and anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does that make sense? So the belief that you're a likable person is realistic and seems like a useful belief, but the belief that she *should* like you doesn't seem to be serving you as well.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, it's not.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It doesn't seem to be. Is there another belief that could be substituted in for that? Think about that belief as very rigid. 'She must/should like me' doesn't leave much room for an alternative. Is there another belief we could work on to put in place of that that may more accurately reflect what's going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, it's okay if or well, I believe that I'm a likable person, but it's okay that others might not feel the same.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, let's work with that. So I like keeping the 'I'm a likable person' part. So you'd say, 'I'm a likable person, but it's okay if some people don't see that.'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So when you resonate with that belief, what goes through your mind?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That I can't really force people to like me, and everyone has their own mind and they can make their own decision, but it doesn't change who I am.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Very good. I agree. So everyone has their own behavior, they're going to do what they're going to do, but it doesn't change your essence as a good person. Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you believe that new thought?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Do you believe it more than the old thought that she should approve of you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's close. Yeah, so there's a bit of a struggle there, right? Both beliefs make sense to you at the same time. So maybe as we continue to work, we can explore the evidence behind each belief and see if one of those beliefs tends to rise to the top. Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So this week between session, would it be possible for you to kind of list out all the reasons that you are likable? To list all your strengths?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you know a particular day this week you might do that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I can probably do it when the kids, the two older ones, are in Kumon. I can do it then while I'm waiting to pick them up.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Do you kind of have an idea of the first few items you might put on that list?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I think I'm sensitive, I'm caring, I'm generous, I am a good mother, I am a good cook.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. All right. So those items, and I hope you'll think of some more. Build that list out. And next week we'll start with that by evaluating that evidence. Does that sound good?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sounds good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Thanks, Susan.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play – Complete Session – Social Anxiety Disorder – Part 1
video_details.description: This video features part one of a complete cognitive-behavior therapy (CBT) counseling role-play session in which techniques including identifying automatic thoughts, using self-talk, and behavior experiments are used to treat social anxiety disorder.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, this is Dr. Grande. I hope you find this video useful. If that's the case, please like it and subscribe to my channel. And as always, thanks for watching.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, Hazel. How you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I know when we met last time for your intake, you were concerned about some presentations that you had to give at school.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You want to talk about that today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, so in school, I am in school for teaching and we have to give presentations a lot, as you can imagine, on different things. And so it's something that's recurring. And what happened was I gave a really bad one one time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A bad presentation?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I wasn't feeling very well and I gave, I think I was just really tired from studying all night and I gave a really bad presentation. And then like now ever since, like when I've tried to give subsequent presentations, I'm just so nervous and I'm up there like sweating and like starting to forget what I'm going to say and I'm just like afraid of getting up there and having to give a presentation because I feel like I'm going to vomit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So was there a time before, like recently, when you had to give presentations?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean, like before, in earlier in my, like I'm towards the end of my degree. So you know, throughout my program I have, I have.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, and how'd you do with those?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Pretty well. I mean, I consider myself a pretty good student. So normally I do pretty well. It seemed to, you know, come out of nowhere.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So this presentation that you gave where you received a poor score might've just been an isolated incident?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, like I was saying, I wasn't feeling very well, I don't think. And it really hasn't happened since.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, but that experience has still led to a lot of anxiety with subsequent presentations.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh yeah. Like I'm worried about my grades suffering as a result and, you know, how well I'm going to do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So would it be okay if we kind of step through the whole process of you giving a presentation?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Um, before I start with that, is this something that leads to anxiety like right now or other times or really just in that moment when you're presenting?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mostly, it's most intense in that moment and like maybe like leading up to it, like in preparation that I know that this is going to happen. Like I always know when I'm going to present. Like it'll be like, she'll, the teacher will say, 'Oh, well, you know, you're this Thursday, someone else is next Thursday.' So the closer it gets to that event, the more anxious I am, like in anticipation.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So you start feeling anxiety a few days before presentation or?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I would say a few days, mostly.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, and when does it start to get really distressing for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, like two days before or one day before. Then I'm like, oh my gosh, like, am I ready? Like, what if I mess up? You know, what if I get a bad grade? All these like, 'what ifs.'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So would you be okay if we step into this process and kind of break down the steps of a presentation?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So let's say that you're taking... what's one of the classes you're taking now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, early childhood.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Early childhood. So let's say you have a presentation in that class in a few days from now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, just a normal presentation.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So let's now move to two days out where you would start to feel a little anxiety about it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's going through your mind at that two day out point?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I would say like, am I prepared enough? Like, did I do enough, you know, to study or to write down? Did I do enough?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So your thought is 'Did I do enough preparation?'

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, which leads to maybe I didn't, is what I'm really thinking, like I'm not prepared enough as I should be.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. I'm not prepared enough.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So that's the thought you're having about 48 hours before the presentation. 'I'm not prepared enough.'

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And kind of thinking about that thought and what happens afterward, do you have a reaction like any type of emotional, affective reaction to that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So at that point, I'm usually like more like anxious, maybe like irritable a little bit, mostly.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. And that goes substantially unchanged, that feeling, for how long?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, like the day before, it like kind of gets more intense when I'm like nitpicking like, 'well, I forgot this' or 'I didn't forget this' and, you know, remembering what happened last time when I didn't do so well and worrying about my grade, like more thoughts pop in my head of things that I forgot or 'what if' sort of things.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so the same type of thought just more intense.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: More intense.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, and the feeling is also more intense.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

video_details.title: Video Interview - Clinical Placements in non-traditional settings
video_details.description: Kendra Bell-Hayes discusses the resources developed for the WA Clinical Training Network to facilitate Clinical Placements in non-traditional settings.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: My name's Kendra Bell Hayes and I've been employed as a project officer for the WA clinical training network. I was requested for this project to explore initially a little bit more areas of low growth in student placements.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I started to explore the areas where students traditionally weren't being taken across the sectors. We found three main areas. The first one was aged care, which has seen some growth over the last few years and is starting to improve in the number of student places that they now offer.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The second area was the justice system where obviously there's significant health needs in that population and some scope for students, but it's a pretty new and very fresh area. And the third one we looked at was private practice.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The private practice industry is growing and there's some degree of student placements there, but certainly probably not as many as they have the scope for. So we felt that it was important to start looking into that area specifically a little bit more.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We initially surveyed private practices in Western Australia to see what the barriers were and what they found, as well as the benefits, which obviously is what we need to increase people's awareness of how much having a student on placement can really benefit an organization.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The toolkit actually works through a little bit of the information from the surveys that we found, where we talk to practitioners who have had students and those who were very reluctant to have students as well. And then we designed a simple model or framework that the private practices can start to look at based on three key themes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The first theme was around the idea of benefits. For the private practice industry, they really needed to start to think about and explore more in depth what benefits a student actually has for them and to start to really look at both the tangible and intangible benefits of having a student.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The second component was obviously the big one for private practices: the cost. Cost was often cited as the most frequent barrier and in lots of different ways, like loss of time, loss of income, difficulty supervising, and those sorts of elements.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We factored that into the model, and the toolkit helps private practices explore some of the assumptions that are being made about whether they actually can charge for student time. But we wanted to flag for private practices to really just sit down and say what actually would it cost us to have students and would the benefit outweigh that?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The third part of the toolkit explores the thing that most places have difficulty: any sector needs support for implementation of placements. Yes, I'm convinced I want to have students on placement, but how do I start? Where do I start?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We have some templates around orientating students into a private practice and some of the preparation students may need because it is quite a different sector and organization and very differently structured. We need to prepare students better for the environment and the context.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This goes down to things such as client consent and even how to script it so that clients are interested in having students rather than being fearful of what a student might mean in that private practice context.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Private practices should find it a really simple, easy tool to access and to start thinking about whether they could take a student, and if they're already taking students, how they could do that better. It would be easy for them to implement and there's huge potential and scope for students to really have a big impact.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We'd encourage private practices just to sit down and take a bit of time to have a look through it. It's also for the universities to have it as a backup when they start to ask some of those sectors to think about having students, that they actually can refer them to the toolkit and give them some direction.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The toolkit will help to help structure some placements in private practice and it should be of benefit to the university sector as well.

video_details.title: ACT Therapy-Advanced Counseling

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello Joy, I'm glad to have you back today. How are you doing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Pretty good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good deal. Now, did you get some of your homework done that I had assigned with you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I did. I did.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Well, before we go through that list, did you have any moment this week where you had to do any public speaking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. Um, I was assigned to train the other officers that I work with on a field app that we created. I did it with another coworker and we were supposed to train everybody else.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I see. Okay. So, was it distressing? Or did you have better luck this time of how it went?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh no. Oh no. It was very distressing. I just get so nervous before I have to stand up in front of people. For some reason, if it's in a room of strangers, like an interview, I'm so much better. But when it's with people that I work with daily, I just have so much anxiety about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. I understand. Okay. So, you had to do this. If you were to rate that from one to ten, how distressing was this event?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Ten. Really, just as much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so through the exercise that I had you do at home, did you write down a list of things that you do in the moment that you tried to do to alleviate the problem?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I did. I wrote a few things down.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, let me hear them.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's that classic one where if you stand up in front of a group of people, you're supposed to imagine that they're all in their underwear. And so I did that. It didn't work.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, it didn't work. Alright, what else did you have on the list?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I knew what I was going to have to present and for days beforehand, I would go over it in my head and stand in front of a mirror and say the script, thinking that if I prepared more I wouldn't forget. But then I get so anxious that when it's time for me to actually say something, all of a sudden my mind goes blank.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, it actually caused you more anxiety to try to do that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, it did.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Did you have anything else on the list?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I tried deep breathing right before I know that I'm going to have to say something. I try to take really deep breaths and let them out slowly to try to slow my heart rate down. It works maybe for a split second, but then I immediately will start to obsess over it and the fear just comes right back.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it causes you to obsess over it even more whenever you try to do these things. When you try to diffuse the moment and alleviate the anxiety, it just gets worse. Is that correct?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, it does. And I guess the last thing I wrote down was that up until the moment, I just try to think about other things.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And that doesn't help.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Doesn't help at all.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, the reason why I asked you to write down some things was simply because it obviously did not alleviate any of the problems. It didn't alleviate your anxiety or stress. Those self-help steps don't really work. So because of that, I'm going to ask you simply to rip that piece of paper up today because it doesn't help. So we're no longer going to do the list.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We're going to do that simply because I think there's a new identity for Joy in accepting the fear that you have. Through counseling, we'll help you have better self-confidence by accepting the fact that you do have public speaking anxiety, but you do well at it. You're going to have better confidence in being able to adapt to your anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would you be willing to learn how to accept that? I've got several exercises.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, because obviously nothing I've done has worked.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Exactly. No self-help things can actually alleviate the problem. There are all types of exercises to empower you to see yourself as a good speaker, but also accepting the fear, which may never go away. Would you be willing to do an exercise today? I have an exercise on nine emotions that are normal responses to help you understand what's normal.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, Joy, we're going to do this exercise to get a better understanding of some real emotions you experience. I'm going to name nine basic emotions, and you give me a thumbs up if it's a good emotion to you and a thumbs down if it's negative. Love. Joy. Curiosity. Anger. Fear. Sadness. Guilt. Shock. Disgust.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Six of the nine emotions you put thumbs down for, which is interesting because those are normal human responses. This exercise is helpful for you to know that those are normal emotions everyone experiences. Every person you encounter in public speaking has those responses.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If you can think of everyone experiencing these emotions, like curiosity, anger, fear, sadness, guilt, shame... fear is a huge response everyone has. That could help you accept that you're not the only one with fear. You have fear for public speaking, but you are not the only person who experiences fear. Those are just normal responses.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That it's not just me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Exactly. It's not just you. And they're normal. You're normal. Okay, we're going to do a mindfulness exercise if that's alright. I think it would be helpful for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. I'm going to read some things aloud and I would like you to sit up straight and follow the prompts. I invite you to sit upright in your chair with your back straight and your feet flat on the floor. Most people find they feel more alert and awake sitting this way. Check it out and see if this is the case for you. Either close your eyes or fix them on a spot and take a few slow, deep breaths, noticing the breath flowing in and out of your lungs.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now quickly scan your body from head to toe, starting at your scalp and moving downward. Notice the sensations in your head, throat, neck, shoulders, chest, abdomen, arms, hands, and legs. And now your feet. Now zoom in on the part of your body where you're feeling this feeling most intensely. Observe the feeling closely as if you're a curious scientist who has never encountered anything like it before.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Observe the sensation carefully. Let your thoughts come and go like passing cars and keep your attention on the feeling. Notice where it starts and where it stops. Learn as much about it as you can. If you drew an outline around it, what shape would it have? Is it on the surface of the body or inside of you, or both? How far inside does it go?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Where is it the most intense and where is it the weakest? If you drift off into your thoughts, as soon as you realize it, come back and focus on the sensation. Observe it with curiosity. How is it different in the center than around the edges? Is it light or heavy? Moving or still?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is its temperature? Are there any hot spots or cold spots? Notice the different elements within it. Notice that it's not just one sensation, there are sensations within sensations. Notice the different layers. As you're observing this feeling, breathe into it. Imagine your breath flowing into and around the feeling.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: As you're breathing into it, imagine space opening up inside of you. You open up around this feeling and make space for it. See if you can just allow this feeling to be here. You don't have to like it or want it, just allow it. Let it be. Observe it, breathe into it, and open up around it and allow it to be as it is.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You may feel a strong urge to fight with it or push it away. If so, just acknowledge the urge without acting on it. Continue observing the sensation. Don't try to get rid of it or alter it. Changing or getting rid of it is not the goal. Your aim is simply to allow it, to let it be.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Imagine this feeling is an object. What shape does it have? Is it a liquid, solid or gas? Is it moving or still? What color is it? If you could touch the surface, what would it feel like? Wet or dry? Rough or smooth? Hot or cold? Soft or hard?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Observe this object curiously. Breathe into it and open up around it. Notice that you are bigger than the object, no matter how big it gets. It can never get bigger than you. This feeling tells you that you're a normal human being with a human heart. It tells you that there are things in life that matter to you. This is what humans feel when there's a gap between what we want and what we've got.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now take one of your hands and place it on this part of your body. Imagine that this is a healing hand. Feel the warmth flowing from your hand into your body, not to get rid of the feeling, but to make room for it, to soften up and loosen up around it. Hold it gently, as if it's a crying baby or a frightened puppy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Letting your hand fall, once again, breathe into the feeling and expand around it. Life is like a stage show. On that stage are all your thoughts and all of your feelings. For the last few minutes, we dimmed the lights on the stage and shined a spotlight on this feeling. Now it's time to bring up the rest of the lights.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Bring up the lights on your body. Notice your arms, legs, head, and neck. Notice that you're in control of your arms and legs regardless of what you're feeling. Move them around a little to check for yourself. Take a stretch and notice yourself stretching. Now bring up the lights on the room around you. Open your eyes and look around. Notice that there's not just a feeling here, but a feeling inside a body, inside a room, inside a world full of opportunity. Welcome back.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So how did that make you feel?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Wow.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Was it relaxing? Did it enlighten you in a sense of becoming more in control of your body and your anxiety?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It actually made me feel like that feeling just is.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It exists. It just is.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: And it's Joy. And it's okay. It's just another part of me like any other part of me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Exactly. So you did find that helpful. Good. We've got several more exercises. I'd like to see you come back next week if that's okay. Our time has run short today, but I'll see you next week if that's alright.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. Okay. Thank you.

video_details.title: CGT Self-Harm in Teens - Motivational Interviewing Demonstration
video_details.description: In this mock-case study, Dr. S facilitates a therapy session with a 16 year old self-harming teen named Gina. The purpose of the video is to demonstrate Motivational Interviewing techniques.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Gina, I haven't seen you in a few weeks. I know it was hard for you to come today and this has kind of been a hard process. So, I'm really glad that you came today. I just want to check in and see how things are going.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Been in a couple of fights with my mom, cut a few times, but not as much as before.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you've cut a couple times since we've met, but not as much as before. You did have a few fights with your mom. So Gina, tell me about where you're at in terms of your feelings about cutting and what your thoughts are about changing that behavior.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I know it's bad, but sometimes I just want to do it because I know it'll help me feel better right away. I don't know that having a bath will make me feel better right away necessarily.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You have mixed feelings about it. It sounds to me like there's some good things about it and you know it's helpful, it makes you feel better right away. And you're not entirely sure that having a bath and the mini-vacation idea is going to work as quickly or work as well. And so there's sort of two sides of it for you. Wondering if the mini-vacation and having a bath will be as helpful for you. What are some of the drawbacks to having a bath and doing the mini-vacation do you think?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess there's nothing bad about it really. I'm just used to having that immediate release when I cut.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's maybe not as immediate for you, you have to draw the bath and it might take a bit more time. And it's different. What are some of the good positive parts about choosing to do have a bath and self-soothe in that way do you think?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's relaxing. I get to be clean and smell good. I can listen to my music. It's sort of like a treat for me. So, and I don't wake up the next day with scars.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's maybe a big one for you, right? That you're waking up, you don't have any scars, you got to listen to your music, you're smelling good, you're feeling good maybe. So you listed lots of positives, but you know there's still these two parts of yourself. Remember in some of the other sessions we've had, we talked about what you Gina as a person, what you value and what's important to you. Do you remember what those things were you'd identified?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: One was independence and two was privacy. Yeah, those were the main things.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So independence and privacy were important to you in terms of what you value in your life. So when you think about independence and you think about privacy, where do you see cutting impacting that? Like how does that fit with those two things? How does cutting fit with independence, why don't we start there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I decide to cut myself and it's my own decision.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there's independence in terms of those choices. Okay. Any consequences of cutting on your independence do you think?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's not a good thing. Yeah, I'm in control, but it doesn't work out for the best.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you are in control but it doesn't work out for the best. Yeah. And there has been some consequences in terms of your mom curtailing your independence based on your cutting.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Definitely. She takes away my independence and so it seems like a bad cycle.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So your mom is sort of pulling back on your independence when it gets into a bad cycle. And then which makes you more mad, which makes you want to cut again. So it becomes a real vicious circle almost, yeah. How about privacy? What does, how does cutting affect privacy for you, that value?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It impacts it in a bad way because I have to be private about hiding my scars, but it's kind of a good way too because I get to do it in private. Nobody else sees me and so I feel good about having that private thing that only I can do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It needs to happen in private and that being wanting to be in private and cutting, those two things go together. But the downside is that you're almost required to be private because you have to hide yourself and be so conscious all the time of covering up and keeping the secret. So you talked about having mixed feelings about deciding to cut or not to cut, there's lots of different feelings for you about that. One of the things I wondered about is, you know, if you imagine what would things look like for you in a year from now if cutting is still in your life. What do you envision it would look like? So you'd be one year older, you'd be 17. What do you think when you imagine that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just feel like it will probably be worse. I feel like I'll have way more scars, they could even be somewhere else, not just my arms, maybe my legs because if I just keep going then there'd be nowhere else to cut and they just could get really bad I think. Lots more scars. I would not even have a chance of going back on the swim team at all or doing anything like that. I think it would be bad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you just feel like there'd be lots of consequences down the road. There'd be lots more scars, maybe more spots, and really afraid that it wouldn't be an option to go on the swim team. And that'd be bad for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
