diarization.text: Yeah, I feel like right now I could probably go back if I stop cutting but once I heal it could be okay but if I keep going the way I'm going I don't know if I could hide it. It might stick around forever.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you have hope right now that you could return to the swim team and that is important to you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

video_details.title: Interpersonal Psychotherapy for Depression Video
video_details.description:
For the full video, go to: http://www.psychotherapy.net/video/interpersonal-psychotherapy-depression

How do you introduce social efforts into treatment for a condition known for its isolating effects? In this video, three seasoned therapists offer key techniques from Interpersonal Psychotherapy (IPT) that target the most relational symptoms of depression.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You mentioned before that you had felt closer to your daughter at one time than you do now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, before we moved to Canada. We were close.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: But now we seem to, I don't know why I just seem to get so angry with her and I feel she does not honor me as her mother.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there's something about this transition that's been very difficult on your relationship with your daughter. She's moved from one of these inner circles to this more distant one. And I can see as you're speaking of her that this is quite painful for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I love my daughter. But things seem to be different since we have been here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What you described about your daughter being out here even though you would like her to be closer, that's exactly the focus of the work that we'll be doing together. We'll be looking at those important relationships and finding ways to bring those people closer to you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: IPT really focuses on the centrality of relationships and universal problems related to loss, change, and conflict. It's rooted in interpersonal theories that are clinically helpful and there's a strong body of research that has shown it to be a highly powerful and effective treatment for clinical depression in the context of life events.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play - Loss of Hope
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which cognitive-behavioral therapy techniques, including evaluating evidence, identifying strengths, challenging automatic thoughts, and creating self-talk are used to treat sadness and frustration associated with a loss of hope.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi this is Dr. Grande. I hope you find this video useful. If that's the case please like it and subscribe to my channel. And as always, thanks for watching.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And Andrew, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hey Doc, nice to see you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Nice to see you. It's been about a week since I've seen you last. I know you're having some different difficulties particularly at work. Any changes there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really. I mean it's pretty much the same pace. I'm very frustrated with the whole system. I'm working with inner city kids, African-American kids, males in particular. I sit and talk with these kids and realize there's not much I can do for them. It's frustrating and depressing to do this every day.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So as you're working with these youth, you're looking at their circumstances and saying the odds just don't look good for major improvement. And that's leading you to lose hope in your ability to help them.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Absolutely. It's their reality. A kid comes in and mom's either in prison or dad is incarcerated. This kid has absolutely no life skills and is convinced this is who he is for the rest of his life. He sits in front of me looking for answers and I don't know if I have them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What kind of questions do they ask you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's more just statements of 'this is my life, the struggle is real'. I'm trying to draw them out of that mindset but it's years of social conditioning. I just don't know if I have the skills to really break through that way of thinking.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so can you think of a particular case, a particular youth you're working with where you're finding this struggle? One where you don't seem like you have much hope for them?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes I do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's his self-statement that's getting a reaction from you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That he's a drug dealer and he's not going to stop. He's involved with gang activity and that's his family. Even the thought of going back to prison doesn't shake this kid.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Not afraid of that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not afraid of it. For them, jail is like going to the school courtyard because all his boys are in jail. I'm sitting here wondering what kind of options I can give him when I don't even believe he has any at this point.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So your automatic thought is 'I don't believe he has any options'. That's what's going through your mind when he says he's involved in gang activity and wants to continue dealing drugs. Right? That's your thought.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's my thought.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: There's no way out for him.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't see it. I really don't see it for him. He's self-medicating and giving dirty urine to the probation office. He doesn't care. The kid just seems intent to live this life.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So in a sense your mood, the sadness and frustration, is linked to this youth's statements and his philosophy. You're reacting to his belief that success is not an option as you would think of success.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. To a certain degree I understand where he's coming from. I was raised with the understanding that being born black and male with a record means life is over. I'm having a difficult time trying to give this kid any glimpse of hope.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's hard for you to give hope when you can understand his situation and how the deck is stacked severely against him.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Severely, yeah. A conviction in this country pretty much relegates you to a certain level of society in my opinion.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In terms of employment opportunities?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: In terms of employment opportunities and things like that. It's just an absolute sense of hopelessness from this kid. He laughs about it and asks why I care so much. I'm starting not to care anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're starting to mirror that approach, the approach he's using.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes I am.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what's bothering you in all this is not only the circumstances, but also that you're losing hope for him and for others like him. Have you expressed that sentiment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No I haven't. Because to do that I think gives the kid credibility. I don't want to increase his way of thinking or give him a license to be an asshole so to speak.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You don't want to let on that his loss of hope is really something you kind of share. You understand that his lack of hope is grounded in a lot of reality. At the same time, do you believe there's hope at some level?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Absolutely. At my core I do believe there is hope at some level. I believe in resilience. But it's just hard to peel back so many different layers with this particular generation of kids. It really takes a lot out of you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's hard to get through.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hard to penetrate that shell. I leave work some days saying I'm not coming back. I've had enough. It's depressing after a while.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's go back to that automatic thought. When he says his life is essentially defined by narrow parameters like drug dealing, and you're thinking there may not be hope. That's the automatic thought you're having.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Pretty much, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Your reaction to that is to not help them or to not say what you feel to them? What's going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't want to say what I feel because I think for them it's going to be a license to continue the behavior. So I just sit there and BS them because what I really want to say I don't think would be beneficial.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Partially because of the message but partially because of how they would interpret it. What is the message? Tell me what you would want to say to them.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That what they've said is real. Broken homes and racism are real. But at the same time, someone else made it out. I came from the same scenario, so I'm no different. There has to be some quality to be tapped into to center us as we go along. I'm just not sure how it would be received.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So your concern seems to be that they would hear the first part but not really the second part. They would hear their concerns are legitimate but not hear that there is hope.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Exactly. I wouldn't want that. It would tarnish my reputation and probably hurt my employment here. So I bite my tongue.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there a way to deliver your message with realism and heart without including a piece that you feel like they could latch onto negatively?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe if I switched it around and I put the last part first. Or maybe I don't tell them at all and just make reference to have them come to the same conclusion.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Give them the tools to figure it out for themselves.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: If what you're saying is true, then how did this person from the same neighborhood succeed? How do you explain that? I think that might be a better way of taking the sting out of it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If that's the new message, how likely do you think you'd be able to deliver that if somebody told you they wanted to continue in an unproductive lifestyle?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think it would work. I think the problem for me is I gotta buy into it first. I've been inundated with so much negativity. Kids know right away if you're being authentic or not.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you feel like you need to be more genuine in your acceptance of the message before you can effectively deliver it. This is really about you losing some hope.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, it is.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what's your belief about their reality if you unfiltered your belief about their chances of success?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They are very adaptable, but they are missing key life skills that keep them locked in. They are mentally incarcerated. It's frustrating because that message is reinforced by everyone around them. It's easier to think it's all society and there's no personal responsibility.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So they've been exposed to a tough message all around them, but a part of you still appreciates their adaptability and survival skills.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They remind me of soldiers, just numb to the pain. The hardest part is getting them to come out of that survival mode. I'm becoming hardened and realizing it's just a job.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Or exposure to that environment makes you disconnected from believing solutions are possible. How do they move out of survival mode? What's the next stage?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The next stage is growth. Accepting the reality and realizing it's not going to change unless I take responsibility. How do I move beyond this to the next stage of development?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In a similar way, is the solution the same for you? Do you need to accept the reality of your work environment and who you're working with?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think you're right Doc. The same solution applies to me. I probably need a dose of my own medicine in that regard.

video_details.title: Counselling Skills- Diversity
video_details.description: This is a role play of a session where the Helper in a Human Resources Dept. is using counselling skills to enable the man to talk about a difficulty with a black female colleague. She uses the skill of Immediacy to name what he might be finding difficult. This role play is useful for anyone interested in healthy communications but it is particularly targeted at Level 2 & Level 3 counselling students. Jheni and I teach CPCAB counselling courses. If you have any comments or questions we would be

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello there. Donald, isn't it? Yeah, yeah. How are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'm okay. You're looking very nervous. Yeah, I'm a bit nervous, yeah. Mary, I don't know if you know Mary, she's my line manager. She has been a few things going on really in the office and she said it would be a good idea to talk to you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, see what you want to talk about what's going on in the office. Okay. So let me just tell you a bit about everything you say here will be confidential. There are limits, however. So if you tell me that you're going to harm somebody or seriously harm yourself, I'm going to have to do something. I'm going to have to tell somebody else. How does that kind of feel?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's all right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And also as well I work to the BACP ethical framework. And all that is really, it's the British Association for Counselors and Psychotherapists, and they just have a set of guidelines that I need to kind of adhere to. And what that means in real terms is that I'm going to endeavor to work in your best interest and ensure that you're safe and where we're kind of working with what you want to work with. Yeah?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's a relief.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that okay? I can see that, yeah, it's really difficult for you. And as well today we've got about 15 minutes. Is that going to be okay? Yeah, that's all right. So do you want to tell me a little bit about what's going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's one of my colleagues and it's confidential if I say the name, you won't...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Absolutely, whatever you say here will not go anywhere else, apart from as I said before, if harm to self or harm to others, and that doesn't kind of include what you may say about somebody. Okay, so is that okay? Yeah, that's all right.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I feel really bad, but we're not getting on and I think part of it is, oh, I don't want to shop anybody, but it's Claudette. And sometimes she just doesn't pull her weight and sometimes she goes off and I'm left with an awful lot of stuff.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So she doesn't do what's expected, she leaves it for you to do, is that what you feel?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's what I feel, yeah, that I'm being left with an awful lot of stuff to deal with. And I feel absolutely ridiculous because I think if it was someone else, I'd be able to let them know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's difficult you can't tell Claudette what you're feeling. Yeah, I find it really hard. Do you want to say a bit more about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I suppose in the current climate, I'm a bit afraid and it's funny, you look a bit like her. Well, no, you don't look a bit like her actually. I don't know how to say it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it feels as if Claudette's a Black woman within your organization and you're not getting on, she kind of leaves a lot for you to do, a sense that she's not fulfilling her obligation. And it's difficult for you to talk about, and I would imagine being with me, I'm assuming she's a Black woman, I'm a Black woman, so I'm assuming that it might be difficult for you to talk to me about this. I just want to assure you that once again, whatever you talk about stays within this room. The idea is that you can come here and bring whatever you need to bring. I imagine you're kind of thinking, oh, I might offend me. I want to tell you, I don't think you will offend me. I want to hear what you've got to say, what it's been like for you and that's going to be the kind of focus of the work in some way. And we'll look at the relationship between you and your colleague as well, but I want you to be able to be free to say whatever you feel you need to. How does that feel? Because I can imagine it must be difficult for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think it's the whole nub of the problem, because I think I'm afraid of offending her too. And not afraid of offending her by kind of reminding her what our responsibilities are and that you know, I've got a home life too. To be honest, I'm afraid that someone's going to call me a racist.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Someone's going to call you a racist.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: And I don't think I am, but I worry am I? I don't know, it's just really difficult.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So again, there is a conflict with your colleague and you kind of fear if you kind of maybe talk about what's really inside of you, you're going to be perceived as a racist. And I'm wondering, do you think I'm going to perceive you like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I wonder if maybe the minute I met you, I might have thought that you would, but no, I don't because you've been so clear about it's okay to recognize that you're Black and that this person might be Black and turns out she is, and that it's actually okay to talk about things like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It really is okay. As I said earlier on, if and when you do offend me, I'm quite happy to have that discussion with you, but it doesn't feel as if what feels important is for you to have a space to talk about and be open about what you're kind of feeling without fear of, you know, anybody else hearing or anybody accusing you of being a racist.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: And I've talked to friends because it's kind of getting worse and worse and it's at the stage where friends are saying, what do you mean you can't go for a drink again or you can't go for a coffee again? You're working late again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's kind of really infringing on other relationships within your workplace and your kind of social life outside of the workplace. So it feels quite big. Yeah, I think it is actually. And in some ways, I don't know, maybe they don't help or maybe they're trying to do the best they can, but when I tell them about it, they kind of say, you want to be careful because you're going to be labeled a racist. So you kind of haven't found any other place where you can talk about it without people possibly thinking, oh, you may be a racist.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So again, I want to invite you to bring whatever you're feeling here. And how does that kind of feel? Because I can see our obvious difference, but again, does that feel like something that you could do here?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It feels really good actually. And it feels particularly good talking to a Black woman about it. So tell me about your work, your relationship with Claudette. Well, we work alongside each other. We've known each other for several years. But just, I don't know, maybe it's over the last six months or so, it started off with, oh, could you do me a favor? And now it's she saying to me, could I do her a favor and do something that really either we should do together or that is her responsibility and not mine. And yeah, you know, you give somebody a dig out, but that's fair enough. But it's kind of she doesn't even ask anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there's just an assumption that you will do these things. That I'm going to be there and that I won't get up and leave until you know, whatever the job is that we're doing at the moment is done. And I can see that's quite, yeah, it's really, really difficult.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It is, it's really hard. It's really hard. And I suppose I should just get up and go when I've done my work, but I don't know why I don't want to.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me a bit about why you don't. Maybe it's fear of reprisal.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So something may happen if you do what you feel you need to. Yeah. And it feels like a great sense of something awful may happen.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that I'll be blamed. Right. That I'll be blamed. And a fear that I might have to point the finger because actually she and I got on really well to begin with.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And I suppose I wonder what stops you from talking to Claudette? You've talked about you don't want to be perceived as a racist, but it feels as if there has been a relationship between the two of you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, though very much a work relationship. Right. I mean, we don't really socialize together or anything like that, so it's very much a kind of a work relationship.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And the conflict is within the work relationship. Yeah, yeah. But it's just so, so I don't know, like I say, if it was someone else I think and I think in the past I have, but just the difficulty with Claudette. I'm wondering, what would you want to say to Claudette?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think I'd want to let her know that it's not fair, that I feel really put upon, that you know, it's a shared responsibility and I feel that it's all been put on me. And I wouldn't want to say it's all your fault, but just find some way of letting her know that I'm just not happy with the situation.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, what you've just said to me sounds perfectly reasonable. But there's also this kind of backdrop of, oh, I might be accused of being a racist. And in terms of what you've just kind of expressed, does it still feel difficult maybe to go back and have that type of conversation with Claudette?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think it feels easier right now when I'm talking to you about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And of course I don't work in your building, you haven't got to see me every day, yeah, I can appreciate that. But I'm not sure if it will be easier 10 minutes after I leave here. I mean, maybe it will, but... and don't get me wrong, I wasn't suggesting, I was just kind of looking at maybe ways in which you could kind of broach it, we've only kind of just met each other. But I imagine that what we could kind of look at, if you know, you want to kind of continue, is how we might work through this situation and how you might find a place where you can talk about exactly what you feel without causing offense. It doesn't feel as if you would, but I can appreciate that that's kind of at the back of your mind. Is that something that you'd feel that you'd want to kind of pursue?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, absolutely, absolutely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And we could certainly offer you the time and the sessions here. And just to kind of say as well, you know, I'm not a qualified counselor, I've done a counseling skills course. I'm well equipped to listen to, you know, what it's been like for you. I'm well equipped to, you know, almost work alongside you in finding a solution to what's kind of going on. I wonder how that kind of feels.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It feels really good. It feels really good. Because I'm thinking it's not the first time I've been here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In terms of how you're feeling?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: In terms of I know I said earlier that I think if it was somebody else and sometimes I have been able to talk through things, but I think I do take an awful lot on and I think some of that might be me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you want to look at kind of what your role is in within your relationship and what your role is within, you know, the workplace as it were, because you're saying that sometimes you may take things on. And that's something else that we could probably explore in our time together, if you were to kind of take up the option. How does that kind of feel for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it feels really good. It feels really good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We've got a couple of minutes left, but I kind of wonder because it does feel quite big, I wonder how it feels to have talked about it with me as well today.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Lovely actually. It kind of feels like even in a few minutes I've made some sort of start. And you're a Black woman and you didn't accuse me of being a racist.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Not at all, that's not how I've experienced you today. And I don't know what your experiences at work, but we could actually even have a look at that because it may not be that. And then again, it may, but we will have the time and the energy to kind of look at that. And hopefully you'll be clearer in the coming weeks. How does that feel?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Feels really good because I think already I'm thinking a part of it is that, but actually maybe not the bigger part of it, maybe that's convenient.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And I really do want, I want to stress, I want you to be able to bring that here if you feel that that is part of the issue. I won't shirk away from, you know, you exploring your relationship with somebody that is a bit different from you. I really am able to hear that. Yeah? And if we do, then it feels as if we're working with the whole picture rather than ignoring that piece, yeah?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah. And I think maybe that's something that I'd find really useful is to look at the whole picture. Because yeah, if I do need to have a conversation, for me to understand the whole picture might make that conversation...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Absolutely, it's about, you know, maybe we can look at it from a new perspective as it were, or different perspectives, because you have a perspective on it, there might be other angles from which we could view it. Does that feel kind of okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that could be really useful, really useful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, we've come to the end of our session now. Okay. It was a pleasure to talk to you and I just want to kind of say thank you for being so open. I want to appreciate that it must have been very, very difficult for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's feeling a lot less difficult now, it really is. Good, good. So maybe I can get back to work.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Absolutely, absolutely and I suppose in the knowledge that you know you've got somewhere you can take some of what you're feeling. Yeah? So I could keep talking it through with you, could I? Absolutely, we've got six sessions ahead if you want to kind of take that, then we can use those six sessions towards the end. We could look at what happens next, how far you are within the process, you know, whether or not you've got what you want or whatever you need. Yeah? Does that feel like something that's going to fit in with what you need?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Absolutely. I think just being able to talk it through with somebody who's not going to say, oh you need to be so careful, or you need to be whatever. And they probably mean well, but just to be able to talk it through to somebody who's going to be open with it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yes, yes, and you don't need to be careful here. Okay. You don't need to be careful at all, say what's on your mind. Great, yeah, that sounds good. Well it's been great talking to you today, yeah? Thanks. And yeah, if you want to continue, it's kind of Thursday afternoon, early evening, round about 3:00, is that okay for you in terms of time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's good, I'll just have to check with Mary that that would be okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But yeah, and I'm happy, yeah, and I'm happy to kind of negotiate if you need to, time and date. Yeah? Right. Okay, well thanks a million. And thank you, I really want to appreciate what you've shared with me today. Thank you.

video_details.title: Mock counselling session number 1- Mena Practical
video_details.description: Initial Mock counselling session

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Neda, welcome.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hi, how are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good. I've been looking forward to meeting you. Did you find the place okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I did. I'm not very familiar with this area, but I did find it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's good. I was wondering if you got a chance to read and sign the paperwork, the contract given in reception.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I did.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Excellent. I want to go through confidentiality to ensure you understand. This is a safe space to talk about concerns. Everything is confidential, except if you're at risk of harm to yourself or others, if notes are subpoenaed, or if I discuss cases with my supervisor. Is that okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, that makes sense.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If I have to breach confidentiality, I'll discuss it with you first.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We have weekly sessions. They're free for the first six under Medicare, then $70 each. Is that okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yep, that's fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You can cancel anytime, but we require 24 hours' notice. Have you been to counseling before?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, this is my first time. I'm a little nervous and not sure what to expect.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's normal to feel nervous. We'll work together collaboratively toward your goals. Was there anything else in the contract you needed clarified?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, there's a bit about referrals that I wasn't quite sure about.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Referrals occur if we feel you need support from external or specialist services. We'd discuss it and get your consent first. They can happen at any stage.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there anything else regarding expectations from me or yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just understand that I tell you my problems and you'll help me fix them. That's what I'm hoping for.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We don't have a magic wand, but we'll work together to find options and solutions. So, what brought you to counseling?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've been in a relationship for six months and want to get married, but he's not on the same page. My mother is also very unwell, and my boss is putting a lot of pressure on me. I'm having trouble juggling everything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like all of these things combined are making you feel quite overwhelmed.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Very. Coming home to deal with my mother and relationship, then going to work, makes me really upset.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How long have you been dealing with these issues?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's ramped up in the last three months, though the relationship is six months old. It's starting to get worse.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How have you been coping with these pressures?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not very well. I take it day by day. This is my first time in counseling and I don't have anyone else to turn to.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We're here to support you. Between the relationship concerns, your sick mother, and work pressure, which would you say is the biggest concern to prioritize?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Dealing with my mother and relationship are equal because she's pressuring me to get married while she's unwell. That's the number one thing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: By 'dealing with that concern,' do you mean the relationship with your mother or your partner?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably my partner first, because I'm putting pressure on him due to what's happening with my mother.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We can focus on that first, then address the other areas. We have a few minutes left; any other questions?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: What happens if I need more than the six free sessions? Money is a factor.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: After six sessions, it's $70 each. You can continue as long as needed, and we'll work out the best timeframe together.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If there are no other questions, we can book a time for next week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Definitely. Do I speak to reception?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'll come out with you to sort that out. It was lovely meeting you and thank you for opening up. We'll focus on the topic of you and your partner next time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, thank you very much.

video_details.title: Difficult Conversation Theory
video_details.description: These masterclasses were recorded for the WA Clinical Training Network as part of the ‘Leadership Development Program: Leading Collaboratively in Simulation Learning Environments’ delivered by AIM WA in August 2016.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Mrs. Hurd, nice to meet you. Please take a seat.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hi Dr. Young, nice to see you again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How are you doing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, well thanks.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I understand that you wanted to have a bit of a chat about vaccinations for Billy?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just came in for a baby check, so I know you guys always go in about vaccines at the eight-week mark, so I guess we have to talk about it today.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Absolutely. Okay, so we're going to vaccinate Billy today as well as part of the baby check.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, no. Same as the first two kids, we're not doing vaccinations today.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, okay. Can you tell me why that's the case?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've done my research. I know about the formaldehyde, mercury, and antifreeze. We know it's associated with autism. Don't tell me about the studies; they've been sponsored by Big Pharma.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, where are you getting your facts from when you say it's linked to all of these things?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The internet, Cochrane reviews.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so the data out there has been completely disproven. All of the risks about autism, that's not true. All of the toxins you talk about are in very safe doses; there's no evidence behind any of that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: If something happened to my child, I have to take responsibility for that. I'm not willing to put my child at risk, and you can't look me in the eye and say that there's not a single risk with vaccines and it's completely safe.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I mean, there are very small risks with vaccines, but the diseases it prevents are huge and they can be debilitating.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can't help the disease, but I can stop my kid from getting harm from a vaccine. That's in my control. I couldn't live with myself if something happened.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, look, would you let your kid ride a bike without a helmet?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Of course I wouldn't.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Exactly, okay. So the helmet is the vaccine that protects the kid.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, the helmet doesn't have poisonous chemicals in it and cause kids to be permanently brain-damaged. What do you think I am?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The vaccines don't have that in it, okay? That's not true. You can't believe everything that you see on the internet.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Anyway, let's talk about the baby check. I'm not interested in getting vaccines.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Ultimately, that's your decision. My medical advice would be that it would be completely the wrong thing to do, but I can only give you that advice. Whether you take it or not is completely up to you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Alright, let's just get on with the baby check.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, let's do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay Sarah, so the baby check is done.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He's pretty cute.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, and Billy's passed with flying colors. I first of all like to apologize; I feel that I didn't let you get your concerns across and I don't think I was listening as well as I should have done. If it's okay with you, I'd just like to address some of your concerns.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so can I ask, what's the main concern you're having with Billy having the vaccination?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I know that it can be harmful and I just don't think I could live with myself if I had to take that responsibility that it was me that said yes to a vaccine that hurt my kid. I'm not interested in doing something that might be the reason they end up with something permanently wrong.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so it's the harm to Billy that you're concerned about. It's Billy's safety and Billy's welfare essentially. Is there anything else there that particularly concerns you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, it's just scary about all the crap that's in it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, okay. Anything in particular that's in the vaccine that you wanted to discuss or that you're worried about?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I know it's all in small quantities, but it's still there. You can never say that it's completely safe, and if it was that small chance that something happened to my baby, I'd be responsible.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And Sarah, you're right. Of course, there's nothing that we do in medicine which doesn't have a risk attached to it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think our points of view are actually more aligned than what you might think. My primary concern is for Billy, as I can see yours is as well. Ultimately, we both just want Billy to be happy and healthy.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I can tell you're very intelligent and that you understand how research works. The trouble with so much data out there is knowing which bits to take. If it's okay with you, I'd like to share some data with you so you can make a fully informed decision for Billy's healthcare.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'll have a read. I don't think it's ever a bad thing to read stuff.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, perfect. And maybe after you've had a read of that information, we can come back and have a further discussion if you'd like to.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, yeah. Sounds good. Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, thanks Sarah.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Bye, Dr. Young.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Bye.

video_details.title: Emotionally Focused Therapy
video_details.description: This video is a role play about Emotionally Focused Therapy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Vania, Jason, thanks for coming in today.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Super glad we're here. Honestly, things are okay, it's just...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Can you let her talk?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'd like to hear what brings you guys in today. Who wants to start?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Vania, go ahead, because I have no idea why we're here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Vania, you want to start? I'd like to hear from both of you, but we'll start with you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He used to be a very loving person, always calling and texting me. Now he's traveling all the time and he hardly ever has time for me. He leaves me alone.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm working. And one of the reasons I'm working is to pay for all the crap she buys.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The fact that you're working doesn't mean that you can't text me goodnight once in a while.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: If I'm in a meeting, I'll get all these messages and if I don't respond right away, she's freaking out. It's totally obnoxious. I shouldn't have to take care of her feelings all day long.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't want you to text me all day, but you could take two minutes on your break.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: In between my breaks I'd like to have a break. I'm tired. I'm working.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: But you haven't seen me all week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I see her every night, for the most part. When I'm traveling, I'm working too. I feel like she's treating me like a little twelve-year-old. I have to check in with her every time I do anything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Vania, let's come back to you. I understand there's a lot of tension right now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's out of control. I don't know where it's coming from. I'm just working a lot to buy her so many things she likes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So Vania, it sounds like he's gone a lot. Jason, how often do you go away on business?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I go about once a week, maybe overnight or for two nights.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When he's gone, what's the feeling for you, Vania?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I miss him. I want to be with him. Every human needs some contact.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The way she handles it is by sending me messages like 'where are you, what are you doing?' It's like I'm on a leash.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I heard you say that you miss him when he's gone. Are you able to express that to him when he comes home?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I want to, but then when he comes home, he's just so tired.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: First thing she does is hit me at the door with complaints. Can we say hello before we get into all that crap?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like you're both feeling very strong emotions, but when you come together, it's hard to express them.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's not nice to come home when you know she's going to start ranting at you because you weren't entertaining her while you were working. She should get a book or something.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's not about entertaining, it's about acknowledging that you have a wife.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: How many times a day do you need to be acknowledged, seriously?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You could just say good morning or good night, but you don't even do that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That is not true. She needs much more than that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Vania, how are you feeling right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel that he's not understanding. I'm a very emotional person and I need that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: But it's not my job to take care of her emotions.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you feel like he's not hearing you and you're missing him. Vania, could you try telling him how you feel when he's gone?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well Jason, when you're gone, I need you to be there. I want to feel that you are thinking about me and that I'm important to you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Jason, could you turn to Vania while she's sharing her feelings? Thanks. Okay, try again.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Whenever you're gone, I miss you. I want to feel that I'm important to you, but at this point, I don't feel that because you ignore me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How does it feel to say that to him?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It feels good to say it, but if he doesn't understand, then I'm just talking.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like you're reaching out for the connection you had in the beginning. Jason, how did it feel to hear her say she missed you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It makes my brain crash. Can you give me a checklist of exactly what she needs? Whatever I give her is not enough.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We can get to that, but how did it feel to hear that she missed you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like I'm under contract with a very difficult boss. Now it's like I have a second one who is never satisfied.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you feel completely unable to meet all of her needs and responsible for her happiness?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Exactly. Like she can't do anything to take care of her own emotions. I'm responsible for those.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's frustrating that you're trying to connect with her but feel like nothing you do would be enough.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Exactly. What does she want me to do? She says she doesn't want a list, but then tell me what you want.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't need a list. I want you to feel it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It seems like you both want to reach towards each other but aren't able to connect. Vania, let's help Jason understand what you need.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just want to feel that I'm important to you and that I matter in your life. I want to feel like you're seeing me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You want to feel valued and needed.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: But she doesn't say what would do that. Some magic thing has to happen for her to just feel that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You're supposed to know me. You married me.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's like a mystery where I'm just supposed to know magically what she needs.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Vania, have there ever been times in the past where he was able to show you that you are valued?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. Once he came home early from a conference without telling me and brought me flowers. That was amazing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That made you feel like he was thinking about you and valued you enough to come home and surprise you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, it did.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was really fun. We ended up having a nice dinner and dessert. It was really fun.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I loved it. I wish it was like that more.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: She can be really fun. There are these other times where things are okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like you guys really enjoy each other and there's a lot of love here. I know talking about these things is hard, but you obviously care about each other.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, why don't you guys tell me a little bit about what's been going on since I last saw you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's still been pretty bad. I had another trip last week and when I come back, she was just raging and angry. I just wanted to crawl up in a ball.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So when you get home, she's angry and it's really painful to come home to that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, so intense.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You hide away because you don't know how to respond or escape.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know how to respond or escape because she physically follows me from room to room. I just hope that it will pass.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's so painful to come home to that response that you withdraw because you don't know what else to do.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, but what about what I feel? I'm also in pain because he doesn't pay attention to me. He walks in the door and ignores me, which just makes the problem worse.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Vania, what's it like when he comes home after being away for two days?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I expect him to be happy to see me, but instead I feel ignored. I feel like I'm just another piece of furniture in the house.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like you're both caught in a dreadful dance of pain and withdrawal. Vania, could you turn to Jason and tell him more about what you're feeling?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When you're gone, I feel alone and I miss you. When you come home tired and frustrated, I'm angry because I can't get your attention. It's painful for me too.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How does it feel to say those words to him?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's painful and it hurts. It's my way of saying 'pay attention to me, I'm here.'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Jason, how does it feel to hear her say this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's easier to hear that. I don't always hear that part because she says it when she's angry, so I get defensive. I don't always hear that it's painful for her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Jason, what do you need from Vania when you come home that would help you not withdraw?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: If I could just have time to put my luggage down and feel like I'm arriving somewhere nice and not to a battleground, then I'd be more able to provide that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Could you actually turn to Vania now and tell her that you need a little bit of space when you come home?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It makes sense that you feel lonely when I travel. For me, work is very stressful. If I could just have a little bit of time when I get home, I would be in a different place.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I appreciate that. You both did well.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's like the first time you've ever said that to me.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel so valued and recognized.

video_details.title: Behavior Theory:  DBT Clinical Demonstration
video_details.description:
Florida Atlantic University, School of Social Work
Advanced Practice with Adults and Families

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Come on in. Hey, Taylor, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, before we get started, I just wanted to tell you how proud I was of you in group on Friday night, that you really helped Debbie in the role play. You got to be her boss?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it was fun.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It was fun to just kind of reverse roles like that. So I just wanted to tell you that the whole group appreciated it and you did a great job.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, all right. Well, I gotta say you look a little agitated.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, well, my mother's been bothering me so much about all the chores and the laundry and the dishes and I just can't stand it. I'm so busy looking for a job and school.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I tell you what, then, before we get started in our session, let's go through just a real quick breathing exercise just to kind of bring you into the here and now. Let's put your feet on the floor, your hands on where you're comfortable, and close your eyes if you're comfortable.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so let's unclench your hands. Now, take a nice deep breath. Blow it out slowly through your lips. Feel the air as it enters your lungs and feel the sensation on your lips. Your breath is always there for you. On the next inhale and exhale, slowly open your eyes and you're going to be calm and here in the room.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. That's better. You're here in this room and it's safe. So, let me ask you a question. Homework. You were going to bring me something or find something at home.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Homework. Oh, that's right. I found it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yes. Something that you could touch or hold. That's beautiful. So what do you do with this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes I put it on my neck just so I can feel it, or in my lap. It makes me feel better, just a familiar thing to have.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, that's nice. Keep it in your lap now and it can help keep you centered. Now that you're a little calmer, let's talk about what happened with Mom before you came here this afternoon.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: She knows that I'm looking for a job and going to school, but every time I walk in the door she asks me to do the dishes. No matter what. We get in a huge argument and we scream at each other. I always try to scream louder than her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So it's back and forth and the situation escalates and you slam doors and leave.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Slam doors, bang stuff around.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I get the impression. Today I wanted to work on some interpersonal skills with you called the GIVE technique. I have a handout here. It's an acronym: G-I-V-E. Why don't you read what those letters stand for.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. G: Gentle, be gentle. I: Interested, act interested. V: Validate. E: Easy manner, use an easy manner.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When a situation starts to escalate, you can just say: GIVE. In your situation with your mother, if you thought: 'okay, G.' How would that look?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I could not yell. I could be quieter than talking to her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, that would probably soften your tone of voice. What about 'act interested'?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I could always make eye contact with her and stuff.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, that's important so that she knows you're paying attention. And what about 'validate'? How might you validate what your mother is saying?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I could tell her that I understand that she would like me to help out more around the house when she asks me to do the dishes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is it important that you work together and get everything done? Can you validate what she's saying? You can still validate her concerns too. And then 'easy manner.' What would that look like for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, I kind of am aggressive, so I guess I could try to be more lighthearted about the situation. Maybe try to tell a joke?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It might be difficult to tell a joke, but you could slow down and stay calm. Think of the letter E: easy. What are the four letters again?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: G, I, V, E. Gentle, interested, validate, easy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good. You're going to take that home and look that over. It's a really easy acronym to remember.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Speaking of acronyms, I used the STOP technique that you taught me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You did? I want to hear about it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The other day I was in traffic and I was getting so nervous and anxious. I almost had a panic attack. I calmed myself down, I stopped.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Stopped, that's the S.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. I stopped, I took a breath.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: T, you took a breath. What does O stand for?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Observe. I observed the situation. I said, if I can't get onto the highway, I'll just get off and then I can get right back on. And then P, I proceeded.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Proceeded with driving. I'm thrilled that it was quick and easy to remember. How did that make you feel to be able to change a behavior like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, it changed my focus and I had that to focus on.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I am so proud of you. That is awesome, Taylor. Wait until we tell the group.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: One more tool for your toolkit: the Opposites. Whatever it is that you ordinarily do in response to situations, you do the opposite of that. When you feel angry, what do you usually do with your hands?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Fists.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So what would be the opposite of that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I could have them up, out, gentle, relaxed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Exactly. What about your stomach muscles and your chest when you're angry?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Tight, hunched over.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So if you want to do the opposite of that, what would that look like?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sitting up straight with stomach relaxed, taking a deep breath.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good. What about your face? What happens when you're angry?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I clench my teeth together.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what would be the opposite of that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Relaxed face, maybe a little smile.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good. I want you this week to make a list in your journal of the times you've used your STOP, GIVE, and Opposites techniques. At least once a day, do your breathing technique too.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sounds good. Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You seem very different than when you walked in. You're making progress. I'll see you in group on Friday night.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, see you then.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Bye-bye.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What you just saw was an example of behavior therapy. Because behavior is learned, it can be changed. The therapist has been working with her to change some of her behaviors and improve general functioning through techniques like distress tolerance and regulation of emotion.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In the video, we were able to watch the four modules of the skills training part of DBT: mindfulness, distress tolerance, interpersonal effectiveness, and emotion regulation skills. Each was demonstrated through exercises like breathing, the STOP acronym, the GIVE technique, and the Opposites.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In summary, I noticed the therapist used empathy towards the client and a lot of positive reinforcement.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, she did. We definitely think that DBT will work for this specific client and Taylor is going to be very successful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you.

video_details.title: Simulation Scenario - Responding to a Client who Dissociates
video_details.description:
A video depicting how a counsellor responds to a client who disassociates. 

For more clinical simulation resources please visit http://ww2.clinsim.health.wa.gov.au/

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So Jess, how'd the police interview go? How'd that play out?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, well they came to my house on Tuesday and I had my mom with me and I had to tell them everything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, it's hard.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like I had to go into so much detail. Um...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hey, Jess, just come back to me. Just come back to the room a little bit. Can you just look up, look up at me? What color eyes do I have? Can you check that out?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Brown.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Brown, okay good. I was just trying to get you back, back into the room with me, okay? So just look around the room. Can you see maybe this painting that's up here? What do you see? Can you tell me what the paintings are?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Beach, sun.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, cool. Okay, okay. Hey, I want you to do something. I just want you to catch this for me. See if you can catch it. Throw it back to me. Okay, just throw it back to me. That's it. That's it. Good, good. Just throw it back to me. Good. Okay, just see if you can stay here, stay here in the room with me, yeah? Yeah, and also, can you catch that one? That's it. Okay, so I just want you just to keep in the room with me a bit. I know sometimes it's a bit, bit stressful and a bit overwhelming, okay? But we're still connected, okay? You're not back there, okay? How you feeling?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um... oh... yeah, really, it was just really hard to talk about that stuff.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, it's completely understandable. These are really, really tough moments, and those sort of conversations with the police sometimes can be very stressful for you. Yeah, I get it. Yeah. So maybe, how you feeling now? Where you at?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, a bit better. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so maybe just, why don't we keep talking and you can just remember that we're connected, okay? And you're here with me. Yeah. So tell me a little bit more. So your mom came with you to do the statement?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, yeah, so Mom was with me. They came over and there were two detectives, and they, yeah, they just wanted to know everything and it took like hours. And...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how you feeling now after you've done it? What's that like?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like, I'm glad it's over and done with. I didn't realize how hard it would be to talk about it here. For some reason I was thinking it was, it was all over and done with, but I'm okay now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, well it's really understandable. It's completely, you know, understandable that sometimes it's difficult to talk and sometimes you can kind of float back to tough times. Yeah, so why don't we just keep talking? We'll keep talking like this, okay? Yeah.

video_details.title: Simulation Scenario - Orientating a Client at the First Appointment
video_details.description:
This video depicts a counsellor demonstrating skills to orientate an anxious client at their first appointment. 

For more clinical simulation resources please visit http://ww2.clinsim.health.wa.gov.au/

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Jasmine, hi. My name is Heidi. I'm your counselor today. We're going to meet in a room to our left. Something a bit more private than this area here. Um, should we go there now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, let's go. So, we're just going to go up the hall and to the right, and then there's a room on the left. Should I go first?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Come in, Jasmine. This is the room that we'll be meeting in today and if you come back again, we'll be in this room again. What I want you to do first is perhaps have a look around and choose where you would like to sit, where you'd like to be. Just the big chair over there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. So when you're ready, just make your way over to the chair and I'll close the door. And from where you're sitting now, where do you think you'd like me to be in the room? Which chair would you like me to sit in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That one.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In this chair here?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. I've got you a drink of water. I'll just move my chair around to face you, if that's all right. How's the distance between us? Would you like more room? Would you like me further back or more forward?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's okay? Okay. So I want to invite you, yeah, to look around. Look around the room. Take in this new space. You've never been here before. See if there's something your eyes want to rest on or if there's anything pleasant to your eyes. Have a really good stickybeak around the room. Most people, most times we come into new environments, we want to have a good stickybeak and we don't. And you can in here. I imagine it's pretty tough for you to be here. Yeah. Yeah. What would help you to spend a moment here?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The pillow?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The pillow? Yeah, yeah. Take a hold of that pillow. Yeah. What's it like to have that pillow against your tummy?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's nice.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. And what's it like to have your hands holding tight there like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. Does that help you to be here?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How did you, how did you get here?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My mom dropped me off here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Your mom dropped you off. Is she still here?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: She's not here. Um, is there an arrangement to pick you up?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. And you're looking at the time. So what time did you arrange for mom to pick you up?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, in like half an hour.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In half an hour?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. So notice you're looking around a little bit more now. Helps a bit more with that pillow, doesn't it? That was a good idea for you to put the pillow there. So how long do you think you'd like to be here? If you had a choice of how long you were going to be here with me in this conversation, how long would it be?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe like another 15 minutes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Maybe another 15 minutes? Yeah. Maybe? Maybe. If we just took then that 15 minutes just to get used to the room, just to get used to being in this space, being in that chair, what it's like to have your feet on the ground, what's it like to feel your seat and your back on the chair with the support of that pillow. That was such a good idea to get that pillow. It's a good resource. Yeah. Because it's helping you to be here. Yeah. So notice how it's a struggle to be here, but there's still something that helps you to be here. So on one hand, there's a struggle and then on the other hand, there's some kind of a little bit of support, even if it's a tiny bit, takes the edge off. Because both is there in the room. Yeah. What's it like for you to consider that it's not going to be half an hour, that it's going to be 15 minutes?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I feel better.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Feel better? Yeah. And we can just call mom and tell her that the first session is shorter. Yeah? Because it's enough. It's really confronting to be here. A lot of people find it confronting to come here because of the name of the agency, the issues that we may talk about in the future. It's pretty confronting. So just getting used to being here is a pretty big deal. And you're doing a great job. You're doing really well. Yeah. And I'm here with you. Yeah.

video_details.title: Counseling Session #1
video_details.description: Description

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So hi Tanya. My name's Solana. It's nice to meet you. Before we get started, I want to talk about a few things. Sessions are 45 to 50 minutes once a week for six weeks. Everything is confidential except for court orders, risk of harm to yourself or others, or suspected child or elder abuse. These sessions are recorded for educational purposes, and I may consult with my supervisor. Is that okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yep, that's fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Excellent. So why don't we get started? What brought you in today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm just overwhelmed with work and I just started school, so things have been piling up. I'm struggling to balance everything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I understand. Where do you work right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I work at Whole Health as a case manager, working in the community with clients who have schizophrenia and similar conditions.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're working full-time and going to school full-time? What classes are you taking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Theories, techniques, and ethics—the core classes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How has the workload been for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've been managing, but I don't have time for friends or myself. I feel bad saying no to people because I don't want to upset anyone, but I have to do homework.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, just trying to find that balance.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Exactly. My husband is also frustrated because I don't talk to him as much. He works from home and wants to chat when I get back, but I just want to decompress.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I can imagine just wanting to relax without having to maintain a conversation.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, but I don't want to ruin our relationship. I'm just so busy with school that it's hard to give him that time. I want to fix it, but I don't know how.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're confused about how to divide your time. What have you been doing to manage it lately?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I set time aside. I have Wednesdays off for homework, and I use Friday nights and Sundays too. I try to finish everything before I go out on Saturdays so I don't feel guilty, but I still feel stressed and overwhelmed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that system working for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really. My family gives me a hard time and doesn't understand that school and work are my priorities. They pressure me to come over, saying I don't need to do homework right now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you feel guilty choosing school over social obligations?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. None of them went to college, so they don't see the importance. It was easier when I lived further away in La Crosse because distance was a natural excuse. Now that I'm only 30 minutes away, the pressure is constant.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That constant pressure sounds like a lot to take on.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It is. I tell them it's important for my future, but I still feel bad. Sometimes I even come up with other excuses because I feel they don't respect 'school' as a reason.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My family is harder than my friends. One friend sent flowers to say she understands I'm busy, but my parents just guilt trip me. They never come to my house; it's always me going to them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It would be easier if they made the effort to come to you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it feels like they expect something from me without reciprocating. I can't cut back on work because I need the money, and I want to finish school quickly. I know I can handle it because I worked 60 hours a week during undergrad, but the proximity to everyone here makes it harder.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you don't want to lose those close connections.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I don't. But I struggle with school being the priority without making them feel less important. I'm wondering why it's so much more stressful now than in the past. My husband confronting me about it is probably the hardest part.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Were you together during your undergrad?

diarization.speaker: Patient
