It's about a 20-minute walk and I've made it numerous times before and it was never an issue. However, this one time, I was about a mile away from work, or a mile away from home, um, and this group of guys, I saw them on the corner, I was just like, "uh, whatever". Um, and when I walked past them, they were like, "yo, give me what's in your pockets". And I was just like, "well, what?". Um, and then like three of them walked up to me, they were like, "yo, you can give me what's in your pocket now or we can have an issue." So of course, since I didn't want to have an issue, I was just like, "here, take whatever's in my pockets". And after that they were, they ran off. And so then I ran home, called 911 and made a report and everything. Um, and that's how I thought I left the situation.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So that would be very stressful.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It, I found it to be really stressful at the time, and for like a day or two afterwards I was really, really stressed out. Um, but I thought I had moved on from that, like it, I, I'm seemingly back to my normal self, I'm back to my normal work routine, um, and everything's back to normal.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No fears about going outside or anything like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, no fears about going outside. Um, I know the one thing is I, I never walk past that corner late at night. Um, sometimes I do have to walk past it um, in the morning time when I miss my ride to work. Um, but it's the daylight hours, I, I'm not stressed then, I'm not worried.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so there are occasions when you do walk by it in the day, you're saying.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there are occasions you walk by in the day. What happens then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When I walk past the corner during the day, I'm really, really hypervigilant about who's around and if there are cars on the street, if there are other people walking, um, just so that I know if something were to go down, other people might be there to assist me. Um, but then when I get to work, I'm still antsy and hypervigilant and um, and then probably two or three hours into my workday, that's when I can actually start to calm down and get back to my normal routine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. And, and do you notice any connection between the voices and the shadows to that event or to being stressed?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So generally, um, yes. So, um, the reason why it probably happens like once a week or every other week is because generally I get a ride to work. Um, and when I'm riding past the corner, it's not an issue or problem. Like it's just like "whatever, it's a corner". But when I walk past it, um, like an hour or two into my workday, that's when I hear the voices. Then like two hours after that, that's when I see the shadow.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. So you're still, you're still stressed from that, from walking by that corner when the-

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I, I don't think I'm stressed from it. No. I don't think I am. But I, I don't understand why it's a delayed reaction if I, I should be freaked out when I'm walking past the corner, but I shouldn't be freaked out when I'm at work, when I'm in a safe environment with people who would never do something like that to me. But it's still happening there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And is there any other time when you have the voices or see the shadows other than in proximity to passing that corner?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not that I'm aware of. Like, not that I can think of. Um, I think it's been, I think I've heard them so much this week is because normally my ride, they, they pick me up like basically every day, but this week my ride is on vacation. So I've had to walk to work a lot more. And I just haven't had the money to catch the bus or do anything else like that. So it's been happening a lot this week.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This week's been a tough week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: This week has been a really, really tough week.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright Jason, um, I appreciate you taking the time to explain to me what's going on, and if you're okay with it, I'd like to get you in to see a counselor here. Okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I, I think that might be a good thing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. I'll get that set up for you and again, I appreciate you spending this time with me.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

video_details.title: Counseling Diagnostic Assessment Vignette #34   Symptoms of Schizophrenia
video_details.description: This counseling diagnostic assessment vignette demonstrates an interview with a client (played by an actor) who exhibits symptoms of schizophrenia.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Jason, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're good?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm here, that's, that's all I can say, I'm just here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're here?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's been going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So I've been made to come in and talk to you because something happened on the bus and I might have said something to somebody and they're just like, oh you can't say that, so they actually said, oh we're going to take you to jail. From jail they just brought me here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you know what you're charged with?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They didn't explain anything. The government never explains anything. They just don't want me to understand what's going on because they just want to keep me held in captivity.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The government? Do you have anyone specific?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, it's the entire government. Entire government.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how long have they been wanting to do this to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: All my life. They've done this all my life. They, they're always listening, they're always around, they're always there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Always there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Always there. Like for example, they're in the lights right now. They're listening to everything that we're talking about, so that's the reason why I really can't talk about what happened on the bus because they're just going to use that against me and then just lock me up again and make me take more meds.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You've been taking medications?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I take the medication because if I don't take the medication, the government comes and takes me away and puts me into a hospital where they force-feed me the medication and then the lights are always on and they could always hear everything that I'm saying and what I'm thinking and what I'm going to do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you know what they want to do with that information?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They want to use it to take over the world. Take over the world, of course. They want to use everything and use everything that everybody knows to use it against them so that they can actually have the world that they want and that they need and make everybody pretend that they don't know what's going on. So therefore, they're using everybody's thoughts against themselves so that the government can use it to their benefit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what can you do in this situation?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: What do you mean what can I do?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, you say the government's monitoring everything and that they want to put you in jail if you don't take your medication. Do you have any options? Are you stuck?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. So when I'm home I think I'm perfectly fine because I set up my house and my room to actually make it government-proof so that nobody can actually hear or see what's going on in there. So when I'm home I'm perfectly fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. So one option is that being home, being home you're safe.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Being home I'm safe. Being home I was safe, my mom's safe, my brother's safe, everybody's safe. And being out in the world, the world, I'm not safe. Nobody's safe.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you safe here?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I told you, they are in the lights and they can hear everything that we're saying right now. So no, we're not safe here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so it's not safe here, it's not safe out in the world, but at home you're safe.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: At home I'm safe. In my room that I made government-proof.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So if you could have your way, you would just stay home most of the time, all the time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would stay home all of the time, but I can't stay home because I'm made to go and see doctors and talk to people and do the things that the government needs me or wants me to do, but I don't want to do those things because it's using my thoughts and they're trying to use everybody against me and I just can't do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So how do you know that they're in the lights? Like how did you discover that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Everybody knows that they're in the lights. It's common knowledge, everybody knows that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you ever hear things that other people can't hear or see things other people can't see?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, of course, everybody hears the lights talking to you. I don't know what you're talking about. Like everybody hears it. Sometimes it's a whisper for some people, sometimes it's a yell and if you want to not pay attention to what the lights are saying to you, then I don't know what's wrong with you but everybody can hear it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Everybody can hear it. What's it sound like to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It just sounds like a robot talking. It sounds like we need to know this information. We need to, what are you doing?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, I'm just making some notes. Just making some progress notes. Does it worry you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. Where are your notes going to go?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, they get, well this chart will get locked in the chart room down the hall.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Who has access to the chart room?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Mostly everybody that works here.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh. Can I get a copy of your notes after you're done?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does it worry you that there's notes?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, because I might trust you and I don't know if I do yet but I don't trust the other people who work here because I don't know if they're working for the government, which they probably are working for the government. So they could actually have access to all of my notes and the things that you're writing down, which I don't know what they are because you're not going to give me a copy of it yet. And I just don't trust that they can actually get that information because they're going to use it to their advantage and they're going to give it to the government which I can't have that happening. So could you please not take notes?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I could not take notes. What kind of information in the notes are you worried that the government's going to get?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, because I made my room at home government-proof, I think they're going to try to steal that technology that I actually created so that they can then disrupt my room and then everybody else's rooms who are just like mine so that they can then use their mind control to then control me to do the things that they want me to do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So without the protection that your house offers they could control your mind?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Correct. Without my room and without the technology and the systems and the things that I created then the government will be able to control everything that I do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. So can you tell me about your mood through all this? This sounds really stressful. You're describing an environment where the government's frequently looking at what you're doing. What are the feelings there? You feel sad or angry?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel fine. I feel fine. I don't really have, yeah I just, I feel fine. I don't feel happy, I don't feel sad, I'm just here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Kind of resigned that the government's going to do this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, the government's going to do what they're going to do anyway so it doesn't matter if I'm happy, sad, pissed off, angry, any of that. The government's going to make me do what they want me to do anyway so it doesn't matter how I feel.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you worried that something is going to happen similar to what happened on the bus?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, because I've learned my lesson to not say those things out loud and to talk about what the government's doing because I can't actually inform anybody else because nobody's listening to me because they're already controlled by the government because they don't have a room like I do at home.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you'll avoid that in the future because it didn't really work. You weren't able to help them understand what's going on.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, if people don't understand what's going on then that's their fault and that's their problem. They should have listened to me and I could have actually gave them the technology that they needed to actually create the room so that the government can't hear them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But they weren't open to that idea.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Quite the opposite.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Completely the opposite.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How are your family relationships? How's that going?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They're okay. I live with my mom. She does what she's supposed to do, she doesn't go in my room because she knows that if she goes into the room it's going to mess up the technology so she stays out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you get along with her okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Perfectly fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Anybody else you have contact with? Friends, family?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, just, I talk to people all the time but they're just in my head and we have conversations all the time about how we can actually make the world a better place and then how we can actually go through and then destroy the government. But yeah, I just talk to them in my head.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright Jason, well I'm sorry to hear that you're under stress. I'm glad to hear you feel like your mood's okay, like you're not down or anxious or anything. This answering these questions for me this has been helpful and I'm going to recommend you continue to see a counselor here, if that's okay. I realize you're court ordered.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Can this counselor be you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It could be me. Would that make you feel more comfortable?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That would make me feel much better.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well then I'll put it on the schedule and we'll set a time up front where I'll see you, let's say in three days. That works?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Three days works.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And we'll go from there.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. Thanks Jason.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

video_details.title: Counseling Diagnostic Assessment Vignette #29 - Symptoms of Alcohol Use Disorder
video_details.description: This counseling diagnostic assessment vignette demonstrates an interview with a client (played by an actress) who exhibits symptoms of alcohol use disorder.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Jackie, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm fine, how are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing fine, thanks for asking. I understand you've been having some difficulties that brought you into our agency.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'm really worried about my drinking.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're worried about your drinking? Tell me about your drinking.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, my family are all big partiers, they all really like to drink. So it's something I've been surrounded by a lot. But I've been having these really intense cravings that I really feel like I want to drink when I'm at work. I'm just like, 'oh, I could really use a drink right now.' And that really worries me. I'm just nervous it's becoming a problem.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So sometimes at work you've been having cravings for alcohol. Any other times you've been having cravings?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, just kind of when I'm at home, you know, not really doing anything. Just like, 'I could go for a beer right now.'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So other than that feeling of having the craving, is there anything you do after you have the craving?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, sometimes I'll have a drink and I just feel like I want to give into it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How much do you drink?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like a beer or two.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is this when you're at work in the day or...?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh no, after work I'll go and have a drink.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So when you're having cravings at work, you're not drinking there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, no.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So tell me about your typical alcohol consumption in a week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: On Fridays after work, after a long week, that's kind of when I really crave it. I go have a drink with some friends. I'll have a drink sometimes with dinner. If I'm at a social event, I kind of feel like I want to have a drink then. I don't really want to feel that way. I feel like that might be a problem.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're worried the craving is indicating that you have an alcohol problem. Have you ever tried to cut down your drinking and were unable to do so?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Usually I'm able to limit my days. If I say I'll just go to a party this weekend, I'll have one. Usually I can stick to it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you spend a lot of time trying to obtain alcohol?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I guess not. I think about when I want to have it when I have a craving, but I don't really spend a lot of time thinking about it or trying to get it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about in terms of your responsibilities? Have you failed to uphold any of your responsibilities because of your drinking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe I haven't gone home from work right away when I have to put my clothes away or do some laundry, because I'd rather just go have a drink with my friends. But no major responsibilities, no work responsibilities or anything like that have been missed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Do you have any social problems because of your drinking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I guess not. I get really friendly when I have a drink, so I don't really think that's a problem.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It hasn't caused any social problems. Do you find yourself giving up important activities because you're drinking instead?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. I usually do what I need to do. I still attend the things that I need to attend, but maybe I think about it while I'm there, like 'why isn't there any beer here?'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so you're thinking about it, but you're still participating. Are you engaging in any activities that are dangerous because of the drinking? Drinking and driving, anything like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Nothing like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I guess not.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: There's nothing like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Do you have any physical or mental health problems that are made worse by the drinking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. I wouldn't say worse.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have any medical or mental health problems in general?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, none.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Do you find that you have to increase the amount of alcohol you're drinking to get the same effect?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I usually have around the same amount every time, so I would say no. I never really go all out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you noticed that the effect has been diminished? Like you're not getting the same effect from the alcohol?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I usually feel the same.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It feels the same way?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever noticed any symptoms when you stop drinking, like a withdrawal?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, what do you mean really by withdrawal?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Like when you stop using alcohol, are you finding that you're anxious, depressed, or you have physical reactions?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh no. No, none of that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, Jackie. I appreciate you telling me about what's going on and answering my questions. If you're okay with it, I'll get you in to see a counselor. I'll get that scheduled and we can go from there.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, thank you very much.

video_details.title: Counseling Diagnostic Assessment Vignette #31 - Symptoms of Alcohol Use Disorder
video_details.description: This counseling diagnostic assessment vignette demonstrates an interview with a client (played by an actress) who exhibits symptoms of alcohol use disorder.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Jackie, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm pretty good, I guess. How about you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing okay. Thanks for asking. I understand you've been having some difficulties that have facilitated you to come into our agency.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, well, I mean I've been drinking a lot more than usual but it's kind of just part of my life. But I don't know, I think there is an increase so it's worrying me a little bit, but...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so you feel like you're drinking more than usual. How much are you drinking now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, you know I go out with my friends a couple nights a week, and then about once a week I'll go out with my co-workers. So yeah, maybe three or four nights a week.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, three or four nights a week you're drinking. And how much are you drinking each time you go out?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, you know it kind of depends on who I'm with, but usually when I go out with my friends on the weekend I'll stay for a pretty long time. I mean I think the problem is when I'm going out during the week with my co-workers, you know I'll stay longer than I want to and then when I have to get up in the morning it's kind of like 'ugh I should've gone home a little earlier'. But you know they're all out with me so when I get there they understand. So...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so do you know how much alcohol... you talked about the time period, do you know how much you're actually drinking each night approximately?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well before I used to drink like maybe two beers an hour, but you know they really like to party so and I try to keep up with them, so...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Your friends?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, so I've been drinking like a shot with the beers I have, so maybe like three or four drinks an hour.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you find that you need to drink more to get the desired effect?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, yeah you know everyone else is getting to that level so I feel like I need to keep up with them and usually before I would get that from maybe one or two drinks so now I've been drinking a little bit more I think to get there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, have you made any attempts to cut down on your consumption?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You know at the beginning of the week I'll kind of say 'I'm only going to go out twice this week' but then they invite me and I'm kind of like 'oh well I don't want to miss out, they're my friends, you know this is my social time during the week', so so I usually go. I don't really stick to the plan so that's kind of been a little frustrating but I don't know I still... it's okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So I want to talk about the time you spend using alcohol. Are you okay with the amount of time? You mentioned that you're using for longer periods, but are you okay with that or is that something that's distressing you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, you know I think I could probably be doing better things with my time, but it's not a huge problem. I think a lot of people do it, so you know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you find that you have a craving for alcohol?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah. I would say like when I'm at work I always just ready to get finished so I can go to happy hour with my coworkers or um, you know if I'm just kind of at a barbecue or something with family, think about how I want a beer. So yeah I cravings, but you know everyone kind of does that like 'oh I could go for a beer right now'.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're thinking about it, but are you also like feeling the craving?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You mentioned work. Are you having any trouble with responsibilities at work or any other area?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, my work life's been pretty going pretty well and I haven't missed work because of it or anything like that, so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Because of the drinking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. All right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about any social problems due to the alcohol?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I think my social life is actually great because of it. You know I hang out with my friends and we all get along really well, so no it's my social time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so no social problems.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, no problems.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you had to give up any important activities because of the alcohol use?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Important activities... well usually the important activities involve drinking so I haven't given up important activities that don't involve drinking but that's been pretty easy because there's usually alcohol at the important things so...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so you haven't missed any important activities because of that. How about engaging in any activities that are physically dangerous because alcohol's involved?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, no I'm usually pretty safe. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Safe? Yeah. All right. Do you have any medical or mental health history?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, well like when I was a kid I was diagnosed with I think maybe ADHD or something like that, but I think my teachers were annoyed by me because I just like to have a good time, so but that's not really been an issue lately.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's not been an issue? No. Has any medical problem or mental health problem become worse because of the alcohol?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, no you know I started drinking after that so not no it's not become an issue with it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So you mentioned alcohol use, has there been any drug use?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, not with my drinking or anything. You know typical teenage smoking marijuana and stuff when I was younger but I don't anymore so...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so it's just alcohol?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, just alcohol.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Do you have when you stop drinking, do you have any physical symptoms or anxiety, any symptoms of withdrawal?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, mm-mm. I usually feel fine afterwards. I can go a few days without drinking.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so that's not a problem for you. All right. Jackie are you open to receiving counseling services at our agency?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I don't see why it would hurt anything. I don't really know if I need it, but...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But you're okay with trying it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think I'd be okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, I'm going to get you scheduled in to see a counselor. I want to thank you for telling me about what's going on and for answering my questions, it's been helpful.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, sure. Yeah, thank you.

video_details.title: Counseling Diagnostic Assessment Vignette #26 - Symptoms of Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
video_details.description: This counseling diagnostic assessment vignette demonstrates an interview with a client (played by an actress) who exhibits symptoms of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Jessica, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm doing okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're doing okay? I understand you've been having some recent difficulties that brought you into our agency. Can you tell me about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I've been having a lot of anxiety lately.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Anxiety?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Um, just getting really nervous in the morning when it's time to go to work. Um, just like butterflies in my stomach, kind of pounding heart.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're anxious when you're getting ready to go to work? Do you know what might be causing that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I noticed it a little while ago. Um, when I went to get in my car to go to work one morning, I was putting some stuff in the trunk and um, I saw some damage that had happened to the car from a previous car accident. And just out of nowhere I started feeling nervous about driving to work.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so you went out to your car, you saw some damage, it reminded you of an accident?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I was in an accident um, at the end of last year. And you know, I didn't get hurt, there was no real damage to the car that I noticed. Um, I just went on about my business, I didn't have any issues after the accident. And now all of a sudden, I'm thinking about this car accident again and I don't know where that's coming from.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now you said the accident occurred at the end of last year?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, um, I can't really remember exactly when, but it was cold out when it happened.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So maybe about eight months ago, that sound right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, around Halloween or so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And when did the symptoms start of being anxious when you're getting ready to go to work?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would say at least a month ago, maybe six weeks.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. And you've been having those continuously from then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, every morning I get up I'm just really nervous about going to work. And you know, I come out to get in the car and sometimes I can barely get in, just thinking about being in a car accident again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever been late to work because of the anxiety?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm late almost every day.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Almost every day? So this has been a problem for you in a few different ways.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I even called out a couple times because I was just paralyzed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you tried anything to reduce the anxiety, like using another car or anything else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well yeah, I live in a house with multiple cars, so I tried driving my mom's car to work one day. And you know, I had the same feelings. And initially I thought it was just my car because I did notice some damage to the back of the car, I was hit in the back. And um, I was going through the trunk one day and I saw that the car was actually pushed in. I didn't think there was any real damage and then I noticed damage to the back of the car and I was like 'Wow, I could have been seriously hurt in this accident'. And that's when I started having these feelings, like I just started thinking about how bad the accident could have been. So you asked if I tried to do anything different, I tried driving my mom's car, I tried driving my dad's car, but it seems to be just driving any car, I'm having all of this anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, and you're having kind of physical distress too? Like you're feeling it physically?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Overwhelmed, yeah. A lot of like swelling in my chest, like really panicky.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. You ever have any dreams about the accident or anything related to the accident?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, no, not really.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you ever have any point when you're not asleep where you feel like you're kind of taken back to the time the accident happened, like you're reliving it in any way?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, nothing like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you remember the accident well?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I remember it pretty well. I was waiting at a stop sign and I think the person behind me, they must not have been paying attention, but they rear-ended me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Who do you believe is responsible for the accident?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Nobody really. I mean, it was an accident. There was no real damage, you know, accidents happen all the time. Just a fender-bender.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So from the time that you noticed these anxiety symptoms, have you had periods where you were happy and kind of positive emotional experiences?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've been really down since I've started having these symptoms.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The whole time you've been down? Or have there been moments where you haven't been? Or has it been consistently down?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would say more down than not.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: More down, but but sometimes up?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can't really remember any times, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. How about your relationships with other people? Have they changed from when the anxiety started?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, not really.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you feel detached from people, anything like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Detached, do you mean like separated? Not wanting to be around... no, not really.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Nothing like that. How about any feelings of irritability or anger outbursts or anything like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you feel like you've been behaving in a more reckless way at all?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: What do you mean by reckless?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Like taking more chances in relationships or in other... nothing like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're aware of like when something surprises us, we kind of have this startle response, like we jump. It's natural. Have you noticed that response has changed at all?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I have been a little on edge. Things have been like scaring me. The phone ringing, people knocking at the door, dogs barking. Just kind of had me on edge a little bit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you feel like your response is more than it used to be, more than just the natural startle response you had?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's kind of worrying me a little bit too.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any trouble concentrating?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You've been okay concentrating? Staying focused has been all right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'm good in that area.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about trouble with sleep? Trouble falling asleep, staying asleep?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No trouble falling asleep, but I have had trouble staying asleep. I've been waking up pretty much around the clock throughout the night.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're getting to sleep okay, you're falling asleep okay, but just having trouble staying asleep?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you thinking about anything specific when you wake up?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really. Just maybe like thinking about going to work in the morning. But no, nothing major.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any use of drugs or alcohol?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about medical problems?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are there ever points from when this anxiety started that you feel kind of outside of your own body? Kind of an unreal feeling where you're separated from your own body?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about times when you feel disconnected from the environment? Like an unreal feeling about what's going on around you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, nothing like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright Jessica, I'm going to get you in to see a counselor here, if you're open to that, if that's something you want to do.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, and I appreciate you taking the time to tell me what's going on and answer these questions. It's been helpful.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you for seeing me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sure.

video_details.title: Counseling Diagnostic Assessment Vignette #28 - Symptoms of Acute Stress Disorder
video_details.description: This counseling diagnostic assessment vignette demonstrates an interview with a client (played by an actress) who exhibits symptoms of acute stress disorder.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Jackie. How you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm all right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You all right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I've been having a rough time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Having a rough time? I understand there have been some difficulties lately that brought you into the agency. Tell me what's going on.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: About a week ago, I went out with some friends to a boxing match. I didn't really want to go, I've never really been to one. I watched a few fights and this one guy got knocked out right in front of me. He fell right on his face and I saw him lifeless. Ever since then, it hasn't been the same. I had to leave right away. I just couldn't be there anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what did you notice right away? So one of the boxers was knocked out and you saw that. What did you notice right away was happening?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just felt really scared. My heart started racing. I couldn't focus on what was going on around me. I just had to get out of there. I don't even know what happened to him, if he was okay or not. I just couldn't handle how I was feeling.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you left and the symptoms continued?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, pretty much daily for the past week. I got home that night and I couldn't sleep. At work on Monday, I was having a lot of problems there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What kind of problems?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I couldn't focus when anyone was talking to me. I had a meeting on Tuesday and my boss was talking and I feel like I couldn't concentrate at all. Everything was kind of just a blur around me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you find that you're having memories of the incident at the boxing match that are intrusive?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think about it a lot. Pretty much all the time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And it's bothersome for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, if I'm at work trying to get some paperwork done, it just pops in my mind and I can't make it go away.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you try but the memory stays there. Any dreams related to it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I haven't really been dreaming about it. I'm barely sleeping.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any times when you feel like you're reliving what you saw, like you're seeing it again?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, not really. I just think about it a lot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is anything reminding you of the boxing match that's causing you to have symptoms?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, at the end of my meeting people started clapping and cheering, and that made me feel really bad. Again my heart was racing and I started sweating. Pump up music when it comes on the radio, the same kind of music they played there, that makes me feel the same way.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you find yourself working to avoid music that was similar?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I've been trying to really avoid the radio and avoiding crowds.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you find that you've had any trouble remembering what happened?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I can pretty vividly remember it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you been irritable at all since then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, out of nowhere, I just kind of snap on people. I yelled at my boyfriend for not putting the toilet paper on the roll. That's not something I'd usually care about. It's just not me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about your awareness level of what's around you? Do you find that your awareness level has increased?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes I feel like I'm in a daze. But one of the students I work with popped out from behind the door. Typically I would laugh, but he did it the other day and I just could not control myself afterwards. It really scared me and I couldn't calm myself down.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you feel like your reaction to that was stronger than it normally would have been?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Definitely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you used drugs or alcohol recently? Any medical problems?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm going to get you in to see a counselor here at the agency if that's something that you're okay with?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think that would be really helpful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'll get that arranged on the schedule and get you in to see somebody.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks.

video_details.title: Counseling Diagnostic Assessment Vignette #27 - Symptoms of Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
video_details.description: This counseling diagnostic assessment vignette demonstrates an interview with a client (played by an actress) who exhibits symptoms of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Jessica, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're okay? I understand you've been having some difficulty with some symptoms lately. Can you tell me about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I've been having a lot of anxiety, just been stressed out lately, irritable, you name it, I have it. The thing that's been troubling me the most though are these memories that don't seem to go away. No matter what I do, I just keep remembering this event and it's really taking a toll on me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're having anxiety and a lot of other symptoms and you're having intrusive memories. Can you tell me about the event?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I was in a car accident a couple months ago and it was a pretty bad accident but I was okay, I didn't get injured. My car was messed up really bad. The driver of the other car, I think they were injured pretty bad, more severe than I was. And I just can't seem to get that accident out of my mind.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does it keep replaying, that accident?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, over and over.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me about how you're experiencing that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I could be just in the kitchen making a pot of coffee and all of a sudden I'm back there in the accident. I'm back in the car with the airbags deployed and sirens coming from a distance and I try to shake that feeling and I just can't. And that just overwhelms me so much that I can't do anything, I just have to go and sit down and I'm stuck in the house just scared to do anything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So these times when you're reliving the accident, does something trigger that or does that happen just on its own?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes things trigger it and sometimes they just come out of nowhere. I mean I could be watching a movie and there's a bad car accident and I start thinking about it or I could be just doing nothing and the memories just come back like full force.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So this has been causing you, clearly causing you distress. Has it been interfering at all with relationships?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, yes, I would say. I haven't been able to go out with my friends, I just don't want to do anything. My friends are always trying to get me to go out and you know, get things off of my mind and I just don't have a desire to, I don't really want to be around anyone.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you find that your mood's irritable or any anger outbursts?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: All the time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That happens frequently?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'm on edge a lot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you feel like your behavior has become reckless, like taking more chances?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Somewhat.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Somewhat?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about your memory of the accident? Is it constant or does your memory change, like you lose some of that memory?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, there are times where it's clear as a bell and then other times people ask me details about the accident and I can't remember a thing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You can't remember any of it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the memory kind of comes and goes.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It does, yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Who do you hold responsible for the accident?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, everybody tells me that I shouldn't but I hold myself responsible for it. I mean I tried going a different way home from work one day, it was a way that I've never gone before and you know, somebody cut me off and I slammed into them, but if I hadn't gone that way I would have never gotten into the car accident.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Did the other driver get a ticket for the accident?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think he did. I think he got a ticket for reckless driving or failure to yield or something, but I mean if I wasn't on that road then neither of us would have been in the accident.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you still blame yourself.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about your emotional state since these symptoms have started? Has it been mostly unhappy or down, neutral, any time when you're happy?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, nothing seems to make me happy anymore, I'm just always depressed. Just...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Your mood's always down?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about with driving? Have you been avoiding driving or have you driven since the accident?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have, but I don't if I don't have to. Like I definitely avoid going places, like if I'm making dinner and I'm missing an ingredient, then I'll just go without it before driving to the market. I just don't want to be behind the wheel of a car.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so you're avoiding it, but you have driven.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me about the experience when you go to drive.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh boy. So I have to almost prepare myself hours in advance because it's so hard for me to get out the house.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In terms of anxiety or what's going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah. I'm just having like knots in my stomach and you know, shortness of breath, my chest is pounding, I'm just fearful, just... it's a lot, it's very overwhelming.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Very stressful.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It is.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you find that when you are driving that you are more aware of what other cars are doing and what you're doing in your car?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, probably more so now than ever. I'm just always looking out making sure that I don't cause another car accident. I'm driving slower, I'm waiting longer to switch lanes, it's just yeah, definitely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're more aware of your surroundings.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Definitely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So when something surprises us, there's a natural response where we're startled. This is called the startle response and everybody has that. Have you noticed that that's changed for you since these symptoms have started?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How's it changed?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Anything, everything startles me anymore. The doorbell ringing, the phone ringing, just you know, somebody getting up to move their chair, any little sound, it just has me like looking over my shoulder to see what's going on.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you find yourself jumping?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, a lot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about your ability to concentrate? Has that changed at all?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It has. It's decreased a lot. I haven't really been able to concentrate on anything. I have things all over my house where I've started things and moved on to something else because I can't concentrate on one thing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, how about sleeping? How you doing with sleep?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not too good. I'm not getting a lot of sleep at all these days. I'm up all hours of the night, sometimes I just wake up for no reason, sometimes I'll wake up out of a dream just scared. I'm just, I'm not sleeping well at all.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So a lot of challenges with sleep.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you use any drugs or alcohol?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about medical problems?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, nothing like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are there times from when these symptoms started when you feel kind of separated from your own body, like it's an unreal experience?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've had a couple experiences like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me about those?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, there was one time I was at work and we were sitting in the cafeteria and just all of a sudden everything seemed to start going in slow motion and I could hear people talking but it sounded very slow. It was like... it's hard to describe but I could see everything but it just wasn't moving at a normal pace. I kind of felt like I was watching a movie almost. And that's happened at least two or three times and I didn't really understand what was going on. A friend of mine told me she said that I was kind of like spaced out and she was like snapping her fingers in front of my face and I could see her but I couldn't really hear what was going on and then I just like snapped out of it. And everybody was sitting around staring at me and you know, they were talking about what was going on and I had no idea what was happening. But it was very embarrassing, you know, they were watching me like I was a movie.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And this has happened a few times.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, in a couple of different locations. One time I was at work, one time I was at school and these things just happen out of the blue.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about a time when you felt like the world became unreal? So you're not detached from your body but the world becomes unreal or dreamlike or distorted. Have you ever had that happen?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No, it's more being separated from your body, more that feeling.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you mentioned like the time slowing down.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, very slow motion, like you were watching a movie in slow motion. The sound and everything was just dragging.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Jessica, I'm going to get you in to see a counselor here if you're okay with that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I think that would be okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I appreciate you taking the time to explain these symptoms, I know they're distressing for you, and for taking the time to answer my questions. It's been helpful for me to help figure out what's going on and help manage your care.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you, I appreciate your help.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks.

video_details.title: Counseling Diagnostic Assessment Vignette #24 - Symptoms of Acute Stress Disorder
video_details.description: This counseling diagnostic assessment vignette demonstrates an interview with a client (played by an actress) who exhibits symptoms of acute stress disorder.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hey Rebecca, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're okay? I understand recently you had a difficult experience and that's what brought you into the clinic.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, yeah, actually I did about, uh, nine days ago. We own a horse farm, and my family does. And my sister and I were loading a horse to take to a horse show. The horse is pretty young and she'd only been loaded a few times. My sister was in the horse trailer with the horse, and all of a sudden the horse just totally freaked out, and she started really thrashing around the trailer, kind of throwing my sister around. She got really banged up. She's okay now, but the horse ended up escaping back out of the horse trailer. I've worked with horses before, but just this particular incident, I just can't get rid of the thoughts of it, and it just really scared me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, it sounds like a scary experience. So your sister's injured by the horse, she's okay. But you've had things like this happen before, but this is different.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, this is different. I'm having trouble sleeping at night. I wake up from recurring dreams about the incident.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you're dreaming about the accident.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I work on a horse farm, so I'm surrounded by horses, and just the slightest little noise they make, I just almost jump out of my skin. I'm having a hard time even handling them. I'm just real short with people.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So your work experience has become unpleasant.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're more aware of the horses and you're more startled by what they do now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, definitely. Even just little things when they're whinnying or just kind of getting, when they're tied up and they're just maybe roughhousing a little bit, it really kind of freaks me out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you been having difficulty concentrating?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, yeah, actually I have because I'll start a task and all of a sudden I'll just be thinking about it. My mind just goes to the memories and just kind of replays it for me, and I have a really hard time staying on task and staying focused.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the memories seem to be coming back automatically.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're more aware of your surroundings there as you're working.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I'm very much aware.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you had any positive emotions? When did the symptoms start?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Pretty much the next day. That day I was just trying to recover from the incident and then by the next day, I had a really hard time being around the horses, and just the thoughts coming in.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the next day?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So from that day, have you had any positive emotions?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really, no.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's been tough for you since then.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, just kind of been fearful and just kind of upset that I can't shake this. I work around horses, it's happened before. I should be able to get over it, so I'm kind of mad about it too.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This time's been a bit different, that's upsetting. Have you had your memory of what happened compromised at all? Do you feel like you're missing pieces of what happened?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't think so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You remember pretty well.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think I remember pretty well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you had any experiences where you had this sense that your surroundings were altered, kind of unreal?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really, except maybe when the memories come and stuff, I think they really hit me strong.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. How about any episodes where you feel like you're reliving the accident? Not just an intrusive memory, but actually like you're reliving it, like you're back in that moment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think it's mostly just the memories.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Memories? Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I want to try to understand what maybe going on. I'm going to ask you a few questions. Do you have any medical problems?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No. Have you had any recent use of alcohol or drugs?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Nothing like that. All right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Rebecca, I'm going to get you in to see a counselor. Okay. I appreciate you spending this time with me and answering these questions and telling me what happened, it was helpful.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

video_details.title: Counseling Diagnostic Assessment Vignette #23 - Symptoms of Intermittent Explosive Disorder
video_details.description: This counseling diagnostic assessment vignette demonstrates an interview with a client (played by an actress) who exhibits symptoms of intermittent explosive disorder (IED).

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hey Tiffany, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm all right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You all right? I understand you've been having some recent difficulties.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The thing with the cops?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The involvement with the police.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was so blown out of proportion. Stupid neighbors were having a party, I'm trying to get sleep. It's like, you know, 10:00, 11:00, I'm trying to wind down, they're having a party. I go over there, yell at the door, yell through the door, yelled, 'I'm trying to get sleep, bring it down some.' No response. So, I let myself in, with a little force I let myself in. They're all, I just confront whoever's there, who's having this party. Everybody's just, like, everybody's ignoring me. So I just go over, take the stereo, open the window, throw it out the window. Then there may have been people walking by, this woman swears she was walking by, says I almost hit her. But to me, and then she called the cops.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what story were you on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe third floor.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Third floor. So you threw the stereo out the window and it landed on the ground.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It did not, it was nowhere near that woman. She was way across the street, but she says I almost hit her, so whatever.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So she called the...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: She called the police, said I was out of control, and then the people from the party had the nerve to go down when the cops got there and they agreed with her. They said I broke in, but I just came in. But anyway, and they said I threw the stereo out, and then the police are threatening to put me in jail and they're threatening to press charges and it was just ugly, but it's blown out of proportion.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You feel it's blown out of proportion.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has anything like this happened before?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, not with the police or anything, but...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about anything where you found your anger kind of strong?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, maybe. Um, there was the time, it was my daughter, she's 16 years old. You know how teenagers are, they don't listen. She wasn't listening. She has a smartphone, brand new smartphone she got for Christmas, you know, out of my money, from my pocket. Brand new smartphone, got it for Christmas. I'm up here, 'Hello, it's time for your homework. Did you do your homework?' She's just gabbing on the phone, not listening. I took the phone, threw it out the window. Broke, shattered. But...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how long ago was this with the phone?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Ah, four or five months ago.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Four or five months. All right, so do you find that you're angry often?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I wouldn't say I'm angry often, I just think it's if people did what I wanted them to do when I wanted them to do it, I wouldn't be so upset as much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you find yourself upset on occasion.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: On occasion, but again, it's just if people would listen. Like, I don't know if it was last year, year before, I don't know when it was, like, it was one of those Thanksgivings, and just, my whole family's around, watching football. I'm cooking dinner. You know, busy all in the kitchen, everything's hot, what not. I've got this whole gourmet meal made. My brother's there, his family's there, my husband's family's there, everybody's there. Everybody, it's time to eat. They think this football game's more interesting than my food, I spent all day making this. So, I just went, took the TV, thought about throwing it at my brother, he's 45 years old, he should be listening, you know. But just threw it on the ground, smashed it. Now you will listen. I stood there, screamed for a little bit, got it all out, it felt so good. Stood there, screamed, they're all staring, but you better believe they ate.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you feel like you planned to throw the TV or is it just something that came up in the moment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It just happened. I didn't plan it or anything, but I just want them to eat, you know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It was more of a spur of the moment thing.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Spur of the moment, completely spur of the moment.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: But it got their attention. They ate.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It got their attention, the TV being broken.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so this has, your anger and some of your behaviors caused some recent trouble with the law. That's why you're here.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Everything, like I said, is blown out of proportion. There's no need for the police, no need for the courts or anything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But now they're involved and you feel like counseling might be helpful?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: If I want to keep my job, yes. I can't go to jail, I can't face any charges, I can't do that. So counseling would be helpful in that regard. But I don't see it as a problem.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You don't see the anger as a problem, but...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't see what everybody's talking about. My husband says I have these anger issues, my kids say I throw a temper tantrum like a two-year-old. But I don't see it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're just not seeing it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't see it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Do you have any history of medical problems, mental health problems?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mm-mm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You ever use drugs or alcohol?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Nope. Clean as a whistle.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Nothing like that. Okay. So, it seems like you are open to the idea of counseling. I'd like to get you scheduled with one of our counselors. I can get you in a couple days, if that works.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That'll work. It'll have to work.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right Tiffany, I appreciate you answering these questions, this has been helpful and I'll get you set up with the counselor.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: All right.

video_details.title: Counseling Diagnostic Assessment Vignette #25 - Symptoms of Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
video_details.description: This counseling diagnostic assessment vignette demonstrates an interview with a client (played by an actress) who exhibits symptoms of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Jessica, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're doing well? That's good. Yeah. I understand you've been having some difficulties recently that brought you into the agency.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I was in a car accident about a month and a half ago. And I've just been having these issues that are preventing me from doing the things I'm used to doing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me about the accident?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I was on my way home from work and I was sitting at a stop sign and waiting for my turn to go. And as I proceeded through the stop sign, a car just came and blew through and hit me on the side and pushed me straight through the stop sign.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Were you hurt?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, not too bad, no.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Scary, though, huh?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was very scary.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And when was this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: This was about a month and a half, I guess maybe two months ago.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: About two months ago? Yeah. All right, and when did the symptoms start?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Shortly after. Um, I've been feeling pretty bad for about a month or so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Can you tell me about those feelings?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've had a lot of anxiety, especially when it comes to getting in my car and going places. I just get really overwhelmed with fear, just scared that I'm going to get in another car accident.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. You are still driving?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not a lot. Not a lot, no.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, you're not driving a lot, but you are able to drive. But when you do drive, there's a lot of anxiety, there's a lot of fear. Are you more aware of what's going on around you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Definitely. I think I'm over-aware. I can't sometimes I can't even focus on where I'm going because I'm just paying attention to all the drivers on the road, just making sure that I don't get hit again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so you're driving with more awareness of what's going on around you. Anxious. Any irritability?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, yes, a lot more than usual.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I have two dogs and I love my dogs, and just lately everything they do just gets on my nerves, you know, just barking, walking, I mean everything just. And I don't know where that's coming from. I've never been like that with them before, but they just they bother me so much that I don't even want them around sometimes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
