diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: More often than not, yeah. Do you find yourself struggling to control the anxiety?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, to control it, um, I'm just anxious all the time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yes. Alright, so it sounds like you are struggling to get it under control.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. Tell me about how it's been affecting... you mentioned school?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's... I'm not doing too well in school right now, not at all.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In what way?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I thought I would be a better student. I was always a straight-A student back before when I was in undergrad, I was always a straight-A student, but now I'm failing, and I just can't, I can't concentrate in school. I'm failing. I'm just so worried all the time about how I'm going to do in this class, what assignments are due, if I'm getting the work done in time, and it's just controlling, it's taking over everything I do in school. So I'm so more, I'm more worried about how I'm going to do than having time to focus on my grades. Like, it's just to that level.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's really distressing for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And that's at school. How about at home?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: At home, I'm so worried about school that it's affecting my life at home. Like I'm, okay, I have this assignment, but then, oh my goodness, I'm so focused on this assignment, will I have time to make dinner for the kids? Oh, my husband's going to... oh, the house is such a mess all the time, and it's just causing so much conflict at home. My husband thinks I should be doing my housework, and I'm so consumed with school, and then it's just such a big mess right now. So I'm constantly worried when I'm at school, I'm worried about home, and when I'm home, I'm worried about school.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, so a good deal, a good deal of worrying.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: All the time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You know, all the time. Okay. So I want to ask you a few questions about this, and some that might be related. Do you drink or use any drugs?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, not at all.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Not at all. Do you have any medical conditions?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, not at all.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Nothing? Alright. Have you ever been diagnosed with any other mental health disorders?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: None? Do you ever have panic attacks?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therist
diarization.text: Do you... have you ever had one in the past?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, no.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No? No. So a lot of anxiety but no panic?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just the, just the anxiety, like overwhelming anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Intense anxiety, yes, but never a situation where you felt you had to flee from a room or anything like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No. Alright. Any past trauma?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, nothing like that. Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you sometimes feel keyed up, on edge, or restless?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm restless, yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Restless. Alright. Do you find yourself easily fatigued?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, tired all the time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tired all the time. Alright. Do you have any trouble concentrating or finding your mind going blank?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, not really.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No? Just no. How about, uh, irritability? Find yourself irritable?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Not really. Not really irritable. Any muscle tension?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, not really.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No. Okay. How about any trouble sleeping? So this would be falling asleep, staying asleep, having unsatisfactory sleep, anything like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I have unsatisfactory sleep, but we just moved and we live next to a factory. There's trucks in and out all the time. Who can sleep with that? There's chronic, just noise.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you think that might be causing your sleep disturbance?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, it's entirely possible, but like who can sleep when you got trucks in and out all hours of the night, overnight, and in the wee hours of the morning? So it's pretty much impossible to fall asleep when you have just this noise.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about before you moved there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I don't remember. I really don't remember.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How long ago was it that you moved to where you are now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, a couple years.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Been a couple years? Yes. So you've had this noise at night for a couple years, yes, and symptoms started eight months ago.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. Alright. So I don't know if they've made it worse or if it's just the noise has just been, so I don't know if it's the noise or what, but I can't sleep through a truck.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. How about any vacations or anything? Have you slept...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No! I'm sorry. I'm sorry.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No vacations, huh? All right. So you've pretty much been sleeping at your home every night for as long as these symptoms have been around.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Ah, yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. All right. All right, Sarah. I appreciate you answering these questions for me. This has been helpful. I'm going to get you scheduled with a counselor, and they should be able to see you in a couple days.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, thank you. Thank you. I would, I would so appreciate it just to get this under control.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Absolutely. Alright. Take care, Sarah.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

video_details.title: Counseling Diagnostic Assessment Vignette #8 - Client with Features of ADHD
video_details.description: This counseling diagnostic assessment vignette demonstrates an interview with a client (played by an actress) who exhibits features of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD).

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Lisa, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I guess I'm doing okay, but I'm having some problems.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're doing okay? You're having some problems? What's going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I find myself getting really distracted, kind of fidgety and stuff, and I think I might have that one disorder that I hear about all the time on TV.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Like ADHD?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's the one.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You think you might have ADHD?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so let me ask you some other questions and then we'll get into some questions specifically about that and see what's going on there. Okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you ever find yourself depressed?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Anxious?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any trouble with drugs or alcohol?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh no, nothing like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When did you first notice you had the symptoms?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: In my early teens, maybe before.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you know what age?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But you think early teens, maybe before?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do the symptoms, are they really bothersome to you? Are they causing you problems?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What kind of areas do they cause you problems?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean really everywhere, I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you work?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does this cause problems at work?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about college?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about at home?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so tell me a little bit about the symptoms that you think might indicate ADHD.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, when I go to class and I find myself going off into my own little world when the teacher's talking. Sometimes I just can't stand sitting down, and then I'll stand up and the teacher's looking at me like I need something.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you feel compelled to stand up in class, even though you know it might draw some attention?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, unfortunately. I mean I know it, but I still, I need to do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so I'm going to ask you a few questions in two categories. Do you feel like you have trouble establishing attention, specifically in school?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about when you have established attention? Do you find yourself struggling to hold onto it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is the school environment a place where these symptoms bother you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, they bother me in a lot of other places, but school is a big issue.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have trouble listening in class?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about following through on instructions provided by the professor?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. Class projects are the hardest.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you find yourself organized?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I am pretty organized.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you find yourself avoiding activities that require a lot of mental effort?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. They give me a headache and I just don't want to do them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What are some things you avoid?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Board games. I can't stand chess. People explain to me the rules and I just zone out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you ever find yourself losing things that you need to function at work or school?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Distracted?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I do get distracted fairly easily.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about forgetfulness?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I am pretty forgetful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so now I'm going to ask you another category of questions. Do you find yourself fidgeting?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How do you do with quiet activities, like reading?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I really struggle with that. I can play a video game, but I can't read or draw.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So when you are engaged in quiet activities, do you find yourself kind of wandering off?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you ever feel like you have an internal motor that won't shut off?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I wouldn't say that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you feel like you talk excessively?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. Almost to the point that I interrupt people a lot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In what settings do you find that's a problem?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: School's a big one. I'll get off track when called on by the teacher, and then I'll interrupt others. I feel horrible but I just can't stop it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you ever find that sitting in class you blurt things out and interrupt people?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I do interrupt people.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In situations where you have to wait your turn, like in a line or a drive-thru, do you find that's a problem?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, like at a drive-thru? It doesn't really bother me. I guess not.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so I'm going to get you in to see one of our counselors. It'll take a couple days to get you in to see somebody, is that okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, that's fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Lisa, I want to thank you for spending this time with me and answering these questions. This has been really helpful.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks.

video_details.title: Counseling Diagnostic Assessment Vignette #9 - Client with Features of ADHD
video_details.description: This counseling diagnostic assessment vignette demonstrates an interview with a client (played by an actress) who exhibits features of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD).

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, Elisa, how are you today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I guess I'm doing pretty good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Doing pretty good?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, so I was looking up online during break between my classes. I go to online school...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Like college?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. And they have this, I was looking up my symptoms, I guess, of difficulty paying attention, difficulty staying still, just stuff like that, and you know, I think I might have that, that one disorder, ADHD?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, that one. You think you might have ADHD?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. Is it, are these symptoms bothering you, you said you go to college online?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, it does.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. I'm going to ask you a few questions and try to get a better understanding of what's going on.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: These symptoms you've been having, what age did they start?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: About 8 years old.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: 8 years old. All right. And you feel like they're bothering you with your classes that you take online.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, but I still get good grades.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You still get good grades? All right. So let me ask you some questions about that. So I'll specifically be asking about how it affects you in class, but if it affects you in any other area, tell me about that too.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have trouble establishing attention?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When you have established attention, do you have difficulty holding attention?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you, for example, with a professor, do you listen to the professor in your online classes?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I have difficulty listening. That's a problem for me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about following through on any instructions that the professor gives you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, I have a real big problem.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you organized?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I am actually organized.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you find yourself avoiding activities that require a lot of mental effort?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What type of activities do you avoid?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, anything that, just like riddles, I can't stand them. Chess, can't stand it. People try to explain me the rules, I still don't get it. I get a headache and I quit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you ever find yourself losing things that you need for class or any other place?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: All the time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you easily distracted?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. Big time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you forgetful?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So, I'm going to move to another series of questions. Okay. Do you fidget?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you find it difficult to stay in your seat?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, there, we have these videos, and sometimes I just got to pause them and I just got to walk around my room for a while. You know, then go back, sit down, get it out of my system, click, and we're good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you feel kind of compelled to stand up and walk around and then you can sit down and resume?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How do you do with quiet activities, like reading?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, no, I don't like doing them because I just can't, I can't deal with the quiet.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you ever feel like you have an internal motor that's always running?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about talking? You find that you talk excessively?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about blurting things out?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, but people don't really notice it because, especially at class, I'll like yell out the answer, but you have to hit a button. And I forget to hit the button.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, you have to hit a button so that like the camera turns on and the audio turns on, okay. So you'll blurt something out, but they won't hear it because you haven't pressed that key. Okay.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, they won't. So I guess that's good, but...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about interrupting people?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have trouble waiting your turn?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Back to the blurting out, I forget to hit the button, I then hit the button to answer and it goes into like this line. I hate waiting for my turn. I can't, I can't deal with it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, that's not a strong suit for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. Go, answer.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you mentioned that this is causing some difficulty in school, but you also said that you're doing okay in school.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there any other area of your life where this is causing you problems?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mmm, not that I can think of, no.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What else do you do? So you go to college?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Really nothing. I got a full course load, trying to get it done, really don't do anything else. I mean, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about like relatives?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't see my relatives a lot. Like my parents retired, they moved, so I don't see them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about friends?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's kind of embarrassing, but I really don't have any friends. Just kind of live, eat, and breathe school.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you ever socialize with any of your classmates from college?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you feel that's because of these symptoms or that you wouldn't anyway?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I feel bad about it, so I mean it's hard for me to you know get over it because I notice it, but it's hard for me to get out there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Do you think it's hard for you to engage with your classmates socially because of any concentration or hyperactivity type symptoms?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's what I believe, yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And any other areas, like shopping or cleaning the house?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, doing pretty okay with that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Elisa, I'm going to get you in to see a counselor. It'll just take a couple days to get you in, so I'll set up an appointment for a couple days out. I appreciate you spending this time with me and letting me ask these questions, this was helpful.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks.

video_details.title: Counseling Diagnostic Assessment Vignette #7 - Client with Features of ADHD
video_details.description: This counseling diagnostic assessment vignette demonstrates an interview with a client (played by an actress) who exhibits features of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD).

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Lise, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm doing pretty well, but I'm kind of concerned about something.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm aware you have some symptoms that have been bothering you. Can you tell me about those?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes I have problems with my attention. I've been looking it up online and I'm worried I might have ADHD.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We'll talk about that. First, do you ever feel depressed or anxious, or have trouble with drugs or alcohol?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, nothing like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Why do you think you have ADHD?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've always had a problem with my attention and I get distracted easily.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have trouble establishing or holding attention?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I have trouble with both. I'm easily distracted.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is this at work or school? How old are you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm 24. It affects me everywhere, at work and school. It's part of my everyday life.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When did you first notice the attention problems?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've always had it, even in elementary school.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How much is it interfering with your functioning?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It really does. It's very problematic.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's talk about the school environment. Do you have trouble listening, following instructions, or organizing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I'm actually very organized. I don't have problems with those things.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you avoid activities that require mental energy? Do you lose things needed for tasks?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. I actually like activities like chess. I don't lose things.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you find yourself fidgeting, having trouble staying seated, or feeling like you have an internal motor running?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really. I do well with quiet activities and don't feel like there's a motor running.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about being talkative? Do you find yourself interrupting people?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm very talkative. I often interrupt people because I feel like I just have to get it out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you find it difficult to wait your turn or blurt things out in class?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, not really.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I have what I need. I'd like to get you in to see a counselor in a couple of days.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's great, thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I appreciate you taking the time. This has been helpful.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you very much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks, Lise.

video_details.title: Counseling Diagnostic Assessment Vignette #6 - Client with Features of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
video_details.description: This counseling diagnostic assessment vignette demonstrates an interview with a client (played by an actress) who exhibits features of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD).

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Emma, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm doing good, thanks. How are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing well, thank you for asking. I understand that you've come here today because you've had some symptoms that have been bothering you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, um, I have anxiety sometimes and, um, I've lost about three jobs within the past year.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You've lost three jobs in the past year. Is it because of the anxiety?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, well, I'm scared that something's going to happen at my apartment, so I need to unplug things. But it has to be in order. So when I unplug things, it has to start with like the TV and then my computer and then my phone and then the lamps. And then I've been late to work.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I see. You have a system you go through of unplugging different objects in your apartment. And you're worried that they're going to cause a problem if they're left plugged in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, like if they overheat, it could like burn it down.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're afraid that if you leave them plugged in, they'll overheat and your apartment will catch on fire. And you have a particular order you go in as you unplug.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What happens if you're unplugging the items and you get distracted or something interrupts that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I mean, sometimes I'll get like a text message and I'll hear my phone go off. Um, I'll have to just start all over again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Will you plug the objects back in or how will you do it for the items that are already unplugged?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I would just have to unplug them and then I would have to plug them back in or vice-versa.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you go back and plug them in and unplug them. What's your anxiety level like as you start that process?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's really bad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about towards the end of the process?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It goes away, but it's just kind of temporary, just for a little bit of time and then it comes back and I have to go check it again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So when it comes back, everything's unplugged, so you have to plug everything back in and unplug it and go through the whole process again. So it's pretty distressing. And you think that this is what led to the problems with employment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, cause I also, um, I have to lock my door, but I like to lock it twelve times. So I'll put the key in and I'll hear it click, but then I just like doing it twelve times just to make sure it's locked. Um, and that made me late for work. And then when I was at work, I have a drawer, I'm a cashier. Um, so I would just make sure it was locked, but I would have to do it, you know, twelve times just to make sure it was locked and I didn't get back in time to like help the customers.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I see. Your employer wasn't happy with that and that led to you losing your job. Are you working now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, um, I had a job for a little bit of time. It was again a cashier position, but I was on break and, you know, I was like in the room and I had the lights and I just wanted to make sure like they would go off all the way because I didn't want to leave the light on. Um, and by the time I got done turning them on and just make sure they were off, I didn't get back in time on the floor and, um, my employer just said I wasn't a good fit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so these symptoms have caused you some real problems with employment and how about with your anxiety level? If we were to put it on a scale, like where 1 was very little anxiety and 10 was the worst anxiety you've ever experienced, what kind of anxiety are you having on a daily basis now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably like a 10.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And checking doors, checking light switches, unplugging everything, this reduces your anxiety for a while?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just for a little bit, but then it comes back.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there anything else that you do that helps to reduce the anxiety?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's just, I guess when I'm in the act of doing it, it will relieve it and then I'll be okay for a little bit of time. Um, like even coming in, you know, I saw that you had chairs and, um, some pictures and I just, like I had to touch them, like I had to touch the chairs, um, but I wanted to touch the chairs first and then the pictures and that's normally what I do in a room, like I have to touch the chairs first and I feel okay when I'm doing it, um, and then when I'm finished, I feel a little better, but then it comes back, the anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you know how long you've had these symptoms?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably since, I guess like third grade, maybe.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so sometime. Did they start off like they are now or were they different?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, it started off with a little bit of things, like I would just get a little bit of anxiety and I just would want to play with the doorknob. And then, as I got... it went away for like a year maybe, and then I would start to play with the lights and just make sure that they were off.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And was it the same thing? Did it help reduce anxiety?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. My parents didn't really like it. They kind of were like, you know, 'something's wrong with you, stop playing with that.'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Were you ever taken somewhere and diagnosed or treated?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, no. Um, my parents just thought it was like nerves.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And now it's the worst it's ever been? Do you feel like you're able to go back to work with the symptoms the way they are now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably not.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Because they're so disruptive. Have you ever had any medical conditions?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, nothing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. And have you ever used or do you use any type of drug or alcohol?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, none.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Emma, I want to thank you for coming in. I'm going to get you scheduled to see one of our counselors. I appreciate you spending this time with me. It's helped me to understand what you're going through.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks.

video_details.title: Counseling Diagnostic Assessment Vignette #5 - Client with Features of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
video_details.description: This counseling diagnostic assessment vignette demonstrates an interview with a client (played by an actress) who exhibits features of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD).

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Emma, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm good, thanks. How are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing well, thank you for asking. I understand you've been having some symptoms that are bothersome to you. Can you tell me about what's going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh, yeah. I moved into my apartment, um, about a year ago. And I've been having, I guess like, anxious thoughts and um, sometimes I'm scared I'm going to lose my apartment.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, so you've been having anxiety, you've been having thoughts about possibly losing your apartment. All right, so tell me more about that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Um, well when I write out my check for the rent, um, I usually would pay it online, but then I would click the button and it would submit it a couple times. So after I just wanted to make sure it got paid, um, so then I started to actually go in person and pay it, um, but then I'd like check my statement just to make sure they cashed it and they got it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: To make sure they really received your payment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. And, um, I'm also nervous that, you know, something might happen where I leave my straightener on and the apartment like burns down or something.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Do you uh, find yourself like acting on that thought, like say specifically that thought with the straightener?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'll check it. Um, and I'll just make sure that it's unplugged, and then I look around and make sure everything's unplugged because I don't want anything getting hot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What, when you say everything, what do you mean?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, like the toaster and um, my computer, like my laptop charger, and my cell phone, um, the charger for that, and just anything that's plugged in like the television, I just want to make sure everything's unplugged before I leave.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Before you leave your apartment. What do you do when you come back?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Um, I check to make sure they're still unplugged. Um, but then when I need to use it, I plug it back in.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So if you need to use, for instance, your television, do you plug it in and watch it and then unplug it immediately or only before you leave?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Before I leave.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Before you leave? So you leave it plugged in while you're there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. When did you first notice the uh, anxiety?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hmm. I guess like six months ago.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: About six months ago? How did it start out?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Um, it started with just thinking about things, thinking about leaving, you know, the door unlocked or being unsure if I paid bills, just like thinking about it and then I'd have to like double check it and triple check it and just kind of make sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Did it start there? Did it start with the door locks?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. It started with just thinking and making sure the door was locked.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And do you still do that now? Do you check the door several times?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I just make sure it's locked.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. And so how do you do that? Do you get up and look at it and see that it's locked and then go sit down and think about it and come back, or do you operate the mechanism back and forth?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I just go and I look and I make sure it's locked and then I'll go back down and I'll just sit back down and I'll be okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: For a while? And does that thought ever come back and you have to go check it again?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Sometimes. Not not really. I'll just check it and then it's fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Do you have kind of a checklist in your mind for when you leave your apartment? Do you do um, like unplug everything in roughly the same order and check everything in a similar order?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I haven't really thought about it, but I I make sure everything's unplugged. Like I I know what needs to be unplugged.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So you do have kind of a a list in your mind of what has to be unplugged and you make sure it's all unplugged.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Exactly.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. And how about when you lock your door from the outside when you're leaving? Do you check that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I'll check it, um, and then if I'm sitting in my car, I just might go back just to double check it and just make sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So you're you're checking the door, you're unplugging various items that may create heat. Um, you're careful with your uh, paying your rent. So fear and anxiety surrounding uh, losing the apartment in some manner. How is this affecting your daily life, these symptoms?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I mean it's time consuming. Um, sometimes I'm late for work um, because I'll think I left something plugged in and I'll have to go back inside. Um, sometimes I'll lock the door and have to go back and make sure it's locked. So I'm usually late for things because I'm double checking.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so it's causing some problems getting places on time. Um, how about your level of anxiety or worry? How high would you say that is?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Um, I guess it would be like high, I guess, thinking about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's troubling for you. If you think about from when it started, it started out it sounds like with a few thoughts, right? If we say that's um, relatively low anxiety, yeah. How would what you have now compare to that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I guess moderate. Like a little higher.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Just a little higher? All right. But you have noticed it's worsened over the six months. Is it the most anxiety you've ever experienced?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Um, I kind of consider myself an anxious person. So I guess, yeah. Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This is the most you've experienced? So this is particularly troubling? Now you said you've always been, you said, anxious person. Tell me about that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. Um, just like in group settings or um, I remember just something when I was younger, um, I was like just playing with a door or something like that and my parents took me to some I don't know, some doctor, and um, they just said I was anxious.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Did they give you any treatment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I I don't know. I don't think so. They just said I was anxious.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So other than saying you're anxious, was there any diagnosis provided?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, not really.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever had any mental health diagnosis?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just I guess just feeling anxious, but not necessarily like a diagnosis.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Not from a provider? Okay. How about any medical conditions?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Nope.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: None? Have you ever been in the hospital or anything?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mm-mm. Just to like get my tonsils taken out, but not like anything else.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. How about uh, drugs or alcohol? Any any usage of those?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Nope.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Never?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mm-mm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Um, Emma, I'm going to have you see a uh counselor here, and get you scheduled to see somebody. I appreciate you taking this time with me explaining the symptoms. It's been helpful.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks.

video_details.title: Counseling Diagnostic Assessment Vignette #3 - Client with Features of Social Anxiety Disorder
video_details.description: This counseling diagnostic assessment vignette demonstrates an interview with a client (played by an actress) who exhibits features of social anxiety disorder.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Sasha, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm alright, thanks. How are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing okay, thanks for asking. I understand that you've been having some difficulty with some symptoms. Is that right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, definitely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me about what's been going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: For the past few weeks, I have these morning meetings once a week at work where I have to make a presentation. Every time it's my turn to present, I start getting really nervous.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You start getting really nervous. So at the morning meeting, does each person present in a row?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, we all take turns.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When do you start to feel nervous? Is it when it's your time to talk, or before or after that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Usually at the start of the meeting, because I know I'm going to have to. There's about 10 of us, and I always seem to be one of the last few to go.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Around 10 people and you tend to be toward the end. Can you describe what you're experiencing from the beginning of the meeting?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When I walk in, I'm usually okay. Then my boss calls the meeting to order, and that's when it starts with butterflies in my stomach. Then my heart starts beating faster, my palms get sweaty, and I start to feel really nervous. I kind of tune out the other presentations because I'm focused on how I'm feeling.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're focused on the physical and mental sensation of being nervous and you're not really listening to what others are saying?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you have these physical symptoms and this nervousness. What happens then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: By the time it's my turn, I'm almost shaking. I'll keep my hands in my lap so nobody sees them shaking. I read from a paper, but my voice is shaky, I stutter and trip over words. I feel like I'm not making good presentations and it's not looking good to my boss.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So when it's your turn to present, you're still feeling that same nervousness and it doesn't go away?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you're trying to hold your body still to keep control, and your voice is crackly as you read from an outline?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. What happens when you have read the last point?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When I'm done, it takes a little bit to calm down. Then I'm consumed by the idea that my boss thinks I did a terrible job and regrets putting me in this position. My mind just shifts on what I'm anxious about.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The stronger feeling of nervousness is replaced by a more general nervousness about how your boss will think of you because of the presentation quality?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Because your voice is crackly, he's picking up on that and you're aware of that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How long have you noticed these symptoms appearing in this way?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: In college, I'd get nervous when I made presentations, but I figured it was normal since most people are afraid of public speaking. It never really bothered me then, but it's been an issue in the last few weeks.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you had some nervousness in college, but it didn't impair your ability to present. You've really noticed it recently?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have any other symptoms that you think may be related or unrelated?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My mom doesn't like to speak in public. When I was in school, she'd say, 'You come by it honest, honey.' So I don't know if that means anything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you think maybe she has the same set of symptoms?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe. She hasn't been in this kind of situation with a small group, but she says she's gotten nervous before.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any feelings of sadness or anything like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: After the presentation, I start feeling really sad because I feel like my boss isn't satisfied and will regret giving me the position. I feel disappointed in myself.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have any substance use, alcohol or anything else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I have a drink very rarely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has the nervousness ever caused you to leave the room before it was your turn?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I've managed to control it. I've zoned out sometimes when others present, which I feel bad about, but I'm focused on my heart beating and my hands shaking. I still push through and do my presentation.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you ever worried about what the other workers at the table are thinking about you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes, because I'm the newest member of the management team. One person has been really supportive, which helps, but at the end of the day, it's my boss's opinion that matters.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever felt nervous well in advance of the meeting?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When I'm preparing that morning, I start thinking about it, but I don't start feeling anything until I'm actually in the room.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you have this intense nervousness at these meetings for the last few weeks. We'll get you set up with treatment in the next few days if that works for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that'd be great.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I appreciate you spending this time with me. It's been helpful.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks Sasha.

video_details.title: Counseling Diagnostic Assessment Vignette #4 - Client with Features of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
video_details.description: This counseling diagnostic assessment vignette demonstrates an interview with a client (played by an actress) who exhibits features of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD).

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Emma, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm doing good thanks, how are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing well, thank you for asking. I understand you've been having some symptoms that have been bothering you lately. Can you tell me about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I just moved into an apartment and it's the first time that I'm on my own. I heard that someone got robbed and ever since then I'm kind of nervous about my apartment getting robbed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Someone was robbed near where you live?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, someone in the same complex. So sometimes when I'm sleeping, I'll wake up in the middle of the night and I'll think, did I lock the door? Is the door unlocked? And I can't fall back asleep.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How long does it take you to fall back asleep?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes it takes maybe an hour or two.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what are you thinking about during that time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm just worried that I left the door unlocked. Sometimes I'll hear sounds and I think maybe someone's in the apartment. I just get scared that the door's unlocked.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That sounds scary. And you say a couple hours you stay awake? That's a while.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So this is troubling for you. Have you ever gotten up and checked the door?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I stay in bed and I just think about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so you just keep thinking about it. Does it get worse as that time goes on, or does it get better?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It gets worse. I try to fall back asleep and I stay in bed and I just think, you know, maybe I did leave the door unlocked, and then I just keep thinking that maybe it is unlocked.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it kind of keeps cycling through the same thoughts. Do you ever do anything to try to get those thoughts to go away, like focusing on something else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have a ceiling fan above me, so sometimes I'll just count how many times it goes around and try to distract myself, but I still think about the door being unlocked. Sometimes it helps.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so you have a fear that somebody's going to break into where you live, and you're staying up at night thinking about whether the door's been secured. Anything else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes if I'm leaving for work, I'll get to my car and think I left the hair straightener on. I'll debate whether or not I should go double check. I'm just worried that if I left the straightener on, something bad would happen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you think might happen?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, if I left the straightener on and it's on a cloth, that could burn. I just don't want the place to burn down, that's what I'm nervous about.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So when you leave, you're thinking about the hair straightener, whether you unplugged it or turned it off.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how long do those thoughts go on for?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Normally I think about it before I get into my car. Then sometimes at work I can't focus because I'm thinking about my apartment burning down because I left the straightener plugged in.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, I remember with the door you struggle with those thoughts but don't get up and check. Have you ever come back and checked to see if something was left on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I haven't. But I just think about it. What if I did leave it on or plugged in?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're worried, anxious...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Afraid?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, definitely. All three.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how often does this cycle of thoughts happen?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Throughout the day. Every day, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how long has this been going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Ever since I moved into the apartment, so about a year.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This has been going on for a year? Has it become any worse?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. It started with waking up and thinking, did I lock the door? But then I'd be fine. As it progressed, I would wake up multiple times throughout the night and it would keep me up.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: As you've thought about it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, I want to ask a few other questions. Have you ever been diagnosed with any mental health condition?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about a medical condition?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Never?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Nope.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever used alcohol or any other substances?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is this the first time in your life you've experienced these symptoms, starting a year ago?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Never anything like this before?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Nope.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Emma, I'm going to get you in to see one of our counselors here. I appreciate you spending this time with me. It's been helpful to understand what's going on.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks so much.

video_details.title: Counseling Diagnostic Assessment Vignette #2 - Client with Features of Social Anxiety Disorder
video_details.description: This counseling diagnostic assessment vignette demonstrates an interview with a client (played by an actress) who exhibits features of social anxiety disorder.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Sasha, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm alright thanks, how are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing okay, thanks for asking. I understand you've been having some symptoms that have been bothersome to you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me about those?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Um, for about the last six months or so, I have this position at work where I have to make a weekly presentation to other managers, about 10 people. And every time I have to do this, I lose it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You lose it, every time you have to make a presentation?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me what is involved with losing it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I'm usually one of the last people to go, and I just keep feeling more and more nervous. It starts where I feel butterflies in my stomach, and that just becomes more intense. I start to just sweat all over. I feel like my face is turning red. My palms get really sweaty. My heart just feels like it's going to beat right out of my chest. I just can't.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This is very distressing. Tell me about the nature of this meeting that's leading to this anxiety. You said you had to make a presentation? Tell me about the structure of it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: There's about 10 people, the executive director and then the managers of different programs, and we all have to do a weekly update report. None of it's very detailed, maybe a few minutes each person. We all take turns.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How long do you have to speak?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Usually just a few minutes, maybe five, at most 10, unless there's something major going on in my program.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And when in the course of this meeting occurring do you start to feel nervous?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The day before.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The day before?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. So the day before the meeting you start to have symptoms? What are you feeling?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I start to feel nervous. Usually the day before is when I'm pulling together my notes. When I'm preparing that I start to feel nervous, and then it usually lasts through the rest of the day, into the evening. I usually don't sleep well that night. By the time I get into the meeting, I'm pretty much panicking.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're panicking as the meeting's starting.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: At the meeting, everybody takes a turn. Tell me what's happening with your feelings as they're moving around the table and coming closer to you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I'm just becoming more and more terrified. I feel like I'm being drenched in sweat. I'm breathing faster and I feel like everybody notices. I feel like everybody can hear my heart beating, that it's just so loud that any minute everybody's going to look at me and say, 'What is wrong with you?'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: They're going to notice you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. There have been times recently where I feel like I've had to run out of the room. I couldn't take it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you run out of the room?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I have. I ran out and couldn't go back in. I tried and my hand hit the doorknob to go back in the room and I walked off. I couldn't do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Too much anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I felt okay in the hallway and then when I tried to go back in the room, everything just right back up again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, so you would push that door open, they would all be looking at you. They would wonder why you left.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you just rode out the meeting somewhere else? Did anybody notice after?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: After a few weeks in a row of running out, my boss was like, 'I noticed you didn't make your presentation,' and I just made up an excuse. But I feel bad because this is my job and I want to do my job. I had a terrible time making presentations in high school and college, and here we are again. I'm trying to be a professional and have a career, and I can't because I can't perform my job.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This is frustrating for you. Have there been times where you've fled the room and then since then you haven't?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: There was one time, the very first time I ran out and nobody noticed. Then the following week, I started to feel that way again, and then two of my co-workers actually started to get into a fight. It was getting really intense and I don't know what it was, I was fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Something about that intense interaction changed how you were feeling or distracted you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess. I felt normal.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: From that meeting on till now, have you been able to stay in for any of the other meetings?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You've had to leave because of the intensity of the symptoms.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. There have been a couple times where I've purposely gone in late, or I've actually just called in sick for the day. There were twice I sent somebody else in my place, but it gets noticed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you're experiencing symptoms when you avoid that interaction in the room too, right? Because you don't feel good about letting them down.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I want to do my job. I really like where I work and I like the people. But the thought of making these presentations every week just terrifies me. I don't want my boss to regret putting me in this position. He chose me and I don't want to let him down, and I feel like I am every week with this meeting.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So you're kind of stuck, right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any other symptoms that you think may or may not be related to this intense anxiety?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm not sleeping the night before the meetings. I have started to drink a little bit to try and take the edge off. I've tried a shot or two before going into my meeting.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does that have any effect?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably not a good effect. I was able to sit through the meeting, but everybody kept asking if I was okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: They're picking up on the alcohol?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I really feel like they were. I didn't want anybody to get close to me because I think they could smell it. I was too scared to do that again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any sadness or anything like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm miserable. Every time I think about how much I must be disappointing my boss, I just feel terrible.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You feel really down.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sasha, I know it's been tough going through all this. We'll get you scheduled in here to get treated in a couple days and you can start working with a counselor to address these symptoms. I appreciate you spending this time with me.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks.

video_details.title: Counseling Diagnostic Assessment Vignette #1 - Client with Features of Social Anxiety Disorder
video_details.description: This counseling diagnostic assessment vignette demonstrates an interview with a client (played by an actress) who exhibits features of social anxiety disorder.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How's it going, Sasha? How are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Good, thanks. How are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. I understand you had some symptoms recently that have been bothering you. Could you tell me about them?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, probably for the last eight months, maybe a year even. I have this position at work where I have to make these weekly presentations, and it's killing me. I can't do it anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me about how these presentations are set up.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's the executive director and ten managers sitting in a circle. Everyone goes around and does a weekly program update for five to ten minutes. Everyone takes turns, and depending on where you sit determines what order you present in.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you say that this situation with the presentation is killing you. What feelings are you having?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel like it's constantly on my mind and I'm constantly worried about it. I'm so consumed by this part of my job that I can't do anything else. I don't sleep the night before, and then by the time I get to the meeting, I'm panicking.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So this is distressing for you. At the beginning of the meeting, what would be your anxiety level? What's going on then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When I've sat down, I feel like I'm breathing harder, I'm starting to sweat, my face turns red, and my heart is racing. The closer it gets to my turn, I feel like everyone can hear my heart beating. My stomach gets in knots and I feel nauseous. Even when I make it to my presentation, I stutter and stammer and my voice doesn't project well. I feel like it's a mess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're not happy with the quality of your presentation, even when you're able to conduct it. Tell me about what you're feeling as the presentations come around the room to you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: If I can get an early seat next to my boss, I'm okay because I can get it over and done with. But many times I'm nervous or even hungover because I've been drinking to not feel as anxious. Then I wake up late and have to take one of the last seats. As it gets closer to me, I feel more panicky. In the last few weeks, I've had to just get up and leave.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So before the presentations come around to you, you get up and leave the room?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In those times when you've stayed and done the presentation, the symptoms are increasing as they go around the room. What's your anxiety level like during the actual presentation?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: During the presentation, I feel almost like everything stops. When it's done, there's a physical sense of relief. But then I feel miserable and upset with how I performed. I feel like I've disappointed my boss and myself. This has always happened to me; back in college, I would drop classes if I had to make a presentation. Even in group therapy as a teenager, I bolted out of the room.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you've had these symptoms for a long time. What about periods of time where you haven't had to be in front of other people?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Then I'm kind of okay. I can go to the movies if I sit on the end. I can go out with friends, but I don't like to go to new places. I like familiar places where I know the layout of the stores.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so it interferes with your functioning a little bit, but if you're not having to present, it's not as big a deal. Are you taking any other measures besides the drinking to avoid the situation?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I run out of meetings, call in sick, or arrive late. I've even talked to my boss about transferring to another department, which would be a demotion and a pay cut, because I can't live like this anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This is too painful. What has been the result of that discussion? Has anything happened as far as a transfer?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He thinks I'm doing a good job and doesn't want me to change positions, but I just can't do this anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you've tried to cope but haven't felt successful. You've had this problem in other circumstances too. Have you seen any symptoms like this in your parents?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, both of my parents and my sister actually. My sister found a job where she doesn't interact with anybody. My parents actually met in college after my mom made a presentation; my dad told her she did great even though he could tell she was nervous. They bonded over that nervousness they both had.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there may be a family history of symptoms like these. We'll get you in for treatment in the next couple of days to see a counselor. I think that could help. Thank you for spending this time with me, Sasha.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

video_details.title: What is Trauma-Focused CBT for Children and Adolescents?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My name's Christine and I'm concerned about my 6-year-old daughter, Jenny. About a year ago, Jenny had a babysitter touch her inappropriately when I wasn't home. Ever since, she's been experiencing terrible nightmares about it. Jenny also becomes fearful and starts sweating when a babysitter gets mentioned. I've noticed that Jenny's having difficulty sleeping and concentrating, she's often irritable and has loud outbursts, and she becomes very jumpy in response to loud noises. Her difficulties led me to consult with a clinical psychologist to explore my options to help her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Traumatic events tend to include situations where someone feels extreme fear or helplessness during the situation. Therefore, traumatic events typically involve situations where death or serious injury occurred or could have happened. Examples of traumatic events include violence, physical abuse, sexual abuse, serious motor vehicle accidents, or natural disasters like hurricanes, fires or earthquakes where people are seriously injured or killed. Immediately after a traumatic event, shock and denial are typical responses that people can have. Other reactions include unpredictable emotions, sadness, anger, flashbacks, relationship problems, and even physical symptoms like headaches or nausea. While these feelings are normal, especially within the first few weeks after experiencing a traumatic event, they can also become problematic if they don't improve over time. Some people have difficulty moving on with their lives. Therapy can help these individuals find more helpful ways of managing their emotions.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it sounds like your family has been dealing with some really heavy stuff, and I think it's really brave that you came here because I know it's hard to talk about and even think that Jenny went through something like that. A lot of what you're describing to me, how she's responding to this trauma, are actually really common reactions that we see among children who've experienced something like what Jenny went through. And we have some really good forms of therapy that can actually really help her cope with this and improve what's been going on for her. In particular, we have one form of therapy called Trauma-focused CBT, and it shows that 80% of kids who receive this kind of treatment show improvement after experiencing a trauma and even improves family functioning. Is that something you want to hear more about?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, absolutely, I think that'd be really helpful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Trauma-focused CBT tends to last three to four months because it lasts anywhere between 12 and 16 sessions. And we'll meet once a week for about an hour to an hour and a half. The therapy was designed to treat a lot of different kinds of trauma, including domestic violence, sexual assault, sexual abuse, and natural disasters, things like fires, floods, tornadoes, things like that. So I'll meet with you individually, I'll meet with Jenny individually, and we'll also have sessions where the three of us meet to kind of just talk about the thoughts and feelings that you guys are having about what happened. Any questions about any of that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess I'm just kind of wondering what specifically treatment will look like and kind of how it'll help her get over her symptoms.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, that's a great question. Why don't I go through the different phases of treatment to give you a better idea of what the therapy would look like.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The psychologist told me that the first part of treatment would involve laying the groundwork to help both Jenny and I understand the trauma that happened to her. She said this would include information on sexual abuse as well as the common reactions on the parts of the victims and their families. Secondly, she introduced a sex education component. She said that based on the nature of the trauma, it would be important for us to give Jenny information on healthy sexuality and body awareness in order to clear up any misunderstanding she might have as a result of the trauma. I was skeptical about this piece at first, but she assured me that my family's values would be emphasized during this piece.
