Finally, the psychologist told me there would be a risk reduction component. She said that this would involve teaching Jenny about warning signs to avoid high-risk situations in the future. She said this would involve teaching her how to communicate assertively and formulate healthy physical boundaries.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So basically I'll teach Jenny a series of exercises that she can use to help calm herself down when she's feeling overwhelmed and relieve the tension in her body when she feels stressed out. Examples of this include just sort of breathing exercises to kind of control her exhale, muscle relaxation when she's feeling tension in her body, and also a thought-stopping technique, so if she's having negative thoughts about what happened or negative thoughts in general, she can kind of combat those until she's in a better place to process them. So I'll cover these with Jenny and I'll also go over them with you so you can practice them with her at home.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We also spend a good portion of time in therapy talking about Jenny's emotions. And to do this we kind of teach her how to identify her emotions and how to talk about them and express them with other people and to a certain extent how to control them. And this is really important so that then when we do start talking about the actual trauma, she sort of has a toolkit for how to help her cope with her strong emotions. And we definitely incorporate parents a lot into this portion of the therapy because we find that it's really important that they're sort of modeling how to cope with emotions positively at home and also help her reinforce and reinforce in her when she is coping with emotions in a positive way.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, that sounds really good and really important. I like that this therapy seems like it does quite a bit to safeguard Jenny and her emotions. Are there any other kind of coping techniques that you're going to recommend throughout the course of therapy?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The other day, I overheard Jenny saying something to her dad about feeling like the abuse was her fault. And obviously as a parent, that's really difficult to hear. But then I just kept worrying about it and thinking about it and I talked to my friends and I talked to my mom and they all just told me that neither of us were thinking about this in a helpful way, but what happened to her was so terrible I don't know how else to think about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. So what you're describing is actually pretty common for parents and kids who've gone through what you guys have gone through. And it's actually one of the things that we'll talk about in therapy. And we'll kind of help you identify what thoughts you're having about it that might be more inaccurate or unhelpful and kind of help you reframe it so that you can think about it in a different way to alleviate some of that distress.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So as I told you before, one of the things that people can often do after they've experienced a trauma is try to avoid thinking about what happened or talking about what happened. And although that seems kind of logical, it actually hinders people from being able to get over what happened to them. So one of the most important things that we would do with Jenny, if you guys choose to do this kind of therapy, is we would have her retell the story of what happened again and again in session until she can retell what happened without getting really upset.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, okay. I'm not sure I understand though. I just kind of want her to move past it. How will telling the story over and over help her?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, I totally understand why you'd be concerned about this, but it is actually the most important and the most helpful part of this therapy. And the reason why is that it will actually help her to process the emotions in session so that day-to-day reminders or thoughts of what happened won't make her become as upset and then she won't be as likely to try and avoid certain places or things or people. And it just also helps her feel like she's in control of her emotions and able to move past what happened.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Will I ever hear the trauma narrative?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, that's a really good question. So once Jenny feels comfortable sharing the story with me multiple times without getting upset, I will share with you what happened without her in the room. And then over time as you can hear the story without getting upset, Jenny will share it with you in a session where the three of us are all present.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Wow. Um, that sounds really difficult, but I'm willing to try it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So once Jenny is able to go through the trauma narrative and remain calm, we'll start identifying what thoughts and feelings she might be having that are unhelpful and cause a lot of emotions and reframe them. So common themes that can come up for kids are feeling like they're responsible for what happened, they can have a lot of feelings of shame, and then also kind of just like general changes in trust for people overall, just to name a couple. So we'll kind of just talk about those and help her through those. And also it'll be important for us to talk about any strong emotions and thoughts you're having because that can happen for parents as well.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I definitely feel responsible about what happened to her. And I think she feels unsafe sometimes. I can see her get anxious or agitated in situations where maybe it doesn't call for it, but I just don't know what to do when that comes up.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. So cognitive processing can definitely help with your emotions and hers as well, but also we have the next phase of therapy we'll kind of help you manage her behavior at home when those strong feelings come up.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I informed my psychologist that following the trauma, Jenny was dealing with behavioral issues for the first time in her life. The psychologist reassured me that children often react to traumatic events with anxiety and emotional outbursts. She also told me that other common reactions include disruptive behavior, aggression, anger, or having trouble following rules. The psychologist told me that in the behavior management portion of therapy, several strategies would be introduced that would help me deal with these kinds of behaviors when they come up. The psychologist informed me that behavior management techniques help parents make desirable behaviors, like following the rules, more likely to occur, as well as making less desirable behaviors, like acting out, less likely to occur. She said that we achieve these things through the use of praise and things like timeout. She also told me that although it might feel difficult at first to punish Jenny for the undesirable behavior due to the trauma, that it's an important part of recovery. I agree that setting firm boundaries and discouraging the disruptive behavior is going to be important for Jenny's prolonged success.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: As I mentioned earlier, there will be a point in therapy at which Jenny is going to share the trauma narrative with you while the three of us are meeting together. And we include this in the therapy for multiple reasons. One, it's an important opportunity for Jenny to be able to share the narrative with you so that she can see that you're responding and being able to talk and hear about it in a calm way and so that you can model effective coping for her about what happened. It also gives you both the opportunity to clear up any misunderstandings or confusion about what happened and any emotions that might be stemming from that miscommunication.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Um, does this mean that I should be talking with her at length about the trauma outside of therapy?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, that's a really good question. And although that is the eventual goal of therapy, we kind of discourage parents from talking about it early on in therapy because we want to make sure that the communication is healthy and productive and that effective coping is getting modeled. And we just want to make sure that you're both comfortable communicating about it before that happens.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So do you have any other questions or concerns that you want to talk about in regards to this therapy?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't think so. Um, you've done a really good job explaining it and thank you for meeting with me. I feel like I have a much better idea of what our options look like.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: In order to find a trauma-focused CBT therapist, visit effectivechildtherapy.org and click on the link that says how to find a child therapist. Thank you so much for your time and for listening to our story.

video_details.title: CBT for Adolescent Depression
video_details.description:
This video addresses an effective psychological treatment for adolescent depression, Cognitive Behavioral Therapy. 

- http://effectivechildtherapy.org/

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, I'm Kendall Binyon.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And I'm Brooke Merrell.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And we are current doctoral candidates at the University of Wyoming clinical psychology program.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, we are making this video because we want the world to know more about adolescent depression.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This is such a big important topic to talk about because adolescent depression affects so many people and it affects so many different aspects of people's lives such as with family, friends, work, school and so much more.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, and depression is something that responds very well to treatment when somebody's able to get the treatment that is designed to best treat depression.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And that's that evidence-based treatment, which pretty much means that research shows that it works. So, what is depression? And how do you know if you or a loved one or your teen has depression or is just going through something that kind of looks like it?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, and this is a really important question that, you know, it's very difficult to know the answer to. But bottom line is if you are concerned about your mental health or the mental health of someone you care about, that's the perfect time to seek help.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And depression can look very different for each person. It's very individualized. In this video, we're going to cover kind of the common symptoms of depression, things that you can kind of look out for. We're also going to talk about how to find a therapist in your area, things to look out for when looking for a therapist, as well as what a typical course of treatment looks like.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And we really want to see how these mood changes are impacting your day-to-day function. Most of us can kind of picture what we're talking about, you know, these feelings of sadness or worthlessness or loss of pleasure, and we can picture what it looks like to have your mood impairing day-to-day function. And just remember that it may not always be exactly what we picture from movies or TV or references or friends, that it might look different for other people and that it is really common.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You know, this is a really important topic and it's also very common in adolescents. In fact, 7% of adolescents meet criteria for depression. That's huge, right? That's equivalent to one in 14 adolescents each year. And the median age is 13 to 14 years old.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do we do? So, you know, I am feeling sad or I am feeling down or someone I know is having these problems. And where can we go?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, one of the best things that we recommend is going to visit effectivetherapies.org. Luckily though, we've already done the work for you because we're that nice.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yay! So we're going to talk about some effective treatments for adolescent depression.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yep.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, we are going to focus on cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT for short. And this is proven to be one of the most effective treatments for adolescent depression. CBT is the model that we practice from here in our clinic because we practice what works. For other disorders or other problems, it might be something different. We are going to focus on individual CBT because that's the most easy to access throughout the US.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hold up. So by therapy, do you mean me going laying on a couch while some old guy takes notes on a tiny notepad and talks about my childhood?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Even though that might be a common picture, it's definitely one that I have. And even though your psychologist might be an old guy in a cardigan, that is not quite what we're talking about.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So if it's not on a couch, then where is it?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, this is actually one of our therapy rooms that we use here at the University of Wyoming. Like I said, you might have an old guy in a cardigan, but you probably won't be laying on the couch. And we don't focus too much on your childhood. Instead, we focus on your current problems and how to find solutions to that. The biggest core component of CBT is this collaborative relationship between the therapist and the client.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Exactly. So let's talk about a typical setup for CBT. Treatment typically lasts anywhere from 6 to 20 sessions.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hold up. 6 to 20 sessions? I thought therapy was like the chiropractor and you see them once a week for the rest of your life.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Actually, treatment usually lasts 6 to 20 sessions, but here in our clinic, it's actually even smaller, usually 12 to 15 sessions. Usually meeting about 50 minutes once a week. So, you know, it's very manageable. It's time-oriented.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And this is really important because the time-oriented piece helps keep this end goal in mind for both the client and the clinician. For the client, that means you know you're going to stop seeing your therapist after a while, so you want to make sure you are working on the things that are causing impairment and make the most out of treatment.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: For the clinician, it's also very effective because we're having to constantly re-evaluate the progress that the client is making to make sure they're on the right track.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, and the reason why this is so important is because with CBT the goal is teaching the client how to gain control over their life and kind of become their own therapist and figure out ways of coping that they can use in the future.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. And with that goal-oriented direction, one of the things we also like to do with CBT is assign homework.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Wait, what? She just said homework. Did you catch that?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I did, yes. But keep in mind even though it might seem a little tedious, it's pretty easy to follow. We're asking you to do things to reinforce those skills, like looking at your behavior over the past week or keeping track of your thoughts and feelings.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, and it's really just like implementing the skills you are learning and putting them into practice. It's helping you gain control slowly, one day at a time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Absolutely. The basic premise is that your thoughts, feelings and behaviors are all interacting. Cognition is the C for CBT, and that's one area we focus on. We can change these things in therapy and by changing one, we can see changes in the other areas. If we can help you change your patterns of thinking, we can see changes in behavior which then translates to changes in feelings.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's awesome. Typically, CBT starts with one to three sessions of information gathering. In this assessment period, there are two main goals. The first is understanding the symptoms and arriving at a diagnosis. Second is understanding the symptoms well enough to have an effective treatment plan in motion.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, and the client and the therapist work together to develop a treatment plan specific to that individual. We like to think of the therapist as the expert on depression, whereas the client is the expert on them. We need their expertise mixed with ours to make the best treatment possible.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's deep. So once this treatment plan is in place, then treatment starts. A typical session often involves a mood rating, so like filling out sheets about how your symptoms are each week.

diarization.speaker: Thererpist
diarization.text: A check-in.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yep, how the client's week has gone for them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yep. And then we review the homework together with the client and help problem solve any issues or celebrate successes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yep. Then we go through the main skill development area, the big chunk of therapy you might think of.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yep, and then we do an assignment of the next homework, a summary and then a final check-in. So you want to tell them more about that core skill development piece?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, absolutely. The goal is to really help the client understand the principles of CBT, meaning how one's thoughts, feelings and emotions all interact and influence one another. This can be accomplished by reviewing the homework and seeing why it did or didn't happen, or looking at any negative thoughts impacting their mood.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you may be wondering how effective CBT is for treating adolescent depression compared to other options.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, so with CBT we typically see that clients have relief from their symptoms of depression after just three to four sessions.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But how long until the client's feeling better all the way?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That is the question. Usually, we stop seeing clients when they are feeling better, and that's an average of 12 to 15 sessions. They learn the skills they need to help prevent future depressive episodes. Usually, after CBT, the client no longer has depressive episodes, or if they do, they're less severe.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I know one of the big questions is how does CBT relate to medication?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, that is a huge question. Generally, CBT provides the same amount of relief as medication, but without the negative physiological side effects. CBT tends to be just as effective without those bodily reactions.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, and like I mentioned earlier, with CBT we're teaching the client to become their own therapist. The outcome of treatment for CBT lasts a lot longer than medication.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, that's right. CBT allows for treating the root cause of depression, whereas medication doesn't really allow that. Even though medication can work quickly to alleviate symptoms, usually once people stop taking it, the symptoms return. Overall, CBT is better at reducing relapses.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. It's important to know though that not everyone who says they practice CBT actually does. So make sure you talk to the therapist and ask them about the model they practice. So I'm guessing you're wondering how exactly to find a CBT therapist.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: There's a lot of different ways. One of the easiest ways is to Google search ABCT therapists, which stands for the Association for Behavioral and Cognitive Therapies.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, you can also look at the American Board for Professional Psychology website. Additionally, you can contact your insurance provider. Most importantly, make sure they're licensed in your area.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, for sure. Sometimes when you're looking for a therapist, there are barriers, and one of the biggest can be cost. First check with your insurance provider. You also can sometimes contact the therapist directly and they can work out the insurance for you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If you live in an area near a university, oftentimes they provide services to community members.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, by Google searching clinical psychology doctoral programs.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yep. Besides cost, another additional barrier is just general apprehension, feeling embarrassed or worried about seeking treatment. But it's important not to forget that sometimes it's just difficult taking that first step.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. All that we ask is just try it. Just get out there and try to find the therapist that you need and be proud of yourself for looking for help.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, definitely. It's a huge step to take just that first initial appointment or even just calling the therapist. It's really awesome when people are courageous enough to take a chance on it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But again, the end goal is just really to help anyone who's experiencing distress to find the resources they need to get help. Besides, who wouldn't want to talk to us?

video_details.title: Communication Goals of Care OSCE
video_details.description:
Vijay Daniels (MD, MHPE, FRCPC) discusses "goals of care" with a standardized patient.

For OSCE scoring guideline information, visit: http://mcc.ca/wp-content/uploads/osce-booklet-2014.pdf

These videos are for educational purposes. Any communication strategies demonstrated in videos should only be applied when deemed necessary based on the particular OSCE station. Videos are intended to familiarize students with the type of language and interactions expected in OSCEs.  

For more information,

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi there, Ms. Stone? I'm BJ Daniel. Let me just wash my hands.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just call me Dorothy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The nurse mentioned you wanted to talk about your care. What's going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Five days ago I was in emergency and they put a tube down my throat. I tried to tell them I didn't want it. I hope it never happens again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I understand that's scary. I've looked at your chart, but did anyone explain why they did it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really, I was gasping for air. I'm really worried and I don't want that tube anymore. I'm okay to pass as I am.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We will respect your wishes. What is your understanding of what brought you here?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Congestive heart failure. There was water in my lungs, and the ambulance brought me in.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So they put the tube down quickly. Did anyone ask if you were okay with that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I tried to gesture that I didn't want it. I've had it three times and don't want it again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you know why they would have put the tube down?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess because I was short of air. They tried to save me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Usually, we only use a tube as a last resort to save you. It suggests you were close to dying when you arrived.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess so, but I'm okay with dying. I've lived a good life. If the Good Lord says it's my time, I'm okay with that. Just no tube.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I hear you. For you, quality of life is more important than quantity. Is that correct?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That is correct. How can I be assured my wishes are respected?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'll document this in your chart and create a 'Goals of Care' form. I'll also notify your family doctor and update the provincial emergency system.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you. I was so concerned about that. It was a horrendous experience.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I need to ask a few routine questions. How is your mood?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm feeling fine. My mood is fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how were you feeling about life before you came into the hospital?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I am enjoying life to the best I can.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you willing to have medications for your breathing, just not the intubation?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Certainly. Medication is fine, just not intubation.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If you were to pass away, would you want chest compressions or shocks to bring you back?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. The Good Lord knows when it's my time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What about BiPAP? It's a mask that pushes air in. It's a bit uncomfortable but not like the tube.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Would it be for a long time?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Usually only two to six hours. Also, would you be okay with the ICU for close monitoring without a tube?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I would be okay with that. It doesn't sound as invasive.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Summarizing: medicines and the mask are okay, but no breathing tube and no restarting your heart. Anything else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I just needed to be reassured. I'm glad it's on my chart.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You can change your mind anytime, but this is the plan for now. I just want you to be aware of that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. I don't think I'll change my mind, but I'll talk to you if I do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's go through some routine history. Heart failure, and anything else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's it, though there was something else starting with an S. I have a list of my medications here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're on Furosemide and Diltiazem. Any allergies? And you're 70, correct?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's correct. I don't smoke, drink, or use street drugs or herbals.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Whereabouts are you living right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I moved to a convalescent home six months ago. I'd prefer my own home, but I'm learning to adjust.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think I have all the information I need. Is there anything else you wanted to talk about?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, you've answered my question. I was so worried about that tube.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It was very nice to meet you, Ms. Stone. See you later.

video_details.title: Psychotherapy Counselling Session
video_details.description:
Richard Counselling Eric (Mock Counselling Session)

PLEASE LIKE! SUBSCRIBE! COMMENT! AND HIT THE NOTIFICATION BUTTON! AS I WILL BE RETURNING TO YOUTUBE WITH MORE VIDEOS REGULARLY AT THE END OF SEPT 2019. AS WELL AS EXPLAINING THE REASON BEHIND MY ABSENCE ON THIS CHANNEL. THANK YOU GUYS FOR YOUR SUPPORT!

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good afternoon, Eric.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How's your day going?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So just before we start, I just wanted to brief you on confidentiality within this therapeutic session. So anything you disclose to me is and will remain confidential between me and you besides the circumstances in which I would have to breach confidentiality and those would include if you may have been involved in physical or sexual abuse, if there's child abuse, if there's self harm or immediate harm to others. So these are certain circumstances that I would have to break that confidentiality and pass on information shared in this session and also if it's court mandated as well. So is that okay with you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yep. This is just for your information only, I'd like to, and just to brief you on that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: With all that being said, can you briefly explain what brings you here today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've been referred here by a few of my professors in school.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So this is school related, you would say?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I guess why they think I'm here, yeah, it's school related. They think my marks are slipping, my attendance is going down, so they wanted to send me here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now, in terms of your marks slipping and your attendance going down, how was your performance before?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, I guess it was better, I assume. I mean, I attended class, I got decent grades. Never the best, but they were, you know, decent. I got 70s. I was an average student.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So with that being said, is there any reason why your grades are slipping or is it just kind of a normal phase you're going through, a high stress phase you're going through?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, I'm definitely going through I think a bit of a high stress phase. It's exhausting. So honestly, school's just not as important to me as it once was and I don't feel like it's a huge problem, but they think I should come here anyways. So.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So with that being said, Eric, could you elaborate on the high stress event that you're going through right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, there's been a rearrangement of living conditions, I guess you could say. I've had to be sent to live with, I've had no choice but to go live with my aunt and her new boyfriend.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you said that you've been sent and there's been a change in living arrangement. What is this change due to, Eric?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, my mother recently got into a car accident and she passed away. She battled her injuries for a couple of weeks and eventually succumbed and died to them. So having nowhere else to go, I unfortunately had to go live with my aunt and her boyfriend out in Toronto.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I'm sorry to hear that, Eric. And it definitely isn't easy to lose a family member, especially a mother. So if you could explain to me like how did that affect you when you experienced and heard that your mama passed away? How is it resonating within you right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, just like anyone else would feel, it's terrible, it sucks. You know, I lost my mother, I never had a father. You know, those couple weeks she's in the hospital, you know, I couldn't do anything but go see her, take care of her. And then I had to watch over my little sister as well and she's about 10 years younger than me so she's very confused, upset, lonely, I guess you could say. So it's, yeah no, it's a shitty time right now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So have you spoken to anybody within the school in regards to what has transpired in your family setting with the loss of your mom?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A few people know, but I haven't really talked to anybody about it. It's, I don't like self-disclosing to other people, opening up to other people, I just keep it to myself.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Understandable. Sometimes it's best to sometimes give an individual space when they're mourning the loss of someone they've loved. And also with that being said, I can definitely see why you are dealing with a lot of problems in school because of course with the loss of your mother, it's taking a real toll on you. But I am grateful that you came here today and you currently now are talking about it, so that is a step forward and I'm very grateful for you being here and allowing me to even have this information between us and help you through what you're going through right now. So with that being said, how are the settings with your aunt because you say you don't want to be there, it doesn't seem like you're comfortable being in that setting nor does it seem like you're comfortable being separated from your little sister? So how are the settings now? Where's your little sister and where are you currently in terms of distance?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: She moved quite a bit of distance. I'm in Toronto now with the shitty aunt you can say and she's all the way up in like Thunder Bay area, you know, with a good, you know, parental figures you say or guardian figures, sorry. But yeah, so that, yeah, yeah, yeah, that's all I can say about it. I really don't.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I really sense the frustration when you're talking about this particular aunt. Is there anything going on within the household that's really bothering you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, we've never got along. She, I don't like her, she doesn't like me, she didn't like my mother. The only reason I'm there is because I'm currently at school in Toronto and I can't afford to leave my job and my schooling to go, you know, live up north with my aunt and uncle and sister, so I had to stay back. So I'm only there kind of because this was the only option I had. She didn't even want to take me in, it was just I didn't want to go, my other aunt had to kind of be the mediator between us. So it's tough.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's definitely a tough situation you're currently in right now. But you say that you're there for school mainly, so there is that time, that period within the academic year where you do visit your other aunt that you like, that's currently with your sister and you do get that communication again?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, but that's only once in a while, you know, I can't be there for my little sister all the way around, you know, she has no family, I have no family really, it feels like. She has no immediate family up there, you know, she doesn't have me anymore, she doesn't have my mother, so it's like to her everyone just died, you know, my mother passed, she has no one anymore. So.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So how have you been coping with this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, I work, I might go out by myself to a bar occasionally by myself, but for the most part I just stay in my room, maybe watch some TV, maybe play some video games. That's if my aunt doesn't barge in my room mind you and start yelling for no apparent reason.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you use the bar as a coping strategy?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Occasionally. Bar's expensive, I can't afford much, it's just for me to get out of the house. But I more just like to stay in my room personally, just keep isolated by myself and just yeah, hope my aunt does her own shit and stays out of mine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how is this coping strategy working for you, this isolation?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's okay, you know, I'm alone with my thoughts, so being alone it's not terribly bad, you know, people don't seem to mind so I don't mind.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So apart from the grades and the high stress situation of course with your mother, is there anything in particular the school has seen from you that led them to recommend you to come here today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, I just I don't talk to anyone anymore. I guess I used to be a little bit more outgoing, but it's just kind of like, you know, people will get used to me not being around as much and talking as much, so that'll be good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you mean people will get used to you not being around as much or talking as much?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You know, it was a habit, I'd come in, I'd be loud, boisterous, and talk to everybody, but you know, things change and you know, it just won't phase them, won't bother them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What won't bother them?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just me not being around anymore. I feel like it's not, you know, as important. You know, my little sister also will get used to it as well with being all the way up north, her not me not being around for her anymore so, you know. My aunt doesn't care if I'm around or not and I frankly don't give a rat's ass if she's around or not. So, she has a lot of alcohol too so I do take a lot of her alcohol and I can at least escape for a little bit using that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you've been abusing alcohol?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's I wouldn't really say abuse, I don't use it frequently but when I do use it I use large consumptions of it just to black out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: To binge drink?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess, but I get, I know I'm, pass out, I blackout and I don't feel anything anymore which feels great. So.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there any other things that you abuse to cope with all these negative stressors in your life?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A lot of sleeping pills. I mean, I've been prescribed them, but I do take more than I should and I will combine it with the alcohol too. I'm not too sure if that does anything, but I'll mix the two for sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now, Eric, there's a lot of concerning things you've brought up in the past couple of statements. I just wanted to know, like, have you, are you talking about suicide?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, it's been a thought for sure. Like I said, me and my aunt we don't get along, me and her many boyfriends don't get along, you know, my sister is all the way up north, my mother's not around, it just I don't see a point really in going on. So, and like I said, people will get used to me not being around. I haven't been at school for a while, you know, people will get used to the idea.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you thought of a plan?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Never actually thought of a plan. I, maybe one day the pills and the alcohol combined will take my life, who knows. It's a risk, but at least in that moment me taking the pills and the alcohol, I feel good. Blackout, I don't feel anything, you know, I'm not lonely anymore, you know, I don't overthink my everything, my situation, my sister's situation.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But Eric, you said that based on the statements you've said, that a lot of them have surrounded your sister and her well being. I sense some sort of discrepancy with what you're implying you want to do with what you know is currently in your life right now. Now you you do have a loving relationship with your sister, as can be seen by the way you're hurt with the separation. But you are now saying you want to remove yourself from that relationship. How do you think that would affect her?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, like she doesn't get a chance to see me anymore and pretty well dead to her anyway, so I don't think it would bother her as much as you think it would.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Eric, I just want you to step into the shoes of what you're going through right now. The loss of your mother was very detrimental to you, of course. And would you say the same for your sister?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, no, for sure. I spent, you know, every night comforting her, staying beside her until she fell asleep, you know, until my mother's passing and then after a while yeah she got sent away.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So how would she feel now losing you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like I said, she pretty well already lost me. I can't see her anymore, I can't comfort her anymore, I can't be there for her anymore, so I'm not there on a regular, I'm not always there for her, not as much as I used to be able to be.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No, I definitely understand with the circumstances that you're not always there for her, but there is possibility for you to be there for her. You don't always have to be there for her and I guess that's understandable because you are going through school, you have to hold down a job, but there is opportunity for you to be there for her at the times you can be. And don't you think that that would be a good way to keep that communication with you to maintain that relationship? Because I'm sure your sister would definitely be in turmoil if she lost you as well. Wouldn't you say so?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe, but she does have her aunt and uncle now watching out for her. She's living with a few other cousins so she has a nice support system already in place, you know, a lot better than the one I have down here. So.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So Eric, there's a couple of things I want you to also take from this as well as a couple coping strategies I might want to add that you use as well when coping with this. And one of them is being seizing the opportunity to communicate with your sister because it seems like she is based on what you've said a very positive feature in your life. Wouldn't you agree?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean when I get the opportunity to talk to her I always enjoy it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yes, so that would definitely be beneficial with the way you're feeling as well. I believe you've said that she's you've lost your main support system which was your mother. At this time maybe it'll be positive for the both of your lives if you be together through all this turmoil, through all this negativity and this high stress situation that you're both undergoing with the loss of your mother. Having each other will be beneficial. And in terms of your circumstances with your aunt, have you communicated that with your aunt?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: There's no point. There's no point. She hated my mother, she hates me, she hates my sister. So I just have to put up with it until I get enough money to move out on my own or until I graduate and I can move. And it's just constant fighting, there's no stop there's constant verbal, constant confrontations.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I understand that, but you've never actually expressed how hurt you are by the verbal confrontations to her directly?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, like I said, I don't think there's a point. So I just yell back or I just go to my room and do what I do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think that also another take home message that you could take from this session too is to give it a try. Communicate, communicate the negative feelings you have towards fighting because it doesn't seem like you want to fight your aunt. It doesn't seem like you want to have a poor relationship with your aunt. It just seems to be like something that just happens circumstantially, but it's not necessarily communicated how hurt you are.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like I said, her and my mother never got along. I don't know why, and that's just transferred to me as well. So I didn't have much of a relationship with her, but she doesn't like me and I'm not particularly fond of her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And in terms of suicide, that's definitely something concerning and alarming. I just wanted to go back to that point. You didn't say that you necessarily had a plan, but you said that there were thoughts of it. Correct?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean I could do it any way, you know, anything's available. I can OD on my sleeping pills if I wanted to, you know. My aunt's current boyfriend is an avid hunter. There's many weapons lying around the house I can use. It's easy, possible.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So Eric, I have to inform you that a lot of the things you've said are quite alarming and they seem to be putting a risk of self-harm. So because of that, as I said in the beginning, I will have to breach confidentiality unfortunately and inform those people closest to you of your suicidality so that they can remove anything that you basically stated within as a vague plan for suicide such as the sleeping pills around the house and the armory around the house as well. They would have to remove that from that setting just to ensure your safety. Is that okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, it's not an active plan, it's only thoughts.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I understand that, but you're still at risk because you've stated that there are ways in which you're thinking of taking your life which include the pills, the sleeping pills around your house and your aunt's boyfriend's weaponry.

video_details.title: Motivational interviewing- Client reluctant to join AA
video_details.description: This video is about a community health nurse engaging in an interview with a client, utilizing the principles of MI. The client is 25 years old and was recently involved in a bar fight.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Alex, my name is Tony, I'll be your nurse for today. Um, how are you doing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, I'm okay, I guess. Just waiting for these stitches to come out, it'd be nice.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, what happened?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, got into a bar fight.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me a little bit more about this bar fight?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, story time, you ready for this? So, out with my girls, having a fantastic time, looking all on fleek andish, and then this girl, like she has the nerve to stare at me from across the room and gives me this eye kind of like this. And then she comes up to me, she bumps into me, she spills my drink, and she comes up and then she's like, I slept with your man. So I'm like, excuse me? So obviously I pushed her, she pushed me kind of thing, and yeah, one thing led to another, it's a blur from that point on, but all I know is that cops showed up, I'm here, and I've this to deal with. Fantastic, right?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, from what I'm getting here is you were intoxicated at that point in time and then you had a confrontation with this girl, which led to the bar fight, and am I missing anything?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, I was more than intoxicated, I was smashed. Oh, you should have seen it. But like, this type of thing doesn't happen often, so I don't want you to be sitting here and referring me to some AA, because yo, I'm not an alcoholic.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so it seems like you get offended and you feel offended being referred to an AA meeting.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'm not an alcoholic, no.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, because it labels you as an alcoholic. That's what you feel, right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, exactly.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Well, we do have some time right now. If it's okay with you, I was wondering if we could talk a little bit about your drinking habits?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, sure. What do you want to know?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: To you, what does drinking do for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, you know, being 25, that's what we do. Like, we get together, we hang out, we get a couple of drinks, it's me and my girls, we do this all the time, and I love this. Um, it breaks the ice when we go socializing, so meet new people kind of thing, you know, grow our friend circle. It's fantastic. And it definitely relaxes me after a stressful week, and my weeks are so stressful that I need this, you know? So, I mean, yeah, but just so you know, I do drink responsibly and I never drink and drive and I don't intend on doing that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So, to me, it seems that drinking is your way of relaxing with your friends, it's your way to socialize and it breaks that ice for you, it helps you socialize and, you know. Um, I also want to say that it's very responsible of you to be drinking and not driving. Yeah, how has it affected your life?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Ooh, has it? Well, I mean, now that this happens, I do have it because of that bar fight. And oh, my Dad's gonna kill me, oh my God. He's gonna be disappointed. So I guess you could say that my relationship with Henry, it's been great, fantastic, but he says that when I drink, it's like I'm not myself, it's like somebody he's never met before. And obviously you can imagine the arguments, the fights, and oh my God, all that stress. It's just... I love him so much, but you know, but it's the stress and it's like I don't know if we're gonna make it. It's just, oh my God.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I see. So from what I'm understanding, drinking, um, it helps you socialize with friends, it relaxes you, it's, you know, your way of just, you know, it breaks that ice for you. But on the other hand, it's causing that a lot of arguments with you and your significant other, Henry. Yeah, and it's causing a lot that all those arguments are leading to a lot of stress in your relationship at this point in time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean, we're engaged and look how pretty this is. Oh, and I don't want to lose that. Like, you put it that way, I mean, I'm worried because what's he gonna think of me later on in life? What's he gonna tell our children? Oh, your mom's an alcoholic? She drank this and they got into a fight? I don't want, I don't want anyone to ever think of me that way. But at the same time, I mean, I don't want to quit cold turkey. I mean, you must understand how hard this is for me to even be here and talk about it. But I love him so much, I mean, I would do anything for him. And he's going to be so disappointed in me and hasn't even seen me. Oh my God, I don't know how I can face him. I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: He seems like a very lucky guy to have someone love him that much.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mm-hmm. I mean, boy, seriously, he's not gonna find anybody that loves him as much as I do. Trust me on that. Not gonna happen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, what I'm getting here right now is that you do, um, want to quit. Yeah, and it's just partly because, um, this alcohol is leading to the arguments with Henry and it's causing that stress in your relationship. Um, I know we spoke about AA earlier, and um, I know you don't really like the idea of it, but what do you know about AA? Like, do you want to shed some light on that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's a place where alcoholics go to discuss their problems and, like I said, I'm not an alcoholic.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, you're right, they're from all different walks of life, and they share their drinking stories and everyone just kind of helps each other through this journey of being sober together. Um, I know you don't want to join AA at this point in time, perhaps, but hypothetically speaking, would you ever consider joining it maybe later on down the road?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: If this is what I have to do to get my guy back, then I'll do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, well, on a scale of one to ten, ten being like for sure and one being not really sure about it at all, um, what would you say, where you are on the scale with um, joining an AA group?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Now that you put it that way and everything I told you, I would say a six.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A six. Hmm. Uh, why would you say a six instead of, say, a three? I mean, you were really adamant about not joining AA earlier.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it's all about, it's all about Henry, at the end of the day it matters to me if I want to keep this engagement. And I will do anything for that man. So of course, if this is what I have to do, then this is what I have to do. This is him, let me tell you, his relationship with me and I with him is so much more important to me than drunken nights at a bar.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, he's a very lucky man, like I said again.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'll tell him that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. So right now we're sitting at a six. What needs to happen to say maybe we can jump that to an eight or a nine?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, you know, like flexible hours maybe? Okay, if that is even an option. Um, also maybe if there's a place nearby somewhere, like nearby my house, that would be great so I don't have to waste gas because... it's expensive. I already go to work and it's far anyway. And um, like I guess, I guess it has to do with attitude as well. I don't want to sit there in a circle like this and somebody judging me because of the way I look and my drinking habits and all of that. So I guess I'm just looking for a good vibe, you know? I don't want to be judged or labeled.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, all of these are like very understandable. I mean, it's, of course, you want some, an AA meeting to be close to you so you don't have to commute so far. And we all have very busy schedules, so something that fits within our busy schedule definitely makes sense. Um, and of course, the environment, I mean, if you're not happy there, just a good human learning environment, if you're not comfortable there, then it's very hard for you to, you know, to be in that environment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, exactly.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, actually today, um, I was wondering if it's okay with you, I can give you this brochure? It's just, um, for an AA meeting that's really close to your location where you live. And my number is also on there. You can always give me a call if you have any concerns. And also, I just want to thank you today for sharing your experience with drinking and I know it's not, you know, easy to just... this is a very sensitive subject, yeah. So, you know, I want to thank you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you for listening to me. Like, no one has actually sat down and talked to me about anything. I feel like you shed some light on an issue. So thank you, it really means a lot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're very welcome. You're very welcome. And uh, if it's okay with you, perhaps maybe we could schedule another follow-up meeting, say in about like two weeks or so?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that sounds fine. I think two weeks works.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, well, we'll go from there.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Two weeks. Okay, well I'll see you then.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: See you then.

video_details.title: Person-Centered Counseling Role-Play - Coping with a Work Related Stressor
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which person-centered therapy is used to help a client (played by an actor) cope with a work-related stressor. The role-play attempts to demonstrate being non-directive with both words and non-verbal behavior by using encouragers, reflections, and paraphrasing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello Carl, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Good. I'm good. How are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. Last week you were talking in therapy.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I mean, and I thought a lot more about it this week after I mentioned it last week, but Jill. I was telling you about Jill, my coworker, and you know, she was kind of bothering me the past couple weeks, but really this past week was like the worst, right? So she's not doing her paperwork. And the thing is is that she has to do these reports in order for me to do my reports. So if she doesn't have hers, I can't do mine, and then I can't get mine out in time for the next person to do theirs, and it's a mess. The whole thing's a mess. And it's just annoying.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So her work slowdown, or not being efficient at work, is affecting your work productivity?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, definitely is. And it's one of those things that like... you know, has... it gives me a bad... a bad evaluation. You know, like if I'm not handing my stuff in on time, then it reflects negatively on me. You know, and it's all kind of... she's the first level, you know? And then all the other levels are kind of dependent on her turning things in on time. So if she doesn't, then I don't, then the next person does, so forth.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It makes it seem like you're not doing your job.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right, yeah. And my boss doesn't like it. My boss's boss doesn't like it, and so forth. You know, and I try to explain to them, you know, she's the problem, but it doesn't always... I don't always have the time to go up and tell them like, 'Here's what's happening,' or just somehow it doesn't come out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You don't always get the opportunity to tell people that are important at your work about the situation.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. And that's pretty annoying too, because you know, it's one thing if people get mad at me, but then I'm able to tell them why I'm not doing my job like I'm supposed to. But it's another thing for them to get mad at me not realizing it's not my fault, you know?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You have an explanation for why the work's not getting done.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I do. I do. That's the thing. But I can't always get it out, you know? I can't always tell the person that has the complaint about it. And yeah, I mean, I've tried talking to my boss and I've tried talking to other people too, you know, but it really hasn't gotten anywhere.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're feeling stuck with this whole thing.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah, I am. And I mean, I talked to Jill a little bit about it too, you know? And I tried to ask, I tried kind of gently reminding her, you know, like such-and-such needs to be turned in by Tuesday at 12 o'clock. I didn't want to be real abrasive, but I tried to remind her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's a polite approach.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah. And it didn't really seem to work because it's still happening, you know?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Your attempt to fix the problem hasn't really worked the way you want it to.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, no, it really hasn't. And that's just... I feel like I've tried everything that I could try. You know? And even like, I came home and I was talking to a friend about it, and I was trying to think of other solutions, right? You know, I was trying to think like, what else I could do, what else I could say, who else I could talk to, things like that, you know? And I mean, my friend, you know, he was listening and stuff and he had some good suggestions, but he didn't know what to do either, like, because he doesn't know the way the company works, you know? So like, I just... I got nothing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're not getting the help you need for this.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, not at all. I'm feeling pretty lost with it, and I wish there was just like a clearer way to do things, like, 'This is what you should do now,' but there's not. And I don't see anything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Some sort of clear plan.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah. But yeah, I don't... I don't see a way to go about it. I mean, I've... okay, so this is the way I've laid it out in my mind. I've tried talking to the people above me. Didn't work out the way I thought it would. I tried talking to the people below me, so to speak, just lower on the... before me in the process, that's what I mean. Um, and that didn't work out, which is just Jill, and I talked to her and that didn't work. So like, there's nowhere else I could turn.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The options are exhausted.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's what it seems like to me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And this is frustrating for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it is. And I've been trying to rack my brain, you know, like what else could I do? You know, like maybe if I could... maybe if there was like a committee or something that I could go to, you know, and be like, 'Well, this person's not doing what they're supposed to be doing,' but there's not, there's no committee like that. Or even if there was like a person, you know, like a resolution person or whatever, but there's nobody like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: There's no other avenue.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's what it seems like to me. Yeah. And that's... I mean, that's... and you know, I was even trying to think like... I don't know, should I like write a letter to somebody maybe? But I don't even know who or what.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You thought about a letter, but who would you send it to?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Or like just something else that I could... I could do instead of going to this person, going to that person, that didn't work. Could I... could I call somebody? Is there anybody else in the company that, you know, might handle stuff like that? But I mean, there's HR people, but that's... I can't really see where they could come in. I don't know how human resources could deal with something like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You don't view them as a potential solution.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. No, I don't. Um, I wonder maybe if there's like... but there's... I mean, I'm thinking now that there's gotta be something or somebody or somewhere that I could put in like almost like a complaint or something, like something's out of my hands and I don't know what to do about it. Like there's gotta be something. And now that I'm saying this, I'm thinking that there's gotta be.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Some other resource you haven't tried yet.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah. And I mean, now I'm trying to think back to my training, you know, initially. You know, maybe there's... You know what, I think now that I'm... now that I'm thinking a little bit harder about it, a little bit differently about it, I'm thinking that there's like a... man, I forget what they call it now, but maybe like a complaint... that's not the right word, but maybe a complaint box or like suggestions or something. And I think if I remember correctly, those suggestions and those complaints get brought up at every staff meeting, which we have like every other week.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: They're discussed at this regular meeting.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. And I'm... I'm thinking now, I mean, nobody really uses it, but I'm thinking like maybe that's an avenue that I can use, you know, and like maybe that'll get brought up and maybe that's something that then might actually work.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This could be another option for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah, it could be. And then if it... if it does work, it'll get brought... or rather, if they do read it, it'll get brought up at the staff meeting where everybody's at. My boss, my boss's boss, Jill, everybody's there. And um, maybe that's a way for it to come to everybody's attention that deadlines being missed affect other people in ways that you don't really know about.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So everyone will hear your complaint and maybe react in a way that would help you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe, yeah. I think that's... I mean, that's gotta be the way to do it. And maybe that's the best way. I really think, yeah, I mean, after saying all that and after going through that, I really think that that's probably the best way to do it. And if it... and if it doesn't, then I guess I could find another way, but I really think that's the best way to do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You feel as though you've found an option here.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah, I do. And even if that doesn't work, then it'll be brought up, and maybe it'll allow me to talk to my boss further about it, and maybe he'll understand really where I'm coming from. But this will at least be a start to something, you know, and make me a lot less stressed with deadlines and stuff, you know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You are frustrated with all this.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. But maybe... maybe after I do that, you know, put in the complaint or suggestion, maybe I won't be as frustrated. I mean, I'm feeling a little bit less frustrated now even thinking that there is another option, you know?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It feels better now as you're contemplating another potential avenue here.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah, it does.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, this might be a good place to wrap this session up if that feels like the right move for you. And we'll schedule so I'll see you next week and we can pick up from there.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sounds good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, cool. Thanks, Carl.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

video_details.title: Intake and Assessment Role-Play - Substance Use Appraisal
video_details.description: This video features role-play of a substance use appraisal section of an intake and assessment (clinical interview) of a counseling client (played by an actress).

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, I appreciate your participation in the intake so far. I want to change to a new section, if that's okay with you. And this section is on substance use. Is that an area you feel comfortable discussing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. So, are there any substances that you currently use?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I drink a bit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me how often you drink?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess it's more than a bit. I would say I have probably three drinks a day.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what are you drinking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, beer.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you know what size?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, the bottles, I think they're 16 ounces.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Three bottles of beer a day?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how much time does it take you to consume those?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably a couple of hours.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, every day, three beers in about two hours?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that do anything to you in terms of your mood or feeling?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It just kind of helps me unwind after a long day of work, relaxes me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's relaxing for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has it ever gotten you into any type of trouble?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: There was one time that I, my friends and I kind of got into a fight after I had been drinking, and we almost stopped talking because of it, but we were able to work it out. But I've almost lost friends over it before.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. Is there any other areas where it might disrupt functioning?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes it's hard to get up and get to work the next morning if I drink it later in the day. It's hard to get up and get to work on time, so I've been late a couple of times too.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. So, three bottles of beer pretty much every day?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Pretty much every day.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has there ever been a time when you've consumed more or less on a particular day?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not typically during the week, but I'll sometimes I'll drink more on the weekends. Maybe drink my normal three in a couple of hours and then maybe three or four hours later I'll have a few more.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You'll have a few more?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how long have you been drinking alcohol?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I started when I was around 17.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Around 17?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now you mentioned beer, have you ever consumed any other type of alcohol?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I've tried wine and shots before, but I always kind of just gravitate more towards the beer.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Back towards beer?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any other substances that you use currently?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, on the weekends every once in a while I'll smoke some pot with my friends, like Saturday night.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that pretty much just weekends?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes during the week, before I go to sleep I'll have a joint just, it helps my anxiety and my worries before I go to bed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. When did you first start using marijuana?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Ah, that was probably a couple of years ago when I first started college.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: About two years ago?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And on the weekends, sometimes other times?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Actually, I guess it's more on the weekends, but I would say maybe every other day during the week.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So mostly on the weekends, occasionally during the week. Has it ever led to any trouble or change in functioning?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: On the weekends no because I don't really have anywhere to be, but sometimes during the week, if I smoke it too late, it's hard to get up in the morning and my boss is really starting to get irritated with how often I've been late.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever tried to cut down on the substance use, alcohol or marijuana?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've tried to cut back on the alcohol before, about a year ago when I started this job. I was able to get down to like one or two beers, but then the job got stressful and I started drinking more again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you think perhaps the alcohol use is connected to the stress of your job?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I, yeah, I'd say it's definitely connected.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. Have you ever been annoyed by people that perhaps criticize your substance use?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, my family can be critical. They don't really know about the marijuana, but they can be critical of my alcohol use.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And that bothers you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever felt bad or guilty about your substance use?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've felt guilty with my mom because it upsets her so much. And sometimes I'll feel bad if I have a fight with my friends if I'm drunk, because it's usually over something silly.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. Have you ever had to drink or use drugs first thing in the morning to steady your nerves or to lessen the effects of a hangover?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not during the week, but on the weekends when I'll drink a little bit more, sometimes I'll have just a little bit Sunday morning to just get going.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So on occasion that happens?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I wouldn't say it's often, but on occasion.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So alcohol and marijuana, two substances you currently use. Can you tell me about substances you've used in the past?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: At a party one time I tried ecstasy, but I didn't like it. In high school I smoked cigarettes, but it just made me feel sick and I didn't like it very much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you discontinued?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that didn't last long at all.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any other substances or just those two?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just those two that I'm currently using and then the smoking and the ecstasy previously.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have a family history of substance use?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My grandfather. My mom claims that my grandfather was an alcoholic.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any other history?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, not that I'm aware of at least.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Before I move to the next section of the intake, is there anything else you want to add or any other comments you want to make about this section?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think that covers it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does that cover it pretty well?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I appreciate you answering these questions and if you're okay, I'm going to move to the next section of the intake.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.
