video_details.title: Intake and Assessment Role-Play - Family History
video_details.description: This video features role-play of a family history section of an intake and assessment (clinical interview) of a counseling client (played by an actress). Areas covered include the collection of information about parents, grandparents, and extended family.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well I want to thank you for your participation so far in this intake. But I want to move to another section of the intake, specifically your family history, if that's okay with you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. So I'm gonna be asking you various questions about your relatives. Is that okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you adopted?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. They're not married to each other anymore. My dad's remarried, and my mom has been married four times.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: She's married four times? What age were you when your parents divorced?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was about sixteen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And then your father, you said remarried?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He did.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How long after the divorce?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think I was about eighteen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And then your mother remarried and was divorced a few times you're saying.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well yeah, she married some guy about six months after, and then that didn't last very long. Then she was dating numerous people, and then she met somebody in an AA meeting and they married. That lasted about a year and a half to two years. Then she had another one when I was about 25, and that one lasted the longest, about close to three years.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That was her third? Well she was married to your father, and then married quickly after that you said, and then she met somebody at an AA meeting.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, so that's the third, and then this one would be the fourth.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And is she married now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, now she's just dating or whatever she's doing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How long did the last marriage last?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That was three years, that was the longest one.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How is your relationship with your father?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's good I guess. My dad is a genuine guy. He stuck around for a lot of things with my mom. I think we have a decent relationship considering what we've been through.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about your relationship with your mother?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Honestly, there's no other way to describe it, it's just chaotic. She's all over the place, and it's just hard to catch her on a good day. It's kind of a surface relationship.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. So who raised you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My parents raised me. They were good parents I guess, according to my standards, because my mom was just always a mess. I guess they both did the best they could given the circumstances.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you think the way that you were raised has an impact on who you are now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think so, definitely. My mom was constantly spending my dad's money and shopping. She was preoccupied with herself and obsessive with cleaning. She was always kind of gone, like hi-bye, throughout my childhood.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Some tough memories in there too. Can you tell me about your siblings?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have two siblings, a brother Jeff and a sister Kendra. We kind of all went our separate ways when my parents divorced, just because we didn't want to relive the memory when we're together.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. So what's your relationship with them now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's okay. I don't really see them quite honestly. Maybe at a family party once every five years, and that's okay with me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's alright? You're satisfied with your relationship with them?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think so. It's not my fault that they won't accept who I am.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you aware of any medical conditions that your mother and father may have, or your grandparents?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My grandma had heart disease. My grandfather had colon cancer, but he beat that. As far as my parents, they don't have any medical issues that I know of.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about mental health conditions?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like my mom was crazy. She was just completely all over the place I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you aware of any formal diagnosis she had?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: She was just manic, like I guess bipolar, but she never really got a definitive label in therapy or anything like that. She was definitely a mess, with anxiety too.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So symptoms of bipolar and anxiety? Any other mental health conditions in your family?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, just my mom with her obsessiveness and she'd get depressed after. But as far as any other siblings, no.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have any special family traditions?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We would go on family vacations together down to the beach when I was a kid. And for holidays, we would have our family over for Christmas and stuff like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me about holidays, like what were the most important holidays to you and your family?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Christmas, Easter, and Thanksgiving.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how did you celebrate those holidays?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes at my cousin's house on my dad's side, and Christmas would be at my parents' house. Easter would vary back and forth between the two houses.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. Can you tell me about your extended family?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: On my dad's side, my uncle was super successful. I don't really see him now at all. On my mom's side, she has a sister who is also a bit crazy. I hadn't seen her probably since I graduated high school.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so not many active relationships there in your family history, it sounds like.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well yeah, there's not many, no.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there anything else you want to tell me about your family history?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My mom would drink sometimes when I was growing up. She was actually friendly to me when she would drink. I don't know if she was an alcoholic, but she would drink often to calm down, and sometimes she would actually be nice to me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Anything else you want to tell me?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Nope.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. So I want to thank you for helping me complete this family history section and we'll move on to another section.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Definitely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright.

video_details.title: How Do You Partner with an Unengaged Patient?
video_details.description:
© 2021 Institute for Healthcare Improvement.


More and more, health care providers are trying to partner with patients to ensure care helps meet their health goals. But what happens when the patient isn’t interested in working with you? In this video, Dr. Andrew Peterson, a Professor of Surgery at Duke University Medical Center, demonstrates how providers can use communication skills to build partnerships with patients, based on the work of Dr. Neil Prose.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, Mr. and Mrs. Allen, how are you? I'm Dr. Peterson. It's nice to meet you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hi. Nice to meet you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hey, I really need that chair to get into. Do you mind if you have a seat over there for me?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure. What's wrong with him sitting in that chair?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, oftentimes it's the chair that I need to get to the computer so I can review your history. Remember all those forms that you filled out?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's just, I don't see what the difference is, but that's fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I looked earlier on and it looks like you've got some erection problems or impotence?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He's having some... we're having some issues together.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I got that, but I'm talking to him right now if that's okay.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you mind if you put the cell phone down?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You should put the cell phone away. Just put your cell phone away and listen to him. All right, I'm listening to him.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, okay, has anybody tried you on any medicines for your erection problems before?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. He's been in denial about it and he thinks it's me. He's trying to accuse me of being the one having an issue here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I mean, is this something that you're interested in getting treatment for? Because there are therapies for this that are out there.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, you haven't told me what any of these therapies are.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, we talked about the pills early on.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You mentioned pills. You might need to debrief him a little better because he's a CEO and he's used to people just laying it out there in a really organized way.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, you know, I see people with this problem all the time. So let me just talk to him a little bit. There are pills, there are injections, and then there's an operation where we can put an inflatable pump in the penis to help you with erections. Are you interested in any of those kind of things?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think the pills would be better than the pump. I hope it doesn't make any noise.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. So, I mean, but you could have gotten the pills earlier, but you've never asked anybody about the pills.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I've never had a problem before. That's not true. Can you just tell him this is normal? That it happens a lot?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hold on. I'm sensing a lot of head-butting here and I really think that you two have a lot to work out before we can help you with this. I'm going to let you two work this out and we'll just make another appointment later. Because this is a family issue.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Are you serious? You're walking out? I don't think you've approached this the right way. Can't believe he just walked out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, Mr. and Mrs. Allen, how are you? I'm Dr. Peterson. Nice to meet you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hi, nice to meet you. We're not married.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, I'm sorry. My fault. Sir, do you mind if I have that chair? I have to sometimes get to the computer while we do our interaction. Is that okay with you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, sure. That was his chair.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, it's very nice to meet both of you. Can you let me know what we can do for you today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I'll speak for us. We've been having a little problem and it's affecting our relationship and so we decided to come in and see what can be done.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what kind of problem are we talking about?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We filled it out on the form. It's a functional problem.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I read the forms and it looks like there's some erectile dysfunction that's been going on for several years. You've never been under any therapy for this, is that correct?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's right. He thinks it's me, but it's not. I'm just trying to help him figure it out for us.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I can sense a little bit that this is really becoming an issue in your relationship. Is that correct? And you're moving forward with a marriage?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's an issue definitely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I can tell you by reviewing your medical records that I saw there's some diabetes and high blood pressure there. Erectile dysfunction is a problem that happens in millions of men, often secondary to other medical problems.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: See, you're not the only one. There are other people that have this problem too. So it's not about your age.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I don't want to take anything that's going to interfere with my diabetes medication.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. Well, the therapies range from just a pill that typically doesn't interact with a lot of stuff, to injection therapy, to even a surgical therapy. I'm pretty sure we'll be able to get you some sort of erection for enjoyable intercourse.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You're pretty sure about that?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When we go through these algorithms for treatments, we tend to be very successful.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's good. That's good news.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So is it something you'd like to discuss a little bit more?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. What kind of questions do you have right off the bat about erection medicines?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, do I have to take it all the time or can we do some sort of one-time fix?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If the pills work, oftentimes you take a simple pill about an hour before intercourse. If the pills don't work, we can move on to different types of therapies.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sounds good. See, it's pretty easy. That's good. Yeah, she'll be happy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay.

video_details.title: Intake and Assessment Role-Play - Social History
video_details.description: This video features role-play of a social history section of an intake and assessment (clinical interview) of a counseling client (played by an actress). Areas covered include friendships, social media, talents, interests, and recreation.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I want to thank you for continuing to participate in this intake. As I mentioned, I want to move to a new section now. This one's about your social relationships. Are you okay with answering some questions about your social relationships?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, sure. Why not?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Tell me about your friends.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh, okay. From when I was in high school or now? Just...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You could start with high school.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Well, I had a lot of friends in high school. I mean, you know, I guess you could say I was popular in high school. I was constantly at parties and hanging out with people. And then as the years went by, they slowly started to peel off for whatever reason. I guess my behavior could have turned them off. Who knows, but...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What behavior do you think did that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess my gambling and my promiscuity. For instance, this one friend from high school, we were really close and I ended up getting with her boyfriend when they were together. But I mean, people forgive each other, like what's the big deal? And she couldn't get over it. And then my other friend got mad at me for that because I slept with her boyfriend, but I was drunk. And I mean, I was gambling that night, so really, who cares? And then I would post on Facebook just constantly about different guys, or that I was gambling and that I was winning. And I think it turned some people off, I guess, but I don't know why because I was just having a good time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And this was all back in high school?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, no, this was just this past couple years, you know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Recently.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh yeah. I mean, because they were my friends in high school, but through the years they kind of just peeled off, so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so you had a good number of friends in high school, but because of certain occurrences, you don't have as many now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: About how many close friends would you say you had back in high school?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: There was like eight of us in a group of girls that we were really close.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how about now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't have any of those friends.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How many close friends do you have?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't really have any close friends. I mean, just acquaintances really. I kind of just like doing it that way better.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sure. How many acquaintances?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Men or women? Like just as friends or...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, how many women?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: For friends, maybe like two at work that are like my acquaintances.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And how about men?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: For men, there's a lot, like ten that I see...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Fairly regularly?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Mhm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you describe to me your relationship with these twelve acquaintances?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The women at work, I usually just tell them about my fun times, like gambling and meeting men, they buy me things and me buying them things and winning all this money. And then I usually go back to work and tell them that I don't have any money left because I've used it all. First because I'm gambling, second because I want to show off for the guys and just the thrill of it. So that's just usually what I talk to them about. And the men usually are just that I encounter while gambling or shopping or when I'm drinking, and I could just meet them just at the blackjack table or whatever, or just online.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you mentioned social media before. Can you tell me about your interaction with social media? Your use of it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I actually enjoy social media a lot. I think it's a great outlet, especially when you have a lot of ideas and you just want to get it out there. And I think that it's really great for me to express my ideas and just what I'm going through, so I use it a lot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A lot?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I do. Especially when I'm out, like on Facebook, I'll post like every 10 minutes when I'm out. I just will post about my night or a cool idea I had about starting a business or anything like that. And like Twitter, it's pretty much like every two minutes because it's super fast. So I'll do that like every two minutes when I'm out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Do a lot of people follow or read the posts?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They do. A lot of people do and some people are like, 'Oh, that's a great idea.' And then an hour later they're just like, 'Is everything okay? Are you fine?' And I quickly unfriend them because they're not following what I'm saying. And then I have people that unfriend me because they don't like that I'm posting all the time. But really, that's what it's there for, it's there for me to express myself and if they can't handle it, then oh well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. I want to ask you about interests, like sports, music, the arts, television? You mentioned social media, that seems like an interest. Any other interests?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like hobbies? I like shopping. I love shopping, going away, I like vacationing in nice places, just enjoying myself. And obviously gambling is one of my favorite things. I like to do that, it's a great social outlet for me. It fulfills me at certain times in my life, you know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. And how about talents? Do you have particular talents?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Talents? I think just meeting people. I have really good talents with meeting people, especially when I feel really good. I have this ability to just talk to everybody and they seem to like me. And I think that's one of my talents, one of my strong points, which is why I probably do really good in sales because I'm in sales.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you have a talent for meeting people and having conversations.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like charismatic, yeah. Okay. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any other talents you'd like to tell me about?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So anything regarding social relationships like your friends, interests, talents, social media, anything that you want to tell me on this before we move to another section?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. I just like to have a good time and I just want people to understand that, you know. So that's it really.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you feel like the people you mentioned that would see you on social media or your acquaintances, do you feel like they understand you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, because they've all unfriended me, so I guess they don't understand me. They just don't get it, you know, which sucks, but...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All of them? Or are there some that...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: There's some like that I'm still friends with, but people that I went to high school with or college, they have all unfriended me, but as far as like those acquaintances, you know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have any friends that are willing to engage with you at certain times but not at others?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I do. I think when I start to like post a lot when I'm out and drinking and gambling, I think that they get frustrated with me. But there could be times where I'm not doing that and actually times when I'm depressed or just even-keeled, which I could be both. But when I'm even and I just have a little bit of energy and a little bit of sadness and I'm just this even person, I think that I'm able to have better conversations with people, I think I'm more tolerable, I guess you could say. Where I won't go on Facebook as much and I'll just post about, 'did anybody watch this show?' or something like that. I think that people respond better when I'm more even-keeled.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. I want to thank you for helping me complete this section of the intake, and if you're okay we'll move on to the next section.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

video_details.title: Motivational Interviewing for Drug Usage - Dr. Wendy Nickerson
video_details.description: Demonstration of motivational interviewing techniques used to help change behaviors leading to decreased drug usage.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good afternoon, Bruce. I'm glad you could make it in today. Last week, we discussed ways you could cut down or extinguish marijuana use. How did you feel about our talk last week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was okay, I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Just okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We developed four strategies: running more, staying away from certain friends, getting a pet, and joining a support group. How did you make out with the running?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was raining and cold, so I didn't get around to it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the weather took away from your motivation to go running?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I wasn't in the mood.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What could you have done to get in the mood?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm not sure what I could have done.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Did not exercising make a difference in your marijuana usage this week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I used a bit more.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How do you tie those two things together?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When I'm not exercising, then I generally turn to more usage.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How could you change your perception about the rain so it doesn't stop you from running?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I could wear a rain jacket or something.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's a great idea. The other goal was staying away from friends who are bad influences. How did that go?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I tried to stay away, but I still saw some of them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like it was difficult to cut them out of your life. Can you tell me what was difficult about it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I didn't want them to think I was avoiding them or to hurt their feelings.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And as a result, what happened?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I ended up going to see them and hanging out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Because you were worried about hurting their feelings, you ended up using marijuana, correct?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, we did a little bit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How could you do that differently this week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I suppose I could just try harder not to go and see those guys. I guess it's as simple as just not going.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have any friends who do not use marijuana that you could associate with?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I do. I could start to see them more.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: On a scale of 1 to 10, how motivated are you to reignite those friendships?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe about a 3.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What made you say 3 instead of 1?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Because I know I have a problem, so I feel like I need to start doing something about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What kind of activities did you do with those healthy friends in the past?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mostly outdoor activities, getting fresh air. They tend to do more healthy activities.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you can recall a healthier life overall without using pot.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think you're right. It might take my mind off of it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The other goal was to get a pet dog. How did you make out with that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I had second thoughts about the commitment and the time. I didn't feel like that was the right idea.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Recognizing that is wise. Would you consider a different pet that doesn't require such a commitment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: What do you have in mind?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Maybe an animal like a snake or a fish. Are those animals you like?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's a good idea. Snakes or fish or something.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The final goal was to join a support group. How did you make out with that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I went to a meeting, but I felt like those people were bottom of the barrel. I'm not where they are.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you left early because you didn't feel you fit in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. I'm still higher functioning.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What might be some positives you would get out of a support group?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd probably be able to relate to people in the same situation and have that connection.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You mentioned playing hockey as a kid. Could you see a support group as a team?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, people in a support group are all there for the same goal, like in hockey. Everybody's there for the win.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you remember how it felt to be on that team?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it was good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How committed are you to trying two support groups this week if I send you a list?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably an 8 out of 10.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Wow, why an 8 instead of a 4 or 5?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The team analogy is good. If I think of it as a team, maybe I'd be the star on the team since I'm not so bottom of the barrel.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I love that analogy. To summarize, you'll run rain or shine, embrace positive friends, look into a pet like a fish, and try two support groups. Overall, how would you rate today's session?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was good, very good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: On a scale of 1 to 10?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: About an 8.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We did good then. I'll see you next week and check in on these goals. Way to go.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thanks.

video_details.title: Intermediate Phase

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, Liz, how are you? Good. It's good to see you. I was just looking at your binge record that we've been keeping weekly, and I noticed that last week you were at five episodes of binge eating, and this week you were down to three. So awesome. Help me understand what's been going on this week. What was involved with the change?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean, good week with the roommate. I had a good conversation with her about what times are good for her boyfriend to be over and kind of giving her a better heads-up on when I really need silence.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Terrific. So what specifically did you say to her or how did you bring it up?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was just telling her that my studies are really important and I understand it's also important that she has time with her boyfriend, but that I would really appreciate that this is both our space and that there are times when we really need to respect each other's space. And yeah, she responded really well and she was just like, just really give me a good heads up before you, yeah. And then we kind of decided like certain times are more appropriate for them to have the living room and not.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, right. Yeah, because I think that's really similar. I know we kind of talked about that, because you remember a few sessions ago, I was kind of wondering whether or not she really got it in terms of what you were feeling, because it seems like one of the ways that you've talked about that before in terms of when we were first starting that often times one of the ways that you manage your feelings is you kind of think you're letting people know what you're feeling, but it doesn't really come out. And I know that was something that you and I had to really kind of work out, but it sounds like you were able to talk with her and that she heard you. And as I kind of thought, she was actually really responsive in a very positive way. So...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think being a little more direct was helpful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's really nice. Well, I think, too, you've been able to do that more with me and I feel like that's been really helpful. I know I've been kind of pushing you on that and that's been hard, but I feel like it's been really nice because I feel like it's really been helpful with your relationship with Kathy. So that's fantastic. And also, you know, again, I know that I keep saying this over and over again, but as you've worked on these things, it's been notable that it's really had a nice and positive effect on your eating because it seems like you're really seeing a lot of real nice improvement. So awesome. Anything else that, so you had a really good conversation with Kathy. Anything else go on this week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I got to spend some time with Brooke. I went home for two days and was with my mom and Brooke.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So is she still six or did she have a birthday recently?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: She's almost seven.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, that's great. Almost seven. Great. Any plans for a birthday for her or what are you guys going to do?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: She's really into Frozen, so anything Frozen's good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Anything Frozen's good. Okay. Yes. Okay, that sounds terrific. And so then you spent some time with her, so obviously that was real positive for you. Did you, when you were there, did you have any opportunity to visit with your mom or how did that go?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, my mom was around, like we kind of all spent time together and she asked about school and I was able to tell her a little more about school and how things are going and yeah, we didn't really get one-on-one time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How did that feel for you in terms of like for her? I know that you've talked about not really liking that she all of a sudden is deciding now that she wants to really be kind of like the good mother and kind of be involved in your life, but how was it for her to kind of want to know how things have been going for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, I've kind of like allowed myself to tell her, I guess, how things have been going, but I mean, to an extent. Like it was with Brooke and what not, like we didn't really sit down just us two together.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So kind of what we had discussed kind of that you've been, you've like been allowing yourself to be more connected with her, but you're still kind of keeping a little bit of a boundary. Yeah. Well, I'm sure it would be really hard to trust her after everything that's gone on. You know, with the infidelity issue with your dad, or at least the suspicion about that. I mean, I think you kind of know that was probably what was going on, but then, you know, and then moving you, how harsh and critical she was, issues with Brooke, you know, even I still even remember too, for her to have gotten to the point where she wouldn't even let you like go to your grandmother's funeral. Or at least, you know, kind of, so all those things have been so like, you know, front and center. And so now to feel like that she's made this real dramatic shift in wanting to start being a mom, but sounds like that you're really working to try to manage that in a better way.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean, like we still butt heads a little bit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm sure. Yeah, but when you do butt heads, what is it, what happens in terms of your eating when you guys kind of, when you feel like there's a little bit of a friction?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, I guess that's like kind of what leads back to things. Like things were really good this weekend for the most part, and then kind of when I was leaving, she just like either brought up things about wanting to know more about life and what's going on at school and if I'm seeing anyone. And yeah, it just, I'm like we don't have that relationship yet.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So that really felt really stressful.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So I feel like when I got back to school, like right after that is, and she like called me and...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, it makes a lot of sense because again, you know, like I know that we've really reviewed this quite a bit, but historically that's how it's been. You know, that's really been a real, and it really clarifies why we're working on this is because it's so clear that when the two of you have these rough patches, that it really all of a sudden evokes all these like negative feelings and that's when food like really kicks in.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: She makes her little comments still, like seeing what I'm wearing. She's like, oh, that looks cute.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, right, yeah. So it's really hard to let that go. I mean, because obviously there's a lot of feelings that you have about that. But on the other hand, too, it seems like that, you know, things have been going really well. How have things been going in terms of just in general, like school, friendships, you know, anything else that's kind of on the horizon?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, kind of seeing a guy. So that's been...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I won't get too excited about that, but tell me about him, tell me about him.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You sound like my mother. His name is Alan.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alan. Okay, okay, all right. Well, did you like, all right, I'm not going to blow this out of proportion, but how did that kind of come about?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We had class together and kind of went and studied at a coffee shop. Yeah, and then just kind of asked to like do a movie night and it was like chill and good and yeah, no like, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Nice, nice. That's great. I'm really happy. That's great. So a lot of really nice things that are going on. Yeah, that's terrific. Yeah, so then for you to go like from you know, because when we kind of got going with this thing it was kind of like you were full-on binge eating, you know, virtually every day, sometimes twice a day and now to be down to three like in the space of like you know, just like seven, eight weeks is you know, pretty remarkable. So no, I'm really pleased with how hard you've been working because you really been pushing yourself and I really appreciate it. And I know this stuff with your mom is particularly hard. It's been really hard for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess like not being able to tell, like I don't feel comfortable really telling her yet about...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you may not. You know, I mean, it's like, you know, I know that we talked about there's like maybe there are times when you just don't really want to share some of that stuff. You know, and I think sometimes my experience has been some parents like, you know, the goal is not to make her feel bad. If you would want to share it, you'd want to share it knowing that she would hold on to that and keep it and really connect with you around it, want to be helpful rather than like, oh, yeah, you were so mean to me and now I have an eating disorder. You know, because then that feels you know, that doesn't feel quite right. And I know that's you know, I know that you have a lot of hard feelings, but I don't really feel like that's how you'd want that to go. You know. And I know we've talked about it a lot, but how are things going with your dad?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Good. Yeah, good. He's doing well. Hoping that he's coming up here to school to see me in like a couple weeks for football.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, nice. That'll be really nice for you to spend time with him. That's great. That's really great. So let's talk some more about this thing with your mom because I feel like that I mean, I know it's tough, but I guess I've been thinking about this a lot and especially after last session that given the fact that you and Brooke are so close and it does feel like that your mom is at least she seems like she's making she's trying to make an attempt to connect with you. Whether or not, at what point would you feel like that you well, let me try to say it this way. What would you need from her in order to feel like that you could kind of like maybe not let down the walls, but kind of soften those a little bit? I mean, is there something is there something that like if you could ask her like, okay, mom, if you did this, then I would do this? Not that you would do that, but I just wondered if like what would you ideally what would you like to see in order to feel like that you could connect with her more?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, like I wish she really recognized like kind of the pressures that she put on me back in the day. video_details.title: Gestalt Therapy Role-Play - Two-Chair Technique with the Internal Critic
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which the two-chair technique from gestalt therapy is used to help a client (played by an actress) confront her internal critic regarding an important life decision.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Erica, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Good. Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're doing good? I was hoping today we could revisit the two-chair technique. We used it a few sessions ago, you might remember. And I know in the last session, I felt like we were kind of getting to a point where we identified a conflict. Do you know what I'm referring to?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Kind of. Between part of me that wants to settle down, but then part of me that also wants to pursue my career and what I'm doing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So we have a part that wants to settle down and a part that wants to keep going with the career. For this two-chair, what I'd like to do is in the chair where you're seated now, this will be the emotional self, the side that wants to pursue the career.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's what I really want. Yes. That's what I want.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're more emotionally connected. That's what you want. So this will be the side of you that has the needs and the wants and more the emotion. In the other chair, let's have that internal critic that's advocating for settling down, getting married, and having kids. In a way, it represents a societal pressure. Do those two sides seem separate to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You feel like you can be the emotional self here and the internal critic there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You'll be talking to the internal critic on the side of settling down and getting married. Then when you're ready to have the critic respond, you'll switch to that chair and respond to the emotional side. Whenever you're ready, go ahead and speak directly to the internal critic.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I want to finish what I'm doing and I want to finish what I started. I've worked so hard on my career path and I'm so close to finishing. I want to finish for me and accomplish those goals I've set for myself. It's something I'm passionate about.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Ready to switch? Okay, go ahead and switch. Now you're the internal critic.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: There's always time to pursue a career, but I need to focus on what's expected of me at this time. I'm the best age for having kids. I have a loving boyfriend who is ready and wants to get married and settle down. You are being selfish by just following a path that you can take at any time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's an internal critic accusing the emotional career side of being selfish. I noticed your posture is very linear and upright. Try to act out the internal critic's body movements a little bit.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think it's accusational. I just want to tell the emotional part that it's being stupid and that you're not acting in the best interest of everyone else. I just want to jump at it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You want to jump at the emotional side? Are you ready to respond back to the internal critic from the emotional side? Go ahead and switch. The internal critic has just called you selfish. What is your response?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel like I'm being attacked. I don't think it's wrong to think about myself and what I am truly passionate about.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Your hands are pointing back toward the career emotional self. What can you do with your hands that really embody what you want to communicate to the internal critic?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They're pointing towards me to protect myself from what the critic is saying. I just want to push that back towards the critic.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, continue and use that motion of pushing the internal critic away.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't need to feel guilty or selfish for wanting to follow my dreams.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does the internal critic have something to say back?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. I think the critic lost its drive. I think the critic feels like it understands where the emotional side of me is coming from. I can recognize why working so hard is worth that sense of accomplishment and how it's going to help provide for my family in the future.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now you have your hands down as the internal critic. Is the internal critic less angry and assertive now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Less pushy, not as critical. I feel like the pressure isn't weighing on either shoulder. It's more quiet and not yelling at me with the urgency it had before.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the critic has lost some of its vigor. Move back to the emotional chair and face toward me. What have you gained here through your communication back and forth with the internal critic?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel calmer. The critic is a part of me, but it's not as intense right now. I think the emotional part of me was able to win the argument because that's what I want.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The end of this conflict is eventually a decision to pursue a career or to settle down. Do you feel you've gained more clarity in that decision?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, because I can stay on my career path but now I feel less guilty for doing it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So that's been your decision all along, but the internal critic was harassing you. Today you were able to shove that back and allow the critic to see how strongly you feel. Was this helpful?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I think that separating the two sides helped me realize which one felt stronger and gave me clarity.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Great. Reflect on what's happened here before the next session. We'll pick up then and see if that internal critic is still harassing you or if you have more peace. Thanks, Erica. I'll see you next week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thanks.

video_details.title: Social Anxiety Disorder: CBT behavioural experiment case example
video_details.description:
Case study example for use in teaching, aiming to demonstrate how a behavioural experiment might be used in CBT for social anxiety disorder. The character of Hannah is played by an actor (Malak El-Gonemy), but the scene is not scripted, and as such it represents a natural therapeutic exchange.

The video was filmed and produced by Ishan Siddiqui and Christopher Werrett.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You've said that when you're in work, you worry a lot about how you come across in social situations.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it really makes me feel really anxious, like what I look like and what people are thinking.

diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.text: How red? Like the chairs in this room?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably like the chairs.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So as brightly pink as these chairs? Out of 100, how pink would you say these chairs are?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: 90 out of 100.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What else are you worried is going to happen? What else might you see on the camera?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm worried I'll say something stupid and not be able to kind of get what I'm trying to say across properly.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how stupid out of 100, if 100 is ridiculously stupid?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably like similar 90, I'd say.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Anything else you might see on the camera?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think you'll probably be able to see that I'm sweating.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how much will you be sweating?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Again 90, like really visibly sweating down the face.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you think will happen the second time around when you stop doing the things you normally do to cope? When you maybe start to make eye contact?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think it will be even worse.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How much worse? Twice as bad?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Twice as bad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, can you give me your phone?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Should I just use this?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah, it's probably best. Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, so I was just wondering if I could talk to you about maybe doing my wedding photography?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, what kind of things do you see? How do you want it to be like?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'd like lots of shots of our family and our friends, quite a lot of natural shots of people talking. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Do you see it being outside? Is that something that you're interested in?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, it's going to be a summer wedding so a lot of outdoor shots if possible. Quite some arty ones too.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I've done quite a few things like that before.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you got anything that you could show me about your past work?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I recently did some shoots outside in a wood environment so I could show you that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, let's do the second one now. You ready to put down the bottle and make eye contact? Hi, so I was just wondering if I could speak to you about doing my wedding photography?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, what kind of thing are you looking at? How do you want it to be like?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'd like lots of shots of family and friends and quite a lot of natural shots.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Are you interested in having things outside maybe?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, it would be really great if we could get lots of shots outdoors of people chatting and maybe some arty ones as well. Have you got anything you could show me?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, actually a lot of the things I do are outside and I'm really interested in getting natural shots. I could show you some of my work.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, let's pause it there. I'm going to give you this back now to look at. Watch that and then we'll chat about it in a moment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's weird seeing it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So going back to your predictions, you said you thought you were going to visibly shake. Could you see yourself shaking on the video?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Definitely not as much as I thought. It's obvious I'm anxious, but I don't think you can tell I'm shaking that much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You said 90 out of 100. How much shaking would you say you saw there in the end?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe like less than 30.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You said you were going to go red or pink, 90 out of 100. Did you notice yourself going pink?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really, actually definitely less than I thought.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You were worried you were going to say something stupid. Did you notice yourself say anything stupid?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really, I thought it was going to be a lot worse than it actually was.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In the end, did you pick up anything? Could we maybe put that as a zero?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe like less than 10.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You thought you were going to be visibly sweating. Did you notice yourself sweating in the end?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really. Definitely not as bad as I thought.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What score would you actually give it in the end?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe again less than 10. I don't think you could tell at all.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You also said it was going to be twice as bad when you stopped using your normal strategies. What did you notice watching that video?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was actually probably better when I wasn't doing any of those things. I think I looked a lot more natural and was able to say what I was trying to say. I think I come across more personable.

video_details.title: CBT for PTSD: Example of how grounding techniques can be used in therapy
video_details.description:
Case study example for use in teaching, aiming to demonstrate how grounding techniques might be used in CBT for PTSD disorder. Catherine Corker, qualified CBT practitioner and Clinical Psychologist, demonstrates the grounding techniques. The character of Sarah is played by an actor (Catriona Burke), but the scene is not scripted, and as such it represents a natural therapeutic exchange.

The video was filmed and produced by Ishan Siddiqui and Christopher Werrett.

video_details.title: Intake and Assessment Role-Play Part 6 - Risk Assessment and Goal Setting
video_details.description: This video is part six of an intake and assessment (clinical interview) role-play of a counseling client (played by an actress) who is having symptoms of anger, substance use, and inflexible thinking. In this final section of the clinical interview, risk assessment and goal setting are demonstrated.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, I want to switch gears again. I want to talk about risk, like suicide or harm to others. I know all these things don't apply to everybody, but I want to make sure I go through and ask certain questions. Is that okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever had a suicide attempt?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. No. It's a sin to kill yourself. Only God can take your soul away, so, no, I can't do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So no attempts. Have you ever had thoughts of suicide?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, sometimes when I get really sad I think that the world would be better without me, but I bring myself out of that. I don't think it's anything I'd ever do, but...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Not something you'd ever do, but sometimes a thought crosses your mind like that. Do you remember the last time a thought like that crossed your mind?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When we were getting evicted from our last place, because I just felt like a complete failure. That was about a month and a half ago. All my friends in the house turned against me because I couldn't pay rent, and it had been like the third month, but not consecutive, so I didn't see the big issue. They told me that if I didn't get out they would call the police, and I had to stay with my sister. I just felt like a failure to myself, to my kids.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it was a tough time for you. Sounds like maybe passing thoughts?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, like I said, it's not anything I could ever do. Ever.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If that ever changes, would you tell me?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'll tell you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So how about harm to others? Meaning, do you ever feel like you have thoughts or you've ever developed a plan to hurt someone else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When I was younger, not anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When was the last time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably when I was in high school. Yeah, when I was still in that violent stage in my life where I would fight, but it never went to anything like 'I'll kill this person.' It was always just, you know, 'I'll knock you out,' but I won't kill you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, that was a while ago. So presently, no thoughts of harming anybody else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. If I ever feel really, really angry, I'll just punch a wall. I have special plates that I'll throw on the ground and break them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Like the suicidal thoughts, if thoughts of harming others do come up, would you tell me about those?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh yeah, I don't want to go to jail over hurting somebody, so I'd tell you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, thank you. Have you ever heard or seen anything that other people have not heard or seen?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Never? How about under the influence of drugs?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, when I used to do cocaine, sometimes I would think that somebody's at the door and they're not at the door, or think somebody's in the house when there's nobody in the house.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But not under the effect of drugs, it never happened?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. I want to switch gears again. I want to talk about the goals for counseling and your general goals in life. Let's start with your goals in life in general.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I haven't really thought much about it, but I would like to just have a really nice, cushy job.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A better job?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, where I can just relax. My kids will have a good future, I'll have a good future.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A better future for your children?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any other general life goals?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess be drug-free. Like I said, I'd really like to quit, but it's hard.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about goals specifically for counseling? Like what you hope to get out of this counseling?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd like to learn to be less angry, bring my blood pressure down a little bit, sleep more...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: More sleep?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, eat less and try to quit drugs.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How confident right now are you that you can meet these goals, specifically the counseling goals?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Kind of, I guess? Is that an answer?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's an answer. Kind of confident?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean, every time I go to a counseling place I haven't really moved forward. So I'm willing to give it another shot, but because of my history with it, I'm just willing to try again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so you're kind of confident and willing to try again. Throughout this intake, I've asked you a lot of questions. Do you have any questions for me?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, not really.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The next time I see you, is it alright with you if it's about a week? We'll start with the actual counseling sessions. I'll still have some questions, but not as many. Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so we've completed intake. Next week we'll start working on the specific details of what's happened to you and how we can treat it. I appreciate you taking this time, and I'll see you next week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: All right, thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks, Rhonda.

video_details.title: Intake and Assessment Role-Play Part 4 - Education, Work, and Legal History
video_details.description: This video is part four of an intake and assessment (clinical interview) role-play of a counseling client (played by an actress) who is having symptoms of anger, substance use, and inflexible thinking. In this section, data about education, work, and legal history are collected.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I want to switch gears again and talk about your educational and work history. Is that okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me about school, starting from the earliest you remember?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When I was around my daughter's age, I was really active in school. I didn't want to go home, so I threw myself into activities and clubs to stay as long as possible. My grades were okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: They were okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And no behavioral issues or anything like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not that I remember, no.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about moving ahead a few years?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Around middle school, I started getting angry. I still did clubs out of habit, but I didn't really participate. I eventually stopped going or would drop them and pick them back up.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. How about high school? Did you go?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: High school was a disaster. Teachers were always on my case, even though I was barely there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How were they upset with you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They said I didn't take school seriously and had a disrespectful attitude. I was expelled in the 11th grade.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that the highest grade you completed?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right now, I'm working on my GED.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how is that going?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It goes. I have to get it, so I'm not happy about it. I know I'm smart, but I choose not to do anything with it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have any special training for work?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really. All my jobs have been retail. I was fired from my first job at 17 for not showing up because I was partying. At my second job, I quit after an argument with a customer.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So first job fired, second job quit. How about moving forward from there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Now I work at a warehouse, so I don't have to talk to people. They have personal days I can use if I party too much. It's meaningless work, but it pays the bills.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I want to switch gears. Are there any other behaviors you're repetitively engaged in, like gambling or the internet?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I stay on the internet until early morning, sometimes 4:00 AM, even when I have work. It's easier to talk to people there because I can just exit if they annoy me. I also get the scoop on everyone.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you consider it a problem?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It interferes with work sometimes. I get annoyed when I see it's 2:00 AM and I have work at 8:00.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I want to talk about your sexual history. Is that okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me about your sexual orientation?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I am heterosexual.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever been abused sexually?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My father was accused of it, but I don't remember much because I was so young and things were really bad when he was around.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about your drive? Is it normal, or more or less than normal?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would say less. I have other things on my plate. It's been reduced for at least a year.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I want to talk about your legal history. You mentioned a DUI?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was caught with a DUI and possession. I got a slap on the wrist for going to NA and paying a fine, though I found NA really boring and stopped going after a few times.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any other legal history? Does the DUI affect your employment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No other history. It was hard to find my warehouse job; a friend had to help me get in.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have any history of military service?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

video_details.title: Intake and Assessment Role-Play Part 2 - Family Relationships
video_details.description: This video is part two of an intake and assessment (clinical interview) role-play of a counseling client (played by an actress) who is having symptoms of anger, substance use, and inflexible thinking. In this section, data about family relationships are collected.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I want to change gears a little and talk about your family. Is that okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, that's a lot, but it's all right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A lot of information there, huh? Yeah. All right, let's start with, can we start with your parents and tell me what you feel comfortable telling me about them?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, my father was incarcerated when I was four for drug trafficking.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Drug trafficking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, and he died a few years ago from a stroke.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How many years ago?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: About three years ago.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: At what age was he when he passed away?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: To be honest, I don't even remember. I don't really talk to him.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, how about your mother?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My mom is crazy. She's always been very eccentric, I guess. We don't talk anymore because she has chosen gambling over the family.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me about that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When I lived with her, sometimes there was no water or electricity because she gambled the money. I had to hide cars from being repossessed. I moved out at 16. She calls sometimes for money or to talk, but I don't really talk to her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So how would you describe the quality of your relationship right now with her?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Not good. And it sounds like there is not much communication.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not anymore, no. She's tried, but I refuse to speak to her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you know if your father or mother has any history of mental illness?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My mom was diagnosed as bipolar. My father had an anger problem and physically abused us.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You remember that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I do. From what I remember of him.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so that's your father and your mother. How about any siblings?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have an older sister and a younger sister.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Two sisters? Tell me about them.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My older sister pretty much raised us since Mom was never around and Dad was in jail. I love her to death. She's my best friend and godmother to my kids.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And this is your older sister?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, my older sister.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about your younger sister?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We don't talk much. She says I'm a bad influence on her and her friends. I think she's stuck up.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A bad influence on... why does she think that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: She thinks she's better than me just because she went to college.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so it sounds like you have a positive relationship and admire your older sister. Is that right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I love my older sister.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And the relationship with the younger sister is a little bit different.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I love her too, and I can deal with her in small doses, but that's pretty much it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How often do you communicate with each one?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I talk to my older sister almost every day; she's my rock. The younger one, maybe every other week just to see what's up.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so quite a bit closer to your older sister. Any mental health history with either sister?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My older sister had depression and anxiety from dealing with my dad. The younger one, I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Does your older sister or your younger sister know that you're here?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My older sister does. I haven't spoken to the younger one this week yet.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you planning on telling her?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, maybe it'll humanize me and show I'm not the bad person she thinks I am.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you feel a need to make a positive impression on her?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, but it's easier not being viewed as the 'bad sister.'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's how you believe you're viewed by her? All right. How about grandparents?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: On my dad's side, I don't know them. On my mom's side, Grandpa died before I was born and Grandma had dementia in a nursing home.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any other mental health history with grandparents? Aunts, uncles, cousins?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just that Grandma's dementia. I have a lot of cousins; we were the family central. I keep in touch via social media.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. How about children?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have two children. They are the loves of my life. One is in second grade and the other in kindergarten.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me about them.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The one in kindergarten is a handful and prefers my older sister for diaper changes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Your older sister watches them? Okay. And you mentioned the son in kindergarten and a daughter in second grade?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. My daughter is being a bully at school lately, getting referrals for pushing and yelling at other kids.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does this behavior worry you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I got in trouble at school too, and I don't want her going down the same path.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How often do you see them?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I see them daily, but if there are parties with 'stuff' around, I drop them at my sister's to protect them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: By 'stuff' you mean drugs?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, drugs and alcohol. I'd rather my kids not see me like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're protecting them from it.
