diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh yeah.

video_details.title: Intake and Assessment Role-Play Part 5 - Spiritual, Cultural, and Abuse History
video_details.description: This video is part five of an intake and assessment (clinical interview) role-play of a counseling client (played by an actress) who is having symptoms of anger, substance use, and inflexible thinking. In this section, data about spiritual, cultural, and abuse history are collected.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me about your or any spiritual beliefs you might have?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I was raised Catholic. So, I mean, it just it get kind of worked because it has so many rules of what you can and cannot do and I'm like that's not living. But I mean I still believe in it I guess I was raised that way.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you consider yourself Catholic but you feel like there's a lot of rules.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I mean there's a lot of dos and don'ts. Our church was very like hell-oriented, like if you don't if you do this you're going to go to hell, if you do this you're going to go to hell, and I'm like well what's left that's fun?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How do you think those spiritual values influence your daily life?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh, I mean sometimes I do feel guilty about what I do. I feel guilty about, you know, spending more money than I'm willing to admit on drugs and um parties, but I mean I think you know God would forgive me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. How about racial ethnic identity?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I am Mexican.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Mexican. And how do you think that affects you in your daily life?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I'm very very family oriented. That's why the family that I'm close with I try to stay close with. That's why I stayed as close as I can to my sister. And you know that when things are at my house that I don't want my kids to be exposed to, they go with her. You know I'm looking out for them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Can you tell me about your living housing situation?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Unsteady, I guess would be the word. Yeah. I mean usually it's about there's a lot of us in one house. Like right now I'm living with about six other people. And you know if a fight happens or somebody can't pay the rent or I can't pay the rent, you know I've moved probably about 12 times within the past year.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In the past year? That's a lot of moving. Has it been stressful on you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Meh. I mean sometimes I enjoy the new environment. Feels like a fresh start to me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So there's a part of it that's not so bad.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, but I mean I could see it having an effect on my kids.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. How about your financial outlook?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My financial outlook? Well, I I get assistance from the state. Um and I mean I usually have enough to pay for everything. I mean there's been some days that I've had to tell, you know, my roommates hey can you lend me some money or my sister's always there if I need that from her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So occasionally you'll borrow money?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. How about your sleep? Do you feel like you sleep as much as you should, more than you should, or less than you should?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Much less than I should.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Much less. Tell me about that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Ah, I mean just two kids and getting them down and then taking trying to take some time for myself and you know sometimes I'm up late with, you know, being with people smoking, drinking. I just don't sleep that much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Is that a problem that you want to work on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess. Yeah, I would really like to get some more sleep.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. How about food intake, eating? Do you feel like you eat more than you should, less than you should, or about right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: More than I should. I find myself like snacking a lot during the day. And I'll still have regular meals so it's like meals on top of snacking on top of meals on top of snacking. It's just a lot of food.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that an area that you want to work on? Do you see that as a problem?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess I could work on that. I don't think of it as a problem but I guess now that you mention it, yeah, that would be interesting.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It may be. All right. Uh I want to switch gears again here to trauma history now. You already told me about what you think may have happened or could have happened with your father. How about any physical abuse? I think you mentioned that earlier, right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. Um well my dad would hit us when we were younger and then after he went to jail, um me and my mom would get in a fight sometimes. Physical fights. Yeah. Had a few cousins that, you know, would step over the line. But I mean I was involved in it so is that considered abuse?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me what you mean by involved in it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You know, I punched back.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, what do you think happened in those situations?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, they were they were picking on me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You were targeted.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, because I'm small. I'm short. You know all my cousins are like towering over me so they would try to disrespect me because they thought they could.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you would act out physically against them to defend yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mm-hmm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Were you ever the initiator of abuse?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: On occasion. How about emotional abuse?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh well my mom always tried to make me like I was the scapegoat a lot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me about that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Even if it was her fault that the lights weren't on and there was no water, it would somehow be my fault. You know, oh well I had to bail your sister out again so you know this happened and I had to drive around town to find your sister because you know she was just off doing her own thing. So I had to spend all the money on gas couldn't pay the light bill and it was always my fault. Everything was always my fault even though I knew it wasn't. But it still hurt.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That was painful for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you think that had an impact or that or the physical abuse had an impact on your life what's happening now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, the physical abuse I guess I try to end fights with violence I guess because I know how bad it can get so I try to shut it down really fast, but probably not in the most healthiest way. Um see that's why I think my sister and me aren't close and so I blame my mom for that because she used me as the scapegoat and then my sister was like oh well that's the bad sister.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you think your mother's behavior led to the way your sister treats you now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mm-hmm. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Any other instances of physical or emotional abuse?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, not really.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Not really. All right.

video_details.title: Intake and Assessment Role-Play Part 3 - Social, Medical, and Mental Health History
video_details.description: This video is part three of an intake and assessment (clinical interview) role-play of a counseling client (played by an actress) who is having symptoms of anger, substance use, and inflexible thinking. In this section, data about social, medical, and mental health history are collected.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I want to switch gears a little to social relationships. This would be like romantic partners, friends, coworkers. Anybody notable in that realm that you can tell me about?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I have a few friends, but mainly how I meet friends is I move around a lot. If I can't pay rent at one place, another friend will offer me to stay at their house. They'll be my friends until I move again. Some of them are strong friends, some of them are weaker friends because I'm just there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How many close friends do you have?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: One or two.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how often do you talk with them?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: One I live with, so I talk to her every day. And the other one, you know, talk about every other day.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about any romantic interests?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've had a few boyfriends, but they get kind of annoyed because I make them do everything. I don't want to do certain things like clean or pick up, so I'll just tell them I'm in pain because of my accident. They call me lazy or whatever.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You were in an accident?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The DUI. Sorry, I didn't mention that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, we'll get to that in a bit. So you've had some boyfriends and they became annoyed. Do you have one now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not currently, no.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I want to switch gears again a little bit and talk about your medical history. How old are you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I am 24 years old.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have any health problems currently?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can't breathe sometimes, I guess I have asthma because I smoke cigarettes. I have that limp from the car accident.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me about the damage sustained in the car accident.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I was under the influence of cocaine and I crashed into a parked car.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you were driving a car under the influence of cocaine and you drove it into a car that was parked. What kind of injuries did you sustain?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My left leg was just shattered.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you said it still causes you to limp now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Some days are better than others, some days are worse.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In terms of the pain?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you take any medications for the pain?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really, no. If I feel any pain, I kind of just smoke.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Did you have surgery for that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, after the accident happened.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any other surgeries or health problems?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I sprained my right wrist in school before.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sprained your wrist? What hand is your dominant hand?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My right hand.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does that affect you at all?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any other health concerns from the past or currently?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are any of these problems you mentioned tied in with the problems you mentioned earlier, like the anger or marijuana use?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, my drug use did kind of cause the accident, and I sprained my wrist in school by fighting.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so there's some connection there maybe. I want to switch gears again and talk about your mental health history. Is that okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever been treated before for mental health conditions?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: After my accident, they sent me to a psychiatrist to talk about possible PTSD.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Post-traumatic stress disorder? Were you ever diagnosed with that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: To be honest, I didn't stick around long enough.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How long were you treated by the psychiatrist?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not very long. I honestly don't even know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any other mental health professionals?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Once in high school, a counselor talked to me about my grades, not going to class, and my behavior.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Was that just a one-time thing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It happened maybe three times and then I just got annoyed and stopped going.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any other diagnoses you're aware of in the past?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I'm not sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How would you characterize your experiences so far with the mental health treatment system?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I haven't had much experience. People try to tell me things are wrong with me and they're not. That's when I get annoyed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So far you don't seem like you're impressed.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

video_details.title: Psychodynamic Therapy Role-Play - Defense Mechanisms and Free Association
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which psychodynamic therapy is used to help a client (played by an actress) identify the cause of feelings of anger and frustration. The defense mechanisms of sublimation, reaction formation, and displacement are featured and a free association technique is used.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Jasmine, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hi, I'm okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're okay? Yeah. What's been going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just been dealing with so much anger that I'm having difficulty controlling it in my everyday life.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A lot of anger, huh? Yeah. Can you give me some examples?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like for instance, um, I go to the dry cleaners to pick up my fiance's uniforms and the lady had them like all bagged together... I began to yell, causing a big commotion because I was so frustrated and angry... she actually was about to call the police to escort me out and I don't think I'm even allowed to go back to the dry cleaners anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hmm, so quite a bit of anger.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Um, my neighbor's dog was barking late at night... I get into a huge fight with my neighbors and an argument... I feel bad now that it's over with, now that I thought about it, and I just don't know why I was so upset that the dog was barking.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so from your perspective, it doesn't seem to make sense why you got so angry.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I just it's been going on for some time now and I just get little things just I just explode. So I don't know why.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Did anything change around the time that the anger started?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Nothing that I can really think of. Just when I'm overwhelmed and I have so much to do, I kind of just break down and just become extremely upset with everything around me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so you're getting upset, you have some anger. Any other time that you're feeling angry?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When I go to the, um, I go work out at the kickboxing class... I'm like the, I go all out... I'm punching the bags extremely hard. I actually had hurt my wrist last week... it's just relief kind of getting all the anger I have out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so that experience for you, you feel like you're releasing more energy than maybe the other people in the kickboxing class.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, way more. Way more. I'm like loud, I'm sweating bullets, I'm just going all out like extreme anger.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so the in recent memory, your anger has increased, but it's still not really clear what's going on that's causing the anger.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really. I just feel like frustrated. I just have too much going on at the moment, so it's just kind of like I just feel overwhelmed, I guess, and I take it out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You feel busy, like in your daily life? Like a lot of responsibilities?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, a whole lot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, what kind of things are you doing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mainly take care of home is my main. I don't work or anything. So I kind of just take care of home and you know, with the kids and everything, it's just a lot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you have a lot of responsibilities in the home? Yes. All of the responsibilities. All of them? It feels like all of them.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm cooking, I'm cleaning, now I have to iron all of my husband's uniforms and get everything ready for him... helping the kids with their homework... it's constant cater and cater and cater and it feels like I just really don't get a break or any other help. It's just me doing everything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're doing everything? Yeah. And has it always been this way?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not always, but it seems it's been like this for some time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Well, you're really just doing everything in the home. All right, I want to ask you or mention a few words, right? Tell me the first thing that comes to mind... try not to invest a lot of thought into the response, but more just what occurs to you. So the first word is home.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Structure, responsibility, repetition.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. I'm going to give you another word: relationship.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Conflict, power struggle, disagreements.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Let me offer you another word: work.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Independence, freedom, able to express creativity.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good. All right. And how about another word here: power.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A constant struggle, extremely controlling.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So do you see any themes in the words that you provided back?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It just seems like everything is like really controlled and structured.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Controlled and structured. And what's the source of that control and structure? Or is there a source of it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A lot of it may come from my fiance, now that I'm thinking about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me what you're thinking.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Because I feel that he doesn't give me the freedom or the ability to do a lot of the things that I would like to do, like work. And I think he should help more with the kids around the house... I feel that I don't have any help. It's like I'm single and I'm doing everything on my own, so that's probably where the bulk of my frustrations come from.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So as you're telling me this and you're explaining kind of that relationship with your fiance, what are you feeling?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm feeling angry and disappointed. Like I don't really know if I want to further anything because will it be like this forever? So I'm kind of just like angry and frustrated.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is this similar to the anger that you've been experiencing recently, like at the dry cleaner and other places?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's far worse than that, but I think that's why I'm always so upset and angry.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're thinking now that maybe that relationship or some part of that relationship is what's really causing the anger.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, because I feel alone at the same time, completely like I'm not in a fair relationship. It's like I'm in a controlling one, and I don't have freedom to do anything, I don't have help, and it's weighing a lot of stress on me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So as you talk about this, do you feel like this is new information that you're kind of realizing something that you didn't realize before?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, because honestly, I kind of I never really focused on that aspect of it. I kind of just thought that's the way it should go and I just thought I was angry because I just had bad days... I try so hard to make everything in my family right. So I kind of really don't pay attention, I kind of ignore it, but now that I'm thinking and pointing out different things, it's all stemming to how I really feel.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you feel this is kind of a big moment in terms of awareness?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Definitely, because I don't think I would have, like I said, I think I'm kind of I try to hide it and really don't focus much on it because I want things to be perfect, so I think I kind of ignore it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So maybe through this session, you've developed more insight about what's contributing to the anger.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, definitely. Because I would just go off for no reason at all and just later just think about like why did I even do that? But this source of anger, this relationship, I definitely can see the reasons why I'm angry in my relationship.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, Jasmine. Well, I feel like we've made some progress here. And I'd like you to, between now and the next session, if you're comfortable with it, kind of reflect on what themes have maybe come to the surface, what information's maybe been revealed to you a little bit, and we can pick up there and explore this further with the anger issue. Does that sound like a good plan?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, definitely. Definitely that's a good plan.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Well, I appreciate you coming in today and I'll see you in a week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Thank you.

video_details.title: Intake and Assessment Role-Play Part 1 - Referral and Presenting Problems
video_details.description: This video is part one of an intake and assessment (clinical interview) role-play of a counseling client (played by an actress) who is having symptoms of anger, substance use, and inflexible thinking. In this section, data about the referral and presenting problems are collected.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Rhonda, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're fine?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm glad you could come in today for this intake. I want to explain a little about the process. I understand you've already completed the informed consent?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. Yeah, I've done this before, so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You've done this before? So you understand my obligations to report certain things? Okay. Okay. So, you answered some other questions in that packet that you filled out with the informed consent. Factual type questions, information that might be on your driver's license or insurance cards, things like that. I'm going to be asking you more emotionally oriented questions as part of this part of the intake. Some of the topics we'll be covering are sensitive for many people and you may not want to talk about it and that's okay. So if I stumble upon one of those topics you don't want to discuss it, just let me know and we don't have to talk about it. If it's an area that you don't want to talk about right now, but you want to talk about it later, we can talk about it later. Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yep.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So, how were you referred here to our agency?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I have this friend that I've known her forever and um, she told me that she was really concerned about the way I was living my life and that you know I should be coming here, so as a favor to her, I'm here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so you're here as a favor to your friend. Do you feel committed to counseling?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, I guess there's some things I can work on, but I mean, they say I have problems that I really just don't I don't have.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And when you say they, who are you referring to?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh, some of my other friends, the friend that referred me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so there's some elements that they're observing and reporting to you, but you're not quite seeing them. And you think they might not be there at all.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Fair enough. So, I want to talk about what we refer to as the presenting problem. And I know you indicated you're here because a friend referred you, but in terms of the any symptoms or any problems, issues that might be going on in your life, any of those you can identify, could talk about?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I mean I will admit I do get angry a lot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Anger, okay.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. And sometimes when I get mad, I break a few things, I'll punch a wall, I'll I won't hit anybody, so I mean that's not a problem, you know, but I'll take it out on something that doesn't feel pain, I thought that was a good thing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, so inanimate objects are the target of some physical and angry behavior, but not people.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, not people.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So do you view anger as a problem you want to work on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I could work on being less angry, I don't think I have an anger problem, but I can be less angry.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So one of the symptoms would be anger, you don't necessarily feel like it's a large problem, but you could be less angry.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I mean I think everybody can work on being a little more peaceful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. That makes sense. Anything else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Now this is something I have tried to stop before, but I'm having a problem. I do smoke marijuana a lot. I'm not going to lie to you, a lot. Um, and recently I've been getting into like snorting some drugs.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me what drugs?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like Xanax. And I've tried to stop before and it didn't work, but I mean I like it so it's kind of like that do I really want to give it up? I'm not sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, you seem a little more torn on that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you say a lot of marijuana. Uh, and that can mean something different depending on the person. What's it mean to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh, several times during the day. Um, even when I'm at work I'll go to my car on break.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does anybody notice that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, the place I work at isn't very professional I guess. I mean, there are managers that I hide it from, but everybody there pretty much knows.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, and they're okay with it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you mentioned specifically Xanax, a benzodiazepine. Any other drugs?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, no. It's just mainly the marijuana and then I've started the Xanax.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And that seems like it's more recent.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean within the past four months a friend introduced it to me and started to like it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, and how often do you use that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That one's less often, I'd have to say about maybe twice every weekend.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And the marijuana sounds more like an everyday thing.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Any other drugs? Pretty much it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, no more drugs.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. How about in your past?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: In my past I have, um, experimented with cocaine. But I kind of got in trouble with the DUI for that, so I had to stop that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. And anything else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any other problems you identify to work on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I can sometimes let my pride get in my way.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Pride. Tell me a little bit about that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't like being told I'm doing something wrong, because most of the time I'm not or I'm doing it in a way, like just because I'm not doing it your way doesn't mean I'm doing it wrong. I know what I can do and I know what I'm capable of.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. So is somebody telling you that you're acting in a way that's proud?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Uh, I've had several people, I've lost a few friends because uh, over, you know, little things that I won't budge on. Um, for example, things like even like what the best TV show is. I know what the best TV show is and anybody who says any different is wrong. And I've lost friends. But you know what, maybe they're not real friends.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're indicating pride, but it sounds like maybe inflexibility is a part of it too.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has anybody ever said that to you or...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, not in that word, but I mean now that you say it, I guess, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. You think that's kind of together with the pride?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I feel...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that a fair adjective, inflexible?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it is.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. So we have anger, mostly at objects though, not at people. Marijuana, a lot. Xanax, not as much, occasionally. And then inflexibility and pride.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean that, yeah, that really would be accurate, as much as I hate to admit it, it does.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's tough for you to talk about this part?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah.

video_details.title: Initial Phase and Interpersonal Inventory 1

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I saw on the thing that your name is Elizabeth and I'm not sure if that's what you go by.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh, I mean Liz would be the best thing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Liz would be the best? Okay. All right, great. Uh, so Liz, one of the things I wanted to talk with you about is I know that you did some assessments over the last couple of days, and so I wanted to talk with you about that and just talk with you about kind of the treatment and how things are going to go. And based on that, it sounds like from what you were saying in terms of the assessment process is that you have an eating disorder called bulimia nervosa and I'm not sure if you've ever heard of that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, a little bit, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so what I want to do is kind of describe that for you a little bit. So what you talked about was that there are periods of time when you have eating episodes where you eat kind of a large amount of food, that you feel like that you've lost control, and that you feel, you know, like overly full, may vomit, and that this happens fairly regularly. And there are times too when you're, you know, you're maybe really overly concerned about your shape or your weight. Does that feel familiar to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, so...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And then it sounds like that's been going on now for quite some time, at least, you know, two, three, sometimes even upwards of five times a week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh, yeah, I'd say, yeah, at times, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. All right. So I just want to let you know too that it's not unusual for a person in college like yourself to be struggling with an eating disorder like this. In fact, we see upwards of 5% of women on college campuses who struggle with that and even more upwards of 20% who have variants of that in terms of excessive dieting. One of the things we know about bulimia nervosa is that for a lot of women it really starts by excessive dieting. So like going for long periods of time without eating, and it sounds like that was something that you endorsed as well, that there are times when you kind of diet excessively.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, especially when I was younger I'd say, but yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. And one of the things that we know about bulimia nervosa is that when people overly restrict or stop eating a lot, that oftentimes that kind of leads into that kind of binge eating cycle. The other thing that we're aware of is that a lot of individuals who struggle with eating difficulties like this also report a lot of difficulties with managing stress, managing relationships, or managing feelings. Is that something that you've experienced?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. All right. Well, that's okay because in many respects I think both things go on for individuals that struggle with eating difficulties like that. So we know that there's a lot of dieting and restriction that goes on, but we also know that there are other things that are happening in terms of managing feelings, managing stress, etc. So one of the things that I like to focus on in terms of working with individuals like yourself is I take an approach that's called interpersonal psychotherapy. And what that means in essence is that I like to approach the eating problem by looking at kind of the social and more interpersonal context. And so what I'd like to do is really talk with you over the next few sessions about periods of time in your life currently and in the past where you've had overeating episodes and really start looking at patterns perhaps in your relationships. And then what we'll do is kind of sum that up at the end of the time that we're together and see if we can kind of come up with a little bit of a game plan and some goals to help you reduce your binge eating. How does that sound?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sounds good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, good. Yeah, and there's really good evidence for the things that we're going to be doing. In fact, you'll note pretty quickly that you're going to start feeling a lot better and it'll have a pretty positive impact on your eating. Okay, great. So this is what I'd like to do. First of all, let's start with, I want you to give me a recent episode within the last couple days where you've had one of those episodes where you felt like you ate a lot, that you lost control, and that you ended up vomiting, and kind of get an idea about that. And then what I'd like to do is go kind of back in time and then I want you to tell me the first time that you had an episode like that. So why don't you tell me like a recent episode where you felt like that you'd lost control of your eating.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I mean like just this Saturday night I guess. I went out with my friends and it was a good night at first and then we went to a party. I guess what sparked it would be I saw this guy that I kind of liked for a little while and I just wasn't, was a little nervous about what I was wearing and it just didn't feel that good to see him. So I kind of left pretty early on and went back to my apartment and yeah, kind of what typically happens is in the kitchen grabbing some different food, bag of chips my roommate had left out, like a sleeve of cookies or something and then I just ate on the couch. Yeah, finished most of it and yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Had you been restricting your food prior to that or had you been dieting prior to that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean I guess like dieting is what you would consider it. I try to eat more healthy typically. And yeah I mean I've been like dealing with like different assignments and stress around that, so um yeah it's kind of fluctuated at times.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. I meant to tell you too, I like to take a lot of notes at least initially so I have a good sense of what's going on. So, what else was going on? Okay so it sounds like Saturday night out with friends, see person that you, did you say you dated some?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh no not really but like we've kind of been like interested in each other.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Interested in each other. Okay. All right. So you're kind of interested, and then it sounds like what you then you began to feel more concerned about how you looked and how your outfit felt?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And then it sounds like what then happened is that you go back to the apartment, food's there, and then you kind of sat down on the couch and you felt like that you'd lost control.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean I didn't plan on seeing him, so yeah, it just didn't feel like the right outfit to see him in.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, and so then what happened is that you sat down on the couch and you felt like that you'd lost control.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, and then I guess after that like before bed I made sure to go into the bathroom and yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Is this kind of a typical scenario?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean with the eating and then just before bed and yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And then so you went home to an apartment, you're in school, so tell me about that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh yeah junior year, so my third year in school.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what are you working on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh English as a major. Um yeah so I guess junior year is kind of the more tough year, more papers and whatnot. This year just been a little more work and a little more stress.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, because I was thinking about the time of the year, so is this exams coming up or projects coming up? So anything big on the horizon for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh I mean like midterms, big midterms, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. What else has been happening for you over the last week or so? Anything else that's been happening this week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh yeah studying for one of my midterms, my test was on Friday, and my roommate kind of has had her boyfriend over a lot. And it's pretty annoying because like she knew I had a test to study for and they're constantly in the living room on the couch and yeah, they're pretty loud so it's kind of frustrating and yeah, it was pretty stressful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Sounds like it. And what's your roommate's name?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh Cathy.

diarization.speaker: Therist
diarization.text: Cathy, okay. So then Cathy has her boyfriend over quite often, this last week they were there quite a bit.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Her boyfriend.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Her boyfriend, okay. And then you're trying to study and did you talk with them about the noise or that bothering you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean she knew I had a midterm coming up. And like I've mentioned that I enjoy studying at home but that's kind of all.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it sounds like you feel like you've tried to let her know in various ways that you've got something coming up and that you like studying when it's quiet, but that their constant commotion is really distressing to you, right? Have you talked with her like one to one about how that bothers you or that that's a real problem for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh not really.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Do you know what's hard about doing that in terms of talking with her?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh I mean we're kind of like newer roommates to each other, we haven't known each other for a long time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, I got it. That makes sense. Has this been something that's been kind of ongoing? How long have you been roommates with Cathy?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: This semester.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And has this been kind of an issue that's gone on for the two of you for a while in terms of her being disruptive or having the boyfriend over?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean he's over a lot, so yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. That's helpful. Tell me how old you are.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: 20. Okay. And you're a junior. Okay, great. Now let's do this. Let's go back to the first time that you can remember having an episode like you described where you felt like you either lost control of your eating or that you were concerned about your shape or your weight. When was the first time that you remember that happening?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess middle school, so eighth grade probably, 12 or 13 years old.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Middle school, 12, 13 years old. Good, so we'll start from there. Tell me about your parents.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh so my mom Lisa and my dad Steve, they actually got divorced when I was 10. So she then remarried soon after.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so your mom and dad divorced when you were 10? Okay. And then you say your mom got remarried.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like two years after that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Two years. Do you have any siblings?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh well I do now from her second marriage.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And is that a boy or a little sister, and what's her name?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Brooke.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Brooke. Okay. So mom remarried. What's your stepdad's name?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh Bruce. I thought I told you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. All right, so mom and Bruce they have a little girl and her name is Brooke. How old is Brooke?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Brooke is six.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh she's six. Okay. Tell me a little bit about what happened during the divorce and leading up to that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh you mean like after or what led up to the divorce?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, do you have a sense about what led up to the divorce or what was going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean I guess they were fighting a lot. Lots of fighting and dad had just they weren't around each other as much anymore and mom was kind of out of the house more.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And then so they divorced when you were 10, and so how soon after did your mom marry Bruce?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just under two years.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Under two years. Um how was that for you to have her remarry so quickly?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean I didn't really like it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. During that period of time when they were having difficulties with their marriage, what was your eating like or how were you managing that during that time in terms of your feelings about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When I was 10? Um I mean I guess I didn't really recognize too many issues right then necessarily.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Were you talking to anybody, or did anybody else know what was going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean I was like pretty close with my grandma, my dad's mom.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And she was aware of what was happening.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, so she was definitely there for me. And I'm closer with my dad I'd say, even at that time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And it sounds like that you're pretty close to your dad's mom.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, she's not around anymore but yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, I'm sorry about that. When did she pass away?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: High school.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. I just want to make a note of that. Okay, so at 10 mom and dad divorce, less than two years your mom remarries Bruce. Um so then what happened to you after the divorce? Were you with your dad or with your mom?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh no with my mom more. We moved to a different area. Not too far from my dad. So I saw him a decent amount, but definitely was with my mom more.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so then Bruce, your mom and you moved to like a different town?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, just like a town over. But changed schools and whatnot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Prior to moving to a new school, were you in a public school or private school?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So I was in a public school and then switched to a private school.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, switched to private school. Okay. How was that transition for you going from public school to private school?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean I wasn't excited about it. It was kind of like a more uppity area and yeah, it was kind of hard because I feel like in a private school these people have kind of been together for a little while and they kind of all know each other and have their groups and whatnot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And so that would have been in around the time when you were 12, 13 when you made that move? Okay, so then sounds like too that was the time when you first were aware of struggling with your eating.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think I felt more pressure from my mom. She was very vocal towards me about my eating and my looks and whatnot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When you say pressure from her, in what way was she pressuring you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean like she wanted me to look good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so that you would fit in more? Okay. And it sounds like you weren't excited, like you weren't happy.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I don't really like Bruce, so yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you don't really like Bruce and you didn't really like the new school and you didn't like that transition. Did you talk with anybody about that, did you let your mom know or let your dad know how kind of like you were unhappy?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean I let them know that I didn't like the school.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And then what would be the response?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's kind of just like 'oh you should feel lucky, like it's a good school,' 'this takes time.'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Well, so in many ways like kind of 'get over it' or 'deal with it'. So you were feeling pressure from her, sounds like also too that you weren't really feeling like there was as much concern about your feelings about where you were. Was there anything specifically that your mom would say to you about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean you mean in terms of the school or my body?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, in terms of the school.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh i mean like 'get over it,' 'it'll get better with time,' 'you just have to put yourself out there to meet people.'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. That kind of pressure. And then you said that you didn't really like Bruce, what kind of person was he, what was making you not like him so well?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean he's just kind of like a sketchy guy. Yeah, I don't know, he didn't really try to get to know me that well and just like the timing of it all was just like a little off and i feel like he kind of is the one who partially caused the divorce.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In what way do you think that that...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: There were some signals.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, so that maybe there was something going on between Bruce and your mom prior to the divorce. Yeah. I'm sorry to hear that, must have been really hard. And were you keeping in touch with your dad during that time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Like were you I mean how what was the arrangement, were you spending time with him sometimes and spending time with your mom?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, so I was with my mom during the week and I guess my dad like every other weekend.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So given the fact that you weren't happy in school, you said it was a private school, kind of clicky, and your mom really was pressuring you so that you fit in a little bit better. So when in this process did you find yourself turning to food or being excessively concerned about your weight or starting to diet?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Dieting was definitely eighth grade, ninth grade definitely. And that definitely came from like my mom telling me that I had to look a certain way to fit in. And there were times like there was unhealthy food around the house because that's what Bruce eats and it was there and accessible. So at times I would eat that as well but I would say for the most part I would try to like really eat and restrict myself to healthy food.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, okay. And do you recall the first time that you then vomited or used vomiting as a way to kind of manage the overeating?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess like ninth grade.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So that started in ninth grade. What was going on during ninth grade? You move to a new school, not really happy, feeling some pressure from your mom. And then in ninth grade the vomiting starts, so what was going on during that time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean just like pressures of starting high school and whatnot. I heard from some of the other girls about vomiting as like an option that they've heard some of their friends talk about before. And like the dieting, even though if I was eating healthy, like it was still here from my mom like 'oh like you need to look like this' or 'there's this outfit I want you to wear but you can't wear it if your body's like that.'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, so she was really critical of how you looked.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Very critical.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And so what did that do? Let me take a step back. So sounds like you've always been a little closer to your dad. So what effect did that have on your relationship with your mom after the move and some of that transition?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean I don't even really remember like a really good time with my mom, i guess i'd say.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So the two of you don't get along as well.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, we've butted heads a lot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Was it getting worse during that time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean i guess i was getting more vocal towards her and speaking my mind more.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And then she was then coming back more harshly or more critically. It's not unusual for girls at that age, part of that culture. But it also sounds like there was external pressure from your mom, it almost even sounded like she was saying that you were too heavy for a particular outfit. Do you remember how that was feeling to you at that time when she would say things like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just sad, cuz i yeah i feel like nothing i could do was right, so yeah, just a lot of sadness.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Kind of trapped. Did you talk with anybody about that, did you talk with your dad about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just like no, not really.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you kept a lot of those feelings to yourself. Okay. That's helpful. Because obviously the divorce, the move, the transition from middle school to high school, also sounds like you didn't have a very good relationship with Bruce and that your relationship with your mom was deteriorating. And i know you said your grandmother passed away in high school but during that time eighth, ninth grade did you have more contact with her?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A little bit, as much as i could. She also didn't live in the town where i was living. But like when i would see my dad, occasionally we'd go to see her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Okay. So if Brooke is six, okay, i'm just doing my math here, she was born in and around that time, so around when you were 14? Okay, so then Brooke is born. How was that for you in terms of having her come on the scene?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean i love Brooke, we're really close and i love her. But it's a little frustrating so as an only child and then your mom gets remarried and soon after a new baby. And then also my mom and stepdad both worked a lot, so i was kind of the one looking after Brooke a lot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So not only was your relationship with your mom kind of deteriorating, then all of a sudden you have a baby sister, they're working and now you're also feeling a pressure to take care of her. During that time you are feeling what?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh i don't know, just a little heavy. Like a lot of weight on my shoulders.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Emotional weight on your shoulders. And then what was your eating like between 14 to 16 when you were more actively involved with that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean i guess kind of similar to what i described now. I try to eat super healthy, but then at times especially because there was the food available around the house and whatnot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So were you bingeing more during that time then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, and i mean because i kind of found other ways to make up for the bingeing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Such as?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Throwing up.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So vomiting began during that particular time. Okay. That's really helpful. So take me to when you were getting ready to transition from high school to college. So what, 17, 18?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, i mean i was, well actually soon before that my mom and Bruce actually also got divorced.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Ooh, okay. So that was when you were 17, so probably middle of senior year. And Brooke would be four years old. So what was going on then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean i never really got close to Bruce, but the only hard part would have been figuring out with Brooke because i feel like i raised her almost. And it's just frustrating that my mom left my dad and then gets married and then divorced again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. And so what did that do? How did that impact your relationship with your mom after the divorce?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean we were still arguing a lot. She kind of started trying to say sorry and feeling bad for certain things, but i didn't feel like it was sincere.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so it's almost as though now she didn't have anybody and you felt like she was trying to reach out to you, almost like too little too late. So continued anger and frustration with her. And did you notice any changes in your eating during that time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean it was definitely still...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Okay. All right. And after graduation, you're in college now. So tell me about that transition from high school to college.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean i was excited. Hard to leave Brooke, but definitely excited to get out of the house to really try my own thing, do something new. So it was good.

video_details.title: CBT for Social Anxiety Disorder: Using downward arrow and thought challenging techniques
video_details.description:
Case study example for use in teaching, aiming to demonstrate how the downward arrow technique and thought challenging might be used in CBT for social anxiety disorder. The character of Hannah is played by an actor (Malak El-Gonemy), but the scene is not scripted, and as such it represents a natural therapeutic exchange.

The video was filmed and produced by Ishan Siddiqui and Christopher Werrett.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you said that when you're at work, you really worry that you're going to say something stupid.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's something that's always on my mind.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what would be so bad about that if you did say something stupid at work?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Because people would think I was weird.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what would be so bad if people at work thought you were weird?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They wouldn't want to be friends with me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what would be so bad about that, if people at work didn't want to be friends with you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I'd just have no one to talk to at work.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Then what would be so bad about having no one to talk to at work?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, the shoots can go on for the whole day, so I'd just be by myself the whole time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what would be so bad about being by yourself, you know, for a whole day?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, I guess I should be used to it now. I spend a lot of my time by myself, so...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That must be tough. What does that mean to you, that you spend a lot of time on your own?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, I guess it's just like, I spend so much time by myself that it's kind of like I'm not even worth being friends with.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it sounds like deep down that you think that you're not worth being friends with. And that's quite a negative belief. I mean, how much would you say that you believe that out of a hundred? If a hundred is where you believe it totally and zero is where you don't believe it at all.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd guess like 90 out of 100.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When did you start believing that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I think it was probably at school. Yeah, I think at school.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what was it about school that made you start to believe that you weren't worth being friends with?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just like quite a lot of things. Like, I wouldn't have anyone to sit with at lunch, or like people's birthdays and stuff I wasn't invited, and you know, like I was the last one picked for teams and stuff like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what is it now that makes you think that that's still true?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, it's kind of similar at work. Obviously, the difference is that it's work, not school. But, you know, people go for drinks and stuff after work or after a shoot and I'm just kind of excluded a lot of the time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That sounds tough. Um, is there anything that makes you think that it's not true, that you are worth being friends with?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess my friends and family would say that I am. Like, I try to make a lot of time for my friends and stuff.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so it sounds like deep down you have this thought that you're not worth being friends with and that started at school when you had trouble making friends at school and that you weren't always picked for teams. And that now at work, it feels like the same thing is happening, that you're not always invited out for drinks with people after work and that sometimes you feel that you're excluded from their social groups. But then that's not the whole story, that on the other hand, you are close to family and you do have friends who would say that it's not true, that you are worth being friends with. In CBT we do a thing called thought challenging where when we have these negative thoughts, sometimes we actually put them up to scrutiny, we weigh up the evidence for and against them. I like to think of it as putting the thought on trial. Could we do that now, where we just actually try and weigh up the evidence for and against that thought a bit more?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So if I just put two columns here, so 'for' and 'against'. And it sounds like the evidence for this thought that makes you think that it is true is difficulty at school, making friends, being picked for teams and difficulty at work, feeling excluded sometimes from groups.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But actually in this other column, we have that you are close with your family and that you have some close friends. Okay, now moving back to this first column, is there anything else that makes you think it's true that you're not worth being friends with?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, just like I kind of don't go to a lot of stuff. People have like gatherings and things and a lot of the time I just don't go and rather just stay at home.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Don't go to parties. What kind of parties are we talking? Like big parties, small parties?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, mainly big ones. If there's a lot of people there I just find it really, it kind of makes me really anxious, so a lot of the time I just prefer not even to be in that situation in the first place.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So you don't go to larger parties and events. Okay. Is there anything else that maybe makes you think that it's not true, that actually you are worth being friends with?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I mean I guess my friends would say that I was. I do have close friends and when it's stuff that's important to them, I always make sure that I think about that and even if I find it stressful, I'll always make sure that I can kind of put them first.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so your friends would say that you are worth being friends with. Um, and it sounds like you put your friends first.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I do make sure and I try and do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what kind of ways do you put your friends first?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I guess when it's birthdays or you know something important to them, I'll always make sure that I'm there and that I put a lot of thought into presents and stuff like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you give me an example of a time that you've done that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, it was my friend's birthday a few weeks ago and we did like a big surprise at hers and I made a cake and stuff like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you actually help to organize events for your friends.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there anything that you do that you wouldn't do if you weren't a good friend?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I guess that I kind of always put myself in a situation, even if I find it kind of makes me anxious, if it's for my close friends and I know that it's something that's important to them, then I'll always put them first and make sure I'm there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you'll tolerate your anxiety if it means something to a friend of yours. Okay, so at the moment in the 'for' category we've got that you had difficulty making friends at school, that you're having difficulty now at work making friends and that you don't go to larger parties or events. But actually there's a lot of evidence in the 'against' column, evidence that would suggest that actually you are worth being friends with and you're a good friend. That you're close with your family, you're close with your friends, your friends would say that you're a good friend. You put your friends first, even when you're anxious, you tolerate that anxiety if you know it'll mean something to them. That when things are important to your friends like birthdays, you'll make a real effort, you'll even actually go to the effort of organizing events and baking cakes and doing things like that for other people. Is there anything else that you do that makes you think that maybe you are a good friend, you are worth being friends with?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean I still have my friends, so I guess if I wasn't worth being friends with, I wouldn't have these friends that I've had for quite a long time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so it sounds like you've got long-term friendships as well. So that you might have trouble making friends, but when you make them, you stick with them.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. I'm just going to give you this list now to have a look at.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How do you feel now that you're looking at that list?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, it's weird, there's actually kind of more stuff in the 'against' than there is in the 'for'. I guess also a lot of the stuff that is in the 'for' column is kind of things that I make happen, like I don't go to things. Um, yeah, it seems like some of it is kind of in my hands.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's not that you're not worth being friends with, but actually that you're choosing not to engage with people always.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah, I think so, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And if I was to ask you now, you know, this idea that you're not worth being friends with, how much do you believe that now that we've done this exercise? Where 100 is where you really believe that you're not worth being friends with and 0 is that you don't believe it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I guess I'd say maybe 40. I think I do still think that it might be true, but I think I believe it less than I did before.

video_details.title: Psychiatric Interviewing: Asking about substance use
video_details.description:
Demonstrating how to ask a patient about their substance use. 

For more information on Psychiatry in Primary care and treating patients, please visit https://www.camh.ca/en/professionals/treating-conditions-and-disorders.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Ms. Watson, nice to see you again. Dr. Goldblum.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Nice to see you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm glad you came back in. I've got the results now of the blood work that we did after your checkup. And before we go over any of that, I really wanted to find out from you how things are going and what you're concerned about.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I mean, I'm curious about them because I haven't been very well, right? I haven't been feeling very well. Well, last week I threw up some blood.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that the first time that's happened?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, the first time. I mean, I threw up blood last week and then again yesterday. So there's something bad going on. I know there's something bad going on.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you think is going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Cancer, right? I think I probably have cancer. I'm not doing very well. I just... not doing very well. Headaches and it's just...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Look, let's try to figure some of this out, okay? When you said you were throwing up blood, were you throwing up bright red blood? And was it like little spots, big spots?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was, it was almost filling the toilet. It wasn't that much, I wasn't like... but it was enough that I could see it in the toilet when I was throwing up.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And did you have any other symptoms?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I was feeling sick, so and I had headaches and I...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What time of day was this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have headaches a lot throughout the day, but throwing up the blood, that was in the morning. And then again the other time it was sort of later in the day. But you know, I also wake up in the middle of the night and I'm just covered in sweat. And I know that's another cancer thing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, look, I can understand why you're worried, alright? Because throwing up blood is scary, and waking up soaked in sweat in the middle of the night, that doesn't feel right either. Let me ask you a couple of questions that might help explain things. When did you have your last drink?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Actually just before I came here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so that was earlier this morning. Alright, what did you have?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I had orange juice and I had some vodka in it. It's the only thing actually that like steadies me enough to get out the door. I don't go out that often but you know...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So tell me how it helps you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It just steadies me, steadies me. Like I'm you know, I'm shaky all the time. I'm just like...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So over the course of a day, in order to steady yourself, in order to feel calmer, how many drinks do you end up having?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Five, maybe?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Singles or doubles?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't measure anything, so...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is it mainly vodka?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes if my stomach is really upset I'll drink cider, so it's cider or vodka because it's just...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And do you ever get that feeling in the morning that some people describe that they wake up feeling so edgy they need a drink to calm down?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's like the only thing that works for me. It's the only thing that works to...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So in the past week do you think you've been drinking more?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: In the last week, not so much. Maybe last couple of weeks, maybe.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has it been daily?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
