diarization.text: Right. So the longest you've gone without a drink in the last month would be how long?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know actually. I mean, I don't know. I've got, you know, I've got a lot going on, right? I mean so my sister is in Boston, she's got cancer and I know like I should be calling her and I can't do that. And my mom is really sick and she's horrible and I'm the only one who can go see her. And I go see my mother and she just yells and screams at me and she's got emphysema and it's just...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And so for all of those things, the alcohol helps?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. And does it ever happen sort of by the end of the day that you have trouble the next day remembering what happened?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess. I mean you know, my days don't differ that much but you know, I'll fall asleep in front of the television and then I don't really... like I'm not seeing lots of people so you know, there's not big events in my life that I would be remembering. I just you know, and especially now that I'm feeling so not well, that yeah, there's not much that I would have to remember like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you tried at all to cut down on your drinking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I did. I did. You know, I had a boyfriend who you know, was sort of casual, coming over and we... and he basically said he couldn't be with me anymore because I drink too much and so I tried at that point, I tried and it's like...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's hard.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, yeah. And then he left, so who cares, right? I mean...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. But have you found yourself feeling guilty about the alcohol?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel guilty about my sister. I feel guilty that I can't, like I just can't, I can't even call her. Like I can't, right? So if I, if I could pull it together then I could...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Because what I understand from what you're telling me is that the drinking helps meet a certain need for you in terms of trying to hold things together with all this stuff going on. And it meets a need in terms of trying to keep you calmer. But at the same time it's getting you into trouble. It's getting into trouble in terms of relationships, but it's also the most likely explanation for why you've been throwing up blood and why the lab results that I've got are consistent with an amount of alcohol that's too much for your body to handle.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Really?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Really. And that means ideally that we're going to work together to find a way to do something about it.

video_details.title: Psychiatric Interviewing: Active listening
video_details.description:
Scenario on active listening in a primary care setting. 

For more information on Psychiatry in Primary care and treating patients, please visit https://www.camh.ca/en/professionals/treating-conditions-and-disorders.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Ms. Spencer, hi, Dr. Goldblum. Nice to see you again.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hi. Nice to see you too.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's been a while since I've seen you. I think not since your last general checkup.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, last year.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, it's nice to see you. But tell me, what brings you in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't even know if this is something I should be bothering you with.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Try me.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My son is really struggling. Josh is basically living in our basement. He's 22. He's not doing well. He's not eating, sleeping. I don't even know if he's talking to his girlfriend anymore. It's that whole transition from university to jobs. He had an internship but it didn't go anywhere. We were really hoping he'd be able to get this job and now it's just slowly gone downhill.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So how long since Josh finished his internship?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was the end of the summer. We really hoped it would continue, they'd pick him up for something else.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Looking back now, when was the first inkling of worry for you about how he's doing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably around Thanksgiving actually. Probably in the fall. He usually gets together with friends, he usually goes out a couple of times, and he was just not. It's come to a point where he doesn't even come out of the basement. He doesn't have to come out of the basement. Everything's down there except the food. It's like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And do you have any kind of communication with him?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not effective. He snaps at me. So when I ask him what's going on, it's none of my business, get out of his hair. It's like he's 14 again. So I'm sort of worried. I'm thinking he needs to see you, but I have no idea how to make that happen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's your worst fear about what's going on with Josh?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, that he really is depressed. That he really is in a place, and I don't know what that is. I don't know what he's thinking, and I can't get to him.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You can't reach him.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can't reach him.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And who's got the best connection with Josh?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would like to say I do. But I mean, I think there are things that his dad talks to him about that he's closer with his dad about.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Of course, it's hard for me to know exactly what's going on with Josh without having a chance to talk with him myself, right? But you're worried that he's depressed.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's the bottom line. I'm worried that there's really something...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you worried that he's depressed to the point of thinking about killing himself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: See, I don't know. I don't know. It has crossed my mind. I mean, it's sort of why I'm here. It's reached a point now where I don't even know if he's having showers. I don't know, right? It's like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. Do you ever hear him talking out loud when there's no one else there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. Not unless he's screaming at the television or something. But I don't know what's going on. We're not welcome down there. We're just not.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When he emerges, though, does he look different?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, he looks disheveled. He looks...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has he lost weight?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So the most important thing is going to be figuring out with you and with your husband together. We need to strategize on how we can get Josh to come in and to talk with me. And I think that's going to work better if I see you and your husband together and we put our heads together to figure out a solution because I understand why you're worried and it's right to be worried. But we're going to have to figure out a way to connect with Josh.

video_details.title: Clinical Interview Role-Play Part 3 - Abuse, Risk Assessment, Recreation, and Goals
video_details.description: This video is part three of a clinical interview role-play of a counseling client (played by an actress) who is having symptoms of anxiety and is using alcohol. In this section, data about abuse, risk, recreation and goals are collected.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I want to switch gears again and talk about any potential trauma or abuse. Are you comfortable with that topic?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You mentioned earlier there's been no occasions of non-consensual sexual contact. What about physical abuse?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about emotional abuse?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know if it really counts as emotional abuse, but my dad can be really intense. When you don't meet his expectations or you're not as successful as your sister, he can be kind of harsh.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you give me an example of something he might have said?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like, 'why can't you ever be good enough' or 'don't tell people you're my daughter when we go out in public' or 'I wish we had two of your sister and didn't have you.'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Those are fairly strong statements. What's that feel like when he says things like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess now I'm used to it. Before it was terrible, but you just kind of grow numb to stuff like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you feel like you're numb to it now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've heard it enough that I know it's coming, so you just kind of get used to it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's still got to be a little painful.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it is, but you can only hear things so many times before it's like, alright, I'm hearing the same stuff.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has there ever been a change in your anxiety levels or your drinking when he would make comments like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes. If he got off on a tangent and got really insulting, generally I would need to blow off some steam and I'd go out with my friends. I think that's when it started to get into the heavier drinking during that time, because I would get anxious and stressed out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would you consider this a significant part of your history?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It seems a little upsetting to you. Something maybe we can talk about later. All right, so I want to switch gears again. What do you do for fun for recreation?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Other than partying?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, okay, partying is one thing. Other than that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I like to shop and I like to hike in the mountains.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When's the last time you were hiking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably two years ago. It's been a while.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I like being out with my friends or I like going to see live shows, like music stuff.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Like theater or music?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like music, like bands and stuff.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When's the last time you've done that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably a year.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you consider your life to be fun?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has it ever been?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. I can think of instances that were fun. I don't know if I would call my entire life situation fun.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When was the last instance that you could remember?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When I go out with my friends and blow off steam, that's fun.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So these little moments here and there, but consistently not the case.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I want to switch gears again and ask you about any time in your life when you may have had suicidal thoughts or behaviors. Have you ever had a time when you contemplated suicide?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, never.

diarization.speaker: Ther therapist
diarization.text: And right now, it's not something you're thinking about?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you think has protected you against having any type of suicidal thoughts?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I want to succeed. I want to do more.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now, how about harm to others? Have you thought about harming someone else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, never.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you think protects against that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think I'm generally a nice person.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You ever get angry?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, who doesn't?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But it's never translated into anything where you had any desire to hurt anybody? So you deal with anger pretty well?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think so, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, has there ever been a time where you heard or saw something that other people did not hear or see, like a hallucination?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Other than perhaps under the influence of alcohol, was there ever a time you felt out of touch with reality?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How would you describe your judgment when making decisions when you're sober?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think it's pretty good. My anxiety plays into it a little bit, but I think generally it's good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now when you're under the influence?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not as good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any questions for me so far? I know we're almost through. I'd like to talk about your goals on two levels: your general goals in life and your specific goals for your time with me.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I want to get a job when I graduate. I want to be self-sufficient. I'd like to not be so worried all the time and just be more at ease in general. Maybe get my own apartment, live on my own.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any other life goals? Any goals surrounding family or anything like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe figure out how to communicate better with them, I guess. And for sure have my own family.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If you think of any other goals later on, feel free to just add that in. How about goals for treatment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The drinking is one, the anxiety, and maybe making sure I graduate through this last year of college.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Anything else that would be a goal for therapy?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think those are the big ones I'm really concerned about.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So if you could meet those three goals, you feel like the counseling would have been successful. What do you consider your strengths that are going to help you meet these goals and your life goals?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think I'm ready now. I think I'm dedicated to getting better and the future that I want. I'm a hard worker, and I think I'm pretty understanding.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about intelligent?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess so, I haven't really thought about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about social skills?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think I'm good at maintaining my friendships.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you think about the future a lot? How's it look to you right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes. It looks not the way I want it to look.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, we'll try to work on that. Any other questions you want to ask me before we wrap up intake?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't think so, that was a lot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We did cover a lot. As I mentioned, if you have any other questions, we can revisit this. I'm going to get you scheduled to see me in about a week and we'll get started with the counseling sessions. All right, Sam?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: All right, thank you.

video_details.title: Clinical Interview Role-Play Part 1 - Family, Social, and Mental Health History
video_details.description: This video is part one of a clinical interview role-play of a counseling client (played by an actress) who is having symptoms of anxiety and is using alcohol. In this section, the client’s family, social, and mental health history are collected.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Sam, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: All right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You doing all right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I see that this is the first time you've come in, you filled out some of the other paperwork.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, 20 of them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A lot of pages?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therist
diarization.text: How did that go?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It went, I mean I've seen that stuff before, but it wasn't too bad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Nothing surprising in there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, pretty standard.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Pretty standard, nothing distressing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not yet.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Not yet? Okay. I'm going to ask you a series of questions as part of a process called intake.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So this document that I'll be making notes on will go in your chart and it'll help guide your care for the time that you're with me.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: These questions are going to be more detailed and more emotionally oriented than a lot of those questions that you were answering on the forms you filled out before.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That was more like factual information that we need for insurance or record keeping. This is more about you and what you've been going through.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You comfortable with that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's okay. All right. If at any time you don't like one of the questions or you don't want to answer one of the questions, just let me know and we'll just skip over that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, fair enough.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So what brings you in today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I brought myself in. Things have just not been fantastic, so I figured I might as well get some help before it got worse.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, things haven't been fantastic and you're worried they're going to get worse.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Seems like it. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What would you say that your main problem is that motivated you to come in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably my anxiety. I'm just nervous about a lot of things a lot of the time and it's kind of trickling into every area of my life now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, so anxiety. You said like a nervousness that's...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, just like nervousness about going places, nervousness about doing things or school or work or graduating college, just kind of that whole stage and it's been like that for a while.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How long?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can remember as far back as like 13 or 14 maybe.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how old are you now?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So this is around 10 years you've been coping with this.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, off and on, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Off and on? So there's times when you're not anxious?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not as bad. I mean I'm still anxious, but not as extreme or I don't deal with it in the same way.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If you were to rate your anxiety on a scale of 1 to 10 with 1 being really no anxiety and 10 being the worst it's been in the last 10 years, how much anxiety do you have right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like a six.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When was the last time you were a 10?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Last weekend.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When was the last time you were a one?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Approximately?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe like a couple months ago when I was just hanging out with my friends, we went out and we were partying a little bit and it was nice, I wasn't too anxious.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: About a couple months ago?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So the anxiety is one problem. Any other problems?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't think it's a huge problem, but I have been drinking a lot, but it helps with the anxiety but it makes going out and I'm more relaxed that way. But I can be kind of a compulsive person so once I start, I keep going. So it's not all the time, it's just happening when I'm going out, but I end up drinking too much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So sometimes when you go out, you drink more than you want to?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What happens then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I make bad decisions or I get sick or the next morning I'm showing up hung over going to class, if I make class. And you know, it's fun for the time being but it's not fun afterwards.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the consequences of drinking in the longer run, you're not too fond of those, but in the short run...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it helps in the moment.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So you want the anxiety to be lessened. Do you want the drinking to be lessened?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably. Yeah, I mean I'd like to still have fun, I'm in college, but I would like to not be like blacking out or being able to stop would be nice.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that what happens now, you blackout?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Occasionally, not every time, but sometimes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sometimes?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You remember the last time you blacked out?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe a month ago.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Month ago?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. It's not all the time, though.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: At what age did you start drinking?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: 14? All right. Any other problems? So you have the anxiety and you have drinking alcohol. Any other problems?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't think so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So those are the two main things that are bothering you. Okay. So I want to ask you some questions about your history. And I'm going to try to divide this up into different areas and just kind of move from one area to the next. There'll be some overlap. So if I ask you the same question more than once, it's just kind of part of that overlap that occurs. First, I'd like to cover your family history. So can you tell me about your immediate family?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I have one sister, mom and a dad. Pretty typical. My sister is really successful. She's a doctor. Both my parents are really successful too. So basic family.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. What type of relationship do you have with your sister?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Kind of like a Merry Christmas, Happy Easter type of relationship where more like acquaintances than we are siblings.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would you describe it as distant?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'd say so. I mean we're nice, we're not like... but we're not going to be like involved in each other's lives really.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you know what caused the relationship to end up that way?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. She was always kind of the like ideal child. She went and did everything that she was supposed to do and it was easy for her. So constantly being compared to that doesn't really foster a great relationship.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Who compared you to your sister?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My dad usually. Sometimes my mom, depends on the day.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Was this a frequent occurrence, the comparison?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, for sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you feel like it had an impact on you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably. Um, you know, it wasn't like I wasn't trying, but not everything can be as easy as it is for some people. So a little acknowledgement might have been nice.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So let's move out a little further. So you talked about your mother, your father, your sister. Any other siblings?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No? How about grandparents?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They're around. Typical grandparents, not super involved, but they're there sometimes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good relationship?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I mean, you know, grandparents show up and it's always like, "Hi, how's it going?" and you see them at the next holiday type of thing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So there's not one grandparent you're particularly close to?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I do have one grandfather I talk to on a more personal level than I would my other ones, but that's gotten more distant in the past couple years.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. How about aunts, uncles, cousins?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have a couple of cousins that I would hang out with or I'll see out when I'm hanging out with my friends or whatever. So we'll hang out if we run into each other. Aunts and uncles, I do have. They're not super involved either, but everybody's cordial. Nice when they see you type of thing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So when's the last time you spoke, say for example, with one of your cousins?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think I ran into one of them like two weeks ago when we were just out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Couple weeks ago?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Do any of the relatives that you mentioned, are any of them aware of your anxiety and or your drinking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My parents are.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Nobody else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My sister knows about the anxiety part of it. And I think I'm pretty sure she knows about the drinking but she doesn't bring it up. But if my parents know, I'm sure she knows.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you believe that they told her?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But she's not mentioned that to you directly?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, we don't have those types of conversations. It's more like, "Oh, she messed up again." And it's just sort of like this funny thing and then they move on, so...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I can see this bothers you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's annoying.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Some of these topics that we're going to touch on in this intake we can talk about in greater detail later on. And maybe your relationship with your mother and father and your sister would be topics we touch on later on. Maybe not. But I want to let you know that we can come back to anything and review it. So I want to move kind of out of family history a bit and move to social relationships. Again, it's kind of similar, a little bit of overlap here. Can you tell me about any romantic interests, friends, anything like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I have a guy I've been seeing for like six months. So it's pretty serious for college. And some of my college friends I'm really close with, so they're there with me through a lot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: About how many?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: There's three girls that I'm super close with. And, you know, college like there's a lot of people I'm acquaintances with or I'll see or talked to in class or whatever. But those three girls are kind of the ones I would go to if I needed something.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. And then you have some other friends that you're not as close to?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I mean we're nice and we have fun and, you know, I'm sure if something happened they would bail me out, but they're not like people I'm going to talk to about my problems or anything like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do they know about your problems?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. I guess you could know like when I show up to class hung over, but I'm sure I'm not the only one doing that, so...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how about the... you said the guy you've seen for six months, does he know about the problems?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Somewhat, yeah. He knows about definitely knows about the anxiety. And he's with me a lot when I go out. So if something does happen, he's usually helping me out or making sure I get home or whatever.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So he's supportive?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, really supportive.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So some of the questions I'm going to ask you, this gives me a good opportunity to talk about this. I could probably guess the answer to but I still want to ask not to be presumptuous. Do you have any children?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. How about nieces or nephews?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any other social relationships that I've missed here that are important to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't think so. Those are the main ones right now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. You said you were 23. I want to ask you some questions about your medical history. Have you had any surgeries in your lifetime?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Got my appendix removed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Appendix removed?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any other serious medical conditions?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, had my wisdom teeth taken out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Wisdom teeth extraction?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you on any medications for physical problems?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. How about your activity level? Do you stay fairly active?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I try to. I go to the gym like twice a week or whatever and I go to yoga sometimes. So yeah, I try to get out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you consider yourself an active person?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I try to be in between classes and everything else, but when I do have the time, I enjoy going out and doing things.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would you generally say you're in good health then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, physically, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Physically. All right. No other illnesses, surgeries, procedures of note?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So I want to shift gears a little bit again and now talk about psychiatric history. And what I'm getting at here is kind of a history of any diagnoses, medications, other times you've been treated by a counselor or somebody like a counselor. Let's start with medications. Any medications for mental health?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, no, no.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about history of diagnoses? Ever been diagnosed with a mental health condition?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I was. I was seeing a therapist before a couple years ago and I saw him a couple of times and I think he said I had some sort of anxiety disorder or something.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you remember specifically what he said?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Something more general, so like it wasn't about any particular thing. So I saw him for a little while, but I just really wasn't on board with the whole therapy thing at that point. I didn't think it was going to help.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How old were you when you saw him?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: 15 or 16. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. And that was a counselor?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So you saw the counselor, the counselor indicated you had some type of anxiety disorder.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you feel that was a fair assessment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think so. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how long did you see the counselor?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think I went five or six times maybe.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Five or six sessions?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And why did you discontinue the treatment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, I just didn't really feel like I was really involved in it and it felt like it was more waste of my time and his. Wasn't ready, I don't know that I was super on board with the whole anxiety thing at that point. I mean, he was nice, there wasn't like an issue with him. I just don't... I wasn't there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any mention at that time about the drinking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I think I brought it up, but I didn't really see it as an issue then.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about other mental health professionals like a psychiatrist, a psychologist, a marriage family therapist?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My parents sent me to see a psychiatrist like maybe once or twice but didn't really stick with that either.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you weren't prescribed any medication?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what do you think happened there that you didn't stick with that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think kind of the same thing. I knew there obviously there was something going on, but I don't think I was ready to deal with it and I kind of felt like I had it under control at that point.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me about when you saw the psychiatrist in relation to when you saw the counselor?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was all within that same time period. I think I saw the counselor first and then maybe the psychiatrist like a week or two later and then followed up with the counselor, but I just wasn't really present during any of it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you feel you're in a different state of mind now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I realize now that I'm not handling it like I thought I was and it's affecting other areas of my life and you know, in my senior year of college I need to get my life together and I'm not really doing that so well. So I think it's time to figure something out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So you feel like you're ready to commit to treatment a little more vigorously at this point?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I want the help now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And back then...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No. Okay. No other treatment providers?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Nope, just those two.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Just those two. Okay.

video_details.title: Clinical Interview Role-Play Part 2 - Educational, Vocational, and Legal History
video_details.description: This video is part two of a clinical interview role-play of a counseling client (played by an actress) who is having symptoms of anxiety and is using alcohol. In this section, the client’s educational, vocational, and legal history are collected.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We're going to shift gears again a little bit and I want to talk about your educational history. So can you tell me about your schooling?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I went to public elementary and middle and high school. Um, got my diploma. Um, I like school and I was, you know, I was pretty good at it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good student? Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, yeah, I was okay. I mean the anxiety definitely made it tough. Um, I didn't always get the grades I wanted. And then, you know, the the drinking young kind of affected my attendance at some points. Um, but I do I do like school.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so you got through elementary school, middle school, high school and now you're in college. And how's that going?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's okay. Um, I mean I like it. I like being surrounded by people and whatever. Um, but it's just really, really stressful. The course work is tough. The professors are tough. Um, a couple of my professors have confronted me about not coming to class or showing up and being hungover. Um, and I'm, you know, they're not as lenient when you miss assignments like they are in high school. Um, where it's always like it's okay, you can do it again. That's really not applying in my program. So experience is a little different.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What did you say when they confront you about the performance problems?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I generally just say, you know, I have a lot on my plate and I'm trying to balance everything and I'm just really tired or exhausted or I'll get it done.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is performing better in school one of your goals?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. We'll keep that in mind. Um, let's I want to talk now again I'm going to switch gears a little bit to the vocational history, like the history of working. Have you worked before?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Um, well I babysat in high school that was my main thing. Um, and then I um just worked at like a department store after school, like one or two days a week. Um, and then like now that I'm in school I'm not working as much, um but I nanny sometimes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And how do you feel that you've done with employment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think okay, I like to work. Yeah. Um, yeah. I don't mind it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has the anxiety or the alcohol use had any effect in that area?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes. Yeah. Um, the anxiety is is a lot at work usually, like performance or um like the pressure of being there knowing I have a boss to answer to or if I do something wrong, um especially like with nannying working with the kids, I get worried I'm going to do something and they're going to get hurt or um you know, there's been if I it's just like all these scenarios could happen and that's stressful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever lost employment because of the anxiety or the alcohol use?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I've given up things because I've gotten uncomfortable or whatever.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's affected you in your education and in your work a bit. Does that concern you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, a lot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that another goal would be to address the employment performance? Okay. What are you in college for?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Education.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what do you want to do when you graduate?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I like kids, so maybe something like school with little kids, early type of stuff.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so I'm going to switch gears again a little bit here. Move to some other areas. Um, we've talked about the alcohol use, and that's something that you would like to work on as the focus of treatment. And then the anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you consider um in terms of the alcohol use, your goal there would be to use less or to discontinue use?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, less.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Use less. All right. And you mentioned to me earlier the age you started drinking, was it 14?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. How has the drinking progressed from when you started using at 14 to present day?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I think then it was more because I was hanging out with people that were doing it, it was kind of like a cut loose, have fun, fit in type of thing. Um, and now it's more of a like helpful, it gives me peace of mind type of thing. Um, and I would say it's probably more frequent now than it was then.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's more frequent now? Does drinking reduce the anxiety?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It does, it makes it easier to just be out and have fun and not be consumed in my mind all the time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you tried before going out and not drinking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I have.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what happens?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I usually get uncomfortable or I feel like I said something or I can't talk or I don't know, I just don't have a good time. I'm so tense and confused and I just I end up feeling worse. It wasn't an enjoyable experience.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And those times when you do drink...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It helps me relax and I get to have fun and not be like bothered with all the anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's a better experience for you. But as we discussed earlier, in the long run, that's not working out so well.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So before we get into the next section, I want to remind you again, any of the questions you don't want to answer or if you'd rather talk about it later on or not at all, just let me know that. Because I'm going to get to some areas that are a little more sensitive than some of the other areas we've discussed so far.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So in this next section I want to talk about your sexual history. Is that okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me at what age you first had consensual sex?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about non-consensual?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I've never.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Never? In terms of legal history, have you ever had any involvement with law enforcement, criminal justice system?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You have. Do you feel comfortable talking about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, um I think I was like 14 or 15, it was right around when everything started. We were out and I shoplifted something from a store. Um, so it ended up being an issue. We got caught and they called our parents and they called like the police came down and so, um and because we were drinking and we were shoplifting, so it was like underage and stealing, so it ended up like community service issue.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. And that was when you were 14? Around that time. Any other legal issues?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, that's the main one. Well, probably the only one.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Were you left with any type of criminal record? Did your legal history ever come back to interfere with employment or anything now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, not so far.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have any history of military or government service?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about your um spiritual beliefs? Do you have any spiritual beliefs?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I believe in God.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any specific religion?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I'm Catholic.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would you say you're a practicing Catholic?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I go when I need to go.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. How important is Catholicism in your life, your spirituality in your life?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would say it's there. It's not super important right now. I have other priorities, but it's there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has your belief system changed throughout your life?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. How about while I'm thinking of it, how's your family? Any spiritual beliefs in your family? Your mother, your father?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They're Catholic too.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has that been an influence on you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I don't know. Maybe a little bit. I mean, we went, you know, to services and stuff.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Is there anything in your spiritual belief system that you feel like you could draw upon as a strength during treatment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, maybe prayer.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So I want to ask you about your financial situation. Shifting gears again. Um, you mentioned you're not working right now, is that correct? How do you support yourself now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My parents help me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you live independently or with them?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I live on campus but I'm only 15 minutes from home, so I go back and forth a lot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what's a lot? Once a week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, maybe like once a week I go home for something and come back, it's so close.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you like that financial arrangement? What would be more ideal for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I don't love it, but it works for now. I'd like to be independent of them, taking care of myself. They would like that too. They've made that clear, so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And that's a goal of yours as well?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Again I want to switch gears. I want to talk about your sleeping habits. Do you feel like you get more sleep than you should, less or the correct amount?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, probably more.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: On average how many hours do you sleep at night? And what would you like to sleep?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, 10 maybe. 7 or 8.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How long has this been going on? Do you know why you sleep more than you want to?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably college years, so 3 years maybe. Um, I'm just exhausted and drained and it turns my mind off so it's a nice way to just block out everything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you ever find yourself down, like your mood down? When was the last time you felt down?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes. Not all the time, but sometimes, when the anxiety gets really bad. Um, 2 weeks ago.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how down were you? What does depressed look like?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I mean I wasn't depressed or anything, but I was kind of upset. Um, I don't know, I guess like hiding out in my room, avoiding everybody, turning my phone off, sleeping.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But you indicated you weren't depressed. So that's what you were doing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, that's what no. I was just upset. I was more like sad or frustrated about a situation and a grade and another one of my professors confronted me and that made my anxiety worse so then I was coming down on myself worse and it was just like I just wanted to block everybody and everything out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So a bit down but in your opinion not depressed. Did it change anything in terms of your drinking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I tend to drink more the more upset I am.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that what happened this last time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Okay. I'm going to shift gears again. I want to ask you about your eating habits. Do you feel like you eat in a healthy manner?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. A lot of eating on the run between classes and everything, so it's grab what's there and getting to the next thing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Busy lifestyle? Do you feel like your appetite is stronger or weaker than it should be or about where it should be?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Typical college student. I think it's pretty normal.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has there ever been a time when it has not been normal?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I don't think so.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play - Fear of Driving Over Bridges
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which cognitive-behavioral therapy techniques, including evaluating evidence and reframing, are used to treat fear and anxiety related driving over bridges.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Elisa, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm doing well, thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Doing well? What's going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have family coming into town and I have to go to the airport to pick them up.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you have family flying in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, and that's something I get very anxious about because I have to cross two bridges each way, the Ben Franklin and the Girard Point bridge.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you have to cross four times. What kind of feeling is this bringing up for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I get very anxious even just thinking about it right now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If we use a scale of 1 to 10, where would you be right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right now, probably an 8. On the day I have to do it, it reaches a 10.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So even a week out, this is an 8. Do you normally have to cross bridges for work or local travel?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I've planned my life so everything is within the vicinity and I don't have to cross any bridges.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But for the family, you will be crossing. Let's move forward a week. What are you thinking 15 minutes before you leave for the airport?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm thinking I have to do this for my parents because they are elderly and need me. A taxi is too expensive and I want to make sure they are safe.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Your reasons are positive. Where does the anxiety come in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The thought of the bridge. I'm afraid I'll drive off or fall off. I stay in the middle lane and go slow. I even keep a hard tool in the car to break the glass if I fall into the water.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about when you start driving toward the bridge?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I say a prayer. My anxiety gets higher as I get to the toll point, because I know there's no turning back.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When you can still exit, what's your anxiety level?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's probably a 9. Once I cross through the toll, it's at a 10.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Your fear is that your car will go off the bridge. When does that anxiety start to go away?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: As soon as I'm getting off the bridge. But then I know another one is coming up, so it starts all over again.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Once I'm descending the second bridge, the anxiety is almost gone, but then I start thinking about the way back.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you aware of any time a car has actually gone off one of these bridges?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've heard things on the news or in movies, so I think it's possible. I've even tried to measure the distance between the metal poles to see if a car could fit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you've concluded it's unlikely, but possible. How do you feel once you get home with your parents?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't even recall the anxiety then. I'm back down to a 1.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You do this for your parents' safety. How important is that to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Very important. It's worth the anxiety, but I wish there was a route without any bridges.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How long have you had this anxiety?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It developed as I got older and had more responsibilities like marriage and kids. I didn't have it when I was younger.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'd like to try reframing. You can challenge the automatic thought of falling off by remembering it's very unlikely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The reframing is that you are the hero of this situation because you are willing to suffer through this fear to make sure your family is safe.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I never thought of it like that. It makes me feel like the hero of the family.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Apply that reframing when you're feeling anxious. You're voluntarily being brave for the good of your family.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever had any close calls on a bridge?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Once during a storm I had to stop and call for help. Eventually I calmed down and was able to cross on my own.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You've always managed to overcome it. Try to remember that and be assertive next time. I'll see you in two weeks.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play - Anxiety Related to Being Away from Home
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which cognitive-behavioral therapy techniques, including evaluating evidence, using self-talk, and identifying automatic thoughts, are used to treat anxiety related to being away from home.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hey Anna, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Doing well?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess so. Yeah. I've been working still on the fear of leaving the home for extended periods of time, like vacation, and it's been a little harder recently because I have this planned trip with a friend of mine coming up in a few months, and that's kind of been weighing on my mind.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And where's the trip to?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Georgia.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how long will you be there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: She wants to go like 6 days, but yeah, I'm not sure with work and school and everything I can make the full 6 days, and plus I'm a little nervous to go that long, so...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's a long time for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient

video_details.title: Interpersonal Psychotherapy: A Case of Postpartum Depression Video
video_details.description:
For the full video go to: http://www.psychotherapy.net/video/interpersonal-psychotherapy

What, exactly, is Interpersonal Psychotherapy (IPT), and how is it applied across populations? Watch Scott Stuart, MD, present the core elements of this evidence-based method in a course of therapy with a woman dealing with postpartum depression.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, it's just been a difficult week, frustrating week. Okay, so Emily, my friend Emily, we had thought that it would be fun to just have an afternoon together. We were going to hang out on Wednesday, and we wanted to go to the farmers market and just bum around a little bit, maybe get some coffee and that kind of thing without our kids. And so, I mean, I asked Todd, you know, 'Would it be okay if you watched the girls?' and he said, 'Well, I can't watch both of them.' And I was like, 'Oh really? You can't? I watch both of them all the time,' but for some reason for him it's impossible.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In the segment you just saw, there was a wonderful example of interpersonal communication between the patient and her husband. One of the techniques that's been extremely helpful in IPT has been interpersonal incidents, and what those are basically are a description of a communication, specifically not a global communication, but a specific communication between the patient and somebody else close to them, in this case, the patient and her husband. So an interpersonal incident, in contrast to a general statement—in other words, a statement like, 'My husband and I never get along, we always fight'—is a specific description of an interaction that occurred. And the idea in using an interpersonal incident is to try and find out what's going wrong in the communication. What's not working well? What is the patient saying that may not be quite as adaptive? How is the other person responding to that in a way that's shutting down communication or causing more conflict? How does the patient respond to that? It literally is a description, statement by statement, about how the interaction goes from start to finish, and getting the finishing part is particularly important.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play - Anxiety and Counting Ritual
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which cognitive-behavioral therapy techniques, including evaluating evidence, self-talk, and behavioral experiments, are used to treat anxiety and an obsessive-compulsive counting ritual related to shopping.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Emma, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm doing good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Doing good? What's been going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh, been a little anxious, um, about a shopping habit that I have.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Yeah. Tell me about that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I have to buy everything in pairs or in twos. And if I only have one thing, I won't buy it. I'll put it back or I'll look around the store for another thing so that I have two things to buy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So when you go into a store, if you just have one thing you want to buy, one item you went there for, you'll buy a second item or even more? Or just second?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes it can be more, as long as it's reached the minimum of two.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So you have to leave having purchased a minimum of two. Or if you can't find something else, you won't buy it at all. So zero would also be acceptable.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Zero would be acceptable, yeah. No, no, no, no. I can't do just one.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can't do one. Okay.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, it's gotta be two or more.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what happens, has there ever been an occasion where you've only purchased one thing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can't really remember one. I'm sure there has been, but I can't really remember one.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, and how long has this been going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A number of years. A long time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Long time. Okay. So for all this period of time, you have successfully either purchased nothing or two or more items.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, yeah. I have to. It's very anxiety-producing if I don't.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How anxiety-producing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, it, I just feel like something bad will happen if I don't keep it to two or more.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you know what would happen? Like, do you have a specific...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, for example, like my family would be in a car accident or I would hit a deer or, you know, get fired from my job or, you know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so something really, really bad would happen. So this is hurtful for you. This is causing you pain. And this would happen, this would really happen on any shopping trip where you just want one thing. You'd be reminded. So if you went in wanting more than one thing, it's not a problem, right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. It's if I only really need one thing and then I can't just buy that one thing that I need.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So how often does this happen where you are in a situation where you want to make a purchase of just one item and you have to change because of the anxiety?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Daily. Yeah, because I mean, if I go grocery shopping or if I go clothes shopping or if any kind of money transactional thing, you know, which I would encounter daily pretty much, it happens.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about like filling up your car at gasoline?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, then I'll buy a pack of gum.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it has an effect at that level too. So you're thinking of it almost like the number of transactions has to be more than one? I mean, has to be two or zero?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess so, yeah. Number of items or number of transactions. Yeah, because see, if I get gas, then I have the gas is in my car, that's a thing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's one transaction.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: And one thing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so that's one product. And you need another product. So you really can't fuel your car without going inside the station store. Okay. So it doesn't matter that there's more than one gallon going in? Just because it's the same product.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Exactly. Exactly. Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I could see now this, this would be more of a daily thing like you said, right? Because it applies to all transactions. So this is a fairly significant source of anxiety for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, it is. It does, I get, you know, it like builds up in me and I feel it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So let's talk about that and help me to understand this better. So let's say that you went to a convenience store and you just had one thing in mind. What might be a potential item that you would buy?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Gum.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Gum. All right. So you want to go in and you just want to buy a pack of gum. That's all you really want. That's why you stop at the store. So you go in. Do you have any thoughts, we've talked in the past about automatic thoughts? These thoughts that just kind of come in. So are there any thoughts that are happening when you're walking into the store?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I start, I start with what do I need, why am I here, you know, I need the pack of gum. And then it's instant anxiety that what else am I going to get? What else can I get to make it the two?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So the thought is, 'What else can I get?' That's one of the first thoughts.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it has to be two, has to be two.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It has to be two. That's another thought. So that thought's a little more demanding. So it has to be...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I guess the first thought is 'What else, what else do I have to get?' Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And then you said jumps right to the anxiety. So is the anxiety relieved if you can decide on a second item and you select it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it starts going down.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So it's relieved gradually. But it is relieved. And when's it completely gone?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When I'm done that, when I've left the store, I'm done the transaction, I've left the store.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So really the worst anxiety would be approaching the store, entering and that moment of uncertainty when you don't know the second thing that you're going to buy. All right. So that's really the target area.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, it is.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So if you could relieve that anxiety, that would be one of your goals. All right. So let's think about it this way. Do you know the reason that you do this? Do you have any guesses?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would guess that, I mean, we've talked about some bad experiences I had... they they were difficult, so I wonder if that's not somehow linked to this behavior somehow, possibly.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So you've been through some really tough times, to put it mildly. And what you're afraid of if you only buy the one item is something safety related happening.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, yes, like the car accident or the... safety, definitely, my personal safety or my family's safety. And I guess security, like the job security.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: And security, yeah. And yes, security.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So safety and security, they're at risk for you when you don't follow this rule. So if we think about it in terms of the cognitive model, we talk about the core beliefs and the intermediate beliefs. So the core belief here, do you have any thoughts on what it might be?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, now that you pointed out the safety-security issue, I didn't really realize that, but it is. Um, maybe that just that I'm not okay, I'm not safe.

diarization.speaker: Therist
diarization.text: I'm not okay, I'm not safe, I am vulnerable. Exposed to danger, so you're at risk.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So with that core belief, we move down to kind of like the assumptions, in this case the rule. All right. So the rule is, 'I can stay safe if I transact involving only two or more products.' All right. So that's your rule.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's my rule.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And then when a situation presents itself, which would be an impending transaction, when they come together, what's that automatic thought?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: What else am I going to get?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So that's your automatic thought. And then what's the behavior that's a product of that automatic thought? You buy the second item. And the feeling, what's the feeling that follows that, that follows that purchase of two?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, that follows the automatic thought... oh, anxiety. And then what's the feeling that follows the purchase? Relief.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Relief. All right. Yeah. So can you see how the mechanism, what's happening to you could be explained through the cognitive model?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Very much. It fits it very well, I think, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So let's talk about the rule of two. Do you think that sitting here now, do you see a causal connection between purchasing two items and a safety or security breach or something bad happening?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. I mean, there's no, I recognize through our work and stuff that it's not, it doesn't make sense. It's not a useful thought, maybe.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's not a useful thought, maybe not a useful intermediate belief. So you recognize that, you appreciate that there's not a link between the purchasing behavior and safety in either direction, though, right? Meaning you realize that if you buy two, that doesn't necessarily keep you safe either. So you can't introduce safety or risk of being unsafe through your transacting behavior.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: True. That's very true. I... yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it does. It really does. I can't... what you're saying makes sense, but it doesn't make sense to introduce safety or either side of the coin.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. Safety or risk, they're not influenced by your behavior. But that's not what your mind is telling you. Right. That's not what your thoughts are telling you. Right. That's logical and you can sit here with me and you can say, 'Yeah, I don't see a link.'

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I, I don't see a link, but I know what I feel. And what I feel is that impending doom, if you will.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So let's talk about that moment. So in this moment, maybe a little anxious now, but you can kind of see how you can't protect yourself or cause harm to yourself or anyone else by buying two or failing to buy two. In the store or wherever you're making the transaction, different story. So let's go a different direction. I want you to kind of stay with me as I go through another scenario. Let's say that you forgot your credit card or cash or whatever, and you only have enough money for the gum and you want the gum. It's really important to you. So it's not something you want to turn into a zero.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I need it in your scenario, okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So you go into the store, you realize you only have enough resources to make the one transaction. So now walk me through the thoughts and the feelings.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: What I would normally do or what I...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No, what do you think would happen?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I, I would panic. I mean not panic like, you know, break down or something, but I mean it would be very, very stressful. Um, if I absolutely had to get that item. Um, I would probably try to scrape change out of my car, but I know we're not going there. Okay, I know, stay with the scenario. But um, it would be very, very difficult for me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Could you do it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm physically capable of doing it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
