diarization.text: Okay. And that is one level of being able, but how about in terms of your thinking and your feeling?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I, I could do it. I could do it. I could get through it somehow.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what would happen? How much anxiety would you experience and would the anxiety fade off?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It, it would fade off, I think. I mean it would have to, I would imagine, so. It would fade. I think it would take a longer period of time to fade um, than if I had just gotten another item, 'Okay, the world is going to be safe for another five minutes, we're good.'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me what you're feeling right now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Very anxious. Very anxious. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you worried, is it the kind of anxiety where you're worried that something catastrophic's going to happen?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mm-hmm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So even talking about a transaction of one can lead to anxiety connected to this safety and security thing. So you can trigger that without a transaction even pending.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. Yeah. Huh. Yeah. Sitting here. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's really scary for you. Is it bearable, the anxiety you have now, is it bearable?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, it's bearable. It's bearable. But it hurts, though.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. It doesn't feel good. What do you feel is going to happen? What's the anxiety about?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Your scenario of having to, having to get only one item or having, only having the resources for one item and...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so it's not a safety and security, it's a concern about following through and buying one item.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: On the rule. The rule is two. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And I'm talking about breaking the rule. Yeah. It's scary for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Because, so you're anxious about that and you're also anxious about the consequence of that. You are. Yes. Yes. And that's the safety and security. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So the anxiety you're experiencing right now in this moment with me, right? Be mindful of that. Keep that in your awareness. So is there something on your mind that you need to buy within the next couple days?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. Coffee.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Coffee. Hmm. And that's a transaction of one.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, so I'll get something else.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You'll get something else. Okay. Understandable. But what if I challenged you to a behavioral experiment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you guess what that might be?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: To buy one coffee? This scenario, too. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, to buy one, to buy one cup of coffee and then leave. So what are the possible things that could happen? Knowing that logically you can't connect it to a safety thing. Now you might be anxious about that and that's real, that anxiety is real, but knowing that the event isn't prevented or caused by the transacting behavior.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Exactly.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's go through what happens. So you buy the coffee, you're really anxious, right? But let's say you follow through and buy the cup of coffee and you leave. Nothing, it doesn't change the safety and security aspect. What is different about that than if you bought two items?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would have a lot more anxiety, but I would really have to talk myself through that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would it go away?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I, I believe it would. The anxiety? I believe it would.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it'd be a more painful experience to buy the one. But it wouldn't actually harm you in terms of the safety and security. But it would cause you more internal anxiety. Exactly. So what would happen if you did it again?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would hope that it would be less anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Could be. What if you did it a hundred times?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It could, I would get old, I think, the anxiety would get old.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Anxiety would get old. So really what you're doing is you're conditioning, you'd be conditioning yourself, right, to surviving just buying the one item.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd have a lot more money.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It would be some financial advantages to it certainly, yeah. And there'd be a freedom advantage too, which is the freedom to buy any number of items.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, that would be nice.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what, what scenario of purchasing could you see yourself being most likely to follow through with this? I guess would there be another item that would be easier to actually follow through, like for example the gasoline because you'd be at your car, you'd buy the gasoline and you'd leave.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that would be easier. I wouldn't be tempted by the other... I wouldn't have to walk through the cold to the store.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would that be, do you think that'd be easier to actually be successful?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think that would be much easier. Okay. Yeah. Because the other thing about the gas is that even though it's physically with me, the product is in my gas tank, I'm not holding it. I think that that could be, make it easier to follow through, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So we would consider that kind of a step in a direction that would result in fewer symptoms. And maybe another step in the future would be to go into the store and buy one, but let's not, let's not do that. Okay. Let's stick with the gasoline.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. I, I feel more confident about that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You feel like you could succeed with that experiment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We'll see when I actually get there, but yes. I would like, I feel like I could actually try that more so than the coffee, so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you afraid with the coffee that you might just end up buying two things? All right. So let's go with the fuel in your car. So the next time that your car needs fuel, go in, buy the fuel, drive away.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. And they have the pay at the pump, so I don't even have to go into the store, so that would be great, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So how's your anxiety now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel better that I don't have to just buy one cup of coffee. But I feel um, it's, it's mild. But, but okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Better than it was a few minutes ago. Yeah. Yeah. But mostly because the experiment that we're talking about is a little easier. All right. And because I think like the insight that you gave me on I hadn't connected all the dots, so that was very helpful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so as you're trying to kind of push through this experience of just fueling the car, you're going to have those thoughts still come up. And the adaptive response could be something like 'I know this won't actually have a consequence in the real world.' Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, absolutely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there's a few things I'm asking you to do, right? One is to just buy gasoline when you need it and only buy gasoline. And at the same time when those thoughts come up to respond to them with the adaptive responses.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: To kind of pair the two. Yeah, I got you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Pair them together. 'I know this won't have a real consequence in reality,' that could be one. 'I know that I can tolerate the anxiety.' And maybe another adaptive response would be 'This is painful for me, but if I can be successful here, maybe I can get rid of the anxiety someday.' Keeping your eye on moving up to coffee and other behavioral goals. Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I like that a lot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So we're kind of attacking the anxiety from a lot of different angles here. And my hope is that the more we can replicate the behavior of just buying one item, the more your anxiety will decrease. So do you, do you believe that you could succeed with this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I do. I do. It's been a long time, but I think it'll be a challenge but I think, you know, it's time. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well that can be very positive. What I detected there was courage. You're ready to say I've had enough and you're ready to take the anxiety on. That can be a positive adaptive response, like being assertive and saying almost like you're talking to the anxiety in a way, but I'm, I'm not going to let you beat me this time. That's what you'd be saying to the anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I like that. I like that one. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So make a note of all these and you can use the same one more than once. But keep applying them as needed through the whole process until you're home. You've permanently recorded just buying the one thing. So that's a victory.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That'd be a huge victory.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So do you foresee needing to get gas between now and next week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, yeah. I will. I will need to do that, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So if you could try that out and if you could record kind of in the moment, the experience in terms of your feelings at different stages, that would be helpful. Write them down right in the moment, that'll be the most accurate record. And that also I think is therapeutic in a way, you're documenting the experience and bring that in.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. I can do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So try that out and make an appointment and I'll see you next week and we'll go over the different stages and everything and see how we did. Thanks Emma.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. All right. Thank you.

video_details.title: CBT Role Play - The Premack Principle
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which the Premack principle is applied during a cognitive-behavioral therapy role-play to treat low motivation to complete assignments. The Premack principle states that a high probability behavior can be used to increase participation in a low probability behavior.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Lisa, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm good, but um there has been issues. You know how we've been working on like my motivation?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sure.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it's kind of related to that. Um, so I'm in school and every few weeks we have like papers to write. And I know I know it, I know I can do it, it's just actually sitting down and doing it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, well tell me about the papers.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, they're usually about five pages long. And I just I just look at it and I'm like it's five pages, but I'm like okay, so I go sit down, you know at my computer, I'm like alright I'm going to start on references. So I get I start off good, I do the references, but then it's like I get sidetracked so easily and then I end up killing like two hours checking the news, checking and then it goes to my phone and then just looking up recipes, I mean it gets really off topic and then I realize I haven't done anything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so you have the five page paper, you sit down to work on it, you have the references, you get that part taken care of, but then it sounds like you kind of wander off a little bit.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh big time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, okay. And then what happens after you're done wandering a little bit?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well I get kind of annoyed with it and then I'm like well you know I've already you know it's already night time, I'll try to do it tomorrow, and then either tomorrow doesn't happen or the same thing happens. And it's just and then I end up you know rushing right at the end, of you know it's due tomorrow and I'm getting all these five pages done and it's really hard for me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you are finishing the assignment on time, so the problem isn't lateness.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I mean I get it done. It's just all at the last minute.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's really the how the time breaks out isn't working out well for you. You'd rather not be doing it at the last moment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I mean I I try not to. I mean I set time aside to go sit down, I'm like alright, you know we're going to start on this paper, then sidetracked, I'm watching TV, I'm on my phone, I'm on some other website.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So these so these activities that you're engaging in between when you start the work and before you start writing, so you've gathered the references before you start writing, you said checking email and other kind of it sounds like unplanned small activities.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean there's small things that keep my attention, but it's not where my attention needs to go.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: These aren't particularly engaging activities, like something you need to do at that moment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I mean I look up you know right I start on one reference and then ooh this article looks cool, ooh this article, you know next thing I know I'm researching octopuses or something.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So like distracted.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, distracted's a good word.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And then there's a moment you kind of catch yourself and realize you haven't really started writing.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, but it's like two hours later.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's too late, yeah, so you're consuming time in there. All right, so you have a few different levels of activity here, you have the paper which it sounds like you're okay writing but you're maybe not highly motivated to write, but you seem to be getting the references done okay.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean I get the references done okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You collect the material and then the writing part, that's the part...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's the difficult part.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And then you have these behaviors in the middle which you enjoy doing a little but they're not something that...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean they're not something that like you know I'm jumping for joy about, it's just something to procrastinate so I don't have to do my paper. And I don't think that, you know I'm not like oh I need to check my email so I don't have to do my paper, it's just oh I should check my email, oh I should check my phone, oh I haven't done this in a while, oh I haven't seen this in a while.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But these behaviors still fulfill a purpose, they do delay the writing of the paper.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's true.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, you may not be fully aware of that in the moment, but then you kind of become aware of that later, that that's the purpose of those behaviors accomplished, was that they kept you distracted from the writing. All right. So the writing of the paper is an activity that's something you're not really looking forward to. What's a behavior that what's an activity that you really do look forward to?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, there is this new TV show out that they just started a new season and I have it all recorded, like 24 episodes, but I can't find time to watch it but I'm really, you know I've seen the first season I'm so interested in it. And now I can't wait to see the next one. You know I guess that that would that's I guess what makes me really happy right now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So so you're excited about this television show and you have the episodes already recorded. And maybe one of the reasons you can't find the time is because the time you're using between the two parts of writing this paper.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean this paper's taking me a lot longer than it should.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so let's try this. When you do write the paper, you're really writing the writing part, not the preparing part, but the writing part kind of all at the end, right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're getting it done but it's the night before it's due. All right. So I want to try a couple different behavioral strategies here. One is I think that it might be helpful to break the five page paper up into more than one night because right now functionally you're doing a lot on the last night. What would be a more comfortable pace? Like for example how long does it take you to write one page?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: About an hour, hour and a half.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so around an hour to an hour and a half you can complete one page, edited, proofread. Okay, so it would take about five days for you to complete the whole paper. And how much time do you have from when the paper's assigned to when it's due?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh they give us about a week and a half to do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay so around ten days.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So if you could maintain the pace of an hour to an hour and a half a day, you would be done in plenty of time. Is there a good time to start writing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um I guess around six o'clock. Like uh because then I'm I'm already done eating, I'm home from work and I've kind of de-stressed already. So six o'clock's like a pretty good time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so if you could work without distraction you would be done by around 7:30 at the latest with the one page.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, with the one page.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so no distractions and just one page.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So let's talk about the the episodes, the TV episodes that you want to watch. How long are they?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They're an hour.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: They're an hour, okay. And what's a time that you could watch those that you'd get the maximum enjoyment out of watching them?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess around eight o'clock, because that's when I'm starting to get ready for bed, I'm starting to like really relax. And um you know my husband's home by that time and we watch it together, he loves the show too.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So eight o'clock's a really good time for you to maximize what you'll get out of the show, the enjoyment you'll get out of the show.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So what I want to do is try to pair these behaviors together. The behavior of writing, which is not something that you're necessarily thrilled about all the time, and the behavior of watching the show, which you are very interested in. I want to try to use it as a motivator, kind of like a reward. So what I'd like you to try to do is pick five nights that you want to work on it, clearly within the ten day window. Set that time of six o'clock is when you're going to start. When that period of distraction might encroach, focus on, I really want to watch that show at eight o'clock.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So just keep thinking about that when I feel like I'm getting off track?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, that's your reward, that's your motivation. You're going to be using what you do enjoy a lot to help push you through that. In the process, I hope that the writing becomes more enjoyable, but whether it does or it doesn't you still want to be able to complete it and not have to stress right at the end. Right, that's really eating more time than your show takes.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Really it is. I mean I could I mean you're right I could watch that show with the amount of time I waste just doing other things.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the key here is to try to keep it structured. Like if that plan that I've laid out works for you, does that make sense for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It does. That does.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, because we can modify it if it doesn't. Try that now and we can always change it up if we need to. But I think that does make sense and it divides it into manageable periods of time. But the key is here, to start on time at six o'clock, and to intend to and try to start the show on time at eight o'clock. Try to keep that structure.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No I see where you're getting at. Yeah, absolutely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does this make sense to you? Do you understand?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, you know that will help me power through and not do things unrelated by thinking, well if I get this page done I get to watch my show later.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And I think that's a helpful way of thinking about it. That's the cognitive piece, when you find yourself wandering, you have to detect that and say, oh I want to watch my show, I'm really looking forward to it. And that's your motivation to keep moving through the paper and then you know when eight o'clock comes...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I get to watch my show.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You get to watch your show. All right, that sounds like a plan. All right, very good, so let's try that. I'll see you again in roughly two weeks. Do you have a paper assigned between now and then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I actually do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You do? So let's try it with this next paper. The one that will be assigned before I see you again. And let's try the five day and we'll evaluate how it goes and make any changes if we need to.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: All right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sound good?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. I'll see you in a few weeks.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: All right, thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, thank you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thanks.

video_details.title: Counseling Assessment Vignette - Client with Features of Social Anxiety Disorder
video_details.description: This counseling assessment vignette demonstrates an interview with a client (played by an actress) who exhibits features of social anxiety disorder.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, Nicole. How are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm doing well. How are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. What brings you into our agency today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I've really just been feeling kind of anxious every time I go to work.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Feeling anxious every time you go to work? What type of place do you work?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I work at an insurance company, sort of an admin assistant.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Work for an insurance company, and how long have you been feeling anxious there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I started a little over a year ago, and I guess you could say ever since I started there I've been feeling kind of anxious. It's my first time in that type of setting and it just never really went away.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever had anxiety like that at a previous employer or any other place?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I would say when I've started new jobs or even in new academic environments, I would feel somewhat anxious.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So this is a somewhat familiar anxiety. Alright, tell me about the anxiety then.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it starts, you know, when I wake up in the morning and get ready to go to work. Even when I'm driving in, I just start to get anxious. And then once I'm there, I really just go to work and I do what I'm supposed to do, but I try to keep to myself. You know, I don't really enjoy interacting with some of my coworkers.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is it that happens when you try to interact with them?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I just haven't really connected with any of them and I tend to worry about whether I'm doing my job right or if they like me, things like that. So it's just easier to stick to my own office.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you have an office and they have separate offices and you find yourself maybe isolating a little bit?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess you could say that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so what is your experience of the anxiety when you more or less have to interact with other people?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You mean how I'm feeling or what type of situations it happens in?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, let's cover both. Let's start with what type of situations trigger it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Whenever I'm in a big crowd or with a bunch of coworkers, like meetings, I tend to get nervous and wonder if I'm saying the right thing. And then when I start to feel nervous, I get some stomach pains, I would prefer to stop the meeting, and then I get a little red and blush as well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you ever have a desire to leave? Like if you're in a group, just to kind of exit the area?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh yeah, all the time. I try not to because I don't want to do a bad job or perform poorly, but sometimes the anxiety just takes over and I would prefer to go back to my office and be by myself.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how distressing is this for you? How disruptive is it to your functioning?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel anxious every day and I've really just been thinking about leaving my job and finding something else where I could potentially be more secluded and not have to go to meetings or make presentations.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So meetings and presentations in particular trigger the anxiety?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would say so. Anything where more than a few people are looking at me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me a little bit more about the physical symptoms? You mentioned your stomach hurt; any other symptoms you feel physically?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes my palms get sweaty, my face gets red or I'll get overheated, but mostly it's just some stomach pains throughout the day thinking about what I have to do that makes me anxious.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When these anxiety episodes are more intense, are you worried about it happening again?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm not always worried about it happening again. I mean, sometimes I can anticipate it and I would like to avoid it, but it's not every time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me about the meetings. How many people are in a typical meeting?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's a pretty small company, but I would say probably anywhere between 5 and 10. Most of them are in positions above me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, and how often are these meetings scheduled?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: About once or twice a week regularly, and then sometimes more if something needs to be addressed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so some are unplanned?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm, and then some happen weekly.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So for the ones that are planned, you get anxious in advance of them?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh yeah, I mean, I think about it as soon as I know it's coming. I'm always thinking about the next meeting I'll have to present at or how I'll have to contribute, and it's a cycle.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the meetings trigger it generally. But there's other times where you're not anxious, like when you're isolated in the office. How about at home?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really, when I'm by myself I don't really feel anxious.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so really it's when you get up for work and start thinking about the work day, especially if there are meetings.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. If I have off work for a couple of days I don't feel anxious at all. It's really just when I'm going to work, when I know I'm going to have to talk to a lot of people or make presentations.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You suffer the anxiety in advance of these planned meetings. How about the unplanned meetings?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The unplanned meetings I don't really have a lot of time to think about them happening, but even when I'm put on the spot, I would still say I get pretty anxious.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so both really cause anxiety that's really troubling you and you're suffering with.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. Nicole, I'm going to schedule you to see a counselor here. It'll probably be later this week. Would that be okay with you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yep, that'll work.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'll take you out to the front, we'll get you scheduled and get you treated later on this week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, great.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What you told me has been very helpful. I want to thank you for coming in.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

video_details.title: Counseling Assessment Vignette - Client with Features of Narcissistic Personality Disorder
video_details.description: This counseling assessment vignette demonstrates an interview with a client (played by an actress) who exhibits features of narcissistic personality disorder.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Sam, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm good. How are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. So you're here at the agency today to seek counseling services?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, my boss sent me over, so I figured I'd come.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Your boss sent you over? What reason do you think your boss had for doing that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: There was this issue with a couple other people I'm on a team with. They couldn't relate to my ideas and my boss saw it as not working super well, so she wanted me to come over and talk about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: She wanted you to come over and talk about your relationship with your coworkers?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think more just so that my ideas were just kind of higher than what they could really understand, so maybe learn how to talk to other people so that they can understand me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, and what do you mean by higher? Like your ideas are higher?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just a little bit more intelligent. I'm just at a level that other people can't always reach to. They just couldn't understand my language or see the vision that I had.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so they were unable to reach your level of expression for a project you're working on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, and my boss recognized this difference and thought that counseling might be helpful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you think counseling will be helpful?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think it's good so that my boss is happy, but it could also be useful. Other people are just jealous of me a lot and they just can't really relate to me, so it might be great to learn how to understand what they're going through at their level.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Again you say at their level. Are you meaning that they're below you with skills?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, they just haven't accomplished as much, they don't know as many people, they haven't been educated to the quality that I have been. So sometimes it's hard for them to understand where I'm coming from.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so counseling can help you bridge that gap to be able to communicate more effectively?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, so I can be even better. I'm here but I want to be like here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so tell me where you are currently in terms of how you perceive yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe like a seven, but I want to blow it out of the park. If ten is here, I want to be higher than that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How do you plan on accomplishing that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I'm always getting recruited for prestigious classes and speaking engagements. I have a really large social media presence so people are constantly asking me for advice. I've accomplished so much and I can really help people because I'm good at so many things.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it sounds like you have a lot of strengths and maybe people are just getting jealous because you seem to succeed at so many things?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's hard to admit that you're just not as good. I think I make them uncomfortable because I can do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How would they describe you given this level difference that you're talking about? What would they say?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think they would say that I have a lot of people that look up to me, that I'm excellent at my job, and that I should really have a more significant position. It would be clear for everyone if I just did all the presentations.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It would be easier?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It would be easier, better, it would just be a great presentation if I did it. It would just cut away all the grunt work type stuff if I just did it myself.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does it frustrate you that you're not called on for every task or recognized?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes, but I've gotten really good at reminding people that they should be calling on me for every task. I've been able to secure a lot of positions because they realize I'm better at it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So they can see your talent and recognize you most of the time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, definitely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How long have you been with this particular employer?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe like six or eight months.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me about the job you had prior? What happened there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I outgrew them. I had a large leadership position and the other VP couldn't really relate to me or see where I was going. So I made a more strategic move to this company where I could reach more.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you wanted to shoot higher and accomplish something greater?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I want to be remembered, legendary. I want my name to be out there. More so than most people my age.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You really want to take it further?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, people really rely on what I have to say on my social media platforms. The more people that are following me, the more people that are with me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me how the interaction went when you left your last job? Did you quit or did they encourage you to leave?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I quit. I initiated it. They had some issues, but I was the one that initiated it because I needed to go elsewhere.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What type of issues did they have?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They said I talk too much or something like that, but it was really that we just weren't communicating well. Afterwards they were calling me and trying to get me back.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So after you quit they pursued you to come work for them again?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, which I told them was gonna happen because I'm the reason this company is flourishing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what did you tell them when they offered you the job back?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That I had gotten a phenomenal job that was way better and that they could just deal with it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. So you feel as though you could benefit from the counseling here to better relate to people at different ability levels?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, and I want to make my boss happy. I don't want to make people feel bad because they're inferior to me or not as successful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is your boss putting any pressure on you, like is this mandatory?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think it's strongly encouraged, but she has a promotion for me in mind, so it's probably just to set me up for that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So she's trying to help you for another advancement. I'm gonna get you on the calendar to see a counselor later this week. Does that work for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh, yeah, okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. I really appreciate you taking the time with me. We'll get you set up for that and we'll go from there.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you.

video_details.title: Basic Counseling Skills: Kim Lampson, PhD
video_details.description: Demonstration of effective & disastrous counseling skills. Great for classroom instruction. Developed by doctoral students and faculty at Northwest University in Kirkland, WA. Based on Ivey & Ivey text.

video_details.title: Counseling Assessment Vignette - Client with Features of Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder
video_details.description: This counseling assessment vignette demonstrates an interview with a client (played by an actress) who exhibits features of obsessive-compulsive personality disorder.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Alice, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm doing okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I understand you're here to receive counseling services.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My boss sent me here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Your boss sent you here? What's going on with you and your boss?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's not even between me and my boss. I'm a good worker at my job. I get everything done on time, but they're calling me inflexible and a perfectionist.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So who's calling you inflexible and a perfectionist?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, my boss has called me that. I've had several coworkers. There was a recent incident where somebody wanted to change days with me, but I told them the schedule's out. I'm supposed to be here on Wednesday. You can't change it. It's right there, black and white. I work Wednesday. You can't change that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And they felt that it would have been more reasonable to change?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, they wanted to change and I really don't agree with that. If they needed a certain day off, they need to go through the order of command and ask for a day off.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And they didn't do that, instead they asked you to switch days?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: And then they called me inflexible because I got upset about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In what way did you get upset?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I told them, I said that's irresponsible, that they didn't think ahead, that they wanted to change with me. I am there at a certain time. I am there from 8:00 in the morning until 5:00 in the afternoon. I take my lunch at 12:00. That is my Wednesday. That's always been my Wednesday. I don't know why they want to upset that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so that upset you and that upset them, that whole incident. Anything else that your boss may have as a reason for...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They call me a perfectionist because I like things done by the book, which I think makes me a great worker because I get everything done on deadlines. Not before, not after, right on the deadline. Everything is just exactly filed and organized. Some people like to take a file to fill out a report, but I say no, it's in the file. You can't touch it. You can't move it. That's where it needs to be.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you consider yourself a fairly well-organized employee.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, absolutely. Absolutely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you mentioned you're there from 8:00 to 5:00 and take lunch from 12:00 to 12:30?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How many days in the last, say, three months have you been late or left early?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Zero. No, I'm there 8:00 to 5:00. I wake up at 6:00, get ready, leave for work at 7:00, and get there at 8:00. The whole day has a schedule and I meet that schedule. It's the best thing for me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so this is frustrating for you that your coworkers can't understand where you're coming from.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just don't get it. I'm doing everything by the book and by the rules, and I'm in trouble somehow? Something's wrong with me because I do it right? I do it the right way and that's wrong somehow. I don't get it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever had to work in a group or a team with any of your coworkers?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They've made me, but I don't like it because I know the way we need to do things. If we're given a project, it starts with A, B, C, D, but everyone wants to jump around. No deviation from that. And then they get mad at me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So working in groups hasn't worked out too well for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really, not unless people listen to me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So in instances where people listen to you, how have things worked out?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: If I oversee everything, I still get uncomfortable because they're out of my sight. I don't know what they're doing. If it's not done right, it's not done right, and that's bad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me anything about your mood in general? In terms of, have you felt sad or anxious recently?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I feel anxious sometimes when things aren't going the way they need to go because then it throws off the whole day. If I have to adjust my schedule even by a minute, that causes me anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Even by a minute?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Even by a minute.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So if your day's not going the way you planned it, you're feeling some anxiety from that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Absolutely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does your employer ever have unscheduled meetings or anything like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He does. He will schedule some unscheduled meetings and I've tried to calmly approach him and say if there's a meeting we need to know about it. I need to schedule my day around it. He once scheduled a meeting at 12:20 when I'm at lunch. Why is that appropriate? I feel like I'm the only person who knows how this needs to run.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so you have some different stressors at work and some disagreements with your coworkers. Can you tell me anything about your home life?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My home life is very neat. Everything's nice and where it needs to be. I have my meals scheduled out on a calendar. Thursday's chicken, Friday's tamales, and so on.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so your home life's a bit like your work life in terms of being organized.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's the right way to do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In terms of your home life, do you ever collect anything?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me about that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That also causes me some anxiety because I like to collect things. If I have a good day, I like to keep the newspaper from that day. I have newspapers from years ago. I just can't seem to let them go.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you keep them in your home?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So newspapers. Anything else that you collect?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Receipts. I've always known you have to keep receipts. You never know when you'll have to prove a purchase or return something.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What percentage of the receipts that you're given do you think that you keep?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: All of them. Every single one. I get very upset if I don't get my receipt, even at a fast food place.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm going to ask you some questions going back to work regarding your work schedule. Do you wash your hands regularly at work?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I wash my hands before I eat, after I eat, and after I use the restroom for 30 seconds every time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you ever find yourself having washed your hands and then going back and washing them several other times?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, there's no need to do that. You wash your hands for 30 seconds, and that's all you need to do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have any particular concerns about germs or anything like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I try to keep neat, but not particularly, no.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever found yourself in a situation where touching something repeatedly, like a doorknob or a light switch, seems to lower your anxiety?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not at all. That seems like a waste of time and inefficient. There's no need to do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about double-checking, for example, light switches or making sure the doors are locked?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I make sure my doors are locked the first time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you check, but just the one time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When I come in the door, I lock it, and that's it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what do you think the solution here is? Your employer sent you for counseling. What would you like to change?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He wants me to be more flexible, to not get as upset if there is an unscheduled meeting or if somebody needs to switch shifts. I don't really understand it, but I'm in trouble at work, so I have to look into it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You like your job?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I do like my job. I like being able to have everything organized and available. I love it; it's like a machine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so you like your job and how you're organized, but there is some conflict with coworkers and your boss and you want to try to work that out.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess. I don't want to lose my job, and if this is a problem, the right thing to do is to come speak to you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're open to attending counseling sessions and taking a look at what's going on here?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Absolutely, if my boss requires it. If my boss requires it, then that's the right thing to do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I appreciate you answering my questions; it's been very helpful. We'll get you on the schedule to see a counselor here in about a week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, so in a week. All right, thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks.

video_details.title: Confrontation: "This is a waste of time"

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't want to talk to you anymore. You're all the same, all of you. I've been wasting my time. You ask me to come in and talk, but I don't get anything out of it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When you say we're all the same, do you mean...?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: All therapists! I've been to four of you and nothing is working. You all just sit there and stare at me and don't do anything for me. There's no help, just talk.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm having a couple of reactions to what you're saying. One is that you're saying we're all the same in this way.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You are. Nothing is working. You're all the same.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm feeling lumped in with everybody else right now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Because you are. There's all this abstract metaphysical stuff and no concrete way to fix it or goals. There's nothing, so what's the point?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there something specific right now that I could say or do that would give you what you're wanting or needing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: How do I get from point A to point B? How do I get better and fix what's going on? That's why I came here, to fix things and make them better.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you want a sort of step-by-step description of how...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Something! I need something to grab onto.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I see you desperately want something to give you hope, but the intensity of your demand makes it difficult for me to respond in a way that gives you what you need. It has to come out of an organic process between us, and your desperation makes it hard for you to be receptive.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's just the way I am. I'm either full throttle, or I don't do anything at all. One way isn't good enough, and the other way isn't good enough either.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's like being damned if you do and damned if you don't.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Exactly. If I go one way, it doesn't make a difference, and if I'm quiet, it doesn't matter either.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like you feel you only have two choices: approaching a situation on the attack, with both guns blazing...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's a good way to describe it, both guns blazing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Or the alternative is to go along and compromise yourself in some way.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right, right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Of those two, which feels better or worse?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Both guns blazing always feels better because I've said my piece. If I don't say anything, it just eats me up and I get even angrier.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I can imagine that. At least with guns blazing, you can feel okay about yourself even if your needs aren't met. Giving in is like giving away part of yourself. The dilemma is that you have no good way of getting your needs met right now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: There's just no middle ground.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm not sure what that middle ground is yet, but I'm willing to work with you to discover it. Does that seem worthwhile?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have to. I have to find a middle ground.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What are you feeling right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It bothers me. I try to do one thing and I can't, and I try the other way and I can't do that either. I'm just stuck.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there's a real sadness there, and maybe hopelessness.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know what to do. It feels like there's nothing I can do, so what's the point?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: My sense is that it's almost as if you're asking for something, yeah?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I need something. I can't get it myself.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I hear your desperation, sadness, pain, and hopelessness. I'll do my best to help you.

video_details.title: Counseling Assessment Vignette - Client with Features of Antisocial Personality Disorder
video_details.description: This counseling assessment vignette demonstrates an interview with a client (played by an actress) who exhibits features of antisocial personality disorder.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Lisa, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm well. How are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. It's nice to meet you, I'm glad you could come into the agency. Could you tell me what brings you here today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, well, I am here now because I was caught stealing money, and now I have to pay the price, I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So were you ordered by a court or...?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how long ago did the crime occur?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: About a month ago.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So I'm going to try to get an idea of what's going on with you to see where you fit in in terms of treatment. So it's an assessment, so I'll be asking you some questions about your history and kind of things that you've done, any feelings you've had, thoughts you've had.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like diagnosing?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Like diagnosing. Is that okay with you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So how old are you now?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So you say about a month ago you got into some trouble. Can you tell me what happened there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, well, I stole money from a friend of mine and, you know, I just needed the money. They had more money than me, so I took it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And this was a friend of yours?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How do things stand between you and your friend now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, she turned me in, so we're no longer friends.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you had any other trouble with the law?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, they say when I was younger I used to get into a lot of fights.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And who's they?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My family. I used to get into a lot of physical altercations and there was this one time when I beat this girl up and they told me that they had to pull me off of her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You remember doing it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I remember doing it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how old were you when that happened?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: About 12.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Were you ever treated for that, like any type of mental health treatment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, they put me in some sort of detention center and I guess they gave me some sort of therapy one-on-one, but nothing like serious or like I'm doing now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you aware of any diagnosis that you've been given related to mental health in the past?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So you got into the sounds like a fairly serious fight when you were 12 and you're 25 now. Can you tell me what's happened in terms of any other problems between 12 and 25?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess the usual. I mean, I drank and got into some drugs and would use and do stuff like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any other thefts or assaults or anything?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, yeah, I still kept getting into fights and stuff, but yeah, I think my last real fight was when I was about 20.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. And how much danger were the people that you were fighting? Like, did you seriously hurt them or...?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. How many times did that happen where you seriously hurt somebody?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably every fight that I ever got into. So many. I don't have a number.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you explain what happened, like what caused the fight?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So the one girl, she just I felt looked at me wrong and I didn't like it, so I punched her in the mouth and continued to do so until she was on the ground, and then I still continued to do so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What are your feelings about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: She deserved it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Because of the way she looked at you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mm-hmm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you ever have any feelings of guilt or remorse about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever apologized to any of the people that were hurt?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've apologized, but just to appease people so that I didn't get into any more trouble.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, so in some of these situations, apologizing was kind of required?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you apologized to them but you didn't really mean it? Or what were you thinking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I didn't mean it. It was just to get out of trouble and go on with myself.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Were you successful in getting out of trouble?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Absolutely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You say that with a little pride. Is it something you take pride in? Being able to get out of trouble?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I mean, wouldn't you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So that's like something you look at as like a skill that you have?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Absolutely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever for the theft type activities, you ever felt any guilt or remorse there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's kind of the same thing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Same thing. They, I mean, they had more money than me, so why not? They probably would have done the same thing to me, so I did it to them before they could do it to me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Were you ever the victim of a crime?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. I'm smarter than most people, so I can probably I can one up people.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you feel that you're good in working with people, like in terms of social skills?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean getting what I want. I can always get what I want.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're effective at managing relationships to get what you want?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How would you describe your mood most of the time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, I guess I can get a little irritable.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How often does that happen?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A few times a week.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Does that irritability ever lead to or has ever led to some of the aggressiveness you've...?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're more likely to be aggressive when you've been irritable for a while?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When was the last time you were involved in a physical fight?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So that was around 20.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: About five years ago?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you think has caused that to stop?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I guess I'm moving on to bigger and better things.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What type of things?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Stealing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the stealing's more gratifying than the fighting?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So irritable and any other emotions, any other feelings?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm not sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. You have a job?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Well, I did.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me about your work performance and your experience there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, you know, I'd show up when I needed to most of the time and do what I have to do.

diarization.speaker: Therist
diarization.text: You show up most of the time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How would your employer describe you as an employee?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, I'm pretty good at doing what I do. But I guess my boss would like me to be there more. But when I'm not there, they'll go on without me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So in terms of your feelings about missing work, that's not too worrisome for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How many jobs have you had?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably like six.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Six jobs? At what age did you first start working?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So six jobs in about six years?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And would you say that your experience with all the employers was the same in terms of how you showed up for work and missing work, or were any of them different?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, they wanted me they tried to get me to conform, I feel, and I'm just not a conformist.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Kind of do things your own way?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yep.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you want to gain out of treatment here?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just want to get out of trouble.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're in trouble now, and you'd like to get out of trouble?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, Lisa, this has been helpful. I'm going to get you scheduled for treatment, and they'll probably get you in about a week, and we can go from there.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

video_details.title: chris withdrawal

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So, you know, I wanted to kind of mention this other thing that happened over the weekend. It happened on Sunday. Um, I was with Jane, we were both at home, and, um, she has been wanting me to kind of help her build this sort of shelving unit thing. And, um, I've been, like, putting this off for a couple of months and I haven't really wanted to do it, but she kind of was asking me more and more on Sunday and I finally kind of agreed to do it. So we started working on it together and we started off in the morning and we had somewhere to be in the afternoon, so I was kind of a little bit anxious about the time and trying to make sure we got it done. Um, and she was kind of wanting to help out, but, um, it wasn't going so well. I was, like, trying at it and, um, I've always kind of been bad at construction and stuff like that. And I don't really know why she bought the thing in the first place, but, um, so she kind of insisted on helping and kind of wanting to keep helping me and I kept saying, I, you know, I can just do this, I can do it on my own. And, um, so she started to help me and I was trying to kind of get this fastener piece to kind of fit in properly and I, like, I broke the thing and and I was saying this is why I wanted to do it on my own. And, um, and you know, she kind of fired back at me and said, you know, can't you do anything right? And, and I just don't know why, I don't know why it's so hard for me to, like, get that done. I don't know why I, you know, let it go for months like that. Um, and you know, it was just, it was frustrating.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, so it sounds like it was a pretty upsetting and maybe you were even angry with Jane?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Did I use the word angry? I wasn't really sure if...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No, I don't think you used it. I just had a sense that you were particularly frustrated with her. But, but maybe I misunderstood, so...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean maybe I was a little bit upset, you know, I think in the moment and, um, but I, I mean, I think I dealt with that in the moment and I think we were able to kind of move on. Um, yeah, I don't know. I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's going on for you right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess, um, I'm, I'm not sure. Yeah, I mean maybe, maybe I was a little bit angry. But, um, I don't think I want to talk about, about that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can, can you say more about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. I just, it makes me uncomfortable to talk about that maybe. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah. Well, can you, let's focus on being uncomfortable. And, and give me a sense of what you're uncomfortable about.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. I think it's, it's tough to, I think it's tough for me to even say to you that I don't want to talk about this. Um, you know, you've been so helpful to me and I've been, you know, coming here every week and, right, right, I just, I feel like I feel like an awful person even kind of, even saying I don't, I don't want to go there.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play - Fear of Driving
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which cognitive-behavioral therapy techniques, including evaluating evidence and problem solving, are used to treat a fear of driving after an automobile accident.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Rebecca. How are you doing today? What's been going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, nothing too bad. I kind of got in a little bit of a fender-bender accident.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A car accident?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What happened?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We were at a red light and the car behind me hit me, and then I hit the car in front of me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh. You okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was jolted back and forth. I've got a couple of bruises, but physically I'm okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So physically you're okay. Were you checked out by your physician?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, everything's okay there. I didn't break anything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. How about emotionally?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's been hard to get in my car. My boyfriend asked if I wanted to go on a trip, and I'm hesitant.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What was the thought that came into your mind?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm going to get hurt.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it was really all about the car, not anything else about the trip?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, it was being in the car, driving the car.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you felt you were going to get hurt?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'm going to get hit. I would normally be excited about a trip, but now I'm just scared.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Even coming here today, I didn't want to drive. I was more aware, but very nervous.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Much more nervous than usual?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How did you feel about driving cars prior to this accident?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was fine. I enjoyed driving and going on trips, but now I'm too scared.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're taking every opportunity to avoid driving.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, except for essential things like work or coming here, and that takes a lot of motivation.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you tell yourself to motivate yourself to get into the car?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have to think about it for a long time. I'm very nervous, and I avoid stoplights if I can.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This is disturbing and painful for you. Prior to this accident, how many car accidents have you been in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe one small thing years ago, but this was the worst one.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The other one didn't bother you as much? Why do you think this one triggered this nervousness?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: This time I was by myself and it was rainy. In the other one, I had someone with me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Did the driver that hit you tell you what happened?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, they left before the police got there. I was just left to deal with it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're worried about getting hit and hurt every time you get into the car now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, even after driving, I'm still worried about another accident.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Driving always carries risk, but there are things you can do to minimize that risk.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I wear my seatbelt and try to avoid stoplights, even though it's difficult.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What about driving habits you can use to stay safer?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I watch my speed, keep space around my car, and make sure my lights are working.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Following traffic laws and being aware of your environment can reduce the risk of an accident.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Ultimately, you need to be safe but recognize that you can't eliminate all risk.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What are some adaptive responses you can tell yourself when those automatic thoughts come up?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can tell myself that I'm doing everything I can to stay safe and that I'll be okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's hard when the thoughts are strong, but remember you've had many safe trips in your life.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
