diarization.text: Statistically, accidents are low-probability events compared to all the times you've driven.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's true. I can tell myself I'm likely not going to get into an accident.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You can reduce the risk by being careful, but you also have to accept that the risk exists.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you feel like you can apply those adaptive responses when those automatic thoughts come in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can try.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'd like to give you some homework. We'll use a 'thought record' to track your automatic thoughts.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Record the thoughts, the adaptive responses you apply, and how you feel afterward.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We'll use this to measure your progress. Can you complete two thought records before our next session?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think I can do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Great. Let's meet again in a week and review them. Thanks, Rebecca.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play - Managing Anger
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which cognitive-behavioral therapy is used to treat anger and frustration. Techniques demonstrated include identifying automatic thoughts, forming adaptive responses, and identifying cognitive distortions.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm alright, how are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. What's been going on in the last week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's still the same. Nothing at home is going right. We're still yelling, we're still fighting. My boyfriend just can't get it together. He doesn't do anything right and I just end up screaming every day. It takes it all out of me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so he can't do anything right and you're arguing and being angry every day.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what are you taking away from this? Like what do you think's going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel like he does nothing wrong and I end up screaming at him when I come home from work. And that's a lot out of me every day and I don't want to feel angry every single day.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But that's what's happening.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What types of things do you think are triggering your anger response?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's anything. I come home, he's just sitting on the couch. I've had a long day at work, he gets home before me, and the dishes aren't done, nothing's even started for dinner. He could just do one thing and I just lose it. I start screaming at him that he does nothing, that he could just have the sink empty. One thing. And it's every single day. The trash is full, you name it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So every day when you come home from work, there's something he's done or failed to do that triggers yelling.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's his response to this? Like what's he do when you yell at him?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He gets mad back. He starts screaming back at me that I expect too much, and why am I always yelling at him. But I don't understand it. You could do one thing and I just can't help it, I scream at him.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are there other things he does other times that you feel are helpful?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: On anniversaries he'll make dinner, so that's nice. He makes good money, so he keeps that together. But that's about it. The rest is just I just get angry at him.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So if you were to pick adjectives to describe him, what adjectives might you select?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Stubborn, condescending, and intelligent.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Stubborn, condescending, and intelligent. Do you see him as this way kind of all the time, or does this change?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't think it's all the time. Like a month ago when a friend at work died and I had a long day, when I came home, everything was good. No trash, no dishes. So it's not all the time, but just lately it's just, I have no words.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So lately it's all the time, but there's been prior occasions when this hasn't been a problem. After you yell and argue, what's it feel like to you then? Like what's your mood?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm still irritable. The dishes still don't get done. The problem didn't go away. It didn't fix itself while I was yelling. It just sucks being that angry, I hate it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's not productive for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right, right, it's not productive.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But there's a part you mentioned earlier where you said you just can't help yourself.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just lose it. That's what it feels like.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you just see the dishes aren't done and immediately there's the...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just go off. Why didn't you do the dishes? You've been home an hour and a half. You could have done one thing for me. I had a longer day and you knew it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so let me take an example from work. Do people there ever frustrate you in a way similar to what your boyfriend does?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Occasionally, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there's times you kind of have that moment with them where you just can't believe they didn't do something.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I just can't stand them sometimes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what's your reaction in terms of anger and yelling to those events?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I get pissed, but I just can't yell.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You can't yell. Why's that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd get fired.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So in those instances, because there's a consequence like being fired, you're able to control the outward expression of anger. Inwardly you're still angry, but you're not yelling.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So they don't really know you're angry?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I just walk away. I don't think they'd be able to tell.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And they're not being yelled at, so no reaction.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right, they would never react.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there is a thought process that occurs between the trigger and when you act. Because at work, you're thinking 'I don't want to be fired'. And the consequence is 'I'll be angry, but I'm not going to act angry'.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right, I can't act angry or I'll get fired, and I don't want to get fired.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So knowing that there is a thought there, when you come home and you see the dishes aren't done, what would that thought be?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, just that he never does anything right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so you see the dishes, 'he never does anything right' is the thought, and the behavior is finding him and yelling at him. So you see how there is an intervening thought between the trigger and the behavior.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess there's a thought where I'm looking at him thinking 'You never do anything right'.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Remember we talked about cognitive distortions? Consistent errors in thinking. I'm wondering if 'he never does anything right' is similar to all-or-nothing thinking. It's kind of blocking off your path in terms of thinking.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, it's absolute tunnel vision at that point.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. But you mentioned earlier there are times when he does do things right.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, there are occasions where he must have thought about me, he was more thoughtful, more considerate.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The thought 'he never does anything right' could be challenged. What might be an alternative to the behavior, to the yelling? What might be a thought you could insert to disrupt that connection?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe that he has done something right in the past. So it's bound to happen again, it is possible.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so an adaptive response that says 'He's not altogether bad because he has done things right in the past'. It's more flexible. And on the other side, I'm wondering if we can't challenge the usefulness of yelling. It hasn't worked.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The dishes don't get done. And the next day I might still find the dishes there. It hasn't worked.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So when you're yelling, there's a hope it will change his behavior, but it's not. When was the first time this was a problem?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've had previous boyfriends where this was a problem and that relationship has long gone because of it. I really do like this guy, and I don't want my yelling to be a problem, but it's hard to control.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Rationally you understand it doesn't work, but somehow it feels like a release. Do you have an idea of what might be a more productive path as an alternative to the yelling?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess walking away is what I do at the office. I've been able to take a minute and either remove myself or intervene more calmly. So I guess walking away and taking a minute.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, that would be one behavioral strategy. How much time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Honestly, like five or ten minutes of just me time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So let's say ten minutes. Then you can respond more constructively. But it seems you're just going right to the yelling.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We're not getting anywhere.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The yelling is really an impediment to what you want to achieve. Do you kind of recognize that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I didn't think that there was anything between me seeing the dishes and yelling at him. But I guess there is a moment in between because I don't yell at work. So there is something else I could do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now you're realizing there's a gap where thinking takes place.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, there's a sliver that is also there at home.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm wondering if you think about it in advance to inoculate yourself. Like you know you might see chores not done.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, I definitely have that thought when I'm driving home. I know he's not going to have the trash taken out or the dishes done, or the chicken thawed, anything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thinking in advance can be good if you prepare yourself for the moment you'll apply that adaptive response. But it can be destructive if you start getting worked up and angry in advance. You want to consciously say 'I'm prepared to take a few minutes to calm down'. Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It does. It's like one more non-productive piece that I could change.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's within your power to change. Start yourself off by thinking 'he's not all bad, it'll be okay. I can just take a minute to myself'.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Adaptive responses don't have to be short, they just have to be inserted right after that automatic thought. We'll work on building some and test them out.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That'd be great.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I hope you'll be successful, but it could take time. I'm going to give you a document called a 'thought record'. Familiarize yourself with the format. We're going to see what the process is and how well the adaptive responses are working. Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It does.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, pick up next week. For this week, try the adaptive response and the behavioral response of walking away for ten minutes and see how that works.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'll definitely try that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It does.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, try that out, and I'll see you in a week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Perfect. Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks.

video_details.title: The Mini-Mental State Examination, 2nd Edition (MMSE-2) - Client with Cognitive Impairment
video_details.description: This video demonstrates an administration of the Mini-Mental State Examination, 2nd Edition (MMSE-2) with an actress playing the role of a client with cognitive impairment. This type of exam is also referred to as a Mini-Mental Status Exam.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Kathleen, how's it going?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Good, how are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. I'd like to ask you some questions about your memory. Okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Listen carefully. I'm going to say three words. You say them back after I stop. Ready?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mm-hm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Here they are: milk, sensible, before. Now repeat those words back to me.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Milk, sensible, and before.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now keep those words in mind. I'm going to ask you to say them again in a few minutes. Okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What day is today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Monday.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is the year?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is the season?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Summer, still hot out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is the month of the year?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: September.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is the day of the week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Monday.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is the date?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The 14th.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Where are we now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: In your office.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is the state?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Delaware.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is the county?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: New Castle.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is the city?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Smyrna?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is the name of the building we're in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I didn't know it had a name.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. What type of building is it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A school.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What floor are we on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The second.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What were those three words I asked you to remember?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Milk, cup, and book.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Now I'd like you to subtract 7 from 100, then keep subtracting 7 from each answer until I tell you to stop. What is 100 take away 7?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Keep going.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Keep going.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Keep going.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Keep going.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, good. What is this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Your eye.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what is this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Your ear.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now I'm going to ask you to repeat what I say. Ready?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mm-hm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It is a lovely sunny day but too warm. Now you say that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It is a lovely sunny day and it's warm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Listen carefully because I'm going to ask you to do something. Look at these pictures and point to the circle, then point to the square, and then point to the triangle.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Circle, square, and triangle.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Please do what this says to do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. You'll find a piece of paper that I left for you on the floor. Using that blank piece of paper, please write a sentence.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I see it. Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Please copy this design. You can hold onto that if you want.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Kathleen, that's the end of the test. I want to thank you. This was very helpful.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

video_details.title: Treatment Planning in Counseling - Goal and Objective Setting Related to Unstable Relationships
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which counseling treatment planning is demonstrated. The treatment planning includes setting a goal and the corresponding objectives related to unstable relationships.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Sarah, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hi, I'm doing alright.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Doing alright? I was hoping that today since I've seen you for a few sessions that we could do some treatment planning.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, would that be okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I'd like to divide the treatment plan into a couple levels, goals and then objectives which are like steps that you would engage in to meet those goals. Right? So you have like a kind of broad goal and then these specific objectives. All right? Are you familiar with this process at all?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think I had a treatment plan before with another therapist.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, great. So I know we've talked over the last few weeks about some relational struggles you've had and various elements, but I want to know and today I just want to work on two goals, and we might add to that later, but I would like to know a couple of goals that you would have for our counseling. Okay? And then we'll just kind of start with the first and then work on some objectives for that and then we'll move to the second and work on some objectives for that. So what would be a goal of these counseling sessions that you might want to achieve?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, you know, lately I've been really having a hard time. I'm not getting along too well with my with my brothers. So I would like to try to maybe work on work on that. Get a better relationship with my brothers.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Work on a better relationship with your brothers. So let's say maybe improving the relationship with your brothers. Does that sound right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what do you think is getting in the way of having a good relationship with your brothers now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, they always are you know they say sometimes I call them too often and then I only call them when I have when I need something or if I can if I want to complain. I don't feel like that's the case but that's what they tell me. And so like they don't return my phone calls that much anymore or you know they just won't they're not there for me supportively like like I'm there for them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so they're detecting like a difference in the level of support. And you mentioned before maybe last week that sometimes when you call you're angry with them. Like you'll say some some things that might be...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah because sometimes they you know they act like fools and somebody needs to you know I'm their sister somebody needs to be honest with them and tell them what they're doing is wrong.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you think that's contributing to the relational difficulties?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean they know that I'm gonna tell them like it is. They know I'm gonna be honest. That's how I am. So maybe maybe it is.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So maybe before calling them kind of looking at the content you're going to put in that call and if it's angry maybe waiting until you can adjust it to something more neutral or positive.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So not call them when I'm angry with them?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah waiting until that emotion kind of dissipates a little and you can replace it with something more positive. And we can get into ways later on how to do that with you know cognitive therapy, but I'm wondering if that might be a good objective, one of the objectives.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think that might that might help a little bit if I'm not as angry when I call them. It would help me to not you know be so mean.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so that'd be one objective. So no no calling when angry. Okay? And and I guess part of that too we'll get to would be applying the cognitive techniques so that you're able to do that. But that'll be the objective. Okay. How about other objectives for that goal of improving the relationship?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I know my one brother, you know he got really mad at me because I had called my other brother and and told him all this stuff you know that my brother did and I kind of was talking badly about the one to the other.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Kind of like a little device like splitting them apart.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah like kind of pitting them against each other.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: And I know that caused a big problem. He didn't talk to me for a couple weeks after that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So that really bothered him. Mhm. How'd you feel about it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, you know, it's kind of like I said. If you make me mad or you do something I don't like I'm gonna tell you how it is. I'm gonna tell everybody else how it is too. So I kind of felt like I wasn't making I wasn't lying. I was just being honest but he didn't like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That didn't go over so well.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, they sort of got in a fight between each other and they both kind of stopped talking to me for a little while.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So how important is this goal of improving the relationship with your brothers? Like say on a scale of one to ten with ten being the most important.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh it's important. It's like a nine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's like a nine. Okay.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You know with my parents gone it's just my brothers. That's all I have and I just love them so much. So...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So they're a big part of your big part of your life. All right. So even though you feel justified in being direct with them that seems to be hurting the relationship a little and that relationship's important to you. So you're kind of a little stuck between those two things. So how about an objective like not not talking to one about the other.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think that's a good I think that's a good one because that's what got me in trouble last time with them when they didn't talk to me for a while. That's what they seemed to be the most mad about.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So if you're gonna gonna say anything about one to the other it have to be kind of positive. So no negative no negative talk.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No negative talk. Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. And again we'll look at cognitive techniques really for for a lot of these objectives we go through to help you to be able to do that. But that would be the objective. So no negative talk to one brother about the other.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does that sound like something you can do?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think I can try it. Mhm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. I know you mentioned before too that even though you've had a stressful relationship with your brothers that they keep extending invitations out to you...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. To go to dinner at their house and you know go to the like their kids' sports games and stuff like that. Um yeah. That's a big part of what we do as a family.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So that's important to them. What's happened when they've extended those offers to socialize?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well sometimes I go but sometimes something things come up. You know like maybe I have a date or I'm spending time with someone else. Um and it's like last minute so I figured there's gonna be lots of baseball games and there's lots of times that we can have dinner together. So sometimes I don't always go when I say that I am going to be there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how do they react to that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well they don't like it at all. I mean I missed my niece's school play and my brother was really upset because I missed the play but also because they had bought tickets that were $25 each and you know he was just really angry with me and called me demanding the money for the tickets since I didn't show up. Um it was kind of a big fight and I didn't really quite understand it because I mean I told him I was going to go but at the time my boyfriend at the time had a really bad day at work and he just wanted to stay in and you know that had that had to come first. That came first for me. So...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So that you prioritized that over socializaing you know social events with your brothers.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess I did.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And and that's certainly a decision. Do you think that if you gave your brothers more priority with the social events that would improve the relationship?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think they would feel better about that if I showed up when I said I was going to show up.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So maybe the objective would be if you commit to join them at a social gathering that you follow through?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Mhm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now you mentioned there are some things getting in the way of that though.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, like um I mean I don't have a boyfriend right now but when I do sometimes things will come up and I would rather spend time with the with my boyfriend than do some other then do other stuff sometimes. So...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hmm. So this will be this will be work for you. This will be a little tough. Do you think that's an objective you know the showing up is an objective you can fulfill? Is it realistic?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean I don't see why I can't do it now. My worry would be if I got into another relationship I think it might be harder for me to it might be harder for me to always keep my commitments like I can when I'm single.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So this objective right now fairly easy. Later on maybe not.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So we'll have to keep this in mind that if and when you develop another relationship like romantic relationship this might be an objective that is in jeopardy of being fulfilled so...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean in the past it's been that way.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Historically it's been that way for you. Okay. All right. So we'll go with those three objectives for improving the relationship with your brothers. So that's one goal. Mhm. What would be a second goal?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, like I said I I don't have a boyfriend right now um but you know I really I really feel like um I would like to be a wife someday and having a real relationship is important to me so a romantic relationship. So one goal would be to try to keep and maintain a healthy relationship because my last one didn't go so well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It didn't. It didn't end well. All right. So really finding a new relationship but also maintaining it. Mhm. What do you think has made that difficult in the past?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well my last boyfriend he would always complain that I just was too needy and too clingy and you know I didn't give him enough space and all those kinds of things that guys say.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You do you believe that? Do you believe that's true?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just think that maybe he didn't love me as much as I loved him because if you really love somebody of course you want to be with them all the time. I mean that's isn't that what love is?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're in your value system as you kind of look through that lens right? We all have our own values. You look at relationships and think that if someone really loves you they're going to tolerate a lot of communication attempts and calls and everything. Mhm. So those relationships failed because they weren't really loving you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, they weren't they didn't they didn't seem to. I think maybe like in the beginning everything was fine but then all of a sudden it's like you called me too many times today or um I don't feel like going out tonight and you know if they loved me then they would do what I wanted. Wouldn't they want to talk to me during the day? I mean it's a long time to go without talking to somebody you love all day long.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How how many times would you contact them in a day?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh maybe like 10 or 12 maybe 15 times.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Maybe 15. So could you appreciate that for some people their value systems maybe different like the way they would manage relationships might be different and that might seem like crowding?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean yeah it must be different because it's been a pattern of a problem for me. So a lot of people probably feel differently.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You've you've heard this feedback before. Mhm. All right. So one of the objectives might be to maybe restrict the number of contacts to something that's maybe more common. I know...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like maybe like five times a day?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What have what have boyfriends in the past indicated would be...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well my last boyfriend said that it would be ridiculous to call any more than once a day. But I thought that was a little bit extreme.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're thinking five and and from one person in the past he would suggest one. Maybe for a objective we'd try three? There's no perfect answer here. It's just trying to get close to a number that would maybe not have you appear as clingy or needy or whatever they're seeing you as but still satisfy your need to communicate.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think I could try three. Like maybe once in the morning and once in the middle of the day and maybe once in the afternoon. I think I could try three.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So again like I asked you about the other goal how important is this goal of finding and maintaining relationship?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh really important. It's really important. Mhm. Like a ten.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Like a ten. Okay. So again keep that in mind as you're working through this objective. Right. And and maybe this is something we revisit depending on the relationship. Right? Maybe you'll find a boyfriend that wants to be contacted more or less. But we'll go with three for now. All right. And see how that works. What else has been a barrier in the past?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well some you know it's kind of like being needy. It's kind of the same thing but some of my past boyfriends always say that I um like I move too fast or I want a commitment that's too like too early. I want the commitment too early or whatever.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So again this is kind of example another example where your values or your style of relationships is a little different than the men you've encountered. Right. So you're you're looking for commitment a little earlier on. Is that is that...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean I just feel like if you meet somebody and things click you know pretty soon you know soon if it's a good match or not and why waste time if you have a good match and if it's somebody you really like you know why wait some why waste time? Why wait?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And that's what you believe but the men that you've encountered they don't seem to reciprocate that belief.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not all the time, no.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the talk or the gestures suggesting commitment seem to be scaring them away.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm. Yeah, I think so. I think that's happening. Mhm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have they ever kind of phrased it that way?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, they don't always say that but they will say you're getting too serious too fast or I'm not that serious about all this and then they'll just stop calling.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there's a sense that they're being scared away a little bit. So if you look at your past relationships and we'll just call it commitment talk right as commitment talk. I know you've had a few relationships in the past. How many times were you the one to initiate the commitment talk before they did?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh probably me all the time. Mhm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All the time. Mhm. Okay.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Because you know men don't like commitment at all. So the woman has to sort of jump in and bring up commitment.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So do you think that I'm wondering here if there's not a way to strike a balance with that level of engagement meaning kind of engage at the same level or a similar level of commitment as they're expressing. And that's really hard to make concrete. Right? That's kind of an abstract concept. Right? You see what I'm getting? It's like a balance between how much you would bring it up and how much they would bring it up. So I'm wondering if instead if there could be maybe something we could measure a little better like a time limit. A time limit from when a relationship starts until you introduce the idea of a commitment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well um one relationship that seemed to last a little bit longer than most of my others um I think that I did sort of move a little slower. It probably wasn't until probably a couple months in until I started talking about commitment. I kind of gave it a couple months. So maybe like two months? Try to wait two months before I talk about commitment.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So in a past relationship that was more successful you were able to or you chose to wait two months and that seemed to facilitate a good relationship. Mhm. All right. So you want to make that an objective? Is that something you think you can do is to restrict commitment talk or gestures to to two months? Like wait two months. All right. So we'll make that a goal. And I'm thinking as I'm looking at the other objective that the improving the relationship, the other goal rather, the improving the relationships with your brothers, that anger was a factor there. And I'm wondering if for the the finding and maintaining relationships with the romantic interest um is anger has anger been a factor in that in the past?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it has been. Yeah. I mean there's been many a times when I you know if somebody didn't do what I wanted them to do or didn't call me back, you know, it would be you know a two hour lecture when they came home from work about why it's so important to call me back or just you know I can get really mean about things if I feel like I'm being rejected or not treated the way I think I should be treated. You know or if someone's acting in a way that I don't think is right. I'm pretty blunt about telling them about it. So definitely been a lot of big fights in a lot of my relationships.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So this is similar to one of the objectives in the first goal which was the not calling when angry. Um but I'm wondering if in your exchanges that maybe weren't angry if the anger comes up while you're on the phone or while you're with them in person. Like so it could start out not angry. Like so with your brothers you were calling them and kind of letting them have it. Right? But I'm wondering in these relationships is that the way it's working or you're having a good discussion with them and it turns angry?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's more like that. It usually starts out okay and then they'll say something that I don't like or they'll do something.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's what I was thinking because you mentioned rejection. Yeah. So when when that rejection is felt or perceived.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm. That's when the anger comes? Yeah. Like if they cut me off too quick on a telephone call or they say they're not going to be home till late or something like that I can get really angry pretty quick.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Pretty quickly. Mhm. So this would be maybe I'm thinking of the objective here, maybe applying some of the coping skills that we'll be reviewing later on when you have feelings of rejection. Because it seems like the feelings of rejection are kind of leading to these or contributing to these angry responses. Does that sound right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Mhm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so you perceive rejection and then if it feels like you're going right to anger.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Because I feel like if you love somebody you're not going to reject them. You're not going to do that stuff. And I just want somebody to love me as much as I love them. And when they don't, yeah, I get really angry about it. It hurts. So...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's painful for you. Mhm. So there's an intervening thought when somebody rejects you. There's this intervening thought that somebody who would love you would not reject you. And then that thought's leading to this anger. So we'll call that an automatic thought and we'll work on that later on. Um how to identify automatic thoughts and how to respond to them. But for just for this point we'll say uh apply coping skills when perceiving rejection.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Mhm. You're going to teach me some coping skills?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'll teach you the coping skills. Yeah. We'll work through them. Yeah. We'll work through them. Uh there's some cognitive techniques. So part of this is going to be recognizing the rejection which it seems like you're able to do pretty well. This would be you know adding a coping skill when you recognize that rejection. Okay. Does that sound like something that's achievable?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think I can try it. Yep.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Are you satisfied with the two goals and the the two sets of three objectives that we've come up with for...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it sounds like a lot. I've got a lot of work ahead of me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A lot of work ahead of you. Yeah. Something you're able to follow through with and...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, because it's really important to me to have a better relationship with my brothers and to you know find a good relationship for myself. So yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Well I'm going to uh type this up and give you a copy of this. Okay. Right? And then next time we meet we'll we'll look at maybe a third goal. But I want to give you some time to kind of review this. Make any changes you might want to make and we can or we can talk about that. So look at it make any notes and we'll talk about if it needs to be you know anything added or taken away. Okay. And then we'll we'll work through the rest of the treatment plan next time I see you and then we'll move forward from there. So this kind of structures what's going to happen right in the future sessions so it's important we get this right but we can also change it if it's not working. Okay. Or when goals are met which hopefully will be the result we can take those off and if there's other goals we need to substitute in we can do that. Okay. Does that sound like a plan? Mhm. Good. So I'll get this typed up for you and get you scheduled for another appointment. Okay. Great. All right. Thanks Sarah. Thank you.

video_details.title: Withdrawal: "You're giving me wonderful advice"
video_details.description: Withdrawal Rupture

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was thinking about what you said last week about talking to my boyfriend when I get frustrated with him. And it's a great thing to do. I think it's important that I should do that. I do get frustrated with him sort of often, but it's only over little things. He works very, very hard and he's so wonderful. I just moved in with him and he's basically supporting me. He's so nice and he has this wonderful job. He just got promoted and I'm so proud of him. But because of this new promotion, he works a lot harder now and so he's a lot more focused on the job and less focused on other things.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I got frustrated the other night when he didn't do the dishes, as silly as that is, and he'd had a really, really hard day. I think it's wonderful advice that you've given me. I'm very glad that I'm here and I feel comfortable talking to you. It was awkward for me when I started thinking the other night when I was frustrated and I had a lot of trouble even broaching the subject to the point that I wound up not saying anything at all. I guess I just need more practice or maybe it's something that I need to get more comfortable with, but it just didn't feel right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. I mean, it sounds like you're feeling perhaps like you have to sort of apologize to me for not telling your boyfriend about the way you were feeling?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I just mean I recognize that the advice you're giving me is wonderful advice. I'm just unsure of how to use it. I really enjoy coming and talking to you. But in this one specific instance, I found myself unable to follow the advice that you had given and I feel as though it was my fault.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you blame... I have a couple of reactions. One is, it's nice to hear that you find the therapy useful and so on.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's very useful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But there's also a way in which I'm feeling protected by you. You blame yourself for not being able to talk with your boyfriend, but somehow it feels like I'm being protected and you're taking all the blame or the criticism.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I guess that's just how I feel. I don't think it can be your fault that I couldn't talk to my boyfriend. I couldn't talk to him and even though I thought about it a lot, it's been on my mind. I just don't see how it could be your fault.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Maybe I'm giving unrealistic advice or maybe there's a way in which I'm not really fully understanding or appreciating just how difficult the situation is for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think that's part of it, but it's not... I was the one who couldn't talk to him. I guess I just feel a little confused because I think your advice is very good and I would like to follow it. But when it came down to it, I just couldn't do it. My boyfriend works so hard and he's so stressed out right now. In the past when I've tried to talk with him, he doesn't respond or he leaves or he starts yelling at me. He's very hard to talk to. So I felt like in that situation, especially with something as stupid as dishes, I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It strikes me that you're so appreciative of your boyfriend's situation and so sort of belittling of yourself, like the dishes. In the same way, you're so appreciative of me as a therapist and so belittling of yourself in our relationship.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, you're definitely right. I hadn't thought of that actually. That's definitely true. I do sort of defer to other people sometimes. I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I just want to check something with you right now because we're talking about you deferring. On one hand, what I said seemed meaningful to you, but on the other hand, I'm wondering if maybe you're agreeing a little bit too readily.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe I am, but I think I do agree. I really do agree with what you're saying. Maybe I'm too eager. I think you're absolutely right in what you're saying. Does it mean something?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What would it be like not to agree with me right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's hard to say. I do agree with you, so it's hard to say.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What does it feel like to agree with me? Any sense of what that feels like inside?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's two-sided. I'm obviously here for your help, so anything you say is going to be very valuable. I want to work with what you say. I don't want to fight against it. I think it's important to take what you have to say and really understand it. And on the other hand, I feel just sometimes when you told me to talk about being frustrated, it seemed like a hard thing to do. I really want our conversations to be productive. So I guess by agreeing with you sometimes, I forget a little. I guess I just get torn because when you told me to talk about my frustrations, sometimes it just can't be done, I feel. And that in itself frustrates me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It feels to me like maybe I'm asking you to do the same thing right now with me that I was asking you to do with your boyfriend. I was asking you to talk about your frustration with your boyfriend and it couldn't be done, and it's like I'm doing the same thing right now with me. It's like putting you in an impossible situation.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I feel that way. I definitely do.

video_details.title: Confrontation/Withdrawal: "I'm not getting anywhere"
video_details.description: mixed withdrawal + confrontation Confrontation/Withdrawal: "I'm not getting anywhere."

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, like it's uncomfortable because it sucks. This therapy is just, like, I'm not getting anywhere. It's just not doing anything. It's uncomfortable talking about it because it's just like, I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: My sense is that you were trying to say something and then you just kind of, almost like you gave up there.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I'm trying to talk about it. I don't know what else you want me to do. I told you that I'm not feeling like I'm getting something out of the therapy. I feel like I'm being pretty clear, but I guess I'm not.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you feeling angry at me?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, I'm feeling angry that the therapy isn't working, like I've been saying. I'm feeling angry that I'm still in the place that I'm in even though I've been trying. I'm just feeling pissed in general, you know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So I understand that you're pissed in general, but are you angry at me? It sounds to me, my sense is that you're feeling angry at me right now and if you are, I really want to know about it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I guess there is a part of me that's a little angry that you're not helping me. I came to therapy because I wanted to feel better, and I guess I am feeling angry that that's not what I'm getting from you even though that's what I'm trying to get.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're sounding really exasperated to me. How does it feel to tell me about this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It feels hard. It feels hard to say that I'm angry because it's not a comfortable thing to say or a comfortable thing to feel. It just makes me feel like, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So I don't want to push you too hard, but can you say anymore about what's uncomfortable about this? I do understand that it's uncomfortable.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's not something I would ordinarily say to someone that I'm angry at them, so it feels like I feel kind of anxious now even saying it. I don't want you to think it's your fault. It feels like something I'm really not supposed to say.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So part of it sounds like you're concerned that I'm going to feel like you're blaming me.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, yeah, I guess. I don't want to do that. But it is hard to feel like I'm alone in this therapy. I've been coming here and trying and I'm just not getting anything from you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so that sounds really important. It sounds like you're feeling angry at me, maybe you're feeling disappointed, and you're feeling all alone and like you can't even really talk with me about this.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it feels really hard. I want to be able to.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. All right. I'm really glad that we're talking about this and you're able to tell me more about how you're feeling about talking about it and my response right now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm still feeling a little anxious but I think it feels better that it's out there, I guess, that I've said it and I think maybe that helps a little.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so at least it's out there, right? Okay, so maybe we can go from here.

video_details.title: Administering the Mini Mental State Examination, 2nd Edition (MMSE-2)
video_details.description: This video demonstrates an administration of the Mini-Mental State Examination, 2nd Edition (MMSE-2) with an actress playing the role of a client. This type of exam is also referred to as a Mini-Mental Status Exam.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Lauren, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Good, how are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. I'd like to ask you some questions about your memory.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Listen carefully, I'm going to say three words. You say them back after I stop. Ready?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Here they are: milk, sensible, before. Now repeat those words back to me.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Milk, sense, and before.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let me repeat those again: milk, sensible, before.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Milk, sensible, and before.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, now keep those words in mind. I'm going to ask you to say them again in a few minutes. Okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What day is today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's the weekend.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is the year?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is the season?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hottish.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is the month of the year?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: September.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is the day of the week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thursday.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is the date?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Where are we now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We're in a building.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is the state?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: East Coast.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is the county?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Dover.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is the city?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Delaware.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is the name of the building?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The college.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is the floor of the building?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Two.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What were those three words I asked you to remember?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Milk, sense, and before.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now I'd like you to subtract seven from one hundred, then keep subtracting seven from each answer until I tell you to stop. What is one hundred takeaway seven?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Keep going.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Keep going.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Keep going.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Keep going.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, that's good, thank you. What is this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: An eye.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Your ear.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now I'm going to ask you to repeat what I say. Ready?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It is a lovely sunny day, but too warm. Now you say that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It is a lovely day, it's too warm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Listen carefully because I'm going to ask you to do something. Look at these pictures and point to the circle, then point to the square, and then point to the triangle.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: One, two, three.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Please do what this says to do. Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I put a piece of paper next to your chair if you could get that. Please write a sentence.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: About what?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Write about where you live.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can I see that? Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: On that same piece of paper, please copy this design.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, let me see that. Okay, thank you. We're finished up with the questions, Lauren. I want to thank you for your help.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play - Setting an Agenda for a Counseling Session
video_details.description: This video features a cognitive behavior therapy (CBT) counseling role-play that demonstrates setting an agenda for a counseling session. Checking in, reviewing the prior session and homework, and prioritizing goals for the session are demonstrated.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Ashley, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm doing alright.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How have you been feeling over the last few days?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, a little bit overwhelmed with school work and my boyfriend has been getting on my nerves quite a bit, but otherwise pretty good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you have a few things going on, but overall you're feeling okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I remember during the last session you had some difficulties at work.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, um, they seem to have been getting a little bit better with the homework that you gave me. It has helped me to identify when I'm getting a little more overwhelmed at work, and when I'm able to identify when I'm feeling that way, it's helped me to I guess meet my supervisor in the middle more or less, so I'm not as argumentative and she seems to be a little more impressed with my work performance, which has been good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So identifying the automatic thoughts has helped you kind of negotiate that relationship more productively?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, absolutely. Definitely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're able to complete the thought record, the homework?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm, yeah, and that's actually helped me a lot, not just with work, but when I'm out say grocery shopping and I start feeling that way, it's helped me to bring myself back down so I don't get overwhelmed and I don't get so anxious.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good, good. So that's a positive result. So I want to kind of set our structure for today, like what we'll be talking about today during this session. And I was wondering if there was a few things kind of on your mind, like what you wanted to discuss today.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, oh there's a couple things. All right, um, my coursework has been really bogging me down lately, and then while I'm still doing better at work, I'm still not where I want to be. I don't want to have to consciously think, you know, this is why I'm... I want to keep working on not being so argumentative at work. And then my boyfriend has been just like I said earlier really grating on my nerves and I... like I told him the other day that I wanted to break up with him, but he told me he was going to change and that things would get better, so I'm kind of torn with whether or not to continue in the relationship or just let it go. And at the same time I'm having a hard time keeping up with my schoolwork and getting everything done on time and it's... my homework isn't where I want it to be. Like I feel like I can do better.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now you're being pulled in a few directions here and all of these things are important to you, like all these things are bothering you, right? The school work lateness, the relationship at work, like you're doing better with that but you still want some improvement there, and then some relational challenges with your boyfriend.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I know it's difficult to prioritize concerns when they're all important to you, right? But if you only had say one thing to choose for today's session that you really wanted to work on as a priority, what would you choose?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Ah, that's really hard.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well tell me about your thought process as you answer that question, as you think about that question.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I've been with my boyfriend for about nine months now and I thought that we were going to go into like marriage and children and I thought we had a future. But at the same time, my work, I need my job. I need it to pay bills and basically live. And at the same time, my schoolwork is very important because progressing in school and getting a better education will... I'll be able to get a better job, which will hopefully... it'll be a job in which I don't find myself where I am right now, budding heads with my supervisor all the time and everything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So again, it comes down to all three goals really are important to you. They all matter to you and you want to work on them. So I'm wondering as we think about trying to rank them, which is what we're really doing, right, is like trying to pick one as the most important. Which area do you think is interfering with your functioning the most? Like what's getting in the way of your mood being good or you accomplishing goals you need to accomplish to survive?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably my schoolwork.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Probably schoolwork? Tell me about that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I think it's most important because, like I said, it'll set me up later in life. So not getting a good grade on an assignment really brings me down because I view it as a threat to my future. Because if I don't get a good grade, then I could possibly fail out of school, and failing out of school means I won't have a good job, if I don't have a good job, then I won't have a good relationship and everything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so that's the priority. So we'll look at that problem, the schoolwork issue. We'll make that the number one priority for today. And if we get through that and we have time, we can look at one of the other things that's going on. But I want to make sure we kind of set a structure so we know what we'll be talking about and what we want to accomplish. So what we'll do is I'll have you tell me a little bit more about that and kind of your thoughts and feelings and behaviors surrounding that schoolwork issue. And we'll go through some techniques and I'll assign some homework related to that, more or less like I did last time when it was the workplace challenge, the workplace relationship that was the challenge. Does that kind of make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, definitely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does that sound like an agenda that you're comfortable with for the session?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Absolutely. I think that getting my anxiety and being so overwhelmed with schoolwork will help me with sleep and... because when I'm overwhelmed I can't eat and it's hard to sleep and everything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, so you could see it really helping you out. Great. Well give me just a minute to go grab some of the homework that I'm thinking of for today's session. I'll be right back and then we'll continue on.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, cool. Thanks.

video_details.title: REBT Role-Play - Postponing Gratification
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which the Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy (REBT) technique of postponing gratification is used to treat cannabis (marijuana) use. This REBT technique, which is also referring to as delaying gratification, is used to reduce the occurrence of less-than-useful behaviors and increase insight.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Carly, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We're good. What about you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. How'd you do this week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Better. Last time we talked about postponed gratification and you wanted me to try 10 minutes. I did better, and was able to put it off several times. One day I went for a walk and ended up putting it off for an hour.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So it sounds like you were able to maintain waiting 10 minutes to smoke marijuana, at least in most cases.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was rough.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It was difficult for you, but you held off for 10 minutes and sometimes longer because something else came up.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mm-hm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And it sounds like there were a few instances where you were able to hold it off longer because something else kind of came up.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I talked to a couple people on the phone and before I knew it, half an hour had gone by.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So another activity presented itself and you forgot about the marijuana?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Kind of, I just wasn't thinking about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So have your feelings about marijuana changed since we last talked?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, not really.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me about that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't see it as a problem. It's legal in many states and it's not that bad for you. It doesn't endanger me much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You still believe you should have the right to smoke, but you want to go back to work for your uncle and you need to be clean for a few months.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'm not hurting anybody else.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But at the same time you want to go back to work. I guess you'd go work for your uncle. And you need to be clean for two or three months?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think two to three months.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you have opposing forces: your enjoyment of marijuana and the need for that job.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My parents want me to move out, and it'd be nice to have that job, but I don't see why I have to sacrifice something I like.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It doesn't seem fair to you, but you recognize it's the reality. It comes down to marijuana use or employment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it really does come down in your instance to marijuana use or employment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's pretty accurate.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So you're not happy about that choice.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not at all.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: With the postponed gratification, I asked you to wait 10 minutes and you did. Were you able to track the number of times you smoked this week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, for the most part.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you remember how many times that was?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I think I did like 15 to 20 times.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How many times did something come up in that 10-minute span that distracted you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Almost closer to 20 times. Phone calls or texts distracted me and I was able to put it off for a bit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In that 10 minutes, things can happen that help you avoid using. Was the experience tolerable?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it wasn't bad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: For next week, could we try postponing that gratification from 10 minutes to 20 minutes?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, that seems like a long time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That seems like a longer time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It definitely is a longer time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know about that. Maybe 15 minutes?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Want to compromise at 15? Do you think you could maintain waiting 15?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think I could try. It'd be a lot easier than 20.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's go with 15 minutes. Consider alternatives like walking or watching TV to distract yourself during that time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What else would you do instead? Like binge watch TV?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Binge watch TV.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Perhaps in those 15 minutes you could start watching a show you like. Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it doesn't make it easier but I see how it helps.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's tough. If we're successful with 15, we can move it up from there.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe. We'll see how 15 goes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm hoping that will give you more opportunities for something else to get in the way. I want you to plan an activity for that time and track each instance. Does that sound like a plan?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think I can give that a try.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good. Write down each time you initiate a wait period and what the outcome was.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, I think I can manage that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. We'll go with that and I'll see you in a week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Thank you.

video_details.title: REBT Role-Play - Understanding the Difference Between Self-Judgment and the Evaluation of Behaviors
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy (REBT) is used to improve understanding the difference between self-judgment and evaluating behaviors. The REBT role-play features a client (played by an actress) who is struggling with alcohol use and feelings of shame.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hey Carly, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm good, how are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. What's been going on this last week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've just been feeling like kind of in a rut. I've been looking for a job and hadn't really gotten anywhere. And then I had a drink the other night and I just felt like me not having a job and me going out and having that drink was just, it wasn't deserved. I just felt like such a loser because that was a time that I should have been at work if I had a job and instead I was at the bar drinking. So I had one drink and then it led to another because then I just felt worse and I figured I'd had one, so...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so how much did you drink in total?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think I lost track after four or five.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, and how long had it been since you had a drink before that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I did really well. It was, I think like three weeks. Three weeks or so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so you did really well and then you had one drink and that just made you feel like you weren't successful.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I felt like a loser.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you feel that kind of led to drinking some more.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you had a rough time of things. Yeah. And how about now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean now I just kind of, I don't know, I'm afraid to go back. Like I'm afraid to go out with some friends. They invite me out to dinner, but I know there's alcohol and...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that where you were when you had that first drink? Was that with friends? Yeah. All right, so there's a few things going on. We've talked in the past about separating the behavior from the person. Right? So behavior is what we do, not who we are. You remember those discussions? And correct me if I'm wrong, but it sounds like when you had that first drink, you're kind of ashamed that you had a drink and you had it during the time when you would have been working.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's pretty accurate.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so taking yourself kind of back to that moment where you had that first drink, like you finished that first drink, what was your thought at that moment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just like shameful. Like I did really, really well and then here I was and I had just finished a drink and I knew I wanted another one.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so shameful's kind of like the feeling, but the thought is I did really, really well. Right? So that's what you were thinking was I did really, really well. And was that the end of the thought or was there more before you had that next drink?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess just I was doing well and then I had the drink and I just felt like an awful person. So I figured what was the hurt in having more?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
