diarization.text: Alright, so the sequence would have been you had the drink, you felt shameful at the same time you're thinking that you were doing really well and then you just, as you've said before, you just felt like a loser and then you decided might as well just have the second drink. Yeah. So you could see how there's some thoughts and some feelings at work right as you finished that first drink. Was it fairly quick? Were those thoughts and feelings occurring right away after the drink?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I would say as I was finishing and then finished.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So right away you regretted it. And in that regret, as you thought about it, thought might as well just continue drinking now because you kind of blow it at that point.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I already messed up, I might as well keep going.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And that's a common cycle to fall into. And you had three weeks where you hadn't had a drink prior to that. So let's look at this, let's try to separate the behavior from the self a little bit. If you had a friend who was in the same predicament, right, who had a history of using alcohol and then had three weeks without any alcohol use and then their behavior was to have a drink. What would you think of them?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would think that they had a rough day or something must have happened where, I mean it's just one drink.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, they had a rough day but one drink. And what would you think of their behavior? How would you categorize that behavior?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess just they made a mistake.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So not ideal. Depending on their point of view, maybe a little irresponsible.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think irresponsible would be...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Irresponsible. But you wouldn't necessarily characterize them as a bad person. But their behavior was a bit irresponsible, you know, in terms of like their recovery plan, which would be to not drink. But when you apply that same examination to your own situation, how do you characterize yourself after you had that first drink?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was my mistake, and it makes me a worse person for doing it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you see how you're being a little, well quite a bit rougher on yourself, like your evaluation of yourself is fairly harsh. You mentioned loser earlier and ashamed, whereas you wouldn't necessarily evaluate someone else that way. How would you evaluate your behavior? How would you judge your behavior of taking that first drink?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Shameful. I mean, irresponsible, just bad overall.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So bad, irresponsible, shameful. Is there a way to separate that behavior in terms of the way you evaluate it from yourself? Like, are you and the behavior together, enmeshed, or can you be separated?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would think we could be separated, but it feels like we're, like I am that behavior.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In that moment, it's very congruent for you. Right, the shame matches the behavior, the behavior matches shame, like they're one at that moment. But really, logically, rationally, you're you, right, and you have an identity and values, and your behavior is something you do. But in the moment it's hard for you to see that. Looking back on it now, are you able to see the distinction between what people do and what they are?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I mean, just because you have one drink doesn't make you a horrible person, I would think, right?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Certainly not, no. And you were clean for three weeks and you had one drink, so really your behavior was a slip. Right? It was, and irresponsible in relationship to your goals, I suppose, but still a slip. And you could have stopped. But that shame got a hold of you, right, that thought, well now I've done it, I blew it. Yeah. So with that mentality, you kind of set yourself up for drinking more. So I think this is important because we've seen this cycle, like where you have weeks of sobriety and then you'll drink a bit and then have weeks of sobriety. And I'm wondering if part of the difficulty you're facing is you're not coping with the slips as just slips.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're allowing them to be gateways into a lot more drinking than a slip. Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that sounds pretty accurate.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you see how the shameful feelings kind of just interfere with the behavior that you really, with what's really consistent with your goals, which would be to not continue drinking. Another piece of this too is the associating with friends who drink. You're putting yourself in a treacherous situation. And again, that's a behavior. Right, that doesn't make you one way or the other, it's a behavior. How would you judge that behavior, going out with friends?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, I mean it's difficult because I like being around those people, but I guess it would be, it's risky.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Risky, okay. It's a risky behavior. And what does it make you? Who are you because you do that behavior? Like how do you feel about yourself when you take that risky behavior?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Guilty.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So you have guilt when you go out with your friends, and then you have shame if you drink. And both, in this case, both emotions that kind of point you the direction of more drinking. So part of this behavioral strategy here is to avoid those circumstances, like to recognize that that's a risky behavior which you have, and the other part would be to deal more effectively if you do slip.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does that separation of what we do and who we are make sense to you rationally?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Kind of. It feels a little unnatural though.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. So maybe as you're confronting similar situations over the course of the next week, you could be aware of behaviors that might put you at risk and try to separate your identity from that behavior. So just judge the behavior. Okay. And don't pass any judgment on yourself. Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Kind of, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It might help you to, since it's a little tough to, because right now the feeling and the judgment are intertwined, right, it might help to write it down when these things happen, and kind of write down like one row for this is how I judge this behavior that I'm thinking about doing, and this is how I judge myself. So if you see a lot of self-judgment, that might be a clue that you're falling into that cycle a little bit, where you're making your decisions based on that emotion instead of a rational judgment of behavior. Would that help a little bit?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think that would probably be beneficial.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so that'll be our plan going forward until next week is note, document your judgment about your behavior and any judgment you may have about yourself. Alright, and there's some insight that can be gained there, right, if you kind of distinguish the two, and make a note of those and try to use that evidence before making a decision that might put you in a risky spot. Okay. Sound like a plan?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think I can try that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, good. I'll see you next week and we'll see how you did with those goals.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play - Anxiety Related to Dishonesty in Social Situations
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which cognitive-behavioral therapy techniques are used to anxiety related to dishonesty in social situations.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Maria, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm doing well. How are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. How have things been going?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, okay. I've been having some trouble with some friends and stuff and, I don't know, I just think people just don't get me. I just don't think people get me. And...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: They don't understand you? Your friends don't understand you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, they just don't and right now I just, you know, I just don't want to be friends with anybody right now because they just don't understand me and I don't know, I think I'm just not going to have friends for a while.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That seems like a fairly large shift from kind of your position before on having friends. You seemed to really like spending time with them. Has something happened that precipitated this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, you know, I just said some things and now it's just gotten out of hand and um I just think I need to break from this friendship group for a little bit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You seem upset about this.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean, we were just talking about some things and, you know, uh I was just telling them that uh I play tennis and I enjoy tennis and I was just, and then maybe went on a little bit about how I play tennis.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me about that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it's a little embarrassing. I just, I was exaggerating about how I play tennis and they were telling me how they uh want to go to the US Open and they want to go every year because they they love it. And uh I've never been really, but I wanted to, I wanted to be part of the conversation a little bit so I told them that um I had studied under a famous tennis player and then um they were really impressed with that and so I just kept talking about that and all the stuff that I learned and told them that I was really good at tennis. So...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And in reality...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've maybe played a couple of times. So, and I've never met that person, let alone studied under them. And I really don't know how I got to the point where I was elaborating the story and so um they want to, they want to have some lessons, they want to learn what I learned under this person and um, you know, they started talking about getting together and at that moment I kind of got caught up and I said sure and um yeah, we'll schedule it like Saturday mornings, we'll we'll get together and we'll just kind of hit together and play some sets and I I don't know, I don't know what to do. It's just really embarrassing now because they're going to know that I really don't know how to play tennis. Um, you know, I could maybe have faked it a little bit, but now they think I've had professional training, so...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's going to be very obvious to them that you weren't being completely honest if you have to play tennis with them.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. And they're just going to know and and then they might question some other things I've said.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Things that are not tennis related?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. So...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Um, do you feel that in your relationship with these friends that you have not been honest uh frequently, a few times? Like how would you categorize...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: This is really hard to admit. It's just stupid, I just, it's stupid, it's just something I do sometimes. Um, I get kind of caught up or I'm feeling left out of a situation and they're all talking about a topic and I want to fit in, so um I might say a couple of things that make it sound like I know what I'm talking about or that I can relate to the topic when I can't.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In social situations when you're feeling isolated from the conversation or or maybe detached from the the uh people, you create a story that helps reintegrate you back into that conversation.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah. Um, you know, it's it's hard, I feel stupid just standing there like having no idea like when they talk about traveling and seeing different cities and stuff, I haven't really been outside of my small town, you know, I've gone to Florida, um I went to Disney World, I went to Epcot. So, you know, when they're talking about going to Paris and seeing the Eiffel Tower and seeing Notre Dame or they're talking about going to Rome and and I just I can't I don't really have anything to say, I don't really have that kind of a life and it's not very exciting. So sometimes I might say stuff about that and it's a lot of little things, you know, that I just I find myself saying things that aren't true and trying to just go along with what they're talking about um when I don't even know what what they're saying, you know. Um when they talk about fashion or they talk about um just different things and I I don't know what to do in that situation then I'm just finding myself just making things up and saying things that I think that they want to hear. And I don't even know if they believe it, you know, I I kind of got the feeling this time that they were kind of calling me out because they were they were getting an idea of what I had been doing and it was really embarrassing and I feel like I just want to run away from the situation and I don't want to talk to anybody and I just want to break off friendships.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So so a possible solution to the what you consider the inevitable embarrassment if you have to play tennis with them is to to just not see them, just not return their calls.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. I just I don't want them to know what you know that I have a really boring life and that I don't I'm not as smart as they are and I'm not as successful and I just I don't want them to know and I don't that I'm kind of like a loser compared to all their exciting things that they do and and say and I just don't match up.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You feel you can't keep up with them on on really so many levels. You talked about travel and fashion and of course now the athletics area with the tennis. So there's a sense of being inadequate when you're with them?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, yeah. Yeah, definitely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So your options here are somewhat restricted, right? Um just let them go as friends um or go and play tennis and they'll figure out that you might have been making up that story, or I suppose telling them the truth, right, would would be an option as well. Have you thought about the different options available?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, I have. Um, and I don't want to lose my friends, you know, I enjoy being with them but it's like I'm going to be mortified if I go out there and try to teach them things I don't know, I mean I guess I could maybe watch some YouTube videos but you know they're going to realize that I've never played and they're going to realize that they're better than I am, um you know and I I wonder if they'll still accept me if I tell them the truth.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you fear you might have lost them either way at this point?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, but maybe there's a chance if I tell them the truth that they might have, you know, some understanding of what I've been doing because I don't even understand it myself. But...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Um, how long has this been going on? Like the exaggeration or or less than complete honesty in these social situations?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it's really when I get really nervous about being around a group or you know get around people that I really admire and and I feel like I can't match up to them so, I don't know. I probably did it here and there in high school when I was a kid but it's just lately it's it's been more as I started um, you know, I got a new job with this really big company and um I have more responsibility and and I got promoted so I'm kind of in circles with people that really intelligent and successful and um, you know, financially secure and so it's probably when I get into to situations socially with people that I really feel are above me, you know, whether it be socially or just intellectually.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So your circle of friends is one group that you've been less than honest with. Any other individuals or groups that you've been less than honest with?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, no, not really. It's just really been in these friendship groups. Like I think with my family they know me and they know who I am so I feel comfortable. Um, I take a lot of pride in my job so I I don't do anything there, you know, I'm pretty honest with my um with anyone who's under me and and above me obviously. So it's nothing like that, it's just this really strange pressured social situation, I just kind of I lose all confidence at that point when I'm hearing what other people are doing and and how successful they are.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I wonder, has there ever been a situation where you're with your friends and they're kind of doing what you described where they're talking about their accomplishments and you have chosen to to not be less than honest? Like either you've made no contribution to the conversation or you made the contribution that was within you know that was truthful? Has that ever occurred?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Have I ever been truthful? Um, only if it's an area that I feel confident in.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, but but you have been a few times, right? But only if you start out confident.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How is um, how's that worked out?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it's been great. I mean, it's fine. It I guess it works like normal. It's fine. Like we have good conversation and we get along, we laugh and it's I feel I feel comfortable. I get really anxious when I start telling lies like it doesn't feel comfortable and I know I'm telling lies and I'm getting caught up in it and then it's just building and building and building and then I don't even know, I don't even know what I've said anymore. People say things to me sometimes I'm like, oh yeah, yeah, that's true.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You can't remember what you told them.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't remember.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So really, I mean from what you're describing, there's two outcomes to these social situations that occur. One is that you're less than honest and you don't feel good about yourself when you do that, or if it happens to be an area where you are confident you can participate in that discussion. But but it seems like what you haven't tried is when you're not confident, kind of still being honest, right? Because that's when that sense of inadequacy is really strong for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you suppose would happen if you weren't as impressive as they were and you relayed that? Like in the particular area that they're discussing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, you know, I think they would think I was I didn't belong there, I didn't belong with them, you know, that I wasn't really good enough to be their friend and kind of as I'm saying it out loud, it seems kind of weird to say it out loud, but I guess that's what I'm thinking. I'm thinking that if people see who I really am, you know, they're not going to like it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But you've not really tested that theory.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you know what the outcome is from being less than honest because you're stuck in that situation now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: With some difficult choices, right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you know no one's good at everything so you can't always count on having that feeling of confidence that would allow you to be honest with them and fully engage in the conversation. Right. So you'll have to decide what to do there, but it seems like it might be worth trying that, right, trying the honesty route and and see if that see what feelings come out of that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well I feel like I just like even with just this situation, I just don't want to be here again. You know, I know that I took this way too far and at times when people are coming up to me and I don't even remember what I said, I was I was starting to get that sense. This is the first time that I'm really caught red handed and so I'm almost forced at this point to make a decision and you know I don't want to hit the nuke button, I don't want to just decide to just disappear from my friendships. So I maybe it'll help if I just say this is this is what I do sometimes and it's not okay but I did it this time and I'm sorry. You know I don't know if I'll end up with any friendships anyway but...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well there's no doubt you have hard choices. Um and I think you can see you've kind of constructed that the the less than honesty policy has led to this situation and you don't want it to repeat.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, definitely not.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But only you can really decide this, right, and we can continue to talk this through. When do you have the tennis thing scheduled with them?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, it's supposed to be Saturday. So...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so that's coming up quickly. Yes. I want to touch on the automatic thoughts. Right? We talked about this before. These are the thoughts that come up in the moment, right, when a stressful situation is introduced. And it sounds like the stressful situation in this case is your friends talking about successes or or interesting things. Right. What what's the thought that pops into your mind in that moment? Like try to try to take yourself to that moment where your friends are talking and you talked about feeling isolated. What was the thought? What were you thinking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I I'm just not that interesting. I'm not that smart. I'm not that successful. I mean, it's almost like a mantra.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm not that successful, I'm not that interesting, I'm not that smart. So really all automatic thoughts that are putting you down.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are those automatic thoughts defensible? I mean is that realistic?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess it's a matter of perspective, you know, it's um you know I just got a promotion so in terms of success like I I have some that was something that that I just did. But I don't know, like interesting is is kind of relative, you know, I don't know what makes somebody interesting over another person, you know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But that automatic thought is telling you you're not interesting.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When the reality might be that for every every time they have something really exciting in their life you may not have done that exact thing but that doesn't necessarily mean you're automatically not interesting or that your contribution would be definitively less than theirs. Right. So there's kind of a those those thoughts are are really patently negative.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And kind of puts you all to one side of the scale, like you're just not interesting. Not that you may not be as interesting on this particular topic.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. That's yeah because there might be other topics that I know a lot about.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And is it okay to be somewhat interesting? Right. So you know if they've if they've traveled to Paris and you you say the furthest you or the farthest you've traveled is Florida, well Florida's interesting. I guess I could see how some people wouldn't think it's always as interesting as certain things in Paris. Right. But it's not like you're completely isolated from travel. You've been to other places.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean I've been to other places too, it's just you know Europe sounds so much more exotic and interesting than places I've been, you know, so...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, so you're not completely out of the discussion. It's just on that one topic of world travel. Right. And and do you always have to have the most interesting stories about or or even equally interesting stories about what they're talking about?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. It's silly to feel like I have to be on top of everything all the time. So no, no I don't have to dominate the conversation all the time, it doesn't always have to be about how interesting Maria is.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And if it's not true, then I mean this is something you're doing to fit in better with this group, but these statements aren't true. Right. So it hasn't really changed anything about you except that you were less than honest with them.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And maybe that's where some of these feelings of now, like you seem like you're regretting these decisions and...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah. Because I should be able to just be myself, especially in a friend group. Um, so I definitely want to stop doing this.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You want to stop.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, this has been this is causing you stress, anxiety, right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So notwithstanding the hard choices you have to make with this particular situation, I'd like to put some a plan together to help you with this in general. I don't know what the best choice for you is in terms of your friends. It's difficult and really only you can make it. I'm certainly open to talking through the possible consequences and your feelings about it if you want to meet again before Saturday. But that kind of put aside for a second, you're aware of the automatic thoughts that are coming in.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, so in that moment you can realize your cognition. And I wonder if we could build, I mean this could be kind of like a homework assignment, that you could build what we call some adaptive responses. We talk about the self talk. So these are the thoughts we consciously think to really counter the automatic thoughts. Right. And I guess I've touched on some of my my thinking in terms of the adaptive responses, like is it okay to be somewhat interesting, do you have to be the most interesting in the conversation? But more more of interest to me than what I was thinking is what are your ideas on some on some adaptive responses for these thoughts?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I definitely don't need to be the center of attention all the time, you know, it's okay to be learning and and getting something out of somebody else's adventures rather than always presenting myself forward, I mean it's exhausting trying it especially trying to come up with things and stuff starts coming out of my mouth and I don't even know what I'm saying so it's exhausting and you know once in a while it might be nice to just learn and hear and appreciate my friend, you know, and just kind of be there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let me stop you there. So one so one adaptive response could be it's uncomfortable and anxiety provoking to feel isolated but I don't always have to I don't always have to be at the top.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. I don't always have to impress. Or something like that. I mean I want it to be in your own words.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I don't that's I think that I think that's it, you know, I don't always have to be the center of attention, I don't always have to be the one with the most interesting story in the group.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And further, this may avoid an uncomfortable situation like the being less than honest, but it's exhausting to you. So there's consequences that that are unpleasant from it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: And I just want to be able to be me with my friend group and be accepted for the non traveling me, you know. So...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's okay not to travel. Any other ideas for adaptive responses?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, well not feeling successful, you know. Um I sometimes just have to remind myself of what I've done so far. And I mean I'm always feeling like I have to move forward and do more but you know...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so that would be like they've just said something impressive so the thought would be that was that was pretty impressive but I've had successes too.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah, because at that moment I I think I forget and then I just want to top their success. So um but you know I know I've done okay for myself, it's just at that moment I kind of get really caught up in the just the feeling that I'm not good enough because I immediately compare myself to that person and what they've done.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah and successes can be difficult to compare, right? I mean are they really measured in the same units so to speak? Right. Like how do you compare your promotion to somebody that traveled? Two completely different things. I'm not sure there's a calculation that makes those so you can compare them, right. So some of this is about self esteem.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. Yeah, I definitely struggle with that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So do you want to try to meet before Saturday so that we can discuss...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh yeah, I think I'm going to think about it and think about what I want to say to them. Um I think it would be worse for me to try to play and just keep this farce going and I don't think I can keep doing that, I think I'll I think I'll have a panic attack right on the court, it just won't work. And it's a little immature to think I'm just going to shut them off completely as friends at this point, so...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, well just want you to think about that and if you want we can schedule another appointment before Saturday so we can process that. Okay. So in the meantime and kind of working on the larger problem, right, that you're that you brought up today. How about identifying to the best of your ability identifying those automatic thoughts we talked about um as they happen, if they happen during this week, but also maybe identifying some of the ones in the past like you've talked about. And working with the thought record to build those adaptive responses. Okay. So it's something that you know with adaptive responses, something you want to become a habit. You want to have those responses ready to go, so when that thought comes in, before you act on that thought, you can um inject that automatic or that adaptive response, that self talk. Right, you could talk to yourself and avoid the behavior that you're trying to avoid, which in this case would be the less than honest...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah, definitely need to stop doing that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so does that homework sound manageable?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I can do that. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So if you can get a few of those kind of written up, the automatic thoughts and the adaptive responses um and then we can try to get you scheduled in before Saturday.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That would be great, I really appreciate it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. Thanks Maria.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

video_details.title: REBT Role-Play - Addressing Belief Regarding Expectation of Respect
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy (REBT) is used to treat frustration. The REBT role-play features a client (played by an actress) who believes she must have respect from her coworkers.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Lisa, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Good, how are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. How has the anxiety been going?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, since last session it seems to be in check. Nothing really major has been going on with it, so I think I'm getting to a point where it's under control.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, subsided a bit? That's good. How have things been going at work lately?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So work's a little bit of a different story. We have our daily meetings and I actually had to pull one of my coworkers aside because I feel like they undermine me all the time and they don't give me the respect basically that I deserve. So I took her outside after the meeting and laid into her about it. And afterwards, the next day, she came back at me again but it was worse even after talking to her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so talking to her didn't improve your situation. You mentioned she's not showing you respect and that you deserve respect. Tell me about that belief. Remember the ABC model we talked about—activating events, beliefs, and consequences in REBT? Tell me about that belief.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I just feel that I do a good job and I deserve to be respected by my coworkers.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, are there levels of respect? Like is there a certain level of respect that you demand or need?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know if there's a certain level, but I feel just like I deserve it, you know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what did she do that convinced you that she wasn't meeting that level of respect?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well she was shooting down my ideas and just kind of made me feel like a fool, basically. I just didn't understand.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so she had criticisms of your ideas. That would upset anybody. But were those criticisms unusual given the tone of these meetings? Is this a type of meeting where people criticize each other in a constructive way?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you criticized other coworkers?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So do you think that her criticism was within normal limits, within what you see there regularly?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean now that you point it out, I guess I can view it in that way that it wasn't too far out of line the first time. But then after I talked to her, it just felt like she was purposely trying to nitpick, if you will.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so maybe the second time around she was actively showing you disrespect just because you came after her, or was that within normal limits too?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean I guess I may have gone at her a little harshly, but I felt at the time that it was reasonable.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so you felt that she was a bit harsh, you talked to her about it, but then she's become more harsh. So where do you stand with her now with the meetings?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I've just been trying not to talk to her, and obviously in a work situation, that's not convenient.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, let's work this through using the ABC model. What would the activating event be here in this situation?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So I guess the confrontation I had with her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You could look at that as an activating event. Another way is her criticism of you was the activating event and your conversation with her was the consequence. Let's work it through with the activating event being what she said. Does that seem reasonable?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright so all activating events are filtered through our belief system. So what would your beliefs be in that scenario?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: She criticized me and I felt disrespected. My belief is that I deserve respect.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, so you have the activating event, the criticism, processed through your belief that you deserve respect. You mentioned a feeling—tell me what that feeling was.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Being upset and disrespected, aggravation, frustration.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, the frustration would be one of the consequences. You have the activating event: she criticizes you. Your belief is that you deserve respect and clearly she violated that belief. Were there any other consequences?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it's the kind of disarray or the tension I guess now in the office.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's definitely a consequence. I'm thinking there's an intermediate consequence though. You had that feeling of frustration and what's the next thing you did after that meeting was over?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh well, I confronted her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You confronted her. And that confrontation it would appear has led her to come on more strongly with her criticisms, which is another activating event. You see how the A and the B and the C paradigm can fit into what happened at work?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It does. Yeah, when you put it that way and say it's cyclical, I can visualize it going around like a carousel.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Exactly. It helps you see what caused what and what could be changed in the future. We try to help people move from rigid thinking to more flexible thinking. A rigid belief system would be 'I demand and deserve respect' at this particular level. Is that a fair assessment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Maybe a more flexible way of thinking would be that you'd like respect, but if you don't get it, you can still function. I can see that's tough for you. Tell me about that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean I understand what you're saying. I guess it's just like the anxiety we worked on, it's just getting there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you willing to challenge your beliefs in this instance?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How long have you had this belief that you deserve respect?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh gosh, since I was like a teenager, so a long time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So this has been a relatively persistent part of your life. Changing it's going to be work. So next time she is criticizing you in a meeting, if you filter that through a flexible belief system... how do you feel it now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it starts in my stomach and then goes all the way up.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So that'll be your first physiological reaction. But if you can pause that moment and apply more flexible thinking like 'I'd like respect, but I can function without it.' Are there other areas of life where you do get respect?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, from my friends and my family, it's actually mutual respect. I give them respect and they give me respect.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so that need is being met elsewhere. Maybe she never really intended to be disrespectful because criticism is part of those meetings. What do you think would happen if you ran that criticism through the flexible belief system next time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I think over time I wouldn't get that initial punch to the gut and I wouldn't have the urge to lash out at her, especially if it is constructive criticism, resulting in less tension in our office.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Functioning in the office would improve and stress would be reduced. Is there a way to smooth things over with this coworker and explain you understand more about her criticisms?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think I'd be able to approach her and maybe ask her to get coffee and talk it over. Maybe I misunderstood her in the first meeting and she didn't mean to undermine me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Having a discussion would be helpful. You can't control someone else's behavior, but it would give you an idea of her intentions and how to repair the relationship so it functions.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, because I certainly don't want upper management to get involved and there be a bigger issue.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That would be a good application of coping skills and flexible thinking. Is that something you can try over the course of the next week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I will definitely try.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Our plan has two parts: smoothing things over with her, and moving from the rigid 'I deserve respect' to 'I would like respect but I'll function adequately without respect from everyone.' Does it all make sense to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's pretty clear, you explained it really well, so thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so let's work on those two elements and check in next time you come in. Does that sound good?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sounds great. Thanks.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks Lisa.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thanks.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play - Exposure and Response Prevention - Later Session
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which exposure and response prevention is used to treat obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). This later session role-play addresses symptoms including fear or germs, repetitive hand-washing, catastrophizing, and anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Victoria. How are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm doing okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're doing okay? It's been a while now, you've been practicing with the waiting after you wash your hands. How's that been going for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I think it's been going pretty well. I've been able to wait pretty good. I started out slow, like you suggested, with three minutes, then five minutes. I got up to about 15 minutes. There were some times I was really proud of myself because I actually forgot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You forgot to wash your hands entirely?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So when was the next time you washed them?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When I would go to eat dinner.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Which is when you would normally wash your hands.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So really, you touched something that had germs, and you had some anxieties, you had to get to that waiting period, but then the anxiety subsided to a point where...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I forgot about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It just wasn't a priority. You just completely forgot and went on with your day?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I was really proud of myself, but I got really concerned because I got sick recently, and I'm afraid it's from one of those times that I didn't wash my hands.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, tell me about the sickness.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, my throat started to hurt real bad, and I was just really congested. All I could think about was, 'it's because I didn't wash my hands when I went to the store or when I went to my car or when I touched a jacket that's been everywhere.'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How many times do you normally get—it sounds like a cold?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, it was kind of a light cold. It went away in a few days.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So how many times a year would you get something like that normally?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I get sick quite often because of my job. I'm around a lot of people and hand sanitizer can only work so much. I do get sick.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's been six weeks since you started waiting. I think it was around session three where we talked about putting a time gap between when you touch something and when you wash your hands. And you got a cold once. Would that be out of the ordinary to get a cold one time in six weeks this time of year?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I suppose not. The rational part of me knows that I get sick, but then just because I'm trying something new with the waiting and then the not washing, I'm just afraid that there was a correlation.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're afraid they were linked—that one caused the other. And that could have happened. But let's talk about the cold. You said it was a couple days?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it wasn't severe. I took some over-the-counter medicine and slept it off.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it wasn't a catastrophe.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I've definitely been sicker in my life. It did seem like one of those ones that I get every now and then.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So when we spoke, I remember you said the worst case scenario, the reason that you're thinking so much about the germs on your hands, is that it could make you sick. But you did get sick, and you were able to tolerate it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I was, which I found kind of odd because I was panicked at the beginning when I started to feel the itchy throat and headaches.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sure, it's miserable, right? Nobody wants to get sick.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: And I got concerned that it was because of that, but then it just subsided. I felt a little better as the days went on. I felt better about it happening.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: About the whole getting sick?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: And just starting to recover, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the worst case scenario occurred and you survived. And again, we don't know if the amount of hand washing you were doing before the Exposure Response Prevention would have prevented the cold or not. You do get sick several times in a year. So we do know that you survived it and it wasn't as bad looking back at it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: In my head, not washing my hands and the sick that I would get is a lot worse, like hospital worthy. And this was, like I said, over-the-counter and relaxing a little bit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So not pleasant, but survivable?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it definitely wasn't pleasant, but it wasn't as bad as it could have gone in my mind.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So presume for a moment that it was a consequence of not immediately washing your hands. What would you rather have: the occasional cold like that or the excessive hand washing and the anxiety?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I definitely don't like the excessive hand washing. It ruins my skin, it's expensive, and it makes me feel bad about myself. I guess the trade-off is if I get a little sick, then that would be okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And again, that's presuming that it did cause you to get sick, which it may not have.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I suppose that's true.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I want to point out too, that I remember when we first started the exposure response prevention exercise, we did it right here in session by touching the arms of the chair. And I see now your arms are...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, I didn't even notice I was doing that. I don't feel like I need to go wash my elbows or anything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You don't feel that compulsion?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I don't. I know that it's dirty, but I don't feel that need to go wash my hands right now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So your anxiety increased a little when I pointed out that you were touching it, but not as much as it did before. About a two?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, on that scale, I think it'd be about a two.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: About a two. With one being the lowest anxiety and ten being the highest. When I pointed it out, you were a one before that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So now you're aware of it a little bit, and you're a little anxious?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, not so much anymore. You mentioned it, I got anxious for a moment, and then it's just kind of like, 'Oh well, you're already doing it,' and nothing bad's happening right now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well good, you've made a lot of progress. You're still going to have some anxiety from time to time; it's part of life. One of the things I hope you've gained from this is that just like you tolerated being sick, you can tolerate that anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The fear of being anxious kind of causes a vicious cycle. You'll do many things to get rid of that anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Because it gets really bad. It starts consuming me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I remember many weeks ago you had the urge to go wash your hands right away. You were anxious. You've become less anxious by waiting. At some point you have to learn to tolerate that remaining anxiety. And it sounds like that's the direction you're moving.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: To kind of live through it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I would really say that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So tolerating that degree of anxiety, is that better than the frequent hand washing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The little bit of unpleasantness versus the depression and the anxiety that comes with washing my hands, I'd really rather take the little unpleasantness. In the grand scheme of things, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So where are you now in terms of how many minutes do you wait after you touch something?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: On average, because I write them down, I wait a good seven minutes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I want to continue ramping that up. If you had no awareness of germs, how many times would you normally wash your hands in a day?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd wash them after eating or before eating, or touching anything like a toilet. It's definitely a fraction of what I do now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So maybe ten times, a dozen times would be normal for you. And you were way beyond that before. We'll keep working those minutes up, trying to get to the point where you're only washing your hands when you normally would.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Choosing to wash my hands instead of needing to wash my hands.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sometimes you'll touch unpleasant objects and you won't be in a place where you can wash your hands. You have to be able to tolerate that anxiety until you get to a place where you can wash them.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So let's move up to 10 minutes between now and I see you next week. And you're timing this, right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I am timing it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good. We'll move from seven to 10. We'll keep getting further away and hope that we can get you onto a normal schedule. Does that sound good?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It does.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Thanks Victoria.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

video_details.title: Motivational Interviewing for Tobacco Cessation

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello, Maria, it's nice to see you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hello. I wish I could say it's nice to see you, but it's never good to go to the doctor.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Unfortunately for me, I hear that a lot. So we're going to be talking about ways to manage your blood clots and options for treatment, but first I'd like to check in on a few things. The first is your smoking. You were at a half-pack during your last visit, and we talked about how important it is for you to quit. I'd say it's even more important now that smoking is associated with DVT. So, have you quit?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I haven't quit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, do you remember our conversation from our last visit? That's when I gave you the information about quitting smoking and the contact number for a tobacco treatment specialist.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I remember. But no, I didn't quit and no, I didn't call her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And why is that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm not ready. I'm too upset to talk about this. I don't mean to be rude, doctor, but I've had a hard time lately and I'm not in the mood for you to get mad at me for not quitting. I'll let you know when I'm ready and we can talk about it. But here now today, I'm here to talk about my blood clots.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, we're on the same page then because that's exactly why I'm talking to you about quitting smoking, because smoking is a major risk factor for DVT. Even if we treat you now, if you don't quit smoking, I'm afraid the blood clots will return again.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Let's just talk about my treatment right now, okay?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello Maria, it's nice to see you again.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hello. I wish I could say it's nice to see you, but it's never good to have to come to the doctor.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Unfortunately for me, I hear that a lot. So we're going to talk today about how to manage your blood clots and some options for treating, but first I wanted to check in on your smoking status. In our last visit, I recommended that you begin to think about quitting, and I'd be interested in hearing your thoughts.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I haven't really thought about it, actually. I thought about canceling this appointment because I knew you were going to bring it up again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Talking about smoking with me is hard for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, it's because you're going to tell me to quit like you always do. And then it feels like you're just like everyone else—like my caseworker, the building manager. Everybody seems to think they know what I need to do and nobody thinks I know anything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So when it comes to smoking, you feel that other people want to tell you what to do and make your decisions for you. You don't feel heard or respected.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No respect. That's it, yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I just want to say that I am very glad you decided to come in today so we can take care of this blood clot, because blood clots are very serious and I know you're concerned. As your provider, I have to be honest and say that smoking can cause blood clots. But hopefully, some of the information I give you today will help you in your decision to quit smoking. Having said that, I know my opinion is not the deciding factor. Quitting smoking is a decision only you can make.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I'm really glad I came in, too. I have to get this blood clot condition under control, I know that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would it be okay with you if I share some information about smoking and blood clots? I can tell you what I know and then we'll see what you think.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. I mean, I don't know that I will quit, but I will listen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, what do you think?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I always thought that the blood clots came from my mother, you know, like passed down, like genetics. I didn't know that smoking could cause this. I just thought that blood clots ran in my family. I guess I also didn't get how dangerous this clotting can be.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You seem surprised and a little more aware now of the smoking risks.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess so, yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So Maria, I'd like to get a better sense of what you think about smoking. So on a scale of one to ten, with one being you don't think it is at all important that you quit and ten being you're ready to quit today, where would you put yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, if you had asked me when I first came in, I would have said a less than one. But now, I would have to say a four.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Why a four and not a lower number?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's a good question. Let me think about it. I guess it's a four because of the blood clots. The blood clots are really heavy on my mind right now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So having a better understanding of how smoking adds to the risk of blood clots increases your desire to quit.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A little, yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What else, if anything, makes quitting important to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You know, the bigger thing for me is the fear of being evicted from my apartment. There's a rule that we can't smoke in the house, and I stick to it for the most part, but the other day I smoked out the window. That was only the second time I've done it. But don't you know the building manager caught me? So now I am sure she's going to be watching me even more. I can't lose my apartment.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The possibility of losing your apartment because of smoking really upsets you, in addition to your health.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would hate to think that Santi and Teo lost their home because their mom chose smoking over abiding by a stupid code, even if I hate that rule. I smoked when I was pregnant with them, and thank holy mother, they were born healthy. I don't think I could live with myself if they lost their home because of something I'm doing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it sounds like your priority in life is taking care of and providing for your children. It's obvious that you're a good mom, and if you had to leave your home because you were smoking, that would be tough to bear.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, it would.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So let me ask you a slightly different question. On that same scale of one to ten, how would you rate your confidence to quit?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Confidence? Ooh, I'd have to say a two.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you are not feeling very confident right now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, no, not confident at all. I mean, I've tried to quit so many times and I just can't do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you've been persistent in trying and haven't been successful yet. Still, you said a two and not a one. I'm curious about that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, the only reason I said a two is that I tried quitting smoking when I was pregnant with Santi and Teo both. I went for two months without a cigarette with Teo, and I didn't make it past that. And I was really mad at myself for that. I really wanted to quit for my babies, and I failed. I guess I'm just hopeless. I mean, who keeps smoking when there's a baby inside?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like you really feel like you've let yourself and your children down, and that's hard to accept given how much you love your kids.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, and I'm doing it again right now by not following the rules. I'm addicted to cigarettes, just like a drug addict. In the end, the cigarettes always win.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what do you think Santi and Teo think about your smoking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Santi yells at me. And sometimes Teo cries when I go out to smoke. He says, 'Mama, smoking is bad.'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you know it would be best for you and your children if you quit. If you had the right support and tools to manage this addiction, if you believed you could do it, you would.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd like to think so, but I just don't think I can do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You quit for two months when you were pregnant with Teo. How did you do it then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, I just did it. I fought the urges with sucking on straws and some hard candies. I just did it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, so you were able to quit on your own for two months. That's impressive. Have you ever used any other form of help, like nicotine replacement or support groups?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. I think people can quit if they really want to. I'm just too weak.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Ah, well, you must be pretty hard on yourself. What would you say if I told you that very few people—only 4% of us—are able to quit successfully cold turkey?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Really? Is that true?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yes. And most people try many times before they're successful. There are medications and groups, and I'd be happy to share that information with you. I'd like to help you if that's something that you'd like.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I don't know, let me think about it. Can you give me the information again—the booklets and brochure you gave me before? I didn't want to tell you, but I threw them away when I got home. But I really want to read them this time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's great, Maria. You can look them over, and I'll have our tobacco treatment specialist, Sonia, follow up with you. We have an excellent tobacco treatment program here, and I believe that Sonia can help you quit when you're ready. When would be a good time to check back in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: She can call me next week and I'll let you know. I may be ready to try again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Absolutely, and I'll have Sonia call you. I just want you to know that I understand how hard it is for you to talk about quitting smoking, and I really appreciate it. So, would you like to talk about how to manage your blood clots?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, that sounds good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play - Exposure and Response Prevention - Early Session
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which exposure and response prevention is used to treat obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). This early session role-play addresses symptoms including fear or germs, repetitive hand-washing, catastrophizing, and anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Victoria, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Very good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Very good. How has the anxiety been around the germs?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I still catch myself almost like double-touching, like going to touch it and then reeling back. I'm starting to notice it, but I still have that anxiety. I still don't want to touch anything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What were some things that you've touched between the last session and this session that have distressed you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I had to go to the store, which is always a nightmare. I don't even like touching my credit card because it's been in so many machines. I keep thinking about the food and how many people have touched it. Shopping's a nightmare for me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So really in a supermarket, everything can be containing germs. And that's what you're thinking about as you're walking through and shopping.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, everything does.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We talked last time about exposure and response prevention. I indicated that we might try some experiments right in session to see how we can move forward in treating your fear and obsession with germs.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It is, it really is.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there anything in this office that you would look at and think, 'I don't want to touch that because it could have germs on it'?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm really not liking the covers on this chair. My clothes are protecting me from the rest of the chair, but I have no sleeves on, so I don't like touching the armrest and the covers.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So even thinking about your arms touching the back of the chair and the armrest?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm not liking it. I feel like I should probably go wash my arms.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What would happen if you put your hands right on the arm covers? What would your usual reaction be to that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: To go wash my arms until I feel like it's gone. Until all the dirt is gone.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how long would that take you to be sure?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Something like this, I'd probably be in there for a good five, ten minutes just washing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how many times a day would you end up washing your hands?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't keep track anymore. It makes me upset how many times.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'd like you to try to put your hands on the arms of the chair. Try to stay like that. Tell me what's going through your mind.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just feel the chair and I don't like it. I feel like I can feel everybody who's ever touched it. They probably didn't wash their hands before they touched this and it's making me uncomfortable.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you're anxious now. Is it tolerable?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Scaling from one to ten, where are you now as you sit here with your hands on the armrest?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd say about a six or seven.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And are you feeling an urge to go wash your hands?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I am.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I want you to sit with it for a few seconds. What's the ultimate fear? What's going to happen if you don't go wash your hands now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm going to get sick and I'm going to die. And I don't want to die.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you feel yourself getting sick?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel like it's harder to breathe. My chest is kind of tight.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tight? You can still breathe though.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can breathe.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Go ahead and lift your hands up. Is that any better, now that you're touching the seat of the chair?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: But I feel like if I touch my clothes, that's even worse. Then I'll have to go home and change my clothes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The thought now is probably that you'd really like to wash your hands. I'd like you to try to hold out for a little bit.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: At this point I feel like they're already contaminated. I'm just trying to avoid touching anything else.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So your anxiety was a six or seven before, where is it now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It is a little better. I want to say about a three or four. I feel better that my arms are off it and I'm focusing on breathing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's a little easier to breathe now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A little, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If you did wash your hands, what would the anxiety move to?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A one. It would take a little bit to get there after actually washing, but then I'll feel okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you've moved from a six or seven to a three or four without washing your hands at all.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh wow. I didn't consider that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you doing okay? I want to use this moment to give you some ideas for the next few weeks. Try progressively to wait more and more time between feeling that urge and when you actually wash your hands.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Try to delay and not wash them immediately. Eventually, I want you to have more control over it. Where's the anxiety right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel like it's at a two. I'd still like to go wash my hands, but I don't feel that overwhelming anxiety anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And no trouble breathing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Actually I haven't even thought about that in a while.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Go ahead and wash your hands now. When you come back, we'll lay down structured amounts of time between when you touch something and when you wash your hands.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play - Subjective Units of Distress, Anxiety, and Public Speaking
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which the cognitive behavior therapy technique of implementing subjective units of distress is used to treat anxiety related to public speaking.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Danielle, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm good, how are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm good, thanks for asking. What's been going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, last time we spoke, you know, I just got a promotion.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's great news.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, great news. I'm really, really excited about the opportunity and the career advancement, but I just really—it just hit me that I'm going to be having to give presentations and really kind of be a team leader and kind of be the face of a group of individuals and it's kind of making me a little shaky.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A little shaky. Are you a big fan of public speaking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not a—I wouldn't say a big fan. No, it's been bearable, but the thought of having to do it continuously is definitely a little frightening for me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's frightening for you. How often would you have to do—you say continuously, how often would it be in this new job?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: In this new job, I would actually have to meet with them every week.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Weekly? And how many people on the team that you now supervise?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: There's 10 people, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so you have 10 people that you're going to have to speak to, right? And how long is the talk each week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Normally it's about like half an hour.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Half an hour? Have you ever had to do it in the past or anything like it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've done something like this for school, but definitely not for 30 minutes, not for half an hour.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so the length of time is a major stressor. How about the number of people? How about like 10? Is that...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's—that's a—I mean, when I did it for school, it was a group of us, so it was less anxiety, but to be doing it by myself, for, you know, and all attention on me, that's... yeah, and 10 people, that's a lot of people looking up to me and, you know...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so the number of people being 10, that stresses you a bit. A little anxiety there. A good amount of anxiety. And then the duration.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, absolutely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, so 10 people for a minute, that wouldn't be too bad?

diarization.speaker: Patient
