diarization.text: That's not too bad. I could handle that. I could handle that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Or half hour with like one person?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I could definitely handle that. One-on-one's not too bad. One-on-one's not too bad. Um, but the thought of 10 people staring at me, hanging on my every word for that long, that's—that's—definitely puts me out there in terms of anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so there's a lot of anxiety there. And that's painful for you. Let's—let's do this. I know that you'd mentioned that you're taking over for somebody, but they still work there. How long do you have before you need to start taking over that responsibility?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have about six weeks.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: About six weeks. All right. So you have six weeks to become reasonably comfortable with speaking in front of 10 people for half hour once a week. So what I'd like to do is, I'd like to develop some steps that you can take at work. Okay? So I know, you know, you do a lot of different things at work and you mentioned that you're good with people individually. So I'm going to create some steps that you can actually conduct at work, you know, collaboratively with you. I want you to be a big part of this. And I want to rank them from the least anxiety-provoking to the most anxiety-provoking. Okay? And let's use about five levels, five steps. So we're going to develop together with you five steps. So the fifth one will be the hardest. And I'm—I'm going to take a wild guess and say that would be speaking in front of all 10 people for half hour.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. So that's the most stressful it can get.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, definitely. That's the most stressful part of your job now, or what your job will be when you take that over.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Definitely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So let's make that a—if you agree, we'll make that kind of a five out of five.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so five is the maximum level of anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can agree to that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So let me think of some other ways you can approach this. You said you're really good one-on-one. How about with two people? Like if you're in a room with two people and you talk to them.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's not—that's not too bad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's not—that's not too bad? That's definitely not a five out of five.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, it's definitely not a five out of five.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So let's make that one of the steps. How about speaking to two of the people for around 15 minutes? We'll make that one of the steps. Okay. And how about another step would be speaking to four people for 15 minutes. Okay? Which—which of those two would be—would be scarier?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The four people for 15 minutes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The four people for 15 minutes. All right. And then if we were to say four people for half hour, what would that rank?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would definitely say that's like a four and a half or four.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so that's—that's high up then. All right. So so far if we're to rank these in terms of anxiety from the least anxiety-provoking, a couple people, 15 minutes, you think you could do that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's manageable.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Double that number of people to four for the same amount of time, that would be the next level up. Taking those four people and talking to them for half hour, maybe one more level up. So where would all 10 people for 15 minutes rank? Would that be more anxiety-provoking than four for half hour?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Definitely because of the duration, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But not as anxiety-provoking as 10 people for half hour.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, not—no. I think that would definitely be my...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's still the top. Yeah, that's at the top. So nothing I've introduced as a step as as anxiety-provoking as all 10 for half hour.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So if that's a five, then a four would be 10 people for 15 minutes, and a three would be the four people for half hour, and two would be the four people for 15 minutes, and the one would be two people for 15 minutes. And and I can write all this out for you. Okay. All right. Uh, would you agree that's an accurate ranking from the most stressful, most anxiety-provoking down to the least?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I would absolutely agree to that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you'd agree that the first step, the the least anxiety-provoking, the two people for 15 minutes, that's not a huge deal for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You think you could handle that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I could handle it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So what my hope is, is that as you move into each step, you conduct that step, you take part in that behavior enough times to where even though it's a little anxiety-provoking at the beginning, you you do it enough times to where the anxiety comes down. Okay. So you have six weeks to get through really four of the steps because the final step will be the all 10 people for... yeah. So you have six weeks to get through these four steps. Okay. So for this—let's use this first step for this next week because I'll see you again in a week. Okay. And meet with two people and you probably want to vary it, like two different people, okay, each time. Uh, if you didn't, they also might wonder what you're doing if you meet with the same people over and over, right? So, but you know, make it productive, make it part of your job, you know, make it something that's necessary for your job, like you could see an opportunity where you have to talk. Remember it's about 15 minutes. Okay. If it ends up being 10 or 20, you know, about 15 minutes. Okay. All right. And meet with them a few times this week. And I'm hoping that through this week, you'll notice that your anxiety decreases. So right after the meeting, if you could just take a quick second, um, and note kind of how stressed you were at the beginning, maybe a scale one to 10, 10 being really anxious, and how stressed you were at the end. And any thoughts you might be having in terms of like what you were thinking while it was going on or what you're thinking afterwards. Like maybe you're going to think, well, I I handled that pretty well.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Or maybe you're thinking, that was still a little stressful. Okay. Or somewhere in between.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That makes complete sense to me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So we're going to take this in gradual steps. Okay. And we won't move to the next level until you're somewhat comfortable with the first one.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's great. I really appreciate that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. I think I think that'll help you to kind of transition gradually because because I think part of this for you is that all-at-once. Yeah. Like you've been promoted, this is all new. Yeah. And all of a sudden 10 people for half hour. Yeah. Whereas if we just kind of move up the level of anxiety-provoking stimuli gradually, you might become accustomed to it. Mhm. And by the time you you get to 10 for 15 minutes, you might think, ah, 10 for half hour's not that much different.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A little more relaxed, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Um, I want to add to this too, that you're in a setting—like one of the things you might be thinking when you're presenting is you're kind of you're kind of stuck there. Like you mentioned all eyes on you. Mhm. And you're in an office setting, we've talked about your workplace before, where if you needed to, you could always say, 'I need a minute,' and you could step out.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you always have an escape plan.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you may have to use that from time to time. Even when you are somewhat comfortable later on down the road, you might be having a day where you're particularly anxious. Remember you always have that plan there.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right? Not everybody that speaks publicly has that option or at least not that conveniently. Yeah. Right? Because some public speaking, if you said you need to take a minute and leave, like if you're at the podium in front of a hundred people...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: People might wonder what's going on.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But with 10 people they might think, you know, you might have to go grab some paperwork or...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Get a drink of water or something, yeah, something small.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, any variety of things. And you could even put another person, you know, — give them something to do, like 'Can you take over this part? — can you discuss this or figure this out while I go and...' All right. So keep in that keep in mind as we as use the self-talk which we talked about before, that you can tell yourself, 'I can always escape.' Right? And you do, it's actually true. You can always escape and you can return to the meeting. Right? If you if you need to. Okay. And if that does happen, try not to interpret that as a huge setback. Okay. This safety plan is there to keep you safe. Yeah. To reduce the anxiety, it's it's an escape plan.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So we're going to ease you into it. Right? And then I want you to keep in mind you have a way out. All right. And know that anxiety levels do, uh, change from time to time. Mhm. Meaning you might get comfortable with one level and the next day it might be a little more distress with that, but the next day it might be a little better.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're not always going to see a decrease, but in general, I think that you will. I hope that you will.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. But that's one of the reasons it's important to kind of jot down what you're thinking so we can develop some adaptive responses to try to increase the chances that you will feel less anxious.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So on the way out today, um, before you set the next appointment, I'm going to jot down those levels for you. Okay. But this week, I want you to just work on Step 1.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Two people, 15 minutes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Two people for 15 minutes.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Because we have—we have time. So there's no—you have six weeks.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So if you feel ambitious and you want to see those same and there's a reason to, and you want to see those same two people for a little longer or you want to see four people, you can do that. But primarily we're just focused on getting through Step 1. Okay. And seeing how the the anxiety changes. We hope it decreases.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. That makes sense to me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So I'll get you set up with another appointment. I'll get that information jotted down and then I'll check in with you next week and we'll see how things are going.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Awesome. Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Thanks Danielle.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play - Behavioral Activation and Postpartum Depression
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which behavioral activation techniques are used to treat symptoms of postpartum depression. Behavioral therapeutic components represent a key part of cognitive behavior therapy (CBT).

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Sarah, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Doing well?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A little better than last time, or worse?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Kind of no change.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No change?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're still having sadness?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And frustrated?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me what's been going on this last week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mary's been crying a lot and I'm really tired. I've needed extra help with her because I just can't get out of bed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How much have you been sleeping each night on average?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe eight or ten hours, maybe more.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how long did you sleep each night before you had Mary?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe six or eight at the most.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So your sleep habits have changed. What else has changed besides feeling sad?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm feeling like I'm not doing well with Mary and maybe I should think about getting a job again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What specifically is contributing to that thought?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: With George, I would hop right up when he cried. With Mary, I just want to roll over.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're less enthusiastic about caring for her than you were with George?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's a good way of putting it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You still do care for her though?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Anything else that's changed?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can't think of anything, but I'm sure there is.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me more about the sadness. Where do you think that's coming from?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe because she's crying all the time and I don't feel like I did with George. People say I'm doing a great job, but I don't feel like it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: People are giving you the same input, but you're feeling differently about it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Their feedback hasn't changed, but your feelings have.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: To the point where you feel you should get a job and put Mary in daycare?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, she's only six weeks now, so she would go to daycare.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What comes to mind when you consider working full-time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mixed feelings. I stayed home with George until school, and I feel Mary wouldn't get the same experience, but she's not getting it now anyway.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Like you're just not doing the same quality job.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What kind of things did you do with George that you looked forward to?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would sing to him and read books. We'd go to the playground often.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Like most days?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Pretty much, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you done those same things with Mary?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I try, but she's fussier and doesn't respond to singing or reading like he did.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Each baby is different, but you'd prefer if her temperament was more like George's.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If it were, do you think that would break you out of these feelings of sadness?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would like to hope so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So part of this could be adapting to her personality.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What else could be a part of it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Some of my girlfriends are going back to work, and I feel like they look down on me because I don't.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So they look upon you negatively because you don't work?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have evidence that's the way they feel?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's just a feeling. One friend said she's always working while I have 'so much time'. It felt like she was judging me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I can see how that would hurt. But this sadness is markedly worse than what you've experienced before.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: After you had George, there was no period of sadness?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, just adjustment. I was ecstatic to have him.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you don't have that same feeling now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's not that I'm not happy to have her, but I have George to take care of too. Mary's constantly crying and I get frustrated.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're adapting to her needs and George's changing role. There's a lot going on.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're sleeping more, not enjoying Mary like you hoped, and seeing things negatively.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When Mary cries, I just give up and hand her off, and others seem to soothe her right away.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Which makes it more frustrating. Have you had feelings of guilt?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I feel like I'm not a good mom to her like I was with George.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It comes back to the feeling that you aren't providing the same quality of care.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I want to look at behaviors. Thoughts are what you're thinking; behaviors are what you're doing.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's important to engage in activities that would normally bring enjoyment, even if you don't feel it right now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Makes sense.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What activities were you looking forward to doing with Mary?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Reading and singing to her, and holding her when she's calm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Reading and singing. Anything else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was looking forward to taking her to the park, but it hasn't happened.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you tried to go to the park?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We went once with friends, but she got fussy. The next time I planned to go, I just didn't.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What led to you not going?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I got sad thinking about the last time and didn't want to be unhappy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So sadness and negative thoughts are the obstacle. Let's schedule reading, singing, and the park.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How many times a day did you read with George?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Every day for about 20 minutes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's set a goal of 20 minutes of reading a day, Monday through Friday.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What time of day would be realistic?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe right after dinner, around 6:30 PM.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's set 6:30 as the target. Can you push yourself to do that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you believe it would be good for Mary?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When you feel derailed, remember 'this is good for her'. What about singing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd like to start singing favorites like Twinkle Twinkle again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When would be a good time for that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe right before bedtime, around 7:30 or 8:00.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Shortly after reading. Do you think that would be good for her?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How many days a week would you like to sing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Eventually, every day again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's start with four times a week. And what about the park?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe once or twice a week.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's go with once. What were you thinking when you sighed just now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's just draining to think about going because I'm so tired.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Could family help you get out once a week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My mom and mother-in-law live close. I could ask them for help.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does that external motivation help?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I feel I have to show I'm as good a mom as I was with George.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Evaluating the evidence, you do seem to be as good a mom. There's just a disconnect with your thoughts.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, we have reading five times a week, singing four times, and the park once. Does that seem realistic?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If you miss a day, accept it as an isolated incident. Don't let it predict the next day.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you stick with those levels? We'll follow up next week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks Sarah.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play -  Problem Solving and Decatastrophizing after Job Loss
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which cognitive-behavioral therapy techniques, including problem solving and decastatrophizing, are used to treat alcohol use, depression, and anxiety after a job loss.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Hazel, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not well. Remember I told you they were downsizing at my job? I've been there 20 years and they let me go.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, that's terrible. I'm sorry to hear that. Do you have any type of severance or anything like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. They let me go and I have nothing to go on. I don't know what to do. I've been at that job so long, I don't know how to do anything else.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You used to talk about that job. You were happy there.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I was. I envisioned doing that job for forever. Now that's not going to happen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How's this affect your financial outlook, like your bills and such?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, it's awful. It's really spiraled out of control. This was half of our income and it's gone. Because it was sudden, we didn't have time to prepare.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it caught you off guard. Do you have enough income with your husband's job to cover your basic bills?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We're a little bit behind so far. But if I don't find a job soon, I don't know how bad it's going to get.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you know about how long you have before you fail to meet any financial commitments?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My husband usually deals with the bills, but probably in another month or so it's going to get really bad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What thoughts have you been having?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I worry we're going to lose our house and be homeless. It's embarrassing. My kids are relying on us to meet their needs. I'm afraid that I won't get another job.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now you said you were laid off. Are you eligible for unemployment? Also, what about your educational background?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm not sure about unemployment yet. I just have my bachelor's.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's more than most. You have a bachelor's degree, you just haven't had to look for a job in 20 years. You probably thought you were going to retire there. This is a big identity shift for you. Did you ever have co-workers who voluntarily left for other jobs?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not that I was aware of. It was a pretty good job, so a lot of people stayed. One of my friends in a similar field left and eventually found another job, but it took a long time, like two years.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would you need to replace that full income to pay your bills or part of that income?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Full would be ideal, but we could probably survive on part of it. It's just not as well as we were living.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We've talked about problem-solving skills before. Have you applied any of those concepts to what's going on now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've been trying to think of different opportunities and being able to spend more time with my kids. I've been trying to think of the situation in other ways.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: At some point you need to replace the income. If a full-time job doesn't work out, could you look at part-time jobs?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've thought about it, but I'm having a hard time. If I only had a part-time job, I'd feel like I wasn't qualified or good enough for a full-time one.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you would internalize that and feel less valuable. That kind of thinking can impede your goals. What do you do when you're feeling worthless?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's not going well. I've been arguing with my husband and drinking a lot more. The depression has come back worse. It's become a cycle that just keeps snowballing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: These behaviors can be a self-fulfilling prophecy. You worry, then you drink to take away the pain, which leads to more dysfunction. It all starts with that thinking.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: But it's hard when I'm really depressed. I'm just home sitting about drinking while everyone else is carrying on with their life and I'm stuck here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're fulfilling that role of being worthless. Is that really what you want? Is that the most useful?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I know it's not helping. I've been thinking about trying to get more organized with the finances and figuring out exactly how much income we need, taking baby steps so it's not so overwhelming.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That makes sense. Figuring out the minimum you need is a logical first step. What do you think would get in the way? What obstacles do you see?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just the fear of the unknown. Worrying 'what if I don't get a job?' or 'what if we lose our house?'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That worry is nagging you. It's likely you'll get a job, but let's consider the worst-case scenario. Say you never find a job again. What would happen?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We'd probably have to get a smaller house or find a way around it. We've been through tough times. We would probably get through it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's an adaptive response. If you tell yourself you would survive even the worst-case scenario, what effect might that have on your mood?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When I really think about it, I feel less depressed and more able to cope. The reality isn't as bad as what's in my head.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: There's peace in accepting the worst-case scenario, even if it's unlikely. Probability is on your side. If you accept the worst case, you can reduce the alcohol and the depression. Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it makes a lot of sense.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's end there. For next week, try applying that adaptive self-talk when automatic thoughts come up. Fill out the thought record when you can. I'll see you in a week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Thanks.

video_details.title: Motivational Interviewing: Reflective Listening in Challenging Conversations
video_details.description:
This is a demonstration and comparison of styles between "business as usual" and Motivational Interviewing with a family member of an individual with a developmental disability.  In the first section, the professional does not use Motivational Interviewing. In the second section at 1:43, Motivational Interviewing trainer, Liz Barnett, uses Motivational Interviewing and reflective listening to establish a healthy and productive working relationship. 

This clip is taken from "Challenging Conversa

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Each of the programs had I spent one day and none of them worked and it was so it was so frustrating because I took so much time out of my work to go and I still couldn't find an appropriate placement for her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: My advice would be for you or your daughter to at least spend a week at the program. Again she needs to get the feel...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, we can't do that. I there's no way I can take her back I couldn't drag her back there. Either any of those programs.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what are you looking for then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I need your help to find a a program that fits her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If I give you three more programs will that work?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: But but what if they don't work? How about if I-

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You need to give it a chance. You need to go and visit again to at least one out of your busy-

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I actually came across a program which is perfect for her and I'd really would like for you to help me see if this could work. Um and I I'd rather for you to try to do that instead of me shopping around for other programs because so far the ones that have been offered me have not worked.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the program that you're interested, you want me to go with you or you want me to what do you want me to do?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I want you to I want you to see if um if if I could choose that program instead of one of the others that you have offered.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay well looking at my schedule it probably won't be until maybe two weeks. My schedule is pretty much tied up.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The case just got transferred to me so I'm not very familiar with your situation.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right, I um well my daughter's 17 years old. She um she's actually very high functioning thankfully and you know I went to three of these programs and none of them worked.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're look- you're looking for a day program. Right. Uh and something that really is good for your daughter.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right, right. And I mean I was looking for a a program that would stimulate her, you know, that would um that she'd really enjoy going to but um I mean they were either like babysitting programs or they were just um the participants were all at like different um developmental levels so that she couldn't really she couldn't make friends. Um they were they were not not good for her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You while you were there it was difficult your daughter didn't really kind of fit in or connect with anybody while you were visiting.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, no she did not. She um she just there just wasn't that that sense of like um that commonality you know just there was no um no basis for like friendships. There were there were some um young young people there who were like screaming yelling and um who were talking to themselves um and she didn't know how to engage.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And so so just there wasn't when when you visited they didn't sort of the program didn't help you to connect or help your daughter to connect to anything that was going on that you were just sort of a viewing it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right and well I mean I observed for a whole day each of these programs which was which took a lot of time. Yeah yeah I mean like you know I work full time and I don't it was very difficult to schedule time to go to these places and once I did it was just so disappointing.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play - Behavioral Activation and Depression
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which behavioral activation techniques are used to treat symptoms of depression. Behavioral therapeutic components represent a key part of cognitive behavior therapy (CBT).

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, Carly. How you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Doing okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're doing okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Not sure?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, it's just the same.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Still a little down?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I've been sleeping a lot. Um, going to work is a struggle. I don't really ever want to go. Um, just haven't been eating much. So, I think I've lost like ten pounds since past like four months or so. Um, just the guy, I don't know, I just haven't really been doing anything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Just been working.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But not much else.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I usually just go to work and go home.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me what happens after you arrive home? Like after work?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, well my fiancé tries to talk to me and really I just kind of want to go to sleep or just, I don't know. I tried reading the other day because I used to like that and it's just I think I got like into two pages and put the book down and decided to go to bed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What were you thinking when you put the book down?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just that I wasn't really happy doing it. I didn't really get any enjoyment out of it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And before you were depressed, which is I guess about eight months now, you did enjoy reading.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm. Oh yeah, all the time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what would you have thought if you had to put a book down back then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, I used to fall asleep reading. I would be up until like two in the morning just reading books.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Something you look forward to?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But not now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I just didn't really get any, I just wanted to try it and then I put it back down and was like...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Were there other things that you used to enjoy doing that you don't feel motivated or comfortable to do now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I used to be a runner. Um, and then I tried going for a run the other morning with my dog and I think we walked a block and that was pretty much it. I just couldn't wait for it to be over.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so it wasn't a pleasant experience. Was there any part of it you connected with when you were running? Like when you first started?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really. I mean it was a change to be outdoors. And I realized I hadn't really seen the sun in a while. But other than that, I just, I had the intention of going out to run, I had my running shoes on and my dog was really excited. And then by the time I got out there, I was like, yeah, we're gonna walk. And then I thought about walking like our normal route and by the time I got to the corner, I was like, yeah, we're gonna turn around and walk back.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what was the feeling like when you returned to your home after planning to run and then kind of walking and coming back?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Kind of a mix of like relief, just because it was over. And then I guess more sadness because I didn't do anything. I didn't do what I had intended to do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sadness, maybe disappointment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. So, I've seen you a few times now. And based on those conversations and of course what you've said today, it seems like you have for a variety of reasons given up on the activities that you used to enjoy. You're not motivated toward them anymore.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess you could say that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And that's a common symptom of depression. Right? I think we've, we've talked about this a little bit before. So it's, it's tough when you're depressed to find joy, satisfaction, happiness in activities that you once enjoyed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right? So we've been working with the cognitive piece, right? Like we did last time where we talked about the automatic thoughts that come up and kind of how that leads to some of the feelings of sadness and what we can do with the self-talk. But I'd like to talk about a different technique today that approaches the problem from a different angle. And we'll, we'll continue to work the cognitive angle, but I want to add a new angle.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And the technique is called behavioral activation. All right? So the theory behind it is that if you engage, if you schedule and engage in activities that you once enjoyed, even if you kind of have to fight your way through it a little bit, right? Like with the running. That that will connect to your mood. Right? Remember we believe in cognitive therapy that affect and behavior and cognition are all connected. Right? So what you're thinking affects your behavior and your mood. And what you do, your behavior, affects your thinking and your mood. Does that kind of make sense based on what we've talked about?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It does, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you mentioned the reading was one thing you, you liked to do that's, it's tough to do now. You tried unsuccessfully with the reading and the running. Anything else you could think of that maybe we could plan for you to do, even if it's just for a short time, even if it's a little bit uncomfortable, that we could plan to do that would be an activity you used to enjoy?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, my fiancé and I used to go out with two other couples and we used to go out once or twice a week and even if it's just a, just each other's houses. Um, but we haven't really seen them in a while. Um, they've tried to schedule things, but I've kind of come up with reasons of not feeling well or to kind of just stay home.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So they're trying to initiate reading, going out, doing something and you're, you're kind of pushing them off.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I just, I haven't really wanted to see anybody lately.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so that's, so we have reading, running, and then going out with these two other couples. Anything else you could think of that you used to really enjoy before that you can't quite motivate yourself to do now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I mean I used to like going for like just walks and shopping with my fiancé. Like we used to spend a lot of time together and lately it's just kind of I come home, I say hello, we eat dinner and then I kind of do my own thing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So spending time with your fiancé outside the house in some manner. Shopping was one example.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any other, any other activities?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Like movies or going out to eat or...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I would kind of put those in with like the things that we would do outside together. Like we would try to switch it up every now and then.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so that's distinct from what you did with the couples because that's just you and your fiancé.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So let's do this. Um, we'll make collaboratively with you a schedule that involves those four activities.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But I want to make it realistic. Right? You've tried a couple times, you weren't successful, so we don't want to be too ambitious. But I want to try to plan a schedule you can get in the habit of doing these activities again.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right? So let's start with the kind of I guess the simplest in terms of logistics, which would be probably the reading. Would it be possible say five nights out of seven to read for ten or fifteen minutes? Like I know you're gonna have to force your way through it a little bit, but...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think it's something I could try to do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're going to have automatic thoughts that come up, right? Like just like you did before. And you're going to be tempted to give up. But I want you to try to push through, say at least ten minutes. Okay? So focus on that as you go into it. This is a behavior exercise, but of course it has a cognitive component. So kind of think, you know, I just have to make this ten minutes.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right? And again, you might not really enjoy it the same way you did before, we kind of know that. But over time that may change.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right? So is five nights a week seem reasonable? That's fifty minutes a week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that seems fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Then, um, let's move to the running because you just recently tried that. You run with your dog, you said?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. How about that twice a week? Would that be possible?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I can try to do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What days of the week you think you could do it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, probably the weekends. So probably like Saturday or Friday night or Saturday morning.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So Saturday morning and Friday night. Now, would you run Friday night and then again Saturday morning?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, no, I guess not. So probably let's see, maybe Wednesday night and Saturday morning.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So Wednesday night and Saturday morning. Run for say a minimum of half an hour?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can try for that, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now again, remember you're going to have these automatic thoughts likely that will be telling you that you should stop and but you have to kind of talk your way through that or do the best you can. Right? The adaptive response maybe being something like 'in the end this will help me'. Like 'it's tough now but this will help me'.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So let's look now toward the more social aspects, um, logistically moving up the ladder here to the most complex, it sounds like going out with your fiancé would be the next at the next level.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, he's I don't know if he's kind of just been mad at me lately or if he just thinks I need to be alone, but we've kind of been getting some distance there. So I think that out of everything, that would be the relationship I'd want to work on the most.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Focus on. All right. So maybe so you're running Wednesdays and Saturday mornings. Could you go out and do something with your fiancé twice a week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think we could manage that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, because sometimes you said you just walk around the neighborhood, so it's not even doesn't have to be necessarily like a lot of time, it's just something.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. What do you think you can do to motivate yourself to do that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, I guess just having like him maybe remind me or suggest it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you could you could tell him that this is something that you're planning to do and you might need a little push to to do it. All right. Or to maintain it. Right? So you might get outside the same thing when you're running, you might want to come right back in.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. And moving to the most complex, but also the one with the highest social engagement, going out with the other two couples. Now once or twice a week you'd mentioned before, how about we shoot for now once every couple weeks?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think I could handle that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Like maybe a Saturday night or a Friday night?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think that could work.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What can you see being an obstacle there? Like what what might help you motivate be motivated to continue that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just having to actually like go to their houses or go somewhere because they don't really live close to us. They're not far, but just the fact that we'd have to get in the car and drive over there and I would actually have to like look relatively nice. I can't just go in my pajamas.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So for this to work, that is for you to do it, you really have to schedule at their house. You can't have them come to you. All right. So that's one thing we know. You have to you have to make some time and drive over there or maybe if your fiancé drives, whichever, but you have to physically have to go over. Right. So once you're there, like so it might be tough like to get in the car and make the drive over, once you're there, how do you think you would feel?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. It's like the run, I'd probably just want to turn around and come back.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do these couples know that you've been a little down?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think they've noticed, and I think that's probably why they've kind of started to back off with asking us to do things. Um, so I think they've noticed it but they don't know like any they don't know what's really going on. Um, so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are those relationships you're worried about losing because they're backing off?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah, um, I mean they're our closest friends, so like we've known each other for a really long time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And could you see this behavior being one that brings you closer together with them? Like restores some of that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean I think it would definitely just us going, they might be a little hesitant because the past couple times they've invited us we've backed out, but I think it would probably be a step in that direction of restoring the relationship, so I mean I would like to do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So I want to review the plan. Okay? And just make sure that we have an agreement because we're constructing this together. So I need your buy-in. All right. Reading five times a week for minimum ten minutes. All right? Um, the next level up was the running and that was that was Wednesday night and Saturday morning. Okay. Going out two times with your fiancé, all right? And then once every couple weeks driving to your friends', going to their houses and spending an evening with them. All of that realistic?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think so, yeah. I mean I can try to get accountability with my fiancé just to let him know my plan and then see if he can help me follow through with it I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good. All right. So let's set that as the plan. Okay? And I want you to be aware that as I mentioned, the automatic thoughts might come in right and and kind of tempt you in a direction away from that. I also want to let you know that if you are unsuccessful in any one of those things, that doesn't mean you have to stop and not try again. Right? Just take it as a small setback and then the next time, you know, for example it's time to read or go out running, just try again. Okay. It's not unusual in this exercise that you won't be able to complete all the behaviors that you've planned for yourself. Sometimes life gets in the way, things happen, sometimes the depression gets in the way. So can you appreciate that that might be discouraging? Like if you try it and you stop like you told me in the beginning.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. So just take that as a, you know, what it is, just a small setback and try to push forward the next time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And I want you to informally kind of keep a record of it. When I see you next week, we'll see how you did. And specifically, I want you to keep track of what you were thinking and feeling through different stages of the behavior. Okay? Can you record that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So we'll go from there. That'll be your plan and I'll see you in a week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks, Carly.

video_details.title: Communication Skills: A Patient-Centered Approach
video_details.description: This video shows an example of a communication skills assessment between a student and a standardized patient.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Come in. Miss Bellamy?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, I'm Honey Harris, I'll be your doctor today. Let me just wash my hands really quickly. Would you prefer Miss Bellamy or could I call you Pat?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Pat's fine, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Great, well, it's nice to meet you. Can you tell me why you're here today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have a terrible headache.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That sounds really bad. Is there anything else besides your headache that you want to address here today at the clinic?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, just that, except I am concerned. I just recently changed insurance companies and I'm not sure this is going to be covered yet.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Well, what we can do is while we're talking and I'm doing your history and physical, I will have my office secretary look into the insurance plan that you have so you don't have to worry about that. Does that sound good?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that sounds good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, sounds great. Is there anything else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I just, this is just really bad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So what I'd like to do today is let's take a look at what's causing your headache. I will go over history, physical, and then we'll do a physical exam and look into your insurance policy. Does that sound like a good plan?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Perfect. So tell me a little bit more about this head pain that you're having.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it started about three days ago and nothing has helped. It's just laid me flat. I haven't been able to go to work. It's all over, and it's really bad when I move, and the light is bothering me a lot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Unfortunately, I can't dim the lights in this room, but I'll try to go quickly. Would it be okay if I took some notes?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So you said this headache started about three days ago. Was there anything that brought it on, anything unusual that happened then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really, no.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Can you tell me anything that makes it better?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Nothing's made it better. I took some Tylenol and tried Motrin, but nothing helped. I just try not to move too much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Is there anything that makes it worse?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, movement and light. And it's just constant though, it's all over.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So if you had to rate it on a pain scale, zero being no pain and ten being the worst pain you've ever had?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, it's a 10. I've never had a headache like this.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Now as far as radiation, does it move? You said the pain is all up here in the front of your head?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's kind of all over, but I've also got this shooting pain down my neck and my neck is very stiff. It's the entire head.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Entire head, okay. As far as the timing, you said it's been constant since it started?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. It started gradually, but once it got there, it hasn't gone away. It doesn't get better or worse, it's just the same.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. I want to get your perception of what you think is going on.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, I can hardly think because it's so painful. I was afraid because my neighbor had a headache and ignored it last year, and he ended up having a brain tumor. So I thought I should come in.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I understand your concern. How is it impacting your daily life?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can't go to work or do anything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like it's really impacting your life. If it's okay, I'd like to talk about your medical and social history.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me if you have any medical conditions I should be aware of?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was diagnosed with high blood pressure about three years ago, but we've been addressing it with diet and it's well-controlled. Other than that, I haven't had any problems.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Any surgical history or hospitalizations?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you said the only medicine you're taking is Tylenol and Motrin?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, and they didn't help.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Do you have any drug allergies?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What about family history? Any medical history of headaches in your family?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My mom used to get migraines in her 20s and 30s. My sister's healthy and my dad has high blood pressure, but he's healthy otherwise. I don't have any kids.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'd like to ask some social history questions for the records. Do you smoke?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is it cigarettes or chewing tobacco?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Cigarettes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how much do you smoke?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: About a half a pack a day.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. What about alcohol?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't drink.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Also, are you married? Do you have children?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm married, no children.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Looking at your GYN history, when was your last menstrual period?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm in menopause.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Going back into history, have you been nauseous?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I've been nauseous. I threw up twice early on because when I move, it makes me nauseous.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Any trips or anything out of the ordinary over the past couple weeks?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Actually, a week ago I was in North Carolina for a family reunion. There was a four-year-old who was sick there and ended up going to the emergency room.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Let me just summarize. You've had a severe frontal headache for three days. It's a 10 out of 10 pain, worse with movement and light, and accompanied by a stiff neck. You have high blood pressure controlled with diet. This is impacting your daily life, and Tylenol and Motrin didn't help. Your mom had migraines, and you smoke but don't drink. You also recently took a trip to North Carolina.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it was in North Carolina. I've just never had this kind of pain before.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I understand that. So what I'd like to do is complete a physical exam and do some testing. Is there anything else I need to address first?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That sounds good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, sounds great. All right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, I'm Deb. I'm your standardized patient. Nice job. I'm going to give you some feedback on your communication skills, but how do you feel it went?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Pretty good. I was nervous at first, just trying to make sure that I was getting all the patient information so we could get the correct tests.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How did you feel when you walked in? Did you feel comfortable?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think I got more comfortable as we sat down and got to talking.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I could see that. Well, I thought you did a nice job. You had an appropriate introduction and a very warm demeanor. You elicited my chief complaint and asked about other concerns to set a mutual agenda.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Your first open-ended question was nice, and you followed up with pointed questions for clarification. You were an active listener with good eye contact. You could do a little more reflective listening just to verify accuracy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You asked my perspective, and that's when you learned about my fear of a brain tumor. I thought you had nice flow and a logical sequence of questioning.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A little bit of signposting between sections would be good as interviews get longer. You moved through quickly, attending to the timeline. You did ask permission to ask social questions, but you might want to clarify they could be personal or uncomfortable.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You were non-judgmental about the smoking. You have nice vocal range and a comfortable demeanor. You did a summary at the end and asked if there was anything else before the physical exam. So, it was a very nice encounter.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, thank you so much. Nice meeting you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You too.

video_details.title: CBT Role Play - Catastrophizing and Decatastrophizing
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which cognitive-behavioral therapy techniques, including decatastrophizing, are used to treat anxiety related to castastrophizing after a job loss. Catastrophizing is a cognitive distortion in which an individual predicts disproportionately negative and often unlikely outcomes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello Jordan, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Good, could've been better.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Could be better? Yeah. What's going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, you know I have two jobs. And I lost one of them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You lost your job? Yes. Which one did you lose?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I lost the one at the grocery store.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That was your part-time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm sorry to hear that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Me too. And I'm just... it's all I think about now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And when did this happen?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It happened about two or three days ago.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Two or three days ago. Yeah. So if I remember right, you took that job not too long ago to kind of supplement your income.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So certainly that would be upsetting, but I know that's not a major part of your income.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's not, but I mean I'm still very worried about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me about the worry.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean I worry that, you know, I only had so much money and now I have less than that. I mean, without my money, you know, God knows how many things can happen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So before you had the job, you were paying all your bills. You wanted some extra income. You've lost that extra income, and I can certainly understand how that would be disturbing. But as I understand it, you were doing okay before with your full-time job.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was doing okay, but I mean I got comfortable with that extra income. And so now my fear is that I've gotten too comfortable with it and now that it's not there anymore, it's going to affect the fact, you know, I'm not going to be able to pay for food or my rent.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you adjusted to the new income level with the full-time and the part-time job together. And you're worried you can't adjust back?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm worried that I mean things are just going to get worse from here. I mean, it's a big deal losing your job even if it was part-time. I've gotten comfortable from having so much money, from the money I had, to now that's, you know, been divided. And I mean God knows how many things, like I said, God knows how many things can happen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, what can happen? So you had that income... your income's reduced now to just your full-time job. What can happen from this point on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I can, you know, stay in the mindset that I have that extra money and spend what I think is that extra money, digging into the money I pay for my rent, my food, my gas, my insurance. And I mean, who's somebody without all that?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you could fail to pay expenses that need to be paid.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: And they help me go to my full-time job that, you know, that I still have. So I mean if I can't... if I spend the money that was from my insurance because I thought I had extra, then I'm not going to have insurance on my car. I can get pulled over, lose my license, not going to be able to get to work and then I'll get fired there too.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so the kind of chain of causality you're seeing is that without that part-time income, you might not adapt with your expense management. You might fail to pay, for example, your car insurance. You could get pulled over for something, the police officer could see you don't have insurance, give you a ticket...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Which is just more money I don't have.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Another expense, right. And how would this... how would that connect to losing your job?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Because I wouldn't be able to get to work.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the ticket would be so expensive you would lose your...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, the ticket would be expensive so I wouldn't be able to try to pay the next month's insurance, so I just wouldn't have insurance on my car, so I'd lose my insurance.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And then by losing your insurance, you'd lose your transportation altogether because you can't drive without insurance, and then you'd lose your job.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, it's either go to work with an uninsured car and then I can get pulled over and go to jail for driving with no insurance multiple times. I don't want to go to jail.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No, that's serious. Yeah, you wouldn't want to do that. Well, so there's two... so you have two kind of causal chains: one is losing your job and now you've introduced the idea you can end up incarcerated.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. I mean, which I would definitely lose my job if I'm in jail.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I would imagine.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: And so then that would have... so then I wouldn't even have like any money to help me through jail. Like to... for the commissary and stuff.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Because you would have no income.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would have no income. And then when I get out of jail, I'm... no one's going to hire me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Because you'd have a criminal record.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Exactly. Which makes it challenging to find employment in some instances.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what's happened is kind of in your mind... you've moved from losing additional income to this possibility that you could be in jail or lose your job because of this.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mm-hm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. So I remember maybe last week... you were talking about the letter that you received from... it was like a late notice, but it wasn't... it turned out it wasn't you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it was sent to me but it was somebody else's credit card.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It was a mistake, right? Do you remember the conclusions you drew from when you believed that was actually for you, that late notice?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That my credit score was going to go down, that I'd be stuck in that apartment, and then I'd go into depression, I wouldn't be able to do anything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, so you ended up in a situation where you just couldn't function at all. And you moved there from a letter that you believed was addressed to you... which of course you don't want to be late on a credit card, but you moved from there to being so depressed you couldn't work, couldn't function.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you see a pattern that's emerged over the last few times I've seen you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, I've seen that, you know, sometimes I can think the worst. And I know it didn't happen last time, but that was, you know, a stroke of good luck.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That it wasn't you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that it... you know, it wasn't me and that was a relief. But this is something that's solid. I don't have my part-time job anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. You've lost real income.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I mean this isn't a mistake. This is real. And so there's real concerns here, unlike last time where I was lucky.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So this situation you see as different than the first situation... is there a reason why you could survive well again, that you could adapt to this lost income?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I suppose there is, but I'm concerned about whether I won't adapt.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, let's look at this in terms of probabilities... how many times have you ended up in jail or losing your full-time job?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean they haven't happened yet.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It hasn't happened.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not yet. But I mean I've struggled a little bit when I lost a part-time job or when I was younger.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you had to adapt. And it was painful.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: But I did struggle a bit. Yeah. But I'm older now and these are... even though grocery store is not a serious job, it was income.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sure. Yeah, and again to lose income would be disappointing for just about anybody. Are there any upsides to not having that job?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I suppose I have more time to focus on my full-time job because that I mean that is really intensive.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there a possibility that you could find another part-time job just as you found that one?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean because... well will somebody else take me because I was fired from that job? I mean that's my concern...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That they're going to find out about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, and then they're going to 'oh she was fired', you know, 'we don't want her'.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But you've had other jobs that didn't work out before, and that didn't affect you getting that job.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's true.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the worst case scenario, I guess is what I'm getting at... ending up in jail or losing your full-time job... it seems like they like you there.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I hope they do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Pretty well, right? Yeah. So those scenarios, I guess, are possible but they seem based on what you're saying as pretty unlikely. So I wonder how useful it is to invest a lot of energy in kind of tracking that causal chain to jail or prison or unemployment when that's really not the most likely outcome. Do you invest as much energy in tracking the positives or the probable outcomes?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, not even close. I know that. I don't think about the positive things. I don't get fired and then go 'what's good about this?'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
