diarization.text: Or get a letter in the mail and say what's... but this has still been a theme that I've seen over the last eight to ten weeks where you really emphasize the negative possible even unlikely outcomes... Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But you don't do the same thing for the positive side. You don't look at how something could work out well. Would you say that's a fair assessment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, no, that's pretty accurate.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But still you're worried about this.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, yeah I am worried. I'm not going to be thrilled about it, but I suppose I don't have to go to 'I'm going to go to jail' or 'I'm going to lose my full-time job'.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think there's a lot of intervening factors that could occur... there's other things that you could do.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I suppose I could get a family member to drive me or take the bus if I lost my insurance and lost my car.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So alternate forms of transportation. There's adapting your spending back to where it was before.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's true.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Part of your fear was that you wouldn't be able to adapt your spending, right? But that's something you would have control over.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I can keep better track of how much I do spend and keep track of my bank accounts and exactly how much money I have in them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So having talked through this a little bit, what I'm going to refer to as catastrophizing... remember we talked about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That sounds familiar, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's where the negative is taken and just making it way more negative than it is... does that lower your anxiety about the situation? Does it change it in some way?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, knowing that I'm thinking about it wrong makes me feel a little better.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I would say you're thinking about it in a way that's less than useful.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, that actually makes me feel better. Knowing that, you know, these things can happen but they might not.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean I would even say probably not. So one way potentially... one way to address catastrophizing... would be to find some sort of peace with the worst outcome... being in jail would be survivable. Being unemployed would be survivable.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean people weaker than me have gone through jail, I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A lot of people have been to jail... it's at the point where you can accept that that could happen and that you would survive that you could find some peace with the catastrophizing... you would survive.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I mean one thing you've shown... is that you're a survivor. You find a way to make it work.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean that makes me feel better, thinking about me as a survivor.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, so in a sense kind of reframing... your circumstances as you're somebody that's surviving adversity.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean I'm right in thinking that that's not a good thing, losing my job.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's certainly not ideal... you can be defeated by it... or you can survive. You'll be able to develop more solutions... focusing on it isn't going to change it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's not going to change...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's not going to decrease its likelihood.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think it does.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In a way it almost increases its likelihood because you're... I'm thinking about it too much. You're investing in the negative outcomes without really looking at the positive side. So that's kind of how cognitive distortions work... We'll work on helping you to reframe circumstances like this. Granted this is certainly more distressing than receiving that letter... I remember back then you were kind of on the fence about taking the job.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Because I wanted to invest all my time in my full-time job, but it's always nice to have some extra spending money, especially with the holidays coming up.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sure... you had other possibilities, kind of investing in those could be a route. I'm trying to give you more options than just the catastrophic ones.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I mean it seems like that there's better ways to go about it than thinking I'm going to go to jail and I'm going to be unemployed forever.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sure, there's ways that are more useful to you... either adjust to not having the income or replace the income.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I suppose it's not hard to get a grocery store job again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well you did it before, right? That's true. And again, even if it is hard, it's a struggle, you survived on that other income for a long time without that. Right? So we'll try to identify some of the automatic thoughts that are coming up around the job loss.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But for now, I want you to just try to get a general understanding of the theme, which is that you tend to catastrophize.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And it is what it is, but it's not so useful for you... it's just not particularly useful.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's not the best I could do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you want to try to do the best for you. Absolutely. So does that sort of make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it does.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So think about that theme... and think about the reframe... focus on those two elements for this week... broken down like we did before to develop adaptive responses. Does that sound like a plan?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it does.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. So consider those two things and we'll pick up with this next week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right, thank you very much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks, Jordan.

video_details.title: Treatment Planning in Counseling - Setting a Goal and Corresponding Objectives
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which treatment planning in counseling is demonstrated. The treatment planning includes setting a goal and the corresponding objectives.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello, Lisa. How you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm fine. How are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. Uh, I'd like to get started today, and we talked about this last time, with some treatment planning.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I've seen you for, uh, four prior sessions, right? And I want to try to get the treatment plan at least started today.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that okay with you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So tell me a little bit about what you think a goal might be that you want to set for your counseling time with me.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would like very much so to start turning in my assignments on time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now we talked about this before, this was something you sort of used the word discouraged about. Is that accurate?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I feel very discouraged when they're not in on time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how many assignments have you not turned in on time? Like as a percentage, say?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Unfortunately, a good 87% probably.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's a very precise number, 87%. You been keeping track of it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. So it's something you're really attentive to. I really have. I mean, it really discourages me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So you're aware of it precisely and you know it discourages you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So what would the goal be there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: To start turning in my assignments on time, in time all the time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What percentage would you like to turn on time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would like to aim for 100, but I'd settle for 95.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: 95% turn in on time, so only 5% not on time. A little leeway.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you want all or substantially all of your assignments to be turned in on time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I really feel like that would just make me feel better about school, about myself, about...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Do you want to make that one of your goals, to turn your assignments in on time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I think that would be fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And that would help with feelings of being discouraged, which have been unpleasant for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So think of a goal as what you want to get out of the counseling in general. So I think that's a good goal, right? That's something that'll help you. And then I want to talk about something that contributes to the goals that we call objectives. Right? So objectives are tasks that we attempt to complete that we believe will contribute to the the goal being met. So like steps to reach a goal. That kind of makes sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think it does.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what's important about objectives is that they're specific and that we can measure them in some way. So I can know and you can know when you've actually completed an objective versus when you haven't, or to what degree you've completed it. Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you think some objectives might be to help you reach your goal?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, my school has a writing center and they offer tutoring there and it's a really quiet place that you know, it's just you and the studies. And I think that if I were to go there and, you know, be able to work on feel comfortable working on my assignments, then I would be able to start turning them in on time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so the writing center's available to you and you feel like if you could go there with your assignments in progress, that you're working on them, or before you start them or in progress?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think, I mean, it depends on the assignment honestly.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. But you'll kind of know when you need to go.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, and I want to take full opportunity of it because there are some things that I just either don't understand or don't understand completely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And they can help straighten some of that out for you, work with you on that. All right. So how often do you think you can get to the writing center?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think about a good three days a week.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Three days a week you can get to the writing center. How many assignments do you have due in any given week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: In any given week, probably about two.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, a week. So three visits to the writing center should be sufficient to address them.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, because they're very difficult and I don't want to spend, you know, three, four hours in there my whole day, but you know, get, you know, kind of take chunks out of it so I'm not so overwhelmed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good. Okay, so that'll be one of your objectives is to try to get to the writing center three times a week. So that's the number we'll use, that's how we'll measure it. We'll look for three visits a week. And what's the average, you know, I don't know the rules for the writing center, but what's the average amount of time that you would spend there if you bring an assignment to them?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm not sure, I've never been.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Never been there, okay. Let's assume maybe a half hour to 45 minutes, okay, and find out and let me know if I'm wrong. So, but approximately you'll be going there three times a week for roughly a half hour to maybe 45 minutes.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there anything they do to ask, that they ask of you like in advance to have ready, like specific questions or anything like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, specifically what am I you know not understanding, what do I need kind of comprehension on, what is the assignment I'm working on so that way they can be prepared to help me. If I need a tutor or, you know, if I need computer time, just making sure that I have all the tools accessible to me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, good. So you like that as an objective?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think it's, I think it would help.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is it one you think you can follow through with successfully?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I know it's possible, I know I physically can and I want to say that I'm mentally prepared to start trying to tackle this.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, because in addition to being specific and measurable, it's worth mentioning that objectives need to be achievable. So if at any time you feel like we're setting an objective that's just not realistic, let me know. Okay? But if you feel like you can get to the writing center three times a week and that's realistic, we'll go with that. Okay? That good? All right. So that's one thing. I'd like to have a few objectives for each goal. All right? We have the one goal so far of just turning in your assignments on time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And we have the one objective, which is getting to the writing center three times a week. Is there any other objectives you could think of? Think about what impedes you in terms of achieving your goal or what facilitates you achieving it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: As much as I hate to admit, I kind of start the day before it's due a lot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So if assignment's due on a Wednesday...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'll stay up till 5, 6 in the morning Tuesday night, Wednesday morning, trying to get it done because I just haven't done it. And I've known about this project or this assignment for usually weeks in advance.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So starting that late is resulting in you not turning in on time, you're not finishing.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, because I get tired. I mean at 6 in the morning I start getting tired, I don't want to do it anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That seems reasonable, yeah. Anybody would be tired working that late into the night or that early into the morning. So what can you do that would help you get around that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I want to start beginning my assignments, even if it's just beginning outlines, something, at least a week early.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So if assignment's due on a Wednesday, the prior Wednesday you want to get started.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Even if that Wednesday it's just writing down my ideas or organizing it so I know what to do. Just something.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So that's specific and that's something we can measure, the number of days that you in advance of an assignment you start working on it. Is this something you can achieve?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Again, I want to say yes, I do. I know I know I can and I'm ready, I'm done feeling like this about my assignments.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're motivated.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think I'm at the end of my rope to the point where I'm motivated.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Motivation comes in many forms, okay? Being at the end of your rope is one of them. So you you made me think of something here as you're talking about the number of days you start prior. And then you also mentioned how you work late into the night or early into the morning. Is there a specific time of the day that would be better for you to start these assignments?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I could definitely not stop, I start starting them at like really late at night because sometimes I get home from work, I just want to eat and I want to lay down and I want to watch TV, and then I don't start until 9, 10 at night.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So before you know it, it's late at night, assignments still due, and it's not done. So what would be, a lot of students have like good working hours in their schedule? Like a certain time range where their house, their residence is distraction-free, they have access to the the items they need like a computer, background noise is minimal. What is, do you have a time like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I get home from work at 5. Uh, and I do like to set aside time to, you know, eat dinner. So I think between 5:30 and 8 are optimal because then at 8 I go take a shower, I get ready for bed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So one of the objectives could be, and tell me if you like this or not, to try to confine the hours you work on assignments from roughly 6 to 8 or 5:30 to 8?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that makes a lot of sense.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. Is that achievable? Are there a lot of distractions that occur right after you finish eating?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: There's really not a lot of distractions, it's again honestly really just me being lazy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You feel like it's laziness?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I just eat, I get off work, I just want to watch TV.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You just want to relax, you worked all day. That makes sense. But you know if you're gonna complete your assignments, your best opportunity is probably between...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, I can definitely do better things than just sit on the couch and watch TV.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So we have three good objectives. You like that objective?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I do. Thinking about it now, I really do, especially if I start a week early. If I only work, you know, those few hours a night, it should be done in no time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So we'll make that the third objective. Now we've been talking about the feelings of discouragement over like I said the last four sessions or so, right? And we talked about the self-talk, the adaptive responses when you get these thoughts. Remember the thoughts you're having that you're never going to be able to...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: And I'm gonna fail out of school, I'm not good enough anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And we talked about the adaptive responses and I gave you the homework of the the thought record to work on that. Uh, so I'd like to, if it's okay with you, to make one of the objectives to continue to apply those adaptive responses when those automatic thoughts come in.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So we can kind of work to your goal at a few different levels. So we have some behavioral things we have in place, right? So that's working 5:30 to 8, starting earlier, and going to the writing center. Those are all behaviors. I'd like to have some cognitive, or at least one cognitive intervention in place.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that something you can do or that you have done since we've been meeting?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The talking myself down that we've done when those things start coming in my head, they have made me feel better and made me feel that, you know, even though I feel bad doesn't mean I can't not do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So used in conjunction with some of these behavioral ideas, you'd be okay with that objective being? I don't think I would think like that that I can't do it anymore as much if I started getting a head start on things.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, because if you got a head start on things, those would be successes, right? And and one of the thoughts you had is you wouldn't be successful, you'd be a failure, right? So you'd have some evidence to say, well, I'm successful. I'm doing, I'm following the objectives and I'm meeting all of them or percentage of them. So you think that would help you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I really do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good. Okay. So we have four objectives there. So we have the one goal, we have four objectives, I have this written out. I want to, if we can, I want to take a break, kind of get these into the system and get this typed out for you. And then maybe we can work on another goal and finish up the treatment plan for today. Does that sound like a plan?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, sounds like a great plan.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good. So we'll take a break now and I'll catch up with you in just a few minutes.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play - Cognitive Reframing an Experience of Emotional Abuse
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which cognitive-behavioral therapy is used to cognitively reframe an experience of emotional abuse. Automatic thoughts, adaptive responses, and the use of homework are featured.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Marty, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'm doing alright.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Doing alright? I know last time you were here, you were discussing some relational issues. You want to continue with that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it kind of came up again. Every time my wife yells at me, I feel like a failure. Like I told you last time, I just feel like I can't do anything right. Everything I try to do is met with arguing and yelling and I just feel like there's nothing I can do right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So no matter what you do, it's not going to end up the way you want?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's frustrating. How is what's going on impacted your relationship with your wife?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's rocky because I feel like I can't do anything right. She doesn't understand that, and then we don't get along ever because we're just always yelling and I'm always feeling bad and then it just keeps going like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When you mention you feel like a failure when she yells at you, can you think back to the last time you guys argued and try to remember that thought? We talked about automatic thoughts before. Remember that thought that comes in that moment when she starts yelling at you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When she yelled at me, I feel frustrated. Like, why are you yelling at me right now? And as I was thinking about it more this week, it kind of felt like what happened with my dad. I guess I kind of felt that same way when I was younger. If my dad would yell at me or when he would yell at me, I kind of feel that same way and it's kind of the same thing. That's kind of the first thought that comes to mind.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The first thought is 'I've been through something like this before'?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess. I mean, I'm not really thinking those exact words, but that's definitely what it feels like.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Like just a sense that this isn't brand new, and the feeling you're connecting with it is the same feeling you had when your dad would yell at you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, pretty much, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So in a sense, these arguments are taking you back to another point in time. That's distressing.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess so, in a way. It feels pretty crappy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now in these arguments, she yells at you, you mentioned before that you do some yelling of your own in the midst of all that. How would you rate it in terms of any physical violence, nothing like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, it's just words. We're just yelling.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what level of yelling would you say, how severe compared to what you've experienced in the past?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes it can get up to like the eights or nines, but generally it's down closer to a seven.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: On a scale of one to ten? So sometimes it's, seven would be pretty bad, but some other times it's not.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you feel like your reaction of being frustrated is disproportionate to what's really going on, or do you feel like it's on the money?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know what else to do, it's kind of my gut reaction. I think I'm justified in it because she doesn't understand how much she yells at me and how much that hurts me. I do feel justified though.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's talk for a moment about your father and his yelling. You've discussed this with me a little bit before in past few sessions. I remember you saying that most of it was in the afternoon when you were both home.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mostly when I'd get home from school. I was in high school and then I went to college, so I wasn't home much during college. But I'd get home from high school, he'd get home from work and kind of be aggravated, start yelling. Yeah, usually when I got back from school.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, so he would get back from work, you would get back from school, and how long would that last, the period where you were vulnerable to being yelled at?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes about an hour. He'd be yelling because he's frustrated from work and from the drive home and whatever else. At some point he would usually start drinking. So maybe about an hour or so where you knew you were gonna get it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So kind of every day you could predict that between when he came home after you were already home from school and when he started drinking, he was gonna find something to yell at you about?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, and there were some days like, I knew when he came home at the same time every day, I knew I could get out of the house. Because at some point I had a car and my friends had cars, and at some point I had a job, so sometimes I'd work after school. So I knew I'd be able to leave the house at times when I knew he was gonna start yelling and stuff. But there was a period of time, probably like my senior year of high school, that I just didn't. I just came home and you knew what was going to happen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Even though you were able to escape it. You could have stayed out long enough for him to start drinking, instead you stayed in the house.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Pretty much my whole senior year. I would come home, I knew what was gonna happen, and I just took it. I just knew he was gonna yell, I just took it though.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Was there ever a period when you first got your freedom that you tried leaving?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh yeah, I did. I don't know why I didn't just keep doing that, probably would have been easier. But the whole senior year, I just was back there at the house when he came home from work.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So in that period, those times when you did leave, what did he do instead of yell at you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess he'd yell at somebody else. My sister, my brother were home. I guess he probably yelled at them. It felt good to not be there, but I guess he probably yelled at them. Which sucks. I guess whoever was there was gonna take it. Somebody was going to get yelled at. Yeah, I guess it was them when I wasn't there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how do you think you took it when you were there? How well did you respond?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just got used to it. I knew what was gonna happen, I knew he was gonna yell, I knew that it was gonna make me upset, I knew just those repeated times, just like now, I'm gonna feel like a failure, which ultimately I did. Maybe I just became numb to it. It happened so often and the same thing every day. Probably became numb to it and just kind of stopped caring and kind of stopped believing in myself or something. Yeah, probably.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how many years total did this experience go on? You endured the yelling?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It would have been while I was in middle school and most of high school. I told you at some point I was able to leave, but probably all of middle school, most of high school, and then for the rest of senior year I would be there. So quite a few years, I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A long time to suffer. And now if we move back forward in time, you're in a relationship where you're getting yelled at a bit, and sometimes quite a bit, and that's causing you distress. You're yelling a little bit, you feel like you're back in the same place.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean obviously she's not doing anything like he was, like drinking or anything like that, but it does, it's like the same thing that happened is happening again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So that's, in your opinion, that's the consequence of what happened to you. All this yelling that you endured before, in some way is significantly contributing to what you're going through now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe. I guess it could because it is the same thing. So maybe there could be some connection. Maybe not 100% explain it, but it explains part of it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So your functioning's been affected a bit, to the point where you're here with me now and we're talking about it and you're frustrated and it does sound painful. Now, I'm curious. You mentioned you had a younger sister and a younger brother and they grew up in the same house. How are they doing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My sister, she's three years younger than I am, she's doing great. She graduated from college top of her class and she's about to get married, too. A really great guy. She lives the next town over from me and I get to see her a lot. And she's great, though. My brother, he's five years younger than I am. He's doing pretty good, too. He's just about to graduate from college. I think he gets really good grades too from what I hear, what he tells me. I don't get to see him as much as I do her because he's in college, but I think he's doing really well, too. They both do some really good stuff, they have really good goals and stuff like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You seem like you have a good relationship with them, you're proud of them.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, definitely. I think they're doing some really good stuff, trying to make something of themselves.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: They're doing pretty well, you're doing okay but you're having a rough time right now. How would things have been if you had taken that opportunity to not be there? Like you said, you had a car, your friends had cars, you could have avoided the situation directly between your dad and you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. I mean, I took the yelling and stuff, so it's obviously affecting me now. I bring it up to them sometimes and they're like, 'Yeah, dad yelled sometimes, but it wasn't that bad.' Definitely different experience from what I had. They don't see it like I do. Maybe things would have been worse for them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In a sense, your father verbally abused you. Nothing makes that right. But in a sense, because you were there and you were the target and could ride it out, you shielded them from that abuse. You mentioned it would have been somebody else, right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, probably would have been them. Probably was them when I wasn't there. I guess you're probably right. They are doing pretty well. I think they're doing better than I am, I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, probably no small part because of your protecting them. You were in an impossible situation and you made the choice to stay there. There was some negative consequences for you, which we'll try to work through, but some really positive consequences for your siblings.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess so. I mean, I feel like a failure most of the time, but they don't, they're doing good stuff. I guess you're right, that could have been it. I'd love to ask them what they think would have happened if the yelling would have been more towards them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And maybe you'll find out that when you weren't there, that is what happened. So you feel like a failure, but at the same time, you're happy for them and proud of all their accomplishments. It seems like you were a part of that success.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe. I guess that makes sense. I hope so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, in cognitive therapy oftentimes we try to do what we call reframing. That's where we take a situation and we don't change the facts, we don't move from the truth, but we try to cast it in some different lights. Certainly being yelled at and abused, like I said, nothing makes that right, that's awful. And what you're going through now possibly because of that is awful. And that's a reality. But at the same time, it's a reality perhaps that you protected your siblings. Both those things can be true at the same time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess so. I guess there's like a positive that comes out of that negative, maybe. I hope that's true, I'd like to think it is.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Another thing that occurs to me is that you were mentioning how you're being yelled at now and you're having some strong reactions to that, but also you do some of the yelling. Do you think some of that comes from what you learned from your father?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably, yeah. I mean, I saw him do it for so many years, it's probably all I know how to do if I'm trying to resolve something, whatever. Probably all I know how to do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have there been occasions where your wife starts yelling at you and you don't respond with yelling?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think so, it's happened a few times. I was trying to think of that this week, too, and I was trying to be a little bit more aware about my reaction to her and I kind of started to realize like maybe I'm yelling a little bit more than I think I do, or a little bit more intensely than I think I do. That's probably the case, it's all I knew how to do, it's all I was taught. That's what you learn.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So again, just like your father yelling at you, your wife yelling at you isn't what we want. But maybe in that case, maybe your reaction to it is making it worse. Maybe you're contributing to an escalation because of what you learned, which is understandable. But perhaps in that moment, that automatic thought, whatever it is, is contributing to that behavior of yelling back. And we can get in there and try to interrupt that. And maybe get your reaction to be, maybe the more she yells, the more you calm down. Because we know what you're doing now is not working, and you want it to work, you want your marriage to be successful.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, absolutely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: For this week, I want you to reflect on the reframe, kind of how the past is connected to what's going on now, but also how things would have turned out if you had just left that whole situation, how it might not be as positive for your siblings. So you contributed some good to a situation that was really miserable for you. And I also want you to try to, I've given you the thought record to work on for homework, I want you to try to capture that automatic thought when she yells at you. But think about how you can respond to the variety of automatic thoughts that you're having with adaptive responses, with the self-talk we talked about. There's still a real focus on the feelings, but in there is a thought. We believe that directly leads to them. So what I want to work on with you is interrupting that process and let's see what's actually happening at the cognition level before just to the feeling, and see if we can get some self-talk in there. If you can complete one to three thought records on that. Remember to ask yourself that question, 'What's going through my mind right now?' so when that yelling starts, try to maintain focus and say 'What's going through my mind right now?' Think about that thought that's automatically coming into your mind, and then we can build some adaptive responses, some self-talk.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think my wife's gonna like that one because she likes it as I'm working on this stuff. I'm sure she'll like it, though. It's tough, it's not easy, but I know it's worth it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's not easy work, but I feel like we've made some progress today. This reframe is something you can consider, and then getting in and recording those thoughts on the thought record, we'll work on those and try to make some concrete progress, and we can work on trying to adjust your reaction to what's going on. Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that sounds good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so I'll see you at the same time next week and we'll move on from there.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Cool, sounds good. Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So Chris, I wanted to talk to you. You're one of our star athletes and I value you as a team player. As athletic director, I keep tabs on the players to make sure everybody is performing at their best. Something came up this weekend about a party you attended, and I wanted to talk to you about how alcohol fits in your life right now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Actually, could I confide something in you? I'm an honors student and my parents kept me away from social life. A month ago, I used studying as an excuse to go to a party and started drinking. This past weekend, I lied to my mom and promised her I wouldn't drink, but I did. When she picked me up, she knew immediately. I feel terrible because I betrayed her trust.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you've been doing everything you were told for years, but recently you got involved in the party scene. It was fun at first, but now you're noticing some consequences.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. I've been more lethargic and apathetic towards schoolwork. My mind is elsewhere, and instead of studying on weekends, I'm caught up with friends trying to find where we can get alcohol since we're underage.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's really changed your focus.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm a reserved and self-conscious person in social environments, but when I drink, I feel relaxed and I'm able to engage with people more easily.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it helps you loosen up and feel more relaxed.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Exactly. But the people I'm hanging out with have changed because certain friends are associated with that scene.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there's a little tension now with the friends you were hanging out with before?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A little bit, because not all of them are into that. I've been hanging out more with the group that invited me to that first party, but it's not fair to my old friends that I'm not there for them as much as I was before.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Given all these changes affecting your friendships, studies, and your relationship with your mom, where do you think you should go from here?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel I should stop. It's not worth it to not remember the night or be sick. I have to slowly build back trust with my mother because that was a big blow for me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Your mom is really important to you, and how she feels about you is important.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Exactly.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How important is it to you to make an adjustment in your drinking or even to quit?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A lot, because it's a big factor in gaining back my mother's trust and getting back on top of my schoolwork and athletics.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How confident are you that you could actually change your drinking or even cut down or quit?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm pretty confident.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: On a scale of one to ten, where one is not at all and ten is completely, what number would you give?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably an eight or nine. I'm determined to make it happen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Why an eight or nine rather than a six or seven?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm determined because I don't like how I felt after betraying my mother or the physical experience of vomiting. Even if I do drink, I don't want to drink to the point where that happens. It's not worth it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you think is a realistic goal for you then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: To focus on my studies first and regain trust with my mother. If I go to a party, I don't have to drink, or at most have one cup, but I'd prefer not to do that at all.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So your goal is to not drink at all, or if you are at a party, a maximum of one.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Exactly, just so I can take part in the social convention without overdoing it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Chris, I really appreciate you talking with me. I care about you as a student and athlete and want what's best for you. It seems like you have a good plan, striving not to drink or limiting yourself to one maximum.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you for listening to me. It means a lot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's my pleasure, it's the part of the job I like best. Now you better hurry up and get changed for practice.

video_details.title: The Ineffective Youth Minister With a High-Risk Teen: Non-Motivational Approach
video_details.description: Demonstration of confrontational youth advising regarding high-risk alcohol use (to contrast with motivational interviewing approach). The content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the official views of the National Institutes of Health, the University of Florida, or the Cher

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So Tommy, I wanted to talk to you because I was on Facebook the other day and saw some pictures that are kind of concerning to me of you and some of your friends at a party. You're such a good kid, like I don't know what you're doing drinking, it's going to ruin your life.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, it was just like a social gathering, it wasn't like I was looking for it. The drinks were there and all my friends were doing it, and it was just... it's not something that I do on occasion, but whenever the opportunity presents itself, it's nice to just let loose and have a little bit of fun sometimes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But Tommy, there's so many consequences with drinking. You're not even 21 yet. You could get arrested, you could have a drunk driving accident, you could mess up your schoolwork. You have such a bright future ahead of you, it just really, really concerns me.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I get where you're coming from, but I thought that I had it under control and I didn't let myself get too far gone. I wanted to be in control and I wanted to make sure that all my friends were okay so I didn't let myself drink too much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: There's really no such thing as not drinking too much. I mean, anything that's drinking when you're underage is drinking too much. Think about all the things that can happen to you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I understand exactly what you're saying and...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How much are you drinking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't think I'm drinking that much. I mean it's mainly for social gatherings, like it's nothing that I do by myself or whatever.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is it like every weekend?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Every other weekend, I would say.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tommy, I'm just so concerned. You know, can't you think of anything better to do?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I can. I could probably be more productive in my schoolwork rather than going out to parties as much, and I do get where you're coming from.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are your friends the problem? Maybe you should just start hanging out with more kids in the youth group and not hang out with those kids you were partying with.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess I haven't really put it on myself, I guess it's really been forced on their account and I've just been following in their footsteps just because it seems like what they're doing is a lot of fun and I just want to make sure I'm getting every bit of the high school experience that I can.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well there's a lot of things that seem fun in the moment that we know aren't a good choice, right? That's some of the things we talk about all the time is making good choices for our life and really doing what's best for you and I just... you know, I really think you should think about making a big change here.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I do see that maybe me drinking not as much would possibly better my life to a certain degree and it does make a lot of sense and I guess I can put more effort into sort of lowering the level of drinking that I...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think you really need to quit.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean alcohol is just so prevalent in our society and it's just around me wherever I go in parties and stuff that I kind of feel like I should just get used to it or at least understand its effects before I should let it get out of my life entirely. I don't really see it as something that will completely destroy my life.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think you're wrong. You know, it really worries me. Anyway, I wish you would quit. If all you're going to do is cut down, that's better than nothing. You know, I appreciate you talking to me about this, but I'm going to keep talking to you about it. It's really important.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I just don't see the problem in it right now and maybe it's because I haven't really had that traumatic of an experience but I'm...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you want to wait for that to happen? Do you want to wait for a dramatic experience?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You're right. I don't want to be too far gone before it's too late. Like I can imagine something possibly happening where it's to a degree where I can't escape. And I guess I've never really had any real experience where alcohol has really affected me that much or affected anybody close to me that much. So I guess it's something that I feel like I'm in control of but in reality I might not have as much control as I think.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, well maybe it's something we can work on together and you know, I think we should come up with a plan that's going to work for you so that you can get control here and stop drinking.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think that would be a good step forward into a life of possibly being sober and just experiencing the true aspects of life rather than the haziness of alcohol.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, sounds good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Watch what happens this time when the youth minister allows the teen to tell his story and guides him to consider how his drinking could interfere with his goals and to think about how he might benefit from making a change.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So Tommy, I wanted to talk to you because I was on Facebook the other day and saw some pictures from a party you were at and made me a little bit concerned because I saw you were drinking and I wonder if you can tell me a little bit about how alcohol fits in your life.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mainly just drink whenever I'm at parties or whenever somebody hands me a beer. I'll take sips every now and then, but it's not something that I feel hovers around my life.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's kind of a social thing for you, not like a major priority. How much do you think you're drinking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I guess I would say like every other weekend, maybe every two weeks. On occasion, maybe if there's a basketball game going on or a football game I'll have a beer just to drink with my boys, but other than that I don't really see it as much of a problem.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're drinking maybe half the time depending on what's going on that weekend?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess you can say that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What, how would you describe the difference between weekends when you drink versus ones when you don't?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, when I'm not drinking I'm usually more involved in doing more productive things like I try and do more schoolwork whenever I have the time or whenever I can go work out or something. But whenever I'm drinking I devote my time to just letting loose and having fun and just relaxing with friends.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So you feel like you get more stuff done on weekends when you don't drink, but maybe you don't feel like you can relax as well.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean, whenever I'm drinking I know that I'm devoting time to not doing other things, so I try and make it so that I don't allow myself to pile on so much work, so I try and get work done before, but I know that drinking gets in the way of productivity, so I try and minimize that as much as possible.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're trying to be responsible and get your stuff done, knowing that the drinking's going to make it harder. Okay. But it sounds like are you getting everything done or is some stuff sort of slipping when you drink?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess when I drink some things do slip a little bit just because when I'm drinking I'm not really focused on what I have to do. I'm focused on the moment and just enjoying the time that I have at that time. And it's really something that I just... it's something of an enjoyment type of thing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What are the things you enjoy about the drinking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just the way that it... it sort of like liberates you. It makes you feel like a more confident, more energetic person. You don't feel like yourself, you feel like a different version of yourself. And it's something that is just empowering to a degree.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So you feel liberated or kind of more confident in some ways. Okay. Are there any not so good things about drinking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Whenever I drink too much, I sort of lose control of myself and I just... like the aftermath of whenever I've drunk too much or whenever my friends mixed drinks and it just has a harmful effect on my body. And that's probably one of the major drawbacks that I have from drinking.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What kinds of things happen?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mainly when I puke or it's just the feeling that I get in my stomach if I drink too much, it's just very overwhelming.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So like you notice it in your body. Okay. How much do you think is the most you've ever drank in one time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Wow. I would say probably at a friend's birthday party recently and he wanted to let loose. It was just all the guys were together and they had a couple of friends over and it just turned into one big party and I just lost it. I drank way too much, I would say like probably a bottle or two and just some beers along the way. It got to a point where I lost count.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That was out of the ordinary for you to lose count. What's a more typical amount that you drink?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I don't let myself drink more than three or four beers on a given night just because I've gotten to the point where I sort of know my limit, but I kind of flirt with my limit just to see how far I can go. And I think that that sort of is very dangerous to play with fire, but I want to see how far I can go just so I know not to go that far.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Got it. So you're sort of testing and pushing it and sometimes crossing that limit and having some of the consequences that you mentioned before.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, just so I know how it feels now so that later on when the situation is more drastic and more out of control, I know what I can do or where my limit is at.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Well, kind of along those lines, looking ahead, you know, five years from now, what do you see as a goal for yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: In terms of career wise?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, in terms of what you think you'll be doing in five years.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would love to travel. I would love to see the world for what it is. And I've always seen pictures and videos of how the world is, but I've never really experienced that. Like, I've always wanted to travel to Europe or China or someplace like that so I can really experience the world that we live in.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So getting a full experience is really important to you, it sounds like throughout your life. You talked about wanting to make the most of your high school experience and now you're looking ahead to think of how you can enrich your life in other ways. How do you think drinking too much would fit into, you know, being able to experience life to its fullest?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess it could interfere with allowing myself to feel the effects of living life to the fullest. But I wouldn't want to tamper with drinking too much often, just because I know I've seen the consequences that drinking has on people and I know that I would never want to get to a degree where I need to drink constantly every single day. I don't want to ever get to that point.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So just to kind of summarize what you've told me so far. You're drinking pretty regularly, but you are trying to limit yourself. You feel like three drinks maybe is probably the maximum that you can drink before you're having some of these negative consequences and you feel better if you limit yourself to three or less.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I feel more in control.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And then kind of looking ahead, you don't want to find yourself being someone who's drinking all the time or someone who feels out of control with their drinking. You've seen that maybe in other people's lives and it's not appealing to you at all.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not at all.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you do have some big goals for your life that you want to achieve that drinking too much could also interfere with. So where do you think you want to go from here with regard to your drinking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe now that I know my limits to an extent, I kind of don't want to push it so much. Now that I know what I can do and where I can go, I would like to mitigate that as much as possible. I just want to have fun being me, but I don't want me to be influenced by alcohol so much. Like I want to live the sober life to an extent, but I know that alcohol is just going to tamper with that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So for right now it feels like a reasonable goal for you would be to sort of limit your drinking and make sure you're stopping at three, for example, or maybe even limiting the number of times that you're drinking.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, or like not drinking in the mornings or just strictly for social purposes, just to not have it around. Like I don't want to have it in my fridge if my parents have it, I don't want to have to deal with that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. What do you see as some benefits to that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Benefits in terms of...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: ...to sticking to those limits.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I could definitely live a more fulfilled life to an extent. Like I could possibly be more productive, more efficient in my work and where I can possibly be in the next few years of my life. And I think that by not drinking it will definitely have a better effect on my life.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. Well, I think taking steps to limit and cut back on your drinking is a really good idea. I really appreciate you taking the time to talk with me about it and being open and honest.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My pleasure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You know, if you don't mind, I would like to talk to you probably about this in a couple weeks or a couple months, just check in how things are going.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. Sounds good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Sounds good. Thank you very much.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This time the youth minister began by expressing concern but relied on open questions and reflective listening to build rapport and encourage Tommy to share his experiences. Tommy provided a great deal of useful information regarding his drinking very quickly, which set the stage for a more productive conversation. By exploring both sides of the issue, Tommy was given the opportunity to open up without fear of condemnation, and was also able to admit to some of the consequences of his drinking. This gave him the chance to consider the reasons he might benefit from making a change. The youth minister also encouraged Tommy to look ahead to consider how his drinking could affect his future plans. By exploring his values and relating them to his drinking, she developed a discrepancy between his future goals and his current behaviors, highlighting the need to make some adjustments to his drinking. Using a summary, the youth minister was able to transition smoothly to a discussion of options, and Tommy identified a realistic goal for himself that matched his values. As a result, he is much more likely to follow through on his plans and actually make a change in his drinking.

video_details.title: Counseling Treatment Planning - Goal and Objective Setting Related to Mild Depressive Symptoms
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which counseling treatment planning is demonstrated. The treatment planning includes setting a goal and the corresponding objectives related to mild depressive symptoms.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello, Allison. How are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm good. How are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. I was hoping we could start today by beginning your treatment plan.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I don't know if you remember from the first session that I had told you around session four that we would start your treatment plan and try to finish around session five.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the treatment plan, I usually like a treatment plan to have two or three goals and each goal to have some objectives. So today I thought we'd just work on one goal, okay? And I'll kind of get that down and then give you some time to think about it until next week and then kind of work on the other goals from there. We'll finish up the treatment plan next week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, sounds good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does that sound okay to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the goal is kind of like your overarching goal for therapy in general, okay? And the objectives, which I'm going to note too, are specific tasks you can do that will help you achieve that goal. So they're specific, they're measurable, and we hope they're achievable. Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So do you have like an overall goal in mind for our counseling sessions?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, yes. I would like to be able to kind of, I've been feeling a little depressed and I would really like to be able to reduce those the depression.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So reduce feelings of depression. That would be your goal. Okay, yes. Sounds like a good goal.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what objectives, what tasks do you think that you could do that would help you to feel less depressed?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess maybe some sort of physical activity. Maybe like walking. I like to be outside, so maybe walking could be one.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Um, have you had a plan before where you've walked regularly?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You know, I used to. I did, and it would give me some relief because I was able to clear my mind whenever I was walking. And so yes, yes, I've had success with walking before.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So walking has worked before. And you've noticed that you're walking less since you've had the feelings of depression?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have been. I really haven't been doing too much of anything. I've just been kind of at home doing homework, stressing out over getting homework done, because I'm back in school and it's been so stressful and overwhelming and it's just kind of got me in this depressed mood.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, since you're on the topic of homework, was there something you think you can do there? You mentioned that it's stressful and overwhelming, and that sounds like the type of feelings that are related to depression sometimes.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mm-hmm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you find that kind of being stressed about the homework is...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, because there's so much work to be done and sometimes I get several assignments due at the same time and I find myself rushing to get assignments in and it can just be a little daunting, just overwhelming sometimes. And I don't know, maybe if I spaced it out and did some time management or something like that to kind of help me with that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you feel like maybe you're starting the homework late compared to when it's due?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So that's where the feeling maybe of overwhelmed...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I would say that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. It sounds like this is just an organizational thing, right? So if you can space it out where you kind of start your homework earlier and do it in small bits instead of waiting more or less the last minute, that would likely reduce some of the stress and feelings of being overwhelmed.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'm sure it would.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you want to make that your second objective then? So you have the walking, and then you'll have trying to space out the homework.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, okay. That sounds doable.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does that sound good? So we have the walking and then spacing out the homework a little more. Both of those seem tied to the depressive feelings that you're trying to eliminate.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What other objectives might work?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Since I've been back in school, I used to love to sing and I haven't done that in a while. And so maybe getting out and singing again and socializing with my friends that I used to sing with, maybe that could help because it would get me out of the house.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has that worked in the past for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was something that I enjoyed doing. And right now I feel like I'm not doing any of the things that I've enjoyed doing because I've been so busy doing homework. So I think that would probably help.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's a good break from thinking about and stressing about the homework for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It has the singing part's fun for you, it sounds like, but also there's a social component, seems like.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I enjoy the people that I would sing with. And we would go and hang out together, go to different jazz clubs or events, different bands that were playing, and it would just be fun. I love music. So I love listening to it and I love singing, making music. So I think that would be a good goal.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Great. You seem to kind of light up a little when you talk about singing.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I just love it. I enjoy doing it. And I just haven't had a chance to do it lately.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So part of this is just making the time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, good. So we'll make that a third objective. So we have walking, organizing your homework differently, and then singing and the socializing that accompanies that. That's great. Three objectives is good. I try to get to four if you have one. Is there a fourth objective that you can think of? Something else that you associate with not feeling depressed?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I used to absolutely love going to the beach and visiting with my aunt. The beach is soothing and comforting, and my aunt is such an awesome person. She's always pouring into me and I just love spending time with her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And she lives down at the beach.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, she does.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so this seems like a good objective too.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're suggesting maybe visiting her more often?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, because I haven't gone to visit her in a while. And the thing is she only lives like an hour away.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's not a long drive.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, it's not. So that's like a trip I can do on a Saturday. Take a break and go down there and spend some time with her. I think that would be helpful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So again, getting away from the school stressors and just taking a break from it for a day.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And then also spending time with somebody that you enjoy spending time with.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good. So I want to go through each one of these and just make sure that we're meeting all the criteria for an objective. These are all specific, which is good. Do you feel these are all achievable? These are things you can do?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yes? Well, some of them you've done in the past, right? So now we have the specific and the achievable. Now I want to get to the part that's a little more tricky, which is making it measurable.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I don't want to be overly prescriptive in terms of objectives, I want you to decide. But I want to see if we can quantify in some manner how often you'll be able to do these different things. So first with the walking. In a given week, what's realistic for you in terms of getting out and walking? How many times?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, maybe I can start out with twice a week.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Twice a week? Okay. Do you have two particular days in mind? Days where your responsibilities aren't too great and you have that opportunity?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, maybe we need to start with one day a week.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, let's go with one day a week. That's a good start. So what day of the week are you thinking for walking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: How about Monday?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there a window of opportunity there you see on Monday?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It is. Um, plus it just kind of I think well No, no. How about Wednesday?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Wednesday? Wednesday, middle of the week, stress from work and school. Yes, Wednesday sounds good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have a particular time range you like to walk? Like a time of the day?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's a good time for you? That's a time you can get out of the house.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, off work and gives me a little bit of time to get home and change and out the door because if I make it too late, I'm not going to go.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So 6:30's kind of the good time for you to get out there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, good. So we'll start with that objective. The walking every Wednesday at 6:30 for however amount of time you're comfortable with. All right, so the homework. This is a little trickier. This is about spacing it out.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the homework assignments that are stressing you out. How much time do they take to complete generally? Like in hours, say.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mm, it depends on the assignment.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If you had to average it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Had to average it, maybe about two hours, two and a half hours, I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well let's go with the worst case. Let's go three hours. And then how much time do you have from when it's assigned to when it's due, usually?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mmm, maybe a couple of weeks.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A couple weeks? All right. And what have you been doing now in terms of managing those three hours relative to that two week period? It doesn't sound like you're doing it early in the two week period.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I'm not.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So a little bit later?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I get distracted. I start reading and then I'll fall asleep or I get distracted by something and then before you know it, the time is gone and I'm rushing at the end to try and get it all done. Three hours worth of work squeezed into the last bit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, I could see how that would be stressful. What day of the week is it usually assigned?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: On Tuesdays.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
