diarization.text: On Tuesdays. So you have three hours of work in those two weeks. What time could you set aside say near that first Tuesday that you could put the first hour in? Maybe divide it in three parts. Is that enough parts?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, should be.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. What would be the first day and time? How about the time when you could start the homework? Just the first hour.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, maybe after I come back from my walk on Wednesdays.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. And how long do you foresee walking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Normally I only walk for an hour.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So gives you some time to decompress maybe around eight?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mm-hmm. Eight o'clock.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: 8:00. All right. So from eight to nine on Wednesday, you'll get that first third of your homework and then you'll stop. Does that sound like a plan? How about that second hour?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I guess I could start it Thursday.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thursday? So that's just one day apart. You want to give yourself more time? It seems like you're not sure.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, let's do Thursday.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Want to go with Thursday? And what hour do you have in mind?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thursdays... at about 7:00.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: About 7:00 to 8:00? All right. So one night, Wednesday, be 8:00 to 9:00 after your walk. And then on Thursday, 7:00 to 8:00. So now just the last hour remains.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sunday. Yeah. Sunday.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sunday. Okay. So you want to get everything done from Tuesday to Sunday night and have the rest of that time off.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. I can try.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That sounds good.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sunday around 5:00.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So five to six.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Five to six, yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What would that feel like to get your homework done by Sunday?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It would be a relief and then I could do some other stuff.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So and there's a potential backup plan I see in here is that if something happens on Sunday, you still have that Wednesday after you walk vacant. Because you still have another six days to have it done after that. All this seems realistic and achievable.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It does.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So how about the singing? I have no idea how long the singing thing takes.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, if I get back in the group that I was in, we would normally get together on a Friday after work.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Every Friday?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Every Friday. But some Fridays it would just be rehearsal. And then another Friday it would be a shorter rehearsal and then we would go someplace if we knew of a group of some friends of ours that were performing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So this is an every Friday commitment, the singing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, but it might be about two hours.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: About two hours every Friday. This is something you really enjoy, though. So Friday, two hours in the evening.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Evening.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's one that you would look forward to, the singing on Fridays. One you feel you could achieve, couple hours on Friday.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. I mean, and if it was something that came up that I really had to get done, it's not like I can't not go. They know I'm in school.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: They understand. Good. So then is the last objective. This is about a whole day commitment, right? Because you're going to the beach. What day...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That would be more like a Saturday, but it wouldn't be every Saturday. Once a month.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So you would go down on Saturday morning and come back that same day. That's something to look forward to.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that something that would be okay in terms of like because on Friday night potentially you'd be out, right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, but on those Saturdays that I know that I'm going, I could not be out too late on that Friday.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, that's a good idea. So you kind of make sure you restrict how long you stay out when you know that Saturday's coming up.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. Restore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So that's four separate objectives and I want to take a moment and print this up for you. We'll work on the rest of your goals next time, but I want you to have this so you can get started on it right away.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So before I print these up, is there any changes you want to make?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I would like to try that. And if it doesn't work, can we tweak it?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, yeah, we can always make changes. We can just make it a document that changes as needed. But if you think it's a good starting place, I'll go ahead and print this up and give you a copy and we can resume with today's session and then next time I see you in a week, we'll work on the rest of the treatment plan.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sounds great.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does that sound like a good plan?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Thanks, Allison.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

video_details.title: The Ineffective Athletic Director With a Lower-Risk Teen: Non-Motivational Approach
video_details.description: Demonstration of confrontational approach to student-athlete advising regarding lower-risk alcohol use (to contrast with motivational interviewing approach). Produced by University of Florida Institute for Child Health Policy & Cherokee Nation Behavioral Health. Funded by NIAAA and NIH Grant #R01 AA020695 (Co-Pls: Komro, Boyd & Boyd). The content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the official views of the National Institutes of Health, the University

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, Chris, so I need to talk to you because, as you know, we have a zero-tolerance policy for drugs and alcohol at this school. As athletic director, it's my job to check in with our student athletes and make sure everyone's adhering to that rule. I've been hearing chatter from some of the other kids about a party this weekend. And from what I hear you were there. I'm not at the point where I can give you consequences, but I do want to talk to you about whether or not you're drinking and how you really can't be doing this as a member of one of our teams.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right, actually, I do want to speak to you about something that happened during this past weekend. Usually, as you know, I'm an honors student and my parents don't let me go out to parties, but I used that to convince my parents to go to this party that my friends were pressuring me to go to. When I got there, I wasn't used to this party environment where people were just drinking out of the bottle to get drunk for no reason. Because I was there in the moment, I felt pressured to conform so I wouldn't be ostracized.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, I get it. Like, we've all been there, okay? I was in high school once too, and I drank too, I get it. There's not a ton to do in this town, but the problem is we have these rules. If you're on a team, you have to stick by the rules.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I know that it's bad for me, it's bad for my body, and it's bad for being on the team. It hinders my performance. I just feel that my friends pressure me. I feel I should go with different friend groups maybe, I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Chris, come on. You're getting peer pressured?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. Like, being on a sports team, you feel very... you have to be unified with the group.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, but you're one of the leaders.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. And as being one of the leaders, my fellow teammates expect me to lead not only in the sports, but also in social environments. If that's the social custom in our society, they expect that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, maybe you can start leading as a non-drinker then.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I could, but that could also backfire on me. I feel that I could be ridiculed for having a stick up my butt, you know?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're a star player. Who's gonna pick on you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, I'm just one person against the voice of the mob.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Well, the issue again is I can't be hearing reports about you drinking, and I can't be seeing pictures on Facebook. There are rules at this school and in my job, I have to enforce them. Like I said, I get it, I understand what it's like and that you want to have fun, but you are a star player and we want to keep you on the team. We've gotta figure out a way to get through this.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Well, I'll dedicate the time not to party or get involved with alcohol to that extent and have it publicized on the internet.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you mean?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like on Facebook, all the pictures that you saw on the internet. I will avoid those situations where I feel pressured to drink alcohol and allow what I do in my own private time to be put on the internet so others can see.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Yeah, I mean, we've gotta have a deal here if you're gonna be on the team, okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. I'll stop.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You promise?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I promise.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Shake?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Shake.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. We'll see you later.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: See ya.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right.

video_details.title: The Folstein Mini-Mental State Exam MMSE - Client with a Cognitive Impairment
video_details.description: This video demonstrates an administration of the Folstein Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) with an actor playing the role of a client with a cognitive impairment. This type of exam is also referred to as a Mini-Mental Status Exam.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi George, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. I'd like to give you a test that measures your thinking and memory. Is that okay with you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I'm going to ask you a few questions and if you could answer as best as you can, I would appreciate it. Okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's today's date?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Today. Today is the 15th.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The 15th. What is today's year?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is the month?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: June.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what day is today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's Thursday.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you also tell me what season it is?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's hot. It's summer.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me the name of the building that we're in right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What floor are we on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The fourth floor's hard.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What city are we in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: New York.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What county are we in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Newcastle.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what state are we in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Pennsylvania.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: George, I'm going to ask you to say some objects back to me. Repeat some objects back to me. They are ball, flag, tree. Can you repeat those back to me?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Ball, flower, plant.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I would like you to begin with the number 100 and count backward by 7 and I'll let you know when to stop. Go ahead.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's good George, thank you. I would like you to spell the word world backwards.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The world... spell the world... W-O-R-L-D.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you recall the three items that I mentioned to you a minute ago?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: George, can you tell me what this is?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's a watch.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's a watch. And can you tell me what this is?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's a pencil.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm going to say a phrase to you and I'd like you to repeat it back to me. The phrase is: no ifs, ands or buts.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No ifs, ands or buts.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: George, are you right-handed or left-handed?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right-handed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'd like you to take this paper in your right hand, fold the paper in half and put the paper on the floor.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you. I'm going to hold this sheet of paper that has some instructions written on it that I'm going to point to. I'd like you to follow the instructions that I'm pointing to.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you. George, on the left side of your chair you'll find a clipboard, could you pick that up?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: There should be a pen on there. On the bottom section of that piece of paper, can you write a sentence for me?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you, George. Now on the same piece of paper, you'll see an image up at the top, you see that? Could you copy that for me on the bottom section?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you. George, this has been helpful, I appreciate your participation.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

video_details.title: The Ineffective School Counselor With a Lower-Risk Teen: Non-Motivational Approach
video_details.description: Demonstration of confrontational student counseling regarding lower-risk alcohol use (to contrast with motivational interviewing approach). Produced by University of Florida Institute for Child Health Policy & Cherokee Nation Behavioral Health. Funded by NIAAA and NIH Grant #R01 AA020695 (Co-Pls: Komro, Boyd & Boyd). The content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the official views of the National Institutes of Health, the University of Florida, or the

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Counselors and other school personnel often have the opportunity to discuss risk behaviors with students, like drinking alcohol. The counselor's approach and tone throughout such conversations are likely to influence the degree with which students trust them. Watch what happens when this counselor uses a judgmental stance and lectures the student about school policies and the dangers of drinking.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Laura, so thanks for coming in. I'm going to be meeting with all the students in the school usually once or twice per semester. We're going to talk about whatever's kind of going on in your life. I'll ask you some questions about your goals and what you like to do for fun. So it's pretty casual, just a chance for me to get to know you, if that's alright?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Why don't we start by just having you tell me a little bit about yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, my name is Laura and I'm 17 and I'm a senior in high school.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And what do you like to do for fun?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mostly just hang out with my friends and stuff on the weekends.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And when you and your friends are hanging out, what do you do? Go to football games, go to parties?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, if it's school related maybe a game or two, or go to the mall, and at night maybe a party or something if someone's throwing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And what kind of hobbies do you have?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I like to read and I like to go outside and take walks and hike and stuff. I'm very outdoorsy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh cool. What are your plans for after high school?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I plan to apply to college and maybe have a good career in something like that hopefully.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's great. What do you think you'll study?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I'm looking into journalism, maybe pre-law.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, that's great. That's a really good goal. Are you doing well in school? What kind of grades do you get?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'm doing okay. I'm getting mostly A's and B's.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. What classes are you not getting A's and B's in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think all my grades are A's and B's.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And do you know where you're going to apply to college?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm not sure yet, but I'm looking into schools like in the area, so maybe I'll leave home or something.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Cool. And what made you decide maybe law school or journalism?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I'm definitely not a math or science person, so I started looking at careers that maybe I would like.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Great. Sounds like you have really good goals. You said when you go out with your friends you like to hang out and also go to parties, so do you drink alcohol?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really, maybe one or two drinks at a party at the most.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how often do you think you drink?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe like once or twice a month at the most.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So like once or twice a month you're having alcohol? That's actually kind of a lot of drinking then.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess you could say that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you think's the most you've ever had?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just two drinks at a party at the most. Getting drunk is not something that appeals to me, so I just have a drink in my hand so my friends won't bug me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But you've been drunk before?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, not really, maybe tipsy but not like drunk.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So the most you've ever had is two drinks in a day? Interesting. Do you know all the bad stuff about alcohol?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: One of the things that's really important to talk to teenagers about is drinking and driving. We have kids die every year from getting in a drunk driving accident. Have you ever done that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I've never drunk driven and I've never got in a car with a drunk driver.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. How much do your friends drink?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, I have some friends that drink more than others. My close group of friends don't really drink as much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What about at these parties you're going to? Are there other kids there who are drinking a lot?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, there are kids that drink a lot more than I do, definitely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And do you hang out with them?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really closely. Like, I know who they are, but they're not really close friends of mine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Even just hanging out around kids who are drinking a lot actually puts you at a lot more risk. Did you know that? There's dangers like car accidents, falling, or being sexually assaulted. Especially if you've been drinking, you're at more risk. Have you thought about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I have. That's one of the main reasons I don't like to drink that much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: People get in fights more often, and kids at this school have gotten in trouble with social media pictures. We have a no tolerance policy that could put your whole college career in jeopardy. Have you thought about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, definitely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But you're still drinking. Do you think it's the thing to do if you want to be an attorney?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Definitely not. That's why I don't try to drink that much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We need to talk about some goals for how to be safer. Obviously, you shouldn't be drinking at all. What do you think about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I definitely agree. I know that there are some other risks involved in alcohol other than the ones you mentioned, so I agree that alcohol may not be the best thing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So do you think you can quit?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean, it's not like a really big part of my life.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so I'm going to write down that you've decided to quit. That's going to be your goal. Can you quit this weekend then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, definitely. I'll just not have a drink.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And then what about your friends who are still drinking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I really can't control what they do, but I'll definitely try to get my closest friends to maybe stop like I will.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what if they won't?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, then I guess I'll just try to hang around them less or find things for us to do that don't involve alcohol.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Probably if your friends won't quit drinking you should just find new friends. They're probably not a good influence. You'll be better set for college too; you really can't be distracted by alcohol if you want to get into law school.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, yeah, definitely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. That pretty much covers all the stuff I needed to go over. We didn't talk about what would happen if your parents found out you were drinking.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They would be pretty upset. They don't really condone alcohol use.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So yeah, just another reason why you probably need to quit then. I'll write down that you've decided to quit and I'll meet with you again next semester. Anything else you'd like to talk about while you're here? Any questions?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I think I'm good. I have no questions.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, alright. Well, that's probably it then. You can head back to class and thanks for coming in.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, thanks.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Beginning the conversation with closed-ended questions interfered with relationship building and made Laura feel like she was in the hot seat. The interaction does not feel personalized; the counselor resorted to lecturing and warning the student. There is very little chance that this student will attempt to make a change to her drinking after this interaction.

video_details.title: The Folstein Mini-Mental State Exam MMSE - Client with a Borderline Cognitive Impairment
video_details.description: This video demonstrates an administration of the Folstein Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) with an actor playing the role of a client with a borderline cognitive impairment. This type of exam is also referred to as a Mini-Mental Status Exam.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Zack, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm doing well. How are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm not doing bad, thanks for asking. I'd like to give you an assessment to test your thinking and memory. Is that all right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I'll be asking you a series of questions. If you could just answer them to the best of your ability, that'd be great. Okay. What is today's date?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The 26th.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is today's year?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is the month?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: May.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What day is today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Tuesday.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you also tell me what season it is?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Summer.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me the name of the building that we're in right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Wilmington University.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What floor are we on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The first floor.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What city are we in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Newcastle.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What county are we in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Newcastle.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what state are we in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Delaware.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. I'm going to ask you to memorize a few objects, so I'll read them to you and I'll ask you to repeat them back to me. The objects are: ball, flag, and tree. Can you repeat those back to me?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Ball, flag, and tree.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you. I would like you to begin with the number 100 and count backward by seven and continue to do so until I tell you to stop.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's good. Thank you. I would like you to spell the word 'world' backwards.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you recall the three words that I read to you a few minutes ago?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Ball... flower... tree.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you. Can you tell me what this is?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Watch.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me what this is?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A pen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm going to read a phrase to you, I'd like you to repeat it back to me. The phrase is: no ifs, ands, or buts. Can you repeat that back to me?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No ifs, ands, or buts.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you right-handed or left-handed?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I am right-handed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'd like you to take this paper in your right hand, fold it in half, and then put it on the floor.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you. I'm going to hold up a sign that has instructions. I'll point to it, I'd like you to follow those instructions.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: On the left side of your chair, you'll find a clipboard if you could retrieve that. On a space toward the bottom, I'd like you to write a sentence.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Mm-hm. Thank you. You'll see on that same paper there's an image. In the same area you wrote that sentence, can you copy that image for me?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Very good, thank you. This has been helpful. I want to thank you for participating today.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play - Downward Arrow Technique
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which cognitive-behavioral therapy is used to treat test anxiety and panic symptoms. The downward arrow technique is used to identify intermediate and core beliefs.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm okay, how are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. How have things been going?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They've been alright. Up and down.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Last time we were talking, it sounded like you were still having some difficulty with the quizzes. Is that still the case?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's still... I still panic when I take them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Still panic? Can you tell me about the process of taking the quizzes? I know we've touched on this a little bit before.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm going to class, I'm fine. I sit down to take the test, I'm fine. The test is in front of me, question one... I'm not going to get that answer.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you take these quizzes in class with other students around? Is having other students around distracting to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, it's happened in previous online classes. It's the same.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're pretty sure it's the quiz itself. And the room is relatively distraction-free?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, everybody's quiet.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you're looking down at the first item on the quiz. What are you thinking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm thinking, 'Oh my god, it's gotta be one of them and I am not going to pick the right one. I'm going to think I picked the right one and it's going to be the one that my second choice is and I am not going to pick the right one.'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so your thought is that you're going to select the wrong response and therefore get that quiz item wrong.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about behavior? Do you notice anything physically going on as you're thinking about that quiz item and how you're going to get it wrong?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd say my palms are probably sweaty. Like I'm probably a little tense. That's really it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so what it could be is that this thought of 'I'm going to get this item wrong' is leading to these uncomfortable physical feelings. So what happens when you move on to item two?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Starts all over again. I'm already like 'Well, I already got the first one wrong and now my chances are higher of getting this one wrong.'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you feel like because you thought that you got the first one wrong, your chances of getting the second one wrong actually increased.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I feel like if I get one wrong, the whole test is all going to be wrong.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever had a quiz where you were confident that you got the first item right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm sure I have. I can't remember any.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But eventually you're going to come to one item that you're going to have these doubts about. Does that pattern continue throughout the test?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What happens after you respond to that second item?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It just compounds. I feel worse and worse as the quiz continues.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's an awful feeling. So by the time you get to item five or six...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm convinced it's over, I've gotten a zero or a bad grade.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how about those physical symptoms? Are they the same?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: If it starts early at the beginning, my heart's like pounding at this point, but I still have the sweaty palms and I'm still tensing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it gets mentally and physically more unpleasant. So the panic's really occurring a few items in. How have you actually been doing on the quizzes?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've been a pretty solid B student. I wish I got A's, but B's are fine. But when I take those quizzes I don't know how it translates.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about your study habits? Do you consider yourself effective at studying?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think I'm pretty effective. I read the chapters, take outlines, and review flashcards.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Your study habits and scores are good, but you're having these distressing thoughts and sensations. So you don't necessarily need your performance to change, just your reaction to the quizzes.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, because I get B's, like I said.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: B is good. Let's go back to looking at the first item. The automatic thought is 'I'm not going to get this one right'. What does that mean to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It means once I don't get that right, I'm not going to get anything else right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're going to fail the whole quiz.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The whole thing, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What does that mean to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: If I fail the quiz, then I'm going to fail the final, then the course. And that's going to affect my GPA.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If you failed the course, what would that mean to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That I'm not going to graduate.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And if you didn't graduate, what would that mean to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can't be a teacher. I can't do what I want to do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What would it mean to you if you couldn't be a teacher? If you were to phrase that as an 'I am' statement, what would that make you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I am a person who didn't make it. I am a person that failed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're saying 'I'm a failure'. Right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's close.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: One of your core beliefs may be that you're a failure. Does that seem like something you've said to yourself before?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can relate to that. Because a lot of times I feel like 'Oh, I'm not going to be able to do this because it's me'.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're personalizing it. You're saying to yourself 'I'm going to be unsuccessful, I'm going to fail'. Do you think that's what's happening?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It must be. Because I study and get good grades. I don't have ADHD or anything intrinsic that would prohibit me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How do you think your friends or family would react if they knew you believed you were a failure?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't think they would see the connection. They'd be like 'Well, you do well in school, I don't understand.'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So they wouldn't believe that you're a failure. And similarly, if a classmate was in the same situation, how would you evaluate them?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I'd say 'Look at the evidence, you're not a failure.'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But with yourself, you're being a little more harsh. So we can go after this at two levels. The first is when you have that automatic thought 'I'm not going to get it right', I want you to apply an adaptive response or self-talk. What could you think that would counter that automatic thought?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess that in my past quizzes, chances are I have a good chance of getting it right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I like that adaptive response. The next time you're taking a quiz, I want you to apply that. It takes work, but don't let those physical symptoms discourage you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, touch and go.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You have 15 items, so you have a few chances to apply that adaptive response. Hopefully, you'll reduce the probability that the automatic thought comes in. Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It does, I think I can do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: At the other level, I'd like you to reflect on the evidence that supports and refutes the idea that you're a failure. Write down both and we'll evaluate it next time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I can do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When's the next time you'll be taking a quiz?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think next week.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We'll set up a session for after your quiz. Try the adaptive response and try evaluating the evidence with the core belief. Does that sound good?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, I'll set the appointment up. I appreciate you coming in and working through this.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, thank you so much.

video_details.title: The Effective School Counselor With a Lower-Risk Teen: Motivational Interviewing Demonstration
video_details.description:
Demonstration of motivational interviewing approach to student counseling regarding lower-risk alcohol use. Produced by University of Florida Institute for Child Health Policy & Cherokee Nation Behavioral Health. Funded by NIAAA and NIH Grant #R01 AA020695 (Co-Pls: Komro, Boyd & Boyd). The content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the official views of the National Institutes of Health, the University of Florida, or the Cherokee Nation.  
ANYONE MAY U

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Laura, thanks for coming in. I'm not sure how much you know already about what you're doing here, so I'll give you a little rundown.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Basically, we're here to talk for a bit about your goals for your life, get to know you better, and talk about some behaviors you might be engaged in.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's not my job to judge you or try to change you. I'm just going to talk to you about how things are going and how I can be most beneficial for you. Does that sound okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so I guess to get started, can you tell me a little bit about yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My name is Laura, I'm 17 years old, and I'm a senior in high school.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And what kinds of things do you have planned for your life?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, hopefully go to college and get good enough grades to get in.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's great. Do you have a plan as to where you might want to go?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm not sure yet. Maybe a few schools in the area, or maybe out of state so I can move away for college.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, keeping your options open. Great. And do you have an idea about what you might want to study?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, maybe pre-law.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh wow, okay, that's exciting. What do you like to do for fun?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: On the weekends, I like to hang out with my friends, go to a party, or the mall to shop, or if there's a school-related event like a football game.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You like to have a good time. And do you have a lot of friends or a few close people?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd say a moderate amount. I'm not really popular, but I'm not friendless. I'm like normal.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, that's a good way to be. It sounds like in general things are going pretty well for you. How are your grades right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They're pretty good, A's and B's, so I'm doing okay for college.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Great. Well, one thing I want to ask about are values. Different people have different things that are important to them, like family or friends.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm going to show you a few things on this sheet like belonging, family, friendship, and respect. Which of those are important to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Family definitely, friendship, and belonging.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's important to you about your family?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I love them so I want them to think well of me and be accepting.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have brothers or sisters?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I have one sister.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Great. And how about friendship?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've grown close to many people I care about, so I'd like them to be accepting of me as well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So being a good friend and having people who are good friends to you is important. And what about belonging?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just a sense of fitting in and feeling accepted in general.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. You mentioned you like to go to parties. I'm curious, when you're there, do you ever have any alcohol?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not much. Maybe like one or two drinks at the most.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How does alcohol fit into your overall social scene?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I pretty much just have a drink so it looks like I'm drinking, so maybe people won't bug me about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're getting pressure from other people and it feels easier to just hold a drink?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, just to have one there and pretend that I have it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how often do you think you are around alcohol?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe one or two weekends a month at the most. It's not really much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In what sort of situations?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: At a party or at someone's house. Even if it's not a party, there might be a few beers around.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you ever places where there are parents around, or is it mostly just with the kids?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mostly just us, but sometimes I'll go to a close friend's house and hang out with their family.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what about driving?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like drunk driving?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, or being in a car after having any alcohol?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Definitely not. I've never drunk driven and I've never been in a car with a drunk driver.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's a decision you've made, it sounds like.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, because I know that's extremely dangerous.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you know about why it's dangerous?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Alcohol impairs your judgment, and driving under the influence can lead to crashes and accidents.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're trying to be safe. I commend you for sticking with that. What's the most alcohol you've ever had in one day?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No more than two drinks, definitely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what kinds of things do you like about alcohol?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've never been drunk, so I can't really say, but it just puts you in a good mood.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it just kind of makes you feel relaxed? Any not-so-good things about it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Definitely. When people drink too much, they start throwing up, they get hurt, or they get loud and obnoxious.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you've seen the consequences for other kids and decided that's not for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's just obnoxious things.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Underage drinking is illegal and considered risky. What do you think about how that fits into your life?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I know it's definitely risky, but I guess we still do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How does alcohol play a role in you fitting in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not with my family, but with my friends at parties there's usually alcohol involved.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So with friends you feel like it's easier to hang out when it's there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess, since it's just there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Looking ahead 5 or 10 years, how do you think drinking might fit in with your life?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It will have a very small role because I have big plans for my future.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you expand on that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I wouldn't be drinking as much if I'm studying in college or law school.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So alcohol is something that might make it harder to reach your goals?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, definitely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How often do you think you might be drinking when you get to college?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe less than I am now, maybe one drink every once in a blue moon.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you have a plan to cut back eventually. How might that go?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would try to stop in high school, and then later just socially once in a while.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: On a scale of 1 to 10, how important is it to make adjustments to your drinking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe a five or six.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And why did you say five or six?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's not something I don't care about, but it's not constantly on my mind.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And how confident are you that you could make a change on that same scale?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm pretty confident, maybe an eight or nine, because it's not a big part of my life.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like you have a plan to adjust because of your goals. What sort of goal could you set today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably to stop. Maybe at the next party I go to, not have a drink at all.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you feel confident you could just stop completely?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I can just tell my friends. I can just say I don't feel like having a drink today.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What might be some benefits of following through with that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'll have all my senses and I'll be aware of everything. And health concerns too.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Great. Should we meet again in a few weeks to check in and see if it's working for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that would be okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Is there anything else that you think would be important for me to know?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: How would you advise me to get my friends to stop drinking?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You can try more activities that don't involve alcohol. At parties, carrying a non-alcoholic drink or an empty bottle can act as a barrier.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, for sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you thought about how you might talk to your friends about your plan to stop?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'll just tell them I don't really want to drink anymore and that it wasn't me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And they'd be comfortable with that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, at least my closest friends for sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any other concerns or questions?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I think I'm okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. We'll meet in a few weeks and see how it's going. If you run into stumbling blocks, we can problem solve together.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, great. Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does that sound okay? Thanks so much.

video_details.title: The Effective School Counselor With a High Risk Teen: Motivational Interviewing Demonstration

Demonstration of motivational interviewing approach to student counseling regarding high-risk alcohol use. Produced by University of Florida Institute for Child Health Policy & Cherokee Nation Behavioral Health. Funded by NIAAA and NIH Grant #R01 AA020695 (Co-Pls: Komro, Boyd & Boyd). The content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the official views of the National Institutes of Health, the University of Florida, or the Cherokee Nation.  
ANYONE MAY US

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Andrea, thanks for coming in.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I thought I'd start by telling you a little bit about my role. My job is to meet with students to talk about how things are going and think about any changes you might want to make. My role is to help you think about your life and how you might like to move forward. Does that sound okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so why don't we start by you telling me a little bit about yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure. I'm Andrea, I'm a junior in the marching band. I play the tenor sax. I'm a bit of a band geek; I also play in the wind ensemble and jazz band.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Wow, you really are involved in music. When did you start?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I started playing about 10 years ago. I started on the violin, then explored the piano and clarinet, and finally found the tenor sax.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Very cool. It sounds like you're in a lot of musical ensembles. Any other hobbies or things you like to do for fun?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just hanging out with my friends or going to the beach.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Tell me a little bit about your family.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have one older brother, my parents, and a dog.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Cute. What kind of dog?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A golden retriever.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, nice.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My big boy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Very fun. And how are things going in school for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Pretty good. Grades have been alright, around a 3.7.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, great. What sorts of goals do you have for after high school?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd like to graduate and hopefully go to an Ivy League school. Then I'd like to become a doctor, study psychology, maybe become a psychiatrist.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Those are some pretty big dreams. One thing I'm going to ask you about is the values you have in your life. Looking at this sheet, which of these are most important to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A sense of community and belonging, and respect.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me why you picked those three?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I enjoy the team setting of marching band, working together towards a goal. Respect is also important to me, respecting myself and those around me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So being part of a group gives you belonging and purpose, and respect is all-encompassing for yourself and others. What things do you like to do when you get together with your friends?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes we go to the movies, the beach, or just play board games and hang out at someone's house.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there ever alcohol involved?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, sometimes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How does alcohol fit into your social scene?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mostly at parties to get things going and get everyone loosened up.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How often would you say you're drinking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: About two or three weekends out of the month.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's different about the days when you drink versus the days you don't?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The days we drink are mostly parties with dancing and fun. When we don't, it's more relaxed with board games and movies.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you notice a difference in your enjoyment level at a party versus a night playing board games?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Board games are relaxing. Parties are energetic and draining, but fun in the moment.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What things do you like about drinking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We tend to have more fun because everyone is loosened up and relaxed. But too much drinking can obviously be bad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What are some of the not-so-good things about alcohol?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It makes people make dumb decisions. We try to be safe by sleeping over at friends' houses so we're not driving, but people still have stupid ideas when they're drunk.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You try to avoid dangerous activities, but things still happen. Can you tell me more about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't like it when me or my friends drink too much and end up throwing up. That's not fun.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How often does that happen?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It happened to me once, the first time I ever drank. Now I have to take care of friends who drink too much, which puts a downer on my fun.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there's relaxation, but also the need for safe planning and dealing with consequences like throwing up. Any other downsides?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: People can get sloppy and do things in public that should be done in private.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're stuck being exposed to things you don't need to see. You mentioned limiting the dangerous aspects. Why did you make those decisions?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have an aunt who is an alcoholic, so I see the issues involved. I know drunk driving is an issue and want to limit the dangers while still having fun.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds similar to your value of respect. How do you think drinking fits in with respecting yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: In a way, drinking is a form of disrespect to my body. But I am respecting myself by limiting my intake to stay in control of my behavior.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're looking for a balance. Do you have a limit you stick to?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I make my own drinks so I know what's in them. I make one drink and try to make it last as long as possible. That way people aren't pressuring me to have more.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And do you feel that's working well for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: For the most part, yes. But sometimes when everyone gathers for shots, I'll think maybe I can take one more, and that's when I start falling into too much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How important is it to you to make adjustments to your drinking to fit with your values and goals?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd like to try to drink less so I'm not damaging my body. I'd also like to have my friends on board with a similar mentality so we can work at it together.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you have a goal of cutting back. On a scale of one to ten, how important is it to work on that goal?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: About a six or seven. I'd like to work on it, but it's not the most urgent thing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Why a six or seven rather than a four?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Because it's still important. Going to med school, I know how it affects your body and schoolwork. Drinking every weekend won't work in college.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Looking ahead, you can't keep drinking this way and reach your goals. How confident are you that you could cut down on that same scale?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Definitely a ten. If I made the decision for sure, I know I could do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How might you go about doing that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe trying to convince my friends to stay in, or being okay with not drinking even if they are.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So planning non-alcohol activities and participating without drinking yourself. Does that sound like a goal you want to work on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think so. It's possible.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would it be okay if we met in a couple weeks to see how it's going?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think so. That's good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I appreciate you talking to me. You have ambitious goals and a supportive social life. It sounds like you have a good plan in place, and I'd be excited to talk with you about how it's going.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'd like to.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, great. I'll plan to see you then in a few more weeks.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Perfect. Thanks.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Great, thanks.

video_details.title: Suicide Assessment of Client with Initially Subtle Warning Signs of Suicide
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play session that demonstrates a suicide assessment of a client (played by an actress) whose thoughts and warning signs of suicide are initially subtle.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now Erin, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm alright.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're alright?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: There's been some changes in my life, but, um, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good changes?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Nah, not really.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Not really? What kind of changes?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You know I lost my job, so, things are kind of a domino effect from that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there's been consequences from losing your job?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, obviously. You have a job to take care of certain things. Like paying your bills. I guess that's really why most people have a job.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you've been unable to pay your bills? How's your mood overall?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, definitely. I mean, what can I say? I lost my job. I'm seeing you because I have a drinking problem. Things are not that great.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me about the drinking now. How's it been going?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I drink a lot. I always say to myself that I'll try to drink less, but at this point it's kind of like what have I got to lose, you know?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you drinking more? A lot more?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess I have more free time now because of not having a job.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What effects do you think you're experiencing because of the increased drinking? Are you feeling good about it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. At this point, who cares? What difference does it really make?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're indifferent? Does it still feel good?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Nothing really feels good. It just gets you back to normal, pretty much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When was the last time you drank? And how much?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: This morning. A lot. I don't know, I don't recall.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that typical? I don't recall you drinking on the same day that we've had sessions before.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: At a certain point it's difficult to wake up and not have a drink to get through the day. I just drink as much as it takes for me to function.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But you feel as though it's worsened. What's your attitude toward the increased drinking right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm pretty indifferent. Like I said, at this point, what does it matter?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You've indicated you're indifferent, but that's not been the way you've appeared before. You appeared before to be unhappy about it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I just don't know why I should keep making myself suffer.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the drinking takes away the suffering?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The feeling bad about the drinking makes me suffer. The drinking takes away the suffering, but that's not what I meant.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So feeling guilty about drinking is what's caused you problems. How would you like to feel instead?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would like to be happy and not drink. But what's the point in this life where I have no job and I'm going to lose my house? Why do you want me to keep feeling guilty?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you no longer understand the point of life?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Why should I keep fighting to be sober if I lost my job? Things are getting worse. Even if I was sober, I wouldn't be able to handle it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you see as your options? Can you tell me about what you've been doing in the last three or four days?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sitting at home drinking. Going to the liquor store. That's about it. There is nothing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You were working on finding another job. Have you been doing that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, not really. I'm going to lose my house, so I'm just biding my time. I'm not looking for a job now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you stopped looking. When are you losing your house and what's your plan for when that happens?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, it will be soon. I don't have a plan.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Before, you were always pretty careful about planning things out.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've just decided that I'm not going to worry about it anymore. I can't. My whole life is just full of worrying.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what do you see as your alternative to all this worrying? What do you do?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I sense at this time you're much more negativistic. Do you recognize that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, things have taken a turn. If something were to happen to me, there wouldn't be anything that needed to be taken care of.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's going to happen to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like if I died. My house is gone, my job is gone. My drinking will be gone.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would your family miss you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't really care. They probably would have wished they'd done things differently, but that's not my responsibility. My responsibility right now is nothing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So no one would care if you died? Correct me if I'm wrong.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They'd probably care a little but do I care if they care? No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have anything else that you care about? Any goals?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I used to. I drank them away. My life is so ruined, I don't know how you could expect me to come back from this.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You can't see a way to redeem yourself now because all things that happened overwhelmed you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've lost so much. I don't have one scrap of dignity. I don't have anything. Alone, worthless. There's nothing I can build upon.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you've lost everything and you're worthless. This is the most severe I've seen your hopelessness.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The situation is more dire than I ever thought. Things have gotten worse.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Erin, have you been thinking about ending your life? Are you hesitant to tell me that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't want you to feel like you've failed. I really don't want you to try to do anything because nothing that you have tried has worked. I'm a hopeless case.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you planning on ending your life? Do you have a plan in place?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have a plan. I don't really want to talk about it. I don't want you to interfere.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But you're aware that I'm going to try to interfere with your plan. I'm going to do everything I can to prevent that. I see somebody with strengths and resilience.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's not in the forefront of your mind, but they're still there. Do you have an intent to commit suicide?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm going to stop you. I'm obligated to. I'm fairly sure that you won't feel this way a week or two from now. These feelings cycle just like all feelings.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I see somebody with a productive life ahead. Suicide's not the answer. What we should do today is get you over as an inpatient for 5 to 10 days to work on getting your mood stable.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you disappointed that I'm trying to save your life? Do you understand why I'm doing it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
