video_details.title: Motivational Interviewing Role-Play - Preparation Stage - Cannabis Use
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which motivational interviewing is used to treat a client who is in the preparation stage of change. The client is struggling with cannabis use.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Kyle, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm doing okay. I found a great new job working with kids, but they require a drug test. It made me consider giving up marijuana for good, but it helps so much with my anxiety that I'm not sure if I'm ready to give that up yet.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the marijuana has real value for you that you don't want to see go.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's a way to self-medicate.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And at the same time, you would like this job. I can see how this would be a difficult spot for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I definitely want the job, but if I stop smoking, I don't know how I'd cope with panic attacks or anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you been treated for anxiety before?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I tried therapy briefly when the anxiety first started, but it didn't seem to do much, so I quit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you use marijuana for any reasons other than helping with anxiety?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes recreationally with friends, but I really use it when I'm feeling anxious about something.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If you didn't have any anxiety, would that change your motivation to use marijuana?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It would still be tough to give up, but the benefits of the job would outweigh just smoking recreationally.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're excited about the job?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I am, it's a dream job working with kids with autism. My brother has autism, so it's something I've always wanted to do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, tell me about it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's working with kids with autism in the schools as a personal TA in an inclusion program. Since my brother has autism, it's something I've always really wanted to work with.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like you have a real passion for this work, and the big obstacle is the marijuana.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's a catch-22 because starting a new job will make me anxious, and without marijuana, I won't have a way to cope.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you think you have a physical craving for marijuana?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, not really.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you use it recreationally and as an anti-anxiety agent. If you were treated for anxiety, do you think you'd be able to stay away from the marijuana and take the job?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: If the therapy really worked as well as smoking, I think I could do it. I'd need to see results and have real confidence in the treatment.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would having the job you're passionate about eventually reduce your anxiety?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Once I got used to it, yes. I'm frustrated by the drug testing policy though, especially with legalization happening in so many places.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're frustrated that marijuana is illegal and still a barrier.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, but I can't wait for legalization to start working. I need to address this dilemma now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You have a choice: continue using and pass on the job, or stop using to take the job.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It feels pathetic to be like, 'No, I don't want to take my dream job because I need weed.'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How motivated are you to make this change?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm on the fence. I'd need another way to manage my anxiety if I give up marijuana for the job.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So an alternative for anxiety is key to making this change.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, definitely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If you had an alternative as effective as weed, could you quit to get the job?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think so, especially for this job. I could give up recreational use.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What if we start treating your anxiety next week to see if we can reduce your marijuana usage?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's the timeframe for the job?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The turnover is high, so if I miss this one, another will open in a month or two.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When would the drug test occur?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right after the application and interview. I used just a few days ago, so I'll wait for the next opening.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you feel like you can invest in this plan to work on anxiety and move toward the job?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I could do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Next time we'll start talking about the anxiety. All right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sounds good. Thank you.

video_details.title: Suicide Assessment by Counselor Supervisor Not Familiar with Client
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play session that demonstrates a suicide assessment of a client (played by an actress) by a counselor supervisor who is not familiar with the client’s history.

diarization.speaker: Therapist

diarization.text: I don't know. I guess she thinks the things I'm thinking are dangerous.

diarization.text: Do you mind if I do an assessment to measure your risk of harm?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Sharon, how old are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there any history of suicide or suicidal behavior in your family?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, my dad committed suicide.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Your father committed suicide. Any others?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think my sister had an attempt before.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: An attempt. How long ago did your father commit suicide?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: About 15 years ago, I think.

diarization.text: How often do you think about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I try not to think about it.

diarization.text: That must be hard, though. Is that on your mind now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Now that we're talking about it, yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Was it on your mind before we talked?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are there any mental health disorders you're aware of in your family?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me about any disorders you've been diagnosed with?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right now, I think depression, and in the past, I've had some problems with anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how about now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm having problems with anxiety, but not as bad as in the past.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how about depression right now? How bad?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Pretty bad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: On a scale of 1 to 10, with 10 being the worst, how depressed are you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably like an 8 or a 9.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about anxiety on the same scale?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably like a 4 or a 5.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, not quite as bad. Has it been getting worse lately?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think it's been worse lately.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If you think back a couple days ago, how bad were the anxiety and depression?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Anxiety, probably like a 3 or a 4. Depression, about an 8 or 9 still.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have any medical illnesses?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you live alone?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How often do you see your relatives?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe once a month.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about friends?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe once a week. I lost my job, so I haven't seen my coworkers as much lately.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How long ago did you lose your job?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: About two months ago.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How would you characterize the strength of your social network?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, sometimes I feel pretty alone, like nobody really wants me around or needs me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How would you characterize the quality of your family relationships?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They're okay, not really that great. But everybody has trouble with their family.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What about your friends?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's okay. I guess I'm always second-guessing everything, but I think they care about me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any conflict or crisis going on right now besides the loss of your job?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm going to be evicted from my apartment. I'm feeling really lost, helpless, and like everything's pointless.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When are you going to be evicted? When did you find this out?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It sounds like it'll be at the end of the month. My landlord told me at the beginning of the month.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It feels really out of control. I don't know what is going to happen or what I'm going to do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you in the past thought about suicide?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, definitely. Probably every time I get depressed like this.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever attempted to commit suicide?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, one time, about four years ago. I cut my wrists.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You didn't go to the hospital or anything?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever been about to attempt and then stopped?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, maybe three or four times. More recently, maybe once or twice at least.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever injured yourself intentionally?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. There have been times where I cut myself a little bit to see what it would be like.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When's the last time you've done that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The last time I tried to commit suicide. I don't think I would try cutting again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever been abused physically, sexually, or emotionally?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I had a really hard childhood with my mom. I really, really don't want to go live with her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is your attitude and feelings about suicide as a concept in general?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's really sad, but sometimes it feels like, what else is there?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You disapprove of it, but you're considering it because you're running out of options?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever been impulsive in the past? Ever violent or aggressive?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really. No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever experienced hallucinations?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't think so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me about any alcohol or drug use?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes I drink alone when I'm in my house. I don't really do any drugs.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When's the last time you had a drink? How much did you have?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Last night. Probably like a bottle of wine. I drink that three or four times a week.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How frequently are you having suicidal thoughts now? How intense are they?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Really often. Pretty much all the time. They are fairly intense and scary.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have a plan laid out if you try to commit suicide?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I would drink a bottle of wine and then maybe take a lot of ibuprofen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have an intent to commit suicide? Are you going to follow through?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've gotten really close to doing it. So, yeah, I guess I have intent.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me about some of the reasons for staying alive?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I don't really want to die. My family and friends would be really upset.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any religious or cultural values? Any pets at home?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have a cat. I've already asked my sister if she would take her if anything happened to me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What did you do when you worked? Did you like it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I worked at a gas station. I liked the regular customers and my nice coworkers.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you ever look forward to getting another job? What caused you to lose this one?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't see how I would. I went to work drunk.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me about some of your strengths or positive qualities?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can't think of any. My family would say screaming and yelling, maybe. I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I appreciate you allowing me to complete this. We're going to put together a plan to keep you safe.

video_details.title: Motivational Interviewing Role-Play - "Double Approach-Avoidance" - Opioid Use
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which motivational interviewing is used to treat a client in a “double approach-avoidance” decision-making situation. The client is struggling with opioid use.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Anne, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hi Dr. Grandee. About the same.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: About the same? How's it been going?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it might be a little worse. I've been talking about my problems with the perks the past couple times I've seen you. I think at work they might be starting to notice a little bit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: They might be starting to notice that you're under the influence of the perks. Before when we talked, it seemed like you felt safe and that no one was going to find you out.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, because when I take them, I feel normal, like I can function. But definitely last week, my coworker in the cubicle across the way was looking at me really funny. I've also been having a little bit of trouble with the numbers. I'm just not on my game the way I used to be, and I know there's a connection to the drugs.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So in terms of concentrating and focusing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's hard to focus. But if I don't do it, I can barely get out of bed. I'm completely... I don't know what to do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This is tough for you. The Percocet makes you feel normal. It used to give you a high, but not anymore. It's not fun.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, but it makes you feel normal.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And we talked about the detox options...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh God, no. That's not an option.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what's changed to make things more difficult is that you're worried your coworkers are onto you, and that your performance in terms of focusing on accounting work has been compromised as well. Is that about right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, she's definitely noticed and she talks, too. So if she thinks something's off with me, she's going to tell someone. There's the reputation piece and then also the quality of my work. It's a lot harder for me to produce what I used to.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you're afraid that's going to be noticed as well.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, for sure. But I can't go through detox. It's just not an option.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, let's talk about it. I want to do some scaling work and talk about the importance of this change to you. Giving up the perks: on a scale of one to ten, how important is it to you that you make this change?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I go back and forth. I don't know that it's that important. Well, if I lose my job, that would be horrible. So it's important that I keep my job and my reputation.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's important that you keep your job, and that importance appears to be tied to the importance of not using Percocet. They've been tied together a bit, right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, because to get out of bed... yeah, okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so if you had to pick a number, one to ten, how important is it to you to make the change?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't want to answer that. Seven, eight... seven.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Seven? So fairly important.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, fairly. All right, eight. I mean, I gotta keep my job.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, let's talk about another construct: confidence. Using that same scale, how confident are you that you can beat the Percocet?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's what I've been trying to do for about six months now. I've really tried. I don't think I can do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Using the one to ten scale, where do you think you would be?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like zero, one. I've been trying.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So really no confidence that you can change, even though it's very important to you that you do. This is a real bind that you're in.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's pretty depressing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Your confidence is low because you've tried over the last six months and haven't been successful in stopping the Percocet use.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'll leave here swearing to myself that I'm done, but then before I'm in bed that night, I've already taken some.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's easy to see where the low confidence comes in. Have there been any other occasions in your past where you have been successful in making a tough change or beating something like this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, yeah, with the gambling. I used to hit Delaware Park on a regular basis and spent a lot of money. My husband was pretty upset about it, and I had a really hard time stopping that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would you say that you felt addicted to gambling? And are you happy that you did stop?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, yeah, definitely. I would never want to go back to that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When you were in the middle of that addiction, how likely did it seem that you would be able to stop?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I didn't think that I was going to be able to. Probably about a two or three.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there's some parallels here between what happened with the gambling and what's happening now with the Percocet.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I didn't think about it that way. I really didn't think I could do it then, and it's been a couple of years since I've been in a casino.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you were successful at beating that addiction. But you say it's so different now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, definitely. But it's so different. I just find myself popping them in my mouth.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The mechanism is different. With the gambling, you'd have to drive to the casino and have money, whereas the Percocet is so easy.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My cousin just... yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And it's a lot easier to consume a Percocet than to get in your car and make the time. So the mechanism is different.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But I'm wondering if there's any similarities with the potential success. You thought you could never stop gambling, and now you think you could never get through detox.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You're right. It was miserable in that period when I first stopped going to the casino, and I felt that really strong urge to go, but I made it through that. My husband was amazing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Your husband was supportive?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, he would sit with me and talk me through it. He was really encouraging. He'd probably be really happy to see me stop using these perks, too.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Since stopping is important to you, but your confidence is low, this might be a good area to process. You have supports in place and you've successfully defeated addiction before. I know detox is something you're not a big fan of, and I can appreciate your reasons. At the same time, it's important you don't lose your job.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Between now and when I see you next, maybe reflect on some of the strengths and supports and the past successes you've had as you consider this tough decision. Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can definitely do that. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so we'll pick up next week there. I really appreciate you coming in today. Thanks, Anne.

video_details.title: Motivational Interviewing Role-Play - Precontemplation Stage - Weight Loss
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which motivational interviewing is used to treat a client who is in the precontemplation stage of change. The client is struggling with weight gain.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Anne, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I'm okay. How are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm well, thanks for asking. So you say you're doing okay? What's going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, definitely no better than last week when we talked. I mean, it's been... I had some major binges this week and I don't even, honestly, know why we're bothering to talk about it because I've been down this road before. I should just... I should just like give up and buy some mumu's and, you know, just resign myself to the fact that I'm going to get fat and I'm going to stay fat.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me about some of the foods that you've been eating that have been kind of leading to this problem for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Brownies. Brownies, brownies, brownies. And well, that's what got it started, you know, I was great the first half of the week and I was staying away from the sugar, away from the flour. My son stayed home from school, you know, he hurt his head, he wanted to bake brownies. I'm like, well, it's my son, okay, let's bake brownies. So then we ate the whole pan, and we baked two more pans, and then it didn't just stay with brownies, you know. We went out and I had like hamburgers, french fries, um candy, you know, stopped in Wawa on the way out. It's disgusting. I can't... I don't even want to tell you how much because it's just disgusting. And my clothes aren't fitting and it's just really, really sad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You've had a rough week. Yeah. So let's talk about for a second, I'd like to, the... kind of your relationship to this problem. How do you view this problem?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's disgusting. It's like... it's slavery. Food owns me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the... so the food is in control of the situation.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sounds ridiculous when you say it like that, but that's what it is.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's in control. All right. So let me... I want to ask you a couple questions about the... the importance and and the confidence of changing. Clearly, um, you have some desire to change, or you wouldn't be here.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh my God, I would love... yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So if you were looking at a scale of 1 to 10, 1 was... it's not important to change, and 10 was... it's extremely important to change. So this is just how important it is for you to... curtail your eating.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: 10. So very important to you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's very important. Okay. So what if I asked the same question, except this time... your confidence. So 1 is you're not confident at all you can change, but 10 you're very confident you can change.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I could probably change for half a day. I've done it. I mean, sometimes if I'm lucky I'll get a week, but overall...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Overall.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's impossible. Like, you want a number? It's 0.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's below the... below the scale of 1 to 10. It's... so you have no... no confidence at all.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've... I've tried it. I know. I mean, it's like beating my head against a wall.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So... so on one hand you'd like to... you'd like to stop the eating, it's important to you, but on the other hand you don't believe you can do it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can't do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You can't do it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can't.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It can't be done. Have there been any other changes you've been able to make, say, in the last few years that have been positive?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um... I stopped biting my nails.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you've had some small success in terms of making changes.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you think makes the... this... well, I'll just refer to it as the food problem, so much more powerful? So much more difficult to tackle?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I wish I knew. I mean, there's so many things, it's... it's everywhere.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The food is everywhere.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Food is everywhere. And... I mean...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You mentioned before that brownies were the culprit for this last week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Brownies, Hershey bars, Hershey kisses, um... yeah, chocolate.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You enjoy chocolate.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. How about... other foods that could be contributing to the problem that maybe you don't enjoy as much as chocolate?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, potato chips, um... french fries, um... Mexican food, um... what else? Cheese. Definitely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any other types of candies?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Start naming them. Skittles, um... Cherry Starburst, um... basically any candy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Pretty much any candy.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So of... of the candies, I want to focus just on the candies and not the other foods just for now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The thought of... like if I introduce the idea of stopping eating chocolate, how would you react to that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not gonna happen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's not gonna happen. All right.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would love for it to happen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can just tell you, I don't even want to pretend.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you know that for certain. How about the... let's... let's go for example with the Skittles. What if I introduced the idea of... stopping the consumption of Skittles?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just that one candy? Yeah. Why bother? But... like can I not eat Skittles? Is that what you're saying?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, you... it's up to you whether you eat them or not. But if I introduced that idea of stopping the consumption of Skittles, how would you react to that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I don't really understand why.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, it represents a change in the direction that you want to move.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: But if I stop eating Skittles, I'm still going to eat brownies, I'm still going to eat, you know...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But we know... we know that's an area that... you know, you can't really make a change right now, from what you're saying. Like that's... the idea of stopping chocolate is not going over well with you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, it's not gonna happen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And that's fine. But the idea of stopping Skittles...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That doesn't seem as daunting.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Would you agree still on say the 1 to 10 scale that it's important to stop Skittles?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Okay. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How confident are you you could not eat them?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it's kind of funny now you're talking about it, I sort of want Skittles more, but you know... I... like from now till next week when I come in here, I'd say like I'm 99% confident I could not eat Skittles and it would not be a major problem.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so this is a change that you think you could accomplish. Even though you're not sure it'll actually contribute to solving the larger problem.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. I mean, if I don't eat Skittles this week or even for the rest of my life, is it going to solve my problem? No. But will I do it if that's what you want me to do? Yeah, that's fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I would hope it's something that... that you would want to do. I mean, what I want is one thing, what you want's really important here. Is this something that... I mean, are Skittles part of the problem?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, small. Right. No pun intended. It's a small part of the problem, but you'd agree it's still part of the problem?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So... not a huge change, but it's one that we can work on.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: All right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I want you to be able to, you know, genuinely buy into the goal. I mean, if you don't think it's important, we can talk about other areas of change.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I guess I see what you're saying. I mean, if I'm going to be completely honest with you, I... well, that's what I'm paying you for, right? So... I don't think it's going to work, I'll just tell you that, but...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You think you could stop eating Skittles, but you don't think it's going to solve the larger problem.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Exactly.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. But that's what we have to work with right now because the larger problem is not something... you know, the way you put it is, it has control.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So if I introduced the idea of stopping brownies...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. No. Sorry.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So let's... let's go after the change that we can achieve in this case. You know, it's not perfect, it's not ideal, but it's what you can do.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Fair enough.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sound like a plan? So for this week, just... discontinue eating Skittles.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No Skittles, all right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No Skittles, right. And let's see... let's see how we do with that change.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Fair enough.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does that seem to make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So work with that, and I'll see you again in a week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, good. Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks Anne.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

video_details.title: Motivational Interviewing Role-Play - Precontemplation Stage - Smoking Cessation
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which motivational interviewing is used to treat a client who is in the precontemplation stage of change. The client is being asked by his girlfriend to discontinue smoking.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, Kyle. How you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm doing all right. Not doing too bad. How are you, Dr. Galante?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Not bad. Thanks for asking. What brings you in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My girlfriend saw your ad for smoking cessation and she's been nagging me for weeks to come talk to you, so I figured I would just come in so she'd stop bugging me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you came into therapy today because your girlfriend pressured you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's easier for me to spend 45 minutes with you compared to hours of her nagging me through the week.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you weighed the cost-benefit and decided to come in.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's covered by insurance. It's just 45 minutes of my time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Her goal would be for you to stop smoking. Tell me what your goal is.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't really have one. I don't think smoking's that bad. It's never bothered me. My only goal is to have her stop bugging me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you don't have a goal of quitting smoking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not at all. There's so many good things about smoking. It gives me one-on-one time with my boss at work, so that makes it completely worth it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me about some of the other good things about smoking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's how I meet people. I carry cigarettes but no lighter, so I have to ask for a light. It's a way in to meet groups of people.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the way you're presenting it, smoking has been a positive thing in your life.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, and I only do it socially.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are there any negative aspects to smoking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Everyone knows it's unhealthy, but I don't smoke a lot. I might have a heavy cough on Mondays and Tuesdays, but it's usually gone by Wednesday.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you don't seem like you're too worried about the negative aspects.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's unhealthy, but the benefit of being able to meet new people through smoking is better than giving it up for health reasons.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: On a scale of one to ten, where one is not important and ten is extremely important, how important is it to you to stop smoking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe like a two. It would be cool to get rid of the cough, but that's not worth everything else I get from smoking.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So not particularly important.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: On that same scale, how confident are you that you could quit smoking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably like an eight or a nine. I gave it up for a month recently and didn't even crave it, but I missed the social aspect, so I started again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So stopping smoking is not important to you, but you're fairly confident you could if you decided to.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Based on that, what would be a goal? How could we spend this time so it would be productive?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess it would help to figure out ways to explain to my girlfriend the things I get from smoking so she realizes why I do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: To help her understand why smoking works for you. Any other relational goals?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We've been fighting a lot because of the smoking. Maybe figure out ways to communicate better or have productive fights that don't last for days.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Productive communication and productive arguments.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: One goal would be to illustrate the advantages of smoking to your girlfriend, and another would be to work on your relational style so you can end an argument without feeling like you're at a stalemate.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think that would be cool.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you want to make those the goals we work on so we can spend this time productively?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I can do that. It's kind of like killing two birds with one stone.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does that make sense to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Reflect on some changes you could make to be a more effective communicator, moving from arguments to conversations that have a positive result.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that would be cool if we could do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We'll talk about those different goals and small changes next time we meet.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Alright, sounds good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks for coming in, Kyle.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, thank you.

video_details.title: Motivational Interviewing Role-Play - Preparation Stage - Stimulant Use
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which motivational interviewing is used to treat a client who is in the preparation stage of change. The client is struggling with stimulant use.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, Anne. How are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm okay. How are you, Dr. Connelly?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm good. Thanks for asking. What's been going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, not really a lot of change on the drug front. Uh, the Adderall, I'm really struggling.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Still struggling with the Adderall?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I'm not sure what to do because I mean I'm having such a hard time with it, but when I don't have it I'm just not functioning. I'm not able to get as much accomplished.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So, oh, go ahead.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it's like it's always there, too.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's always available to you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's always available. Yeah, or so much of the time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So you're having some mixed feelings about it, I'm sensing.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah, like I know I want to stop, I think.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You think you want to stop.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. No, I do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You do.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh my god. See, I feel crazy, but I mean I know it would be good if I didn't have it in my life.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But at the same time, it is in your life.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: And I don't know how to get out of that. I mean, if I didn't live with my roommate, that would be one thing. Like, it wouldn't be in the apartment all the time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you find you have easier access to the Adderall when you're in the apartment with your roommate.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So if you physically weren't there, like with your roommate in that apartment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, like if I was, oh my god, living at home with my parents again or even living with somebody else, I guess. Oh my god, but move? What a hassle. But that's, I mean, that's the problem. It's just there. It's accessible.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it sounds like you're recognizing that maybe you don't have the willpower to stop taking the drug when it's right there in front of you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe you're right. Yeah, that's good because before I didn't really want to stop. And sometimes I want to stop. My mind will go back and forth. You know, but for the most part, I would like to be without it. I really don't want to deal with this anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So mostly, so there's still some feelings where you want to use it, but mostly you would like to stop.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it makes it so easy to get stuff done. I mean, I just take a couple and boom, boom, boom.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there's some advantages for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, definitely. And I'm so used to it, too. It's just comfortable.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's comfortable and it allows you to be productive. Are there any downsides to it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, yeah. When I don't have it, the crash is like a really bad crash. I'm not productive. You know, and it's gotten worse than it used to be.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's painful.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like I need it. Yeah, it's painful, definitely. It feels like a trap and I want out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And one of the ideas you're having was potentially moving out of the apartment because then you wouldn't have access to the Adderall anymore, or it would be harder to get.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh my god. And sometimes it feels like that's a good idea and then sometimes I'm like, no, I don't want to be, you know, kind of cut off from it. But I think I'm ready.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You think you're ready for that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And that moving out you really see as what you would need to do because stopping while living there is too difficult.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh my god. Yeah. Yeah, I think you're right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I remember before you've tried to stop while living there a few times over the last few months. And with your roommate being the one that gives it to you, it just appears the temptation is so great for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, she really doesn't get it. She doesn't understand what a problem this is for me. She's definitely not supporting me or anything like that. Yeah. God, maybe it would be better.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, are there any disadvantages to living with your parents?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Living with my parents at my age just feels a little bit humiliating, a lot humiliating.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so humiliation would be one.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, and just this feeling of failure, embarrassment. And then my mom just is in my business, you know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there's some clear disadvantages. Any advantages other than the obvious, it would sever you from the Adderall?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My mom would do my laundry. Fully stocked fridge.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hmm.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah, my dad would fill my gas tank up.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are these things that happened before when you used to live there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah, not so bad. Uh-huh.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there's some disadvantages to this plan, but there's some advantages. And then there's a key advantage of being cut off from the Adderall.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. And it wouldn't necessarily have to be the rest of my life, either. Just for now, just to get me out of that apartment with the drug. Right?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That would separate you from the drug and you could potentially move out later on.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh my god, but do I want to? I mean, that's just it. It sounds really good until I like really think about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So when you really think about it, what comes to mind?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, like I start to shake. Like that feeling of when you really want something and you can't get to it. And just that desperation. And like right now, I know that living there, it could be my choice. But at least when I want it, it's there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's right. It would be.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This is tough. Well before, it seemed like you're really more on the side of making this change than not. But clearly there's still some things you want to consider.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, you know, you're right though. I want out. And it's not really a choice when I'm there. Like I say I have the choice, but the choice is always yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You always end up using the Adderall.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So let me make sure I understand the situation overall. You live with your roommate, she has Adderall, she makes it available to you, you use it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You've tried to stop that behavior but that's just not working for you. You don't want to be using it, but yet you are, especially because of the proximity.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's true. God, it would be nice having that fully stocked fridge.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there could be an upside to it that would be beyond just not using the drug, which would in itself be a big victory for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. And my mom would be there to talk to. Yeah. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so let's do this. It seems like that's the direction you're moving. You're thinking that might be a better way to go.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So for the next session, let's plan out the steps that you'd have to put in place to move out, to move back home. Let's just go through the steps and try to get a firm plan together. And of course you can always re-evaluate and change your mind.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: This is kind of exciting.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's exciting?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it definitely is. I can do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good. So I will see you next week and we'll pick up where we left off and we'll start with the planning and see what happens with that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Cool.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: All right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks, Anne.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure.

video_details.title: Psychosis
video_details.description:
This was a short film cooperate I did for National Health Services so they can show examples to their patients.

John is a 20 year old Afro-Caribbean man who is a student in engineering at Newcastle university, He has no past psychiatric history, or anything significantly wrong in his medical health now or in the past. He has done well academically, and had lots of friends at school.
John did find it strange going away to study so far from home but in his first year things went quite well, and h

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: 999, which service do you require?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I need an ambulance for my son.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Ambulance service, what is the address of your emergency?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: 48 Stanhope Road, Streatham.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's the phone number you're calling from, please?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How old is your son?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's the emergency? Tell me exactly what's happened.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, something's going on in his mind. He's talking about going on top of the roof.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is he conscious?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is he breathing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has he been violent at all?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh god no, no.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does he have a weapon?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh god no. I'm just a bit worried about him, he's acting a bit strange. He's talking about the MI5 trailing him, and he hasn't been sleeping well for the last week.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has he done anything to harm himself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is he thinking about committing suicide?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. He's just been acting really strange, and I think he might leave the house, he's pacing around the room.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is he completely alert?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. He's just pacing around the room. I don't know what's wrong with him, can you please get someone here quickly?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, do you want me to speak to John?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I don't think he'll come to the phone.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No problem. Let John know we're organizing help for him now, okay? Please stay on the line and I'll tell you exactly what to do.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Who is it, mum? Come in.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello, how are you doing? I'm Craig, what's your name?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: John.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How are you doing, John?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm here with mum. Mary. And yeah, everything's fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you want your mum to tell me what's going on, or why have you called us?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's not him. I don't know what's going on.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so have you got any medical conditions or take any medications?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I've not got any conditions or taken anything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: John, what's going on? Are you hearing voices?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm doing a project and someone's talked to me, he's helping me with my project.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you on the phone at the moment or... you've got your earplugs in.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I don't have a phone.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is it alright if Emma just does a few checks on you, like your blood sugar?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, blood sugar.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's been going on today? You've got your big bags.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Traveling, walking, hills, and camping.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's not this kind of bag though, is it? So what's been going on today with you, John?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just a bit weak. Tired. Haven't really been sleeping, I've been trying to focus on my project and it's demanding.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does your mum know about this project?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, this project's from university, I've got to create an airflow.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What university do you go to?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Newcastle. Newcastle's up north. Newcastle's near Manchester, near Leeds, near Scotland.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how come you're not there at the moment? I'm just going to take a little drop of blood from your finger, alright?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm strong, it won't hurt me. It's the half term, so I'm allowed to come back.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Basically I can go and come back when I like because it's my project.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What year at university are you in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm in my second year. There's three years, so I'm in my second.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that right, mum?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He is in his second year, yes. But just recently this has started to happen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: John? You alright? What's going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So what's your name?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Craig. I'm from the ambulance service, remember?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hi Craig.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So your mum's a bit worried about you. You're very anxious, aren't you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've been up all night, slept for three hours. I need to get good grades, otherwise I can't make it into the third year.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You said you haven't been sleeping well... how long's that been going on for?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd say about three weeks. This week's been the worst. Counting every day since.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's my choice. I'm just too active, I've got a lot to do. I like to eat food, I like to play football.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: With your food, do you have a balanced diet?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, a lot of bread, sandwiches, KFC. He's not been eating that brilliantly, have you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What about drinks?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Fanta, Coke. Red Bull, probably two bottles a day.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you take any other kind of drugs? Now, when your mum rang us, she said you were thinking about going up on the roof?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, for my project I've got to create this amazing airflow and fly off. It's for a helicopter and it'll get me a really good job.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it wasn't... you were just going up on your roof for this project? It wasn't anything dangerous? John, you alright?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. X, Y. It's quite complicated, but it links all together because when you've got X and Y it equals Z.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, I think we're probably going to need to get you to come and talk to somebody at the hospital.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think that's a really good idea, don't you, John? You should go and have a conversation with them.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Why not?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I think we're going to have to pop you down the hospital, because I think there's a few things going on at the moment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Are you going to come with me? Of course I'm coming with you. Yeah, we could go.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright then. Ready to come out then? Get your bits together.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. I want to stay here. I'm comfortable here, thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We just need to go and have a chat with someone at the hospital, John.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: John, your mum's going to come with you. We're going to go to the ambulance and have a drive, and it's going to make lots of noises.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh no, I don't like that idea. I want to stay here. I feel really warm and comfortable here, I don't want to go outside.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I really would like you to go with them, John. I'm coming with you too. Mary, mum, I'm staying here, I'm okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: John, you're really worrying your mum. It'd make her feel better if you just came and had a quick chat with somebody.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We've spoken.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I know you've had a quick chat with me, but you need to speak to someone who's a little bit more specialist at the hospital.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Don't you want to speak to someone so they can understand this project that you're on? I think it'd be a really good idea.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: John, listen to me. There's somebody I know at the hospital who knows about this project.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah? He could come here and he can help me. Okay, let's go.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright John, just need to do your blood pressure. If you just want to stick this arm out your jacket for me.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, let's take this off.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Come in please. Hello. I'm Ruth. Nice to meet you. John, I understand things have been quite difficult recently.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, it has been. And the big buildings, lots of people around me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: John, I understand you've had some trouble sleeping, and with your appetite. I'd like to rule out a physical cause. I'd like to take some blood and a trace of your heart.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The other day when I was trying to do my project and then I got a bit tired. What's in that pink folder? Is it got pictures of when I was younger?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It hasn't got pictures. It's got your medical notes actually, John. So it's just going back a little bit.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, I'm fine. I just want to go to the gym and do weights again. I've got a project to do, it's helicopters and airflow and I've just got to create this really mad thing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hopefully you'll be back soon. I'm just going to ask you a few questions. First of all, have you had any headaches recently?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. Have you got my sunglasses, mum? No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you felt weak at all recently, John? Weak in your muscles?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He trains a lot, so I don't think so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And John, I'd like to know whether you've had any problems with chest pain recently?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any feeling of your heart beating or racing quite fast? John, you're doing really well.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: On Sundays me and my mum watch Formula One. I want to be a driver, so I looked at helicopters and then I got an airflow. So that's why I come to the conclusion that X plus Y equals Z because it's maths.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, John. Have you noticed any pain in your tummy at all? Are you passing urine okay at the moment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how about passing poos? Is that alright? Great. I'm just going to examine you, if that's alright.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you. What are you doing? I used to do this when I was younger, I used to play games. I'm fine, Dr. Bennett.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: What does that mean, what you've done so far?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm just giving him a brief physical check to make sure there's nothing wrong physically. We'll follow this up with blood tests and a trace of his heart. And then one of the other doctors is going to come and talk to John.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like a maths test and English test and science test and blood test as well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I've seen similar episodes before. Thanks a lot, John, I'm just going to pass my colleague over to speak to you. My name's Ruth, I'm a psychiatry doctor here. I understand you've been having quite a stressful few days.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, he has had a very stressful week. This last week's been really bad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I've got some of the story. John, are you hearing someone speak to you? Who's speaking to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: X. Not telling you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Why don't you want to tell me?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He thinks it's the MI5 that's communicating with him, they're following him and they're giving him instructions. They're trailing him, apparently.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: John, sorry to interrupt. Tell me what X is saying to you at the minute.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's just getting progressively... airflow... Project university.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: But it's not a university project, is it, John? Me and X project.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so what is the project about, John?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I need to create an airflow. X is helping me and be successful. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So X is telling you how to do this project? Does X ever tell you anything that causes you to be afraid?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Stuff. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Does X ask you to hurt anybody? I can't tell you. Oh, that's not his personality, he wouldn't do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you don't think that he would act on anything? John, has X ever told you to hurt yourself in any way?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know anymore. I can't tell you nothing. I can't tell you nothing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can I tell you a bit about what I know? I heard, John, that you were on the roof...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was on the roof, and X helped me, tells me to do all these things. Jump. To jump from the roof. Airflow, fly.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: John, that seems a bit dangerous to throw yourself off the roof. Do you not think that that would have consequences?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Fly, like a bird. What's the time? Yes, please.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It seems he's holding some unusual beliefs. He's described some risky behavior. What I think will need to happen, I think John must come into hospital for a period of assessment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So will he be just coming in the daytime, or he's to stay overnight? Mum, let's go home. I'm not going nowhere. Let's go home. He's told me I've got to go home.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay John, it's alright. I think you need to come into hospital, John. I'm going to try to organize what's called a mental health act assessment. Decide whether John needs to come into hospital as a detained patient.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So when he comes in, I will be able to come in every day and sit with him?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so I'll go and arrange that now, and I'll come back and have a chat with you if you've got any more questions.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, thank you very much. I'm not going nowhere, I've got to finish this project with X. John, this is going to make you feel better.

video_details.title: Motivational Interviewing Role-Play - "Avoidance-Avoidance" - Fine or Community Service
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which motivational interviewing is used to treat a client in an “avoidance-avoidance” decision-making situation. The client is deciding between a fine or community service.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, Kyle. How you been?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, not too good, man. Something happened over this past week. I was driving to my buddy's house and I forgot that my tags for my car actually expired earlier this month. So I got pulled over for that and then the cop asked to search my car and I was like, 'Yeah, it's fine,' because he said he had to search it since it was getting towed. And I completely forgot that I had my junk bag in the trunk. So he opened the trunk and he was looking through the bag, so he found everything. I had my weed in there, I had the bong, the pipe, all my pieces. So I got in trouble for possession. I just went in the court and the judge offered me this decision. He said that I could either do two weeks of community service, like about 80 hours, or I could pay a $1,000 fine. I'm really trying to figure out which one would be better, I guess. They both kind of suck.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're struggling with a decision between two options you perceive as negative.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right, right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now, we've discussed the marijuana usage before, which is probably at the root of this problem, right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But it sounds like you didn't really want to explore change at this time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. I mean, it's really not a problem. Like, the only problem is that I got caught. I'm doing good in school, work's fine, so obviously marijuana, other than just getting caught with it, hasn't ever been a problem.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So let's focus on this decision then. The decision is between a couple weeks of community service. What kind of community service?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just picking up crap on the side of the road.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, or a $1,000 fine. And do you have the $1,000?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I do, but I got a vacation coming up, and I definitely want to keep the money for some fun stuff with my buddies. So I'm definitely, like, I want to keep that money. But I also, the community service is also kind of close to the vacation, so I might have to like give up part of the vacation in order to do the two weeks. So that doesn't really help my decision either.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you see any value in either one of these options, or does it all kind of feel negative?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, really, they both have the same negative. I guess if I do the community service, then I do get to keep the money, but on the other hand, if I keep the money and I'm doing community service, I'm not going to have all the time to spend the money. So neither really have a positive, and both the negatives are kind of equal, too. So it makes it kind of tough to choose.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So let's talk about what's important to you. Try to help you make this decision. Really what you're going to have to determine, and what I want to explore, is the importance of keeping the money. Because that's really what this comes down to. You keep it and you do the service, or you spend it and you don't do the service. So on a scale of one to ten, where ten is very important, how would you scale keeping the money?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's obviously pretty high. I guess keeping the money would be like a nine, because if I keep the money, obviously I can use it for other things. So I'd say probably a nine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So keeping the money, that's very important to you. So that scenario would lean more toward completing the community service.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. Yeah, I mean, I guess that's true. I didn't think about it that way. If I give up the two weeks of time, obviously that would suck, but I guess I have more of a choice of what to do with money compared to my time. So I guess if I think about it that way, maybe.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, let's look at the other side, too. How important is it for you on a scale one to ten to avoid the community service? We know it's a nine to keep the money. How about to avoid the community service?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe like, I guess would be about a seven. Because the community service, I mean, it wouldn't be that bad. Obviously it would be a waste of time. I'd have to do this crap work for so long, but at least I know if I do the community service, then it would be done after this amount of time. So I can always keep that in mind.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so as you're talking, it seems like you're leaning toward completing the service, even though you're not happy with either choice. That might be the least objectionable.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah. Actually, I guess, because I never thought about scaling it like that way, so, yeah, I think so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When do you have to make this decision by?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, about the end of the week. Today's Tuesday, so I have like a couple days to think it over.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you go back before the judge on Friday.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Friday, yeah, when I give the decision.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Why don't you weigh some of the factors, weigh this importance of the money versus doing the community service? Let's meet again just before, maybe on Thursday, and just talk about it and take a look at your decision-making process and make sure that you've made a decision that you can be most happy with. I know neither option is a really happy option for you, but one that's the least destructive or least negative for you. Does that sound like a plan?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: All right. Yeah, I think I can do that. I'll think it over some more.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good. Then I'll see you then.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yep. Sounds good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Take care.

video_details.title: Motivational Interviewing Role-Play - "Approach-Approach" - Selecting a Doctoral Program
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which motivational interviewing is used to treat a client in an “approach-approach” decision-making situation. The client is deciding between two doctoral programs.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Kyle, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm pretty good, Dr. Grande. How are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. What's been going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've been applying to doctoral programs for this upcoming fall and I'm kind of stuck because I got into two of the schools that I was looking at. Both of their programs are really good and have great research track records in what I want to do, but I don't know how to decide between the two now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
