diarization.text: So you applied to two places and you got into both. It sounds like both have programs that are really well suited to what you want to do and you're having difficulty deciding which one to go with.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I've always had trouble with indecisiveness. When I have two choices of something that's very similar, I always get stuck and it's very hard for me to actually make a decision.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, start at the beginning. You definitely want to go on for a PhD? Okay, so we've established that. It's going to be one of these programs either way, so really the only question is which one. Often in these situations we look at pros and cons. Are there any cons to either one?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean really, not any that I can think of. I've tried to write them down and the pros look very close. Both programs are good, they're in the same city, and I have connections with teachers in both. It would be easier if there were some cons to one of them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It'd make the decision easier if you had some negatives. In a way this is a 'good problem,' but it's still a tough choice. Maybe we can help you build decision-making skills because you'll have to make more decisions later on too. What aspects are really the most important to you in general?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Research is definitely up there. I also think it's important for the university to have a post-doctoral plan, connections with businesses for jobs, or a pathway to a faculty position. Those would probably be the biggest influencers.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The research and a high probability of employment. Even without negatives to look at, we can rank these positives. How hard will they work to find you a job? That seems to be what you're saying.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Actually, I never thought about that. I guess I could look online at job acceptance rates or percentages of what people do afterwards. If I see how many of them go on to be professors or work in the industry, that might help me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That might allow you to find a difference between them because right now they're melded together. Creating a bit of a gap between them helps you see if one is slightly better for what you want to do. You can also consider other aspects after you leave to try and view them as two separate entities.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, that makes sense.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Another possibility would be talking to representatives from each university. They may have more information about potential pros and cons, or things they do better than the other school. This information gathering seems like your next step.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I never actually thought about ranking the pros and going from there, so I think that's a good idea.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It might also be helpful to clarify your values and what's important to you to help rank those attributes. We can talk about that more when we meet again.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right, okay, yeah that makes sense.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, let's leave it there and pick up next time, unless you have any further questions.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I think I know what I can do now to help me decide.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Great, so I'll see you in about a week and we'll pick up there.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Alright, sounds good. Thanks, Dr. Grande.

video_details.title: Motivation Interviewing with Survivors of Intimate Partner Violence: Session 1 of 3
video_details.description:
The Portland State University School of Social Work presents:

Motivation Interviewing with Survivors of Intimate Partner Violence
Scenario 1: "Emmy's First Encounter with a IPV Counselor"
Dr. Stéphanie Wahab

Motivational interviewing is a guiding approach to communication used to support individuals to make changes in their lives. The MI approach focuses on evoking and eliciting rather than telling or advising. Individuals are supported to tap into their own motivations for change. The scenari

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Emmy, I'm Denise. I'm one of the advocates here at the center. How are you today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm fine, thanks. Feeling a little strange about being here, but okay. I've never done this before.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Why don't you tell me a little bit about what brings you here today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm not even sure. I heard about this place and that you work with women having trouble in their relationships, so I thought I'd give you a call.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would it help if I explained a little bit about what my role might be today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, because I don't know what to do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm not here to tell you what to do or give you advice. I'm here to help you sort out what's going on and explore what you'd like to do differently. How does that sound?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That sounds hard because I'm not sure I'm very good at sorting things out myself. I'm feeling overwhelmed and confused about what to do next.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're not even sure where to start, especially since any decisions you make affect both you and your baby.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: And my boyfriend. It affects him too, which is why I'm here to talk about us and how we work together.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Why don't you tell me a little bit about your story?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He and I have been together about a year. We have a baby. The relationship has been on and off with fights where he disappears and comes back. Recently, he did something that didn't even look like him. It freaked me out, it freaked the baby out, and it even freaked him out. He said he felt out of control.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there have been arguments and separations, but something happened recently that was significant and scary for everyone.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A male friend came over to help with my resume. My boyfriend came home with a weird look in his eye. After my friend left, he got this dark look and pushed me onto the ground. He said he was possessed and would never do it again. He's usually a good dad and helps us out a lot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It didn't make sense to you because on one hand he's good with you and the child, but then this happened which was something really different.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I didn't know what to do with that feeling, which prompted me to call. I'm not sure what to do next.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What are your thoughts right now about some of the options out there for you to do, if anything?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I haven't talked to anybody for a year. I've gotten pretty isolated. My parents live far away and my boyfriend is jealous, even though he cares about us.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I used to work and I was looking forward to working again, but he says I don't need to because he takes care of us and pays the rent. When he's gone and I run out of money, I wish I could do a little bit by myself.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That leaves you in a real bind when you're there and you don't have what you need. You're trying to find ways to get those needs met.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know what to do next. I'm not very good at it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I really appreciate your willingness to talk about this; it's not an easy situation. There are several things we can focus on, like the relationship, community resources, safety planning, finances, or taking care of yourself and your child.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've been focusing so much on being a good mom and trying to get a job, but I haven't even been talking about taking care of him. It's weird that I'm looking at these other things when I usually spend so much time thinking about him.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Maybe you want to focus on some other areas and see where those lead you. Focusing on yourself and your child might help you figure out what to do about the relationship.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm not sure what to do with the relationship. I don't feel like I've been making any decisions.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like you'd like to focus on the possibility of getting a job and how to balance that with being a mom.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What thoughts do you have about how you might go about balancing that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd need his help more with the baby, but he doesn't do that now. I would have to find some other childcare I trusted and a job with a schedule that allows me to still be there for breastfeeding and naps.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You are deeply committed to taking care of your child and providing the structure they need. It's very important to you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd like him to be a dad, but I realize I spend so much time worrying about him—if he loves us, or why he did that weird thing. Letting go of worrying about him feels kind of freeing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're realizing how much attention it takes to focus on the baby and that it's hard to do both.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I need his help with that, not to be worrying about him. I don't understand what safety planning means.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Safety planning is helping you have plans in place for what you would do if anything scary came up, to make sure you and your baby stay safe.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So if he got that weird look in his eye again? It went further this time, so I'd need to know what to do if I saw that look.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Exactly. We can talk about places you can go, steps you can take, and people to call to keep yourself and the baby safe. Is that something you're interested in exploring?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It sounds freaky to think I have to keep myself safe from someone who says he loves me. But I didn't expect him to do what he did, so planning ahead makes sense.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: To summarize, this was a scary incident that prompted you to seek protection for yourself and your baby. We've discussed your off-and-on relationship, your desire for financial independence through work, and the importance of a safety plan.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When we get together again, we can start looking at planning for both your safety and your career goals. There are resources and people who can help you with things like your resume.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you. I think I'll go get my baby from childcare. Should we make another appointment?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yes, let's make another appointment when we go out front.

video_details.title: Case study clinical example: Session with a client with Bipolar Disorder (fluctuations in mood)
video_details.description: Video for use in teaching CBT formulation, aiming to demonstrate some of the triggers, thoughts, feelings and responses linked with elevated mood. In order to try and provide information to build a formulation, the session moves faster than an average session might and does not include all aspects of standard CBT (e.g., agenda setting). An actor plays the character of Tom [Sam Newton], but the dialogue is not scripted, and as such this represents a natural therapeutic exchange. I am a qualified

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, nice to see you again, Tom. How are you today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I understand that since I was seeing you that while ago, that you're in hospital again.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So can you tell me a bit more about what happened before that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it was a few months ago now. I'd done quite well for a number of years, kept it under control really, but...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, I haven't seen you since your gap year, wasn't it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, so that was four years ago. And so it was quite disappointing to go through it all again. But it sort of started towards the end of university. So I was doing law. And well, I was on course for a first and I was just coming up to my final exams. And I had a few essays and a few exams. And so I just started working really hard. I felt like now is the real time to put the effort in and to put the work in. So I started to stay a bit later, take on a bit more work. So my stress levels sort of started to increase over a while. I was drinking a lot more coffee, took a few caffeine tablets, energy drinks. A few people, or because the environment at the time was a lot of people were pushing themselves that they wouldn't normally do. And some people were taking Ritalin.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh wow, okay. Did you take any Ritalin?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, because it was just like that was necessary at the time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How did that affect you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it sort of increased my confidence at the time. All that was going on, I was becoming a lot more productive, yeah, a lot more confident. I was working harder, my brain was working faster. And so I, yeah, my momentum was building up and up throughout the period. Yeah, and so I was relishing it and I was doing a lot of work.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what did that mean to you then, to be at that time? Because it sounds like you put quite a lot of pressure on yourself, you'd been doing really well at uni and you know, this was it, this was the time. What did it mean to you to be feeling like that, kind of more awake and more energized maybe?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, well, for me it was, it was my sort of time. So I'd spent three years, I was in control, I was doing well. It wasn't really part of my life at the time, I didn't really talk to any of my friends about it. But then I started to just sort of grow into it. And I took the opportunity to enjoy this time. And it didn't really reach its peak until after my exams. Whilst I was still functioning throughout my exams, I have since found out that I didn't get the results that I wanted to.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Why do you think that was?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I thought that I was working harder than ever, but it was misjudged I think. And so I, yeah, I didn't perform to the best of my ability when it came to the exams, so I didn't achieve a first, I only got 2:1.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What else was happening for you around that time? I mean you talked about the pressure of your exams and staying up for them. Was anything else going on for you around the same time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, so it was the end of university and that was the time where as soon as that period stopped of work, then I was sort of let off the leash a bit. And yeah, I just sort of started to grow even further. So I mentioned I was taking Ritalin, drinking a lot of coffee and as soon as my exams had stopped, I just, substance abuse sort of took a bit more of a hold. And yeah, I just sort of grew into this person who I thought was him, was the guy that everyone wanted to be around and to see. And so I made sure that I was just everywhere to be seen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So this was like the gap after you'd finished the exams but before the results were out?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, those kind of few weeks. So we were just going out a lot, if not every night.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You said that you were taking Ritalin and drinking a lot of coffee, and using other drugs as well.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it sort of developed into cocaine, a lot of cocaine and MDMA, M-Cat.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how did they affect you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I honestly was on cloud nine at the time. Yeah, I just, I was the person everyone wanted to know. In my head, I put myself at the center of the universe and I even convinced a friend of mine who develops apps, I had an idea to develop an app about when you go into an alcohol shop that it will weigh up what's the most cost-effective way to get wasted.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean at the time I was spending a lot of money, a lot of my parents' savings. I'd got a credit card which I didn't tell them about. And so in this sort of role as the man, as the man about town, I spent a lot on yeah, alcohol, drugs, clothes. I invested in this technology and yeah, I was...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it sounds like it began with kind of the exam pressure and putting more pressure on yourself to stay up using kind of stimulants to keep yourself awake, and then you started to feel like you were more and more the man. You were kind of popular, you were successful. How did you respond and cope with those symptoms? What did you do once those are kind of begun?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, having not had to deal with my illness throughout university and for it not being a part of that world, I didn't confront those symptoms in a way that's going to have long-term stability. As far as, well, it began with doing the work that I needed to do, that's just what I needed to do in order to achieve my goals and to achieve what I want to. And then it just, I just let it take hold and it was all part of me, it wasn't the illness, it was me. It was just, I was the master of this whole situation and everything that was happening was down to my own doing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it sounds like on the one hand you didn't confront it, you kind of just let it roll, and on the other hand you said that you kind of took it as evidence that you were very energetic, you were powerful, this was all kind of explained about who you were. I guess how did that affect you looking at things in that way?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It just, it was my time. It'd all been leading to, this was the moment where I would sort of become the person that I wanted to be. All the hard work, all everything like all the work that my parents had done for me, all the work that I'd been doing, it was now crystallizing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it felt like you were on the brink of something enormous from the sounds of it. Again, going back to that kind of beginning stage where you started to stay up late and use stimulants, I mean how much sleep were you getting at the beginning?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It sort of gradually diminished, I think. It began at six, five, and then ended up about three and two hours.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What kind of things did you notice? Did you notice any changes from having less and less sleep? In your body maybe or the way you were thinking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think the harder I was working, the faster my brain then would work and how much, yeah, the harder I worked, the more I would do. So it was just, the momentum was building more than anything and my thoughts were firing and my goals were stronger and my determination was bigger.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how did you feel in your body? Did you notice any changes physically?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not that I can recall at the time, maybe I was trying to, maybe I was avoiding confronting any negative effects but nothing powerful comes to mind.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And once you'd kind of, things were a bit further along after your exams, you said you're going out a lot, you convinced your friend to do this app. Was there anything else that you did that maybe you wouldn't normally do that you think might have been a sign to you that your mood was much higher than you'd like it to be?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: There was, I had a lot of savings that my parents had built up for me which don't really exist anymore, either through the money I invested and through drugs, clothes. I had a girlfriend at the time, but because I was the main character in a sense, I was the only person that mattered. And so sort of those around me, especially her, just didn't really have as much importance. And so on nights out, she just wouldn't be in my mind and so there would be other women.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And how do you feel about that now looking back on it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think it's those moments where it's not just me, it's those closest to you and those around you that have to suffer more than anyone else, that brings a lot of the shame. But yeah.

video_details.title: Motivation Interviewing with Survivors of Intimate Partner Violence: Session 2 of 3
video_details.description:
The Portland State University School of Social Work presents:

Motivation Interviewing with Survivors of Intimate Partner Violence
Scenario 2: "Vanessa's Second Meeting with a Hospital Social Worker"
Dr. Stéphanie Wahab

Motivational interviewing is a guiding approach to communication used to support individuals to make changes in their lives. The MI approach focuses on evoking and eliciting rather than telling or advising. Individuals are supported to tap into their own motivations for change.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Vanessa, hi. It's nice to see you again.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's good to see you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. How are you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm doing okay. I've been, you know, things have been settling down a bit, I think.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. The last time we saw things were pretty chaotic and hectic when you were being released from the hospital, discharged from the hospital about a week ago. How's your injury? How's your arm?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's... I've had a lot of pain in it. I've been trying not to take too much pain medication and just kind of trying to keep busy and focus on things that are happening. I've been busy with my church duties and with my kids.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you've been trying to stay busy.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah. It's been hard to think about myself when I have so many other things that are more... way more important than me to deal with.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How are your kids doing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They're doing okay. You know, the little ones were pretty, kind of, stressed out when I first got home and they were a little unsure of themselves and what was going to happen. But the older kids have helped out quite a bit, so I think they're pulling together.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. I imagine that there's some period of readjustment and healing and sadness, or as in... it sounds like also just trying to get things done.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I mean, my motto is just to keep moving, moving as fast as I can, trying to keep the house clean, be good with my duties at my church, and trying to keep the kids focused on their activities and not on what's happening between me and Paul.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're taking care of a lot of people while trying to take care of yourself. I really appreciate you showing up today. Last time, you talked about how important it is for you to do what you can to keep your kids and yourself safe. I was wondering if you'd be interested in talking more about that today.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I made time today to talk about this. I think it's really important to try to figure something out. Things got very out of hand there, and so I'm looking forward to thinking about what things I can do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you were scared. It sounds like you were scared.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was terrifying. I mean, we ended up having to call the police and Paul was arrested and spent some time in jail. I had child welfare folks crawling all over my house, my mom was upset, and neighbors were gossiping. It was just very scary.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So a lot of things were turned upside down. When you say it was scary, I hear you saying it was scary for your safety, but also because all these other disruptive elements were put in motion.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. We had people checking in, asking if I'd get a restraining order. My mom was trying to get me to move in with her. It was just too many cooks in the kitchen. Way too many.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So a lot of people have some ideas about what you should be doing.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, and I'm not going to do that. I'm not going to get a restraining order or call the police. He knows where I live.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Say more about that. Why don't you want to call the police or get a restraining order?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They were throwing him on the ground and they had their guns. You never know what the police are going to do to a black man or whether he's going to make it to the jail safely. So I was terrified for him. And then the next day, child welfare was calling the house.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like that was a very scary experience and moment for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, because I'm a good mom.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And given that experience, it sounds like you're maybe not as inclined to think about calling the police again.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. I've told my mom that that's a last resort and that I'm going to be meeting with some folks and thinking about other options.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And that's what you'd like to talk about today: alternatives to calling the police.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Absolutely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, what have you thought about so far? What other ideas do you have about what you might do in a serious moment where you're scared for your well-being and that of your kids?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think I'm most afraid that something might happen that will be really crazy and out of control. I've thought about talking to my minister about it because he's somebody we've talked to before.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So your minister is someone you're thinking about talking to about what's going on in your relationship. What would you like to tell your minister?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm really interested in telling him more of the truth. He has no idea that Paul has threatened to kill me and the children. He knows we've had some marital and financial problems and that Paul's had some drinking problems, but he doesn't know about the death threats, the hitting, or the rages.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You feel like you've been keeping some significant information from him. What would be some reasons why you would tell him these things? What might be some advantages?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He's been helpful before. We've had counseling with him over the last five years numerous times and he's been very helpful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's someone that you trust and have a relationship with. In what ways has he been helpful?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think Paul respects him as a man and cares about him. My family and friends are bordering on hating Paul and don't have any objectivity, but my pastor does.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Your pastor is able to see him as a whole, complicated human being like you do. What would be another advantage to talking to your pastor, in addition to trust and Paul listening to him?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I don't think he's likely to storm into our pastor's house. He goes storming over to my mom's or my girlfriend's house, but he's not likely to do that there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So your pastor's home actually might be a physically safe place for you all to go to.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right, to cool off. Because things got so out of control and crazy, and that's not going to happen again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You've said that a few times now, that things got out of control. Tell me a little bit more about what that was.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My eldest son got involved, my arm was harmed, and things were broken. He threatened to kill all of us. I had to call the police, and then he called me from jail asking how I could do this to him. I felt like, how can I do this?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So not only was it scary in the heat of the moment, but the fallout was scary as well. So going to your pastor's might be an advantage. Are there any disadvantages to talking to your pastor?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That Paul will know. If he finds out that I've talked to our minister about this, I have no doubt how angry he will be.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So this could really be a significant trigger.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, if he finds out about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's a difficult situation. There's potential advantages, but also significant risk. When you think about the pros and the cons, where do you go with that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's a risk I'm willing to take. Things got so out of control that I feel like it's time to do something different and think about how we're going to do this differently.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're really concerned. A part of you is worried about the next time and you feel like it's a risk you're willing to take given what is at stake—your life and your children's lives.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. Things can't continue the way that they are. I have to figure out something that's going to work for me, for my kids, and for Paul.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would it be alright if I offered a suggestion regarding kids and safety planning? Other moms have had a conversation with their kids about identifying a safe person to call or run to in the moment if things get really out of hand. What are your thoughts on that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: For my eldest son, that would be really helpful because he wants to know what he can do. He's always jumping in, which is how I got hurt in the first place. Helping him identify something that will keep him and us safe would be a great idea.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you see this as a way of having him turn away from a violent situation as opposed to turning into it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Absolutely. He's becoming a man now, and he needs to have an option of what he can do to keep his family safe.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're identifying things you have control over: talking to your minister and having a conversation with your son. I'm confident you'll be able to put a plan together that works. I'm here to support you and can follow up in a few days.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you. I'd appreciate that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks for your time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

video_details.title: Motivation Interviewing with Survivors of Intimate Partner Violence: Session 3 of 3
video_details.description:
The Portland State University School of Social Work presents:

Motivation Interviewing with Survivors of Intimate Partner Violence
Scenario 3: "Liv's Fourth Session with a IPV Advocate"
Dr. Stéphanie Wahab

Motivational interviewing is a guiding approach to communication used to support individuals to make changes in their lives. The MI approach focuses on evoking and eliciting rather than telling or advising. Individuals are supported to tap into their own motivations for change. The scenarios

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, Liv. Welcome back.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hi.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How are you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm feeling pretty intense. Things have kind of gone downhill since I was here last time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, I'm sorry to hear that. I know last time we talked, you and Kelly had just gotten engaged and you were rather excited about plans that you had for your life. So tell me what has happened, what has shifted?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think that we've just sort of fallen back. You know, I was really hopeful that with the proposal also came the promise to work on the relationship and work on her anger and work on being the couple that we hoped to be. And that's not happening. It's not happening. We're right back to where we were.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm sorry to hear that. I know you were excited, you were feeling hopeful for change and I don't get that same sense from you right now. In fact, it seems like you're feeling pretty sad and maybe even a little hopeless about the situation. Well, how can I be helpful and supportive and useful to you right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just don't know how to make change. I don't know how to end this. I don't know how to get out. I just can't do it anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you've decided to make a change and in fact it sounds like you've decided to leave the relationship.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. I mean, I want to. I don't want to be in it but I don't know how to get to not being in it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're thinking about it. It's not that you've committed or decided that you absolutely want to leave the relationship but correct me if I'm wrong, what you're saying is you want to make a change and you don't want this relationship as it is right now. When you think about changing, what ideas - I guess you mentioned leaving - what other possibilities or thoughts have you had about change and what that might look like?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. It just feels so overwhelming when I think about it. I just can't seem to find a way out of it that feels ethical, feels like it - I don't want to hurt her. I just don't want to be in this relationship anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Why don't you want to be in this relationship anymore?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's not healthy. I'm not happy. I can't imagine that she's happy even though she says she is. We're fighting constantly. I feel like I'm walking on eggshells with her. She's overprotective. Yeah, it just doesn't feel right. It just doesn't feel right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It doesn't feel right. Yeah. And so, what would feel right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's a huge question. I'm not sure. Just this isn't right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the way things are is not right. It's not working. You don't feel supported. This isn't the kind of relationship that you want or that you had hoped that it would be.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I mean, when we started it was lovely. She was amazing. She was this super caring and thoughtful woman and you know, lots of same interests, same friends. It's, you know, she was just fantastic. And I don't know, I don't know where that changed and I feel like we did this on-again-off-again stuff and it's just, it just seems to like, it's just not right. And I know, I know I don't deserve to be treated this way. I know that I'm better than that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You really value yourself and your wellbeing and your spirit. And it sounds like you don't feel like you're taking good care of yourself by staying in this relationship. And even though things started out well, they haven't turned out to be the kind of relationship that you want for yourself.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. But you know, but she's lovely and I love her and I can't imagine my life without her in it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're feeling torn. You're torn between your love and affection for her and your sense of honoring yourself. And you've got a lot of mixed feelings and you are saying that you need something to change. It sounds like you're able to kind of hold that complexity if you will, that you've got these strong feelings for this person and you don't feel like this is a good relationship for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. I don't think it's good for either one of us.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: For both of you. Yeah. Well, so then you've talked a little bit about leaving. I mean, tell me more about what you've thought about and when you think about making a change in terms of leaving, what might that look like for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. I mean, it feels - I just can't imagine my life without her in it. So the idea of not having her there feels really scary and the idea of staying the way it is and things not changing feels even scarier. So I don't know, and I don't even know how I would do that. Our lives are so intertwined. I mean, my business, our friends, the queer community is so small. You know, that's my fam - those are not just my friends, that's my family as well. And so it's just, you know, how do you extract yourself from that in a way - for me, in a way that I feel that I'm doing that with grace and respect for her and respect for myself?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What thoughts do you have about how you do that? How do you extract yourself? How might you extract yourself in a way that has some integrity and grace, as you said?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't even know. I mean, I talked to my friend Jay about it and I don't know, he suggested like a break but I don't know, I just don't want to get caught in that on-again-off-again before like we've done before. But the idea of a break feels a little less - I don't know, maybe more gentle. I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Say more. A little more gentle.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. To give us both time to really think about it and I don't know, maybe she'll change. Maybe if I'm - if this is it, if this break is it, maybe she'll be able to change.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I heard you say that moving on and having a life without Kelly is really scary, in fact it's almost impossible for you to imagine what that would look like, especially with the way that your lives are so intertwined. I also heard you say that the thought of not making a change is scarier. And I was wondering if you could say a little bit more about what you mean by that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just feel exhausted. I feel like I'm not who I was when I came into this relationship. I feel like I'm constantly struggling to make her happy and that just doesn't work. There's nothing I can do. And I feel like I've lost my joy and I don't know - I'm just afraid of what will happen if I just keep staying in a place where I feel like I'm falling apart piece by piece.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're concerned about your own wellbeing and your own joy and your spirit if you stay and don't make this change and that's the part that's really scary for you. You mentioned that your friend suggested possibly taking a little break and you said that that was a scary thought for you and I guess I'd like to hear more additional thoughts you might have about that as an option for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I just - it seems like I mean, if it could happen, if we could find a way to make it happen that it would just give me some time to think about what I want and what I need and you know, I feel like I can't sort out what's me in this anymore. And so like if I had that space just to sort of breathe and not have to worry about her feelings and taking care of her and just being able to focus on myself for a little while, I don't know, it seems like that would be helpful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like you're feeling like you're so in it, just so in the mixed emotions and the sense of hopelessness and sadness and disappointment that it's really hard for you to see out of it. And an advantage, a reason to take a break would be just to give you a moment to breathe and look around and collect yourself and not be so stuck in that ambivalence if you will, that sense of not knowing. Well, if you don't mind, I'd love to ask you to take a look at this ruler here. I just kind of wrote this down really quickly, but on a scale of 0 to 10, 0 being not motivated at all and 10 being extremely motivated, how motivated would you say you are to take a break in your relationship right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, like 6.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: 6. So somewhat motivated. Why a 6 and not a 1?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Because I know it needs - I need it. I feel like I'm losing myself, so I feel like it's important.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It is important. Yeah. Well, so why a 6 and not a 9 or 10?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Because I'm not sure how to make it happen. Yeah, I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's important to you and you're not maybe fully confident or sure about the 'how' part, how to make it happen. Well, kind of following up on that, on a scale of 0 to 10, 0 being not confident at all, 10 being extremely confident, how confident are you that if you decided to take a break from your relationship with Kelly, you would be successful at making that happen?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, I don't know. Maybe like a 3 or 4.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so less confident. You're a little less confident than you are motivated. Why a 3 and not a 0?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Because I want it. I mean, I do. It's something I want.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And so wanting it makes you feel confident to some extent that you could actually make it happen.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therist
diarization.text: Well, why a 3 and not an 8 or a 9?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can't control her. I don't know how she would react and I just don't want any more arguments and anger and yeah, and I don't want to hurt her. So.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So when you think about taking this break, you're also thinking about how she might respond and what she might do and that creates this whole other kind of set of worries and it undermines your sense of confidence on some level.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It creates a lot of anxiety for me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. What do you think needs to be different in order for you to feel more confident about successfully being able to take a brief break?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think maybe a plan. Like just knowing knowing what the rules are, sort of like where where I want to go with it and what I'm - I don't know, what I want to accomplish.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So thinking through an actual plan, like what you would say, how long, what the boundaries are might help you in that regard. Okay. And then one final question: on a scale of 0 to 10, 0 being not ready at all and 10 being extremely ready, how ready would you say you are to commit to taking some kind of brief break in the next couple of weeks?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think an 8.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: An 8. So pretty ready. And you've spoken to this already a little bit, I believe, but I'll ask you again: why an 8 and not a 1 or a 2?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Because I know if I just let it drag out that I'm gonna be miserable.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So your sense of readiness is actually really connected to your motivation. That is, that this is something you know that you need to do for yourself and if you don't, things are not going to get any better and that makes you both motivated and even more ready. Well, why an 8 and not a 10?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's, you know, it's scary. Change is hard and thinking about not being with the woman I thought I was going to marry, it's sad. Makes me sad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So your emotions, your sense of maybe sadness and grief and disappointment around this detract from your sense of readiness in some way.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sort of giving up on a dream.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. And so, another aspect then to your whole experience is that you're grieving. The relationship isn't even over yet, but you're grieving the dream and the hopes that you had and that's a heaviness and certainly a factor in what you do next. Yeah. Well, if I could take just a minute and make sure I've captured and understood everything you've shared with me. And I know this is really difficult to talk about, so I really appreciate you spending the time to share with me what this has been like for you. You've been feeling stuck and things were great for a while, you had some hope that things were going to change and now you're realizing that Kelly is not going to change and that you are suffering in the process, that you are really being kept from your aspirations and your dreams in a lot of different regards. You know that you need to make a change, you want to make a change, and you have a lot of mixed feelings about this change. You know it's what you want to do, it's the right thing for you, and you still really care and love Kelly. And you're also concerned kind of on an outer level about your business, about your community, about your family and your friends and how they may be affected by a breakup. In order to make this more manageable, you're thinking maybe in terms of smaller change, like taking a small break as opposed to breaking off the relationship and you feel like you're pretty ready, you're motivated and maybe a little less confident. But you also said that if you were able to maybe think through a concrete plan, that that might help you feel more confident. And that's certainly something that we could do together next time we meet, if that's alright with you. I'd be happy to hear your ideas, maybe even share some suggestions with you about a possible plan. Would that be alright?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That'd be great. Yeah, thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you very much for your time, Liv. I really appreciate it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So I noticed on your diary card that you have that you did cut.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yep.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so let's talk about that a little bit. When what day did that happen on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Tuesday.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tuesday. Okay, so where were you on Tuesday when you first had the thought that you wanted to cut?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Where I usually always am at school. I was at my locker. And that stupid girl...

diarization.text: What was going on at your locker?

diarization.text: Melanie was talking about Tim. My Tim. My boyfriend. And I know it was it was my Tim she was talking about. I just wanted to punch her so bad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you were standing at your locker and you heard somebody say something about Tim that you didn't want to hear.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, she was talking about him and he had he didn't text me the night before, so who knows what's going on.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What were you feeling right then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So angry. So angry.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: On a scale of one to ten, how angry would you say you were?

diarization.text: Pretty angry then. Yeah. And what did you do right then? You're at your locker. What's the next thing you did after you heard it?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so I know that the gym is usually the place where you cut because you said you can go behind the bleachers, people don't usually see you there.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so where between hearing the person talking about Tim and going to the gym, where did you decide to cut? Because you said you were also feeling like punching somebody. So there must have been a point where you decided I'm going to cut.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think it was right after I slammed my locker and thought I can't punch her, I'm going to get in trouble. I'm going to go cut.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So that was when you decided to cut. And you went down to the gym.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what happened when you got there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, nobody was there because gym class isn't in the morning. So I knew that nobody was going to come in the gym. So I went behind the bleachers.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What did you use to cut?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The pencil that I have always used.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The same pencil as usual. Yeah. With the the one with the metal tip?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, that was a pencil that you were saying that you were going to get rid of.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I know. It's just it's it's my favorite pencil. I I use it for school and I just it's my favorite pencil.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you still had the pencil, you got under the bleachers, you say you were feeling angry still. Where on the scale of one to ten, where were you when you got under the bleachers?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was still at like, it's still pretty high, maybe like an eight and a half though, because I I knew I I knew I was going to cut. So it like came down a little bit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What were you thinking at that point?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I thought a couple things. I thought I'm glad I kept this pencil. And that I'm just so pissed that I just want to cut so badly.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you have your pencil. Where did you cut?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: On my leg.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How many times?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Three.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How deep did you cut? Where was it deep enough um that you needed a band-aid? Did you need more than a band-aid?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I mean, I guess I could have used a band-aid, but I mean, whatever.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But it wasn't so deep that you needed something more?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Right after you cut, where were you on the scale of one to ten with your feel with your anger?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like a three.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Three? What were you thinking right afterwards?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That felt good. I feel better. And I'm going to have to talk to Michelle about this.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Did that feeling last you for the rest of the day?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The feeling better?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Mhm.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, for the most part. Yeah, it did.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so that's what happened right afterwards. Later in the day, what were you thinking about the cutting?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I kind of forgot about it. But then I just started thinking about it again right before bed. And I just feeling really guilty that I cut. Because I knew I was going to have to talk about it with you. And I just I mean, I the night time, I just I constantly think about what happened that day and then what the next day's going to be like. I mean, you know, it's usually a pretty hard time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I know night is a really difficult time for you. Everything seems worse at night. Yeah. So you were thinking back at at it then and you were feeling guilty.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sounds like you weren't feeling so good about it then as you were in the afternoon.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. That always seems to happen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like for you cutting works for a little while, but it doesn't last.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I know you've also been working on doing less cutting.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've been doing pretty good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You have. You've been working really hard. I'm just wondering if we can find something that might last that you can feel good about later that you won't have those guilty feelings.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, maybe. I mean, those guilty feelings really suck.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so with the cutting, it sounds like the point where you decided to cut at your locker, what triggered it was hearing that girl talking about Tim.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, because she's stupid.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, it sounds like you're also already having a pretty bad day. You said he hadn't called, you hadn't been texting as much and that was on your mind.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I'm wondering if at that point, if we can think of two things that you can try differently next time instead of the cutting.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That'll bring that anger from a nine down a little bit.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's not going to bring it down all the way to a three though, I'll tell you that much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It might not. But it'll bring it down a little bit. And maybe each thing you try brings it down a little bit more.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: All right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And maybe there'll be things you'll feel good about later. You won't have to worry about that guilty feeling coming back.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: All right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the first thing is that pencil. It sounds like it's comforting to have it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it is.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But it also sounds like it's tempting. What do you think about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, only if I am in the mood to cut it's tempting.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like having that pencil is going to make it harder to try other things. And you've been talking about how you're really committed to not cutting anymore or cutting less.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I am.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sounds like that pencil's standing in your way.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, maybe.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you think about getting rid of the pencil this time? Choosing a different favorite pencil that maybe you can't cut with.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, maybe, only only if it can be like a really cool pencil.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That way you can still have something that can be your favorite, but which won't tempt you. And that'll make it easier to try the two things.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, what do you think our first thing should be? What do you think you can try? You just heard somebody say something you don't want to hear, you're feeling pretty angry, what can you do in that moment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: What I do a lot at home when my mom's bothering me and saying stuff I don't want to hear, I put my headphones on.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have your headphones with you at school?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, they they actually they let me keep them on in school.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that something you'd be willing to try next time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think so. There's a there's a few songs that usually help me, so I think so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, that sounds like a good one to try.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So we have headphones. We need to come up with one more. What do you think you'd like to try?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I really like my teacher Mrs. Eaton, so she seems to always kind of be there when I need to talk. And her room's kind of right down the hallway from my locker in the same hallway. So I guess, I guess I could talk to her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That sounds like a good option.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So that's our goal is to keep pushing cutting further down the list and to keep adding things that you're going to try first. And you're right that the first thing you try might not bring you all the way down to a two or a three, but it might bring you down a little bit and each thing you try might bring you down just a little bit more. So you have to be willing to try a few things. Can you do that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can, but I really want like a cooler pencil though, like like a cooler pencil. So I don't know, maybe maybe we could go look for a pencil together?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think that's a good idea.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, I'd like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Thank you for answering all of my questions on this. You did a great job with this chain and I know it wasn't easy.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. You're welcome.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's go look for that pencil.

diarization.text: So, good to see you again. Last week we were talking about anxiety. Um, do you have your diary card?

diarization.text: Well, I'd be anxious, of course. And it's kind of scary to see that. And what else did you think when you saw that?

diarization.text: And your family wants you to learn to drive this year because you're 16.

diarization.text: They're insane.

diarization.text: Hmm. And yet you keep complaining how you live in the middle of nowhere and if you had a car you could go see friends more and get out of your lame old town and get to go do fun things.

diarization.text: But I can't see my friends anymore if I'm dead.

diarization.text: True. That's true. And I won't get to see you anymore because you're dead. You know I don't treat dead people, right? Remember that? All right. Yeah, okay. So, on one hand, I know the idea of driving is completely overwhelming and I know you're anxious like all the time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, I get that I have to drive because you're right, it's like the middle of nowhere and I can't just not go places, but...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I'm wondering if we can bring it back to some of those things we were talking about to help reduce your anxiety. What do you think?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think that was a lot of puns, Jen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm punning, aren't I?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, here's an idea. Let's get on board. We start treating this anxiety, we do it really, really good job at it. We work hard and the idea of driving might not be quite so scary. And let's face it, being an anxious driver increases your risk of accidents.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, that's helpful. Thanks.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So reducing your anxiety is going to make you a safer driver.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, but all these things you keep telling me that I have to do to be less anxious, they involve feeling really anxious.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Mm. True.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: There's no way to - like you're supposed to just make it go away. You're not supposed to make it worse to make it better.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So here's what's interesting. You're really good at being really anxious, so you'll be really good at this. And it will go away. I promise you. Totally promise you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's just that's so hard.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, reality is, you know darn well I'm the expert here of treating anxiety and I promise you it will get better. I know everything. I know this. What do you think?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think it sounds really hard.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And it is really hard. Oh, I'm not going to lie to you. It's totally, totally hard.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That maybe it's just another insane thing that you have to be more anxious to be less anxious.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I know. It's pretty insane, isn't it? I agree.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, another option is you could just be anxious the rest of your life. Do they have a bus where you live? You could live with your parents for the rest of your life. So you could just live with your parents, be anxious all the time. Maybe we can come up with some ideas on how to maintain your anxiety the rest of your life. You won't need to learn to drive. diarization.text: Shut up, Jen. That's not funny.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's not meant to be funny. What do you think? I mean, I'm trying to help you. I really want to help you. I know being anxious every day is really hard.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So one of the options is to really become good at being anxious and do okay and learn to sit with your anxiety. And another option is, yeah, getting more anxious to reduce your anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. But you're practiced at it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I mean, if those are the only options, we might as well do the one that's going to make it eventually go away rather than just be there forever.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Do you want to review what some of the treatment strategies will be?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess.
