diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Some people say that when they cut themselves, it makes them feel, and that helps them because they just feel nothing otherwise. Is that you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever had thoughts of wanting to kill yourself or end your life?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I dream about putting my face under a pillow and just breathing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever put a pillow over your face to try to kill yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Plenty of times, but I got scared.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What kept you from doing it? What made you stop?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thinking about my family and how much I would be missed by my family and friends.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I wonder if we made up a plan with your sister here today, so you'd go to her if you're feeling sad and she'd have a list of what to do so you don't cut anymore.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: All right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Victor was telling me about some difficult thoughts he was having about wanting to die and hurt himself. He's told me about times where he's cut himself in order to feel. I wonder if the family was aware of this.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Actually we had no idea.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Together as a family, we can make a plan for things you can do and people you can talk to when you're having those thoughts. I'm going to give you this crisis prevention sheet to fill out together.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play - Treating Heroin Use
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which cognitive-behavioral therapy is used to treat heroin use.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Jesse, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not too good. Not the grand day.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Not so good?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Nah, I just got into a fight with my parents.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's been going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've been doing heroin for a few months now and I didn't think my parents knew, but I guess they found a needle in my room. They told me that I have to start shaping up and stop doing any kind of drugs because the next time they find anything, they're gonna kick me out of the house.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so they're at the point where anything else happens and they discover it, and you're out in the street. What are your feelings about being out on the street?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't want to be out there, but it would be hard to stop cold turkey. I know buddies who did that and got junk sick. I'm stuck because I don't want to be on the streets, but it's gonna be so hard to give it up.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there are conflicting feelings here. You don't want to be out on the street, but you don't want to give up the heroin at the same time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't want to give it up, but I know I have to. I'm a young guy, I couldn't make it outside of my parents' house.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so you want to stop to avoid the consequences, but to this point you haven't been able to?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: To this point I really haven't had something that would make me. I've been doing it for a while and it's been pretty great, but nothing too bad has happened until now. This is the first time I feel like I really got to stop it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So this is the first potential consequence that's motivated you since you started using.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How strong is the craving to use?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When I first started, the rush was amazing. But recently the rush isn't as intense and it's starting to backfire. I'll feel a little sick without using it. That scares me, but the cravings are definitely still there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so when you try to cut back, have you tried to cut back?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have before, but there was no reason to, so I didn't try very hard.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But when you did try, did you have the feeling where you were getting sick?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I did, yeah. It wasn't as bad as my buddies, but I didn't feel well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have your parents given you any options? Do they understand that you're a little dependent?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, they do. I have a pretty good relationship with them and I know what I'm doing isn't good for me. They said they would support me and have a place picked out where I can go and they'd pay for it, but if I don't meet them halfway, they're done.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so they have a solution. Is it like a detox place?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It is, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So they have a solution to help get you off the heroin. Is there still a part of you that doesn't want to go that route?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think I'm starting to come to terms that it's time to stop. But I don't know if the detox is gonna work. Sometimes it's hard to focus on anything until I get my next fix.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there are a few problems: can you commit to going to detox, and even if you complete that, will you be able to avoid heroin when you come back out?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's tough because my dealer lives a few houses down. My girlfriend lives in the same community and he's on the way to her house, so I'll just pick it up on my way, go to my girlfriend's, and maybe shoot up at my buddy's on the way back.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're running into him as you walk to your girlfriend's house.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And the temptation is great.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That house is where I shoot up a lot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's in his house.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. Whenever I'm coming up to his house, I start getting excited and anticipating how great it's gonna feel. I get excited when I see his house.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: As you're walking past his house on the way to your girlfriend's, you divert to go to his house. What's the thought going through your mind?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just can't wait for the next hit. Now it's mixed because I think if I do that and my parents find out, it's all over. But on the other hand, I think about how great it's gonna be and how much I'm gonna do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is your plan right now to go into detox?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It is, yeah. That's my definite plan. If it works, I think I could be done with it. But I don't know if it can work and I don't know how good I'll be at it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's presume the detox is successful. Are you worried at that point that you'll go right back?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you worried you'll go right back?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: If the detox works, I think I can stay off it. The cravings will still be there, but now that I realize what I can lose, I don't think I'd go back. It might be hard if I run into my buddy though.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there's a concern you could go back if you run into him. But if you stay away from him, you think you'd increase your chances of being successful.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Definitely. Experiences in his house feed the craving, so if that doesn't happen, it'll probably help.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When are your plans for going into detox?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Monday, after the weekend. So in three days.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You have confidence it'll work, but your worry is when you get out, can you avoid your friend. You don't buy from anybody else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right, just him.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You don't buy from anybody else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, just him.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So avoiding him becomes a key goal. Since you're committed to the detox part, it's about preparing for life after detox.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: If it works, I can try.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's about preparing for life after detox.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In this case, you need to avoid your friend and where he lives. Is there a way to walk around the block to completely avoid his house and still get to your girlfriend's house?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: There is a horseshoe path I could take. I could go up the block, around the horseshoe, and turn right to her house there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you would never even see his house.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right, right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about her coming over to your parents' place instead?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: She has come over before. If I tell her it helps me out, she can make that walk and it'll be easier.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: She can walk right by that house without problem.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. If I can't even leave and she comes, that might be best.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: To get to work, do you have to pass his house?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I drive the other way out of the community.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there's a behavioral strategy: physically keeping you away from his house. The only reason to go by is to see your girlfriend, and there's an alternative strategy for that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I can do that. That might work.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there ever a time where he comes to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really. He doesn't like to leave his house much since he deals and shoots up there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Could you identify a specific thought that occurs when you're in your house that motivates you to walk to his house?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm bored. Straight up. When there's nothing to do and my parents are gone, it's the best way to have fun.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the thought 'I'm bored' directly connects to the behavior. Is there an adaptive response you can interject at that moment?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Assume you're post-detox, sitting in your house, and the thought 'I'm bored' comes. What's a self-talk piece you could use?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I should remember to think about what I don't want to do. Maybe I can call my girlfriend and ask her to come over to distract me from wanting to go over to his place.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the adaptive response is calling your girlfriend. It sounds like she's supportive of you quitting.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, she doesn't use and wasn't happy with me doing it, so she'll be on board.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Consequences motivate you. I'm wondering if another adaptive response could be 'I don't want any trouble,' like getting kicked out. Do you think that's enough motivation to keep you from that house when your girlfriend isn't around?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I do. School and work are going good, and I don't want to lose that. I'm starting to realize that if I keep using, it's going to affect everything else. Telling myself what's at stake will help remind me why I shouldn't go.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good. Are your parents around much?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My dad works a lot, but my mom's usually home at night.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is at night when you've gone over to your friend's house?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's more during the day while they're at work.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So your mother could be an asset when she's there. It sounds like being home alone when your girlfriend's not available is your highest risk time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We have the cognitive adaptive responses. Is there anything more behavioral we can do, like going somewhere else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I always go for a drive to clear my head. If I start feeling bored, I can just physically leave the temptation and go to a bookstore or a comic book store until my girlfriend or parents are home. I could do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think that's a good plan. The more we apply these adaptive responses, the more the risk and craving should decrease. For now, we'll focus on the short-term and keep you away from the circumstances you don't want.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think that'll definitely help, especially being with you right after detox.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I appreciate you coming in, Jesse. I'll see you in a couple days.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks.

video_details.title: DD CARES Best Practices Series: Suicidality assessment
video_details.description: Part of the DD CARES Best Practices series on improving primary care, emergency care and community follow-up, this video demonstrates common practice errors as well as strategies that can help a patient with a developmental disability tolerate a difficult procedure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Victor, sometimes when people are feeling sad, they have thoughts of wanting to hurt themselves. Have you ever had any of those thoughts?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever hurt yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes I grab a knife and just cut myself.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Have you ever cut deep enough so that you needed stitches?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Or had to go to the hospital?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does anyone know that you cut?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. Shh... don't tell anybody.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What you and I say is confidential, but when I'm worried about people's safety, I need to tell someone about it so they stay safe. I wonder if we talk about you cutting a little more, if we can tell someone in your family together so that when you feel like cutting, they can help you. Can you tell me about those thoughts?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I want to stick a knife right here and just slit my wrists.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That sounds pretty rough. Is it all the time that you want to do it or just some of the time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: All the time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Some people say that when they cut themselves, it makes them feel because they feel nothing otherwise. Is that you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever had thoughts of wanting to kill yourself or end your life?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I dream about putting my face under a pillow and just breathing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever put a pillow over your face to try to kill yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Plenty of times, but I got scared.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What kept you from doing it? What made you stop?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thinking about my family and how much I would be missed by my family and friends.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I wonder, Victor, if we made a plan of what to do when you're feeling like wanting to hurt or kill yourself with your sister who's here today? We can make a plan together so you can go to your sister when you feel sad and she'll know how to help you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: All right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Victor was telling me about some pretty difficult thoughts about wanting to die and wanting to hurt himself. He's actually told me about some times where he's cut himself in order to feel. I wonder if the family was aware of this.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What I thought would be a good idea is together as a family and with my help, we can make a plan for when you're feeling so sad of things that you can do and people you can talk to so you don't actually hurt yourself.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm going to give you this sheet about crisis prevention and management. It tells you what to do at different stages of feeling like wanting to hurt yourself, like when to take medications, use behavioral techniques, or go to the hospital. Let's fill it out together.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play - Fear of Voyeuristic Video Recording
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which cognitive-behavioral therapy is used to treat a fear of voyeuristic video recording.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hey, Hazel. How are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's been going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, last time I started to tell you a little bit about my best friend. She found a video camera in the bathroom at our local library.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In the bathroom? Wow.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. She turned it in, but they weren't able to catch the person because her own prints were on it from finding it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So they didn't catch the person?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. Since then, I've been on high alert. I'm worried it could happen to me or my kids, especially since that person is still out there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So he's still in the community. How is this affecting your daily life and what have you been feeling?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A lot of anxiety. I've become very aware of cameras everywhere, like the one in your office or on people's cell phones.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you're feeling anxious and hyper-aware.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. I'm so aware of the possibilities that I don't want to go anywhere. I've been arguing with my husband because I refuse to go to restaurants and I've started dressing more conservatively to avoid hidden shoe cameras.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You've changed your routine to feel safer. Has that helped reduce the anxiety at all?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really. It's really starting to affect my life, which is why I'm here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You mentioned the arguments with your husband. Can you tell me more about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He wants to take the kids out, but I'm nervous about public bathrooms, baby monitors, and laptop cameras being hacked. I'm not finding any relief from the anxiety, even at home.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you taken any other specific precautions regarding the cameras?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I search bathrooms before my kids or I use them. I've also researched how to disable phone cameras, and I keep my laptop and smart TV cameras covered or turned off.

diarization.speaker: Therist
diarization.text: Those seem like reasonable precautions, yet the persistent worry is still interfering with your life.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You'd like to cope more effectively and reduce this anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When you enter a public restroom, what is the first automatic thought that pops into your head?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That there might be a camera I don't see, and someone will record me in a vulnerable way.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the thought is wondering if a camera is there. What feelings or behaviors follow that thought?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel fear, my heart rate goes up, and I either rush or just leave. Sometimes I avoid going out altogether just to use the bathroom at home.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you check for cameras or avoid the situation while feeling that intense anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like a core belief of being vulnerable is combining with these situations to create these automatic thoughts. Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Exactly.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In cognitive therapy, we use an adaptive response or self-talk to interrupt those thoughts. Let's work on a response you can use in those moments.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What could you tell yourself to get between the thought of a camera and the feeling of anxiety?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I could tell myself that while there is a chance, it's not very likely, and I am taking steps to keep myself safe by looking for them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's good. You're acknowledging the low probability and the behaviors you use to minimize risk.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Try that logical self-talk next time. It's unlikely to happen, and you are taking precautions.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We'll write those down before you leave. Now, consider the worst-case scenario. How do you think you would actually react if you were recorded?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd be really upset and feel vulnerable for a while, but eventually I think I would be okay. My friend is starting to get back to her routine, so I think I could adapt too.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It makes sense to be upset, but that distress would likely be temporary. How long have you been in this state of daily anxiety?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's been about two months.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how often are you affected during the average week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Usually every day.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, being recorded is a low-probability event, but you are suffering from anxiety every single day. Does that comparison help?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's true. I never thought about it that way.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: At some point, you might decide the risk of the unlikely event is better than the certainty of daily suffering.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right, because I am suffering every day right now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: With an adaptive response, you can know that even if the worst happened, you could survive it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think I could.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What general adaptive response could you use when those thoughts start before you even leave the house?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can remind myself that most cameras are for security, the risk of illegal recording is minimal, and it's worth the risk to live my life.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's great. It's important to rehearse these responses so they're ready when the automatic thoughts occur. We'll write them down so you can commit them to memory.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, that makes sense.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Use those responses this week. Record the outcome, your feelings, and any physiological reactions each time you apply them. We'll review them next session.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think that would be really helpful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I appreciate you coming in today.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you very much. Thanks.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play - Test Anxiety
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which cognitive-behavioral therapy is used to treat test anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Michelle, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I'm kind of doing... I'm feeling a little bit stressed out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Stressed?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I have an aptitude test for work with math problems and scenarios to move up to assistant manager.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, a job you've been interested in for a while and have been talking about.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. I've been feeling a lot of anxiety about it. I got overwhelmed during the test; my heart was racing and my hands were shaking, so I couldn't concentrate even though I knew the material the night before.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you know the material on this test pretty well?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But the feelings and physiological response got in the way of you completing it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I wasn't able to complete it. They let me reschedule because I said I didn't feel well. Now I'm scared the same thing will happen again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So you weren't feeling great about taking the test in the first place?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The night before I felt prepared, but the minute I walked into the room, all these fears took over.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But did you know that was coming? You had some anxiety in advance?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. I had some anxiety the day before, but studying made me think I could push it down. Once I got there, it all came back up.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you think is leading to this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've always struggled with tests. In third grade, I failed a math test and was held back. It was embarrassing and I felt like a failure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And since that bad experience in third grade, have you had trouble with tests since?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I always feel really anxious. I pass them, but the anxiety makes me think I'll fail again like before.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you've been able to adapt and pass them, but you're never thrilled about it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. Sometimes I even get an A.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's good. But with this work test, it's more of a stumbling block.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any ideas what's making this test such a point of anxiety for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think it's because it's for a promotion. If I fail, I'm being held back again, like in third grade.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's really that same feeling from third grade coming up now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I didn't put them together until now, but yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And other tests in school didn't have that same value attached?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, because there wasn't as much pressure; it wasn't strictly win or lose.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You could retake them or take another test to raise the grade?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you maybe had more options and safety nets in school.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, it wasn't pass or fail.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. It's the pressure of needing to get through this without those safety nets.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. If I fail, I don't get the promotion and have to wait a year to take it again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, that is a lot of pressure. Is there a time limit on this test?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, there isn't.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's multiple choice and you're well prepared. Let's think about cognitive therapy and core beliefs.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What core belief might be operating for you now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That I could fail and end up being a failure at everything I try.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Something like 'I'm destined to be a failure'?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would say that, yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So that potentially is the core belief and automatic thought as you take the test.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's what scares me. If I don't pass, it'll have a domino effect of failure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like a panic response. Are you alone in the room when you take it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So no one sees you have these panic-like symptoms. Have you had these before?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really, only around tests.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What happens once you get worked up?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I try to work through it and answer one question at a time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: One possible strategy is an adaptive response like 'I can ride this out.' Panic only lasts so long, and you have no time limit.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's true.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I could also choose questions I know automatically to relieve some stress.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: To get some minor victories and feel closer to your goal.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, that would validate the feeling that I can pass.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Exactly. Correctly answering items will make you feel more calm.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, knowing those questions are definitely right makes me feel more calm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You can wait out the panic in the room alone. Tell yourself it's unpleasant but temporary.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, so I could use self-talk.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Exactly. Panic symptoms usually only last 10-15 minutes.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So I can take as much time as I need.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yes. Focus on the easy items while telling yourself you can ride this out.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've done that before, so I can apply it here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So that's worked for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, it has worked for me in the past.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Another adaptive response is knowing you can retake the test in a year. It's not the end of your career.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. Even if I have to retake it, I'm not a failure because I still have the chance.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Exactly. You'd just have another year to study. It's important, but not catastrophic.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: In the third grade, being held back didn't prevent me from doing what I wanted in the long run.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's another adaptive response is 'I've survived this before.'

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I definitely have.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Don't let this one event fashion your destiny. Fortunately, your employer is giving you a second chance.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You can ride out the symptoms and remember you've been successful before.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel better knowing I've been here before and can get through it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When is the test?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Next week, next Wednesday.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's schedule an appointment before that to review these strategies and focus on a positive outcome.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That sounds good to help me prepare.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'll see you then, Michelle. I appreciate you coming in today.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, thank you.

video_details.title: A Role-Play Assessment with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment MoCA
video_details.description: This video features a role-play counseling assessment with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA).

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Susan, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm doing good, how are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. I want to give you a brief assessment to help measure functions like memory and thinking. Is that okay with you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mm-hmm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. For the first part of this assessment, we're going to be handing this sheet back and forth. I have the table there so you can write on it. For the second part, I'll get that out of your way and we'll work on some other parts of it. Does that sound good?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So I want you to take a look at this section right here. Please draw a line going from a number to a letter in ascending order. Begin here and draw a line from 1, then to A, then to 2, and so on and end here.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you. I want you to copy this drawing as accurately as you can in the space below.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you. So in this empty space here, I'd like you to draw a clock, put in all the numbers, and set the time to five past four.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you for drawing this clock. Can you tell me the name of this animal?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Giraffe.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how about the name of this animal?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Bear.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And the name of that animal?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hippopotamus.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You're welcome.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This is a memory test. I'm going to read a list of words that you will have to remember now and later on. Tell me as many words as you can remember. Truck, banana, violin, barn, green.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Banana, truck, violin, green, barn.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you. I am going to read the same list for a second time. Try to remember and tell me as many words as you can, including words you said the first time. Truck, banana, violin, barn, green.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Truck, banana, violin, barn, green.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you. I will ask you to recall those words again at the end of the test. I am going to say some numbers. When I'm through, repeat them to me exactly as I have said them. 3, 2, 9, 6, 5.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you. Now I am going to say some more numbers, but when I am through, you must repeat them to me in the backwards order. 8, 5, 2.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you. I am going to read a sequence of letters. Every time I say the letter A, tap your hand once. F, B, A, C, M, N, A, A, J, K, L, B, A, F, A, K, D, E, A, A, A, J, A, M, O, F, A, A, B.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you. Now I ask you to count by subtracting seven from 90, and then keep subtracting seven from your answer until I tell you to stop.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So starting with 90 and then going down seven?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's correct.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's good. Thank you. I am going to read you a sentence. Repeat it after me exactly as I say it. A bird can fly into closed windows when it's dark and windy.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A bird can fly into closed windows when it's dark and windy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you. Now I am going to read you another sentence. Repeat it after me exactly as I say it. The caring grandmother sent groceries over a week ago.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The caring grandmother sent groceries over a week ago.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you. Tell me as many words as you can think of that begin with a certain letter of the alphabet that I will tell you in a moment. No proper nouns, numbers, or words that begin with the same sound but have a different suffix. Are you ready?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now tell me as many words as you can think of that begin with the letter S.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Shoes, socks, stockings, sweater, shirt, stripes, suitcase, safe, strategic, surly, sweet, super.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me how a carrot and a potato are alike.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Both vegetables.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me how a diamond and a ruby are alike?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They're both stones.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And a cannon and a rifle, how are they alike?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They're both weapons.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I read some words to you earlier. Tell me as many of those words as you can remember.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Banana, truck, green, barn, violin.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me today's date?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: February 10th, 2015.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me what day of the week it is?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Tuesday.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me what place we're in right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Montague University.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what city we're in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Dover.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you Susan, you did very well.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

video_details.title: DD CARES Best Practices: Frequent visitors (no talking points)
video_details.description: Part of the DD CARES Best Practices series on improving primary care, emergency care and community follow-up, this video demonstrates common practice errors as well as strategies that can help a patient with a developmental disability tolerate a difficult procedure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi August, I’m Angie. I’m one of the nurses here.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I’m not feeling very well. I’m very sad. I’m really scared. I want to run away.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. All right. Well, I’m sorry to hear that. When you’re sad, what helps you feel better?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Coming to the hospital.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. What else helps you feel better? I see you have a phone there. Do you play any games on that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I know lots of good games.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Well, why don’t you play one of your games? That might help you feel better, and I’m going to go and come back in a few minutes, okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Dr. Lee, so this is our frequent flyer August, and you know, it’s the same story, there’s nothing wrong, nothing physically wrong and he’s here again. So, you know, he’s fine, he’s settled.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, okay. All right, I’ll be out to discharge him.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, that’s good. August, are you feeling better now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A little bit better.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good. Okay, that’s really good. This time when you go back home, can you talk to your group home worker? Let him or her know that you’ve been here again, and that you were feeling sad again.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I can do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You can do that? Okay, great. I’m going to go get the doctor.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi August, I’m Angie. I’m one of the nurses here.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I’m not feeling very well. I’m feeling really sad. I’m scared, and I don’t know where to go.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What helps you feel better when you’re sad?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Coming to the hospital.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay August, so you’ve come to the hospital a few times now saying that you’re feeling sad, and you’re not getting along with your roommate, right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. My roommate is mean to me, rude to me, and I don’t know where to go.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Did you talk to your group home worker?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. He told me to go for a walk.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Mm-hm. And so you came here. All right, so this might help you feel better for right now, but it doesn’t help once you go back home, does it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A little bit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So I think I should speak to someone in your group home. Do you know who the manager is?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Her name is Kim.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And what’s the phone number? I don’t see it in the chart.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, we’ll need to find the number. Can you give me a few minutes, and I’ll go call the DSO to find the number for your group home?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay August, I just got off the phone with your manager, and we talked about how you’ve come to the hospital a couple of times, several times now, and that you’re upset with your roommate. So we discussed if they could help you make a crisis plan.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: What is that?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so it’s a plan that reviews how people can help you. So when you start to get upset or afraid, a crisis, it helps people help you so that things don’t get so bad you don’t feel you need to run away or come to the hospital.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, that sounds good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So we’ll review what we talked about because I want to make sure that you understand.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Great. There’s also something called an exit interview that we can go over together. And in this, we’ll go over what brought you here to the hospital, the... anything that we did today at the hospital, what helped, and also what to do, how to plan for after when you get home. So this needs to go home with you, and we’ll put it in this packet to take home and go over with your group home worker.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And we’ll also follow up with the group home worker.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

video_details.title: DD CARES Best Practices: The depressed patient - No talking points
video_details.description: Part of the DD CARES Best Practices series on improving primary care, emergency care and community follow-up, this video demonstrates common practice errors as well as strategies that can help a patient with a developmental disability tolerate a difficult procedure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Victor, I'm Dr. Sawyer. Victor, can you tell me how old you are?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're 20. Okay. Where do you live?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: At home.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You live at home? Who do you live with?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My mom, my dad, my sister. Who do you think I live with?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you live with your mom, dad, and sister. What do you do for work?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I go to a co-op.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you came to see me because I'm a doctor?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I didn't come to you. My mom and dad and my sister drove me here. I didn't want to come.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are your mom and dad and sister here?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'll let you go back to them in a few minutes, but let's just get through a few questions.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I want to get it done now!

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Victor, tell me how's your sleep been? Have you been experiencing any lack of joy?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I have. My teachers and educational assistants have been mean to me. They always put me in timeout. I'm feeling pressured!

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Victor, I need you to calm down.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I will not calm down!

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Victor, if you don't stay in your seat, I'm going to have to call security.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I never yell. This is the first time I'm yelling, the first time I'm pouring out my feelings on you!

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're yelling at me right now and I need you not to yell. Are you on any medications right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My mom, dad, and sister know medications. Thank you!

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yes or no, are you on any medications?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I am!

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I need you to bring me a list of your medications later. I'm going to give you a prescription for an anti-depressant. Can you bring it home to your mom?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'll say that's none of your business.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm just going to put it in my computer and my receptionist will print it off. Good luck, Victor.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Victor, I'm Dr. Sawyer. I'm a psychiatrist. Do you know what a psychiatrist does?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A psychiatrist is a doctor who deals with people feeling sad or mad. We'll talk for a bit and see how we can make things easier for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. At school, I feel like they're not doing anything. They're not listening to me about my feelings.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you feel pretty unheard.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel unheard at school. My parents and my sister are hearing me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You said you've been feeling pretty sad. How long has that been?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: This one teacher doesn't listen to me. She just tries to keep me down.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How long have you had this teacher for?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: About four years.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you been feeling sad for the entire four years or a shorter period?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A shorter period of time. A couple of months.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I want to invite your sister in because I need to find out about your medical history. I'll be right back.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like Victor's been suffering from major depression. Do you know what medications he's on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I brought a list because there's quite a few. I can give you a copy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you. There's a couple of treatments for depression. It seems like school has been a major contribution to his sadness.

diarization.text: Yes I have. My teacher's been mean to me. My educational assistant has been mean to me. They always put me in time out. I'm feeling pressured.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Victor, I need you to calm down.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I will not calm down.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Victor, if you don't stay in your seat, I'm going to have to call security.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I never yell. This is the first time I'm yelling. This is the first time I'm pouring out my feelings on you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're yelling at me right now and I need you not to yell. Um, are you on any medications right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My mom and dad and my sister know medications. Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, yes or no? Are you on any medications?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I am.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, oh, I need you to bring me a list of your medications later. Um, so I'm going to give you a prescription for an antidepressant medication. Um, can you bring it home to your mom and show it to her and then get it filled?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'll say that's none of your business.

diarization.speaker: Thererpist
diarization.text: Okay, so I'm just gonna go to my computer and put it in and then my receptionist will print you off the medication. Okay? So good luck, Victor.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Victor. I'm Dr. Sawyer. I'm a psychiatrist. Do you know what a psychiatrist does?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A psychiatrist is a doctor who deals with people who are feeling sad or mad. We'll talk about things that might have been difficult in your life and see how we can make things a little bit easier for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. And at school, I feel like they're not doing anything. They're not listening to me about how my feelings are.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you feel pretty unheard?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel unheard at school. My parents and my sister are hearing me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you say you've been feeling pretty sad. How long have you been feeling sad for?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, well, this one teacher. I won't give out any names, but she doesn't listen to me, okay? She just tries to keep me down.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How long have you had this teacher for?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: About four years.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Four years. So have you been feeling sad for this entire four years or a shorter period of time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Shorter period of time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So has it been a couple of weeks, a couple of months, a couple of days?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A couple of months.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So Victor, I want to tell you some of my thoughts, but I want to invite your sister in because I need to find out about your medical history. I'm just going to get her and then I'll come back, okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I've been talking to Victor and he's been telling me about how he's had less interest in things and trouble sleeping. It sounds like he's been suffering from major depression. Do you know what medications Victor's on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, so I actually brought a list because there's quite a few, so I can certainly give you a copy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you. There's a couple of treatments for depression. One is medication and one is interventions within the school and with the family. It seems like things in the school have been a major contribution to his sadness.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah.

video_details.title: Administering a Mini-Mental Status Exam
video_details.description: This video demonstrates how to administer a mini-mental status exam in a counseling setting.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Rebecca. How are you doing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm good. How are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Pretty good. Uh, can I ask you what hand you normally write with?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My right hand.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Your right hand. Would it be alright to ask you some questions about your memory?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I am going to ask you some questions and give you some problems to solve. Please try to answer them as best as you can.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What year is this?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What season of the year is this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Winter.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is the date today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: January 20th.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What day of the week is this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Tuesday.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What month is this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: January.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me what country we are in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: United States.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you know what county we're in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Newcastle.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you know what city we're in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Newcastle.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you know the name or the address of this building?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, Wilson Graduate Center? No, I know the name. 31 Reeds Way. 31 Reeds Way.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What floor of the building are we on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: First floor.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I am going to name three objects. After I have said them, I want you to repeat them back to me. Apple, Table, Penny.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Apple, Table, Penny.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Remember what they are because I'm going to ask you to name them again in a few minutes.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now I'm going to give you a word and ask you to spell it forwards and backwards. The word is 'world'. First, can you spell it forwards?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: W-O-R-L-D.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now, can you spell it backwards?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: D-L-R-O-W.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What were the three objects I asked you to remember earlier?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh, world? No. Um, apple... I can't remember.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is this called?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A wristwatch.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is this called?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A pen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I would like you to repeat a phrase after me. The phrase is, 'No ifs, ands, or buts'.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No ifs, ands, or buts.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I want you to read the words on the page I'm going to hold up and then do what the words say.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Close your eyes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Can I open them?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Mm-hm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Take this paper in your right hand. Fold the paper once with both hands and put the paper down on your lap.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: On this piece of paper, write any complete sentence on that piece of paper for me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Here is a drawing. Please copy the drawing on the same paper.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That concludes this test. I want to thank you for your cooperation.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

video_details.title: Suicide Assessment Role-Play - Ideation and Plan without Intent
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play session that demonstrates assessment of a client (played by an actress) expressing suicidal ideation and plan without intent.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Jill, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm doing okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Just okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I know we've talked before about me thinking about suicide and I'm starting to think about it, you know, like a little bit stronger than before. I think a little bit more clearly. So...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me a little bit more about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, when we've talked before I've had the feelings and the thoughts of suicide but now it's kind of starting to like I'm thinking about it more often and I'm thinking about it a little more clearly and that's alarming to me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you want to die?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, a little yeah, sometimes. Sometimes. I mean, you know, sometimes I know it would be scary to try it and my husband would be so hurt but at the same time I want to end this. I want to end the feeling that I'm having.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Depression?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Do you have any plan as to how you would end your life if you decided to do that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, I know if I wanted to that we have pills in the cabinet so it wouldn't be that hard. I could just take the bottle.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The same pills that you're prescribed for the depression?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you feel like you're going to carry out that plan?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I mean, part of it that's why I'm nervous because like I'm worried that I might but at the same time you know I'm afraid to so sometimes I think that I might and sometimes I think I won't. I don't want to but sometimes I get scared that I will.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And so today you're a little worried that you will or you're a little closer to it than than usual, right? We've talked about this before in the past. You've come in, you've had kind of that same plan with the pills and the thoughts. And what stopped you those times? What stopped you in the past?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: In the past I thought this'll get better. I just have to keep trying. I thought what will my husband feel when I'm gone and my family, my parents, my brother and sister. I thought that this is as bad as it can get and it has to get better eventually but now I'm just starting to feel like I don't think it's going to get better.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So those times before when you had the same feeling, right? You felt just as bad as you feel now. Really down, hopeless. What happened a few days after that? After the the thoughts of suicide went away. What was your outlook on life then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean I'd feel I'd feel a little better, you know, and then I'd I'd say to myself that was silly, you know, I don't want to do that. I don't I don't want to end things. You know, it's it's too rash. But you know it's starting to feel like a permanent problem.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you feel like this time these suicidal thoughts they're markedly different than what you've experienced before?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I wouldn't say markedly but I would say they're different. They're a little they're stronger.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: More intense this time. Right. What do you think's brought this these feelings on? Before we talked about I know it was relationship surrounding relationships. Is it the same thing this time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean I guess that has something to do with it. I guess it's just like when I look to everything. Like everything that could be good or everything just everything like life, my relationships, the future. I just look at it and I see despair. I just see everything going wrong and I just don't see how it could get better. I just don't see it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Get a sense of hopelessness?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So this time's different because you feel it's maybe less situational, less tied to the relationships and more well philosophical. You're looking at your outlook and you're saying it's not going to get any better. What's the point of going on? Alright. So this is a little bit of new territory for you. How long you been feeling this way with the intensity that you have right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably a week, maybe a little less.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what's prevented you from hurting yourself over this last week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm afraid to do it. I'm just scared. It's like it's like jumping off a diving board like you get up to the edge and you stand there. That's where I'm at.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you made any gestures to harm yourself? Like have you went and grabbed the pills or went to the medicine cabinet, looked at the pills, anything like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, sometimes I look at them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You look at them? Have you done anything further than look at them?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well I mean so I have to take them, it's my prescription. So when it's time I start thinking about it like it's more I think about my like the ideations come even more because it's like a trigger like I'm thinking about the pills so I go to the cabinet and I get my pills and and I take the the one that I'm supposed to but I just look at the bottle and I kind of stand there and I just think instead of putting the bottle back I could take it with me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what do you end up doing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It it takes a while but I put it back. It's it's scary. Like I look into the bottle and I'm afraid because dying is scary but...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how about the pain that you would cause your husband and the rest of your family?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I don't want to do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You don't want that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't I don't want my husband to find me. I don't want him to feel like this is his fault. I don't want him to be sad that I'm gone. I don't want him to feel like I feel.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And when relatives of somebody that committed suicide hear about the suicide, who do they blame?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Themselves.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: And it's not their fault. It's not their fault. And I know that they wouldn't be able to get over it and I know that they'll be thinking about how bad I felt. They'll have to know what it really felt like for me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I know this is a tough time, right? But the good news is you're here talking to me about it, right? And you're talking about it. I'm going to guess that you want to do something to prevent to feel better. Right? Are you going to carry out your plan? Are you going to hurt yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't want to.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you going to?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. I think I think if I can just remember what it'll be like for them that'll keep me from doing it. You know, it's the times that I forget to think about how they're going to feel that I get closer to the edge. But when I remember, you know, like it upsets me to think about what it'll be like for them so if I can remember to think about that then it'll help me not do that but I think having the pills there in the cabinet like that is a big temptation for me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So can we can we do this? Uh your husband's at home. Right, you mentioned. Uh you take the pills once a day?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Before bed?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhmm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Can we uh would you be willing to sign a release so I can talk to him and he can hold on to those pills and just give you the pill each night you take one at night? Would that be okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think I think that would be a good idea.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. Is there anything else in the medicine cabinet or anywhere else in the house that could be of danger to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think I think yeah I think it would be a good idea to just make sure that everything that was in the medicine cabinet...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All the pills. Okay. Would he be willing to do that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah I think yeah I think that he would be willing to do that. He doesn't he wants me to get through this.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And if I get a release for to talk to him you'll sign it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'll I'll do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. You're familiar before, are you familiar rather with this concept we've talked about before contracting for safety? Remember the prior times when you've been in states similar to this? Can you promise me that you're going to not harm yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can yeah I can do that. At least until next week when we meet again. I promise.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's meet a little sooner than that. Okay? Let's set something up for tomorrow.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Yeah I can definitely do that. I can do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. I know this is a rough time. Uh and I'm trying to appreciate how rough it is for you. I want you to keep in mind how you felt after the times before and how you do tend to pull out of this and you look back at it a lot differently but in the moment it's hard to see that. Right? That doesn't necessarily make this any easier. Uh but if you can hang on to we can get through this this cycle and the depression you'll probably have a different outlook. If if history's any evidence, right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Mhmm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does that kind of make sense? Alright. So what do you have planned for the rest of the day after you leave here?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm you know, I'm just going to go home. My husband will be home from work and have dinner, watch TV. He'll be there, so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you going to be alone at any time between when you leave here and when you come and see me tomorrow?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh yeah I'll probably be home for a little while in the morning but I have to work so I won't have you know I'll be busy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. If these feelings intensify to where you do feel you're going to act on them would you promise to call me and if you can't get ahold of me call 911?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'll do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. I'm going to go get that release so we can talk to your husband and then uh I'm going to see you for a few minutes and we'll set up an appointment for tomorrow. Alright. Thanks Jill.

video_details.title: Access to Primary Care: Access to care via service providers
video_details.description: Members of the Access to Primary Care study perform skits based on experiences with the primary health care system.  To learn more about the study visit: http://www.camh.ca/primary-care-study

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Mental health facility, how may I help you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hi, I'm calling because I'm wondering about coming to a program that you might have there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, could I get your name please?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, it's Joanna Dean.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. I'm seeing that you have been here before once. We have recommendations for both an inpatient and an outpatient program. Did you have an idea which one you wanted to follow up on today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I've been feeling pretty bad, pretty depressed, so I think that I should probably do the inpatient program, if it's possible.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so we do have a cycle starting in about six weeks. In order to make it into that cycle, we need a medical package back from your doctor within the next two weeks. I can fax that package to your doctor today. Do you have the fax number?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, I'm going to fax that off. What you need to do is call your doctor today and set up an appointment to have that package completed and returned to us within the next two weeks.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, so I need to get a medical package and I have to call my doctor for it?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You need to have them fill it out, so you need to call them for an appointment. I'm faxing it off to them today for you though.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, sounds good. I'll call them right now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Dr. Bob's office, reception speaking.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh hi, this is Joanna Dean. I'm a patient of Dr. Bob and I need to come in to get a medical package filled out so I can attend a program.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Joanna, we actually got your package in the fax earlier today. Before we set an appointment, I wanted to let you know this package isn't covered by OHIP, so you will have to pay for it. It's generally about $100 to $125.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: $100 or $125? I don't have that money because I'm on ODSP for my depression and I haven't actually been working.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Sometimes local municipalities have extra funds for people on ODSP to help with these programs. My recommendation is to call your worker, see what they can do, and call us back if they're able to help out.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, I'll call my worker right now. Thank you, goodbye.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, you've reached caseworker 43672. I'm away from my desk, but if you leave a message I will get back to you within 48 hours. Thank you, bye.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hi, this is Joanna Dean. I really need to get this medical package done and it turns out it costs $100 or $125. I was told maybe you could help me out with the fee so I can go to a program to help me with my depression. Please call me back. Bye.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hello?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, may I speak to Joanna please? This is your worker calling back. We do actually have some funds available, but before we can release them, we need a quote from your doctor in writing.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: What? What do you mean?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We can help with the package because it is related to your disability, but we need the exact value from the doctor on file. Once we have the paperwork, it usually takes about five to seven business days to release the funds.

diarization.speaker: Patient
