diarization.text: I don't understand, this is such a complicated process and by the time it's done I'm probably not going to get into the next cycle at the hospital.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I am sorry about that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I understand you're trying to help, but okay. Goodbye.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Dr. Bob's office, reception speaking.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hi, this is Joanna Dean. I spoke with my worker and they're willing to give the funds for the medical package, but they need a quote sent to them for how much it's going to be. Could you do that please?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Glad they can help. Before we can do the quote, we need you to come in for a brief 15-minute appointment so we can see which forms we need to do. We have something in two days on Friday at 10:00 in the morning. Can you come in then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: This is so complicated. I actually have a hard time with mornings because of my medications; it makes it hard to sleep and hard to get up too.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's see if we can find something a bit later in the day. We have a 12:30 on the following Tuesday. Would you be able to do that one?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, yes, I'll take that one.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so we'll see you at 12:30 on Tuesday.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, thank you. Bye-bye.

video_details.title: Suicide Assessment Role-Play - Ideation without Intent or Plan
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play session that demonstrates assessment of a client (played by an actress) expressing suicidal ideation without intent or plan.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Jill, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm alright.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Just alright?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, obviously I'm not doing great. I asked you to have this session; we weren't scheduled for today. I'm feeling depressed as usual, but it's stronger and I just don't want to wake up. I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Just a rough time of things?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you know what's causing it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really. It's just the same except worse. I just feel like what's the point? I don't feel like continuing on.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You don't feel like continuing with your life.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, kind of.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you been having thoughts of suicide?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think about what it would be like to just end things. I think it would be a lot easier, but at the same time I can't imagine doing it. I can't say I haven't thought about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, so you've had some thoughts about it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What prevents you from doing it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I know what it would be like for my family. I don't want to hurt them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And they would be hurt.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. And it's scary; the thought of dying is scary, but the thought of going on is painful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it almost sounds as if life's wearing you down a bit.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I kind of feel like I'm stuck between a rock and a hard place. I just don't know where to go from here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Have you worked out any specific plan to hurt yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. I mean, I've thought about ways, but not specific because I just don't think that I could do it. It's starting to creep into my thoughts and it never has before, so I'm kind of concerned about that. It's really scary for me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So how long has it been going on, these feelings?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: In the past couple of days it started more so, and then today it was just the first thought in my head and I couldn't stop thinking about it. That's why I wanted to see you, because I'm starting to feel a little bit out of control.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so today and the past few days, a kind of a new thought that you don't want to continue living, but at the same time you don't want to commit suicide and you don't have a plan.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I don't want to. But like I said, I feel like I'm stuck. I know it's not a good option, I just don't know where else to go.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So if the depression would go away, do you think that would change your outlook?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Definitely. I think that is the reason why the thought of not living anymore comes into my head. I wake up feeling so down and pointless that it makes me wish that I was dead. But if I didn't have that feeling, then I wouldn't wish that I was dead because I know that my life has value.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: These suicidal ideations are fairly common with depression. It sounds like you're frustrated and tired of being sick. Your life has value and I want you to try to hang on to that thought. Tell me what you have planned for the rest of the day.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I didn't really have plans because I really needed to see you. I guess I would go home, but I'm not really sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is anybody else at home?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, but I probably could go to my parents' house if I needed to. I could call them and see if they'd be off work soon.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you do that for me? Can you go there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think that's a good idea.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. We'll play it by ear from that point. If you could spend the night there, I think that would be a wiser choice. Have you ever heard me use the term 'contract for safety'?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think you mentioned it before, I'm not really sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It means you promise to me that you're going to be safe until I see you again; that you don't have any intent or plan to harm yourself. Can you make that promise to me now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Give me a minute and I'll come back and we'll work a little bit today, and then I'm going to schedule to see you tomorrow as well, okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Thanks, Jill.

video_details.title: Suicide Assessment Role-Play - Ideation, Intent, and Plan
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play session that demonstrates assessment of a client (played by an actress) expressing suicidal ideation, intent, and plan.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Jill, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm doing alright.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Doing alright?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'm feeling a little bit better.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Feeling a little bit better? I know you've been down for a while. What's going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just feel like everything's going to be okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hmm, this is unusual for you, because usually when you come in and talk to me, you're kind of down, a little depressed. Something changed recently?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just feel like I've found the solution and I know what I'm going to do, so I'm not really worried about my depression. I guess I'm feeling a little bit better about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me about this solution you found for your depression?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, you know, I know we've talked about it before, I think that I'm going to commit suicide.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You want to commit suicide? Do you know how you'd do that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I have some pills in my house, in the medicine cabinet, and I'm going to take those.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And when do you plan on doing this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably a couple days from now. I have some things to get in order. I want to arrange things and make sure everything's in order and then I'll do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What kind of things you need to arrange?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I want to make sure all the documents my husband needs are in a place where he can find them. I don't want to make things more difficult for him. I want to make sure everything's in order so when I'm gone, everybody has what they need.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Jill, you've been seeing me for almost a year now, and you know by telling me this that I'm going to act to stop you. I'm going to try to stop you from killing yourself.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, I want to do it. I think in the end it's what's going to make things better. But I guess there's still a part of me that doesn't want to die, doesn't want to do that to my family. I guess I'm telling you because I'm not 100% resolved and I wanted to talk it over.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You seem pretty serious though about your timetable and your plan.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean, it's like when you plan to go on a weekend trip. You're pretty sure you're going to go, but if the weather's bad you might not. So I think I'm pretty sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there anything that can stop you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. I think I feel pretty sure about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you feel like it's the depression or something else that drove you to this decision?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel like it's just the same old things I was worried about before: the depression, my relational issues, my job, the stuff that gets me down. It just clicked and it was like I feel like I'm going to feel better.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: As you said, it's a solution. You feel like you found a solution.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, now we've talked about this issue in the past. When you've come in feeling this way, we've sent you over to the hospital. I know that's not your favorite place, but when you go there for about five days, you come out feeling a lot better. Do you feel like this time would be different?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I feel like in the past I've been thinking about killing myself seriously but now I'm not as scared of it. I don't really want you to put me in the hospital because then I won't be able to do it. Before I was scared so I wanted you to put me in the hospital, but now I just want to get it over with.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So a part of you is saying you don't want me to stop you, but yet you came in here and told me. So a part of you seems to be not quite sure?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess there'll always be a part of me that's human and scared to die. I care about you, we've had a relationship and I felt like I owed it to you to be honest because we've had that relationship in the past. I felt like I wanted to talk it over before I did it to gain the final clarity that I needed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has it helped you gain any clarity?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. I guess I see that you're saying I really need to go to the hospital. I guess I was hoping you would be happy for me that I was feeling better, but you want me to go to the hospital so it makes me think about whether it's the right decision.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You mean the suicide?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sometimes, as you've been with me almost a year now and you've been depressed much of that time. It's not unusual when someone thinks they've found a solution to depression, even if that solution is suicide, that their mood becomes elevated because they see an end to the pain. There's other things we can do.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: But we have done them in the past and I didn't feel better and now I am feeling better. So I just want you to accept that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But I'm not going to. It's my obligation to try to keep you alive. I've seen you this way before and I know it may not seem this way now, but when you came out from the suicidal thoughts before, you did well for weeks or months at a time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, but I'm feeling better now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Temporarily, because you feel you've found an end to the pain. I understand you feel better, but you're feeling better because you plan on killing yourself. We've talked about how devastating that would be to your family and friends.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: But I'm just torturing them with my sadness. I'm just making their lives miserable. I don't understand how it helps them for me to stay alive. I'm worth more to them through my life insurance and they won't have to suffer anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So your logic is that if you end your life, you'll free them from having to deal with you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it feels like the right thing to do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And as you know, I've talked to your husband and parents. They've repeatedly said that despite the challenges of your depression, they would much rather have you alive. Why would they say that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think that they're scared of the pain of losing me, but I know that they'll feel better eventually.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So they'll get over the grief?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I understand. I think we've come to have a good relationship. I hope that I've earned your trust and that you value my opinion. Can I share with you something that I know about suicide? You open to hearing it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: There's a lot of ways that people die. It's hard for me to imagine a way more devastating than suicide. When someone dies of an illness or a tragic accident, people grieve, but there's usually not a blame assigned to that. They don't feel guilty. Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: They feel sad because they've lost the person, but they don't feel responsible for that person's death. Suicide is different. When someone commits suicide, their family and friends feel responsible. They have no answers to all the questions they have.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm going to write them a note and tell them everything and that it's not their fault, because it's not. I just want them to be happy without me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you believe the note will take away all that pain?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, but I think that it'll help them realize that they shouldn't feel guilty like you're saying.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It'll mitigate that pain?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I can tell you from experience that notes don't really help. If anything, it's another artifact that they can agonize over. They will miss you and they will agonize for the rest of their lives because they lost you. It's a special horrible type of agony that comes with feeling responsible for causing someone's death. I know you don't want that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just want to feel better. I just don't know why you can't let me feel better.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I know it's frustrating. The times when you've gone to the hospital before, you have felt better. Your outlook was completely different when you came out. Is it possible that if you go to the hospital this time you could come out feeling better again?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's possible.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm going to make arrangements to get you over to the hospital.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't want to go.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I know you don't. We've had this conversation before. You usually do well in the groups. Every time you've been to the hospital, you've come out feeling better. I know you think suicide is the answer, but I can tell you it's not. I'd like you to go voluntarily through this process. Will you do that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'll go.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. I'm going to make arrangements to get you there. Make sure you set up an appointment to see me right away once you're discharged. Can you do that for me?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. I'm going to go make those arrangements and we'll get you over there, okay?

video_details.title: Access to Primary Care: It's a Dog Bite
video_details.description: Members of the Access to Primary Care study perform skits based on experiences with the primary health care system.  To learn more about the study visit: http://www.camh.ca/primary-care-study

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Jennifer, what can I do for you today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have a dog bite and I think it's getting infected. See, it's red and it's getting swollen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Mhm, dog bite. Yeah, I see that there. I'm wondering though, have you been using any recreational drugs lately?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: What? No, I never use them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No, never? Yeah, I see. How about your mood? How has your mood been?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, well you know, I struggle a little bit with being anxious, but it's not anywhere worse than usual, except that I am worried about getting an infection that spreads.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, your psychiatrist though, have you seen your psychiatrist recently?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: What does this got to do with my dog bite? Yeah, I have.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, and your medication, are you still taking it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, yeah, I'm taking some medication, but not for, like, not antibiotics.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, no, I understand, but I'm just thinking, you know, under the circumstances, the best thing for you to do would be to go make an appointment with your psychiatrist, maybe have your medication adjusted, see what your psychiatrist says.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: But my psychiatrist doesn't treat dog bites!

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, I understand Jennifer, but just go see your psychiatrist, see what she says, and then if you still have a problem, you can come back and see me then.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: But the infection will get worse.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Jennifer, I understand you're very worried about this. You see I have a waiting room full of patients who really need to see a family doctor, so I'm going to have to ask you to go make an appointment with your psychiatrist, and I'll follow up with you if the psychiatrist feels it's necessary.

video_details.title: Explaining the Limits of Confidentiality to a Counseling Client
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which the limits of confidentiality for counseling are explained.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Lisa, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm doing okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Did you make it here okay to the office?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I did, traffic wasn't too bad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good, good. So I understand that you've come to see me because you have a situation at home.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I've just been having a lot of anxiety right now. My oldest child is moving out, and I know as a mom the goal is to let them be independent, but I'm still a little concerned it's going to work out and that he's in a good place.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, and I'll try to help you with that. And I'm sure you're eager to get started with the counseling.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Absolutely, the sooner the better.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good. I want to go over a few disclosures about the counseling relationship before we get into assessment, which is the first stage. I'll ask you a lot of questions about your past and what's going on now, and after assessment, we'll move into counseling roughly once a week. First, I want to discuss confidentiality.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, so like attorneys, what you can and cannot do?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Kind of. Attorneys and clients have confidentiality, and counselors and clients do as well, but the types are different. I'll explain how it works between us.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, can you explain the differences to me?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Absolutely. Our counseling relationship, the notes I take, and your chart are confidential, but there are exceptions. Confidentiality isn't absolute.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So there's times you might tell someone else something that I said?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yes, but only in specific situations that permit or mandate it. I want to review those with you before we move on. Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'd like to know that before I tell you anything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I agree. The first exception is when you give me permission to release information. For example, do you have a primary care physician?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I do, yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Depending on what we talk about, you may want them to know, so you'd sign a release. Furthermore, if you want your son to come in for a session, you'd have to sign a release for him to be here.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That makes sense.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Other exceptions involve insurance. Insurance companies have access to progress notes and assessment data in the chart. It's important you know that information is transmitted for billing and reviews.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So whatever progress notes you have automatically go to the insurance company?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The notes themselves don't go for standard billing, but information about the session type, length, and identifying info does so they know a service was provided.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right, they get all your medical stuff too, so they have it all.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Another exception is if I feel you are going to harm yourself or someone else. In that instance, I am obligated to act. If you have suicidal or homicidal ideation, I would only release necessary information to protect you or the person at risk.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right, I'm not planning on hurting anybody, but that's good to know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Confidentiality release is limited to what's necessary. Also, having suicidal thoughts doesn't automatically mean I'll call the police. We have a discussion first because most people with ideation don't have intent or a plan. Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So if someone's thinking about it, you're going to try to get to the bottom of it first?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Absolutely. I have a responsibility to make sure you're safe. Having a thought is different from having a detailed plan. That exception is for extreme cases.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, that makes sense.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Another exception is child or elder abuse. I am a mandated reporter. Even if it's something mentioned in passing about a neighbor, I would have to act to protect safety.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I'm not abusing anyone.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm sure, but I wanted to explain how far-reaching it is. The last exception is if a judge orders me to testify in civil or criminal litigation. I have to comply, though I will try not to disclose if you don't want me to.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It does, yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'd rather you have all the information so you don't have concerns about where the information you reveal is going. Any questions about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, I understand that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Again, most of these are unlikely, but you should have the info. Do you have any questions about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't think so. Seems pretty clear.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. I appreciate you sitting through that. We're going to get started now with the assessment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play - Anxiety Related to School Performance
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which cognitive-behavioral therapy is used to treat anxiety related to school performance.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello Hazel, how you doing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm alright, um, a little bit stressed out right now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A little stressed? What's going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, as you know, I'm in a graduate program right now and I'm just really coming to the end of my program and I'm just finding it increasingly difficult and just really stressed with how things have been going.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, and we've talked about some different struggles you've had as you balance work and school and everything. What specifically is bothering you now? Seems like you're a little more distressed today.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I don't really know. It's just I, as I've told you before, I take school really seriously and I really strive to do well on my assignments and I just feel like I'm not performing as well as I need to be.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hmm. Now what kind of grades have you been getting lately?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh, well I've been getting A's.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Anything else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, just A's.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, that's usually considered pretty good, right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I just feel like it's getting harder to get the A's.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you're working harder to get the same grade.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. It used to be so easy for me to do what my teachers expect and to get good grades. Now I feel like it's really a struggle and I'm constantly worried about not doing as well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you been getting any feedback from professors or your classmates about your performance?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My teachers all seem to think I'm doing well. I seem to get good feedback, but to make sure I'm doing well, I really focus on the details, like making sure the instructions are clear because I'm afraid if I'm not clear, I won't do it the right way.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So before when you got A's, you were working hard but not to this level of precision or detail. You're working harder to get the same grade you used to get before.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. I find myself emailing the teacher almost obsessively trying to clarify the assignment and to make sure they think I'm doing well in class.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When you're having this feeling of anxiety or stress, what's going through your mind? What are you thinking about?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I've worked really hard this whole program and I don't want to mess it up now. If I don't get these grades, I feel like I'm ruining all this hard work or that I'm a failure because I slacked off at the end.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what grade would you have to receive for you to feel like you have failed?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably less than an A. Anything other than an A.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And right below an A is an A minus?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I would be okay with that, but I wouldn't be really happy with it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about a B plus?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I wouldn't be that excited about that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about a B?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I wouldn't be happy with that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So an A you can tolerate, an A minus you think you could.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. To me, a B is a B whether it's a B minus or a B plus. And that's not an A.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what would it mean to you if you received a B?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That I didn't try hard enough or that I was slacking. I just didn't do enough.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What would it mean if that were true?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That I was lazy. That I could have tried harder and I didn't.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We've talked before about cognitive distortions, specifically black or white, all or nothing thinking. It sounds like you feel that if it's not an A, you didn't try hard enough and you're lazy, though it's clear to me you're not lazy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Earlier in the program, A's weren't effortless, but you didn't have to work as hard for them. What do you think has changed?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm not quite sure. It didn't stress me out as much in the beginning, but now I almost dread it because it's anxiety producing for me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You mentioned part of it was getting close to the end. Is there anything else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: There's a new student in the program this semester and it seems like she's really stressing me out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How so?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Throughout the program I considered myself the student who got the best grades. There's an award at the end for doing really well, and I made it a goal to show I really busted my butt. This semester, a new student named Joyce came in and she had a 4.0 in her other program.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So now you feel like you really have competition for this award.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. The pressure's on. She might win it over me, so I need to go above and beyond to make sure I'm still on track.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And paradoxically, that's caused you more stress and you're working harder for the same grade.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. It's causing me a lot of anxiety and school is not as enjoyable as it once was.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What if Joyce won this award and you didn't? What would that mean?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Then why did I do the program? If you're not going to be the best, why try? I could have skated by this whole time. It would feel like it was all for nothing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's all for nothing if you don't win the award.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess it's not the only thing that matters, but it feels like it would negate all the positive things, like losing a race right at the end.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But you would still graduate. The reason you came to the program was to get the degree, and you didn't even know about the award until the second year anyway.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: But it's now taken on some importance for me. Winning this award has been a real goal.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You have a tendency to be a little perfectionistic. Have you ever heard the phrase 'perfect is the enemy of good'?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This desire to be perfect is potentially causing you not even to perform well because of the anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. I'm so stressed about reading the right thing that I'm not retaining all the information. It's starting to impact school.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there any way that you can not win the award and still walk away having accomplished worthy goals?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It sounds silly when you reflect it back to me. There are different degrees of success. I would be happy with just getting the degree and it would still be a worthwhile journey. But in the moment, the possibility of not getting the award is really upsetting.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The award validates your hard work, and losing it invalidates it. But in reality, you're still an excellent student. Would this award have any impact on employment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't think so in the long term.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In a sense, if you could forget about the award, you'd probably win it. But the thought of potential failure is holding you back.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It makes me paranoid to make mistakes or take risks because I'm worried about judgment from my teachers.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: There's no tolerance for any type of mistake. For you to feel better, you need to not place so much value in winning.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's the automatic thought you have when you're working and you sense that anxiety coming on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When I'm just doing the work?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, what's going through your mind at that moment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm just running through a checklist, making sure I did everything expected of me to ensure I get that award.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: One of your thoughts is 'I must win that award.' Is there an adaptive response you could apply at that moment to counteract that thought?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I could say the award is local and won't really impact future employment, so colleagues won't think less of me if I don't get it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you could say it'd be nice to win, but it won't make a difference in your career. You're still a good student and a good clinician. Do you believe that adaptive response is true?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes I do, and then sometimes it's really hard in the heat of the moment to talk myself down from that spiral.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What percentage of the time do you believe that response is true?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe half the time. The other half, I'm not really buying it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What advice would you give Joyce if she were in your situation and obsessing about this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd tell her the class sees she's doing well and teachers give positive feedback, so all signs point toward her being successful in the program.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Your advice to her is positive and uplifting. Why isn't it appropriate for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I hold myself to a higher standard than I hold other people to. It's hard for me to apply that to myself.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You can see the logic, but your feelings don't match. I want you to complete a thought record, specifically working through the adaptive response section to help you form a realistic and useful response. We'll look at that from week to week and hopefully bring you some relief from this anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sounds like a plan.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Thanks Hazel.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thanks.

video_details.title: Managing depression with 10 Minute CBT

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I know when we met a few weeks ago, you were quite keen to look at some ways to try and manage your depression, maybe without medication. Is that what brings you in today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I'd like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, okay. I'd like to take some notes if that's okay, just to keep track of what we talk about. Would that be okay with you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, that'd be fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You can have a copy to take away afterwards. Um, what I find quite helpful is if we talk about a specific situation. I wonder if you could just think of a time, maybe a recent time, when you felt particularly depressed and it affected you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, well a few weeks ago I was due to meet up with some friends from antenatal classes. We used to meet up every week, but I felt so tired and low, I just couldn't go.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So what was going through your mind when you were feeling tired and low that stopped you wanting to go?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, well I started thinking about the other mothers laughing and chatting and I wouldn't have anything to say.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And, and what would that mean if you didn't have anything to say?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They'd probably think that I was boring. Um, why would they want me there if I was just going to make everyone else miserable?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: They sound like some really difficult thoughts to have. And how did it make you feel when you were thinking that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Really low.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. Okay. It's really understandable, I think, that you'd feel low if you're having quite self-critical, very negative thoughts, and that's quite common in depression to have those type of thoughts. Did it make you think anything about how they might see you, for example?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well the other children always seem so happy. Um, I started thinking maybe the other mothers do a better job than me. I worry a lot about Molly and wondered if she'd be better off with one of the other moms.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. Okay. Um, now that must be really painful. And how does it make you feel to think that Molly might be better off with one of the other moms?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It made me feel really sad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What tells you that Molly might be better off with one of the other moms?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They always seem so in control. With my depression, I just feel guilty that I'm not a very good mother.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You've mentioned a number of emotional feelings. You said you feel fed up, low, sad and sometimes guilty. Do you have any physical symptoms or body reactions?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hmm, I get quite tearful, although that's mainly when I'm on my own. I'm so tired, I just don't have the energy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. Are you getting good sleep at the moment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well Molly keeps me up sometimes at night, so that makes me tired. But even after a good night's sleep, I'm still exhausted.

video_details.title: Case study clinical example: First session with a client with symptoms of depression (CBT model)
video_details.description: Case study example for use in teaching, aiming to demonstrate some of the triggers, thoughts, feelings and responses linked with problematic low mood. This section here represents the first 13 minutes of an initial therapy session, but in order to try and outline the vicious cycle, it moves faster than an average session might. The video features an actor playing the character of Gabriella, but the dialogue is not scripted, and as such represents a natural therapeutic exchange. I myself am a qua

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Gabriella. I understand that you're here today because you've been experiencing some low mood.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I just, um, recently I've just, I'm feeling down a lot and I can't really like snap out of it. Like sometimes if it's happened before I can just like get myself back on track but recently I'm just finding it really difficult to do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so it sounds like you've been experiencing some low mood and you're kind of struggling to get going a bit.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah definitely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You've had low mood in the past, but it's kind of you've been able to pull yourself out of it before but more recently you've found that harder. Okay, so I understand that you first went to your GP who referred you here about two months ago. Um, can I ask what what led you to go to the GP in the first place?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, my long-term boyfriend broke up with me and it was it was such a shock, like I really wasn't expecting it and um, it just got me really down and I just felt really lonely and and I didn't really want to see people, just wanted to be in my own space and my mom told me I should probably go to the doctors and I went and he's referred me to you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so it sounds then like you had that breakup and you weren't expecting it, so it kind of came out of the blue a bit and um, and that you've been on your own quite a lot so you're not been seeing people as much and it sounds like your mom noticed that there's been a bit of a change in you. Um, okay, and and how have things been then since then, since that happened and since you went to the GP?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just nothing's really changed, nothing's really improved, I just just feel down, like everything's an effort and I just feel distant from things and like I said I can't snap out of it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And how did you feel about coming here today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I was kind of disappointed in myself because I feel like nobody else my age is doing this, like I should have been able to snap out of it, like it's just another thing that I've not really it's another thing that's making me stand out for the wrong reasons.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you feel like it's kind of odd or unusual to be coming to see a clinical psychologist. Um, I suppose I just want to reassure you that it's absolutely normal to have feelings of depression and anxiety, it's really very common and it certainly isn't odd or strange at all. Um, so it sounds like it was actually quite hard for you to come here today. So what I guess led you to do that because it sounds like maybe there was a lot pushing you against coming here today but you've managed to come anyway?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I'm just hoping that it's going to help. I think I didn't I didn't really want to admit it because like it's just another failure, but my mom was talking to me and I know she's she's not really happy with the way I'm behaving and I don't really want to disappoint her again and so I thought there's no harm in it so I just thought I'd come.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so it sounds like partly you're doing it then for your mom because you're a bit worried that she she isn't pleased with you at the moment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Um, well I think it's great that you've come here and definitely there's a lot of evidence to suggest that psychological therapy um, can help depression and particularly the type of therapy that we're going to be doing which is called cognitive behavioral therapy and I'll tell you a bit more about that as as we go on but I'm just trying to find out a bit more about you today. Um, so I saw from your notes that you're a medic student.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, um, I'm not currently in uni at the moment but yeah last year I was a medic student.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so I guess uh what why what's what's the reason that you're not in uni this year?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I just it was like it was pretty tough first year so they um suggested that I took a year out this is the break.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so just thinking so that would be about six months ago was it that your year out started?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Um, and it sounds then maybe like your first year was also quite tough.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it was. I thought it was tough for everyone but obviously we all take it in different ways, don't we?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you're planning on are you planning on returning?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, yeah I'm going to have to really, so that yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You don't sound too sure about that though.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think returning is probably that's what's going to make everyone happy and I think, you know, at least I'll be able to um finally achieve something and get something right. So yeah like next year I'm gonna I'll get through it. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so it doesn't it doesn't sound like you want to go back.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I do, um, I don't enjoy it, I just I just don't feel like it at the moment and I just it's a lot of work and it's a lot of pressure and but that's what comes with it and, you know, it'll work out for the best if I go.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, um, so I guess then there's quite a lot of thoughts and feelings about going back at the moment. Um, I'm just wondering in the meantime what are you what are you up to, what have you been doing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, well I've not really had much on the horizon, my mom um, her friend owns a restaurant and like she suggested that I did a bit of waitressing in there just, you know, for a bit of like money and stuff because obviously I'm not in uni. So, you know, I've done that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. How many shifts have you done there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I've only done one so far, um, yeah I don't know whether it's something that I'd probably go back to, but...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so when was that shift?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was it was last week actually.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, and and how was it? I suppose I'm intrigued. Can you tell me a bit more about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, it was it was different, you know, because it's like I could I did enjoy it because there's like it's just different aspects and I had to like speak to people and like try to get their orders and try to remember it and stuff, like I wasn't very good but I suppose like it was handy to have some money and to like get out the house.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so it sounds like you quite enjoyed that then.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Um, what makes you think you weren't very good?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just like I was bit slow and people sometimes they didn't understand what I was saying so I'd have to talk louder or quieter or slower and I got a bit confused sometimes with the orders and I just don't really think that I'm not really like a friendly like people don't really think that I'm a friendly person so they didn't really want to to talk to me and stuff, I felt like I was like inconveniencing them by like asking them things and getting things wrong. But yeah, they said they said that apparently um most people get like a few mistakes on their first shift.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Mm-hm.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: But then again, she's my mom's friend so it's probably why she was saying it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the person who owns the restaurant is your mom's friend.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so it says you're saying that you think you weren't very good and that's because you were a bit slow and you got confused with some orders. Is it but you said it's common for people to do that on their first shift?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, that's what she said to us but um but it's probably just she's just trying to make me feel better. She probably felt sorry for me because I'm obviously not very good at it, like I'm not very good at anything recently. I think she just felt sorry for me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so I've just been noting down some of those thoughts that you've been having, you kind of say that you feel like you're not very good, you're slow, you're confused with the orders, um and you feel like you're inconveniencing her and she feels sorry for you. Um I suppose I'm wondering, I mean what makes you think that she feels sorry for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, like I said she's my mom's friend and she's obviously feeling sorry for my mom as well because she's got a daughter that's not like anyone else of her age and she's just like all alone and she's not getting involved, so I think she just feels sorry for me and she doesn't want to like say anything to upset me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. When you're having these kind of thoughts, because that's quite a lot of negative thoughts you're describing, how do you feel?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just feel empty. I don't I'm just calling it as it is, I'm just calling as reality and I feel like I'm being honest with myself by just voicing it and not trying to go around hiding it because I know, like I can see it myself.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it sounds like you feel like those thoughts are very true then. I mean, if you were going to rate them, um, if say I'm going to pick out some of those thoughts you described, so you said "I'm not very good" and "I'm inconveniencing them", how much would you say you believe those on a scale, um, out of a hundred? Where a hundred is like I absolutely believe it and zero is like I don't believe it at all.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm about eighty.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Eighty.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Eighty percent yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you feel quite sure that you definitely believe those. Okay. And you said that when you're thinking those thoughts you start to feel quite empty.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just feel distant and like I said I'm not really myself, I just like it's like I'm not really there but when I am I can't even do a good job and...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Are there any other emotions that you experience?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Feel drained. I don't feel like I'm in touch with anything, just like everything's going on around me but I'm just not there, I'm just it's like I'm just watching.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you feel empty, distant, you feel drained. Um, and how when you're feeling these emotions, how do you feel in your body kind of what sensations do you notice?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know how to describe it. I get like I have a bit of like like you know when you kind of get like butterflies when you're nervous and stuff?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Mm-hm.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Kind of get a bit of that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you feel some butterflies.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Did you have butterflies that night when you were at the restaurant?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I was pretty nervous then but when I got into it they went away and like it distracted me for a bit until obviously I realized that I wasn't doing a very good job.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Mm-hm. Okay. And when you when you have those emotions, how does it affect your energy levels? Do you feel more energetic, less energetic or about the same?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When I'm feeling down?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, when you're having those emotions that you were describing.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just feel drained like don't even have like the energy to wake up in the morning sometimes. Like it all just feels pointless and like my body's heavy and I don't want to... yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it sounds like you feel very tired, you're struggling to wake up.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You said it's pointless. And um what do you do then when you feel like that? So I guess you just talked about when you wake up in the morning and you feel heavy and I suppose you've been maybe having some of these thoughts and those emotions potentially the night before. What do you then do? How do you respond to that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just have to get up I suppose. I don't really have a choice because my mom I live with my mom and I know it's hard for her so I don't want her to be too worried so I just I just try to carry on as normal and get up, it takes longer and I don't want to but I do and I'll get on with my routine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're a bit slower in getting up.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But you are still getting up anyway. And what about your kind of what do you think about when you're doing that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm just thinking that nobody else is like me at my age, like nobody should be feeling like this and I'm the only one that does.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it sounds like you think a bit more about the problem and you kind of spend time thinking about how you feel.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I hate having it, I don't I don't want to feel like this but I do and nobody else I know does so it makes me feel even more alone and that gets me even more down and I just don't want to disappoint anyone and I just don't really want it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so it sounds like you try and toughen up on yourself a little bit, tell yourself to work harder, to be different.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And and when you start telling yourself that kind of thing and how does that make you feel? Does that make you feel better afterwards or worse?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It feels worse because I still can't snap out of it, like I'm aware it's happening and I just and I'm trying but I just can't and then and then it's just another thing that I'm failing at, just another thing that I can't really get...

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play - Depressive Symptoms and Lack of Motivation
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which cognitive-behavioral therapy is used to treat depressive symptoms and lack of motivation.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Elizabeth, how are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm alright.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How things been going since the last time we met?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's about the same, I'm still feeling pretty down. I just feel really stuck and not happy, and I just don't know why.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So there's a few things going on. You said you're feeling stuck, not happy, and sounds like you're confused as to what's causing it. Do you have any suspicions about what might be causing it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've been feeling really isolated lately. As a stay-at-home mom, it's hard; there aren't many people around. My friendships in the neighborhood fizzled out. Now, I don't feel like doing much, I let things slide, and the passion is gone.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how long have you been a housewife?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: For 10 years, since my first son was born. It's been rewarding and I'm not interested in going back to work. I've been happy with it for so long, so I don't think it's being home; I think it's something inside of me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Something has changed. For a long time, you were satisfied, but then somewhere along the line you stopped being happy with it, even though the activities haven't really changed.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. My youngest started school, so I have more time to myself. I filled it with things like Cub Scouts and friends, but that's not happening anymore. It's not boredom; it's that I don't want to do anything, yet I'm frustrated because there's nothing to do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're frustrated with your situation and maybe yourself a little bit.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, mostly with myself. I know that I would feel better if I found something to do with my time, but I don't want to at the same time. I don't really have the volition to do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're not motivated. Has anyone else noticed that you're down?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My husband has. He's supportive but getting frustrated because he has to pick up my slack. My mom thinks I'm not doing as much. It feels like everyone thinks I'm lazy, and now that I'm doing less, I feel like they're right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do they use the word lazy?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not exactly, but my mom said I'm not doing as much as I used to, and that hurt.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That was painful. What has your husband been saying?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He's getting frustrated because it's my responsibility. He told me he needs me to do more around the house.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What was your response when he said that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I started crying because I know he's right. I tell myself every day I need to do more, but I lack the motivation. I know he needs that from me and I don't know why I'm not motivated.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're frustrated for feeling down and lacking motivation. And just a few years ago, you didn't feel this way.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's been more in the last six months. This feels more consuming and stunting.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let me shift gears. Tell me about a recent typical day.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: On Wednesday, I struggled to get out of bed until 10:30. I meant to go to the store but just sat there until the boys came home at 3:30. I made dinner, and then we just watched TV until bedtime.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What would an ideal day have looked like?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd want to wake up with the kids, pack lunches, and see them off. Then I'd do chores, shop, prepare a snack and dinner, and spend quality family time together in the evening.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: There's a wide discrepancy between where you are and where you want to be. Regarding oversleeping: you were awake but went back to sleep. How did you feel about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I thought, 'What's the point?' and felt a sense of pointlessness. I went back to sleep but felt guilty and worse for doing it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you feel guilty for oversleeping, but you think 'What's the point?'. Can you expand on that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When I'm sleeping, I don't realize how sad I am. As soon as I wake up, I do. I feel like what's the point of getting up and experiencing those feelings when I could sleep and not have to.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sleeping keeps the pain at bay, but then you feel sad and guilty for oversleeping.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Definitely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Functionally, you're just delaying the pain, which causes problems for your family. Before this, was it easy to get the kids ready?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it was so easy. I would wake up and be ready to go. I was glad to take care of things and felt accomplished.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We've talked about cognitive behavioral therapy. Sometimes the useful behavior, like getting up on time, has to come first, even if the feeling doesn't match. Completing your tasks might help those feelings of sadness and guilt abate over time. It's hard in the moment, but you want things to be normal again.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I do. I never thought about it like that. Maybe doing it, even if it's hard, will make me feel better. Nothing is really harder than what I'm already going through.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're making things worse by delaying the pain. When you think it's 'pointless,' it's an automatic thought that you can avoid pain by sleeping. Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I also thought it wouldn't be beneficial to get up.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're minimizing the benefit. What 'adaptive response' or self-talk could you use in that moment tomorrow morning?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I could tell myself 'I can do this.' I can get out of bed and push through the pain because I'm strong enough.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good. That's your adaptive response. You also need to recognize the value of seeing the kids off, even if the emotional payoff isn't there right now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I know it's valuable. I used to get pride from it. I need to realize that if I keep trying, that feeling might return.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's logical that you'll have a higher probability of getting that back if you do get up than if you sleep in.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's true. I'll never get the satisfaction of sending my kids off to school if I never actually do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Exactly. You're likely dealing with depression. Just try to get one victory each day, like getting up and seeing the kids off. Build on that. Don't try to build Rome in a day.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think I could try that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Use those adaptive responses, maybe even say them out loud.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'll try not to let the negative thoughts take over. I have to remind myself that even though it's hard, doing nothing won't make me feel any better.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You have a good handle on the adaptive responses. Give it a try this week. It's okay if you don't succeed every day; don't let one setback wash away your successes. Take it one day at a time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mm-hmm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Stay present, recite your responses, and push for that one victory for tomorrow. Can you try that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think I could try that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Work on that and the CBT homework, and I'll see you next week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: All right. Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Thanks.

video_details.title: Case study clinical example: First session with a client with symptoms of social anxiety (CBT model)
video_details.description: Case study example for use in teaching, aiming to demonstrate some of the triggers, thoughts, feelings and responses linked with problematic social anxiety. This section here represents the first 12 minutes of an initial therapy session, but in order to try and outline the vicious cycle, it moves faster than an average session might. The video features an actor (Malak El-Gonemy) playing the character of Hannah, but the dialogue is not scripted, and as such represents a natural therapeutic exchan

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Hannah, nice to meet you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hi.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I understand that you were referred to me by your GP because you've been experiencing some anxiety difficulties.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, um, yeah, I guess it kind of started like five, six years ago. Um, it kind of escalated a bit. Um, I've just recently moved out, um, from living with my parents, so it's made it a bit worse I think.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, is this the first time that you've left home?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I, um, yeah, it's the first time actually, yeah. Um, I was going to a few years ago, I just thought it would be easier to stay at home, so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so it's been quite a big step and a big change and, and it sounds like that's what led you to go to your GP. So how has that change things for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Do you know, it's kind of I haven't really told anyone, so, I mean, it's made it like better in the sense that I feel hopefully this is, you know, this is it, like it'll help, but I don't know, I don't like thinking that I've had like had to do this, I never thought I'd like be the kind of person who'd have to actually go and like get help, if that makes sense.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so how do you feel about being here today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A bit like scared, I don't know, hopefully it will help.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you've been feeling a little bit anxious about today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so I guess just going back to um why you went to the GP and how you've ended up kind of coming here today. So it sounds like you've been experiencing anxiety for quite a few years, but just recently you moved out of home for the first time and, and that was what kind of led you to go to the GP. So how did that change things? How were things after you moved out?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I thought that they'd be better but because I thought I'd have to kind of be independent and stuff but it's actually a lot worse. I'm just kind of staying in the house a lot, I don't really have any friends or anything. I mean, my family come and visit a bit, but it's not, I don't know, it's kind of scary because I've just been kind of literally just in the flat by myself, which I always thought I'd like but I don't actually like it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so what other kind of difficulties that you have been experiencing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, I'm a photographer, um, so I kind of, it's been stopping me a bit, my anxiety from being able to get work and because every time, you know, there's an opportunity that is kind of involving me having to interact with people I just tend to just turn it down. So it was kind of making things hard in that respect and just kind of friends-wise and everything I'd feel like I'm increasingly more alone. So it's kind of stopping me from making friends and, you know, like relationships and stuff.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you said that your difficulties are getting in the way of you doing certain things. So they're stopping you from taking up kind of certain types of work and as a freelance photographer, I guess that can be kind of a problem. And they're also stopping you or you feel like it's stunting you socially. You're not kind of able to make new friends and get to meet new people.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah, um, it was kind of easier when I was at home because I was obviously, I mean my parents and stuff, that's fine, but, you know, they would, I'd go to places with them or I'd kind of have people there. But more and more I'm just finding myself just staying in a lot. I mean I went like two weeks ago for coffee with my friends and the whole time I was just kind of wanting to go home again. So I don't, I just don't want, I don't want that to happen. I don't want to lose everyone.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're kind of worried about how, where this is going to lead to.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you said that you first noticed the anxiety kicking in about 5 or 6 years ago. So you would have been about 19?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. And what was happening around that time? I guess I'd finished school about a year before that um, and I mean I've always been a bit shy um at school but it was never ever a like it didn't really affect things as much as not at all as much as it has been doing the last few years I guess. It just started when um like my friends went to university and I don't know I felt like I was expected to kind of move out or just do something and then it just kind of escalated from there. I'd just stop going to parties or I'd just say no to invitations or I don't know, I thought my job would help because I mean I love it, I really like doing photography but I'm just kind of getting less and less work as it goes on. So which is my fault, I keep saying no, but.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What kind of work is the most difficult for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess when it I have to kind of be working with other people. Um, I don't like that. It's like when I'm trying to kind of do an event or something where there's a lot of people, they'not just photographers but actual you know, if I'm taking photos of people, that I don't know, I just kind of find myself saying no. I mean I want to do them but just it's scary so I just don't do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I guess tell me a bit more about what happens then. So let's focus on maybe an invitation to do a job with you know, it's going to involve photography with a group of people and you're going to have to have social interaction. What kind of thoughts go through your head?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um just I mean I get really hot and sweaty and I don't, I feel like everyone's kind of looking at me and thinking that I'm just like really stupid and I feel like they're all going to be staring and thinking I just can't do my job and I'm just an idiot and I mean they'll think that I just look like a weirdo and I just try and I mean I just kind of just try and get out of the situation or just focus on something else, so that's why I like doing shots where it's just me and the camera because then I can just put all my attention on that instead of having to you know be with other people.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay so it sounds like you have quite a lot of thoughts rushing through your head then at the point where you get that invitation and you think people look, people will stare, people will think I'm a weirdo. There's quite a lot about what you what you think other people will think. And how does that make you feel?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just makes me feel like an idiot, it makes me feel like I shouldn't even bother trying to do it anymore. I should just go home and I just, I think I just don't want to be in that situation. I just feel like everyone else is fine and they're normal and I'm just the freak who can't do normal things.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Can you give me an example of a recent situation? Maybe we can focus on that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like a work situation or?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, a time when you were maybe doing a job with some people and you felt the social anxiety you know that you're describing you felt that kick in.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah um I was doing a job where it was kind of like a nature shoot and I was having to work with a lot of different people. Um and when they told me about the job I thought it would be fine, I thought it was just going to be a few other photographers but there were actually 10 people in you know I was taking photos of people kind of in the trees and stuff like that and...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That sounds quite interesting. Was that a fashion shoot or something?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah, it was a fashion thing. I think it was for some kind of, I'm not sure if it was a campaign or something but it was, yeah, it was really cool but I find it, found it really hard to try and focus on that because I was so I was kind of feeling really anxious.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it wasn't what you expected.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, it wasn't.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So how long ago was that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That was two weeks ago.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so it was quite recent. So on that particular day, what were the thoughts that you had in your head when you were in that situation?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just felt really, just really kind of hot.
