I couldn't really breathe and just felt like I wanted to just get out and I was kind of trying really really hard to just focus and just you know like hold the camera and just not think about anything but I just felt like everyone was looking at me and like when they'd say action and they try and get me to start and I was just felt like everyone was just thinking I was really stupid and I shouldn't have been there and...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I can tell you're getting kind of anxious even just thinking of about that day. Okay so you're describing quite a lot there to me. So you're saying that you you kind of got hot and sweaty. You said that you held the camera. What was do you mean you were kind of trying to hide behind it or what was that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was just trying to focus on it. I was just thinking if I could just hold it really tightly it would, I don't know, I'd kind of just be able to just get through it and just focus.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're holding the camera very tightly. And why was that why was that helpful?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Because I felt like I was getting really like hot and flushed and I just thought at least if I can just, I don't know, it sounds weird, but I was just trying to keep my hands still on it because my hands were kind of sweaty and like shaking like loads, like and I could just tell everyone was looking and they could see and I just thought if I just managed to hold onto it, it wouldn't be as noticeable, but.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so, okay, so it sounds like you had a lot of thoughts going through your head. You said that you're worried that everyone's looking at you. What other thoughts were there that were in your mind?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just that I was just just stupid and I was just really just felt really like kind of like everyone was just going to be staring and just thinking that I just felt like everyone was looking at me and just they could tell and just thinking oh what's she doing and why is she here. Like that I was just really like sweaty and just...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That they could tell or like they could see that there was...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah, um, so I always try and wear black so at least it kind of tries to cover it up and just like a lot of layers so they can't tell. But I mean, my hands, like they were so shaken, I was really red and just was just wishing that I just wasn't there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I mean, you've already described it to me a little bit, but if you think about how you looked that day, how how do you say how do you think you looked?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think just really stupid and like I think my face was really red. I could feel it flushing and I knew that I would was probably sweating and shaking, like my hands were definitely really really shaking. Um, and it was like definitely really noticeable, everyone could definitely see.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, and what did you do about how did you try and conceal that or hide that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um well again I was trying to grip the camera just look down just try not to do anything weird or because I mean they could probably tell I was being weird anyway but hopefully if I just tried really hard to just focus and look down not try like not look at anyone else and just kind of try and get on with it as best as I could, but.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you avoided looking at people and it sounds like you wore black as well in kind of preparation anyway.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. No, I always do that, even if it's really hot or I wear just loads of layers and just because otherwise like I'll just be really sweaty and like people would definitely be able to see, so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And how did it end?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um well it kind of went on for like an hour or so and then um people were going... just after every shoot people go out for drinks after just to kind of celebrate like that we've done it. But I just I went home straight away. Just got in my car and went home. I just didn't want to be around them, especially after they would have seen me being weird and I just wanted to get, get home straight away.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay.

video_details.title: CBT Role-Play - Anxiety and Guilt Related to Balancing Home and Work
video_details.description: This video features a counseling role-play in which cognitive-behavioral therapy is used to treat anxiety and guilt related to balancing of child care and work.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Samantha, how you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Good. How are you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing all right. How things been since last week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, things, you know, I've been really sort of preoccupied and anxious a lot this week. My daughter got sick, so I had to take three days off of work to take care of her and I'm starting to worry she's been sick a lot since I've gone back to work and she's in daycare. And I've had to take a lot of time off work and I'm getting close to going over my allotted amount of days and um, so I'm finding myself being very anxious about that and then feeling guilty because when I'm trying to take care of her, I'm always worrying about work.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so it sounds like a couple things maybe going on. Child, child's been sick, so you've taken off days. So you're a little worried about your relationship with your employer, right? And at the same time, you want to make sure you're taking good care of your child, so you're having trouble reconciling those two.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Um, what was the last time it happened? Can you describe what happened?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The last time I had to take off work? It was just this week. Um, she woke up one morning with a really high fever, so I had to call out that day, and then she still had a fever the next day, and then I had to take a third day because she has to be fever-free before she can go back to daycare. So um, the first day was, I was okay with that, but then like the second and then when I started realizing that I was going to have to take a third day, then I um, really started to get kind of panicky and worry about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so let's see. Let's go through each day. All right, so the first day when you discovered she was sick, what were you thinking then when you had to call out of work?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, well because she's been sort of sick a lot lately, I was a little bit worried and I was sort of, you know, I have this number 10, because I only have 10 days for the whole year, so I have this number in my head and I just thought, 'Okay, well here's one more day I got to take away from that 10 that I have.' And um, but I was able to sort of think about, I was a little worried about any work that I would miss and you know, keeping up with my caseload and stuff at work. So um, but I was able to kind of figure out that I would be okay for a day and I can kind of make up for that when I get back.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so your thinking was, this isn't ideal but I can live with it for one day.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about on day two when you realized you're going to have to take a second day?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Then I got a little bit more worried. And then I did start to also, you know, add the worry of I was going to start to get behind at work, and not only was I missing more time but I was also going to be behind on my work. So then I started thinking when I go back, it's going to be a mad scramble to kind of catch up and keep up with everything and um, you know, so it became worrying about my workload and worrying about taking more time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so a little more stressful version of what happened on day one. And then how about when you discovered that you had to take a third day off?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I was then it was just more amplified, you know, amplified worry and it was a lot harder for me to let it go. I just kept thinking about, I kept going back to it, and then I started feeling guilty because I was so preoccupied worrying about that and I was trying to answer emails and do some stuff and send out some emails to people that I work with to try to help me out with things um, at work since I wasn't there. Um, and then I felt guilty because I wasn't really caring for my child as best as I felt I should have been, you know, I started feeling kind of like a bad mom.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So guilty and a bad mom. And that was mostly on the third day. That was the worst of it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Now this go up against the weekend, was the third day Friday?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so then you kind of knew that by Monday things would be able to return to work.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So tell me what happened when you returned to work on Monday.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I checked in with the main office and you know, I just said, 'I'm really, you know, I'm starting to worry, I'm getting, I know I've had to take a lot of time, but you know, I've done the best I can to try to make other arrangements,' but my, you know, just starting in daycare she's just been sick a lot and I can't control it. I'm doing the best I can. You know, I asked them if there was anything I needed to do as far as providing doctor's notes and stuff, and they said no, that they don't, you know, they don't need a doctor's note since it was my daughter that was sick. Um, they said there's nothing, nothing that I could really do and just try to not have it happen much more if I can. Just do what I can to not miss more.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So they said that to you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. But they... yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how did they frame that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They kind of just said, 'You know, do what you can to not have it happen, but if it, you know, if it has to happen, what can I do about it,' was kind of what they were saying.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So they were understanding?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I didn't feel like they were that understanding, but I also didn't feel like they were going to take any punitive action against me right then and there or anything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Did you anticipate a worse reaction than you experienced?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I did. And I also anticipated that they would maybe have more of a procedure for how to handle it and they didn't have a procedure, which also made me feel a little worried. I can't imagine I'm the first mom that has had to deal with this and they kind of talked like it's never happened before. So I kind of felt anxious because I thought, 'Am I really the first mom that's had to take a lot of time off because their child's sick?' They didn't give me the impression that they had sort of a protocol or like they had dealt with this before.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it sort of like it took them by surprise.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, or they just didn't have a plan for what to do about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: They weren't investing a lot of energy in thinking about that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, no, I guess not.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And when was this again? How long ago?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just this past week. Just this week.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So how has this week been back at work?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, um, it's been very busy because I'm trying to catch up and get everything handled, but that's the way it always is. So um, nobody has said anything to me or anything about the absences.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Other than that first day back.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Other than... yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And there've been no more absences.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Earlier you mentioned being a good mom. What does a good mom look like?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, somebody who takes care of their child and puts them, makes them a priority, like their first priority. And um, you know, does the things that they need to do to make sure their child is taken care of.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you're a little worried through this last experience you're telling me about that you didn't rise to the level of good mom.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I felt like I wasn't being a good mom because I was preoccupied and making work a bit of a bigger priority than taking care of my kid.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so so good mom's more about more than just rather, uh, your behavior, right, what you're doing. It's about what you're also thinking. So you took care of your child.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But your mind, your thoughts were somewhere else some of the time. And that's where you feel like you've wandered out of the good mom area.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. How about on the other side? How about a good employee? Did you mention that? You want to be a good employee?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's what's that look like?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, somebody that you know, takes care of all of their workload and handles all of the tasks that they have each day. And someone that's consistent and reliable and um, you know, puts effort into what they're doing and gets their job done really, you know, reliably.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And that's where you feel like with this out of the last eight workdays you missed three.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. How about in the last year, how many days have you missed?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I missed a lot for maternity leave.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, certainly understandable. But excluding that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, since the school year started, I've missed, if you include the three, I've missed nine days. But some of those were half days. They add up to nine days.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, total nine days. And you're allowed 10.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: 10 for the whole school year. And it's only January and I'm already at nine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I can see where that would cause worry. What happens if you go over the 10?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. I mean I think that they would dock my pay for the for those for a if I was there a day and I didn't have any more sick days left they would just dock my pay for that day. But outside of that I don't know what else would happen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there anybody that you work with that you could ask that question to? HR department?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess I could contact the HR department.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm just thinking because you're just one day away from being at that that number. Might be prudent just to talk with them and see so you know what to expect.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So this this whole thing though, the missing days causing you anxiety and frustration?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, a little bit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about any type of like feeling down at all?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, a little bit sometimes when I start feeling like I'm a bad mom.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So as far as your child's concerned, your relationship with your child, you have some anxiety. Relationship at work, some anxiety. But the sadness mostly surrounds how you feel you're treating your child. Of all the emotions, you know, frustration, anxiety, what I'll refer to as depression, I should say sadness, what's bothering you the most? What emotional response is bothering you the most?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably sort of the guilt and the feelings of not being able to be the best mom.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How would you rate yourself right now as a mother if say 10 was the best mother you could imagine, right, and one was the absolute worst?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, probably like a eight.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: An eight? Okay. That's pretty good, right? What would be the cutoff to where, what's the cutoff score in that little scale I just gave you for good mother and not good mother?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess like halfway, like five.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So five is good enough.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're not, you don't seem like it's good enough for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. I wouldn't be okay with that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So if you looked at somebody else, another person in a similar situation, a five would be acceptable, right? But how about for you specifically?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's not... that's not going to cut it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What would cut it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I don't know, at least a seven.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: At least a seven? And you're an eight.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sure? Not sure. Okay. So you're close to the border, you feel like you're close to the border in your out of your value system of being not a good mother.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. Well, as good a mother as I want to be.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And how good do you want to be?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I want to be like a eight or higher.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Eight or higher. Well you are an eight, you said.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. So you want to be a 10 sounds like.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well yeah, doesn't everybody want to be the best for what they do?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I mean I think people are driven to to do their best. But is it crucial to be perfect? Is it crucial to be a 10?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. There's some leeway, I guess. You have to allow for that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Remember before in other sessions for other situations you've brought in here, we've talked about dysfunctional thinking, irrational thinking. How does when you reflect on that, like the usefulness of of these thoughts, the you know that other mothers can be a five and that's that's good, right? You need to be an eight or higher, eight, nine, or 10. Does this seem useful? Like a useful way of thinking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, in some ways it's useful because it keeps me um, it keeps me on track if that makes sense. It keeps me um, pushing to keep doing the best I can do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Keep you driven. Motivated. Okay. So it does have a useful side. Does it have an unusual side? A less than useful side?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, yeah, I guess it does in the sense that um, if I become too worried about it then I'm wasting energy on worry instead of being able to put that energy into being a good mom.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. So I guess one of the things I'm getting at here is has the worry has the anxiety and the worry paid off for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably not.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Probably not. So you're suffering with it. It might make you a little more vigilant but mostly it's just causing you suffering.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So at the heart of it you're not a bad mom, right? You're in the good mom category. You're a good employee. But your your way of evaluating yourself, your perception is that you're not doing a great job at either one.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Exactly.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And that's the thinking I'm getting at that's not it's not necessarily irrational, I'm thinking it's just less than useful, right? It's dysfunctional.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I can see that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. We were talking about that third day, right? The the third day of work you had to you had to call off. Um, do you remember any of the specific thoughts that were going through your mind on on that morning, was that a morning when you figured it out, like a Friday morning?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Um, no it was really the night before. Um, but uh, well you know, I went as far as to think, 'Am I going to get fired?' You know I had to kind of think about that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So your thought was, 'Am I going to get fired?' Right. And then what was the feeling that that came right after that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Panic. Worry. Oh yeah, maybe some anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Were you able to do anything to address that panic, worry, or anxiety at that time? Like did you tell yourself anything or did you take some action?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I did tell myself that I didn't go over yet and you know, hopefully I won't, you know, there's still a chance that I'm not going to go over on my days and hopefully it won't go so far as to fire me, you know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how'd you feel after you consciously had that thought?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A little bit better but the thoughts still kept hovering around. Yeah, the whole time. Probably all the way till Monday, right? When you returned to work.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah, like I wanted to call somebody at work and talk to them about it and make sure it was okay. But you know, it was the weekend so I couldn't do any of those things. I just had to wait it out. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So we've talked before about self-talk, you might remember me saying the phrase adaptive response, right? So it's the kind of the prepackaged response we have to thoughts that we've identified as not so useful.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So do you agree those thoughts like 'Am I going to get fired' and all that not very useful in that moment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, not useful in that moment.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Understandable, right? But not useful. Um, so what's now you had sort of some some self-talk that you applied on your own. What's some other self-talk? What's some other another thought that you could think or something you can say to yourself that could counter an an automatic thought like that? Like specifically I'm going to lose my job.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well I guess I could say, you know, I didn't, you know, I haven't had any conversations with anybody that have indicated that. So sort of like maybe I just need to not worry about it or cross that bridge when I come to it kind of thing. Like hopefully it won't I don't know if it will happen or not and hopefully it won't happen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So so the the self-talk there is there's no clear indication it's going to happen. Right. So why borrow the worry? Right? How about other how about adaptive behaviors? Now we talk about the importance of support systems before in other sessions. Is there anyone else that could watch your child if you were really running up against that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, my mom can um, can sometimes um, I did call her this this week to see if she could take one of take a day. Um, but she couldn't because of what she had going on. But in in other times she might be able to take a day and stay home. Um, or my sister can do that as well. Um, and my husband can sometimes, it depends on what is going on that week for him at work. So there are some options there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Did you explore those options for this last time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I did. Um, I did but just the circumstances didn't work out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So none of those individuals were available.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are there any other options you have for care or was that it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, that's really it. You know when she's sick that's really it. Because you don't I don't want to put her around any other kids which is why I wouldn't send her to daycare. So...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That seems reasonable. Okay. So there are some things that you've already done. Right? And I think at this point since to address I know this is the lesser of your worries which is your employer, you're more worried about being a good mom. But to go look at the employer side for a second, you can talk to HR, you can try to understand what the consequences are for going over, explain that it doesn't appear to be your fault. Okay. And I don't know what you can do in terms of the support, maybe try to get a better awareness of the schedules when they're available and or convey the nature of your problem to them to get some more support.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So that was one issue. Now you highlighted more prominently though the the good mother. I want to want to touch on that as well. You did everything you had to do to care for your child.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you sure?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Except for my my thinking I was maybe a little not uh as present as I should have been.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay and we'll get to that. But your behavior, you did everything a good mom would do.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So is it okay if you're doing everything you need to do to think thoughts that don't seem congruent with that? You know that distract you away from that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess it's not ideal but it's okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's not ideal. So you'd really rather be have the ability to be really focused on what's going on with your child to the exclusion of what's going on in other circumstances.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, or at least be able to put my worry about the other circumstances aside for the for that time period.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So by addressing the employer issue that might give you a little relief on the good mom issue. All right. So here's another uh opportunity talk about dysfunctional thoughts. I think that as you reflect on whether you're a good mom or not, you're really basing it on this idea that if I'm thinking about something other than my child, I'm in the wrong place in terms of being a good mom. You're being distracted. Right? So that pushes you on that 1 to 10 scale, the more thoughts you have like that you think of it as like pushing you down toward a five.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So when you have those thoughts, what's an adaptive response or you know self-talk? What can you tell yourself in those moments?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, that I'm doing... I'm behaving... doing the behaviors that I need to do and the baby doesn't know what I'm thinking. So probably not. She doesn't know that I'm distracted or worried. So I'm not doing any harm to her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Matter of fact, who does know you're distracted or worried?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess just me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Just you. Yeah. So the self-talk there would be 'I'm doing what I have to do to be a good mom and that's what my child sees.' Right. 'But I have these understandable thoughts that come in where I worry about other things and more or less just is what it is.' I mean you're permitted to worry about things. Life isn't going to be worry-free. True. But we can we can work to not suffer more than we have to.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. Yeah, it makes sense. And you know when you say it back to me, the things that I'm saying, it does sound a little bit irrational or unhelpful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Less than useful. Yes, it's a little less than useful. It's not, you know, I want to and this is an important distinction, it's not good or bad. Right? Um, and those words have a a function, right, in our in our lives. But they're a little dangerous when applied in terms of mental health when they're applied to things like you know good mom, bad mom. Right? That doesn't leave a lot of gray area to talk about improving. Right? Also it seems like from what you described your way into the good mom category anyway. If you're an 8 out of 10, I think most people would be happy with an 8 out of 10.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: True.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's not like you've you've drifted down toward five or four or somewhere. Okay. So there's a couple different, you know I know we talked about two different subjects, right, but they're related. The work situation and then the situation of caring for your child. But those are some self-talk strategies. Right? So what I'd like you to do um when you go home today and I would I would ask that you do it today if you can. I think it's important that it stays um in terms of time, you know near when we're having this conversation, okay. If you could try to document some of those automatic thoughts, I remember I gave you worksheet before, right, and then work on some of your own, we'll call them adaptive responses. Okay? And maybe around this area or maybe around other areas as well. You know that doesn't, it's okay if you have other problems you want to apply the model to but certainly around this issue of the child care versus the work performance. Because that's the real struggle that's going on right now inside of you. Is that right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You think you'll be able to have that um completed next week when we meet?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think I can handle that. Yep.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so we'll leave it there and I'll see you next week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Thanks, Samantha.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I don't think it's the case that people are either not motivated or motivated. And in fact, motivational interviewing was born from conversations with very, very difficult people, who were classified as not at all motivated to change and very resistant to treatment.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, Mr. Smith, that's your medication sorted out. Blood pressure's a little on the high side. I wonder if I could raise the subject of your weight?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: What?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I wondered if we could spend just a couple of minutes talking about your weight?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You are joking, aren't you? I mean, look, I've made time in my day to come here. I'm kept in your waiting room for 45 minutes. It's not acceptable, you know. If I make an appointment with a client for ten, I expect them to start at ten, not quarter to eleven.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. And you—so you're busy enough...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I've got other things to do. I've got accounts to do, I've got clients coming in, you know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, and it wasn't necessarily easy for you to make the time to come down and you had to wait in the waiting room and now I raise the subject of weight just when you're thinking of leaving.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean, okay, fair enough, I've got to have my blood pressure medication changed, but I really haven't got time to talk about my weight. I'm aware of my weight, I'm aware of the problems and the solutions, so I don't really need a discussion. I've just got too much to do at the moment.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, and so it's been a bit of a rush for you coming in, and I'm sorry about the wait in the waiting room.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it's—it's bad form, you know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, and that's not easy for you because you'd like to go really soon and here I am asking you to spend just a couple of minutes with me.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, well basically I've got things to do, I've got to get back to the office, I've got a pile of work. Every moment out of my day means I have to work in the evening or weekends.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It counts.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When you're self-employed you haven't got a choice, you know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, exactly. It's up to you. Just a couple of minutes?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I'm here now, so yeah, okay, if it's a couple of minutes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I promise. Okay, good. I want to simply ask you how you feel about it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: About what? Losing weight? Well, obviously I want to. I'm aware that I'm over my balance weight, and I know that it's causing problems. I get out of breath if I have to do something in a hurry and I realize I'm on this blood pressure medication...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: ...and maybe that's probably contributing to it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So you can see the links between your weight and your health and you'd like things to be a bit better.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, the weight is something I would like to get a handle on, you know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You'd like to if you could.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I know the theories of exercise and diet, but because of my lifestyle as an accountant, finding time to exercise or prepare meals is hard. With me it's very often ready meals and that sort of thing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Food on the run, you know? Grazing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Let me see if I can summarize: you lead a busy life, you run a business, and you've got a lot to do. You're aware of the links between health and weight and you're concerned, but your life is busy and you tend to use convenience foods to get work done.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, because of my lifestyle, food is just fuel. I'm juggling all these balls and I don't want to drop any.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I get it. And so if you could fit it in, you would like things to be different, but that's not so easy.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Can I suggest that you come back and see me in a couple of weeks' time just to chat about this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, okay, I'm up for that, but it's going to be the same problem of finding time, and if I make an appointment I don't expect to be kept waiting for half an hour.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Exactly. I tell you what might be a nice solution: come for the first appointment at 8:30. Then there'll be absolutely no waiting. The purpose will be to see how you could move forward and fit in a healthier lifestyle into your busy work life.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'll look at my schedules and see if anything can be arranged so it's not a wasted interview and I can come here prepared.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good. See if you can fix it up and also give some thought to what we've talked about.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, of course.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good stuff.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, thanks. Sorry I went off a bit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Ah, all the best.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A few well-chosen words, a very thoughtful question, can be worth more than many mouthfuls of busy talk.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, um, I want to try to stop smoking.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Aha. That's quite a decision.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it is because I've been smoking all my life.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We could talk about adjusting your diet, adjusting your exercise, or perhaps anything else that you think is relevant. And I'm wondering what makes the most sense to you.

video_details.title: Mock CBT Therapy Session

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Welcome Erika, how has your week been since we last talked?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My week was fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so your week was fine. How are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I'm still feeling a little bit on edge. I mean, I wasn't able to go to school again today. I don't know, I just felt so overwhelmed and I couldn't handle it, so I told my mom I felt sick, again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, what I'm hearing is when you have to go to school, you become overwhelmed by the idea. Is that correct?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mm-hmm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, last week I gave you a pamphlet to read over about the symptoms of anxiety. Did you find that helpful?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, yeah, I actually never really thought that in depth about it and a lot of what the pamphlet said about anxiety I can relate to.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me more about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, yeah, well I read that like your heart starts to race and your palms get like really sweaty and your breathing like accelerates and that's pretty much exactly like what I experience when I think about going to school.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so tell me a little bit more about school.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I mean I get a lot of homework but I can manage that. Um, it just like it gets harder when I feel like everyone's always talking about me even to the point where I feel like the teachers are even giving me weird looks and stuff.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you always felt this way?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I used to actually really like school up until about like this time last year.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Mm-hmm.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, I mean I used to be like really involved and I had a lot of friends. But then I got really sick last year with the flu and I was out for a while. Um, when I came back there was like this crazy rumor that I had gotten pregnant and had an abortion. And all these kids would laugh at me as I passed in the hallway and they would talk about me behind my back. I just couldn't handle it anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Wow, I can see how that must have been hard for you to go through. Having to deal with things being said about you that aren't true can be really upsetting.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, ever since then I felt like people were constantly talking about it. And all summer I worried about having to go back to school.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What worried you the most about returning back to school?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, well ever since then I feel like I have no friends and no one likes me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what I'm understanding is you believe you have no friends at school and that a lot of your worry and nervousness about school started after you heard about this rumor, is that right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I guess yeah. I didn't really want to go to school after that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, um, so okay I have a question for you. Um, before you got sick and these rumors started, how did you see yourself? Did you think you were unlikable?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I mean not everyone liked me, but I thought I was a good person. I mean, people liked me, I had friends.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: On a scale of 1 to 100, how much do you believe the idea that you don't have any friends at school currently?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: 100. Like I really don't have any.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so let's see how much of this is what you believe and how much of this is really the reality of the situation. When this happened, did you tell anyone about it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, well there was this girl, Michelle, who found me like one day after when I was really upset and crying. Um, and she - it was basically like after I learned about the rumors. And she asked me if I was okay, so I told her what happened and that's pretty much the only person who really knows.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When you told her about the rumors, how did she react?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, she listened to me talk for like two hours and pretty much she was really, really nice.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It must have been nice to have someone to confide in who listened and wanted to hear what you had to say instead of just listening to those rumors. Do you two still talk to each other?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, we actually had lunch together on Saturday.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so I have another question for you then. Let's say, hypothetical situation, we have two guys, and one of them talks to no one throughout their day, and the other one occasionally meets up with someone to walk their dogs. Which one would you say has friends?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, the one who meets up with someone to walk their dogs.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you sure?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, obviously the guy who walks his dog with somebody has a friend opposed to the guy who doesn't talk to anyone.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So based on what you're saying, can you relate that to your situation?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I guess I can because I don't not talk to anyone.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so what did you tell me earlier about you and your friendships?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That I had none.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And based on everything that we talked about, how much do you believe that now, rating it from 1 to 100 like you did earlier?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I'd say like 60.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what do you believe now about your friendships?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess it's not that I don't have any, I do because I hang out with Michelle.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, good. Um, unfortunately our time is up for today. But let me show you this core belief worksheet. This worksheet is an organized way of working on your beliefs because all of your anxiety seems to be stemming from these negative beliefs that you hold about yourself. And the only way that we can work through this is by reorienting the way that you think about yourself. So I want you to do this worksheet for homework and we can go over it in our next session, okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have a great week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You too.

video_details.title: Crisis Planning- Emergency Department
video_details.description: These vignettes demonstrate an evidence-informed approach to engaging youth and families in crisis planning that is person- and family-centred.  This intervention was developed as part of the Peel Service Collaborative. For more information on the project please visit https://www.camh.ca/-/media/files/professionals/videos-and-podcasts-section/holistic-crisis-planning-overview-peel-region2017-pdf.pdf.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So Steph, I know you just want to go home and you don't want to be admitted. However, I'm really concerned that you swallowed a whole bottle of pills last night because you were feeling down. Do you think you're going to do that again?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I'm feeling a lot better now. It was a stupid thing to do. I'm not going to do it again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm still really concerned about you, and I need to know that you're going to be safe when you leave here. I need you to fill out this safety plan to ensure that you have strategies in place to cope when you're feeling down.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't really feel like filling out a plan and I don't need a plan.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I think that you do need a plan. You obviously needed a plan last night when you swallowed that whole bottle of pills, and I want you to fill out this safety plan to ensure you have strategies in place in case you feel like this again. It's a condition of your discharge.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I really don't want to.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This is really concerning for me, Steph. Perhaps you need to be admitted.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Fine, I'll fill out the plan.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So Steph, I know you probably want to get out of here and go home and you don't want to be admitted. It must have been a really scary experience for you. I want you to know though that any time you're feeling unsafe or at risk of harming yourself, you're always welcome to come back to the emergency department. I'm wondering what you think might have been helpful for you if this happens again.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, I don't think it'll happen again. I was feeling really down, but I don't really want to die.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Must have been a really hard experience to go through.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm wondering if you think it would be helpful to have some kind of plan in place or some strategies if by chance you feel like this again?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you think might be helpful for you to think about or to do if you did feel like this again?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, I guess I could have called someone.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, so that's a good idea. Who do you think you might have called?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe my Aunt Jenny. She's great, she's really easy to talk to.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's good you have someone in your life that you can talk to. What do you think stopped you from calling her last night?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was so late. I didn't want to call at like 3:00 in the morning. It would have woken her and my uncle and all of my cousins up, and they'd probably just be mad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're worried about disturbing them. I imagine that your Aunt Jenny probably would have been okay with you calling her given the circumstances and how you were feeling. Do you think you'd be okay with maybe having a conversation with her about her being an emergency contact for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm wondering maybe if I could bring your dad in right now, and we could maybe all talk about this together?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Tom. Steph and I are just having a conversation about safety planning and I'm wondering if you want to join us? Sure. Great.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So Tom, Steph and I were just talking about who she might contact in the future if she were ever to feel this way again and she mentioned her Aunt Jenny.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yes, I think that sounds good. Steph and Jenny are pretty close.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm wondering Steph, are there any other things you can think of that would help you in the moment if you're feeling this down again?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. I haven't been doing the stuff I usually do for fun, like reading or going outside or hanging out with my friends even.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: She also likes going for walks late at night when she can't sleep or isn't feeling good, but I'm just not that comfortable with that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So that's concerning for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It helps a lot. The fresh air clears my head.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm wondering Tom, is there anything that Steph could do to make you feel more comfortable with her going for a walk?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I guess if she were to let me know before she left and maybe text me partway through to let me know where she is and when she might be home, that would help.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Steph, is that an okay compromise for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so we've talked about a few strategies today and sometimes people find it helpful to write them down. I actually have a template for a safety plan so we could write down what we talked about. The other option is you could use the notes section of your phone. Do either of those sound helpful for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe using the notes section on my phone. I always have it with me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, great. So let's recap what we talked about today.

video_details.title: Case study clinical example CBT: First session with a client with symptoms of depression (CBT model)
video_details.description: Case study example for use in teaching, aiming to demonstrate some of the triggers, thoughts, feelings and responses linked with problematic low mood. This section here represents the first 14 minutes of an initial therapy session, but in order to try and outline the vicious cycle, it moves faster than an average session might. The video features an actor playing the character of Lucy, but the dialogue is not scripted, and as such represents a natural therapeutic exchange. I myself am a qualifie

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Lacey, nice to meet you. So I understand that you were referred here by your GP because you've been feeling quite down recently?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I thought I should, I've been feeling quite bad for quite a while, so I thought maybe it's time to see someone about it because I don't want to feel like this anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so from your notes I saw that you saw the GP about three months ago. So how long have you been feeling down altogether?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Quite a few months before that as well, actually, but it's gotten pretty bad these past few months, so that's kind of why I came.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so has it got worse since you saw your GP?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so tell me how things are at the moment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it kind of started just feeling a bit low and wound up about things, but I don't know, just recently I just can't really be bothered to do anything at all. I kind of find it hard to get motivated for things and I want to be, I really want to be better, but it's just kind of reaching the end now where I just want to do something about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you said that you're feeling really down, really sad, and you feel like you haven't got any motivation, but... are you okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'm fine, sorry.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And you haven't got any motivation, but it sounds like you're putting quite a lot of pressure on yourself to try and feel a bit better.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I just, it's kind of hard as well because there's not really anyone to talk about it, so I just kind of stay on my own trying to, I don't like to think about it, but... I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you say you've been feeling quite isolated, there's not many people around.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: There's no one I can talk to about it. No one would listen or understand anyway.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so I'm just going to try and find out a little bit more about you. So I understand that you're an English student at Uni?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you live away from home with some friends, is that right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I live here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you don't live far from the Uni. But you say you feel like you live with your friends, but you don't feel like you can talk to them.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean, they're lovely. I get on really well with them, but I don't know, recently whenever they want to go out or stuff, I just, I don't want to bring them down. They don't understand what I'm going through. They kind of, I don't know, they don't make fun of how I feel, but they don't really understand what it's like. I just don't want to go out with them and bring them down or stuff.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so it sounds like you try and hide the way you're feeling from them.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess, I mean, it's easier to hide it than to try and explain it all the time when no one really wants to know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so it sounds like you've been feeling down, you've been feeling unmotivated, you feel like you want to be better, but actually it sounds like you feel like you can't reach out for help, you can't speak to anybody.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I don't really talk to my parents a lot either, so that's kind of hard.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, I'm just going to go back in time a little bit. I suppose I'm just wondering when did all of this start? You said it's been going on for quite a few months.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess it kind of started when I was actually when I was revising for my exams. I guess the stress, I put a lot of stress on myself, I think I've always wanted to do well for me and I guess for my parents, so the stress of exams and it was also kind of hard because my parents were going through a bit of a troubled time then, so...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so this would be like last March, last April?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Around that time. So about six months ish. And it sounds like a lot was happening. So you had a lot of Uni pressure on, and you said that your parents were having marital problems.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, and it sounds like that was a real shock to you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess it was hard as well because I wasn't doing well at Uni and I guess I just felt a bit guilty. I know it sounds silly, but I felt like maybe if I could do better then they would get better, but I don't know, it just wasn't really happening.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so it sounds like you were trying to work hard and be more successful because you thought that that would make them happier and try and fix things.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I wanted to make them feel better, but it just kind of backfired a little, I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How did it backfire?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It just ended up with them getting worse and I've just been feeling worse since then.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so after the summer, after the exam period, and how did that exam period go for you in the end?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not very well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's an awful lot of pressure to put on yourself to think...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's just annoying because I know I should have done better and I just didn't and I guess I beat myself up a lot about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you say "I know, I know I should have done better". I mean, I suppose hearing it from my perspective, I'm thinking it sounds like you had an awful lot going on at the time and it would be understandable absolutely that you wouldn't do as well as normal. I suppose I'm just wondering if you have very high standards for yourself.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably, maybe more than other people. My parents have always kind of taught me, not in a loving way I guess, but that you should do your best, but also get the best and I agree with that. I think that's the right thing to think, but when I don't do that, I don't know, it annoys me a lot and I worry that it annoys them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it sounds like you feel you should always do your best, "always" was the word you used. And that there isn't any kind of exceptions for that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So I can see then that was a really difficult time for you and that was when your mood started to get lower. And things are still quite bad now. I mean, what's the situation with your parents at the moment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think it doesn't sound good. I don't really talk to them a lot, but I don't think they're going through a very good time. I don't like to talk to them about it because it just makes me feel worse, but I don't think it's getting any better.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Were you home over the summer?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: For a little bit, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how was that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not very fun. No. It was quite tense all the time, stressed me out more than relaxed me over the summer, I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Okay, so it sounds then like quite a lot has been happening. You've been feeling very low. You've had Uni pressure on. You've had problems with your parents' marriage. And sounds like you feel like you can't really reach out to anyone. Like you can't... I understand you can't really reach out to your parents right now. You can't really confide in your friends. So I suppose I'm just wondering if you can tell me a bit more about how you've been feeling, I mean say this past week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Really not good, to be honest. I actually, if I don't have to then I don't really leave the house or get out of bed. I just, I can't find the motivation for the things that I used to enjoy. I used to love doing sports or going out, and now I just prefer to lie in bed and not really do anything. I missed a few lectures this week that I should have gone to, but...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So I suppose I'm just wondering then, if we can think about one thing, say a lecture. What kind of thoughts do you have about going to that lecture before it happens?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't really see the point anymore. If I can't do as well as I should be doing, then what's the point in putting myself in those positions? I just, I can't be bothered anymore to try. It just stresses me out more than it needs to.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so it sounds like the kind of thoughts you've got in your head are "it's pointless", "it's not worth it". Do you have any other thoughts in your head when you're just at that point before you go to the lecture?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel like I don't know, I don't really even deserve to be here if I can't do well enough. I see these other students who are doing well and doing better and want to be there. I don't know why I'm here even at Uni to be honest.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it sounds like you feel like you're not as good as other people here.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. I'm just, sorry, is it okay if I take notes as we go through? It's just I'm trying to I guess understand what you're telling me and it helps me just to write it down, and I'll share this with you later. Okay, so it sounds like those are some quite negative thoughts to have. You're kind of saying, you know, "it feels like it's pointless", "it's more effort than it's worth", "I don't deserve to be here", "I'm unworthy". Those kind of thoughts, it sounds like they just flit through your mind. And then you're kind of describing different emotions that those lead to. You've described sad, anger, frustration, embarrassed. What about in your body, what happens? How do you feel kind of physically?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I used to be, I think from those emotions, very wound up, very kind of stressed all the time. But recently it's just been a lot more draining than anything, just quite lethargic and I just can't be bothered anymore and my body reflects that. But then when I try and sleep I just can't seem to have a satisfied night's sleep. It's really, really frustrating.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it sounds like this is affecting... it's draining you of your energy, like your body can't be bothered. I think that's a really good way of describing it. And you're noticing sleep problems as well. And then what do you do? So this is, say we're back to the point before the lecture. So you start having these thoughts, these emotions, and you know your body I guess it sounds like those thoughts are quite draining so they'd be draining your energy. What then happens? What do you do next?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I kind of focus on the negative thoughts when I probably should not think about them, but I focus on them and then I don't really want to do anything. I kind of stay in bed or...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you think even more about those kind of worries that you have, so you do a bit of dwelling and you stay in bed. And it sounds like you don't, you haven't tried speaking to your friends about it, or speaking to family.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I just stay in bed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And then after you've done that, so after you've not gone to the lecture, you've stayed in bed, you've kind of spent time as you said focusing on those thoughts, those negative thoughts. How do you feel after that? Do you feel better or do you feel worse?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I feel slightly worse, but then a bit numb in a way. Kind of once you've felt that, because I do feel tired all the time, I just try and push it out and then you don't really think about anything and it's almost nicer that way than to keep focusing on how much you're getting wrong and how much you can't do stuff, sometimes it's better just to not think about it at all.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it sounds like in some ways it's a bit of a relief to do that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But in other ways maybe you think it might make things worse.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably in the long run, yeah.

video_details.title: Clinical Supervision for Counseling - Confidence Issues with CBT Techniques
video_details.description: This video features a clinical supervision vignette that demonstrates one way a supervisor may choose to intervene when a counseling supervisee is struggling with a lack of confidence regarding the ability to use CBT techniques.

video_details.title: Clinical Supervision for Counseling - Intervening when a Supervisee is Attracted to a Client
video_details.description: This video features a clinical supervision vignette that demonstrates one way a supervisor may choose to intervene when a counseling supervisee is attracted to a client.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello, my name is Dr. Grande. Welcome to this video on a challenging supervision scenario. This is a completely fictitious situation for educational purposes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Jeff, how you been?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, Dr. Grande. I have something I should talk about, but it's kind of embarrassing. I've been working with a client named Shannon and I've started thinking about her more than I should. I think I might be starting to have feelings for her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you find that when she misses appointments you're disappointed?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, actually. She's one of my favorite clients. When she comes in, it makes my day a little better, but when she doesn't show up, it kind of depresses me for the rest of the day.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What you're going through, being attracted to this client, is normal. We're going to take some steps to make sure everyone is protected. I'm glad you brought this to me. Does Shannon realize you have feelings for her?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I don't think so. She's going through a lot with her boyfriend and has confided in me. She feels safe around me. I wish she knew how I felt, but I didn't want to throw that extra pressure on her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I can see how this happens in a trusting relationship. However, any romantic relationship with a client is prohibited. There are consequences for your license and potential criminal or civil penalties. Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It does, but what about the two-year rule? If she's not my client after two years, then I can reconnect with her, right?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're saying if I reassign her and you wait two years, then you could have a relationship with her?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm conflicted because I don't want to reassign her. We're making good progress and I'd hate to just drop her because I really think I can help her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The NBCC ethics say two years, but the ACA code says five. We follow the more strict rule. Additionally, the rule isn't meant for a planned relationship after stopping treatment. I am going to reassign Shannon to err on the side of caution.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's hard to swallow because I have strong feelings, but I understand. I want to get my license and I'm not a criminal. I want to do what's best for her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A lot of harm comes to clients in these situations, including difficulty establishing trust and increased suicide risk. I suggest you get counseling yourself to work through these feelings. Would you be willing to do that?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I guess so. This is something I should work through. I care about her, but I also want to get my license and I want what's best for her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good. I'll meet with you tomorrow so we can get through this bump in the road and keep things moving forward.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you for watching this video on a challenging counseling supervision scenario. If you have any questions or concerns, feel free to contact me.

video_details.title: Clinical Supervision for Counseling - Addressing Counselor Burnout
video_details.description: This video features a clinical supervision vignette that demonstrates one way a supervisor may choose to intervene when a counseling supervisee is approaching burnout.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello, my name is Dr. Grande. Welcome to this video on a challenging supervision scenario. I'd like to remind you that the person you'll see in this video playing the role of the supervisee is acting and this is a completely fictitious situation we're acting out. Also, this video is completely for educational purposes. I want to offer special thanks to two of my graduate assistants, Andrew and Al, for their diligence and hard work in producing this video. I hope it's helpful to you and thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Bob, it's good to see you again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How you doing, Dr. Grande?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing well. How things been going with clients?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You know, I really thought I was getting better at this, to be honest with you. I got another guy, David, you know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm familiar with that client, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, and he was doing so well. He came in, he was having some trouble with heroin. I've seen that before, nothing out of my scope. But I thought we built a really good rapport. I felt like we were getting somewhere and then he relapsed again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How long was he clean?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I would say about a month.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: About a month. Okay. That's a long time for him, right? So you're kind of feeling like you made some progress and maybe lost some of it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, and I just don't understand. Obviously I took the classes, I've worked with him, but something about it is just not working out and I don't know what to do anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're frustrated by this client relapsing. This sounds familiar; you might remember in supervision where you talked about Debbie. I think she had a problem with cocaine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, yep. Drugs, just drugs.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: She had the same thing, right? You were expressing that you were disappointed because she went for three or four months, had some pretty large successes, and then relapsed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. She was trying to get her kids back, she got out of the shelter, she got detox. She was making progress just like David, and all of a sudden. But that's addiction.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're seeing a familiar pattern here where you're seeing some successes and then they're going backwards a little bit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that my fault?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's not your fault. For every case where progress was lost, you've had a lot of great success stories too. It's hard to keep those in perspective, but you've had people getting jobs, getting clean, and staying out of trouble with law enforcement.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Staying in housing, regaining some support, and getting family members back involved.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, so I'm thinking you might be emphasizing some of your more negative experiences where the clients really haven't succeeded the way you want.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I guess that's a character trait I have.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You think so?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, I'm a little hard on myself.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Being hard on yourself can be very positive, because you hold yourself to a high standard and you're really invested. But the negative is taking failures personally and coming in frustrated.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, I've even tried not to take it home.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So it's almost like you're a little over-invested in the outcome, but your process is good. One of the hard things to accept in this field is you can do everything right and still have clients that don't improve or even relapse.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think I needed to hear that. I've been thinking it's me, I'm saying the wrong thing, or using the wrong therapy, but maybe I need to hear that. I appreciate it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Absolutely. You do a great job here and you're really committed to each client. Remember, a relapse doesn't necessarily mean they're all the way back to square one.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's true too.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It feels that way, but sometimes a relapse can last an hour or a day, and they can be right back in to see you. Now they're even referred to as slips.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's better, I like that word. This way they don't feel like I'm angry with them. I hope that hasn't come through in my counseling, that I'm angry or disappointed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I hope what comes through is that you're invested. It's good for clients to see when their counselor really cares. That's a distinction that's important to you and that clients recognize.
