diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I want to make sure that you're not burning out, because that over-investment makes you a little bit more susceptible. I'm seeing a theme of a supervisee who's frustrated by perceived failures. I'm wondering if you're willing to see a counselor just to help you through this one particular issue, to get ahead of this burnout.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think that seeing a licensed professional counselor may be helpful to work on this one area. Is that something you'd be open to?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You know, I think I remember you saying in a class that every counselor needs their own counselor. So I think I am open to that. I think it's about time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It seems like it's about time now. We can get ahead of this, get you back on track, and reduce frustration. I'll point out some of the successes that you might be missing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Although now it seems like you have recognized some of them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I have, I just want to see more of them, you know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I know. We all want what's best for the client. It is a tough part of counseling. I'll let you find that counselor on your own, or I can give you a referral. I appreciate you bringing this into supervision today, Bob.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you Dr. Grande, I really needed to hear some of these things.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're very welcome. Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you for watching this video on a challenging counseling supervision case scenario. If you have any questions or concerns, feel free to contact me. I'll be happy to help you. Thanks.

video_details.title: Clinical Supervision for Counseling - Confidence Issues after Assessing a Suicidal Client
video_details.description: This video features a clinical supervision vignette that demonstrates one way a supervisor may choose to intervene when a counseling supervisee is struggling with a lack of confidence regarding the ability to use CBT techniques.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Anne, how you been?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good. I'm okay. I know there was some stress over Robert yesterday. I want to give you an update that he's hospitalized and he's safe, okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh good. Okay, alright. I feel really glad to hear that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How are you coping with all that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel like I should be more professional, but I've been pretty freaked out about that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It was a scary experience, sure. What do you think in particular is bothering you about it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I guess it's pretty obvious. Meredith lost a client just a couple months ago.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Just a couple months ago. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Was it a couple months? It seems more recent than that to me and...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That was tragic.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I felt it was sad when I heard about it, but then yesterday when everything went down with Robert, it got real.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, that was definitely a scary experience. I remember you coming into my office in quite a hurry, which was the right thing to do when he expressed those suicidal ideations and had the plan worked out.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, and it was the first time it really hit me that I could lose a client.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Counseling is a serious business. Is this the first time you've understood in a direct way that the consequences of our actions potentially could be very harmful to clients?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's exactly it. It feels really heavy, like so much responsibility. Meredith's been doing this a long time, and if it could happen to someone that experienced...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: And I'm brand new. It made me feel afraid. Do I have what it takes?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's shaken your confidence a little bit.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, definitely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, you might remember at the onset of your internship that I told you you'd be assessing clients for suicidality. It's not typical for your first time to have someone with intent and plan end up in the hospital, so that's not an everyday thing.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh thank God. Oh my gosh.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's what we do in extreme circumstances when we can't control the risk. I felt after evaluating him yesterday that our facility wasn't capable of controlling that risk, and I didn't feel safe sending him home.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. How will I know?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We can go through some additional techniques for assessing suicidal ideation, intent, or plan. Often ideation is passive—hopelessness rather than a high threat level. We'll go through different protocols for you to follow.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's more passive.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's more passive, right. I want you to continue coming to me whenever you have someone with ideation. I'll meet with the client and show you how I assess until you're ready to do it yourself.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Are you concerned about my abilities too?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm not, but I want you to have a structured, progressive learning experience. I'm highly confident in your abilities. You recognized this was outside your competency and came to me, which is crucial.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that makes me feel a lot better about myself too.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I have some reading material on suicide assessment I can give you. Before Robert gets out of the hospital, we'll work on a plan to reintegrate him into services here so you're ready when he comes back.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Good. Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does that sound like a plan that'll work?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Definitely, definitely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Very good. And thanks for bringing this issue to me. I really appreciate it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thanks for being so open and helping me with this.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Absolutely. Anytime. Okay.

video_details.title: Clinical Supervision for Counseling - Countertransference
video_details.description: This video features a clinical supervision vignette that demonstrates one way a supervisor may choose to intervene when a counseling supervisee is struggling with countertransference.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hey Rachel, how you been?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I've been alright. I'm a little frustrated today.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh yeah, what's going on?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I just have this client that I've been seeing for a while and he doesn't like to show up on time to our sessions. This is really frustrating me a lot. I've tried talking to him about it, but I'm usually met with an indifference and he just waves me off or gets a little tone. It's been going on so much that I've noticed my frustration towards him is starting to get in the way of our sessions.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, and which client are we talking about?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This is David.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so what's David doing that you find yourself frustrated by?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Just the lack of respect that I feel he's giving me by not showing up on time. He's not taking his own recovery very seriously. It frustrates me to no end and, if I'm being honest, it also just gets me sidetracked thinking about issues with my husband and some of the same things I see on that end too.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So some of what David's doing kind of reminds you of some of the things your husband does?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any other similarities between David and your husband in terms of behavior?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, my client has mentioned to me a couple times about his money situation with his significant other. He likes to spend the money without any regard for how she would feel about that. I've asked him about that in the past and again, I get the indifference, and that does remind me of my husband as well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so when you have these moments where you're frustrated with David in session, tell me what happens from that point on.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Usually I'm getting frustrated when I'm looking at the clock and I know he's not going to be there on time, which I feel bad about because I should give him the benefit of the doubt. But then I do end up waiting and by the time he gets there, I'm frustrated. I keep a straight face and I try to draw his attention to it, but when he waves me off or makes a joke, I'm kind of angry inside and I notice that sticks with me while we're in session.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And distracted, what do you think's distracting you? What are you thinking about when you're distracted?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How upset I am with him and at times how much he just does remind me of my husband.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you remember a while back before you were an intern, you took theories of counseling? Do you remember what it's called when a client treats a counselor like somebody else important in the client's life?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, that would be transference.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Transference, yeah. Do you remember what the opposite of that is called?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Countertransference.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Countertransference. I see some similarities in what you're talking about with the frustration and the distraction with David and you thinking of your husband. I see some potential countertransference going on. You think that's what's happening?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I do actually. I didn't really think about it too much, but I am making connections there and I think that might be getting in the way. Not to take away from the fact my client still doesn't show up on time, but...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: There's legitimate reasons to be frustrated. But from what I understand, because we've had a supervisor relationship that's lasted some months now, you seem more emotionally invested in this with the anger part than I usually see. Is that accurate?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think so, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's possible there's some countertransference going on here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Definitely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I want you to know this is normal. The important part with countertransference is to recognize it, to have some insight and bring it to supervision. Even though you didn't know the name necessarily, you knew something was off because of these feelings of frustration and anger. Countertransference can be destructive and compromise client care. So we'll work through this and learn from it. You feel you can continue to work with this client now that you know about what might be going on?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think I can. Now that I'm aware of it, I do believe that I can.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I'm going to move forward in that direction, but if at any time it seems like this is not manageable anymore, we can always reassign David. It's not a failure, especially at this stage. There's a value in working through it and being aware of it as long as the client's not at risk. So I want to continue on that path and we'll see where it goes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, that sounds great.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I really appreciate you bringing this to my attention.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you for listening.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Absolutely.

video_details.title: Cognitive Behavioural Therapy- Using a CBT Worksheet
video_details.description: Basic role play of the principles of CBT Dr Grant Blashki with an actor role playing a patient

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So these dodgy little sheets we use for cognitive behavioral therapy strategies. You can see at the top they talk about the situation, at the bottom the feelings, and in between there's discussion about the thoughts.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's easier with a concrete example. I might get you to write in the situation you mentioned—the tram situation—in the little box there.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Of course.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so what have you written in there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Catching the tram.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so what feelings do you have when you go to catch the tram? It's often useful to have a one-word feeling, something really in your gut.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Anxious. That's the one. Anxious.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you want to write that in? Are there any other feelings that really resonate with you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Scared.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, pop that one in there. Anything else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Embarrassed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Pop that one in as well. This is great, you've really clicked with it. Now, I'm going to ask you to imagine what the little voice in your head—that self-talk—is saying when you're feeling anxious. What's the story going on there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm thinking I'm going to get lost. Yeah, I'm anxious because I think I'm going to get lost.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Write that one down: 'I'm worried I'll get lost.' Any other thoughts or self-talk?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I reckon I'd start blushing and going red.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's another good one to write down. What have you written there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Panic that I'll go red or blush.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We've teased out the situation, feelings, and the voice in your head. Now, with CBT, we try and challenge some of these thoughts.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I know they're silly, but...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Some thoughts are realistic, but some aren't helpful and cause problems. Let's look at the evidence for 'I'm worried I'll get lost'. Have you ever been lost in Sydney?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I don't think I have. I make sure I know all the tram numbers and where they go because I'm so scared I'll get lost.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So how likely is it really that you're going to get lost?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Actually, it's really unlikely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Write that in the right-hand column. These are disputing thoughts—alternative ways of looking at things that are fairer and more realistic.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. 'Unlikely I will get lost.'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Look at the next one: 'I'll panic and blush and everyone will look at me.' If you did get panicky, do you think people would really notice?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably not. Maybe not.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you look at other people on the tram and decide whether they look happy or panicky?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really. I usually look out the window or read the paper.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Most people are just doing their own thing. Can you think of a more realistic way of thinking about blushing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel anxious sometimes, lots of people do, and that's okay. It doesn't mean I'm an idiot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Write that in as the disputing thought. People actually probably don't care that much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Reviewing this, you've moved to a new way of thinking: 'unlikely I'll get lost', 'people don't really care if I blush', and 'it's normal to get anxious'. Does that take the heat out of the feeling?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It makes a big difference to see it that way.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This sheet won't instantly resolve everything, but for homework, I'll give you a couple more to play with.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that'd be good.

video_details.title: Cognitive Behavioural Therapy- Explanation of the Principles
video_details.description:
Thanks to the SWFPS program at the University of Melbourne for permission to use this role play video.

familydoctor.expert is a patient education site which aims to help patients with common health problems with short video explanations by a general practitioner. Our hope is that the information is like a brief discussion with your GP providing you with key information that is based on evidence and that is up-to-date.

Of course these brief videos don't replace seeking professional care from a

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Bridget's anxiety has been getting worse. She's been having panic attacks, not sleeping well, and she's avoiding going out unless she absolutely has to. Bridget is expressing faulty thoughts that are causing her emotional pain and preventing her from functioning as she normally has done. The social worker is considering cognitive behavioral therapy as an option for Bridget. Today, the mental health social worker is explaining the basic idea of CBT and how it might be useful for Bridget.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, I just find it really tough getting on trains and trams in the city and just, yeah, just get anxious.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, the reason I've brought you back today was I wanted to talk to you about this psychological technique that some people find really helpful. And I thought we could spend a bit of time today just explaining what it is, see if it's something that you might find useful. Yeah?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, sure. Yeah, that'd be good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's called cognitive behavioral therapy, and it was really developed by psychologists. And it's actually not that complicated, but I'll go through it with you. It's basically a technique that really has a look at the way you think about things, you know, particularly the way you think about yourself or other people, and how that thinking affects the way you're feeling about things. Right? The central idea of it often we say it's the way you think affects the way you feel. Alright? That seems sort of obvious, but as you'll see, that's an important part of this technique. So I'm just going to scribble that down in big letters here and we'll give you a bit more of an example of what I'm actually talking about. So it's the way you think affects the way you feel. Okay, so that's sort of obvious. So why, how does it all come together? Probably the easiest way to understand it is with an example. And we often talk about this concept of the ABC of thinking. Okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. Uh-huh.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, an A is an activating event or, to put in simple terms, any situation that happens to you. So obviously we're going through life, be it struggling with the trams or the trains or the way you're relating to other people, that we call those sort of activating events or situations. It's a bit artificial, so just sort of roll with it and it'll make sense as it goes.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So that's the activating event. And everything that happens to us has a consequence, okay, in terms of the way we feel. In your case you said you're getting a bit panicky on the trams and trains. And also the things that we do, you know, start avoiding going on the trains and trams, yeah? But in between events and what you actually feel and do, there's a whole little thinking process going on, you know, the thoughts, that self-talk in our mind about how we interpret events. Okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, yeah. Yeah, yeah, that'd be good. Thanks.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so say there's a lady walking down the street and she sees a friend who she hasn't seen for a while, and the friend walks right past her, completely ignores her, okay? And she feels quite angry, you know? What could she have been thinking, do you think? Just at a guess, for example, that made her feel angry.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, well maybe she's thinking, you know, my friend just ignored me. What's going on here? That's rude.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, so you can see that the lady's walked past, she's felt angry, but there's been a little bit of thinking. She's had to think all that stuff, you know, why is she ignoring me?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure. Yeah, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's take another lady who's walking past and her friend ignores her, or appears to ignore her. But she actually just feels a bit concerned. Her reaction is she feels, oh, you know, she feels a bit concerned. What could she be thinking that has led her to that sort of feeling?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe, oh, she might think that her friend must be really preoccupied with something and really worried about something because obviously she'd say hello otherwise.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Exactly right. So if you have a look here, you can see that in one case, the activating event, the friend walking past, caused a feeling of anger. And in the second example, it caused the feeling of concern. And the lady who felt angry, I think you said she was thinking, why is she ignoring me? and that sort of thought. And the lady who was concerned, she was thinking, I hope everything's okay. So this is a really long way of getting to it, but it's really getting back to this idea of all our situations we're dealing with, between the event and how we feel, there's this thinking process.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, but I get it. I understand that. That makes sense.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay.

video_details.title: Clinical Supervision for Counseling - Moving Sessions Beyond the Superficial
video_details.description: This video features a clinical supervision vignette that demonstrates one way a supervisor may choose to intervene when a counseling supervisee is struggling with moving sessions toward more depth.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hey Rachel, how you been?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I've been okay. Thank you for asking.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sure. What's been going on?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I've kind of been having an issue with one of my clients. I've been kind of having a hard time moving our sessions out of superficial conversation into more deep and meaningful conversations. And I feel kind of stuck, and I'm not really sure like what I should do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, which client are we talking about?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We're talking about David.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: David, okay. So with David, you feel like the conversation is more conversational. It's been more on tangents?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Very much so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Where would you like it to be?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I'm concerned about, you know, his substance use. He drinks and smokes, and I try to move the conversations towards that and why he does that and what the meaning holds for him. And we'll have these little moments where he'll kind of start answering and it looks like it's moving towards a deep conversation, and then it's like he realizes that it's going in that direction so he'll kind of snap it back the other way and start talking about other things like his car and the girls he's seeing. You know, things that aren't really related to why he's using.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And are you able to predict when these tangents are gonna come about?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: For the most part, yes. But getting him to even talk at a deep and meaningful level is hard enough. So when it does happen, I'm definitely cautious of the fact that he could at any moment take it somewhere else. So I guess yeah, you could say I know that it's going to happen at some point.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And particularly when he starts to get into any type of depth work?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's like he shuts down and switches gears?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: He just kind of laughs and just changes the subject. You know, and I can't seem to get him back there or you know, just be like "Whoa, that was great" and...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you trying to get him back?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I am. I think I could probably do a better job and not be so afraid to kind of... I don't know if "afraid" is the right word, maybe "intimidated", to be like "You know, we don't really need to talk about your cars or this girl. I want to go back to that moment we just had."

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you've been an intern now for around four months, right? Is that right? Four months? And when counselors are new, when counselors are in training, sometimes it's a victory just to have the client talk. Right? You remember those days from your early days in supervision where you just wanted them to say anything?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's a next level skill to start confronting and guiding the sessions a little bit. And I kind of feel like that's what you're looking for is that confidence to be a little bit confrontational and directive and move the session in a direction that you think would be helpful, rather than just let the client take it in whatever direction they choose. Does that sound about right?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's exactly what I would like to do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, so let's look at your options here. Alright? What's the worst that would happen if you confronted David when he goes off on a tangent? So he gets into some deep work, starts talking about the drug and alcohol abuse, and you notice him talking about the weather or cars or whatever it is, right? And you're like "You know, I noticed that you kind of switched gears. Can we go back to what we were just talking about?" What's the worst that could happen there?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I mean, I think the worst would be that he would say "no" and not want to have that conversation.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. What would be the best that could happen?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think the best thing that would happen would be, you know, he would be willing to come back to that moment and explore that with me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And if he explored that with you, what might happen?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: He would gain some understanding about himself and his addictions and that would help us be able to move the therapy, you know, forward.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Progress.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: He would make progress. So is that worth the risk considering the worst case scenario and then weighing it against the best case?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think so, yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think it is too. And it's normal to have these moments where you doubt yourself, especially when you're new to this field. And it is tough to move to that next level skill. So I really appreciate you bringing this up with me, and I want to work with you to confront David just a little more, right? And we'll try it in stages. So a little confrontational, a little directive, and maybe a little more if needed. And each time as we try this, if it's clear it's not working, come back and we'll talk about it, we'll figure another plan and we'll try to move forward from there. So we'll just take it in steps. Alright? So it doesn't have to be anything more than that. Like it doesn't have to be a major breakthrough or anything that you're seeking. It can be mild confrontation and then coming back and exploring that and then moving forward from there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, that sounds perfect. Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does it sound like a plan?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yes.

video_details.title: Sample Problem-Focused Standardized Patient Encounter
video_details.description: By the end of Year 1, KCUMB medical students will have the skills to complete a problem-focused encounter in a safe setting with a standardized patient (actor).  In this video, two students who (years 3 and 4) demonstrated these skills.  Of course, we would not expect a first year student to be as smooth as this, but all of our grads have these skills.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Come in.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, Ms. Alexander. Hi, my name is Brittany and I'm a medical student working with Dr. Parrott today. It's nice to meet you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Nice to meet you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So she sent me in just to ask you some questions and do a brief physical exam, and then I will step back out and talk to her and then she'll be in behind me. Is that okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Great. So what brings you in today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've been having pretty bad neck pain.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh goodness. Well, I'm glad you came in so we can take a look and make sure there's nothing going on. So how long has this been going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably about two days.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Did anything happen a couple days ago out of the ordinary?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I was in a small car accident.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Must have been scary. What happened?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I was at a stoplight and the person behind me rear-ended me. We weren't going very fast though, I think he was maybe going five or ten miles an hour.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And were you wearing your seatbelt at the time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good. And so you said you didn't go to the hospital or anything because you didn't feel any pain initially? No. So when exactly did the pain start? About how many hours after the accident?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would probably say maybe four to six hours after. I think maybe I was just in shock at first and so I didn't really feel any pain or anything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. And where is it bothering you specifically? Can you pinpoint a specific area on your neck?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's mostly just the back of my neck and on the sides of my neck.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Both sides?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And did you hear any pops or have any numbness or tingling that occurred during the accident?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And is there anything that's making the pain worse?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mostly when I bend my head forward and try to turn it to the left, it kind of it's really tight.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Anything you've noticed that's helping it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I took some ibuprofen and I put ice on the back of my neck and that helped a little bit, but it still hurts.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how much ibuprofen are you taking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I took two tablets every six hours or so since then.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. I'm just taking some notes so that way when I go talk to Dr. Parrott, I can be thorough and let her know everything you're telling me. So it's worse whenever you're bending forward and to the side to the left. Is that correct?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. And can you describe the pain to me?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It just feels like a tight, kind of dull pain.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, tight and dull. And is this pain radiating or moving anywhere?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really, it just goes up and down the back of my neck.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So nothing coming down into the arm?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And on a scale of one to ten, with ten being the worst pain, where would you say you're at?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably around a six or a seven out of ten, especially when I try and bend forward and turn my head.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And is it a constant pain?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But it'll get worse whenever you bend forward and turn to the left?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And would you say since the accident, since that evening, has it been constant or is it getting worse, better, what would you say?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It feels like it's getting worse, but I don't know if that's because the ibuprofen's not working.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I'm glad you came in since the over-the-counter stuff's not working and we can do an exam and make sure there's nothing we're missing. If we need to, possibly do some osteopathic treatments, and we'll get onto that later, okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And as far as your past medical history, have you ever had a neck injury before?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you've never had problems with your neck?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, that's good to know. And any medical conditions that you're currently being treated for or that you've ever been treated for?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have asthma and I take medicine for that. That's about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Ever been hospitalized?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Ever had any surgeries?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I had my tonsils taken out when I was a kid. I think that was probably nine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And as far as medications, you said you take the over-the-counter ibuprofen and then you take something for asthma. What do you take for your asthma?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I take Albuterol.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you just take that as needed?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mm-hm.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And do you take any other medications?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I take a Loratadine or a Claritin for allergies.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. What about any herbal supplements, vitamins?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I take a multivitamin.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And I always like to ask all my patients, any recreational drug use?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, none.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And are you allergic to any medications?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I am. I'm allergic to penicillin.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what happens when you take penicillin?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I break out in a rash.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, we'll be sure never to give you penicillin for anything, so thank you. And as far as family history, any medical conditions in the family with your mom and dad?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My mom, she's pretty healthy. She has diabetes though and it's pretty under control. Good. My dad has high cholesterol but he takes medicine for that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any brothers or sisters?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have a brother and he's healthy. He doesn't have any conditions or anything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And no one's ever had problems with joints or arthritis?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Great. And I always like to just get an overview of my patients, kind of get to know them a little better. What do you do for a living?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm an administrative assistant.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, where do you work?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I work for the Fish and Wildlife services.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh wow, that must be fun. You've been doing it for a while?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, for a few years.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Stressful or pretty...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's not very stressful at all.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's good. And are you married?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I am, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Congratulations. Do you have any children?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, not yet.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. And so do you have hobbies that you like to do?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I do, I like to cook and I like to garden. It's been kind of difficult to garden because I can't lean forward as much for the past two days.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, that can be frustrating when you can't do the things you enjoy. Any tobacco use?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I smoke, probably maybe half a pack a day, if that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how long have you been smoking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, I want to say maybe seven years or so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Any alcohol use?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Occasional. I'll have a glass of wine with dinner maybe once a week.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. Well, I believe I got all the information I needed from you. So we're going to go ahead and move on to the physical exam portion. So what I'm going to do is I'm just going to have you take a seat up here.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, for the physical exam, I'm going to go ahead and listen to your heart and lungs and make sure those sound nice and clear. So I'm just going to slide this down and just breathe normal. Good. And go and take a big deep breath and out. Again. Again. And last one. Good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And so I'm just going to do a structural exam here and palpate down your spine. Let me know if there's anything that's tender.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's tender everywhere.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Everywhere? Okay. I'm going to work my way down. Okay. And I want to check the range of motion in your neck. So what I want you to do is try to put your chin down to your chest.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's about as far as I can go.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And then looking up to the ceiling. Pretty stiff. Okay, and what about looking, turning and looking over to the shoulder? Okay. Alright. And turn and look to that shoulder for me. Right there. And then ear to your shoulder. Trying to touch your ear over to your shoulder.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's as far as I can go.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. And I'm going to go ahead and check just some reflexes. This will kind of tell me if there's any nerves that are involved. So just relax your arm. And we're going to rest your arm right here on your lap. And just relax. Okay. And I'm going to do the same thing on this arm. So just relax your arm. And just relax. And then last one, just let your arm hang.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And now I'm going to test and see how strong you are. So place your arms like this for me and don't let me move your arms. Good. And arms up and don't let me push them. Good. And fingers out for me, don't let me squeeze them, and fingers together and try to push them out. Good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright. If it's okay with you, as an osteopathic student we learn some treatment, so I'm going to do some soft tissue to try and break up some of this tension that you're having, if that sounds okay.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, as long as it doesn't hurt too bad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No, it's not going to hurt, and if there's any pain, I want you to let me know. And so I'm just going to do just very gentle, it's called myofascial, and just kind of slowly up. And if this is something that you do get some relief from after this evening, then you can come back and we can be a little more aggressive. But since the car accident was just two days ago, I want to be very gentle.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. I'm just going to hold this right here. All those muscles that are tight and spasming right now attach right up where my fingers are at. So I'm just trying to get them to relax and loosen.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So this is supposed to relax all the muscles in my neck?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Uh-huh, yeah. Okay. Alright, I think that'll be enough for today. I don't want to do too much since it was such an acute injury. So I'm going to go ahead and help you up.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And then I'm going to go ahead and summarize everything that you told me from earlier, if that's okay. Would you prefer sitting back down in the chair? Sure. I'll help you down.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you started having some neck pain two days ago after a motor vehicle accident, you were rear-ended but you were wearing your seatbelt. You didn't hear any pop or have any numbness or tingling that occurred, and it's just been real tight for the past two days, real constant, but it's worse whenever you flex your head down or turn to the left. Is that correct?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And as far as your past medical history, you just have asthma and you're taking some medication for that. Okay. And you're not allergic to anything?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Penicillin.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Excuse me, yes, that's right. You are allergic to penicillin. Alright. What I will do is I will go talk to Dr. Parrott and then we will be back in to put together a treatment option plan for you. Any other questions or concerns you have for me today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I don't think so. Just want to feel better.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, well that is our main goal, so I'm glad you came in today.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Great, thank you. Thank you.

video_details.title: Effective Motivational Interviewing Approach with a Teen

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Chris.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hi.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks for coming in today and filling out our survey. I wondered if it's okay if I go over a couple of the things that you answered in the survey?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. One of the things that I noticed is that you are not using any kind of birth control right now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And I just wondered if we could talk for a few minutes about some ideas. And I wondered what your thoughts are about using condoms?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I've heard stuff about them that I don't really need them and they're not going to do much for me and it's just kind of a hassle to go out and get them. So I don't really use them for that reason.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You've heard a lot of negative things about condom usage. So Chris, is it okay if I share with you some of the things that I've learned about condom usage and some of the things that my clients that are around your age have shared with me about condom usage?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. What some people don't realize and don't know about condoms is that they not only help prevent teen pregnancy, but they can also prevent sexually transmitted infections like chlamydia along with HIV. They're really effective in preventing these things. And there's also a lot of easy ways to get condoms these days that some people don't know. The local health departments have condoms and many times they're free. And local pharmacies, drugstores have condoms and there are a lot of clinics that have them as well, either for a small fee or sometimes they're actually free. And there's some ways too that people have found of carrying them around pretty conveniently, you know, in their car or in their pocket because they're pretty small. What does it sound like as I'm talking? What are some thoughts that are going through your mind?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, definitely changing my mind about condoms a little bit. I think there's no hurt in just carrying them with me and if they do protect against all that stuff that you said, I mean, that sounds a lot better than what I have heard and I definitely want to avoid all those consequences.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, yeah. You're not interested in becoming a father right now, I'm guessing.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, great. Well, can I ask you, so after this conversation today, on a scale of 0 to 10 with 0 being that it's not at all important to you and 10 being that it's extremely important, where do you think you fall with how important taking a chance and using condoms would be to you now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: After everything that you've told me, it sounds pretty important to me. Probably like an 8 or a 9.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: 8 or 9. Okay. Well, that's great. It sounds like you really have a plan in mind. What do you think you'll do next? Like, what do you think would be a next step with you as far as contraception or condoms?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably go out and look for some condoms and really have an open mind to them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Well, we've got some here at the clinic. Would you like me to give you some on your way out? And you can just take them with you? Great. Well, thank you so much for talking with me today, Chris. It was nice to meet you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Nice to meet you too.

video_details.title: The Interview
video_details.description:
If you are taking an online interview, you can get some further guidance from these films:
*  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iw3zCAZk4dM
* https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=goTD0_P-vC8 

In this film, we invited four successful applicants back to Cambridge to share their interview experiences.  

We asked experienced interviewers in four subject areas -- Geography, Human, Social and Political Sciences, Medicine and Natural Sciences (Physical) - to conduct a mock interview with each student.  Foot

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The Cambridge interview process is very important to see this is one part of the assessment. We look at many things about each candidate, whether or not the person has the right kind of background knowledge and if they'd be successful in our teaching environment. Can they think?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hello, hi.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Just to start this interview, I want to give you a bit of an outline. We'll start with a question, then talk about some unseen material. Please don't be thrown by us taking notes. We're looking for students who listen carefully and take us through their thought processes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We'll start by talking about the essays you sent in. In one of them, you discussed the theory of functionalism. In your reading, have you come across that as an idea?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I've definitely come across that idea. There are interlinks between sociology and social anthropology, the idea that society works as a body. I think broad theories like this often generalize too much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In the arts and social sciences, we often use personal statements to ask students to say more about themselves and their interest in the subject. I saw you mention archaeology; can you tell me a little bit about what you've been doing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've been trying to build a foundation knowledge because I've never studied it. My interest started in programs about Egyptology and seeing exhibitions at the British Museum, which sparked my interest to understand it more.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In technical interviews, we're looking for how teachable students are, how they take an idea and develop it. Let's start by sketching the function y equals sine x divided by x between minus two pi and two pi.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: First of all, I'm going to get some main points to work out. I'll start with x is equal to zero.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, let me stop you there because x equals zero is a little bit tricky. Choosing points is a good idea, but we might come back to that one. Are there any other points you know the values of?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Pi is a good one. Sine of pi will be zero, so zero divided by pi is zero.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Even when she was uncertain and hesitant, she would nevertheless draw something. That gave us the opportunity to guide her. Keeping the dialogue going is very important, and Hannah was very good at that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That would be... yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have a scribble if it helps.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: What was this one? That was two-thirds. This one is minus two-thirds of pi. So that would be more like minus two-ninths.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, good to me. Much smaller. Questions are designed to push candidates and make them think hard. You hope to start with something they can answer but get progressively more difficult.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Starting with something we've already covered... what role do bases actually play in the hereditary nature of DNA?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A triplet code, where three bases together code for one amino acid. Different combinations of those codons in DNA build up a chain of amino acids and code for proteins.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, why is it three? Why is a codon made of three bases instead of one?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Because three bases are needed to have enough combinations for different amino acids. With a single base, you'd only code for four.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How many combinations can you have with three? Oliver gave a positive interview; he didn't give up and was listening to the information given. If you have one base, you can code for four amino acids. With two, what's the combination?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'll have to write something down.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well let's think about this. If you have one base, you can code for four different amino acids. If you now have two, what's the combination?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Twelve? Would I have?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A bit more than 12.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd have... oh, and an AA, right, so I could have 16.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: 16, okay. So when you have a triplet, what can you get? Sixty-four. Can 64 code for 20? Yes, potentially. Natalie also handled the interview well by reflecting on her interests.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This shows total fertility rates by regions in Europe. Could you describe the pattern that you see there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: In West Europe the fertility rates are generally higher, but within each country there's variation.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Why do you think the patterns look the way they do, particularly in Western Europe which you identified?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd say cultural factors play a big role, like expectations of family size. Welfare measures and state provisions also encourage or discourage people to bring up families.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Speculate on what you think this map of total fertility rates will look like in 20 years time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would say that possibly the fertility rates in the UK and France might decline a little bit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Why might that be?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That might be due to the changing role of women and expectations of their careers. It's difficult to say because there are so many factors that come into it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We run a holistic admissions process, collecting information from personal statements and school references. The interview is just one component.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: My single piece of advice is to listen carefully to the questions. If you don't understand, ask for clarification. Be yourself, as we're assessing whether we can teach you effectively.

video_details.title: Clinical Interviewing Role Play   Part 2
video_details.description: This video features a role-play of a counseling clinical interview.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello, my name is Dr. Todd Grande. Welcome to part two in my series on clinical interviewing. This is a roleplay exercise with Nell, who will be role-playing the character Anne. This is for educational purposes; remember that all clients are individuals and your agency may have different requirements.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In this second section of the intake interview, Dr. Grande will be eliciting information about the client's childhood, relationship history, and spirituality. Let's get started.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm going to ask you some questions about your developmental history. What city and state were you born and raised in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Wilmington, Delaware.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you speak any other languages other than English?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Spanish, pretty well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me who raised you and if anyone else lived with you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My biological parents raised me. My grandmother lived with us for a little while during middle and high school, but that was it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me briefly what your life was like growing up?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was a pretty normal childhood, but my mother was a very angry person, especially towards me. I have two sisters and we didn't want for anything, but I definitely felt like I got the most of her anger compared to my sisters and father.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've been wondering lately if that's connected to issues I'm having with women at work and in my neighborhood. I wasn't severely abused, but I was hit more than my sisters. My middle sister was seen as perfect, always getting good grades and doing exactly what my parents wanted.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has that family dynamic changed at all?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't think so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: At what age did you move out of your home?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I moved out for college when I was around 19.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How were you disciplined as a child?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mostly yelling. My mother would also hit my face or pull my hair. It happened less as I got older and could push her away.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How was your father during this time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He was quiet and didn't really get involved in the discipline.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's move on to relationship history. You are married; have you been married before?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, this is my first marriage.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is your sexual orientation, and what age were you when you married?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I am heterosexual. I got married when I was 27.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you describe your marriage? Does your spouse know you are seeking counseling?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It is a happy marriage. He gets concerned when I have sad periods, and seeking counseling was actually his idea. He's very supportive.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would he be willing to come in for a session if appropriate?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Definitely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does he have any history of substance use, gambling, or mental health concerns?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, nothing like that. We have been married for 15 years.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me about your previous relationships before marriage.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I had a serious boyfriend in graduate school, and I dated a few people in college and high school.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have any children?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, a 12-year-old son and a 10-year-old daughter. They live with us and I see them every day.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are there any health or mental health concerns regarding your children?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, and we've never been involved with Child Protective Services or suffered a traumatic loss.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you describe your relationship with your children?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's a good relationship. I made a point not to be like my mother, so I don't yell at them. We spend a lot of time together as a family and they do well in school.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you see any of the patterns from your mother playing out between you and your daughter?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really, because I try so hard. I feel myself flare up sometimes, but I don't think it's the same.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there anything else I should know about your children?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A few years ago, my son's teacher was worried he might be depressed. We took him to see someone, and he is doing okay now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm going to switch gears again. Are you comfortable moving forward?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This concludes part two of the series. I hope you found it useful. Please move on to part three for the conclusion. Thanks.

video_details.title: Clinical Interviewing Role Play   Part 1
video_details.description: This video features a role-play of a counseling clinical interview.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello, my name is Dr. Todd Grande. Welcome to my video series on clinical interviewing. This is a roleplay and I'm here with Nell Cawley, who'll be playing the part of a client that's coming in for an initial intake.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: In part one of this video, you'll see Dr. Grande go over the introduction, confidentiality, and several segments of the intake interview, such as trauma screening and getting a client's treatment history.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello, Ann. How are you doing today? Thanks for coming in for this intake. I know you've gone through the screening process, but the purpose of this intake today is much different. I'll be asking much more personal questions.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm doing all right, thanks. Sure, I'm comfortable with that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Before I get started, I want to talk a little bit about confidentiality. When you see a counselor for treatment, the communication is confidential, but there are certain circumstances under which confidentiality might be broken.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The probably largest exception is if you sign a release. For example, if you want me to talk to your physician because a physical condition or medication could be affecting your mood. You might sign a release that allows me to communicate.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, okay. That makes sense.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Similarly, if you have a family member that you want to bring in, you would have to sign a release. You can discontinue a release at any time by calling the agency and telling them you want it canceled.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Another exception to confidentiality is what's called continuity of care. A lot of other people work here and have some investment or duties related to your care, like billing or filing. I'm permitted to speak to those individuals to the extent that I need to.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So you can tell them my deep, dark secrets?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I could, though I generally would try to avoid that. But if there's a treatment team meeting and your particular case was being discussed, then other clinicians and the director would have access to that information.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That makes sense.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Another exception is if I have reason to believe that you're going to harm somebody. It's called a Tarasoff duty to warn. If you were to tell me you're going to go harm somebody, I would have to contact them and warn them.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Again, this wouldn't involve the disclosing of family secrets and all kinds of diagnoses. This would just be to keep the person safe. Another exception is if I believe that in general you're a danger to yourself or others.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, that's not going to happen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If you tell me that you have suicidal thoughts or homicidal thoughts, that doesn't necessarily mean law enforcement or inpatient facilities are going to be involved. We can talk about it, and a lot of people have these thoughts.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But if there's a clear threat and I'm really worried, then I will act. Another exception is if you provide information to me that leads me to believe a child or an elderly person is being abused. I would have to report that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And the last exception to confidentiality would be if for some reason during the course of this therapy you get involved with the civil or criminal legal system and a judge orders me to disclose information from your chart.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, so if I told you that I was feeling really sad and I thought about killing myself, you're not going to...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We're going to have a discussion about that. The first thing I would do is assess the seriousness and we'll try to work out some sort of safety plan. If there's an active plan to harm yourself, then my recourse would be to call law enforcement.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, that's not unusual. All right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's not unusual to have passive suicidal ideation, like maybe wishing that you wouldn't wake up the next day. That's a lot different than you telling me that you have a plan to harm yourself and that you're going to do it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, that's pretty clear.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so let's move to the next step. I'm going to be asking you questions from a wide variety of domains, like relational history and emotional history. This is like the data collection stage. Do you have any questions before we get started?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, okay. No, I'm ready. Let's do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What brings you in to our agency? What's been bothering you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I guess I've been feeling kind of down. But really what it is, I think it's work. I'm not getting along very well with my boss and some of the other women at work. I'm starting to feel like there's something wrong with me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're saying you're a little down but you're also having some relational difficulties with people that you work with? Have you been feeling pretty sad?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, and maybe more than a little down. I've been pretty sad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We'll talk about that some more. Any feelings of anxiety, like being worried, nervous, or on edge?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think a little bit. I'm kind of a worry-wart, so yeah, I'm always pretty worried.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm going to ask you some questions from what we call a symptom checklist. As I touch on a topic, let me know if it's happening currently, in the last 30 days, if it's ever happened, or never happened. We'll start with memory loss.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. I mean, there's some things I can't remember from my childhood, but I think that's kind of normal.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any substance-related problems or issues?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe when I was a teenager. The campus police raided a party where I was and they caught me with a nickel bag of weed. They took me to the station, but nothing really came of it. I drink and stuff, but it's not a problem.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When's the last time you had a drink? And have you ever had any withdrawal symptoms?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yesterday. No, I've never had any symptoms like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever heard the term auditory hallucinations? It means when somebody hears things that other people can't hear. Or visual hallucinations, seeing things other people haven't seen?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. I mean, maybe when I was high in college once, but I don't think so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever felt like or been told that you have any type of delusions or paranoia? Have you ever felt like your thoughts are disorganized? Have you ever felt really manic, with a lot of energy, or racing thoughts?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. My mood is fairly stable, but I do get really sad. I don't think I get really happy right after or anything like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about irritability?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: If you ask my husband, probably. But not really more than anybody else, I don't think.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever had trouble with sleeping? When was the last time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, sometimes. Sometimes I'm sleeping a ton, but then sometimes it might be hard to sleep. It was probably in the spring, a couple of months ago.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever found yourself having obsessive thoughts or compulsive behaviors? Or problems with nightmares?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. I get nightmares sometimes, but not significantly.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever had any trouble with the amount of food you eat? Like too little food, too much food?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, my husband's been concerned lately. He says I'm not eating enough. I'm just not hungry. I don't feel like the energy to get up and eat. I don't have an appetite, I guess that's it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you feel like you are now or ever have been a danger to anyone else? Have you ever had suicidal thoughts?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. But yeah, I have had suicidal thoughts.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We'll touch on those a little later on. How about a suicidal plan or an attempt? When was the last suicidal thought?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, never an attempt. Maybe a plan a long time ago. The last thought was last week.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever harmed yourself, what we call self-mutilation, for example, cutting? Have you ever had any homicidal thoughts, or been violent?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. No, definitely not. I mean, I've yelled at my husband and stuff, but no physical violence. It's rare.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I've completed the symptom checklist and I want to switch gears a little bit to trauma screening. Have you ever been involved in a motor vehicle accident, a fire, or been the victim of a crime?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Vehicle accident, yes. And victim of a crime, yes. No weather-related trauma or flashbacks.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever been physically abused? How often did that happen?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, my mom would smack me and stuff when I got out of line. It wasn't that often, like maybe a couple times a year. No sexual abuse, traumatic loss, or domestic violence.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me a little bit about the motor vehicle accident?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My husband and I were on our way to the movies and somebody rear-ended us at a red light. It was scary, and the airbags didn't even deploy. But I'm not too shaken up about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You mentioned you were the victim of a crime. Can you tell me briefly about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I left my car in Philadelphia when we went to the symphony, and they stole my car radio and CD player. My husband called the police and they recovered it a couple of days later. The insurance took care of the repairs.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I want to switch gears to substance abuse. You mentioned the involvement with the law about the marijuana. How long did you use marijuana for?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: To be honest, I still do occasionally. Not all the time or anything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about alcohol? Have you ever found yourself in any trouble because of alcohol use?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have a couple of glasses of wine at dinner a couple nights a week. I embarrassed myself at a restaurant one time, got a little loud. My husband wasn't that happy about it, but that was just one time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you think you have a problem with alcohol? If you had to stop using entirely, would you be able to?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. Yeah, I could. I mean, I don't want to, but I could. I experimented with speed and cocaine in college a couple times, but I didn't really like that. No use since then.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever been treated for substance abuse? I want to switch gears again to gambling. Do you ever gamble?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. I've gone to Las Vegas and Atlantic City with my husband, maybe once a year. We'll set a certain amount of money to spend, and when that's done, that's done. I don't feel I have a gambling problem.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I want to talk about any previous treatment history. Have you ever seen a counselor, mental health clinician, or psychiatrist before?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I saw a counselor a few years ago, around 2010. It wasn't that long, maybe two months. I just wasn't that comfortable with her. She didn't seem very sure of herself, and I didn't have a lot of confidence in her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me how you terminated treatment? Did you cancel an appointment, or have a session to wrap things up?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I just stopped going. I missed an appointment and then I didn't call to reschedule. I feel kind of bad about that. She didn't get me, and I didn't know how it was going to help me anyway.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
