diarization.text: In our counseling relationship, if you feel that's the case, I'd like you to communicate that to me so we can talk about it. Was there any other mental health treatment you've ever received, either inpatient or outpatient?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, in college, they wanted me to see the counselor there two or three times after the marijuana thing. It was like a mandated group. Are we ready for the next section? Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This concludes part one of my video series on clinical interviewing. I hope that you found it helpful. At your convenience, I would encourage you to click on to part two to continue watching this roleplay. Thanks.

video_details.title: Clinical Interviewing Role Play   Part 3
video_details.description: This video features a role-play of a counseling clinical interview.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello, my name is Dr. Todd Grande. Welcome to part three of my series on clinical interviewing. I'm here with Nell Kelly, who's a graduate assistant here at Wilmington University, who will be playing the part of Anne, the fictitious client in this role-play.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: In this third and final section of the intake interview, you'll see Dr. Grande cover areas such as education and career, legal history, and he will complete a safety checkout and attempt to instill hope in the client.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so I'm going to be asking you some questions about your social situation and what you do in your leisure time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How do you currently spend your day?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, well, right now, I guess I go to work in the morning and then I come home at about 4:30 and take care of the kids, get them from after-care, and then we'll have dinner, help them with their homework, and then me and my husband will watch a TV show or something and go to bed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's a fairly typical day for you? Okay. What do you do for fun?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, well, lately not a lot. I used to love reading, going to the movies, making jewelry, but not in a while.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Why don't you think you enjoy those things now as much as you did?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't have as much energy as I used to. I come home from work and I'm drained. Dealing with that situation, then the kids and homework can be a nightmare. I've been kind of down on myself lately because I just want to go to bed. I feel like maybe I'm not as good of a mom or wife as I used to be.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you think that this change in your mood is related to the problems at work? Do you feel like it's all tied together?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, probably. Yeah. I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you know which came first? The lack of energy or the difficulty at work?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd have to think about that. It was after things started getting really bad at work. I'm just drained. If I just go to sleep, I don't have to think about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Who are the most important people in your life? I'm going to guess your husband and kids are included. Outside of them, who are the most important people?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My sisters, my dad, my mom, and my best friend, although I haven't talked to her in about six months.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When you have difficulties or problems, do you feel like you could talk to these people?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Switching gears, let's talk about spirituality. Can you describe any spiritual beliefs you have?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I believe in God. I pray. I think God takes care of me. I was praying the morning before I decided to call the agency because I was feeling like such a bad mom.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you affiliated with any religious institution?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was raised Roman Catholic, but I haven't been to church in a couple of years.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you describe how socio-cultural influences, like your values and culture, have affected your life?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: What I learned in Sunday school helped me to be a better person. My parents and Girl Scouts taught me about giving back to the community, and I've tried to pass that on to my kids.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you identify with any particular ethnicity?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Italian-American.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Italian-American. Has that influenced your life in any way?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I take pride in my culture, maybe not so much growing up, but now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Let's talk about your educational history. What is your highest level of education?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: One year of graduate school. I dropped out when we got engaged. My degree is in history.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Anything else in terms of special training? Did you enjoy school?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, but I enjoyed school very much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you ever envision going back to school?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, when the kids are a little older. I get sad about not finishing my graduate degree.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have any military history?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now for employment history. You work full-time for a bank as a teller. How long have you been there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: For 10 years now. It's not that challenging.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you in any danger of losing your job?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, but I'm not happy there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Who was your employer prior to that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Another bank for six years. I left because we relocated. Before that, I waitressed in college and graduate school.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What type of work did you enjoy the most?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: None of it, really. I liked it when I was in school best. I don't like work.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you don't feel satisfied with your work?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, but looking for another job seems daunting. I really don't know what I have to offer.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it seems intimidating right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's all I can do to get to work and get home and take care of the kids.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's talk about legal involvement. You mentioned some legal history involving marijuana in college. What happened?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We were having a loud party and campus security was called. I was found with a bag on me and ended up at the police station. It got expunged and hasn't caused problems, it's just embarrassing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. As we move toward regular sessions, we will talk about goals. What are your general goals for therapy?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd like to get along better with other women and feel better overall. I'd also like to be a better mom. I'm boring and asleep a lot lately.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you remember a time when you didn't feel this way?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, like last year. At home, it wasn't as hard and I had more energy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me about your strengths?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Normally I'm a good mom. I love my kids and want them to know it. I'm smart and creative. My sisters think I'm funny, and I'm a good cook.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you think you're funny?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Last year a lot of people were telling me I was. Not now, though.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We'll be starting the regular sessions next week. You mentioned earlier having some suicidal thoughts within the last 30 days. Can you tell me more about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's more like if I just went to sleep and didn't wake up tomorrow, how bad would that be? I don't have a plan or intent.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So kind of a passive suicidal thinking process. You don't have any intent or plan to harm yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you sure? There's a term we use called contract for safety. Can you promise me you're going to be safe?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What would you do if those thoughts became more pronounced? Tell me what you would do.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I could call my sister, my husband, or my best friend.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Family support is a good start. If you feel in danger, call 911 or go to an inpatient facility. Losing your life would be extreme. Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Lastly, I want to thank you for coming in today. These intakes are helpful for your treatment later on. We'll start the real sessions next time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I want to encourage you. These thoughts are understandable given you might be depressed. As you commit to therapy, I hope these symptoms improve. Do you have any questions?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I don't think so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If anything comes up, feel free to call. I look forward to seeing you next week. Thanks, Anne.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This concludes the video series on clinical interviewing. I want to extend my thanks to Nell Kelly for her help on this project. Thank you for watching.

video_details.title: Clinical communication skills - explanation Skills
video_details.description: A demonstration of the explanation skills used in a primary care consultation.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Come in. Mrs. Olsen?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hello, Doctor.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello, I'm Dr. O'Connor. Would you like to take a seat?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How are you today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, Doctor, I've not been feeling very well at all. Feeling really tired and run down, and I've been having this breathlessness, you know, and I've been really worried about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You came in to see one of my colleagues about that recently, didn't you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I did, yes. Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And she sent you for a blood test?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's right, Doctor.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, we think you might be anaemic.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh. Oh, gosh. Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what I wanted to do today was firstly to give you your blood test results and then talk to you a little bit about the condition of anemia and then talk about some potential treatments. Does that sound okay with you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That sounds fine, yes, Doctor.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Great. So shall we have a look at your blood test results? Here it is. So what we're testing for is the level of hemoglobin in your blood. And just to show you the normal range for women is between 11.5 and 16 grams per deciliter of hemoglobin. And this is your level of hemoglobin, it's 8.7.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, that's low, isn't it?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's a bit lower than we would like. So what we'd be looking to do is to get that back within the normal range. Just to reassure you, iron deficiency anemia, which I think you've got, is fairly common. Up to around 15 percent of women can experience this type of anemia. And it's very treatable as well.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh yes, I mean, this tiredness, etc. is just getting me down, Doctor.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It must be, it must be, because you've got quite a busy lifestyle, haven't you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have, yes, yeah. And I just feel as though I can't cope much longer with it. It's, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Shall I tell you a bit more about anemia? Do you know anything about the condition?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't. No. I mean, I've heard of it, but I don't know what it is.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, it's a condition related to your blood. And within your blood there's several components, one of which is plasma. Within the plasma, you have your red blood cells. And within that, you have a protein called hemoglobin, which carries the oxygen around your body to all the different organs. Now, if that's not working efficiently, you start to experience the kind of symptoms that you've been having, like breathlessness, dizziness, tiredness.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Definitely. Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: One of the causes can be blood loss, so I wondered about your periods. How are they?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, they've been heavy these last few months, really heavy. Yeah, I've put it down to my age, you know, they start getting irregular and heavy. But you might be right there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That may be a factor. So I want to talk to you about treatments now. Um, there are a couple of things that I would suggest that you try. The first thing we'd like you to do is to increase the amount of iron in your diet. Can you tell me a bit about the sort of diet you have at the moment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I mean, I'm really busy. Um, I think I have a reasonable, you know, a well-balanced diet. We eat a lot of ready meals. Um, and then on a weekend, we always have a good breakfast, cook bacon butties. Um, so, no, so I think it's quite... quite a good diet. Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The teenage children, they keep you busy.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, they do, yes. I mean, you know, it's like having a taxi service. What with that and then at work, you know, I'm so busy at work. It's just... just so tired.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Just keep feeling tired, it must be hard for you to do all those things.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, yes, it is difficult. I just feel as though I can't cope anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now, you mentioned ready meals. I can understand you relying on those for convenience, but the problem is sometimes you don't get the proper balance of nutrients.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Alright, Doctor.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what I'd ask you to do is perhaps to adapt your diet slightly and include more iron-rich foods in your diet.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, right. Okay. How do I do that?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Before I tell you about what some of those foods are, can I ask if you're a vegetarian?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. No. I'm not.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The reason I ask that is because one of the best sources of iron in your diet is lean red meat.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, yes. Yes. Like steak.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, exactly. Also liver is a good source.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, no. No. Couldn't eat liver.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What about something like steak that you mentioned? Would you consider eating that a bit more regularly?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, yes. I mean, steak wouldn't take long to cook, would it at all? Yeah, we could give that a go.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good, good. There's also leafy green vegetables, things like kale and spinach are good sources of iron.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, the kids wouldn't eat that. But, I mean, they like sweet corn, so they can have the sweet corn, can't they, with the steak? And I could go for the leafy... the green vegetables. Like broccoli? Is it broccoli?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yes, broccoli.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I like broccoli. Yeah, I'll have a go with that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. There's other things too you might want to consider, things like fortified cereals, which have iron in them.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. What are those?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, if you look on the ingredients panel of cereals, you'll see some are enriched with iron. So you could perhaps incorporate some of those.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, yes. Yes, I'll have a look at the supermarket. I mean, if I got some of those, we could have that at the weekend, and that'd give me more time, I wouldn't have to cook, would I?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Could make your life a bit easier.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That would be a help, wouldn't it?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It would, yes. Wholemeal bread is a good source of iron as well.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, yes. Yeah, they only like white bread, but I could buy myself some brown bread cobs and have it for lunch. Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you think you could give some of those things a try?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I will try, Doctor, definitely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Great. Great. The other thing I'd like you to consider is taking a course of iron tablets.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, I'm not into tablets. Why?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Um, this can be a really effective treatment for iron deficiency anemia. And, um, what it does is it supplements the amount of iron you're getting in your diet.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So would that be short-term?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yes, yes. Often people respond very well to those. You can have some side effects. Sometimes they can upset your tummy if you have them on, you know, on an empty stomach. So what you do is you take them after a meal.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Alright, I'll remember to do that. Yes. Yeah. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But I think those two things, adapting your diet and taking a course of iron tablets, I think you might respond very well to those treatments.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right, yes, I'll have a go at that, Doctor.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How do you feel about the information I've given you so far?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's fine. Yes, I'll definitely try if it makes me feel any better. It's worth it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yes, excellent. Excellent. I've given you quite a lot of information about anemia today. I've got a leaflet here about anemia, which I thought you might like to take home and read in your own time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, thank you. Yes. Oh, yes. Yeah. I'll read this, Doctor. It's... it's sometimes difficult to remember what you tells, so yes, having a look at this at home would be really helpful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's right. That's right. So just to check that I've explained things to you correctly, do you think you could just recap on the two treatments that you're going to try?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, you said that the anemia is due to a lack of iron. Um, and I can get this from having some red meat, um, steak, lamb chops, would that be...?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yes, trim the fat off.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. And green vegetables and wholemeal bread. And if I have these iron tablets, that, you know, hopefully I'll feel better. Thank you, yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Excellent. So what I'd like you to do is come back in a couple of weeks and then we can see how you're doing.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'll do that. Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you got any questions?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Are there any other tests I'll have to have?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think at this stage, when you come back to see me again, we'll do another blood test and check on your hemoglobin level then. If it hasn't gone back into the normal range, it might be then that we'd look at doing some other investigations, but I don't want to worry you about that at this stage. I think let's see how you do with the dietary change and the iron tablets, and we can discuss that next time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. Thank you. Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there anything else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I think that's it. Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, well good to see you and I'll see you again in a few weeks.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, thank you. Bye.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Bye.

video_details.title: Anger Management in Counseling and Psychotherapy Video
video_details.description:
For the full video, go to: http://www.psychotherapy.net/video/anger-management-psychotherapy

Watch anger experts Howard Kassinove and Chip Tafrate demystify the challenging work of anger management in this indispensable video! Whatever your professional setting, you'll breathe easier with this practical, empirically validated showcase of exercises, live sessions with real clients, and tools to strengthen your practice.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Carmelo, I want to take a couple of minutes and go over the scale on anger that you filled out when you got here. You had mentioned that some people in your life have kind of commented and they said, 'You know, maybe you ought to look into thinking about whether or not you have some issues with anger or not.' And that's one of the reasons you're here. And I'm hoping that this will help sort of identify specific issues related to anger that might be problematic for you. And so this is really feedback meant for you. You can do whatever you'd like with the information. It's just for you to consider it. And so let's go through each area. And there are a number of questions here and a number of sort of different anger dimensions. And I think the place we're going to start is if you look at all the questions that you answered, it comes up with something called a total score, which is just kind of looking at everything together. And when we look at the total score, you scored quite high, actually. You scored in a range that we would sort of call the 99th percentile, which means that your anger is at a level greater than 99% of the population of men your age.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Are you kidding me?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That high?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, so it's kind of hard to hear it that way.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm kind of surprised you...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It kind of surprised you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, well, I didn't think... yeah, I didn't think it was going to rate that high. I mean, I figured a lot of people were in my category, but I would have figured that I was probably in about the 60%, 75%.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Just a little above average.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Wow, that's way up there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's a little bit high and it might indicate that really anger does get you in trouble at times in terms of relationships and causing you... so you've recognized that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've always recognized that. I've seen it. I've tried to deny it a lot of times, but then I've recognized that I'm at the stage that I know I have issues.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So this kind of just highlights that and puts a number on it, in a sense, and so...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Where the studies have been done?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, right. Exactly. Kind of comparing how you answered the question to the general population of folks your age. That you're really, you're sort of in the top 1% of scores.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I didn't think I was that bad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've gotten a lot of serious problems. I mean, the same thing that they do to me, I do to them. So a lot of times I'm surprised, especially in the environment that I live in, that I haven't gotten shot, stabbed, or killed yet. I mean, that should definitely have happened. And I'm surprised it hasn't.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Because getting angry, saying things to people, not thinking things through, can really put you at risk.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Exactly. Same things I can do to them for angering me to that point is the same thing as me getting them back for what they've said or done. So it could go in a vice versa aspect. They could kill me, or I could kill them.

video_details.title: Example of EFT: Process-Experiential Therapy for Depression
video_details.description: Ellen, Janna, Jonathan, Charlene, Jeremy

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So Bethany, can you tell me what this week has looked like for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: This week, um, I don't know, I guess it was a little bit more productive than usual, but not really. I'm still just usual, dead to the world.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Dead to the world?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, you know, I'm just in my room most of the day. I'm not really part of the world or part of my family. I'm just closed off in my own little sad universe, I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're feeling isolated from your family?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah, I'm just feeling really disconnected. Just really... I don't know, it's just been a really tough week with my husband. We've been fighting a lot, as usual.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So when you say you're feeling disconnected, can you explain to me more what that looks like?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess, I'm just so tired all day and just exhausted, and he has all these demands and all these things he wants me to do and I just feel like I'm not capable of doing them. I can't even get myself out of bed in the morning, how am I supposed to do all the things he wants me to do? Like just last night, he came home yelling at me like usual and all the dishes were still in the sink and all the laundry was all on the bed, but like I couldn't even tell him that like I looked online for jobs, which I was, I thought I should be proud of, but I didn't even... I don't know, I didn't even find a job, so whatever, it's fine, it's not that big of a deal, but I just thought maybe like we could talk about that, but he was just yelling about his shirts needing to be ironed and I just couldn't do any of it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you feel that even though you made some progress by looking at jobs this week, that you didn't feel much accomplishment from that because your husband didn't acknowledge it or appreciate it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, he doesn't appreciate anything I do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How does being unappreciated make you feel inside?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It just makes my whole body just ache. It just makes me feel empty. Like, if he can't appreciate the things I do, then why would I be motivated to do the things he wants me to do? Like how am I supposed to iron his shirts when I can't even get out of bed in the morning, you know? It just makes me feel really just... just empty and just miserable.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I hear you saying that you're shutting down. And not only do I hear you saying that, but I can see you sitting here with me, with the way you're sitting with your arms crossed, I feel like you're closing yourself off to a lot of things, to a lot of people.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah, definitely, I am, because they don't notice anything I do. And I mean, on Monday, like, I actually got out of the house, which I thought was like a big deal in the moment. But I took the cat to the groomers. My husband's been bugging me about that for months and you know, I got out of the house, I drove to the groomers, I changed out of my pajamas, and like all these things are a big deal to me but he doesn't even see that as like an accomplishment. He didn't even notice. Like my daughter didn't notice either. She just comes home and slams the door and doesn't even look at me. And the cat was all groomed, had a nice little bow, and no one even... it's been like five days since then and no one's even said anything since then.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I feel like I've made this huge accomplishment for myself by getting out of the door even and taking the cat to the groomers, but then when I get home and it's not noticed by anyone, it takes it all away. It doesn't even matter to me.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Exactly. Exactly.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So for things to matter to you and for you to feel good about the even little progress steps you're making, you really need to have that acknowledged by your husband and your daughter?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I mean, otherwise what's the point, you know? If I don't have that support... all they do is point out the things I haven't done. Like I'll do something, but it's all about what hasn't been done. Like, 'oh, you haven't vacuumed in two months,' but they don't notice the things that I actually do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I feel, I hear you saying that you're experiencing a lot of hurt.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. It's a lot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So Bethany, you're feeling all this hurt. You're feeling like nobody's recognizing who you are. You have all this laundry and work and vacuuming to do, all these chores. It's a lot. Do you think there's a way we can maybe like put it away somewhere for a little bit to be able to address other issues?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can try.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Um, can you try putting it in a little jar and being able to put all that hurt in a jar?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's hard, it feels like there's so much of it, it won't fit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. Um, maybe do you need a bigger space maybe for it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, let's try putting it in the corner over here. Um, let's try one more time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's hard, it's like it won't disconnect from me, I just can't separate it from myself.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Um, so what do you think that that hurt's trying to tell you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's take a minute and think about it. If it needed something...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, like maybe it's just telling me that this is what I always do, I always try to avoid it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Um, well, let's tell the hurt that maybe the hurt is important and that we'll be able to come back to it once you've pushed it away. So it's not going to be gone forever. Um, so can we do that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess we could try. I just know it's... it's trying to tell me that that's not going to work. It's just... yeah, I feel like it's just what I always do with it, I always just try to avoid it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright, well let's try doing this. Let's try closing your eyes. We'll do some breathing exercises here. Take a deep breath in. Deep breath out. Deep breath in. Deep breath out. Imagine all the laundry, and the husband, and the daughter, and the cat... just put it outside in the hallway, the very far end of the hallway. Breathe in. Breathe out. Okay. Open your eyes. How's that feel?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, I guess I'm so... I'm feeling a little bit more relaxed, but I still don't feel good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Um, is it in the hallway or are you still hanging on to it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess it's in the hallway now, just different things kind of coming up.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Um, so what are you, what are you feeling? What do you want to talk about?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, I guess I'm kind of lost. What should I talk about?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I don't have an agenda today. So whatever, whatever comes to mind, whatever you feel is important.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. Um, I mean, do you have any suggestions?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, let's take a minute and think about it. Close your eyes again. And think about what you're feeling. So what are you feeling right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess what it really is, is I feel guilty, like for even letting go of that hurt. Like I... I need that hurt, or like that hurt makes me feel guilty, like I shouldn't be hurting. Like part of me needs to hurt and part of me just feels so bad for even hurting like I should be taking care of my family and I just feel a lot of guilt.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you feel guilty when you hurt. You're not worthy of feeling hurt, you're not worthy of feeling good?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, exactly. It's like I feel guilty for even feeling hurt, but I feel guilty for feeling good. It's like I don't deserve happiness, but I know I probably deserve to feel better. It's just, no matter what, I just feel guilty.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So I want to kind of delve into that a little bit, that guilt that you're feeling that's arising into this hurt. Would you be willing to try something with me?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I can try.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So what we're going to do is I want you to think about this chair and I want you to picture yourself over here. This is the side of you that says you don't deserve to be able to feel guilty, and that you don't deserve to be hurt. So I want you to focus on yourself. Okay. Um, tell yourself about how it makes you feel to be guilty about hurting.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just feel like I... I feel guilty for hurting because it makes me... it forces me to just stay in bed and it makes me feel... hurt makes me feel like I'm incapable of taking care of my family and I need to take care of my family. And I just feel guilty because while I'm hurting, I can't do that, I can't be there for them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It hurts to know when I'm hurt.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It hurts to know when I'm hurt.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And I deserve more than being hurt.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I deserve more than being hurt.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And I want to be there for my family.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I want to be there for my family.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And I deserve to be there for my family.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: And I deserve to be there for my family.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You don't deserve to be, feel guilty about being hurt.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You don't deserve to feel guilty about being hurt.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you need to take care of your family and stop being so selfish.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I need to stop being so selfish, my family needs me, I need to take care of them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And when you don't take care of them, they get upset.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's why they're always mad at you, because you don't take care of them, you're selfish.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's what it feels like.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How does it make you feel when yourself tells you that you're selfish?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It hurts. It makes me really sad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm sad, it makes me, it hurts me when you tell me I'm selfish.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It hurts me when you tell me I'm selfish. When you tell me I'm not there for my family or that I don't care about them, because I do care about them so much. I'm trying my best.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Why are you making me feel guilty about being hurt? I have needs too.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have needs, I need to be taken care of too. I can't always be... I'm a person too.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you're not taking care of me. You're not allowing me to feel good.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You're not allowing me to feel good. Feeling selfish and guilty doesn't allow me to feel good, and that's the only way I'll even be there for my family.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How's it feel when you hear that your hurt, the hurt and the pain that you're feeling...?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It just feels like I need to... I need to step it up and I need to try even harder.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So when you tell yourself that 'I'm hurt' and then you tell yourself 'I'm selfish,' how does that feel inside?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's just really confusing. It's like I need to break out of this guilty feeling and just allow myself to hurt. I deserve to hurt. I... I need to hurt sometimes. And it's okay.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I need to hurt sometimes, and that's okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I deserve to have my needs met as well.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I deserve to have my needs met as well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, how does it make you feel that your other self understands the hurt that you're feeling?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Actually, it does feel... I mean, I'm still hurting, but it's almost like it's okay to hurt now. I feel... I feel better that you're allowing me to hurt.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel better that you're allowing me to hurt. I feel validated. I need to help my family and I need to hurt and show them that I'm hurting but not feel guilty about it. That way I can be there for them and they can really understand what's going on with me. I need, I need these things too. Yeah, I need things too. I have needs too.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So how do you feel inside right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Almost feel energized. I feel lighter, like some of that guilt is gone. Even if I'm still really hurt and I feel really sad, it just feels more okay to feel that way.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When you hear that you need things, and it's okay to be hurt, and 'I need to be validated,' tell yourself how you can maybe do that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I can do more of that. I can feel hurt without feeling guilty. And I can feel okay about hurting. And I can talk about hurting without... without feeling guilty about it. It's okay to hurt.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And it doesn't make me selfish to need things.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it doesn't make me selfish to need things.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So now you can come to an agreement with yourself to allow that space to hurt without the guilt.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think so. I think so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So we're, we're actually out of time for today. So, um, I want you to take this awareness with you this week, um, and then we'll pick up again next week.

video_details.title: Emotionally Focused Therapy for Gay Couples Video
video_details.description: The therapeutic needs of gay ouples are given some long-overdue attention in this masterful video with Emotionally Focused Therapy (EFT) originator Dr. Sue Johnson, who offers fresh hope to a gay couple using her signature framework for repairing the partners' emotional "dance." For the full video, go to: http://www.psychotherapy.net/video/emotionally-focused-therapy-gay-lesbian-couples

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tim, what's hard? I mean, how does your body feel when you think about showing him that vulnerable side of you? Can you feel that in your body? How does that feel?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The vulnerability... the sadness is like a stone in my belly. Sort of like heavy and wanting to lift that stone out, so to speak.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The vulnerability... it's so painful for you to be vulnerable.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't want to be... it's so painful to be vulnerable. Whereas I think you have seen me in vulnerable situations more because of medical problems. And when someone else is vulnerable, not me, I can be seen as capable.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there's a sadness here when your partner says he doesn't really see that softer part of you. It feels like a stone in your stomach. For you to actually touch that vulnerability and show him, there's something about not being capable then, not being strong. Is that it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really knowing how to do that. How to actually name it or stay with that vulnerability and feel comfortable about doing that. It's associated with trust, but it's very, very difficult to actually do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's difficult for all of us to give that up and we all have that sense of needing to protect ourselves. We've often learned that it's a bad idea to be vulnerable, and you're in a cultural context where that's not encouraged.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: And to some degree we have been vulnerable because of the cultural context of being gay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yes, you're even more vulnerable being gay. There's a vulnerability about being gay, period. So there's an even greater need to protect yourself.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I validate and normalize their need to protect themselves as individuals and gay men in a heterosexual world. So what's happened to them since?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I've continued to work with them. We've had seven more sessions since you saw them. We're still working on de-escalation, which in a withdraw-withdraw couple is getting each of them to engage.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Out on the dance floor. They now describe their relationship as moving from a tribal dance where they were each jumping up and down in one spot individually, into doing a fluid waltz together.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's beautiful. I love that. So they're feeling much...

video_details.title: Cognitive Behavioural Therapy Techniques for Psychosis
video_details.description:
Professor Douglas Turkington
Insight CBT Partnership

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I've just been hearing about this belief that everyone's hearing your thoughts, that they've somehow been transmitted into their heads. And it sounds as though out of all the things that are going on, that's the thing that's most distressing for you, that other people can actually read your thoughts.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I could cope with all of the rest, but I'm really anxious. I'm sweating just now, and I'm really worried about all these people knowing my thoughts.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, okay. I mean, one of the things that I think we need to do is to try and get some more evidence really to find out, you know, what is really going on here.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, I wish we knew.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Because it seems like there's something going on, but I'm not quite sure what it is. So what I'd like to do is to try and do some kind of an experiment so that we can gather some more information and see what happens.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I'd like to think of an experiment in some ways that tests out whether people can read your thoughts. That's really the crux of it all.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's exactly it. That's what I want to do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. I'm just wondering if you've got any kind of creative ideas that you could think of that would find out whether or not people are, you know, that if I was watching, we would know one way or the other or find a bit more information about what's going on.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So we're both going to watch?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What I was just thinking, it might be useful if I was there because at the moment, I mean, how at the moment do you know that people are reading your thoughts?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I stay in my flat a lot, as you know, because I'm a bit too scared to go out. But sometimes, maybe it's like once every couple of hours, I can feel it starting to come on and then there's the whoosh, thought's gone, empty head. And it goes out and I look out the window and I can see that like there's one woman talking to another woman and she turns, she turns her head away. I'm thinking, oh jinx, they've gone out again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's something about how people react at that time. Right, okay. So, any thoughts about what we might be able to do?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Think of a really funny joke. But my thoughts aren't like that. My thoughts are mixed up and sad and shameful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you think of something that would get a real reaction from people in terms of behavior that we could observe? Something that, you know, there would be absolutely no questions about what was going on in terms of how people reacted in terms of behavior.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: In terms of seeing them actually moving. That might be something that would be quite useful, yeah. Well, suppose I think a thought that, you know that band One Direction?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I've heard of them.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Suppose I think One Direction are about to open a supermarket in the shopping center. Because like people go crazy for them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So if you had that thought and it went 'whoosh', what would we expect to see?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I think some people would be disgusted because they don't like them. But lots of people would be running to the supermarket, I think.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So if I was with you and I said 'right, you need to keep having that thought', we would see people running towards the supermarket?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You would definitely see some of the younger end of the market running.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay then. Okay, so that would prove that people were actually getting that thought. Okay, if we were in that situation and people didn't start running, what do you think that would mean?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Might mean they don't like One Direction, might mean they didn't pick it up, might mean they're preoccupied with their own thoughts, I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. Because I'm just wondering if we're going to set this up as an experiment, we've got to think about how we're going to interpret the results when we see them. So I suppose that's one thing. It needs to be something that we're pretty convinced that if we don't get a result, there's a good chance it means they're not picking up your thoughts, if you know what I mean.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It needs to be something bigger than this One Direction thing, doesn't it? I just wonder, maybe some kind of super sale. Things are cut to 20% of their proper price. Really nice furniture and clothes and stuff.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, okay. And what would happen if people didn't run when they got that thought? What would that mean?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I suppose that I'd start to wonder if the thoughts were going to them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So it might make you wonder whether or not it was happening or not.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Because it needs to be a valid experiment, I suppose that's what I'm trying to get at. It's no good setting up an experiment if it doesn't really give us any more information.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: But if it's not going to them, where are they going?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, perhaps that's the next thing to think about. So first of all, is it going to the other folks? And then the next bit is, well, if it's not, because we don't know, it might be that everyone starts running through the shopping center at this stage, in which case we're going to have to deal with that. But for now, I suppose we just need to look at that. So is there a certain time or kind of particular shopping center we need to go to?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, we can look at my window and we can see the shopping center. And it's every couple of hours this happens.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So we could do it from your flat and we could actually observe what's going on outside. And you'd be happy that that was a pretty decent experiment to test things out?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, if you were there, that would really help me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Okay then, shall we arrange a time then and we can set that up?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm.

video_details.title: Clinical communication skills - communication using an interpreter
video_details.description: A demonstration of how to use interpreting services in primary care consultations, identifying post ail pitfalls and good practice.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello there, I'm Dr. David. Can I just check your surname?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Razia Bibi.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Ah, Mrs. Bibi. Can I confirm your date of birth?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Birth? No Bibi born. 42 years old.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: 42 years old. How can I help you today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: For five days, I've had diarrhea, vomiting, and stomach pain. I can't eat anything and I feel very weak.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Where is the pain? Do you have any other symptoms?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The pain is bad all over my stomach. I have vomiting and diarrhea.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you taken any tablets for your symptoms?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My husband got some small pink tablets from a chemist, but I don't know the name.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you been throwing up? Is it vomiting or retching?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's vomiting. Everything comes out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you had any loose stools or diarrhea?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, it's very thin and watery, about every 20 minutes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can I examine you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No check, no check.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I can organize a Punjabi interpreter for tomorrow and we can meet again. Does that work?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Tomorrow? Okay, doctor. Tomorrow.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good morning. I am the interpreter. Let's arrange the seating for eye contact and speak directly to the patient in the first person.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello, I am the interpreter. Everything we discuss will be confidential. Dr. David would like to start the consultation again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me what the problem has been?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's been five days of bad diarrhea and vomiting. I have stomach pain all over and feel very weak.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you still vomiting? What is the diarrhea like?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The vomiting stopped three days ago. The diarrhea is better but still watery and foul-smelling. There is no blood.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How often are you opening your bowels?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It used to be every 20 minutes, but now it's about every 40 minutes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me more about the tummy pain. Is it constant or crampy?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It is a crampy pain that comes and goes, maybe four to five times a day, though I have a mild pain all the time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The notes say you aren't on regular medication, but you took some pink tablets for diarrhea?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, from the chemist, but I don't know the name. I generally feel healthy and don't usually visit the doctor.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can I examine your abdomen on the couch?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm comfortable if the interpreter stays with me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I've examined you and found nothing to worry about. It sounds like a tummy bug called gastroenteritis.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It should get better by itself. I can prescribe something for the diarrhea.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have been taking some herbal medicine from my neighbor. Can I continue that?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's best not to take the herbal medicine so I know how the prescription works. You should also provide a stool sample.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'll stop the herbal medicine. Can I get a bottle for the sample?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You can pick up a bottle and an Urdu leaflet from reception. I've prescribed one tablet to be taken three to four times a day.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Is the medicine strong? I sometimes get heartburn.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It shouldn't cause heartburn. It's just to slow the bowel down. Any more questions?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, that's all. Bye-bye.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Bye-bye.

video_details.title: Emotionally Focused Therapy for Lesbian Couples Video
video_details.description:
To watch the full video go to: http://www.psychotherapy.net/video/emotionally-focused-therapy-gay-lesbian-couples

The therapeutic needs of lesbian couples are given some long-overdue attention in this masterful video with Emotionally Focused Therapy (EFT) originator Dr. Sue Johnson, who offers fresh hope to a lesbian couple using her signature framework for repairing the partners' emotional "dance."

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Physically, physically, why won't you engage, I guess is what I put in and you said...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You're saying I'm inviting you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'm constantly sort of there in the moment and, you know, being lovey-dovey and what-not, and it's like I'm not there. You know, we've still more things to talk...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm the one saying you're not there. I'm the one saying we have more things to figure out and what-not. So it's kind of a brush-off, it's kind of...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Nope. So, does that make me a little bit perturbed? For sure. Because I'm thinking, well, how do we fix this? I'm not saying that sex fixes everything because it doesn't, but how do we get past that part of it if you won't take the step to get past that part of it, is what I'm...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what does happen there? That must be painful for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Nothing, we just continue. Just like, whatever, we're watching TV or...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You know, whatever. But...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That has to be...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Is it stewing inside? Absolutely. But do I say anything further? Yep.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That has to be painful for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yep, a little bit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you think she understands how painful that is for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. No. And it's funny because I'll run things through my head with questions that I want to ask but I don't ask them. You want once in a while ask... it took me a long time to ask you that question, 'why won't you engage with me?' and it was probably two or three days and I'm thinking, 'okay, I'm going to ask,' and just...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you help, can you help Janie right now understand what that, a little bit of what that feels like when you're aware that you're reaching, right? And you're reaching and you're hoping that Janie is going to respond in a certain way and you're going to have more physical intimacy and somehow you experience that Janie closes the door or... can you help her understand a little bit of what happens to you in that moment? That's painful.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think she knows. But it is... yeah, it's... it is painful. It's hurtful. It makes me feel like I... that you don't want me, type thing. And it's... it's not a good feeling. To feel not wanted and... kind of brushed off and... no. So it makes me feel...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You feel brushed off. Not wanted. Small. Is that what you're doing with your hand?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think that you really were able to deliver exactly what I was hoping would happen in the session in terms of helping Janie to reach a little bit deeper and move away from the complaining and the demand to the need to have Kelly really be there for her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: To go on an emotional level.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, her fear, her fear of reaching out and getting hurt. Really helping bring her to that and having that corrective experience with her partner who really, really wants to be there for her. And I think, I think for Kelly, it's a new challenge and an exciting one to be the one that's taking care of her partner.

video_details.title: Clinical communication skills - communication with child patients version 2
video_details.description:
A demonstration of the correct use of communication skills used in an interview with a child patient.

See a video highlighting the incorrect way to communicate with child patients here: http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BZfOYvPmcjo

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello there. It must be Martin, is that right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, Martin, yeah. And Martin's dad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good. I'm Dr. Bay. I haven't seen you since you were little. How old are you now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Ten.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Ten. Gosh. I remember doing your jabs. How can I help you both today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He's been getting tummy pains for about two weeks now and has been off school. I'm worried it might be something more than ordinary pain. Since I lost my job, I'm home quite a bit, so him being off hasn't been a logistical problem.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'll ask a few questions. Martin, what school are you at, and how is it going? Do you have any hobbies?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm at Ladybay School. My teacher is Mr. Pearson. School is going well; I play football and support Spurs.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me more about the tummy pain. Where is it exactly, and what is it like?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's really bad in the mornings but fades away by the afternoon. It's a queasy pain near my belly button.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does it cause vomiting or any issues with bowel movements? Have you been losing any weight?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, everything's fine there. He actually eats for two people sometimes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does the pain happen every day, including weekends?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, not on weekends. Just weekdays.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's examine your tummy. I'll have a gentle feel while you lie on the couch.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The good news is I couldn't find anything to worry about. Martin, has anything happened or changed in the last two weeks?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We have a new P.E. teacher, Miss Croft. She's strict about trainers and isn't very nice. I lost mine and didn't think Dad would be happy because we don't have much money.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Trainers are just trainers; you should have said something. We have plenty of money for new ones. I'm sorry you were worried.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sometimes stress at school can cause physical symptoms like tummy aches, which would explain why it doesn't happen at weekends.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's get new trainers and see how things go. If the pain doesn't settle, come back and see me. Hopefully, it will go away.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Let's hope so. Thank you, doctor.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does that sound all right? Happy, Dad?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, happy. Bye.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Nice to see you. Bye-bye then.

video_details.title: DBT for Anxiety Mock Interview
video_details.description: Dialectical behavior therapy mock interview session for client with anxiety. Includes 5 senses grounding exercise.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well hello Susan.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hello.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good to see you today.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thanks.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So tell me what brings you in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I have an anxiety issue. There are a lot of things that make me anxious and I gotta do something different because I'm really not functioning at the level I need to be functioning. My anxiety just really impacts a lot of my life. So I need help with managing it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so tell me what that looks like for you, anxiety in those situations.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Driving here on the interstate, I'm just panicking constantly about the cars. I've had a couple of accidents and I'm constantly thinking people are about to hit me. In school, I get really anxious when I take a test. I know the information, but I sit down and I can't recall because I'm so anxious about the test.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So is it physical, or is it a lot of thoughts in your head?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's a lot of thoughts in my head and it is very physical. I get sweaty palms, my heart starts racing, I get tense.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what are the thoughts going on in your head?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When I'm in the car, I think I'm gonna get hit. If I'm taking a test, it's like, okay, I gotta do well on this test. I gotta remember this. And I just kind of freeze because I'm panicking that I can't remember.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And so with the test, have you found that to be a problem as far as not being able to complete the test or not doing well?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I know I could perform better if I wasn't so anxious. It wouldn't take me as long. The anxiety subsides after the situation is over, just like in the car when I get off the interstate.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it sounds like we might need to find something that helps you in the moment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I want something at the time to help me in the moment because these are things that I can't avoid. I've got to do these group settings with kids at work. I can't change them, so I gotta figure out how to deal with it better.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, well would you like to learn a skill?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I am eager to learn something that can make a difference.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, well there is something called grounding. Have you heard of that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, just like electricity grounding, you know, that third plug thing. I need to be grounded, that sounds good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Being grounded is getting to a level place. For some people emotions get really intense, like your anxiety. Grounding tries to learn ways to bring that down to a calm place to deal with it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That sounds good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm going to introduce a grounding technique to you. It involves some deep breathing, closing your eyes, and getting into your senses. I have a script here to read to you. To begin, just relax and be as comfortable as you can. Rest your hands and just breathe. Try deep breathing where your chest rises and you breathe out. Now we're going to use the five senses. Close your eyes, listen to my voice, and notice all the sounds around you. Tell me what you hear.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I kind of hear my breath. I hear the air coming through the vent, like a constant noise.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you think you noticed that sound before I mentioned it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I'm just hearing it now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's move on to smell. Do you smell anything in the room?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really, there's not a lot of scents right now. No flowers or anything, just smelly air.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Open your eyes and let's talk about sight. List some things you can see in this room right now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I see you, that picture, that sofa, some books and flowers, and that deer thing over there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What about the colors of what you see?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Blue, red, a lot of beige, and orange. Clashing colors.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And when you first came here, did you notice those?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I might have noticed some, but I'm more aware now because I'm focusing on it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Next is taste. In other situations you could eat a snack and savor the textures, but even without food you can taste the saliva in your mouth. Are there any tastes from this morning?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I had a granola bar, a banana, and some tea. The flavor right now is probably the tea.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Finally, the sense of touch. Where your hands are right now, what are you feeling?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was feeling my hands because I cross my fingers.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Put your hands on the couch and describe how it feels.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It feels solid and soft. It feels secure and comfortable.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Find something else, like your phone, and describe that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: This is hard, but it has a cushy case on it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What about the paper there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Silky, smooth, bendable, thin, and slick.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now, for a moment, get comfortable again and close your eyes. Take a deep breath three times. With your eyes closed, come up with a statement you can say to yourself when you're feeling anxiety. Something like 'I'll be okay.' Say it out loud.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Something encouraging, like 'you can do it' or 'I will be okay.'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Say your statement out loud.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Say it with confidence.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can do it!

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Open your eyes. We went through each sense as a distraction to focus your mind on details and help you calm down. It's important to breathe through it. How was that for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It did calm me down. I was getting revved up talking about what makes me anxious, but I forgot about it focusing on my senses. It got my mind off of that and onto something else.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Was there a certain sense you found most helpful?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably what I'm seeing and hearing. Those two and feeling seem most helpful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Think about how we can use this when you're driving. You can't close your eyes, so what senses can you use?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Seeing, obviously, and feeling the wheel. I could listen to more soothing music instead of NPR to help me calm down.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Also, the sound of the road and cars going by.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The music might help me more because hearing just the cars might make me nervous. I'll try music.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: With sight, focus on the car in front of you instead of being distracted by cars behind you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What about when you're taking a test? What senses can we tap into there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Looking at the questions, feeling the pen or the keyboard, and hearing the quiet or the vent.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Try to tap into hearing. Don't think about the function of typing, just the feel of the keyboard to be aware that it's there.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, being aware that it is there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Next time you feel anxiety, try this. You can even take a five-minute break and dedicate one minute to each sense. Do it before you start a drive or a test. Remember your statement, 'I can do this.'

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can do this! Say it with gusto. I can do this.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When is the next time you could do this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have to drive home today, and I have a test next week. I drive every day, so I can try that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How about before you even leave, while you're sitting in your car?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'll take a few minutes in the parking lot to go through the senses, put on music, and say 'I can do it' before I proceed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That sounds like a good plan. We'll talk next week and see how it goes. Different situations might not need all the senses, so just focus on what calms you down.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sounds good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you for coming in today.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thanks for the tip. I'll try that out.

video_details.title: Communication Skills 1
video_details.uploader: Pass MRCPCH - London Paediatrics Trainees Committee
video_details.description:
MRCPCH Clinical Revision - more videos at http://mrcpch.paediatrics.co.uk

Revise for your MRCPCH Clinical exam, with videos and high quality content created by the London Paediatrics Trainees Committee.

Video Credits: Dr Caroline Fertleman, Dr Hermione Race, Dr Camilla Sen, Dr Chloe Macaulay, Dr Emma McLaren, Chris Knapp

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, Mr. and Mrs. Scott? I'm Chloe McCauley, one of the baby doctors.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hi, yeah. Nice to meet you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Congratulations, I understand you've just had your first baby, is that right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. Happy, although these people have been in and out, so we're a bit on edge and bit confused about what's happening.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Well, that's why I've come to talk to you. Tell me what you understand so far. What have people said to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Basically, after my wife gave birth a few hours ago, they told us the baby was healthy, but they couldn't decide whether it was a girl or boy. No one's really said anything, they're just whispering and we're just confused.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What you say is absolutely right and I'm sorry that you feel confused, but sometimes at the beginning things aren't clear and we need a bit of time to sort things out over the next few hours and days.
