I've actually been to see your baby myself. Sometimes when babies are born you can't be certain what sex the baby is and it's really important not to say one thing and then be wrong. In lots of cases, what you see is you're not sure is either a very swollen clitoris or a very small penis, and that's the case with your baby. It may be that in 24 hours the swelling has subsided and it's very clear the baby's one sex or another, but for now we can't be sure.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So you're saying there's something wrong with our baby?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm not saying that. I'm saying there is potentially a cause for making the fact that your baby's genitalia don't look normal. So what we need to do is various tests in order to get to the bottom of it. The first thing I want to say is it may be that every single test we do is normal and tomorrow when we look at the baby we can say 'this is looking much more like a boy' or 'much more like a girl.' But we'd still like those tests to reassure us. The tests that we do is we'll do some tests looking at the baby's genes to see whether the genes are the genes of a baby girl or a baby boy. And then we'll also do some other blood tests looking at some other salt levels in the blood because they can sometimes be abnormal.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Gene tests... does that mean it's our fault?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's a very good question and no, it definitely isn't your fault. The commonest cause for us seeing this, although it is very uncommon, the commonest cause is a hormone problem which we can pick up on the blood test. So that's why we want to do a blood test.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Is it something you can manage or is it something lifelong? What does that mean?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I can understand that you've got loads of questions and it's a time of great uncertainty. What we can do is we don't know and I don't want to start talking in great detail about the different possibilities until we know what it is. So what we're going to do is we're going to do two tests in the immediate term and that's to see whether the baby has got chromosomes of a boy or chromosomes of a girl. And we'll do this other test looking for this hormone problem. And they will give us a lot of information in the first instance and then we will take it from there thinking about what, if anything, we need to do. As I say, it may be that your baby's totally normal. If they have one of these hormone problems, that is something that we can treat very easily.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So what are we going to do now? Because our relatives keep coming in and they're like, 'what's his name?'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I think the best way to approach it is to just say sometimes it's not clear and it may become clearer and they're just going to do some tests.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Are the tests going to hurt the baby?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the tests that we're going to do in the first instance are blood tests, so that's just a prick with a needle and babies at this age aren't normally bothered by blood tests. And then after that we might go on in the next few days to do some more tests, but I can talk about those if and when we need to do them.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: This is quite overwhelming. A bit of a shock really, I think. Wasn't exactly... will we be able to talk to some more people later on? I'm sure I have a lot of things going through my head that I'd like to ask.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sure. Well, I can leave you now just to kind of get your head around it because I know that it's a lot to think about. But the essence of it is, and I can just go over it again in simple terms if you like, is that we can't be sure what sex your baby is. This sometimes happens and it sometimes turns out to be nothing. Occasionally, and the commonest and most urgent thing for us to work out is if it's a hormone problem, so that's why we're doing the blood tests. And we're also doing some genetic tests to look at what sex, what genetic sex the baby is. So they will help us. So we'll have much more information in a day or two but we won't get those tests back straight away because it takes a bit of time. And so just for now if you can bear to, it's just better if of course you can have the baby with you and you can start bonding with the baby and introduce the baby to everyone but just we can't be sure at the moment and I know that's difficult but we will know in the next few days.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: But the baby is okay?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The baby is fine and whatever it is we'll get to the bottom of it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. I feel a bit better now. At least he's okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there anything else you want to ask?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not at the moment, we'll have a lot of questions later.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I'll come back in about an hour or two and we can talk about it again if you want, if there's some more questions that come to mind. Okay? Thank you.

video_details.title: CBT Mock Session-Bethany

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Jessica, how are you doing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm alright, how about you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing okay. So, how have you been doing today? How's your week been?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's been okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In our last session together, we talked about your lack of confidence. Do you feel like you've made any progress on that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've been journaling like you said, and I think that's kind of helping. I feel like there's still a lot of room for improvement, but it has improved slightly.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So when you say you've been journaling, were you able to write down the negative thoughts when they occurred?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, and I'm noting what was taking place like you told me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And were you able to make it a positive thought?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I tried to do that. It helped some. I think if I just keep doing it, maybe it'll get better. I was more aware of how often it occurs.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you remember what we discussed last time about how CBT works?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A little bit, not exactly, but I do remember how my thoughts are causing things.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, would you like to review it? Say a situation happens, you have a thought, then an emotion, and then a behavior. Do you understand that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You also mentioned problems with marijuana use, depression, and anger issues. Which one would you like to discuss today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably the anger issues. I feel like that's the biggest problem going on in my life right now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me more about your anger issues.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I get defensive, and that's usually when I lash out. It's usually always at my husband.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me about the last time you lashed out at your husband?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We were unloading groceries. I had just had my hair done, and he thought about how much it cost. He told me I was selfish, and then I hit him.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The situation was that you got your hair done and he was angry about that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, he was just saying mean things.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What was your actual thought in that moment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm selfish. Initially, yeah, that was it. He's right, that was selfish.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How did that make you feel when you thought you were being selfish?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Guilty, sad, and then very angry that he had made me feel that way.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So when he was telling you that you were selfish and you felt that way and got angry, what did you do?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I smacked him.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so there was physical contact there.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I hit him upside his head. I felt bad afterwards, but I was so mad that he would even feel that way.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just lashed out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How do you think you could change from smacking him to having a more calm response?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I think if I wasn't able to get as angry.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: With CBT, we change the thought. How could you not feel selfish? Do you think you're selfish?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Now, I don't think it was selfish to want to feel prettier. We have plenty of money. He's just kind of a cheap person.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you don't think you're selfish at all.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: In this situation, I don't think I was wrong. We had enough money for me to afford it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So instead of thinking you're selfish, what could you think?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I deserve this.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If you were thinking 'I deserve this', what emotion would you feel?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would feel confident in my decision. I would still feel sad that he thought that, but not at the same level.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you think that would in turn change your behavior?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think it would help me realize that that's his issue and not mine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How would you behave then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Walk off, or be able to express it in a non-violent manner. He didn't deserve for me to hit him.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Maybe you could say to yourself that he just doesn't understand, and explain that it makes you feel good about yourself.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I could try that. If he understood why I did it, that might help as well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Could you try to change your thoughts in the coming week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can try, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would you like to discuss the depression or your marijuana use?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We can talk about the depression.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. What do you think triggers your depression?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My son's at the age where he doesn't want to be involved as much. He's growing up, and now I'm left alone.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How old is your son?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He's 14.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, that's an interesting age.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He doesn't want me to call as much, and that's normal, but it still makes me feel really depressed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the situation is that your son doesn't want to be involved with you as much.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think he's just growing up.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you think to yourself when he's out doing his own thing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He got upset at me because he felt I was trying to mommy him. It just made me feel like I'm not needed anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what is your exact thought when this happens?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm not needed anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's hard when you've always been needed before.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How did that make you feel?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sad and lonely. I felt really lonely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how did you behave in that situation?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That ties into the marijuana, because then I smoked a couple of joints.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you think you use marijuana because you're depressed?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think they go together.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you don't feel needed, you feel sad and lonely, and then you use marijuana.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you want to use marijuana?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. I wouldn't be a good influence on my son, and I don't want that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Before the next session, I want you to journal and try to change negative thoughts to positive ones.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can try, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Think instead that he's growing up and you've raised an active son. How would you feel then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that might make me feel better because he's a good person because of me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does journaling sound good?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'll try it.

video_details.title: DBT for Anger Mock Interview
video_details.description: Dialectical behavior therapy mock interview session for teen aged client with anger issues. Includes S.T.O.P. technique.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello, Alyssa.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hello.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's good to see you today. I'm glad you could see me. So tell me a little bit more about why you're here.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, well I guess I have anger issues. I just find myself getting mad all the time and I get in a lot of trouble over it. People can't handle it, so they told me to come here for it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So who told you to come here for it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The courts. Okay, so yeah, I'm not really... I don't really want to be here, so...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're not excited about being here. Yeah, I hear you. Well, what is your objective? What do you want out of this today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, I know I'm probably angrier than the average person. So people do a lot of things to make me mad, so I guess I'd like to find a way to not be so mad all the time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And maybe manage that a little bit better.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Tell me, um, is it school you're getting mad, is it home you're getting mad, is it friends? Tell me about that a little bit.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess with my friends I'm cool. It's just definitely at home with my mom. We fight almost every day. And at school I get in fights with the teachers, so I get like detention and stuff like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Before we get into this a little bit, I'd like to tell you a little bit about your brain. Have you ever heard of the amygdala? It's known as the alarm center. It normally indicates fight, flight, or freeze.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'm definitely a fighter.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, you're a fighter. Tell me an example when the alarm is going off and you are really angry.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just yesterday with my mom, she told me to do the dishes. I just wanted the show to end, but she kept yelling and I started yelling at her. I ended up punching a wall.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And that was just yesterday?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that was just yesterday.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Your mom asked you to do something, she pestered you, and it escalated until you punched a wall. Tell me about a situation at school when your alarm center is going off.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My history teacher. I tend to sleep in class and she'll call me out in front of the whole class. We'll start going back and forth and I'll end up cursing her out and going to detention.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I see. Teacher's calling you out and you respond with a lot of anger and cursing. Is there any time when there's anxiety happening before the anger comes out?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: What do you mean by anxiety?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Like, if you ever get anxious where you just kind of freeze? Or is yours a more reactive fight or lash out?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I definitely feel something I have to get it out. I can't even think of a time when I actually stop and think.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. I want to help you monitor and control the anger reactions using a technique called Stop. S-T-O-P.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'd like that. I don't see myself being too good at it, but...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Knowing that you need that is a really big step. I'm hearing you say that you want to make a change and that's really huge.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. But also just wish people would stop messing with me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Let's try this technique this week. It only takes about one minute for when you feel that anger rising in the heat of the moment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it happens real quick.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: S is for stop. T is for take a breath to get oxygen to your brain. O means observe the situation and how you're feeling. P is for proceed in a way that benefits you. Is yelling at your mom working for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It gets you in trouble. In that situation with your mom, do you have an idea that might work for you instead?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess talk to her, but it's hard to talk without yelling. If I stopped I wouldn't be quite so mad. I guess just tell her I'll do it later.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You might try asking if you can finish your show for 10 more minutes and then do the dishes. Put it in a question as a compromise. Does that sound like something that might work?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean that's what I said before but I guess I probably didn't love the way I was saying it and she was getting pissed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, I'm glad you can acknowledge that. That's a big step. So let's step through it again. S-T-O-P. The S is for...?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Stop.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. And what's the T?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Take a breath.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Exactly. What about O?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Observe.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And then what's the P?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh... proceed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Proceed in a helpful way. How are you going to proceed with your mom?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just talk to my mom calmly.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. Ask her calmly and try to compromise. It takes time to make a change, so be patient with yourself.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I see it being a struggle in the beginning. It's hard to just stop when she's yelling at me and stuff.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Be patient. Let's think about at school. You're in history class and the teacher is calling on you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, she always stops when she's calling on me like I have the answer.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is she asking for an answer or just telling you to wake up?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: She knows I was sleeping, so she'll ask me the hardest question and I obviously don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Instead of your normal reaction, what would you do using the Stop process?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't f***ing know, teacher.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Try to stop and take two breaths. How are you feeling then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just anger and frustration because she's just messing with me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're naming that frustration. Now, how do you proceed in a positive way instead of yelling and getting sent out of the room?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess just tell her I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's the truth and then she'll go to someone else. You won't get sent to detention. We want you to get to the next grade.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I want to.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This procedure only takes about 45 seconds to stop, breathe, observe, and then figure out the best tool to proceed. Again, be patient.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's going to take a while.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you willing to practice this once a day this next week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, yeah. Something's always coming up, so yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Try this and then we'll talk about it next week and see how it's going.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, I can do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Thanks for coming in, Alyssa. I appreciate you wanting to make a change.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Alright.

video_details.title: CBT Mock Session

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Glad you came in today. How's it going today for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, pretty much the same as it's been for the last few months. Um, not getting any better. Yeah, still feeling pretty down.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, from last week when we talked, you kind of told me about your situation, getting injured on the job and then losing your job and sleeping a lot. Your wife left you and took the kids and I know that's been very hard on you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. And I had you take that inventory and scored that and you in fact do have pretty severe depression.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think I already knew that. I wasn't surprised. I guess it's nice to get validation on that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Mm-hmm. So what I thought we might do today is a therapy I'd like to try with you called cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT. I don't know if you've ever heard of that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think I may have heard the name before.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'll describe it a little bit to you. We can work on that to help your depression. I want to give you some tools maybe to take home this week so you can kind of talk about the situations of your depression and thoughts and feelings and stuff and then next week we can have some concrete stuff to think about. Does that sound okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean I'm willing to try anything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's a big part of it. CBT takes a situation, a thought that automatically comes into the mind, how it makes you feel, and then how you respond because of that feeling. Tell me about the last time that you were feeling depressed.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably this morning. I woke up like 10:00 or so and just couldn't get out of bed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's the first thought that came into your mind?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I thought, why would I get out of bed? There's no reason for me to get out of bed. My wife's gone, I don't really have many friends anymore, and I don't have a job.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How'd that make you feel about yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Worthless, I guess. Like I don't really even matter. Just made me feel really bad and worthless.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Because of that feeling, what would you do? Were you able to get out of bed or just stayed in bed?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I stayed in bed until I came here. I was in bed most of the day.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, let me congratulate you for getting out of bed and coming here today. That's a big step. Do you often have those feelings of worthlessness?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'd say most of the time that's how I feel. That's what causes it I think.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And typically is your response to that feeling to stay in bed?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, if I'm in bed at the time, I won't get out. Sometimes I'll be on the couch and start thinking and feeling like that and then I just won't move.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tommy, can you remember a time when you weren't depressed?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, before the accident at work. Lots of times spending time with my kids.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me a little bit about those times when you can remember before the accident.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My kids would run and jump and wake me up in the morning. We'd get up and make pancakes and have a big long breakfast and on the weekend we'd go to the park or see a movie.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How'd you feel when those activities were going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just felt good. I felt loved by my kids and I loved them and it was just great.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like the opposite of worthless. Do you think it would help you to think about times when you felt pretty good about yourself when you're feeling down?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I guess I've never tried that before. I don't know if it'll work, but I'd be willing to try.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What about when you were working? How'd you feel about yourself at work?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I worked in a factory. I felt like I was doing something, like I had a purpose. Then the accident happened and I lost that and that's when I started to feel worthless.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm glad you can still remember some times when you felt that you did have a purpose. With depression, what you actually have to do is get up out of bed and do something, and then you feel better.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that makes sense what you said.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me some things that you might enjoy doing, that might be worth getting out of bed in order to do.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I always loved fishing. I always enjoyed doing that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When was the last time you went fishing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was a long time ago, way before the accident happened.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you recovered enough from the accident in which you could go fishing? Are there any other activities besides fishing that you might enjoy?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I think I could. I used to get together with my buddies and we'd usually have a cookout or watch football. I haven't talked to them in forever and since I've been feeling so down, I haven't made any effort.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that something that might be able to be planned, maybe a get together with one or two of your old buddies?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean I think we could do that. I guess I'd be willing to try.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there an activity you should do even by yourself, like exercising or listening to music?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Working out was always something that I did. I felt tired during the workout, but I always felt really good afterwards, like I had a purpose and accomplished something.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Those are some good suggestions. This next week, I'd like you to journal about when you're in bed and can't get out. Write about your automatic thought that's coming into your mind.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: There's no reason for me to get out of bed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Write that down, and then write down how that makes you feel and your reaction. Also, try to schedule one event a day that you enjoy doing and log how you feel after you did that. Does that feel overwhelming?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I feel good about that. It's just going to be different, but I'm willing to try.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: CBT really helps you think about what's going on and why you're feeling this way. You might even rate your emotion on a scale from 1 to 100 to see how that adjusts with time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That sounds like it would be helpful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. All right. Well, we'll talk about that next time.

video_details.title: Advanced Motivational Interviewing: Depression
video_details.description: Dr. Chip Watkins demonstrates Motivational Interviewing in treating depression.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Alvena, how are you doing today? It's good to see you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm just tired.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Just tired?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You know, we did some pre-visit planning with you and your PHQ-2, which is a short depression screen, was actually positive. So we asked the nurse to give you a little longer screening tool, which is a PHQ-9, and that actually did come up with a score of 8, which is in the mild depression range. So how does that feel?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I knew I felt different. I didn't know I was depressed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But you knew something was wrong.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I didn't feel like myself. I haven't been feeling like myself, no.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me a little bit more about not feeling like yourself.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, you know, I just go to work and I come home and I sleep. I wake up in the morning and I'm still tired. I just have no energy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you sleep a lot, but even though you're sleeping, you don't wake up rested.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, not at all.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Doesn't sound like good quality sleep.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. I just have no energy. I don't want to do anything but just sleep.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How long has that been going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess a couple months.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Two or three months.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What else is going on, Alvena?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, you know, I've been drinking more. I mean, I drink socially, but I find myself that when I come home, you know, I have a glass of wine and then I just go to sleep.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And that's worrisome to you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It is, because I don't usually drink that often during the week, so it's increased. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I can see where that would be bothersome to you. What else is going on with you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, you know, my mom died a year ago. So Mother's Day is coming up, so I've been thinking about mom a lot. I miss her, a lot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That anniversary is close.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And that's particularly hard when those anniversaries come around for the passings of our parents. That's a very difficult time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. And I took care of mom. So that's hard because for a long time, well, she was sick and she died from cancer, so I took care of her. So for a long time, that's all I did was take care of mom and work. So now that she's gone, it just kind of brings up everything all over again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Kind of a hole in your life.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, we were really close.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I'm really sorry for your loss, and thank you for sharing that with me. I know that's very difficult. So it sounds like your sleep has really been affected, you're not getting good quality sleep, you're really fatigued, just kind of going through the motions, it sounds like, during the day. And then, how's your appetite been?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really eating that much. You know, because I don't have energy. You know, before I would come home and cook dinner or, you know, meet some friends after work, but I don't want to do that. I just come home and have a glass of wine and just go to bed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you used to be more socially involved than you are now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I don't do anything now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A little more isolated.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, just working and come home and sleep.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So if there was something that you could do about this, what do you think you might like to do?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I don't want to stay like this. This isn't who I am, you know, just sleeping all the time. It's just... I don't want to stay this way.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Kind of feels like you're stuck at this point.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I just don't want to do anything or go out with my friends anymore and just work and come home and sleep. I don't want to do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's kind of the same old routine.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I wonder if it would be okay if we could talk about some of the options that are out there for folks that have some mild depression like you. Would that be all right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Most of the time we typically think about medication as a possible answer.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't want to do medication.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So no medication at this point. All right. Then I think as important certainly, perhaps more important than medication, is counseling and getting you to talk with someone about your feelings on a regular basis and getting some feedback on that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm okay with that. You know, when mom was sick, you know, she was in hospice care, so she had cancer, and the nurses and the doctors, you know, had our family talk to someone, you know, about what we were feeling.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So that was a pretty good experience then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. To talk to someone that understood what we were going through.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sure. Something else might be exercise. Another possibility would be a natural product. There's some things over the counter that I think for mild depression maybe be appropriate, and that's another thing that we could talk about if you wanted to learn a little bit more about those.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe something natural. Exercise, I don't have energy. I don't feel like doing anything, so I know I'm not going to exercise right now. But if it's something that's natural, you know, I could maybe try that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. If it's okay, let's go back to talking about the counseling for a minute, and then we can hit some of those other things too.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there a counselor that you know or that you have a relationship with? This lady that worked with you during your mom's death, is she someone that's out in the community?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: She was really nice, from... yeah, I liked her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it sounds like you're pretty ready to do that. Could you say on a scale of zero to ten, ten being really ready, zero being not ready at all, how ready would you be to do some counseling?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe like a six or a seven.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So a six or a seven. Why a six or a seven and not a four or a five?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, because I don't want to stay like this and, you know, I've already talked to her before and she was really nice, so I wouldn't mind going back to her. And she told me, you know, when I saw her last time, if ever needed I can come back.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it sounds like you've got a connection there already. That's really good. Does that sound like something you're ready to do then and maybe make a plan about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I can definitely check with her and see if she can see me again. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well if that's okay then, would it be all right if we talked a little bit about the exercise? I know you said that didn't really sound like an option for you at this time and that's perfectly fine, only you can make those decisions, Alvena. But if it's okay I wanted to give you a little bit of information about exercise and its effect on the brain.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Exercise is, again, in a number of studies has been shown to be as effective as prescription antidepressants.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. I didn't know that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, it actually raises serotonin. Have you heard about serotonin? Kind of the happy hormone. So it actually raises serotonin and also something called BDNF, which is... well, it doesn't really matter what it is, but it helps actually your brain actually grow and help repair itself. So exercise can help in lots of ways by improving serotonin and decreasing stress certainly and actually improving the quality of sleep. How does that sound at this point?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, if I tried to exercise and if I call her to talk to her again, does that mean I don't have to go on the medication right now? We can try that?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Absolutely. Again, those are your decisions and I'm here to really support you in those. So if those sound like things that you might be willing to do, I'm all for it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I'll try that if I don't have to go on the medication. I have some friends that exercise and work out that I could probably call and exercise with them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you have some friends that are already involved in an exercise program.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is that something you talk with them about and that you possibly could get into that group?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I have friends that run and friends that go to the gym, I have some friends that walk after work.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it sounds like a wide variety of things that you could do. Which of those tend to interest you most?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, then also, you know, my church on the weekends, they have exercise classes too. So yeah, but like I said, I don't have energy really to exercise, but I'll try it. But I'll definitely call the person that I had talked to when mom passed away and I'll do that right away.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Very good. Well, I think it sounds like this is important for you to feel better and it sounds like you're really ready to kind of make a plan. How do you see this fitting into your life at this point, again, kind of getting back to the counseling and the exercise?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, when I saw her, I could see her after work. So I can call her and see if I could still see her after work for therapy. And exercise, I mean, I can do that after work or on the weekends. My friends, they exercise various times, so yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's talk a little bit more about that. If we can use another one of those scales, zero being confident that you could start an exercise program, zero being not very confident at all and ten being very confident, tell me where you are in this exercise thing.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Honestly, maybe a five.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'll try it. Anything... if I have to do that so I don't have to go on medication, then I'll try it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That sounds like a pretty strong commitment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I'll try.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And tell me a little bit more about your plan for exercise at this point then.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, you know, my friends have been calling, but you know, I'm just sleeping all the time, so when they call I'm asleep, so I haven't really called them back. But I can just return their calls and just let them know I'll go and meet up with them and you know, at least maybe just start walking.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think that's a great decision. You have a couple of friends in mind that you could call?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I have real close friends that live not too far from me, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So tell me about a plan that you would think could perhaps get you going with the exercise.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I probably shouldn't come home. I probably would need to call one of my friends and make a plan to maybe walk after work and take a change of clothes and maybe drive to one of my friend's house after work and change with her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it would be difficult to do it in the morning. You don't see that happening.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, because it's so hard when I get up in the morning, I'm so tired that I can't... I can't see doing it in the morning.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you think it would be easier to do it after work.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Because I'm already out, yeah. As long as I don't come home because I come home, I want to go to sleep.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You come home, it's over.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Well good. It sounds like we have a plan for the counselor. And when you check out today, I'll put this in your record, that we'll want to get in touch with the counselor that you worked with when your mom was going through her passing and the grief situation. And then I'll want to depend upon you to call your friends and then get involved in the exercise program.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. I'll try that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. And if it's okay, I'd like to call you in a week to one, see how you're feeling, and two, if the exercise is helping. You may really find that after you give the exercise a good trial, you may actually look forward to it because my hope is that it will actually help you feel better and improve your mood. And then I would also like to see you back in two weeks just to check on things. Now we've talked about medication not being on the table at this point, but I want you to know Alvena, you can call anytime and I will work to get you in, and that might be something that we need to do if our plan is not working.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

video_details.title: Employer Talks: Kayla van Bruinessen
video_details.description: AIPC South Australia (Adelaide) Manager Carol Moore interviews Kayla van Bruinessen, owner of the Adelaide Counselling Practice (www.adelaidecounsellingpractice.com.au).

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, I'm Carol Moore, current manager for the Australian Institute of Professional Counselors in the Adelaide branch. And I'm here today with Kayla van Brunesen, who is the owner of Adelaide Counseling Practice. Welcome, Kayla.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you for coming today. Can you briefly tell us what services Adelaide Counseling Practice provide?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, Adelaide Counseling Practice provides services for people who've experienced depression, grief and loss, abuse in forms of physical abuse as well as emotional, mental abuse. We also provide things along the lines of relationship counseling as well, and we go heavily into those with the approaches learned from the professional counseling diploma.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Excellent. So what role do counselors play in the provision of those services?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, our counselors provide services to clients all over Adelaide. We've got city offices, we've got offices in the western suburbs, but we also allow our counselors to go to the residence of our clients.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So a mobile service.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Mobile service, yeah. And that's working out to be beneficial because a lot of clients don't feel comfortable coming to places where they can still be seen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sure. So what do you see as being the skills and knowledge that AIPC graduates have demonstrated in the delivery of those services?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Yeah, I feel that there's an amazing amount of information that comes from the AIPC diploma. We constantly use many of the articles and the actual forms that we used in the studies throughout the diploma. For instance, the personality profile that's in there. That really helps our clients in relationship sessions understand what their personalities are and how that can differ within a relationship. We also use the five types of conflict that's in the readings that allows us to explain to clients that there's different types of conflicts and how they can upset a relationship. So we use a fair amount of the information that came out of that diploma that really helps benefit our clients.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So how does the skills that our students have benefit Adelaide Counseling Practice?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, they benefit because they're all uniform when it comes to what Adelaide Counseling Practice needs. We like to know that we have uniformity in our counselors, and we know that the AIPC can offer that because we've all done the same base units. And then when it comes to the actual majors that some of the staff that we have have taken on, they can also add to the quality of the service that we can provide.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the advanced study majors in conjunction with their diploma is an additional benefit to you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Absolutely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Excellent. And Kayla, would you consider continuing to source positions for your practice with graduates of AIPC course?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, without a doubt. We haven't had any issues with the people that we've taken on board. They've all been professional and well-educated and fantastic with our clients.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Excellent. Thank you. Is there anything else you'd like to add about the course or the students or graduates you've taken?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I truly believe that this course, amongst others that I've researched before I did the actual diploma, has to be the most in-depth that I've actually seen. Even to the point where I'm now doing a psychology degree, and I don't believe that with the psychology degree, I would have the confidence to counsel clients because it doesn't actually show you how to practice, whereas the diploma shows you exactly how to practice.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the confidence to actually work with clients face-to-face comes from doing the diploma.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Absolutely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Excellent. Thank you. Well, thank you very much for your time today, Kayla.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you, Carol.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks, Kayla.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you.

video_details.title: Role Play: Solution Focused Therapy
video_details.description:
Solution-focused therapies are founded on the rationale that there are exceptions to every problem and through examining these exceptions and having a clear vision of a preferred future, client and counsellor, together, can generate ides for solutions.

Presented in an authentic and flowing style, this video incorporates a role play demonstrating the key techniques of Solution-focused therapy -- demonstrated by counselling professionals and including captions of the specific skill as it is demon

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Terry, thanks for coming in today. Hope you found the place all right.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, no problem at all. Clear instructions, so here I am.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Excellent. Terry, I was just wondering if you could tell me a bit about what it is that's brought you in today.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, a feeling of discomfort within the job that I'm doing at the moment. About three months ago, I answered a job advertisement that looked like it was going to be something that I would really enjoy doing. And three months down the track, it's just felt less and less comfortable. I don't know whether it's the right place for me to be. The place itself is okay, the people are great and supportive, and the work I can do, it's not a problem with the work, but I just feel really uncomfortable. I just thought, I can't do this anymore. I can't really put my finger on what it is.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And I'm wondering why today, Terry, is the right time that you've decided, after three months, I need to do something about it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Because last Friday, I felt like running out of the place screaming. It seemed that there were a lot of demands being made on me in a very short time, and it just got to me. Again, there's this confusion. Am I in the right place? Am I doing something that I really want to do? I thought if I don't do something and talk to somebody, then I don't know what might happen, but I found myself being right on the edge.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So Terry, I'd just like to ask you a bit of a different question. Imagine that tonight when you go to sleep, a miracle happens. And when you wake up in the morning, all of your problems are solved. How would you know that they're solved? What things would be different?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, that'd be great. I would feel different because I knew that I wouldn't be going to the job that I've been going to. There'd be that relief of pressure. I would be living somewhere else that would be cooler, with my wife, and doing something completely different that I would enjoy doing. I'd feel much more relaxed and much more at peace with myself and everybody else.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And Terry, you mentioned doing something different to the job that you're doing now. Do you have any ideas about what sort of thing you might be doing instead?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, yes. What I'd really like to do five days a week is what I do now one day a week, which is work on radio. It's something that I've enjoyed, I grew up with, and it's been part of my life for a long time. If given the opportunity, that's what I'd love to do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What sort of things do you do on the radio program? What does that involve?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I do a lot of interviews on local issues and topics, phone interviews, and face-to-face interviews. What I really like is talking to local people about local issues and help promoting the community sector's activities in the local area. So that's what I would really love to do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Wow, okay. Terry, you've created a really clear miracle picture. You've talked about a different job, being involved in community radio full-time, maybe even living in a completely different area, still with your wife in the picture. Terry, I'm just wondering whether there are times when you've been able to live somewhere else where you felt a bit more comfortable, where things haven't been so hot and humid for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, well, one of the challenges at the moment is the heat and the humidity where we're living. I've got a brother that lives in Tasmania and I've been to visit him a few times and that's a very different place to live. But the biggest experience of not having to deal with humidity was when I lived in Scotland for 10 years. That was absolutely wonderful. I would rather be in a cooler climate than a humid climate.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What sort of differences did you notice in yourself when you lived in the cooler climate?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: More energy. I felt like doing more things and I didn't feel like I was restricted. Sometimes on a weekend if it's too hot, there's not the inclination to go out and just to be part of the outdoors. So that was different when I was in Scotland. I was more active and able to be outdoors more.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Having a bit more energy. Would you say perhaps even a bit more social?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, but not necessarily. It's more just being able to be outside and to move around more freely. And just feeling a bit more comfortable in yourself as well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Terry, I'd just like to ask you a scaling question where one on the scale is oh, that's not really me at all, and ten is absolutely, definitely I'm going to do that. diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, on a scale of one to ten, definitely an eight.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: An eight! That's pretty high. And another scaling question, one being oh no, and ten being yes, absolutely. How willing do you think you are to make effort towards achieving your miracle?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's probably about the same, but it's more likely a seven rather than an eight.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, that's still pretty high on the scale when you think about when you came in and you were saying you're feeling a bit confused. Now you're saying actually, I'd like to be on radio, maybe in a different place, and you're saying yes, I'm motivated and wanting to do that. That's a bit of a shift, Terry.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I think hearing that when you offered the opportunity, I go, yeah, okay. So yes, I think that's probably why the motivation's there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. It feels like you've got a bit of energy about you when you're thinking about that. I'm just wondering if you've got any ideas about how you might be able to take even the next step to move towards making your miracle happen.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, definitely talking with my wife because we'd definitely need to be on the same wavelength. Researching other places in Australia of where we might live that's cooler and doesn't have the humidity. And talking with people who've lived in other parts of Australia.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's getting more real the more you talk about it. I'm wondering whether your brother who lives in Tasmania might be someone who could be a resource person for you in terms of finding out about Tasmania.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, he already has. He likes to send little snippets every so often about real estate prices and things like that. Very helpful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Well, Terry, I'm just wondering do you have a feeling as though enough has been talked about today to give you a bit of where to go from here when you leave our session?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's helped me just verbalize it out and imagine in a bigger picture what it might look like. I've got some very positive moves out of the session.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Excellent. All right. Well, if you'd like to make another appointment in the future, I'd love to meet with you again and see how you've been going.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay then. Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you Terry.

diarization.speaker: Therapist

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And are you having problems with your appetite?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I make the kids their dinner, but I just can't be bothered. I'm not bothered at all about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what about life in general? Have you kind of lost your get-up-and-go? Your energy levels, have you found that they're kind of low?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I used to enjoy going swimming with the kids and stuff, but now I just want to be on my own. I just can't be bothered. I'm just not being a very good mom at the moment as well. I'm just so exhausted, really. I just want some sleep.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Just going back to your sleep, can you tell me a bit more about that? How much sleep are you getting each night?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just lie awake and just think about him and her together. The things that we used to do. And I just wake up exhausted.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sounds like your lack of energy and lack of sleep and lack of appetite... it seems to me that things seem to be really getting you down.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm just such a mess at the moment. I'm just not coping. I'm just exhausted. Look at me. I just need some sleep.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You say you're a mess. Okay. It would be helpful for me just to sort of find out a bit more about home life and work life and ask a few questions in that area. Would that be okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's fine. Sorry, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, do you work?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I work in a job center. It gets a bit stressful at times. We've got to see so many people, and of course they're stressed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I've got some patients who work in the same environment. It's very high pressure, isn't it?

diarization.speaker: Patient

diarization.text: And who else is at home with you?

diarization.text: I've got two kids. Richard's the youngest, he's seven, and Marie, she's nine. They're very good kids.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do they get to see their father much?

diarization.text: No, he can't be bothered now he's got a new family. He doesn't see them at all.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That must be quite hard on both you and them.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I try and be a good mom, but it's just very difficult.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you get any help or support from anyone else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My mom. She's wonderful, but she has arthritis. She does what she can.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does she live locally?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, she's just around the corner. She picks the kids up from school. She's an angel, she helps me a lot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What about your hobbies and things you enjoy doing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I used to enjoy going to the cinema with my friends, even line dancing. But that's been a while ago. Nobody wants a bit of misery around, do they? And I'd rather be on my own now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You must have had thoughts about what's causing all these feelings. Have you thought about those type of things?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I was on automatic pilot when he first left. I guess that's why I'm in the state I am now. Could I resent the kids? I don't know, but I suppose that's why I keep going down and I just feel everything's useless.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What tends to bother you the most? Is it the sleep or the appetite or the energy or not coping with the kids?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's the sleep. I just feel if I had a bit more energy and if I could just have something just to help me out so I can do the normal things.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What were your thoughts about how we could help you today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just thought sleeping tablets might help.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would it be a good idea perhaps if we think about all the options available to you and then decide which one's maybe best for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. What are the other options?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, you might have heard of some of the talking therapies, being able to sit down and talk with a trained counselor about your feelings and about what's been happening.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Will that help my sleep? Will that make me be able to cope the next day?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It may help you deal with some of your feelings. I take on board about the thought about using a sleeping tablet. diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that sounds good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I mean, what about those two options? The option of the counselor or perhaps trying a short course of sleeping tablets?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My friend, she had counseling. I just feel if I had some sleeping tablets that might just give me a spur, and I'm quite happy with the counseling as well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you'd like to try both. I think that sounds like a good idea. And would you be happy to see the counselor here at the surgery?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, that would be fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so I can organize that. It'd also be really helpful if you could complete one of our HADS questionnaires. It's a short questionnaire just asking some questions about your feelings, and it'll help me to find out if there's any more help I can give you when I next see you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, no problem.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: From what you've told me today, it sounds like for the last 12 months or so you've felt really low. Your sleep's not been good, your appetite's not been good. It sounds to me like your self-esteem's taken a real knock, hasn't it? I certainly think the help we can give you with some counseling and a short course of sleeping tablets will be of benefit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Maybe I can see you in about two or three weeks' time. I don't want you to think that you have to manage all this by yourself. That's what we're here for. Let me do the prescription then. Okay, that's gone to reception now. If I give you one of the HADS questionnaires as well, and you can complete that before we see you next time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Thank you, Doctor. Thank you for that. Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, see you next time. Bye-bye.

video_details.title: Role Play: Cognitive Behaviour Therapy
video_details.description:
Cognitive-behaviour therapy involves a specific focus on cognitive strategies such as identification and modification of maladaptive cognitive errors and restructuring of core beliefs and/ or representations of the self. Further focus is on behavioural strategies that are designed to activate clients in the environment with a view to effect desired behaviour change.

Presented in an authentic and flowing style, this video incorporates a role play demonstrating the key techniques of Cognitive-beh

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay Marsha, so, how can I help you today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I'm working full time, I'm a part-time student, I've just gotten engaged and I live at home. There's just so much stress in my life, I've everything happening all at once. To top it all off, I failed an exam, a really big exam, and I just feel like I can't do anything anymore, I can't do anything right. I've just got so much stress and I feel like such a disappointment, such a failure, and I've embarrassed my family by failing. Yeah, I just don't know what to do anymore and I guess I've come here today to tell you I want to leave uni and I guess that's why I've come here to you today.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So it sounds like a whole lot of stuff's on top of you at the moment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, just so much, just all piling on, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hmm. So you're working full time, plus part-time study and then you've got a wedding preparation.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, just got engaged and the wedding's just a month away now, so, yeah. So I've just got so much happening, work is really demanding and, yeah, just failed this exam, it's just, yeah, don't know what to do, all too much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All too much. Yeah. So I imagine you've been sweating on this for a while and it's all been swirling around in your head.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's just been building up and building up and so much pressure with everything, and I'm living at home so my parents, you know, a lot of pressure, need to do everything right. And, yeah, by failing this I feel like I've just embarrassed them and disappointed them and I just don't feel like I'm good enough, you know, to go on studying.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And have they said much to you about failing an exam?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They haven't said much. I was really scared to tell them actually because I knew they'd just be so disappointed and just embarrassed by the fact that I did fail. Yeah, I've never failed anything before and, so, yeah, it's really hard.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, so it's new and you don't like it at all.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not at all, no. And I think leaving uni will just be the way out just so I don't have to go through it again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, okay. Well, I'm glad you've come to counseling because it's good for us to get an outsider's opinion when we've got so much on our plate and we're confused as to what to do and our emotions can get in the way. And you just said earlier that a whole lot of stuff's on your plate at the moment, okay. So, um, I'm glad you've come here. Um, here at the clinic we use the ABC model, which is a cognitive behavioral therapy model. Okay? So Marsha, some counselors have put together a list of beliefs that we often use, and we don't realize that we're using those beliefs and they tend to be faulty ones. Okay? Here's the list here. Have a look through that to see if there are any beliefs that you might be operating on at the moment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I think number two.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Read that one out for me.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That it's necessary to have a high degree of order and certainty in order to be happy and perform well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah, you mentioned that earlier, didn't you? Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Number four, that it's necessary to be competent and successful in all those things which are attempted.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hmm, yeah, that's an expectation from your family.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Possibly number eight, that life should be entirely pleasant and enjoyable and that any frustration, discomfort, or pain would be unbearable.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hmm, hmm, yeah. Which one of those stands out the most for you at the moment, Marsha?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably number four.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. How would you put that in your own words?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That I need to be successful all the time in everything that I do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah. And is that different from what's happening in your life at the moment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, failing that exam, I mean, I wasn't successful with that, so, yeah, it just throws out, I guess even number two because it throws out all the order in my life. I need to have everything, you know, so I need to know what I'm doing, where I'm going, yeah, so...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so if number four's an expectation that your family have and that you have of yourself, how do you measure up next to number four?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't feel like I'm good enough.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. All right. Well, what I'd like to do is put some of those ideas on the board under the ABC and I'll explain as we go along. Okay? Okay. So what do you think the trigger point might be, or the activating event for you at the moment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, there are a lot of things, but I think obviously failing the exam was the main one.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. All right. And the consequence is you thinking of leaving uni, yeah. All right. And that statement that you made earlier about 'I'm not good enough', yeah, that's the B one. That's the crucial one, and I'll explain it shortly when I get up to the board. Okay. Okay, I think I'll put it up there now for you, so we can work through that. So Marsha, the activating event, which is what you stated earlier...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I failed my exam.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's right. And the kind of decision that you're thinking about is...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Leaving uni.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's right, yeah. Okay. So it's important that we consider the jump from here over to here and the kind of thinking that you've been swirling around in your head affects the consequence. And you've mentioned earlier that number four seems to fit, and you've put that in your own words. What were your words before?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That I'm not good enough.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, good. That's really important for us to consider that kind of thinking. Hmm. Okay Marsha, it's good that we've got those things on the board. And what I'd like to do now is focus stepping out a bit from your situation and looking at it from another point of view. Okay. To me, it sounds like you're doing a whole lot of things really well. Can you list all of the things that you're doing really well?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I'm working, it's a really demanding job and I'm, you know, keeping up with it. So, I guess work. Um, things with my fiancé, I mean, we're engaged, so, planning the wedding, that's going really well. It's stressful, but it's going well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hmm. And all of your other university subjects?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I've never failed anything before, this is the first one, so, I guess all the other subjects, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah. And you're succeeding in all of those things together. You're juggling it and it's a lot on your plate at the moment, but it sounds like you've been able to cope up until this point of the one exam.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: This one just threw me off balance, yeah, just failing, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, would you describe yourself as successful most of the time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, most of the time, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what's the evidence for that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Passing all my exams all the time, passing my subjects, not just exams. Um, getting that full-time job, it's a great job that I'm doing, yeah, getting married.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, that's right, yeah. So how do all of those successes compare to that belief that you've written, that I've written on the board for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess in comparison I am good enough.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, that's right, yeah. And all the evidence is there, all of the subjects that you've passed in first year and now second year, your full-time job, that's a success, it's great, yeah, good. Okay. Well, what I'd like to do is get you to write that on the board, to dispute that belief. Okay? Yeah. Would you do that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: All right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well done Marsha, that's a powerful statement. What kind of decision goes along with that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Staying at uni.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good, okay. Write that on the board for us. Great, that's good. Good. Okay. So you've made a bit of a decision there, haven't you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
