diarization.text: Okay. Tell me about it. Does it feel okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I feel like I should stay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Why is that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can try again. I mean, everything doesn't have to be 100% all the time. So, I mean, I could re-sit the exam.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, yeah. And we've talked about all your successes, so it's harder now to believe that top statement that 'I'm not good enough'.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I mean, I am good enough compared to all the things that you helped me realize with all the successes that I've had. I am good enough.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, good. Okay. And so this idea about staying at uni...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I'll stay. I mean, I am good enough, so I'm sure I can give it another go and see how it goes from there. I can re-sit the exam and I'm sure I'll be fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, good. Okay. What I'd like you to do is to keep saying that statement 'I am good enough'. Say it in front of the mirror two or three times a day, um, so that you build up your confidence, because it's going to take some time to reprogram your computer up here with that kind of positive belief about yourself rather than carrying around that other belief. And, um, we tend to carry those other beliefs for years and years and years and so it's going to take a bit of work on your part to deliberately change your thinking and change your belief system. But, um, you've made a great start here today, so congratulations, well done. All right.

video_details.title: Learning ACT // Part 8: The ACT Therapeutic Stance

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In this next set of clips, we're going to be working on the core competencies in chapter nine: the therapeutic stance. Here we're going to be working on the relationship with the client and the therapist, and the quality that the therapist brings to that relationship. This is a genuine, compassionate, and vulnerable quality that allows the therapist to connect with the client on an equal basis. In this next section, we're going to be exploring core competency number two: therapist self-disclosure in session. These disclosures should be appropriate and thoughtful, well-timed. The client in this particular section has been struggling with feeling incompetent and a failure in her schoolwork. It is a barrier for her in terms of progressing in relationships, at school, and just in general.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I'm already taking way less classes than everybody else, and I signed up for five and now I've dropped all except two, and I just can't seem to get myself to be motivated on the weekends or at night to study because I feel like it takes so much out of me to just go to class that I just can't move forward and then I end up getting, you know, Cs or Ds or Fs on the tests. And they post those grades in this list that everyone can see your grade, and I always have one of the lowest scores.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you've talked about this in some of your past sessions and you've linked it up to feelings of failure, sometimes feeling incompetent.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I do feel that way. And I feel like when we have partners, that I can't bring anything to the group. I just, yeah, I feel like I shouldn't even be at school sometimes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, this kind of sense of withdrawal and pulling away. And you've mentioned that this is a lonely place for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I feel very alone. None of my friends, I guess you could call them that... no one has this problem but me. And I go to the college counselor and it just seems no one understands that... I just feel like every time I try to seek help, no one gets where I'm coming from and it's just, 'oh, she's lazy' or whatnot. But I really want to succeed, I just... I don't...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it seems like you're completely alone in this. Well, one of the things that happens for me sometimes is that I too feel like I'm failing or incompetent in some of the things that I do.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. I struggle also and sometimes I don't even know exactly what to do in here, and I'm thinking about failure or incompetence, certainly. Yeah, so that's present for me also. And I wonder, because we know that this has been a part of keeping you out of some relationships, if it might even be a way that it would interfere with our relationship. Like maybe feeling like you're failing and not doing this right even, if it doesn't go a particular way.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I feel that way.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. And so I wonder if you and I could kind of recognize our very human experiences, feelings of failure, incompetence, and then work on the problem together as we move forward. Yeah? In this session, it was an ACT-consistent self-disclosure. The client had been feeling alone and like she was unique in her failure for quite some time. At this time, I joined with her and let her know that she was not alone by disclosing that I too sometimes have those experiences. And then, as she began to open up and say 'really?', in that space, she could connect too that she wasn't alone. Finally, it opens the room up for the two of us to work together on any way that this particular experience of failure or incompetence might show up in the room. We'll be aware of it so we can ask in the future, 'is this a problem right now?' In this next section, we're going to be focusing on core competency number five. Here the therapist models acceptance of challenging content, while also being willing to hold content that is contradictory without any intention to resolve that content.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, well I didn't get to grow up in the same house as my dad, so he's always been really present but I feel like he's tried to raise me from a distance. And everything... I know he's coming from a place of love and I love him too, and I want to have that good relationship with him, but everything that he tries to tell me I just feel like I'm not good enough and it's really judgmental and it's really hurtful. And then it makes me act hostile around him because I feel like he doesn't love me and he doesn't, you know, he can't celebrate me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it sounds like there's a couple of things happening. One is that you love him and want some closeness, but at the same time he's giving you messages that you're not good enough. Let's spend some time thinking about how you could improve the communication with your father so that maybe you could let him know what's on your mind when you're having these experiences. Can you give me an example of a conversation that you've had?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, um, I told him I was really interested in doing this program abroad in Italy. And it's something that I'm really looking forward to, I want to be a chef and it's a culinary school there. And, you know, he just automatically goes back to 'well, you need to stay here, you need to go to school, you need to do something'... he wants me to be a nurse like his mother. And I know he's coming from a safety... he wants the best for me, but he can't celebrate the adventures that I want.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So maybe one of the things that you could do is have him reflectively listen to you. So ask him in your conversation if perhaps he could hear you more openly and repeat back some of the things that you're saying. Because it sounds like he's kind of just missing it. Is that something that you could try in your next conversation with him?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know if he would be able to do it, but I mean I could ask him. But he just... even coming here with you, he thinks is a waste of money.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, so maybe then you can speak with him about how you're benefiting from it and again ask him to hear it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I could try that. Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So in this last clip, there was a very subtle thing happening. We did move into problem solving, which in and of itself isn't necessarily a problem. In fact, problem solving could be quite consistent with something that you're doing in ACT. In this particular case, though, the client was expressing a fairly emotional piece of content. She was talking about her father criticizing her, and at one point she even seemed to be on the verge of tears. I missed an opportunity there to connect with the client in a powerful way by taking an in-the-moment time for our relationship to develop, by recognizing that emotion that's there, being willing to tolerate the emotion that's there. Another issue that might be at hand when a client begins to get emotional is that sometimes it's hard for the therapist too. Let's say, for instance, I had a critical father and it was hard for me to experience that criticalness. I might quickly then move into problem solving as a way to escape my own emotional experience and lose the willingness in the moment. So, the best approach in this one would have been to stay with the issue at hand, the emotion at hand longer, and be willing to experience what the therapist is experiencing too. Additionally, this is related to core competency number nine, where we're talking about the processes that occur in the moment. In this session, I missed those processes that are relevant and ACT-consistent. In this next clip, we'll be looking at core competency one. Here we'll be working with the client from a perspective that they are completely able at this point in time; they have all that they need to move forward in their life in a valued way.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, um, I just have a really hard time getting motivated. I don't have a job again because I just can't get there on time. I have a hard time leaving the house in the morning because I just don't see the point. I just feel like every time I try anything, I fail and I'm just a broken human.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You've mentioned broken human before. And the place that I'm coming from is that you are 100 percent whole, 100 percent capable and able, and able to respond to what it is that you'd like to do in your life. So I'm not going to operate from the position that you're broken. I'm going to hold you as a response-able person who can get out there and bring her values to life. This was a very short section, but the client is holding herself to be broken, having that particular thought. From the ACT perspective, the therapist always wants to hold the client as 100 percent capable and able in the moment. So this was a consistent ACT move.

video_details.title: Role Play: Behaviour Therapy
video_details.description:
Behaviour therapy had its beginnings in the early 1900's and became established as a psychological approach in the 1950s and 1960s. At this time, it received much resistance from the current school of thought, psychoanalysis.

Presented in an authentic and flowing style, this video incorporates a role play demonstrating the key techniques of Behavioural therapy - demonstrated by counselling professionals and including captions of the specific skill as it is demonstrated.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, that's the housekeeping finished with Kathleen, so perhaps you'd like to tell me a bit about what brings you here today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, actually, Wendy, I'm having a lot of trouble coping with my job. The hours I'm working are supposed to be 8:30 to 3:30, and lately I've just got so much work given to me. I've got a couple of teenage boys that I pick up after school every day because they're so naughty they're not allowed to go on the bus. I'm getting there later and later, and it's all getting too much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, well you're supposed to finish at 3:30, and they're the hours you're employed to do. Why do you think you're not finishing at 3:30, Kathleen?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, I've got too much work.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And who's giving you the work? What's happening?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, one doctor employed me, but there are four within the practice and I'm doing work for all of them when really I should only be doing work for one.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, so that's really the problem, that there are four people giving you work and there's no way you can fit it into the times that you're employed to work.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, and I just can't say no to them. They put the work in my in-tray and it's not getting to my out-tray, and it's just all too much for me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yes, I can see that, and I can see you getting quite stressed about it. Have you had any thoughts about anything you might be able to do about this, Kathleen?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I don't want to leave, it's such a good job, but I'll probably have to tell her. I think I'm going to have to tell her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you really do feel that you need to talk to the boss that employed you and explain what the problem is. Is this something you feel comfortable about doing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. She's so busy, and she's so lovely, and I just don't want to annoy her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, you said she was lovely there, so do you think that if you were able to go and talk to her, she'd actually be quite receptive to listening to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, of course she would, wouldn't she? Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What I'm going to suggest, Kathleen, is that we do something called a role play. We act out the situation, in your case, going and talking to your boss and trying to explain the problem. You'll be playing you and I'll be playing your boss. It gives you a chance to practice and get a response that you can then react to.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'll give it a swing. What do you mean?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, we'll practice it right now. I'll be the doctor that you're going to see. What do you think would be the best time of day to do it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably early morning might be best, first thing in the morning.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sounds like a good idea because then you don't have to worry about it all day too.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's true, yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so have you got any thoughts about what you might say? How you're going to introduce it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I suppose I could say to her, 'Is this a good time to talk?'

diarization.speaker: Therarpsit
diarization.text: That's fantastic. Because that gives her the opportunity to say if it's a good time or not. Shall we give it a try?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, alright.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I'm going to get you to stand up and pretend that you're knocking on her door. I'll be your boss and you're going to tell me what the problem is. We'll do the role play now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Come in. Oh, hi Kathleen.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hi Maryanne. Is now a good time to talk?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, sure.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Good, thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have a seat.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, thanks. Well, the problem is Maryanne, I'm having problems coping with my workload at the moment, mainly because it's putting me here too late in the afternoon. My hours were 8:30 to 3:30, but now I'm finishing later and later.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Why is that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've got too much work. And I like to finish on time because I have to pick my boys up from school. So I'm just wondering if we can work...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well obviously you're employed 8:30 to 3:30 and they're the hours we want you to work. I want you to leave at 3:30. But from what you're saying, the work you're being given doesn't fit into those hours. Do you know why? What's happening?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'm getting too much work from the other doctors. I thought I was only doing your work, but there's four doctors here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think I've got the picture. I'm really glad that you came to see me Kathleen, but obviously 8:30 to 3:30 is long enough. So I need to have a look into this and see what's going on.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's only half my day. The other half starts when I pick my boys up and they're so naughty.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well certainly Kathleen, I'll have a look at it but I want you to make sure that you do leave at 3:30 every day.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Well, I feel a bit better actually after that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, let's slip out of that. How did that feel?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I think because I've done that little role play I feel a little bit better about probably going and seeing her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The important thing is to work out that first opening gambit, isn't it? And then to flow on. So that's something I want you to think about. Perhaps if you're going to come and see me next week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. What in the meantime? Should I practice at home or what?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Think about what we've done today, but don't overdo it. Don't sort of keep it going through your mind.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'll get nervous.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Exactly. I can see that you're getting a bit...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I just don't like confrontation. I don't like telling people what to do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I know. So having the right words is a help. But importantly, I think we need to relax a bit, don't we? There are some simple relaxation exercises that I can teach you that I'd like you to go away and practice.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Could I do them at home, can I? What are they, lying on the floor or...?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'll tell you what they are. No, you don't have to lie on the floor. So I suggest you come back in a week's time, having practiced those, and we'll perhaps do another role play. What do you think?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, that sounds good. I feel a little bit more relaxed just thinking about it actually. Oh, thanks for that.

video_details.title: Learning ACT // Part 7: Building Patterns of Committed Action

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So we're going to look at core competency two, which is detecting some of the barriers to committed action. This next clip will be working with a client who is having relationship problems, specifically having a hard time getting close to people in her relationships. She has a past history of having been betrayed and is afraid she's going to be hurt again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So when that choice point comes and there's a way of stepping forward with your boyfriend or back, what's inside? I have that sense that you kind of step back a little bit. What's happening in there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I guess just old stuff starts to come up. I'm an independent person, I have my routines that I do, and when someone starts moving in on that, I get really nervous.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there another level down there? If you go for what's harder to see, maybe more emotional, what do you start feeling as you step forward?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I guess I don't really like people to see me be vulnerable because I don't want to get hurt again. In my past relationship, I was open and then I got slammed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you got slammed hard.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: He betrayed you. Don't run off from that, sort of come back to that. Because I get the sense that as you touch that, there's this part that goes, 'I'm not going there' with this boyfriend who has not betrayed you and has actually been pretty good to you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. But it's hard.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What if it's kind of like this? Vulnerability comes from a root word that means 'woundable', that you can be hurt. When people get close to you, they can hurt you. Yes? Inside when you were betrayed, why did that hurt so much? Isn't it because you really wanted something? What did you have?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Love.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Love. Is that important to you? Even as you say that, part of you is going to want to say, 'but I'm not going to be so vulnerable again.' So maybe the other side is something that you really want but you're afraid to want. If you throw away the hurt, you have to throw away both sides. Is it worth it? Do you really want your life to be throwing away both sides?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not both.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you see that as you detune this, it isn't just that you're more protected from hurt? What's happening on the other side?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just don't want to go there again, which means I can't really experience love.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. And that hurts too, in a different way.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When you encounter barriers to committed action, often the barriers are ones of pain. People are reluctant to move forward because of this sense of pain. Avoidance is one of the barriers. What we just did there was pointing out that pain can be a guide. If you didn't care, things would not hurt. So as you avoid your hurt, you also avoid what it is you really care about. We were looping up from the barrier and having it be part of a pattern of committed action.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And so I have a sense that you're holding your boyfriend at bay a little bit. You take one step forward and then one or two steps back. Am I wrong in that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. Whenever I start to feel closer to him, I get that reminder that if it gets any better it can only get worse. And I get nervous about being vulnerable.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there's sort of a pull to defend yourself or something.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's scary.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what do you think it's going to take to move you forward? If you always do what you've always done, you'll always get what you've always got. As you back up and back up, what's it going to take to move you forward?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Trust.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But you've been waiting for that a long time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so behaviorally, what are you not doing with your boyfriend that you ought to be doing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just feel like even when we're at home watching a movie that I'm not really there. I can't be present fully.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And because you're not present, what would I see from the outside if I were there watching?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe I'll have an impulse to sit closer and then all of a sudden I'll think, 'Oh, this feels nice.' Uh-oh, if this feels nice, then...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, maybe we should target that, sitting closer to him. If we don't move forward, we're moving backwards. Do you value being close to him?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, of course I value that. I just feel like I'm watching from the outside all the time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, maybe we should set a goal in here of you sitting closer to him. Let's just do it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, but I'm still going to be uncomfortable.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, that's part of the cost, I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: There are some things in here that could be helpful, but there's a crude quality to what's going on here. There's a missed opportunity. The barriers coming up must be brought into the work, not simply dismissed as if these other problems will somehow resolve themselves. Although it has some superficial connection with an ACT model, it's not a very sophisticated implementation of it.

video_details.title: Learning ACT // Part 6: Defining Valued Directions

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Chapter 6: Defining value directions. In the first set of clips, we'll be working with Julie, who is a client dealing with some moderate level of social anxiety. She's come to therapy with an interest in overcoming this anxiety and making deeper, stronger friendships, and finds herself, to date, unable to do this, and largely finds herself on the outside looking in on relationships. The first vignette will focus on core competency number one, which is about helping the client clarify value directions.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, Julie, we've talked quite a bit about your struggles with anxiety and feeling like that really gets in the way of your engaging with people and having friendships. And part of what I wanted to focus on today was looking at sort of the larger picture of this, the larger context in which this struggle occurs. You know, we've been sort of focused on all the trees and we want to look at sort of the forest. Like, what is it that you want to be about in terms of relationships in your life? Like, what is it that matters to you in terms of your relationships?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I think that I have a hard time being so focused on my inner dialogue and me doubting myself and my self-consciousness that I fail to be a good friend to a lot of people who love me. And it hurts me to see that, but then I don't know how to stop and listen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you feel like you're not a good friend. So what I want us to do is we're going to walk through some different domains of functioning for you and I'm going to jot down what you say. And our job here with this is to really come up with some really concrete sort of statements of what it is that you want to have happen. And so I'm going to work to help us kind of get really clear on what are your values in this area. What is it that's important to you? And one of the things you just said was you felt like you're not there for your friends. Is that right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how would you want it to be?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I mean, I would like to not always be the person calling up crying, you know? I feel like no one could count on me in that way because I'm not strong.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So in that domain of friendships, what you want is to not always be the one who's calling up crying. Okay. So I'm going to write that down. Does that seem to fit for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, okay.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So what are you writing down?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Just what you said. Not always be the one who's crying. Okay. And that's what you want in that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. What are other things that you want when you think about your friendships?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I want to actually have a good time when I go out instead of, you know, I can kind of bring myself some nights to actually get to the place, but, you know, it's so draining.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, okay. So you want to have a good time with friends. That feels like kind of the way you want to be.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So that was an ACT-inconsistent piece. It wasn't terribly ACT-inconsistent, but it did have a few different aspects. The first aspect was that part of what the therapist recorded as a value was actually more of a goal. And particularly, as you might have read in the chapter, a dead man goal. The client said they wanted to not always be the one who's crying. And this is a sort of inactive, passive goal that are not of the sort that we want to have in relation to values. It's also a problem because it's a goal and not a value. The second part that was problematic in this segment was that it didn't have much of the qualities that we want to have as part of a powerful values conversation, like vitality, willing vulnerability, a present orientation. Those sort of qualities were not very much in there. In fact, the therapist was sort of laid back a bit and kind of behind their tablet of paper and not as engaged with the client in this segment.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So Julie, we've spent a lot of time already talking about the different struggles that you've had with social anxiety. And I feel like you've been fighting this for a long time and it really stands in the way of you having the relationships that you want, and you've been really working hard to overcome it. And part of what I was wondering about is if we could spend a little time kind of looking at the bigger picture of what are your dreams and your goals in terms of your relationships. Like, if you could have your relationships be however you would want them, like if it were just so simple that you could just like you had like a bowl of prizes and you could just reach in and just pull out the kind of relationships that you wanted, what would those look like for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I'd like to have someone who I want to call up and share good news with. I'd want to have good news. And I want to have, I mean, obviously a boyfriend at some point, I haven't had one in years. And I just want to have friends or relationships that don't feel like a chore to tend to.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I hear a couple of things in there. You'd want to have it feel like it was a choice, like you'd really want to have relationships that really sort of felt meaty to you or felt like that they were important to you. Does that seem right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there any other thing else I missed in there? I feel like there was like a first piece that I sort of missed in there.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just being able to share good news.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Feeling close enough to people in your life where you felt like kind of connected enough to and close enough to that you would want to share good news with them. And that they would sort of be there for you. Does that feel right? Like that's sort of the kind of relationships you want?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that feels right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has there ever been a time in your life where you felt like you had those kind of relationships?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, as a kid I had no problems being social. I was always out playing with everyone and it really wasn't a problem until maybe I was 13ish. When I started moving into adolescence I just started doubting myself a lot and...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And who was your best friend back then when you can you remember?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, Megan Myers.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what was that friendship like?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was, I mean I could spend the night at her house and not come home for three days and it didn't matter. You know, I felt safe next to someone, which I haven't felt in a really long time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And is that something you'd want to have again in your life? That sort of like feeling so connected to somebody and like so there with them that you felt like safe to be able to just be just who you were with them.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I definitely would.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So this was more of an ACT-consistent vignette. And in this vignette, you saw the therapist focus more on the client's experience in the moment. And as this was an attempt to illustrate core competency number one, clarifying value directions, the focus was bringing some of these qualities of a powerful values conversation in the room, like vitality, choice. And you saw the therapist kind of hit on the issue of choice at least initially by asking the person to focus on what they would choose. And there was also more of a sense of connection and vitality in the conversation. Where the therapy might have gone next would have been to go more into the experience of what it was like to be with her childhood friend and help the client to really get in contact with that experience in the moment and then using that to help set up a choice in terms of whether she would be willing to experience some of these difficult anxieties if it were able to serve that value.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This vignette continues in what would be a later session with Julie after we've already worked on getting clear on the client's values. And this one focuses on core competency number four, which is helping the client to distinguish between outcomes achieved and involvement in the process of living. What we're going to do here is pick up at what would be the start of a session and where this leads is that the week before Julie has committed to some homework or some actions over the week that would be consistent with her values of connecting with people and being able to be sort of spontaneous and playful in interactions. And she noticed that one of the things she does that gets in the way of that is she'll spend minutes or sometimes even hours preparing and maybe writing notes about what she's going to say to somebody before she goes into a conversation. And so the task was to let go of preparing like that and just to walk into a conversation and to practice this on a daily basis at work this week.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So Julie, I thought we'd check in with, start by checking in with what happened this week in terms of the commitment that you made.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I did do what you asked me to do and I went out and I tried to connect and make some friends, I guess, but it didn't go well at all and I felt every time that it was basically just a failure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you feel like you were sort of going out to connect with people and then like because you felt like you didn't have that feeling of connection, it's like you blew it or something.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But I want to check back to our conversation about last week and like, was that what we were trying to do was get you to where you felt connected to people? Was that what we were practicing in that? Do you remember?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean, getting there was the start and talking, and that's ultimately what I want is connection.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So part of what I want us to look at is the difference between sort of this focus on goals and it sounded like when you walked in there you were really focused on the idea that you were going to connect with these people. And that if you didn't connect with them, then that was going to be something that was like really bad. Does that seem fair to say?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, like I lost. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And I want you to remember when we talked about it, that wasn't really what we were doing. We were looking more at sort of the path that you want to be on. And if you can remember last week, like yeah, you want to create connection with people and you want to be connected, right? But we want to focus more on sort of the side of that that you have control over, which is what you do with your hands and your feet. And what you did here was you let go of one of your barriers that stands between you and other people. Like did you do that part of not preparing before you went in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I just tried to walk in.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Cool. Cool.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: And that felt good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Cool. So you let go of that. And that was like we were sort of practicing a willingness move there of letting go of that barrier. And it sounded like when you got into the situation you kind of got caught up in this whole sort of focus on the outcome of how it was turning out and you got sort of attached to this goal of, am I feeling connected or not? Or sort of, are they liking me in this moment? Rather than paying attention to the process that you wanted to engage in, which was this process of like, here I am moving towards connection with people. And part of that process is going to be, you know, at times it doesn't work out. And so part of what we want to do is see, you know, can you continue to have your feet moving in that direction even as your mind is sort of chattering to you and saying these things like, you know, I'm not connecting or they're not liking me and those sort of things. And it sounded like you did that this week. But then there's this focus on the kind of goal that sort of took it away from you in a way. Does that seem fair?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. That seems right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So that was an ACT-consistent piece. And again it was competency four. In that I was trying to help the client to reconnect with the process that was being focused on in this, rather than so attached to the outcome. What seemed to happen during the week was that the exercise sort of transformed from an exercise that was about getting her feet moving in this direction and into really an attachment to a particular goal that she sets for herself and sort of really is harsh with herself around, which is this goal of feeling like she's connected and feeling like people like her. And she got attached to that as she did the exercise and started to evaluate herself more in reference to that goal, rather than sort of appreciating the qualities of herself as moving towards this value direction while letting go of barriers that often tend to stand in the way. Again we return to core competency number one, helping the client define value directions. And this vignette is specifically focused on the issue of goals versus values. And in this case we're going to be having Derek, who is part of his goals for therapy is having a better relationship with his wife.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So Derek, what is it that you want with your wife? You know, if you could just choose what you'd be about there, like what would that be like?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Quit arguing. Quit arguing. Resenting her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what would you need to do to do that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think I'd have to start with disrespecting her. To stop, I mean stop disrespecting her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yes. To stop, you mean stop disrespecting her. Yeah. Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So this was an ACT-inconsistent vignette. The therapist started out fine with a question that could go either way. But the client gave a response which was more of an avoidance goal or what we might call a dead man goal. A dead person's going to be able to do the job of not arguing better than this client is likely to be able to do. And we want to come up with goals which have a sense of, and values which have a sense of, what's the client moving towards rather than what's the client moving away from. And by the therapist accepting this goal as something to orient towards, we're likely to be feeding that process of moving away.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And Derek, what would you want in your relationship with your wife? I mean, if your relationship could be about anything, if you could be about anything in that relationship, you know, you could just choose it, what would you choose?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Stop resenting her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And if you were able to stop resenting her, like what would your relationship, like if you could just imagine that, like that you just got to that place sort of magically that you weren't resenting her anymore and you weren't fighting anymore, what would you hope that this relationship would look like and how would you be in it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think communicating, understanding, and doing things we used to do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, okay. So both of you would be communicating and understanding.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And specifically you, from your side, like if you were able to sort of let go and that resentment sort of just sort of magically evaporated, you'd be more connected and more present.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. More fulfilling.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: More fulfilling perhaps as an outcome, but maybe you don't have a choice over that, but you might have more of a choice over whether you're going to be present or not.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Exactly. There for her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, there for her, that would be part of the picture. Cool.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's exactly it. Yeah. And her for me as well. Just to enjoy simple things.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So that would be part of the vision.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Exactly. I mean, I'm really striving for that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So that was an ACT-consistent vignette. Again focusing on the issue of developing goals that would be more approach-type goals. The client originally came and presented a goal that was more of an avoidance goal initially. And my job was to help the client to contact what was the value and the quality of action that might be perhaps behind that goal. And so I sort of sidestepped the initial statement and asked, you know, if you were to achieve that goal, then what would you hope things would be like in an effort to hopefully draw out what are the client's dreams and the hopes, hopefully something that the client could connect to in a more powerful way than just not arguing anymore.

video_details.title: Learning ACT // Part 5: Distinguishing Conceptualized Self from Self-as-Context

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The next set of segments will be part of Chapter 5, distinguishing self as content from the self as context. All of these segments will have in common work on helping the client to be able to better observe and distinguish their thoughts and other ideas about themselves, such as roles or feelings that they might have, and to be able to distinguish this from a sense of self as more like the content or the context or the arena or the location where all of these things take place.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Through all of these role-plays, we'll be working with a client named Phil, who is a chronically depressed client who has come to therapy initially with a focus of really wanting to feel better about himself. This segment reflects competency one in the self as context chapter, which refers to helping the client to distinguish the contents of consciousness from consciousness itself. And we're going to try to weave this into the ongoing flow of the session.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So Phil, we've been working on this issue of you wanting to feel better about yourself. I mean, you came into therapy saying that that was something that you were really working hard to do, and you've been working on that for a long time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Seems like it's been all my life.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. And I actually wanted to try an exercise, if you're willing, that would be relevant to that, to see if it's sort of really possible to find peace at that level of really being able to feel good about yourself. Would you be willing to do an exercise with me?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: At this point, I'm willing to try just about anything, you know, to enjoy my life. That ever-impending doom, just that cloud... I can't seem to get away from it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So what I want you to do is I'm going to say just some phrases about yourself, and I just want you to notice what sort of reaction you have in your head or in your mind as I say these things. Okay? So here's the first one: I have some good qualities.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, but... I mean, I don't know, I'm always going on the dark side.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. That's good. So all I want you to do is just notice what comes up when I say one of these statements. Okay. So the next one is, I'm a pretty good person.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think... this is hard. I mean, a good person, but I have too many problems.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Good. So next one: I'm a perfect person.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, right. Okay. So there we went towards sort of the positive side, and you've been sort of working to have those more positive evaluations of yourself for a long time. Let's go the other way. I have some flaws.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Doesn't everybody?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: There are a lot of problems with me.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: But I'm genuine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how about this one: I am completely, utterly worthless.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: But I have a good heart.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I just want you to... do you notice what happened there? Like what happened was as we went to one end or the other, either really positive or really negative sort of statements, it pulled for the opposite. It's like as we got more and more positive, immediately the next thing that came up was a negative thing. And as I had you think about things that were more negative, immediately the reaction was something more positive.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Wow.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This clip with Phil was again meant to help Phil to be able to see self as content, in particular to help to discriminate that from his self as context. We took some evaluations and brought them out to their extremes and saw that when you're operating with self-evaluation, that as you become more positive, it tends to pull for negative, and as you think about more negative self-evaluations, it tends to pull for more positive.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This is Competency 2. The therapist utilizes exercises to help the client make contact with self as context and distinguish that from self as content. This role-play will be with Phil, who wants to improve his self-esteem, he wants to feel better about himself. And here we're going to see how the issue of distinguishing self as content is relevant to this situation.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel like a hamster in a cage. I mean, I start to move forward and then all of a sudden, I hit a barrier, I hit a wall, and I can't go past that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So let me have you sort of repeat that comment again: I hit a wall. And just slow down and let me have you see if you can repeat that again.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I go forward and I hit a wall.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And as you do that, I'd just like you to take a moment and look sort of inward at your body and notice what sensations do you notice showing up there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Fear.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I want you to maybe even close your eyes for a second and just bring your attention down and into your body. What do you notice there? Just directly sort of observe it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just a fear... frozen. I don't have the energy. Crippled.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So feeling frozen and like you don't have the energy. Right. And as you do this, can you also notice that there's a you there that's noticing this sense of feeling frozen? It's not the same as this sense, but just notice that there's a you that's sort of behind your eyes and noticing this experience.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'm just there observing and then I guess making judgment on myself.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And let me ask you for a second to just see if you can notice what thoughts show up when you're thinking about this topic of feeling like a rat on the wheel.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, there's no nowhere to go. Why even bother? It's always been the same and there's no way of changing it. I only know the one pattern.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And can you notice, even just for a brief glimpse, that there's a you there that's having these thoughts? That's not the same as these thoughts?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. It's just an old pattern.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And that thought, that it's just a pattern, can you sort of move that out in front of you? And then notice that there's a you there that's having that thought that it's an old pattern.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That you're in control. I'm the one choosing to make those patterns.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And that thought, I'm the one choosing to make this pattern, can you notice that there's a you there that's having that thought? I don't want you to do anything with the thought, just simply let it be there and notice it as if almost as if it were like an object floating by.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's... I mean, I'm not even aware that I do these things and I'm not even consciously aware of it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And that's a thought too.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This segment was an ACT-consistent segment. Basically, what I attempted to do was to help the client to slow down and step out of the content where the client began the segment. A common way of helping to develop this discrimination is to help the client notice what's present and then to help the client to notice the noticer. There was a piece in the segment where I made a bit of an error by shifting from self as context and I began to refer to the client as you there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I want you to imagine that this is like a chessboard that stretches in all directions. On this chessboard are various pieces, you have the black pieces and you have the white pieces. And all the pieces on this board are your various experiences: your thoughts, your feelings, your memories. They go to war. You've been kind of going to war with these pieces for quite a while now. You have these white pieces that you really like, which are the thoughts that you're a good person, and these black pieces that are like questioning yourself or doubting yourself. I want to propose that in this metaphor, you're not the pieces at all, but you're more like the board, the context where this war takes place.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: But each piece on that board is Phil. I mean, the good, the bad, and the ugly. They all blend in.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, but, you know, you can't see it that way. What we need to do is you need to be able to see it a different way, that you're not those pieces, that you're actually the board. You need to see this differently.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I understand what you're saying, but...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So that piece had both ACT-consistent and inconsistent elements. The inconsistent piece came at the end of the vignette when I attempted to convince the client that he needed to see these pieces in a different way. An alternative approach would have been to have taken the client's expression, that all these pieces together are me, and perhaps picked up an object and said, "And those thoughts you just expressed, those are on the board too."

video_details.title: Learning ACT // Part 4: Getting in Contact with the Present Moment

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In this next set of clips we're going to be working from chapter four, the present moment. And here we're going to be helping the client to contact the present moment and also move away from spending too much time in their history or in their future. We'll also be helping the client to see the moment as an ongoing experience so that they're in the process of contacting the moment with awareness rather than getting caught up in what their mind has to say about past and future. In this particular competency we're going to be focusing on helping the client to contact the present moment. This client that we're working with is having a lot of anxiety and sadness around her feelings of loneliness. And she's also feeling like she can't stand it any longer.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just feel like even when I'm in a room with a hundred people that I'm still by myself and I want to have friends and I want to go out, but I just feel alone no matter what I do. And when I'm at home I'm really unhappy and and really lonely, but I just can't be around anybody.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can I have you go back to this statement that you made? I just really feel alone no matter what I do. Could you say that again for me? A little slower.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I... because I used to have people calling me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I'm gonna ask, I'm just gonna interrupt you gently again and see if we can get you back to this moment, this space where this loneliness is showing up. Could you just for me one time say, um, I'm really feeling this loneliness?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm really feeling this loneliness.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And just stay there. Just be aware of what your body's doing. Notice your hands. Notice the little shimmer as you breathe in. Notice the feel of the tears in your eyes and rolling down your cheeks. And let's just stay in this moment with this experience.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's hard.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, now notice that your mind said that in this moment. And you just took a deep breath. Stay with it for just another few moments.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I really feel that...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, I'm gonna slow you down again and just with from a very gentle place, very gentle place, ask you to stay and notice. That's all. Your breath.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: As you observe yourself, can you feel it changing? You feel it move in and out?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what you notice here is that as a process, like you're experiencing an ongoing sense in each moment of the sadness, your hands moving, tears rolling down your cheek. So one thing that your experience tells you is that you can stand it and it keeps changing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In this clip we did a act consistent piece and essentially what I was helping the client to do was just stay present to the moment. Gentle interruptions to help that process happen are okay. Sometimes therapists will stray away from that because they're taught that they shouldn't interrupt the client while they're speaking, but speaking in certain contexts and situations can really lead the client away from their experience, away from what's happening right now. So those gentle interruptions to help the client show up to that place are one way to help them contact the moment, describing what's happening for them, helping them be aware of what's going on in this moment to the next. Additionally, it helps them contact the ongoing experience that happens in each coming moment. So emotions change from maybe heavier to lighter, you notice that your tear is rolling down a cheek at one moment and that your hands are wringing the next. So you can kind of see the ongoing process of experience there too. There's one place where I think that I made a small mistake when I asked her to do it for me. I wouldn't normally do that and I wouldn't recommend that others do it either because this is really about what's there for her to do in terms of where she's headed in her life.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I just feel really alone most of the time and even when I'm with people I'm still just so by myself and I feel like no one cares or even notices when I walk into a room.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, so let's start there with no one noticing that you've walked into a room. What emotion comes up with that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, sadness.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you feeling it now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, a little bit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So just stay with what you're feeling right now, even the little bit. Just be present to that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it's like I feel like I try a lot of the time really hard to to make efforts to bring people together and even when I'm in a group and I'm formulating something that it's like the whole group ends up clicking except me and I'm always on the outside of it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What other areas are you on the outside?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: At work. I feel like oh we'll be having a meeting or something and I'll end up going into my head about something and then I'll miss the conversation and then everyone will start laughing and then you know I will not have any idea what just took place.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How long has this been a problem for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know it it would happen in grade school, playground stuff. Okay, just...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you could probably describe this all kinds of things about how this happens.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, in the third grade I tried to formulate this cheerleading group for this flag football that the boys did and um I put the whole thing together and we went down to the field to present our new cheers and then the flag football guys they really liked it but they said okay we want to take everyone except you. And it was my idea. Right, right. And I was the one who ended up being on the outskirts again and I really tried that time to...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So outskirts is really part of the problem, being on the outskirts.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Maybe we can think of ways to help you not be on the outskirts anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In this clip we initially started by making an act consistent move, asking the client to show up to what she's experiencing. But then once the client began to offer material after that, then the clip became act inconsistent. The therapist got caught up in the content of what the client was saying. And if you think about this clip as compared to clip number one where the client was being asked to be in the moment, there seemed to be a much more kind of vital and alive emotional connection in that place. In this second clip where I'm caught and off in content of what she's saying, she's crying but she's crying about the past. It has a different quality to it where she's kind of crying about the story of the cheerleader and it's lost some of its vitality, some of its openness and uniqueness in the moment. Um that also might have been a time where I could have slowed her down and asked her to get present again, uh to show up to what she's experiencing in the moment again and to try and get her out of her past and back to this place. In this next clip we're going to be working on core competency three. In this competency we'll be working with the client to help him see his experience as an ongoing process, so it'll be a showing up to each moment. This particular client is very worried about aging and has a urgency about him in terms of getting things done in his life before it's too late.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just don't have a whole lot of time here. I mean I just woke up one day and I was like fifty-seven, okay? I I I'm not ready for this. I keep I keep myself busy with with doing whatever I need to do to I don't want to deal with this. I mean I'm getting older and my hair's falling out, I'm just sick of this. I I don't want it, I'm not ready. I'm not ready for the age to come in yet. No but you don't understand, you don't understand. It's like I'm already fifty-seven. Do you get that? Fifty-seven, how am I gonna... there's too much I have to do in my life yet. I'm not ready.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If I could interrupt you for just a moment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No but you don't understand do you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I do, I'm just gonna ask you to pause and just take a deep breath. Okay.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I do notice what it is.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And notice how it is that you're talking about this. I can feel the pressure and urgency.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you aware of that, where that is, can you locate that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: This pressure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Where do you feel it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Feel it in my heart.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I just want you to stay present to that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't have a lot of time to sit and be present.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, and notice that. What emotion shows up with that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sadness and failure. I don't want to go out like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I'm gonna ask you just to hang in there and notice this place, notice this moment. And also as you notice these moments, as you show up to them, something changed. The urgency left.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Wow. It did.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It did.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In this last segment we worked with the client to contact the present moment. It required getting the client to slow down and observe their behavior. In this contact, the client also slowed down in terms of the experience of urgency. This is act consistent in the sense that we want the client to kind of experience the moment as it unfolds in the here and now. So the urgency does dissipate, but it's not as a long-term goal for the client but as an awareness of what happens when you show up to the moment.

video_details.title: Motivational Interviewing - Good Example - Alan Lyme
video_details.description:
Interview B.

Alan Lyme, LISW, MAC, brings respected and innovative clinical and program management skills as the Director of Training for the Phoenix Center in Greenville, South Carolina. Alan has been an active member of MINT (Motivational Interviewing Network of Trainers) since 2004, is an Internationally Certified Clinical Supervisor, a Master Addictions Counselor, and a Leadership Challenge Workshop Certified Master in Training. He is concurrently the trainer for the University of South Car

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Ms. Clark. My name is Alan Lime, and I'm a social worker here at the Family Health Center. Dr. Seal asked if I would spend some time with you today. I'm glad you're here, but I'm curious why he sent you to see me.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I saw Dr. Seal last week for increasing stress and anxiety. I mentioned that my occasional glasses of wine have turned into three or four glasses some nights. He had some concerns about that and felt you could help me with the stress.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you went to him for stress, and he's concerned your alcohol consumption might be part of that. I see you filled out this sheet for me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You noted here that you have four or more drinks in a week, and sometimes more in one sitting. What kind of drinks do you typically have?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Usually wine with my meals. It used to be one or two glasses, but it's been more like three or four since my stress increased.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Based on your form, you scored six points, which puts you in the 'at-risk' zone. This level of drinking can increase stress and cause physical ailments. For a healthy woman your age, the recommendation is no more than three drinks in a sitting and seven in a week. What do you make of that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's news to me. I thought red wine was supposed to be healthy. Seven a week seems very low.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's certainly less than you've been drinking. Dr. Seal is likely concerned about the interaction between alcohol, stress, and any medication he might prescribe. What is it that you like about alcohol?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It temporarily reduces my stress, and I enjoy the taste of a good glass of wine.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: On the downside, if I have too many glasses, I wake up feeling bad. Also, I like expensive wine, so drinking more increases my financial burden, which is one of my stressors.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like a catch-22; you're drinking to reduce stress, but it's also increasing your stress.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe I need to find another way to deal with my stress.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've exercised in the past and that helped, but my schedule is difficult right now. I hoped Dr. Seal could prescribe something for when I feel overwhelmed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: He may be able to, but he's likely concerned about the alcohol interaction. On a scale of 0 to 10, how important is it for you to do something about your drinking right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: If it's increasing my stress and preventing me from getting help, it's fairly important, maybe a seven.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Why did you choose a seven and not a lower number?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have to get things under control. My kids depend on me and I have to work to ease this financial stress.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What would bring that up to an eight or nine on the scale?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The risk of drug interaction. I certainly can't afford to have any more stress in my life.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you'd rather lower your stress than increase it. How confident are you that you could change your drinking habits?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm pretty confident, probably about a seven or eight.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And would you choose to cut down or quit altogether?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd like to try cutting back. However, if Dr. Seal says I have to stop to take medication for my anxiety, I'd be willing to do that for a period of time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Based on that, how ready are you to make a change right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: If I can find another way to manage the stress, I'd be pretty ready, maybe an eight.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You seem very motivated to make this shift because of your responsibilities and your goal to lower your anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm confident you can follow through. Besides exercise, what is one other thing you think might help lower your stress?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe just having someone to talk to, to bounce some ideas off of.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We can set up an appointment for you to talk to one of our behavioral health specialists. I also have a pamphlet on healthy limits and how alcohol is affected by medication. I wish you the best of luck with these changes.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you very much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're welcome.
