Dr. Becky Spelman uses a technique known as Eye Movement Desensitization & reprocessing Therapy (EMDR) to help a client get over the emotional trauma of a break up.  
EMDR can be used for a range of emotional problems including PTSD, anxiety, and much more.

For more informat

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, um, so what memory would you like to work on today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well I'm going to work on a memory of an ex-girlfriend when I was 18, when we split up. I was really upset. It was the first time being in a proper, very intense relationship. Lovely girl, but when we split up I was really upset for a long time. It took me about two years to get over her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how distressing would that memory be to you now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Eight, nine maybe. Three, four, five, four. That's still a long time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So we'll start processing now. I'll tune you into what to start with and then as we do a set of eye movements, or we might do taps or tones, just notice what comes up for you. Be curious and just notice. Sometimes things will change, sometimes they may not. You may notice other images, thoughts, feelings, or body sensations. Other memories may come up, or you may just be aware of the eye movements or taps. There's no right or wrong response, just notice whatever comes up and report back to me after I stop.

diarization.speaker: Ther therapist
diarization.text: So I'd like you to bring up that image and those negative words 'I'm lost' and just notice in your body where you feel that. Okay, just notice.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's your distress rating for that out of 10 when you think about that now? 10 is the highest level of distress and zero is the lowest.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Zero, one?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Zero or one. Okay. Could I get you to close your eyes and just focus on that memory again and just place yourself in that memory.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. What did you notice?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just going through it again. Yeah, it feels okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. Okay. Just notice that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's just try some tapping. It's a different way of doing it and some other stuff can come up. I'm going to get you to put your hands just on your knees like that. And if you could just close your eyes and I want you to go to that point, the last thing you noticed, that it's okay to love someone. Just notice what comes up.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So can you visualize that memory again and we'll start processing again with that memory? Do you want hand movements or tapping?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Tapping.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tapping. Yeah. Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What did you get?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. What's the distress rating when you think of that memory now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Visualize it. It's okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. If you were to rate it, zero being no disturbance at all, 10 being highest.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Zero.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Zero. Okay. So when you think about the original incident now, how true do the words 'I am strong' feel to you out of seven? Seven is completely true.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh really? Pretty strong.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yep. Out of seven?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Six.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Just hold those words together when you think about that incident. Think about the incident and the words 'I am strong'.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What did you notice?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: More relief.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, just notice that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: More relief.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, just notice that. And how true does that feel out of seven?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Seven!

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Just notice that. And in relation to the actual thing there that we're working on, the original memory, how are you feeling about that now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. Do you feel that that got processed in today's session?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah, I do.

video_details.title: Learning ACT // Part 2: Developing Acceptance/Willingness

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In these next clips, we're going to be talking about acceptance and willingness, and we're going to be focusing on the core competencies in Chapter 2, that include contacting the cost of control when you're unwilling and also looking at the paradox of control. And I'll be working with a client who has a difficult history of trauma, and largely she's been working to avoid the experiences that accompany that trauma.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's a really painful memory. I just... yeah, I just would rather not go there at all. I just don't really like to talk about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And so when you notice that you don't want to talk about it, what emotional experience shows up with that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm just kind of numb to the experience. Over the years, I've blocked it out, tried to at least. So I just find not dealing with it at all, just not trying to think about it is the way that I've been.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: One of the things that I'd like to ask you to do at this moment is to just see if you could let yourself contact the experience of numb. Is it there? Do you notice it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So let's start there with that particular experience. Where do you notice it in your body?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right here. It just kind of feels like a fist, a little bit, and like I can't really breathe that well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So just notice that you're having the thought 'can't breathe', that it's shaped like a fist, and just let yourself be present to it for a moment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's hard.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, notice that one too. Take your time. And then as you notice this feeling, I want you to think back about when this feeling shows up and you're present in it. You're trying to get away from that painful experience. And when you do that, what's the cost? What happens?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm forced to relive it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it shows up even when you don't want it to be there. So one cost is a kind of this paradox: 'I don't want to feel it, but there it is.' Are there other costs?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess it just kind of seems like even when it's not in the forefront of my life at that moment, it's just always there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's almost like it's haunting you. And when it's haunting you, how workable is your life? What's going on in your life?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't feel like I'm a part of my own life.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: One thing that it sounds to me like is happening here is that numbing out and running away actually makes the problem grow, like it's everywhere. Let's just start where you're at in the difficulty of not being able to talk about it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In this clip, the client is asked to show up to the moment of what she experiences, to be willing to experience numbness as it is. We're also looking at the costs of the numbness and the avoidance so that we can link up the unworkability of the agenda of control.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's really hard for me to even try to verbalize what happened and I just feel like I'd rather not go there at all.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what emotion shows up with not wanting to go there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Numbness.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I understand that you would feel the experience of numbness, that makes sense to me. It's very difficult to have these kinds of experiences. I think anybody in your shoes would feel that way. Does that help?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean it's still there but that helps a little bit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good, because sometimes these kinds of things can be overwhelming. And when they're overwhelming, it sometimes helps to just back off a little bit. How are you feeling now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel a lot better being able to step away from it and not have to go there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In this clip, although validation may be helpful in small ways, moving in to comfort her probably will not help this client find a place where she can be flexible and more willing in such a way that her values are actively chosen. I allowed her to escape and reinforced the notion of control.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In this next segment, we're going to look at the cost of unwillingness relative to valued life ends. This particular client is struggling with her relationship with her boyfriend; she's feeling rejected and is trying to overcome her emotional experience around that rejection.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just feel really self-conscious and unattractive around him. I want to be supportive of his career, but I just end up creating this whole anxiety trip around basically sharing my needs and my wants in the relationship.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What happens for you when you begin the process of sharing your needs or wants? I hear anxiety in there, is that what happens?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, anxiety, fear that I'm going to say something stupid or that he's going to disagree with. I just feel like I'm this tiny little speck.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: From this place where you're feeling anxious, what happens to your relationship?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think initially he's open to having the conversation and then just this voice in my head just won't stop talking, and then I just end up shutting out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds to me like it's not going the way you want it to. Is it growing further apart?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it feels that way.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there's this anxiety that's in there, there's this kind of running dialogue in your head about this is going to be stupid. Would you be willing to feel those things if it meant that you got to have a closer relationship with your boyfriend?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Ultimately, yeah. That's what I want.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Part of wanting a good relationship includes feeling the anxiety, letting it be there, and taking steps that are about moving closer. These can be little tiny pieces of willingness; you can move into getting closer and carrying these emotions and thoughts with you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, well that's what I want to do but it's hard to feel those things and carry on normally.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Bring that thought too, and take those steps. Would it be worth it to you if you got to have a closer relationship?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Essentially, I was working with the client on willingness to experience if it means that she gets to attain valued life goals. For her, it may mean holding the anxiety, being present to it, and choosing a valued path while carrying the emotions with her.

video_details.title: Learning ACT // Part 3: Undermining Cognitive Fusion

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We're going to look at competencies two through four in this chapter, which involve helping people to separate from their mind and catch the thinking process in flight. We'll observe a client with panic disorder preparing for an exposure exercise.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, today's the day.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, but I'm not really feeling it. I haven't been able to stop thinking about it all week, my chest is tight, and I almost didn't come. I'm afraid I'll lose it once I walk inside the mall.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Let's slow it down so we can catch it. We agreed to look for Mr. Anxiety, and it looks like he's here. Does this feel like familiar territory to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it happens to me all the time. That's why I came here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's big time and very familiar. How old would you say these urgent, racing thoughts are? One leads to another, saying this is going to happen, then that. Are you with me?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm, I see what you're saying.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How old is that specific process, even if the exact words are different?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's happened since I was a kid. Before I was a teenager, my parents would try to take me to a mall or a street fair and I'd be a wreck in the car on the way there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So this has a long history. Is it fair to say you've been turning your life over to that process? We're working to create a space where something different can happen.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's what I hope for. I've missed out on a lot because I can't keep it together enough to go where other people go.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We're right at the point where the action happens. You aren't in the situation yet, but we're where the thoughts are being conceived. Can we slow down and just watch it? I want to do something odd to show how the mind works. I have a pen here that says something: 'woo.'

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, you do. It says woo.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If I ask you what this says next week, or next month, or even next year, what would you say?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd still say it says 'woo.' I see what you're saying. I've been thinking for years that I'll lose it in a crowd, and here it's happening again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Exactly. Letting that thought run your life is what brought you here. Notice how old this thought is and the cost it's produced. This pen says 'woo,' and your mind says if you go to the mall, you're going to...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Lose it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Your mind is just doing what minds do. Is it really your enemy?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I guess that's just what happens. If I can learn a pen says 'woo' in two seconds, I've had a lifetime of this other thought.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: As we prepare for this session, I want you to watch your mind as it constructs these scary futures. Notice them like you would carry something fragile. It's not your boss, just your mind doing its thing. Are you willing to try that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I can try. I can feel my mind kicking in now, telling me I'm going to fall apart.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good catch. Let's do the same thing with that thought too. That segment was ACT consistent, using techniques to create separation between the person and their mind. Now let's look at an inconsistent example.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, today is the day. Ready for Mr. Anxiety?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm not sure I can do it. I've been petrified since last week. My chest is tight and I'm sweating. I'm afraid I'll pass out or go crazy in the crowds. It's just too much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's not surprising you're thinking this since it's an old thought. But in all the years you've had these thoughts, have you ever actually lost it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, but I haven't really tested it much either. It sure feels like it's going to happen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's just a thought, not a fact. Let's try something silly to look at it differently. Give me a cartoon character you like.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Donald Duck.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Imagine those scary thoughts in a Donald Duck voice. Mentally hear him saying it's going to be bad and terrible. Doesn't that make the thoughts seem ridiculous?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, they are pretty silly thoughts. I guess I'd say I'm going to hyperventilate and lose it. It does make it feel a bit different.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hang on to that when the anxiety hits to remember these things aren't necessarily true. That segment was inconsistent because it focused on ridiculing the thoughts to make them go away, rather than just noticing them. Now we'll see a student struggling with career choices.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's inside this decision for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm nervous because I have one semester left and I'm not sure I'm on the right path. My parents and teachers all want different things, and I feel pulled in six different directions.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What are the two major alternatives you're weighing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Choosing family and friends versus focusing on career success and making money. I always feel like I'm failing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It seems like you think choosing one means losing the other. Is that really true? Maybe you just need to follow your heart and make a choice. Just do it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel like I am doing it, but I'm not going anywhere. I'm trying to cover all the bases.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That was a 'normal' interaction but inconsistent with ACT because we focused on the content of the problem rather than the process. Now let's see a more consistent approach with the same client.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's inside this choice? It feels like your thoughts are very close, almost blinding. Is that a familiar place for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, definitely. It's a very worried space.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Your mind is trying to help, but it's doing something very familiar. Let's notice what the mind is doing and what's showing up in your body. Every time you make a decision, your mind says you're leaving something behind, right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's scary to not know, but I guess I don't have control over that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It is scary when you open some doors and close others. Can you open up to that scariness rather than trying to fix it? You're not doing anything wrong; it's just part of the process.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In this section, we caught the 'mindy' process that pulls people into obsessive problem-solving and created some separation to allow for a more flexible way to explore life's choices.

video_details.title: SCENE 15 Suicide risk assessment
video_details.description: This video is a learning resource for "Psychotherapy: An Australian Perspective" available at http://www.ipcommunications.com.au/title_psychotherapy.html. In this video all characters, 'therapists' and 'clients', are played by actors, and scenarios are fictitious; any resemblance to a real person, living or dead, is purely coincidental. Scenarios are designed and offered for the sole purpose of facilitating the education and training of helping-professionals; they cannot be used to guide the tre

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay Ian, so you've been telling me that you've actually had quite a rough week this week. Can you tell me a bit more about what's been going on for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, things were bad, as you know, last time I saw you, but I had a meeting with my boss this week and it was about my work performance. And I think that my depression's been getting in the way of working properly at work as well. I haven't been able to concentrate and so on. So he didn't really think that I'd been performing too well, so my review was quite bad in a number of areas and I don't know, I just feel as though it's just another thing that I don't really need to deal with at the moment on top of everything else.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so it's leaving you feeling quite overwhelmed.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, overwhelmed and just don't know if I can handle it anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. When you say that you don't feel that you can handle it, what kind of goes through your mind thinking about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's just one thing on top of another, on top of another, and no matter what I do, I just can't seem to see how things are ever going to get any better.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's very very hard with all of this happening, with your financial problems, with then having difficulty at work because you're feeling so depressed with your concentration, to ever even think that things might get better. Does that kind of make you feel that it's kind of not worth it at the moment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I just don't think that anything I can do is going to help me get out of this rut.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So feeling quite helpless. Okay. Does that make you think at all about wanting to end your life?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It does. How often is that coming up for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Quite a lot since the review, in the last few days.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Last few days. Okay. So you're having those kind of thoughts going through your mind. Do you have any time when they're not going through your mind?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Not much. Okay. So tell me a bit more about what actually goes through your mind when you think about this.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just think it would just be a lot easier just to bow out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So that seems like a kind of an option that would work. Okay. Have you thought about how you might do it if you were to bow out?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. It's a bit hard to talk about. Probably the medication that my GP's put me on. I don't know much about it but I imagine if I took enough it would be enough.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So when you think about it, you think 'well, if I took all the medication that I have then maybe that would be enough to end my life.' And you're obviously here today, so what has stopped you so far from actually acting on those thoughts?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not much. I don't know. I don't like the idea of my daughter thinking that I didn't have the guts to stick with my life.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so that's something that kind of stops you when you think about her. Any other things?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm from a fairly religious background I suppose, and so I think it would be seen as a sin.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And are you aware, Ian, of kind of what you're hoping will happen? Because sometimes when we're feeling this desperate and overwhelmed, we can get a sense of we just want things to stop versus maybe wanting to die.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just want it to stop.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You want it to stop. Okay. So it seems that say taking all the pills that you have would be one way of having a solution to your problems. But when you think about that, what stops you is the feeling of what your daughter would feel like and that it goes against your beliefs.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it just seems like the only way.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The only way. Okay. So has it been quite hard for you in the last week since you had the performance review to focus on the strategies we've been talking about?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'm sorry, I haven't really given that much thought.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. That's been really hard to hold on to. Have you still been going to work since the performance review? What have you been doing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just spending a lot of time in bed, sitting around the house looking at photographs of my late wife.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And the more you do that, does it make you feel worse? So it would seem that we're in a kind of a dilemma here. On the one hand you have this option that would seem to solve all your problems by making everything stop, but on the other hand there's a part of you that doesn't want to do that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How strong do you think that part of you is at the moment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not very.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Say in a percentage-wise, which part feels stronger? The one that says 'let's go home and take all the pills'?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's much stronger.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's much stronger. Have you been collecting the pills for that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Only the ones the doctor's given me, the antidepressants and the sleeping tablets.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. This is quite concerning and I'm worried about you going home and feeling like this. Do you have any ideas of what you think might be helpful for support for you at this point in time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I could give John a ring, I suppose. He's my brother. Go and visit him and his family.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you feel that you'd be able to do that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't want to burden him with all of this though. Just because my relationship's in the toilet doesn't mean he has to suffer all of my misery as well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So you worry about being a burden to him. Would he see it that way?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably not. He's quite supportive.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So do you feel that you could contact him after the session, or would you prefer to do it maybe together?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can give him a call when I get home.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. As we can see from that scenario, Ian was quite depressed and feeling quite helpless and was admitting to having constant suicidal ideation. It would be important to take enough time to actually do a thorough risk assessment. Some things that would be important to get from Ian would be how likely he felt that he would actually act on his thoughts, whether he'd done a trial run, or had any previous attempts.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You sound like you feel quite confident that you'll do that. Alright.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's really important to think about how safe this client is to leave your office on their own. He mentioned a couple of protective factors, like not wanting to hurt himself because of his children or his family. Another thing is to engage the client in trying to think of solutions to get involved with what might help him to feel better and engender hope. Knowing the lethality of the means is another important thing to think about and to find out. There's quite a number of things you need to find out: the intent, the means, and the support structures.

video_details.title: SCENE 12 Exploring feelings
video_details.description: This video is a learning resource for "Psychotherapy: An Australian Perspective" available at http://www.ipcommunications.com.au/title_psychotherapy.html. diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Amanda, thanks for coming in today.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Your GP sent me a letter telling me a little bit about what's been happening for you, that you've been having some difficulties since the birth of your son a few weeks ago. Tell me a little bit about what's been happening from your perspective.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's been really difficult. I've been really struggling, and I don't know why. This should be a really wonderful time for me and something that I've been looking forward to.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But it hasn't been a good time for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I could never have imagined that it would be like this. This is not what I thought it would be like.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What has it been like for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm just not feeling how I think I'm meant to feel. It's difficult sometimes for me to actually do what I'm meant to do as a mother and that just feels so wrong.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So wrong.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: This isn't how I'm meant to be. I feel like I'm just meant to love looking after him and taking care of him, but it's just not feeling that way and sometimes it's even hard to want to.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're meant to be feeling this.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, yeah, and this is something that we've been trying so long for and it's just been so important for both of us.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So this thing that has been so important and now that it's here, now that it's happened, it's different to the way that you imagined?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Completely different. I thought that I'd blossom and just love this time and I do love him, it's not that I don't love him, it's not that I don't want to do this, I do, but there's this part of me that is just really struggling with this.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me a little bit more about that part that's struggling.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's really difficult to even talk about because I'm not meant to feel this way, but there's this part of me that would just not like to get out of bed in the mornings. I just want to sleep. I don't want to do anything, just want everything to go away.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And that's difficult to admit that, isn't it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's really hard to admit because I can't imagine that anybody else could understand what this feels like. It feels unnatural almost, but it's kind of a relief to say it out loud.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And this is the place that you can say what needs to be said.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. There's this part of me that almost feels angry with all the stuff I've got to do and I don't feel like I'm getting the support that I need and it's really difficult, and I feel like I have to do it all myself.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So feeling as though it's all on you, that you've got to deal with it all alone.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, and it's huge. It's this little boy that just needs me to be there and I'm struggling to be there and to want to be there even, so it's really overwhelming.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: By yourself with it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My partner John's there, he tries, but I think he's getting frustrated with me too. He had expectations of how I would be and how we would be and how this would be and I think that he's disappointed in me and that doesn't help. And so then I sort of feel like I have to do it to prove that I am okay and that I am kind of holding it all together and I do love this.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So trying to keep a mask up, trying to seem as though it's okay.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I don't want him to know how I feel. I feel like I'm a bad mother already.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's a painful feeling, having tried so hard to have this child.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's all I've wanted and it's all we've been talking about and planning for for so long, and it means so much to John as well and I'm just, it's just not happening how either of us thought and I really want it to.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so at this point, it's six weeks?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Six weeks.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: They've been a really rough six weeks it sounds to me, really rough. Having waited so long to have this child, you've gone through the birth, and I understand from your GP it was a somewhat difficult birth.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was, yeah, it wasn't what I thought either, it was awful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So from the very start it hasn't been as you thought, and now you're at that point where the reality is here, the reality of this baby, and it sounds to me that there's a struggle going on for you but it's a struggle that you're feeling very much alone with.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay.
