diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So Felicity, I think that we've done a lot of good work today and I'm delighted that you didn't have a panic attack last week. That's really impressive and you seem really pleased about that as well.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And so you know I think today we've run through a couple of more techniques that you can use to manage your anxiety and it seems to me that you've got a good grip on those, yes?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah definitely. I think today was really helpful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh good. That's fantastic. Well I guess if we wind up now and then meet again next week, yeah?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah. But did I tell you actually that I had an argument with my mum on Thursday?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, really?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah it was a really really big one. Yeah what happened was basically that mum she was just getting really angry at me for Dave again because you know we've been going out for three months and as I've told you before she really really doesn't like him. Yeah and she had a go at him for the drugs again and then she was saying you know that I can do so much better and she was just you know like screaming at me and I had to take all of that and you know we were just going around in circles and circles and yeah it was really really not very not very good that I had to sit there and listen to her saying that, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah I can imagine. So you must have been really upset by that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah I was because you know she, well you know that I mean I really like Dave. I think that Dave's really good and I would I would I would like to keep on seeing him but that she disapproves of him and I find it really hard that she disapproves of him.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yes I can see that really causes you more anxiety as well that this is happening and you feel criticized by your mum and perhaps torn a bit between your mum's view and David. So have you talked to him about this argument?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well she doesn't, she doesn't want me to talk to him about it because she doesn't want him to know that she doesn't like him and then you know he doesn't really like her as well because she thinks he thinks that she's a snob and so it's really hard you know I just feel like I'm sort of sort of in the middle and sort of stuck in between the two of them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So Felicity, I'm very pleased that you didn't have a panic attack last week and so are you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And I'm hoping that the work that we did today in looking at a couple more techniques of how you can manage the anxiety has been helpful to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah I think I'll be able to give it a practice this week.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh good. And we've discussed your homework?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So excellent. Well then perhaps if we wrap up for today, all right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um well did did I tell you that I had an argument with my mum on Thursday?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No. Yes?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah yeah I had an argument with mum and it was really bad because she was just yelling yelling yelling and you know it was about Dave. I've told you about Dave before because she doesn't like Dave and she was having a go at me for the drugs you know because he takes the drugs and she was just yelling at me because she doesn't like that he takes the drugs but she doesn't understand that I mean I just want to be with him and so but because she doesn't like him she you know she was yelling at me about that on Thursday.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I can see that this is very upsetting for you Felicity and it is an issue that you've raised before. So I'm wondering whether we should decide that for next week we'll start to discuss these issues that you're having with your mum so that we can work out a plan when we've got our next session. How would that be?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well this one this one I mean the argument was when she was saying she was saying to me that I should leave him and she was saying you know that I could do a lot better and that I really shouldn't be with him and I should just leave she was saying. Um but you know and then she wouldn't let me you know because I I wanted to talk to him about it and she wouldn't let me talk to him about it and because they really don't like each other I just feel really sort of stuck in the middle.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And I can see that that's a really big issue so I think we definitely we'll put this on our number one agenda for next week, okay? And so we'll work on it then because this is clearly very important to you and I think that we're going to need a good chunk of time to be able to help you to resolve some of these issues with your mum. Okay, right. So how about during the week in addition to the other homework you have you have a think about what the issues are that you would like to raise with me next week about this.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, all right. So we can spend we can spend most of the next session talking about it?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like that's going to be a very important thing to do because I can see how distressed this makes you feel.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Yeah alright okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay so we'll meet again same time next week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sounds good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks Felicity.

video_details.title: SCENE 14 Assessment feedback
video_details.description: This video is a learning resource for "Psychotherapy: An Australian Perspective" available at http://www.ipcommunications.com.au/title_psychotherapy.html. In this video all characters, 'therapists' and 'clients', are played by actors, and scenarios are fictitious; any resemblance to a real person, living or dead, is purely coincidental. Scenarios are designed and offered for the sole purpose of facilitating the education and training of helping-professionals; they cannot be used to guide the tre

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, and I suppose now we've gone through a quick recap of the stuff that you told me in our last session, talking a bit about some of these panic attacks that you've been having over the last few months, and also I suppose this increasing sense of your range of activities closing in as you've become more and more worried about leaving the house and doing some of the things for fear of having some more of these attacks. What I'd like to do now is I suppose go back over some of those questionnaires that you filled out for me at the end of last session. I think one of the things that's really important about these is that these contribute something to, or add something rather, to the information you've given me in our last session, and I'm going to be interested to feed back those results and see how they fit with your own experience of the stuff that you've been telling me about as well.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I did my best with them so that they'd be helpful, so I hope they are.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And I understand that some of these measures can take a bit of time to fill out too, so I appreciate you having put the time in and taken them seriously and spent a bit of time thinking about those as well.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I just want to understand what's happening.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, let's perhaps have a look at some of the results of those and see if that does help not only you but me as well I suppose understand a bit more about the panic and some of that increasing sense of things closing in. How does that sound?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sounds good, sounds good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The first one that I gave you I suppose is this one right here. And this one was a measure of I suppose some of the physical symptoms of anxiety. Things that you were telling me about last week included your heart rate going up, the perspiration starting and that trembling as well. One of the things about this measure is that it's a quite a good measure I suppose of those physiological symptoms. Now your score on this one was 22. Now that doesn't probably mean a great deal to you just saying the number like that, but what this indicates I suppose is a moderate degree of those physical anxiety symptoms being a concern for you at the moment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Cause it feels like I've got a lot of those symptoms.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So I suppose that sounds like that corresponds with that score. Yeah, that score is around a moderate to high level of these anxiety symptoms and that fits I suppose with what you've said there about that feeling as though you're having a lot of these symptoms and they're quite frequent and quite distressing for you as well.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, particularly the heart. My heart goes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The second one that you completed was this one here and I don't know if you remember that one.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, yeah, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This was a measure I suppose of some of the thoughts that go through your mind in the midst of some of these panic attacks. The kind of things that you say to yourself I suppose when these panic attacks are winding up or continuing. It's a measure of what I suppose we've referred to in our last session as the cognitions, the thoughts that go through your mind during these attacks. Now your score on this one was also quite high, which I suppose gives us a bit of an indication of maybe one of the things that might be driving some of these panic attacks. One of the things that I hope we can talk a little bit about over the course of today's session is how those thoughts often link up with some of the panic symptoms, some of those physiological symptoms that we just talked about.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So the thoughts... I know when it's happening there's so many things running through my head, but the thoughts make it worse in some way, or...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I suppose that's one thing that we'd need to consider, that's one idea that you and I might test out. But at least at this stage what this suggests is that the thoughts seem to go with the panic attacks. Whether they're making it worse or whether they're part of it, you and I will probably have to spend a bit of time discussing that, maybe even trying out a few little experiments and things to see exactly how these thoughts do relate to the panic attacks that you've been having. But for now at least I suppose what this suggests is that they kind of seem to go together, that there's a high level of these kind of worrying thoughts and they correspond with or go together with the panic attacks. Does that fit with your experience that those thoughts are there at the time of the panic?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It does actually. I hadn't actually stopped to think about them being two different things. Like when it happens it just goes... it's like a train coming through. It's just all happening, I'm in the midst of it. But you're right, there are the sensations and the thoughts as well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Obviously it's very difficult to tease those apart when you're in the midst of a high level of anxiety or even a panic. It can be difficult to kind of separate those out, but I think that's one thing that might be useful for us to look at is whether we can separate the two of these out. One of the other things that you told me last week I suppose was that as these panic attacks have escalated over the last few weeks, that you've found that you're not going out and doing as many of the things that you used to. You're kind of reducing the amount or the number of activities that you're willing to go into because I suppose you told me last week that you're quite frightened about having these panic attacks in different situations. That was the third questionnaire that I gave you. It was designed I suppose to... have another quick look at that one. That's it there. Remember that one? This is the one that lists all of the different situations.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I actually felt pretty bad when I went through all those situations. I knew there was lots of stuff that I wasn't doing as much, but just going through made me realize just how things have shrunk for me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. And that I suppose fits very closely with what you've said on that questionnaire. It really does highlight to me that there's a whole range of activities, even ones that we didn't discuss last week, that you have kind of started to avoid. We talked last week about shopping centers in particular, but I didn't ask you about cinemas and going out to dinner and some of those sort of places like restaurants, and I think that's again one of the things that this has been useful is to kind of fill in some of the blanks that we didn't get to talk about last week. It's really highlighted that there's a number of these locations that have become quite difficult for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. I know that I don't go to the movies like I used to. It's whether I ever can again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And I'm hoping that that is something that we can work very hard on together, you and I, making sure that we do the best we can to change that range of activities from shrinking in to expanding back out to where it has been in the past before these attacks came on.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sounds good to me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The other thing that I asked you to do was not just complete this series of questionnaires, but even just keep a log of the number of attacks that you'd had over the last week. And you did write down that you'd had a total of five over the last week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hmm, it was a bad week.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All of this information together I suppose, the reason that we do this is not just so that we can get a bit of an assessment of how things are right now. It's useful for that purpose. But I suppose the other reason that we do this, our aim is also to have a baseline I suppose or a measure of how things are now so that over the course of our work together we can see whether that changes. We can see whether some of these are improving, whether some are improving and others are staying the same. We can I suppose use these as a bit of a gauge of our progress in therapy as well. So what I'd like to ask you to do if you're okay with this is over the next few weeks I'll probably ask you to do these once or twice more as we see each other.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Look, I will do anything that helps.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That'll be useful for both of us, I think, to see that progress or to see how things are moving. So I suppose we've got three bits of information there: the number of attacks that you've been having, these questionnaires as well as the stuff that we talked about in our last session. And I suppose that's given us a good understanding of the panic, that closing in range of activities. I'm wondering if there's anything that I haven't asked about though that hasn't been talked about or hasn't been assessed on those questionnaires that you think's important for us to discuss or important for me to know.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I think that... I think that's it. It covers it and just when you put it all together like that it just... that helps actually. But that is it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Great. If you do think of anything else that you do want to kind of add to this, I suppose one of the things that we need to keep in mind is that this will be an ongoing process and I'm sure there'll be new information that does come up that'll help both of us understand exactly what's going on with these attacks and with that reduced range of activities as well. Okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

video_details.title: SCENE 16 Working with a client in a domestic-violence situation
video_details.description: This video is a learning resource for "Psychotherapy: An Australian Perspective" available at http://www.ipcommunications.com.au/title_psychotherapy.html. In this video all characters, 'therapists' and 'clients', are played by actors, and scenarios are fictitious; any resemblance to a real person, living or dead, is purely coincidental. Scenarios are designed and offered for the sole purpose of facilitating the education and training of helping-professionals; they cannot be used to guide the tre

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Kevin, I'd like to summarize our discussion so far. Your wife, Lydia, feels strongly about you attending therapy. You're unsure why she's so upset but want to save your marriage. You've been married for eight years and have two young boys.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes, but it's not that serious.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When we spoke earlier, you said you didn't think the relationship was aggressive and that you just have a normal relationship.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's right. Every couple has arguments.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: To get a shared idea of what we consider aggressive, can you describe a time when you felt most aggressive towards Lydia?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It wasn't just me. A few months ago, we had an argument on a Saturday afternoon after having some beers. It was about whether the kids should stay outside late.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Exactly what behaviors were occurring? Was there yelling?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, there was yelling, but we were both yelling at each other.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You mentioned Lydia sometimes feels scared around you. Why do you think that is?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Our voices get raised. Maybe she gets frightened because I'm in her face sometimes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you mean by 'really in her face'?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When we argue, we are often pretty close together.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, literally in her face?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, absolutely. We're yelling, and I might move a bit closer to her. It's not just me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like you feel you're both contributing equally to the tension.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I suppose so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does Lydia see it that way?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: She gets easily intimidated and makes a big deal out of things. She thinks couples should never argue.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It doesn't sound like you're scared of her. Her fear seems to be a reaction to your behavior, leading her to give an ultimatum about leaving with the boys.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Regarding that Sunday afternoon, was there any physical contact?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not at first, but towards the end there might have been a bit of pushing and shoving.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If I were watching, who would be doing the pushing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably would have been me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Did she fall over?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, but we'd been drinking, and she probably just lost her balance. I didn't throw her or anything like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: When you talk about it, Kevin, it sounds as though you don't see the seriousness in the behavior.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was just an argument. Maybe I went too far with the pushing, but it's not like we beat each other up with sticks or anything.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Did you hit her that day?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: She would say I did. In the scuffle, I might have accidentally struck her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has that happened at any other point?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's not something that happens often. Maybe a couple of times a year.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Were the children around for that incident?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, we were arguing about them. They would have heard it. They are around sometimes when we argue.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does that worry you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Looking back, it's probably not ideal. At the time, I was caught up in the argument and wasn't thinking too much about them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You get caught up in the moment and don't consider the kids. Is alcohol usually involved?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably most of the time, I'd say.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you think Lydia is hoping for from our discussion?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I suppose she just wants us to argue less because she gets frightened by my temper.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You don't sound entirely sure about that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: We have great times, but we also argue. It's just part of being a couple. You can't expect everything to be rosy all the time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like you're happy enough with the relationship as it is.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't enjoy the arguments, but they are just a fact of being a couple.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How willing are you to address these issues?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel I have to. If I don't, the family will break up, and I don't want that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This session illustrated working with a mandated client. Building rapport is crucial since they may not want to be there. Kevin demonstrated common defenses like minimizing and denying his behavior, showing a lack of shared conceptualization with the professional.

video_details.title: SCENE 9 Younger therapist working with an older client
video_details.description: This video is a learning resource for "Psychotherapy: An Australian Perspective" available at http://www.ipcommunications.com.au/title_psychotherapy.html. In this video all characters, 'therapists' and 'clients', are played by actors, and scenarios are fictitious; any resemblance to a real person, living or dead, is purely coincidental. Scenarios are designed and offered for the sole purpose of facilitating the education and training of helping-professionals; they cannot be used to guide the tre

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So I've been hearing you as you've been talking and it's coming through that perhaps at the moment you're feeling a little sort of dissatisfied about where you're at in your life at the moment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean you get to a stage sort of around 50 where you think, well what's it all been about? And you know, it just, feeling a bit stale and a bit like so much more behind me than ahead of me, that sort of stuff. I don't know if you can relate to that really, I mean given where you are in your life, I'm not sure if that is something you can even understand.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you've reached a point, so what I'm hearing you say is that you've reached a point and you're feeling, gee, am I getting a bit stale here? I feel like I've lived all of this life and that's behind me now, and what's ahead of me and where am I going? And perhaps a little concerned about whether or not I can relate?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No offense, but I mean you remind me of my daughter, I mean sort of at the same sort of age, and so it's a bit hard for me to think well how would you even understand what I'm going through? I don't want to offend you or anything, but yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No, no. So how does that impact on you I guess, feeling that way or remind you of your daughter and how am I possibly going to understand what's going on for you? How is that making you feel sitting here now talking to me about these kinds of issues?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess it's a bit like I'm not sure you really understand or could really, I mean if it's possible for someone to understand with that difference in age, simple as that, I guess I just wonder.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're wondering, you're uncertain as to whether I'm going to get it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean you're a nice person and you're helpful and we're talking, but I'm just thinking, well maybe I need to talk to someone who's kind of been there and done that sort of thing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sure, sure, sure. And I guess this is an issue that might sort of come up a bit and I think maybe we should maybe talk about how in this between us, how is it going to be made I guess easier? How can I for you make you feel like I'm getting it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm not sure. I mean it's hard to say I guess. Either we get it or we don't get it, I just don't know. Yeah, I just don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So with that uncertainty, does it feel for you like we can make progress together, with not being sure whether we can resolve it and feeling uncertain? How do you feel?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean I guess there's some things you can understand thinking them through, I just think there are some feelings that maybe that you won't know about or what it's really like to have been there and been a parent and that sort of stuff. So it's just, you know, levels of connection I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, and I'm sensing that that is important for you in what you're bringing up, that it would be important for you to feel those levels of connection?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, because I just want someone, when I say what I want to say, I just want to know that I'm not just saying it to thin air, it's kind of with someone who really will get it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sure. Okay, well I guess and thanks for sharing that with me, Alf. And I guess from my perspective, certainly I haven't been through many of the same issues that you have, and you are the expert on your life and your thoughts and feelings at this point in time. I guess for me, perhaps what I bring is just some knowledge about generally how feelings, thoughts, stages of life impact on people. And so I do feel that perhaps we can make some progress together if we combine our two forces, I guess, you with your expertise on you and me with the knowledge of general psychology type stuff. And so what I'm hearing is from you that you don't want it to be like you're speaking in thin air. So would it be helpful as a bit of a process thing if I check in with you, reflect back to you what I'm hearing and give you the opportunity to say, "No, that's really not quite it" or "Yeah, that's spot on", so you don't feel like it's talking to thin air?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've just been counseled by Danielle and I've been asked to debrief this from the point of view of the client. For me as a client, the issue was very much intergenerational. How can a young person help an older person? It seems to me to be a kind of reversal of the order of the world where older people are supposed to help younger people rather than the other way around. And so I was having discomfort with that. It was almost like the child was being the parent and the parent was being the child, and I found that uncomfortable. I also found it a little bit shameful that I had to tell a younger person what I was feeling, I would much prefer an older person. So for me there was some reversal of the generations and some shame which I'd rather have shared with an older person. And also a sense that you know, how could you possibly understand without having gone through it? It's just mostly words. But I didn't want to offend her, I respect authority and this person was in a position of authority and competence, so I wanted to raise it in a way that wasn't aggressive but it was important to raise. I felt in the way she handled it, I felt that she actually showed competence and authority and I think I responded to that as much as anything else. The suggestion that I was the expert on me and that she was the expert on the process and that that would be a partnership, I think could get us some of the way and I think that's true. At the end of the day, I suspect that would be less desirable to me than if I had a therapist who was also an expert on process but also had some felt experience of what I was going through. I think I would still feel happier about that. But I thought that Danielle showed sufficient authority and awareness of this issue and she was able to manage it in the moment for me to feel well, maybe that was worth another go. But my gut feeling would be that at some point or other we would hit this, we'd come back to this point again and this wouldn't be the only time we'd come here, there'd be moments where I'd be looking for some insight perhaps or some other perspective from someone who'd been there before. So I think what was done was good, it got us some of the way, but I think there'd be tests ahead of us.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so I've just finished being a therapist for Alf who presented as a man with midlife crisis type issues and was concerned that as a young therapist I wouldn't be able to understand his experiences because I haven't myself been through them. And I guess this is something as a young therapist and starting out was always a big anxiety for me and I guess something that has had to be overcome. And I realized that going through life we can't experience every single thing and we're always going to have clients come in with something you haven't yourself been through. So I guess for me it was just about saying to myself I can still offer these people something and I can still help them. And I can at least I guess have some understanding and empathy for what they're going through, and I think that that is the most important thing. In this part I think it was important for me to really process that with Alf, I think I would have lost him out of therapy if we didn't address it head-on to start with. I feel that the therapy itself in that section went well, I think we came to a point where we could perhaps leave that issue aside for now and progress further, and with that in mind constantly as a therapist, the process then being trying to illustrate to him all the time empathy through my reflection of his feelings all the time to show him I guess that I can get it, or if I don't, at least asking him and checking in with him to see whether I'm on the right path. It was confronting as a therapist and it probably always will be, you have that slight kind of your heart flutters a little bit because you feel like you're being challenged. I think the most important thing for me was to not react to that in a defensive way and try and justify myself to him but to really focus on what was going on for him, which I think started off a nice modelling of that this is always going to be what's going on for him and I'll always be wanting to know that. So whatever comes up for him and he feels that I don't understand, that was a nice starting point for him.

video_details.title: SCENE 8 Working with a difficult client
video_details.description: This video is a learning resource for "Psychotherapy: An Australian Perspective" available at http://www.ipcommunications.com.au/title_psychotherapy.html. In this video all characters, 'therapists' and 'clients', are played by actors, and scenarios are fictitious; any resemblance to a real person, living or dead, is purely coincidental. Scenarios are designed and offered for the sole purpose of facilitating the education and training of helping-professionals; they cannot be used to guide the tre

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Debra, when we spoke on the phone during the week, you were explaining to me that your boss had asked you to come in today and have a chat about some of the stuff that's been going on at work recently.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, honestly, she is just such an idiot. I'm really annoyed about this whole situation. This is just a waste of my time as far as I'm concerned.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You certainly sound annoyed even right at the start here of our session. What's the reason that she's asked you to come in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: She had a whole bunch of these like little training nurse people running to her and complaining about how I manage them. And it's outrageous, you know? They come in, they're hardly trained. I don't know what they do at university anymore with these people. But you know, this one, a shockingly bad attempt which she called giving an injection, it was just ridiculous. And then the minute you say to them, 'this is a problem, be professional, pull your act together,' off they trot with their little tails between their legs, whining about my behavior. And now I'm sitting here with you. No offense, I'm sure you're great at what you do, but I could be out there doing my job.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The impression I'm getting from you is that you don't really see the need to come in here but it's something you've been kind of forced into.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: All this talking about your feelings stuff. No, it's not my scene.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I take your point that you seem to see that some of these other nurses that are working with you haven't done their job well, and the way you describe it, it sounds as though you're just doing your best attempt to improve their skills, improve their training. If I was to ask your boss, what was the issue that she took with the way you were handling this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: She said that I was being too aggressive and that I was, can you believe it, messing with their self-esteem? As though it's my job to look after their little self-esteem problems. Either they do the job or they don't. And so I was just being very clear saying that was just a ridiculous thing you did, this is how you should do it, get it right. I was just being clear.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And that's what she meant when she was saying aggressive?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I presume so. I mean, when I did my training and went through all of this stuff, you just did as you were told and you got things right. You didn't run around worrying about how you felt about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it sounds from just the way you're talking that you don't see the way that you manage this as being aggressive. You wouldn't use the same sort of word.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. It's just getting to the point. No nonsense. They certainly know where they stand with me, absolutely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm curious that your boss seems to have singled you out for this sort of thing and it's not something that they seem to have needed to address with other staff in the workplace. What's your explanation for that? Why is it that you've been the one that's been asked to come and see me rather than anyone else in the workplace?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. Maybe I've just been unlucky with the trainees I've had. That's the most obvious reason I can think about. And they've now got all this anxiety since there's been problems in the workforce about any kind of inappropriate behavior. So I think that they've just become trying to pander to the community and the community's needs, and nurses are precious and we can't train enough of them. I just think they've all just gone totally over the top with all these worries about things.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It does sound as though there's some difference of opinion between yourself and your boss. And it also sounds as though it's probably safe to say though that you are coming into conflict with some of these people in the workplace.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: If they just knew their place and just understood that it's my role to tell them what to do and they do it. I mean if they got that, there wouldn't be a problem. In fact they should be sitting here, not me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Because you are the one sitting here, I suppose one of the things that we need to consider is it's difficult for us to control their behavior, but there is a bit of an opportunity here I suppose for us to consider whether there might be some changes that you might be willing to make in your behavior.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Are you saying that you think I've got a problem in my behavior? From what I've told you do you really think I'm the one with the problem?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I suppose it's difficult for me not having been in the workplace to make an informed judgment about that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: This is typical of you people, it's just fence-sitting isn't it?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I think that one of the things that I have to be very careful of is to not make a judgment about something where I wasn't there. But I suppose to help you maybe come up with some ideas as to whether you might be able to make some changes yourself.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't need to make any changes. I'm fine. They are the problem. Like I mean, you know, can't you see that?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I certainly see that that's the way that you see the situation at the moment. That you see it as something where it's the other staff that are the problem rather than something that you're doing in your behavior.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, good point. So we're done?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, what I'm suggesting to you is that even if there is problems with the other staff, their behavior is a little bit beyond what we can do here. But that as I said before there is a bit of a chance that maybe this might be an opportunity for you to consider whether there are some ways that you might want to change your behavior. Or at least consider that. You may be right, but then again...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You really are starting to imply that this is my fault, aren't you? Is that where you're going with this?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No, that's certainly not what I'm trying to say. What I'm trying to say is that in any conflict in the workplace, you know, there's two agents in that conflict and that one of them is outside our control.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The 'it takes two to tango' story, isn't it?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I suppose that a conflict exists between two people and that we have to recognize that the one person in that conflict that you have some control over is yourself and that as I said this may be a time that you can consider making some changes...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Look, I am just absolutely sick of this nonsense! And I think you are just basically pandering to their stuff! And I don't want to keep on doing this nonsense! I mean honestly what's your problem?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I can see that you're getting quite angry in this situation.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm furious! What do you mean quite angry? I'm furious with this!

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And I suppose when you are so angry like this, it does make it difficult for us to talk about this in a kind of reasonable, calm kind of manner. I'm wondering whether it might be useful for us to take a break for a couple of minutes and then come back in and start talking about what we might be able to do, given that you have come along here today, what we might be able to do to help I suppose resolve some of this conflict in the workplace.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: What do you mean take a break?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, can we just maybe stop for two or three minutes? If you'd like to go outside, grab a glass of water, or we can get you a glass of water, and then come back in here in two or three minutes once both of our kind of arousal levels have calmed down a little bit and we'll try and approach this again with a bit of a fresh perspective.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hm, okay.

video_details.title: SCENE 7 Managing therapeutic boundaries in rural areas
video_details.description: This video is a learning resource for "Psychotherapy: An Australian Perspective" available at http://www.ipcommunications.com.au/title_psychotherapy.html. In this video all characters, 'therapists' and 'clients', are played by actors, and scenarios are fictitious; any resemblance to a real person, living or dead, is purely coincidental. Scenarios are designed and offered for the sole purpose of facilitating the education and training of helping-professionals; they cannot be used to guide the tre

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, Felicity, before we start to talk about what you've come here to see me for today, I just wanted to raise an issue with you. I think that we've both realized when you walked in here that we've seen each other around before.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, you're Jake's mom, I've seen you at Kindy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's right, that's right. We do run into each other a fair bit at the kindergarten. So I suppose what that brings up for me is that I'm a psychologist and there is certain boundaries that I have to uphold with my clients. And I think that we need to talk about what we're going to do about this that we do see each other quite often and how we're going to manage that in terms of, you know, keeping those appropriate boundaries within therapy and outside the therapy room.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So how I see it is we have a few different options. The first one is that we could decide not to engage in therapy together given that, you know, there could be some issues when we see each other outside of therapy. How would that option suit for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I guess part of the problem for me is that I really feel that I really need to talk to someone about what's going on for me and I don't really there's no one else in town I can talk to.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, yeah. Psychology services are quite limited in this area, aren't they?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They really are. They are.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you really feel that you need the help and this is the only option that you've got. So given that that's the case, how do you think we could manage this when we do run into each other outside of the therapy room so that we don't crossover, you know, the boundaries of therapist and client?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So if I see you at the kindergarten, shall we acknowledge each other and keep walking or how would you like to manage it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I mean, I think it's good if we can like say hi and stuff, but I probably wouldn't want to talk to you at Kindy about what we do here in case other people hear it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sure, sure. And I'm really glad that you brought that point up because I think that given that we will run into each other quite a bit at the kindergarten, it's fine for us to acknowledge each other, but we do need to keep the therapeutic issues that we talk here in therapy for therapy. And yeah, I'm glad that you think that that would not be appropriate outside of therapy also.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: And I mean, you wouldn't tell any of the other moms, would you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No, no, I would definitely keep it confidential that we're in a therapeutic relationship together and nobody else needs to be aware of that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. So it's kind of like we've got therapy for in here, but then out there, we're just moms.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's exactly right. So if we could just keep it at, you know, those things separate, then I don't think we should run into any problems in therapy. But perhaps we could check in from time to time to see, you know, whether that's becoming a problem for us.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah, okay. Yeah, that sounds good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you think that sounds okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yep.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. So now that we've discussed that issue, let's talk about why you've come in to talk to me today.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

video_details.title: SCENE 10 Interview with an adolescent
video_details.description: This video is a learning resource for "Psychotherapy: An Australian Perspective" available at http://www.ipcommunications.com.au/title_psychotherapy.html. In this video all characters, 'therapists' and 'clients', are played by actors, and scenarios are fictitious; any resemblance to a real person, living or dead, is purely coincidental. Scenarios are designed and offered for the sole purpose of facilitating the education and training of helping-professionals; they cannot be used to guide the tre

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks for coming in today, Sky. Why don't you tell me a bit about what's brought you in here today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh, well, really like dad just thought I should come in. Um, he took me to the doctor a while ago and the doctor said that maybe I should come talk to someone.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you ever been to like a counselor or school counselor or psychologist before?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So this seems a bit crazy, doesn't it? Sitting here talking to some stranger who's going to ask you questions about about yourself.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How do you feel about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Yeah. Because today I just want to get to know you a little bit and understand a little bit more about you know your life and what are some of the issues that have come up. So why do you think your your dad wanted you to come in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, like he just thinks that I get really angry at home and stuff all the time. I don't know, like whatever I don't really whatever.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you think you get angry? Do you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh, not really. I just they don't let me do stuff, so...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. You feel like they're a bit controlling.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are they?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, definitely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. What kinds of stuff would you like to be doing that they...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just normal stuff. Just normal like all my friends can do stuff. I can't do stuff. It's just like whatever whatever.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What kind of stuff are your friends doing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just I don't know like they can just go and like my friend Kylie, she can go and hang out with her boyfriend all the time. And like I just it's not like I want to have a boyfriend, it's just like you know like just want to be able to go out and stuff. Just you know stuff like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. So can I ask you a little bit about your friends and who who would you say is your best friend? Who would you say knows you best?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I don't know 'cause I had a fight the other day with Kylie, so she was my best friend but then we just we just had a fight so...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What was the fight about?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh, it's just really she's just been she's just been an idiot like she she had a fight she broke up with her boyfriend and then like 'cause I'm friends with them both and I was just trying to still be friends with them both and I think I don't know maybe she got jealous or something.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like you were a bit caught in the middle in that situation.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. So who else do you hang out with? Who do you...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like it's really hard 'cause I see them at school but then 'cause they all do stuff with each other outside of school and it's like I don't really get to do that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you do on the weekends? What do you usually get up to?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well I have to do these chores I have to do chores. It sucks.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What kinds of chores are you doing at home?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, like mom likes me to take out sometimes take out the garbage, wash the dishes, clean my room and just heaps of stuff like no one else has to do stuff like that it's not fair.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you see your friends aren't getting all those chores and your parents are coming down hard on you and making you do all that kind of stuff. Do you feel that's really unfair?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Don't you think that's unfair?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, I can see how you might feel it's pretty unfair. What would you like to be doing on the weekends?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hanging out. Maybe go to the movies, go shopping. Yeah, hanging out. Maybe sometimes have like have friends stay over. I'm not allowed to have friends stay over.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're not?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. 'Cause I don't know, mom just I don't know mom and dad just think that if we all hang out together we're just going to like get into trouble and 'cause like they just don't understand what it's like to be young anymore and 'cause and then then they just think that all young people when they get together they're just going to like drink and do stupid things and we just want to hang out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. So you feel like they don't really understand what it is you want to be doing.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. They yeah they don't get it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. So tell me a bit about your parents. Like what's what's your mom like? What's she...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Uh, like it's really weird 'cause mom and dad are really old.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are they? How old are we talking? I'm I'm pretty old, so how old are we talking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You're not old. No, they're like 70 and stuff.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so they're really old. Yes. So old. I thought you were going to say 35 or something and I was going to feel really really old.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well that's kind of old.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, I'm not quite there yet. But the no that's old, hey.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, they're old.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: They are quite a bit older than you. Yeah. And I wouldn't imagine a lot of your friends would have parents that are quite that old.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, like maybe like I don't know 40 or something.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Yeah. So you feel like your experience is a bit different, being at home's a bit different.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah and so like yeah people just don't my friends don't can't really get it and mom and dad don't get it and people don't get it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Who does get you? Who do you think understands Sky?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. Don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I imagine it must get pretty lonely then. Do you have any brothers or sisters at home?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not at home. Mom and dad have got older kids they've moved out of home.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're the only one at home as well.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah and like they kind of did the whole thing with their parents like with my parents did the whole thing with their my older brothers and sisters when they were kids did all the family stuff like we don't go out even go out as a family anymore 'cause like you know go to the beach I love going to the beach. We don't get to do that 'cause they kind of it's like they did that when my older brothers and sisters were kids and they're too old now and they don't really want to.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it feels like you miss out on that kind of stuff because they've been through that stage with their other kids.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And that's what your friends are doing.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I mean maybe a part of what we can do here is try and help your parents understand a little bit more what it is what life's like for you and what it is that you need at the moment. Maybe that could be part of what we do here. I don't know, I don't know if that sounds like something you'd be keen on.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, 'cause I just want them to understand and so I can maybe hang out with my friends. It's lonely at home.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. What's school like? Do you... what grade are you in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um 10.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: 10. Would you say it's hard? But it's you know like...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I like it. When I get to see my friends and...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's your favorite subject? What do you...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I really like art.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you? So you're pretty creative.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. Sort of.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. Do you do you get okay marks?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, okay. Well because I'm just always at home so I'm just always studying, there's nothing else to do. So I go alright.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sounds like you'd like a little bit more balance, do a little bit more fun stuff on the weekends as well. What would be so the ideal weekend would be going to the movies and doing some shopping with some friends and stuff.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, like that's that's not too much to ask.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds pretty reasonable. When was the last time you got to do something like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, maybe a while ago, a couple of months maybe, something like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So is this the reason why sometimes you get angry? You said the original reason why your dad wanted you to come in and talk to someone was 'cause he sees you get kind of frustrated and angry sometimes.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess. I guess sometimes I like just shout at them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You shout at them sometimes.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Because but like they just that's the only way that they can listen to me. That's that's the only way that I think that they can hear me sometimes is if I shout at them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're feeling not heard so you think that shouting at them might make them listen. Does it work?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That sounds stupid but...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well does it work? Do they listen?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. They bring me here.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah.

video_details.title: SCENE 11 Therapist countertransference and supervision
video_details.description: This video is a learning resource for "Psychotherapy: An Australian Perspective" available at http://www.ipcommunications.com.au/title_psychotherapy.html. In this video all characters, 'therapists' and 'clients', are played by actors, and scenarios are fictitious; any resemblance to a real person, living or dead, is purely coincidental. Scenarios are designed and offered for the sole purpose of facilitating the education and training of helping-professionals; they cannot be used to guide the tre

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Marcia, you told me last week that you had a number of important events coming up. I'm interested to hear how some of those went for you over the last week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It has been a big week. I had to give a thank-you speech to the school principal for the school committee. Until I started seeing you, I never would have agreed to do it, but I did get up and say what I needed to. It went well, so I'm really pleased.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's fantastic. This sounds like a big step for a long-standing difficulty.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was pleased that I did it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you give me an idea of some of the strengths you showed during the speech?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The main thing was simply doing it. While waiting to speak, I was anxious and used those breathing techniques you told me about. Once I got up and made eye contact, it went okay. The preparation really helped.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So in spite of the anxiety, you pushed through, used the techniques you learned, and it went well?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I did it. I'm very happy with that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there anything else going on that you'd like to talk about?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Everything was going well, except there's a school camp coming up for the football team that Tim wants to go to. My husband and I have decided he shouldn't go. He gets silly with his friends and things go out of control, so we don't think it's the right time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you won't let him go?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Tim is upset, but we think it's probably best not to let him go.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: There will be other boys with the same assignments who are allowed to go, but not Tim?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you think that's wrong?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds as though you might be being a bit over-protective, don't you think?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm having trouble understanding why it's okay for all the other kids but you won't let Tim go.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He's always been the kind of boy who is easily influenced by his peers.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is this something you'd reconsider with your husband?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I think we're convinced that this is the right way to go.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We've talked about being willing to try new stuff. You did that with the speech, but you're not willing to let Tim go on the camp.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Do you think it's like that?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think you should think about it that way.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess so. But he is our boy and I know what is best for him.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Maybe that's the case, but I would like you to reconsider that, or at least discuss it with your husband again.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: In that segment, I was playing the client. I'd been telling my therapist about my achievements and felt pleased, but when the topic shifted to my son, I sensed all was not well. I felt unfairly challenged in my decision-making, which is not a comfortable situation for a client to be in.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So Mark, tell me how things went with Marcia this week?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think there was some really good stuff. She managed to give that speech she was concerned about, so she was quite happy with herself.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You should be pleased too. When you started working with her, she wouldn't talk to anyone outside her immediate family. She's come a long way.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: There was one other thing that I was a bit concerned about. Marcia didn't want her son, Tim, to go to a school camp. It struck me that she was being very anxious and over-protective. She seemed unwilling to let him have any freedom.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What were her reasons for not wanting him to go?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Just vague, over-protective stuff about him being different to other boys. It just didn't seem like a good sign. It really concerned me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So was her anxiety spilling over into Tim's life?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's right. Her anxiety has moved from giving speeches to now controlling Tim. It didn't look good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I can see that you're really worried about it. What's the thing that's really bugging you about it?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: He's a young guy moving through adolescence, trying to get emancipation from his parents, and he's being prevented by a mother who is ridiculously controlling and sheltering him from the real world.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you feel it's without cause because she didn't give good enough reasons?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: She gave me some reasons, but they seemed trivial and like vague nonsense. I think she's really got to let go of Tim.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Previously, you've had an enormous amount of empathy for her anxiety, but I'm picking up that you're feeling quite cranky with her at the moment. You find her anxiety inappropriate this time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm frustrated that she can let go in some areas but not this one. I know what it's like when you're a young guy trying to get a bit of freedom and growing up. It must be really tough for Tim.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do we know how Tim feels about any of this?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I can imagine how he'd feel. He's a teenager trying to break away from parents and get some freedom.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The way they describe Tim is that he is also a very anxious boy. I'm wondering if he might even be relieved if his parents say he can't go.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I don't know if I'd agree with that. Adolescent males want some freedom to move outside of that over-protective family circle.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I must say that it's almost as though you've decided that this is how Tim has to feel. I'm wondering whether your own strength of feeling about this issue is interfering with your ability to be objective.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I do have a lot of strength of feeling about this, and I suppose that's because I know what it's like.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In terms of what it's like for Tim or for you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: For both of us, I suppose. It's something I've gone through. I know what it feels like to be struggling for emancipation and being held back by over-controlling parents.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But do we know whether that's Tim's experience?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No, of course not. I'm inferring that's what it must be like for him based on what I know about adolescent males.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: At least based on your experience of adolescent malehood.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I suppose so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This is giving us an exciting opportunity to look at our own reactions as therapists. It's unusual to see you become so emotionally reactive in a client situation. I'm wondering if there's a bit more going on for you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I take your point. It does seem to be a stronger emotive reaction than I've had around other issues with Marcia.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I wonder what it was like for Marcia in that session. If you were this strong in telling her she was being over-controlling, how did she react?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: At the time, I thought she was being defensive. Reflecting on it now, some of that may have been a reaction to how forceful I was being in the session. I was pushing it too hard.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Rapport was great at the start, but it did weaken around this issue. The emotions that I was experiencing probably leaked out into the session.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now with some time to reflect, if you imagine you were Marcia, how would she describe what happened?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: She'd probably say I was pushing it hard and being too forceful, direct, and uncompromising in the way that I pursued the issue.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How effective do you think that was as an intervention in terms of helping her think about whether she's being reasonable?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It probably wasn't very good. I was pushing rather than encouraging. I think I was being a bit too forceful in pushing my conclusion on her.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Which probably resulted in her becoming defensive and shutting down, rather than considering all the options.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I need to reflect on this. When I have an issue like this, I need to be more aware of where it pushes my buttons and try to manage my reactions better.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It happens for all of us. The thing is just about being aware of what pushes our buttons and learning how to manage that. That's what supervision is here for.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you for sharing that openly. I'm really impressed at how quickly you've started to reconsider what happened.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thanks for helping me see that. I'll spend some time reflecting on this and considering how I might respond differently in those situations in the future.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Next week, I'll just check in and see what your thoughts were.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Great. Thank you.

video_details.title: SCENE 6 Working with a distressed client
video_details.description: This video is a learning resource for "Psychotherapy: An Australian Perspective" available at http://www.ipcommunications.com.au/title_psychotherapy.html. In this video all characters, 'therapists' and 'clients', are played by actors, and scenarios are fictitious; any resemblance to a real person, living or dead, is purely coincidental. Scenarios are designed and offered for the sole purpose of facilitating the education and training of helping-professionals; they cannot be used to guide the tre

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Danielle, you were telling me a few minutes ago about some stuff that's been going on for you recently that seems to have been quite upsetting for you. I'm wondering if you can give me a bit more information about that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, look, it really hasn't been a good week for me this week, and like I was telling you about the problems with my boyfriend and we broke up and I just, I'm not coping with it, I just can't cope. And I'm just, you don't understand, I just, it's just happened one more time, just one more time and it's just pushed me over the edge and it just happens to me all of the time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you think it'll get better or...?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No! It's just not getting better, it won't get better. You just don't understand that this happens to me all of the time and it's happened again to me now and it's just something is wrong with me. I feel like there's something really wrong with me because people, they just reject me all of the time and I don't understand and I don't know why.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, I mean, I can see that you're really upset about the stuff that's gone on with your boyfriend during the week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, because he just keeps, yeah, just like it always happens, just... and I'm just... and now he just doesn't want to talk to me and I just feel like if I was... just if I was a better person then this wouldn't happen, so I just feel like that this is because of me and nobody understands and I just can't... I just... I can't do this again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, I mean, I hear the stuff that you're saying about the issues with your boyfriend during the week. Has there been other stuff that's been going on for you during the week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No! This is just... this is it! This is... there's nothing else! This just happened, he just broke up with me just the other day and I can't sleep and I can't eat and I can't stop and he just... and I keep calling and he just won't answer the phone and why won't he talk to me? And he just doesn't want to know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I mean, I know that when you break up with someone it's really upsetting. I suppose over time this sort of stuff should get better, I'd think.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, how long?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Uh, yeah, it just takes a bit of time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A bit of time? And I don't feel like I can make it through the time! You need to help me get through the time because this time it just feels like there's... it's never gonna end! Oh, and it hurts!

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, it certainly sounds really tough. I think it's important that we talk about other stuff also, though, that went on during the week other than the breakup.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No! It just... it hurts! I don't know what to do, it just hurts! It hurts!

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It, yeah, I can see that it's really upsetting for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Because he... because he rejected me! Because... because I'm not good enough, because there's something inside me that's broken or something! And he won't even talk to me now and I just need to be... I just need someone to say that it's gonna be okay and that it's okay! Because I can't...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm sure it will be in the long term, even though it's tough right now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Clients who are extremely distressed are one of the most difficult tasks for therapists to handle in a therapy session. What you just saw in the video there was an attempt by myself to assist Danielle through some very distressing events that have been going on for her, specifically a breakup with her boyfriend. One of the things that I hope you did see in that short vignette that you just saw was that although the therapist at some times was engaged with the client and was being somewhat empathic, the therapist was also very, very keen to move off topic, found the distress that the client was showing very difficult to tolerate and was very keen to move away from that subject matter. And even though the client continually pulled the therapy session back to the discussion of her own flaws and the problems with the breakup with her boyfriend, the therapist really wasn't getting the message there and persisted in trying to derail what the client wanted to talk about and move the content of the session away from the breakup with the boyfriend.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, it's almost like, you know, my son just... his little sister is just an irritation for him. Oh, it just breaks my heart when they fight.

diarization.speaker: Patient

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Patient

diarization.speaker: Therapist
