video_details.title: SCENE 1 Discussing confidentiality
video_details.description: This video is a learning resource for "Psychotherapy: An Australian Perspective" available at http://www.ipcommunications.com.au/title_psychotherapy.html. In this video all characters, 'therapists' and 'clients', are played by actors, and scenarios are fictitious; any resemblance to a real person, living or dead, is purely coincidental. Scenarios are designed and offered for the sole purpose of facilitating the education and training of helping-professionals; they cannot be used to guide the tre

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So thanks for coming along today, Brooke. I've really been looking forward to meeting you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, me too.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Cool. Okay. So I just wanted to ask, did you receive that information pack that we sent out to you in the mail?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I did. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Fabulous. Okay. So would you mind if we just spend a few minutes going through that together now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, no, that's okay. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. All right. So I guess something really important that I would like to draw your attention to first of all is this issue here of confidentiality. Basically, everything that you and I talk about together in therapy is just between you and I. However, because I am a probationary psychologist, the things that we discuss I may need to share with my supervisor.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Yeah, that's all right. Will it only be with your supervisor?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, that's right. There are a few special circumstances though where I may have to break confidentiality. That is if you tell me that you might be of harm to yourself or someone else, if you tell me that you've been involved in a serious crime, or if somebody else wishes to access the information that we talk about in the context of legal proceedings and they take out a subpoena. I'm required to give that information then. But of course if any of these things ever did come up, I would discuss these with you first.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, that'd be good. Yeah, thanks.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Great. All right. Something else I just would like to draw your attention to here as well is just our fee here at the clinic, which as we discussed on the phone is $20 a session.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's fine. Not a problem.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And I understand from time to time that things can come up as well and that you might have to reschedule one of your appointments. We just ask that if you could provide us with about 24 hours notice beforehand, so that gives us a chance to be able to set up another appointment time.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah, that's fine. No worries.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Did you have any other questions about anything that you read on that sheet there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, it all seems fine with me, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Wonderful. Okay. So if you wouldn't mind just popping your signature at the bottom there. Thanks Brooke.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No problem.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Wonderful. Thank you. Okay, so I guess I mean to start off with, have you ever been to therapy before?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I haven't. I'm feeling a little nervous about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I can understand that it can be a bit confronting and scary the first time you come along. So I guess to give you a bit of an idea about how I like to work with clients is that I like it to be a collaborative approach so that the two of us get to work together on your problems and concerns that you're having at the moment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Yeah, that sounds good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the purpose of today's session I guess would be for me to get more of an understanding of what's happening for you lately and give us a chance to get to know each other a little bit more. Does that sound okay with you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that sounds really good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And at the end we can sort of touch base again and see how we went for today and whether we'd like to take it on from there.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, okay. That sounds good. We'll have a better idea then, I suppose.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, that's exactly right. Okay. So, I mean just to start off with then, are there any other things that you've tried apart from coming to therapy as some ways to help you cope with what's happening for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really. When I feel down, like I just stay at home and I don't really go anywhere or do anything. I just sort of withdraw a lot. That's all I've really done.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. So you've been really keeping it to yourself and it's quite a big step for you to reach out to someone today.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it is. It's just got to that point where I just wanted to come in and don't really know what to do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Well I guess to start off with then, would you like to tell me a little bit more about what's been happening for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, sure.

video_details.title: SCENE 3 Therapist being rigid
video_details.description: This video is a learning resource for "Psychotherapy: An Australian Perspective" available at http://www.ipcommunications.com.au/title_psychotherapy.html. In this video all characters, 'therapists' and 'clients', are played by actors, and scenarios are fictitious; any resemblance to a real person, living or dead, is purely coincidental. Scenarios are designed and offered for the sole purpose of facilitating the education and training of helping-professionals; they cannot be used to guide the tre

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sam, I'm interested to hear a little bit about what you've been up to since our last session. But before we get onto that, what did you take away as the main points from the last time we met?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The main thing I took away was the relationship between my thoughts and feelings. The way I interpret the world really influences how I think and feel, even if that might not be an accurate reflection of reality.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's a really good synopsis. Remember we talked about setting some homework? I'm interested to hear how you went with that as well.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I haven't actually gotten around to it. I was really busy this week and I didn't do what you asked me to do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me why? Like, why didn't you do it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm really busy, Mark, and I feel like sometimes you don't really get that. I don't really see the point in recording it all the time when I've got other things to do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I thought we discussed how important homework was and you seemed to get that last week. Can you clear up why you feel differently now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like I said, I didn't really get around to it. Homework can be important, but I don't see the point of this particular exercise.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It makes it hard for us to do a good job if you don't do the work between sessions. It's one thing to talk about it, but it's another thing to actually do some of it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I never asked you to tell me what to do or write my feelings on paper. It seems a bit silly and isn't really what I was hoping to get out of this.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's disappointing that you feel that way.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, that's just the way I feel.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's been a week since our last session. What were the key points that really resonated with you from the last time we spoke?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The main takeaway was the notion that how I interpret the world influences how I feel. Seeing the relationship between my thoughts and feeling crummy was really helpful and useful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's a great job of synthesizing the key points. We also discussed setting some homework to put those ideas into practice. How has that gone?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I haven't actually done it. Life just got in the way this week and I didn't manage to write down my thoughts as planned.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I appreciate that it's difficult to fit extra tasks into a busy life. Let's look at the hurdles that got in your way and see if we can solve those problems together. Would that be useful?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure, that would be useful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you give me some specific reasons why you weren't able to get to the homework tasks?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The main problem is that the times I feel worst are when I'm at work in a team environment. I can't pull out a worksheet there without looking like an idiot. It gets in the way when I need it most.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I understand. Since you can't do it at work, how could you modify the task so you still benefit? What's the next best thing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The obvious thing is I could do it later, like during my lunch break or when I get home. Does it have to be done right in the moment?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It doesn't have to be immediate. Doing it at a later time is a great suggestion. Is that realistic for you to do?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't see why not, as I don't have much to do at home. However, even though it seems like a good idea, I haven't actually been doing it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there's another hurdle. Let's put our brains together to solve why it's not happening even at a more convenient time. How might you work around that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm also not convinced that writing things down and analyzing them after the fact will make things any better. I still feel crummy when it happens and I wonder what the point is.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Besides convenience, you're not fully convinced of the rationale. You accept the idea but doubt this specific method. How could we find an answer to whether it works?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I'd just have to do it and find out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's one possible solution. We could treat it as an experiment. If it works, great. If not, we'll know.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, if it works, that's great. If not, I can just stop and I won't be any worse off. I'm willing to give it a go because I don't want to keep feeling this way.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Great. We've identified hurdles of convenience and skepticism. Are there any other problems that got in the way of the homework?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, that's pretty much it. I'm confident I can go away and try that now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Try it this week, and we'll see in the next session if these solutions were effective. We'll revisit this each session to give you the best chance of success.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That sounds good.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just finished acting as the client for Mark, who was the therapist. We did two takes on not doing homework: one with an authoritative, punitive approach and one with a problem-solving focus. The first left me feeling reactive and defensive, while the second felt validating and helped resolve the barriers to the homework.

video_details.title: SCENE 5 Cross-cultural interview
video_details.description: This video is a learning resource for "Psychotherapy: An Australian Perspective" available at http://www.ipcommunications.com.au/title_psychotherapy.html. In this video all characters, 'therapists' and 'clients', are played by actors, and scenarios are fictitious; any resemblance to a real person, living or dead, is purely coincidental. Scenarios are designed and offered for the sole purpose of facilitating the education and training of helping-professionals; they cannot be used to guide the tre

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just haven't been feeling like too good lately. I've just haven't, I'm not very happy at all. And so my lecturer, my lecturer in my course, they said I should probably come here and talk to someone.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you're feeling a bit sort of unhappy and obviously someone's noticed that as you say your lecturer's sort of made a point of saying come here. Can you tell me a little bit about what's happening for you, what's going on for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, just, I've just come over here from India. Um, so I just came here to study and so I just finished my first semester and um, like I'm missing my friends and um, and my family, so you know, they're back in India so I haven't seen them in a while and yeah, just thinking you know, maybe you know maybe it was a bad idea to come here and study, so not feeling too happy about that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it sounds to me, correct me if I'm getting this right, but it sounds because you've moved from India over here, that that kind of social thing, your friends and your family and those sort of connections seem to be a bit lost, is that kind of right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah, because I moved here, yeah, it's only been six months and I really miss them, like miss back home and I thought it'd be easier to kind of make friends and stuff here, but it's not like that. So yeah, so I've just been thinking about if, you know, maybe I should go back or if this is for me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So that's kind of... it sounds to me that's something you're playing with at the moment, whether this has been a good decision for you to come out here or not, wanting to go back.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mm-hmm. And things are so much different back in India. Like because I went to school in India, um, so things are really different there, so um, I just don't know if like if I can fit in here as well, and like even talking to people like I have very little in common with them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So it must be hard for you, I guess, to come in today as well, if you're finding talking to people and that kind of stuff. So with coming out from India, you're saying that you know, it's different. There's a difference to coming out here. Can you tell me a little bit about what's happening for you now and talking to me and how's that, what sort of things are going through your head?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, like what's happening right now? Um, like I didn't really know what we were gonna do together um, but I thought maybe you could uh you know um give me some things to feel better about things and tell me to do things that you know maybe will help me make friends. I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, okay. So this is just... I'm sort of curious about how you're feeling comfortable in talking to me about you're saying you're having difficulties with talking to people out here and stuff like that. So I'm just curious about are you feeling comfortable in talking to me about what's happening for you at the moment or is it...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, um yeah it's fine I can I can talk about it. Um I guess like I feel like somehow I'm of a lower lower class here like compared to India like like in India we have the caste system and um you know and I'm from a family that's from a higher caste because we're Hindu and you know the people in the lower class you've you've got to think about like they when they're around higher class people they don't talk immediately you know and you have to be respectful and when I'm here like I don't know when to talk and when I say something it it's funny or it's the wrong thing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sure. I need to know a little bit more about India so I'm just trying to get my head around that for myself. So you're saying that there's a caste system where you have higher and lower classes and that communication between those are kind of harder.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um I think like in India like because I'm Hindu um and in Hindu we have like different castes and each caste well um you know it depends on the kind of work that you do like I'm from a um class that's higher up and we're priests like we're Brahmins and we're priests um and so we're of a higher class and they used to have like the people in the lower class are like untouchables so they're the more um like the manual workers and the cleaners and things like that um and so there's this expectation that you know when they're around people like us they should show respect and um not talk out of you know line and be well behaved and um and usually they're quite uneducated and and like when when I'm here I kind of feel like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And that you feel...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel yeah I don't know when to say things and I'm always getting things wrong and you know back in India it's different you know it wasn't like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Just for my own understanding can you give me some examples of when you've felt like you've got it wrong? What's sort of happened out here where you kind of felt like you shouldn't have spoken or said something differently?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um like I guess in the tutorials like you know and it's not anything big but you know if if I say something or because of my accent or you know people kind of laugh and you know that doesn't make me feel very good so um even like talking to people I don't know what to say because um I feel like we don't have anything in common much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sure. Okay. So just for my understanding I'm not sure if I'm getting this right. So you've been having some difficulties since you've come out from India, you've started university here and you feel there's a a difference that you're picking up on. You obviously missing your family and friends which is one of the main things you've talked about but also there's a difference in this cultural thing that over in India there was a class thing in terms of when you talked and how you talked or who you talked to where over here that's not so easy and you're feeling that when you do talk you shouldn't have done it or people are judging you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hmm. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. And it makes me feel like you know like I'm of a lower class like I was born into that and back in India I was more important and um people knew what caste I was from and here it's all different and people like don't understand how I feel and like even when I try to explain it people don't understand it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just feel like in India things were so much different and because of the religion and because of the caste people understood that and but when I come here I feel all these things and I feel like I shouldn't have to feel like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the comparison is in India it seems a lot easier for you because it seems to be an everyone kind of knows. But out here it's it's harder for you because it's not known and I'm curious about how being out here makes you feel of a lower class. Can you tell me a little bit more about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. I just feel like I don't know when to say things and I'm unsure of myself and I feel like I've never felt like that in my life. Um and you know those are the kind of things that maybe in my mind I think you know people of a lower class are thinking especially when they are around people in the higher class. Like we have many workers at home or servants and they always you know they're very careful about what they say and what they do. I feel like like I'm like that now and I shouldn't be like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So I'm curious about you know you're saying that you're wary about what you say and how you say it I'm just curious about our time together and with my not really understanding that kind of background for myself and us sort of trying to I guess help and talk things out and have communication. I'm wondering you know if I'm getting it wrong or if I could do something to make it a little bit easier for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh no no no as in like yeah I mean I think by by understanding how like things work in India I think I can kind of explain you can kind of understand how I feel um and yeah I think a lot of how I feel is because of my religion and my my you know my beliefs and like I I don't know what religion you are but you know a lot of people don't understand that and so I just feel like no one understands me and I can't talk to my parents about it because they just want me to be okay and I don't want to burden them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's really important for me to understand you that's that's what I really want to understand what's happening for you so if there's anything that we're doing together when we're talking that's making you feel a bit uncomfortable or doesn't feel quite safe or right for you if you could let me know that'd be really helpful.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: All right yeah okay I'll let you know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And then I think on top of that I think there's a lot of things going for you as well as this you're saying as well as then feeling socially isolated that kind of moving from friends and family. Can you tell me a little bit more about what's happening with that for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah I miss my friends a lot. I thought when I came here you know I'd have different friends and things would be kind of easy like you see on TV but um it's not and and I feel like you know maybe it wasn't the best decision because I thought people would be friendlier and people understand more um but you know I had a few friends but they they also left and um you know I just don't feel like people understand me and I think I'm a little bit angry as well like I don't want to understand them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it sounds to me and correct me if I've not got it right but it sounds to me you're feeling quite isolated and alone out here and that people really don't understand who you are and when you do talk out you don't feel you're getting it right or people are judging you. Is that am I getting that right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah yeah absolutely yeah and I feel like people just yeah they don't like they don't know what it's like um and you know maybe I don't know what it's like for them but you know I just feel like if they can't understand that like um the gap is too big um that there's so much about me they don't know um that I don't think we can be friends or you know even have good friends like I have back in India.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Can you give me any examples of where you you feel that they really don't understand you like where you've tried to talk to people?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah I guess like even in class and like having conversations with people at university um you know I just feel like whenever I talk about India they're kind of laughing at me okay um it's and I don't feel good about that because you know I I really miss India and I really like the time I spent there and when I and I say that I always get that feeling that they're kind of laughing at me and looking down on me and I don't like I don't like that and like you know like in India they do that with people in the lower class.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So when when you're having a conversation with someone if they laugh at you it kind of gives you the sense that they are putting you into a lower class and it makes you feel so sounds to me that it's kind of like back in India where they're putting you into a different class compared to where you were.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah kind of like uneducated and I'm not like that and I feel like they're only doing that because they don't understand me and you know what India's really about.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you talk to anyone about India or your background and that sort of thing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um I have some family friends who are Indian um but I feel like I can't tell them that I'm feeling sad because you know my parents paid all this money um for me to study here and um if I you know if I say I'm not happy then they'll feel bad and you know that's a lot of money wasted.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So the people that you feel you can talk to you also can't because of feeling like it would get back to your parents and there'd be a sense of disappointment that they've spent this money.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah so I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Makes it very difficult doesn't it when you've got sort of those sort of areas to talk to.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah so I just feel like no one understands and um that you know I can't really talk to anyone and um and so I guess that's why I feel isolated and don't have many friends.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So a lot of it could be coming down to how when you're talking to people, how it ends up making you feel. What kind of outcome does that give for you when you do feel like you've been put into a lower class, what do you then do?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't feel like doing anything at all like um I just think you know what's the point um of doing this um I was really interested in my course and now I'm not I'm really bored in the lectures and um like even assignments I don't feel like doing um I just think what's the point.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um like in the mornings when I wake up I just feel really heavy and um sad and just I don't feel like doing anything at all.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it it seems to be it's spreading to other areas as well that that ability not to be able to socialize and feel connected is sort of taken the passion out of your studies and about assignments and not feeling motivated to do anything. Is that kind of the core of what's happening for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think it might be. I think it might be. I think yeah maybe because I don't have friends and um I'm feeling unhappy and stuff it's why I'm doing badly because there's no like I don't feel motivated um like I don't want to get up and do things and I think you might be right I think it may be because you know I am feeling unhappy about my circumstances.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So feeling unhappy is sort of taking away the impetus and the motivation to do things and the ability to sort of get on with your assignments and studies.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. And I want to do well like my parents have paid all this money and um I really want to do well in my university studies.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's important for you to do well by the sounds of things. How does your parents paying for things affect you? You just mentioned there that your parents paid all this money as well can you tell me a little bit about what goes on for you with that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah like my my family are from a sort of middle-class upper-middle-class kind of family and my father's worked very hard um you know to try and get some money for me to come to Australia um and so I was very excited about it and I you know I feel like I have to work very hard to pay them back and you know grow up and maybe take care of them and bring them back here but um and so I feel a bit selfish because I you know I'm just complaining about friends.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: But at the same time I just feel like no one understands me because of what had happened.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So part of it is it sounds that there's expectation placed on you to do well and that you've been sent out here to do well to be able to look after them. But it's hard to do well when you're feeling as you say isolated and different out here in terms of communicating with people. So there's this as you're saying it sounds that there's a bit of you saying I feel a bit selfish a bit bad about complaining about this when they've spent all this money to send me out here.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: And in India it's not like here you know you have to work very hard um like my father's had to work his whole life to kind of save up money for me to come here and um I feel I don't know like slightly irresponsible for you know I should be happy coming to Australia and doing university studies but you know um I'm just I'm not. It hasn't turned out to be the way I thought it would be and I don't want to tell my parents that because um they'll be disappointed that if I went back home I wouldn't get as good a job.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there's this massive expectation by the sounds of things that you're even placing on yourself that they'd be disappointed if you didn't do really well. But it's been hard for you to do really well when you're feeling so isolated.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah yeah I guess it is yeah and I just don't see a real way out but at the same time I just don't know how I can keep going like I've only finished one semester and the course is you know three years long. I just want to go back home all the time and we can't really afford for me to go back home um and so I just I feel really stuck and unhappy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Seems to be a lot going on for you at this point in time. Apart from all these pressures and expectations of doing well out here and doing your degree there's also the social pressures of not feeling like you're fitting in, feeling hard to connect with people. Going back home is what you really want to do but there's the sense of you've been sent out here to get something. So I can imagine you're feeling quite stuck and isolated and alone.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah and somehow like I feel like it won't improve. Like um I just don't I don't know. I mean like like you understand when I tell you how I feel but you know I don't know if other people will understand that right as much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what is it about us talking that makes you feel that you've been... I mean obviously you've been telling me stuff fairly well I can understand what you're saying and so I'm just curious about our process as to what's been happening here to make you feel that I've understood you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I just feel like you're not laughing at me like you really want to know about about India and about what's been happening for me and my family. But with other people I think it's different compared to that but um yeah I think like there are some nice people but I think if if people kind of just stop and listen and if they knew a little more then it would be easier.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So when people sort of pay attention to you and listen to what you have to say you feel a little bit more at ease about the communication thing.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah I guess so yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Tom, how's things going?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, really good, really good. Thanks, yeah. It's been a good week.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's been a good week? Okay, tell me a little bit about that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, well, I mean, I really have to thank you for the last session. It was just amazing. It's difficult I suppose for me when it's been a long time since I've had someone to talk to and certainly someone as considerate and kind as you are. So I just can't express enough how thankful I was for that last session.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, I'm really pleased to hear that. I'm glad to hear that things are going well for you and you're happy with how we're working together.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean it's not just happy, I mean, I'm really, yeah, I can't say it enough. It was just, almost like it changed my whole week, it really just gave me a really, really nice week, so thank you very much, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, it certainly sounds like it's had a really big impact on you, good.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: And I mean while we're on that I suppose I've brought you, just to thank you, I brought something in for you. It's um, you know because it was such a good session I thought I'd bring you a gift in.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, okay. Oh, that's really thoughtful, okay. Thanks.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You're welcome.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, um, I'll just pop this down here for now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I hope you enjoy it, it's yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yes, yeah I quite enjoy wine, so that's um, yeah, that's lovely.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hmm, good, maybe you could have it, drink it over dinner this weekend or have something, have it with a nice meal this weekend.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, I'll, I'll certainly keep that in mind, good. How's your week been?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, good, yeah you know can't complain, usual kind of work, that sort of thing. Great, yep, yep. Okay, so um, and, and how are things with you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's well, good, good. I've been thinking about a lot of the stuff that we talked about last week and, you know, I think um my mood's lifted a real lot. I've been happy and, you know I've been thinking a lot about the session I suppose, it's really been kind of in my mind the whole week, I've been thinking a lot about the stuff that you've been saying and yeah, it's been great, it's been really good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so what was helpful for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, oh, well I think just like I said, having someone like yourself to listen, um yeah someone who's so kind, someone who's easy to talk to, um yeah someone who's concerned and caring and, you know I don't have a lot of female friends so just to yeah spend a bit of time with someone like a female and talking about some of the stuff that I've been concerned about has been really, really good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Tom, how you doing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, really good thanks, really good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good, how's the week been?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's been fantastic. Yeah, it's just been amazing. Some of the stuff that you said to me last week, I've really thought about it, in fact I've been thinking about the session a lot over the last week and my mood's lifted and yeah it's been a really good week.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm really pleased to hear that, that's really good to hear.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can't thank you enough, I really can't. It's just been, it's been great. I've um just having the opportunity to have someone to talk to and not just someone to talk to, but someone who is as kind and um considerate and caring as you are, I just, you know I just can't express how thankful I really am um for your help, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it sounds like our last session had quite an impact on you to the extent that even through the week you found that your mood has shifted and um it's something that's been going over in your mind, so and I'm really pleased to hear that, it's very encouraging that this therapeutic relationship is working for you in this way.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, and it's something that I don't get to do a lot, as I've said to you I don't have a lot of friends, I don't have a lot of female friends so to have the chance to talk to a a female, a kind, kind of compassionate um female like yourself has just been really, really nice, I can't thank you enough. In fact I've um I really did want to thank you um for the session so I've brought something in for you. Okay, it's not much but I just yeah I really wanted to thank you for it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I really appreciate the gesture. It's um it's good to know that this is working for you so well.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, you're welcome, I think you deserve it because it's really useful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so it sounds like this therapeutic relationship is something that's really helped you through the week. Okay, so the way that we're working in therapy is is obviously having quite quite an impact.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, absolutely, my mood as I said my mood's really lifted and it's been great.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And I guess it it makes sense that this is so important to you given that you haven't sort of you've been having some relationship problems and difficulty sort of forming relationships outside of therapy, that now when you're in here and you've got somebody who sort of listens to you and is very open and accepting and non-judgmental, it certainly makes sense that this is something that would be really important for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's a really valuable experience.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah. And hopefully the way that we work together here in therapy can then help you outside, to help you form relationships um and move towards the sort of relationships that you've told me you would like to have outside of therapy.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah, I hope so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good. Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Gifts represent a bit of a tricky situation in therapy. Um, what I thought was happening in this situation was that this client was maybe getting a little bit confused about the nature of the therapeutic relationship and starting to get a little bit confused about boundaries. Um, this is understandable given his relationship history and what's happening outside of therapy, that once he does experience um a positive relationship, he might misinterpret it. The other option is that he actually is just grateful for the work we're doing together and wanted to express that gratitude and there was nothing else behind it. What I chose to do in this situation was to accept the wine, but leave it on the table so I wasn't actually accepting it as a personal gift to me. What I was very mindful of though was actually not demonstrating that this was a rejection of him. So what I wanted to do was very much validate the reasons for choosing to give me the wine and express his gratitude, but also make it very clear that this is a therapeutic relationship and that there are boundaries here and that what he will need to do in future is actually work at establishing relationships outside of therapy. What I could have also done with this is explore what his motivation was in choosing to give me the wine. However, just at the beginning of the session I thought that might be perhaps a little bit too confrontational for him, um especially if I as I wasn't quite sure whether it was a personal gift or just an expression of gratitude, but that is something that I could have addressed later in the session um or even at a different stage of therapy. This did present a bit of an ethical situation in that the gift was alcohol, and depending on the agency that I work for or the broader context, that has an effect on how I could accept the gift. Something I could have said to him was that um I would share the wine with colleagues at a meeting that evening to indicate that I wasn't rejecting it but it wasn't a personal gift to me. Um, the other thing I would be aware of is being quite mindful of similar gestures towards me in therapy, and so if I saw repetitions of this sort of behavior, I might need to address that in future.

video_details.description:
An example of a CASC exam history taking station

To become a Member of the Royal College of Psychiatrists (MRCPsych), doctors must pass a series of written and clinical examinations. The MRCPsych Examinations consist of three written papers and a practical assessment known as the Clinical Assessment of Skills and Competencies (CASC) examination.

This is the third in a series of videos released by the College to help increase awareness about the CASC examination, and to help candidates prepare

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello Mr. Vance, my name is Dr. Vanita Goves and I'm one of the psychiatrists who works here. Can you tell me what's brought you here today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, well I was referred to you by my GP because my wife thinks I'm drinking too much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, I see. And do you think you're drinking too much?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, looking at it from her point of view, I suppose I do like a drink, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Maybe we can just explore that a little bit more. How much would you say you drank in a day?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Now? Oh, it's crept up over the years. Well if I'm honest, I drink about a bottle of vodka a day.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A bottle of vodka a day. And how long have you been drinking that much for?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well as I say, it's crept up, a few years now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you be more specific? Two years, three years, five years?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, initially I just used to have a couple of drinks after work because I've got a pretty responsible job and I just found a drink calmed me down. Then I got more responsibility and I found a bit more alcohol helped me. So yeah, I'm drinking about a bottle a day now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you'd say for about the last two years, three years?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, about that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And do you drink anything else apart from vodka?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, after work I normally go to the pub and I have two to four pints of bitter or lager.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, okay. And would that be every day?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, especially Monday to Friday when I'm working, but at weekends I normally go down the local pub and have a few at lunchtime.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. And how much is a few?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Again, about two to four pints.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: On a weekday, you have about two to four pints after work and then you come home and drink about a bottle of vodka?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well no, I drink during the day. Not when I'm working mind you, apart from lunchtime, not when I'm at work.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So when do you start drinking during the day on an average day?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: After I'm up and dressed and have my breakfast at home.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, so after breakfast. And again, when did that start?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A couple of years ago.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what about the weekend? Is it the same at the weekend? Would you drink more than a bottle of vodka during the day at the weekend?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It'd be about the same, would it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And are there other regular times when you'd drink more than what you've told me?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And is it just beer and vodka, or would you drink wine or liqueurs?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. We used to drink wine together with an evening meal, but since she started complaining, she sort of nailed that on the head so we don't do that anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And would you say you have to drink more to get the same effect from the alcohol?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, the same calming effect, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you ever have days where you don't drink, or periods where you don't drink?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A few months ago now, when she really had a go at me and I thought to myself well maybe I'll give it a try again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how long did that last for?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: About three days.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And in that time did you experience any physical feelings at all?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I was shaking. I was on edge all the time. I wasn't working properly and I was sweating and I just felt absolutely lousy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you had to take time off work?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I didn't dare take time off work. I just said I had a bit of a cold, but I thought to myself I can't carry on like this. So I had a couple of large vodkas and that made me feel better.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Did you ever get those similar sort of feelings in the morning when you wake up?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, nowadays, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what happens? You have the drink in the morning and that makes you feel better?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, it does.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If you don't have that drink in the morning, what happens?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: By the time I get to work, I feel pretty shaky and very on edge. As I say, I don't touch it when I am at work because I've got a pretty responsible job.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you work as a bank manager?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I do indeed, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has anyone apart from your wife commented about your drinking? Have you ever had any more serious health problems? Seen a doctor, memory loss, fits, or serious shakes?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, no, touch wood, nothing like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And you went to your GP. Did he do any physical health tests at all?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He did some blood tests.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And did that show anything?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He said my liver wasn't too good. My wife threatened to leave me basically, so that's what got me to see the GP. He said I've got to cut it down a bit and then he said he was going to refer me to somebody to talk about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, okay. And how did you feel about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I wasn't exactly over the moon when he suggested it, but if it's a choice of coming to see you or my wife leaving me, I came to see you. I don't want to lose her you see.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I can see that it's had quite an impact at home. What about outside the home? How has your drinking affected jobs or anything else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It hasn't affected my job.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What about relationships other than your wife, with family, friends? Any other serious consequences?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I have to go to family dos and dragged along to there, but I avoid mixing with my work colleagues socially. I find that bores me. I've tried it once and I found I needed a drink and I thought I was going to put my foot in it, so I left early and just make excuses now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, okay. Thanks for coming to talk to me today.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

video_details.title: Downward Arrow

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Today, let's just focus on one or two things that are problems for you. Can you pick something out from the things that you've brought that you can't get rid of but you know you probably won't really use? Now, remember, this is an exercise and the purpose is not to throw things away, but just to learn something about your attachments to them. Okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. How about this purple shirt?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, that looks great. Let's try what we call a downward arrow method to look at the way you think about getting rid of this shirt, so we can better understand how attached you are to it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That sounds okay to me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, what comes to mind when you look at the shirt?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I got this shirt for Christmas three years ago from my sister, and that was just a really good year. I was still married, and I just remember feeling happy. So now whenever I look at this shirt, I remember there was a time in my life when I felt that way.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So it sounds like you have a strong emotional attachment to the shirt because it brings back good memories. If you were to get rid of the shirt, what thoughts would you have?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I'm worried that I wouldn't be able to remember that Christmas and that happy time in my life as well if I didn't have the shirt to remind me. I'm also worried that my sister is going to expect me to have it. She gave it to me for a gift, and if I get rid of a present she gave me, it'll be like I didn't appreciate her gift. She might ask me, 'Where's that purple shirt I gave you?' or 'Why don't you ever wear it?' and I just think she'd be very disappointed in me if I got rid of it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I see. So what would be so bad if your sister was disappointed in you because you got rid of the shirt?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, if she was disappointed, I know that I'd done something to upset her, like I'd betrayed her somehow. And then I'd feel like a bad sister.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what would be the worst part of that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, if I'm a bad sister, she won't want to talk to me anymore because she won't be able to trust me. We usually talk a few times a week, and if she doesn't want to talk to me anymore, I'll get really lonely.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell me more about how that would feel?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I'd hate feeling all alone because then I'd feel like I don't have anyone in my life that's there for me. And if she abandoned me, I'd be all alone and depressed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I see. So when you think about throwing away the shirt, a number of horrible things occur to you, right? You won't remember the happy feeling at Christmas when you got the shirt, your sister may abandon you, and you'll be lonely and depressed. Is that right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's no wonder you can't get rid of it then, is it? I don't think I'd get rid of it either under those circumstances. Let me ask you a few more things. How certain are you that these bad things will happen to you if you get rid of the shirt? Are you 50% sure or 100% sure, or what?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think I'm probably 90% sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I see. And in terms of how badly you'll feel on a scale of say 1 to 10, where 10 is as bad as you can imagine feeling, just how bad would you feel getting rid of the shirt?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Too bad to actually do it. I guess it would be a 9 or a 10. There's no way I would do it, though. It's too much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So if you did get rid of the shirt, how long do you think that bad feeling would last?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, probably for a long, long time. My sister is the most important person in my life. If I don't have her, I'd get up in the morning feeling like, 'Now what?'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. So if I'm understanding you correctly, you're saying that you're 90% sure that some really bad things are going to happen to you when you get rid of the shirt. You'll lose some good memories, your sister will abandon you, and you'll end up lonely and depressed. Not only that, but the bad feeling will be as bad as pretty much anything you can imagine and it'll last a long time. Does that kind of sum it up?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, that's right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's clear that this shirt has meaning that goes well beyond just the physical shirt.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It certainly does. Just like almost everything else I have.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, I see. If we talk about it, do you think the meaning of the shirt will change if we just spend some time talking about this shirt?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. I'm certainly willing to talk about it. I don't think I'm willing to get rid of it though.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, okay. Well, let me ask you this. You've mentioned how you think your sister would feel if you got rid of the shirt. Could you also tell me what your sister thinks about your hoarding problem?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, she thinks it's horrible and disgusting. She won't even come to my house anymore because it's a cluttered wreck.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So if she thinks that, do you think she'd really be upset if you got rid of the shirt?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. I guess I hadn't thought about it from that angle.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If getting rid of the shirt would help your hoarding problem, what do you think your sister would say about it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess she'd probably want me to get rid of it. Anything to help my hoarding.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If your sister wouldn't mind if you got rid of the shirt, would you still feel like a bad sister for getting rid of it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I don't think she'd be happy that I was giving away a gift from her, but I suppose she'd be glad that I was decluttering.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So if you think about it now, are you still 90% sure all those bad things would happen to you if you get rid of the shirt?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. Maybe 70 or 80% sure now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So once you thought about the shirt in a different way, your attachment to it changed a little bit. Is that right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, you're right. It sort of changes my perspective, I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would you be willing to do a more difficult experiment with the shirt?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. What do you have in mind?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, you're certain that you'd be distressed if you threw the shirt away because of your attachment to it, but maybe you're mistaken about that. What if we test your prediction about how bad you'll feel by actually getting rid of it and keeping track of how you feel?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I could try, but only with the shirt.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We call this a behavioral experiment because we've established some predictions and we'll set about trying to test those predictions. Let's try discarding the shirt. So here's a donation bag and I'll take it to the Salvation Army. Do you think you can try that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You won't really throw this away, will you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like this is pretty hard for you. How bad does it feel to put the shirt in the bag?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Pretty bad. I really don't want to get rid of it. But I will. I'd rate this at about a 6 or 7. I'm definitely not happy about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Well, let me try one more thing. Let me take this donation bag and I'm going to put it in the other room and then let's see what happens. Okay?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so it's been about 15 minutes since you got rid of that shirt. How does it feel now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it's not as bad now. I still feel uncomfortable about it, but I can live with it.

diarization.speaker: Thererpist
diarization.text: So before we started, you were 90% sure that some bad things would happen if you got rid of the shirt. You thought you'd lose memories of the holiday, that you'd offend your sister and her friendship, and that you would become lonely and depressed. How do all these predictions seem to you now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I guess it was a bit over the top. So far none of those bad things have happened and I don't think my sister will abandon me over this. I'm still a little concerned about the memory thing, though, and I do worry a little about my sister's reaction.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So how would you rate how sure you were about this? Remember you were 90% before.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I'd say about 50% now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The other thing you predicted was that you would feel pretty bad, that it would be very uncomfortable. In fact, I think you rated that feeling at a 9 or a 10 on a 10-point scale. What do you think about that prediction?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I do feel bad, but I certainly don't feel that bad. I would probably rate it at about a 5.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So did anything surprise you about this experiment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I was surprised that I actually got rid of that shirt. Although I still want to get it back, I think I can tolerate letting it go. I expected to feel worse than I do and to worry more about not having it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you think it makes sense to keep track of how you feel about the shirt over the next week to see how your thoughts and feelings change about it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think that might be a good idea.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, let's do that. And when we talk next week, we'll come back and talk about this shirt, okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Last week we did an experiment. Can you tell me now your reactions to the experiment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, for a while I still had the feeling that I somehow let my sister down and that I should have worn the shirt more than I did. So I decided to call my sister and I told her that I had given the shirt away.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And was your sister disappointed in you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: She had forgotten that she had even given me the shirt because she never saw me wear it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What else happened?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I was surprised I could still remember that Christmas and how good I felt back then, even without the shirt to remind me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So on a scale of 1 to 10, how badly did you feel this week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, when I left last time, it felt like a 5 or a 6, but now I'd say it's a 1 or a 2.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So what did you learn from this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, that the shirt wasn't as important to me as I thought and even though I don't have the shirt, I'll still have memories of that special Christmas. Also, since I gave the shirt to Goodwill, I think someone who needed a shirt probably got it and that's a good thing for them. My sister was actually proud of me for getting rid of something that was difficult. I don't understand why I thought it would be so horrible.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you think you might have the same reaction with other things you've been saving?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I might.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, why don't we try some different kinds of things and see if that's true?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

video_details.title: Motivational Interviewing (MI) for Addictions Video
video_details.description:
Full video:  http://www.psychotherapy.net/video/motivational-interviewing

Learn how Motivation Interviewing is applied to working with addictions in this video with Motivational Interviewing expert and trainer Cathy Cole.

#therapy #therapist #motivationalinterview #motivationalinterviewing

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So let me tell you what I normally do in this interview. We will talk for up to maybe 20 minutes or so. Normally, what I do is just give some feedback from all of those questionnaires that you answered last week and then we just talk together about that. But I always like to just start with wherever you would like to start as well. I am setting the focus and agenda, but also providing flexibility for Sarah. By letting her decide where to begin, I reinforce her autonomy and ability to self-reflect. I demonstrate that I am partnering with her.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean when I was doing those questionnaires, it was weird because I don't really think about drinking being this huge deal, and I don't ever really think about how much I drink. Filling out how much I'm drinking every day was like, whoa, you know? I just didn't ever really think about it like that. If I try to actually count the drinks, it's kind of a lot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You were pretty shocked at what you learned about your patterns. I use a complex reflection to emphasize Sarah's beginning awareness. Complex reflections pick up on the emotional impact for the client and deepen the client's own self-reflection. Change comes when we begin to recognize that our current behavior is discrepant with how we see ourselves.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well yeah, because I also kind of thought that I drank about as much as my friends did. Then I was talking to my roommate and telling her that I was drinking like 10 drinks on the weekends, including Thursday. And then she was like, 'Sarah, that is crazy, why are you drinking this?' And I guess my friends didn't know. Anyway, yeah, I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, this information has opened your eyes in some ways, and as you talk to your roommate about it, she was even shocked to know that you were drinking as much as you realized when you did the questionnaire.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, and I guess it was just like I thought that everybody was doing it, but that's not really what was going on.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, the fact that you're drinking stands out from others is clearly not something you had ever really taken into consideration before. Thus far, I am very careful about using the conversational style of following, focusing on demonstrating my understanding of Sarah's situation and allowing her to continue to talk. The reflections I have done have reinforced Sarah's alarm about her drinking.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah. So that was the thing that was really the most weird about doing those forms.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: One of the things, I mean motivational interviewing did start out in the addictions field and is widely used there. Traditionally, addiction counselors often have backgrounds as addicts themselves, and there is this hardcore approach of breaking through resistance and denial where people have to be abstinent. This is a very different approach.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It is a different approach. The others have certainly been traditional and perhaps for some people those have been effective. But in motivational interviewing, we really want the client to be the one who determines if they have a problem and give them the full opportunity to examine this and establish their own goals. It was quite revolutionary to approach the client from this direction.

video_details.title: Cognitive Behaviour Therapy example

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So Jane, it sounds like you're angry with your supervisor. Would I be right in saying that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I think I'm pretty angry.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Well look, maybe to help me understand more about that anger, I'm wondering if you could choose two or three pictures here that look like how you were angry at the time. Which of the cards here would show how angry you were?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, that's fine. I'll just have a look at those. Okay. It does look like anger, doesn't it? It's a pretty big anger.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So after you'd had that big thing with your mom, you went to your room, is that right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, she got really angry at me because on the way to my room, my idiot sister got in the way. So I pushed her out of the way. She's just annoying. So then I went into my room, the only place I really feel safe, slammed the door, and then mom's favorite picture fell on the floor.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you for sharing that and being so honest about your anger. It's helping me understand that this is really big for you. Surprisingly, anger is a good thing because it lets you know something wasn't fair. But what happened next was that your anger took charge and did more than it's meant to do. It just pushed you out of the road and said, 'I'm taking control here'.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So Jane, when you were angry, did you feel it anywhere in your body?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, my neck is really sore and it's really paining. And my shoulders. It just feels like I've been hit by something.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: At the end of the day, with pushing your sister over and yelling at your mom, did anything change?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, it made it worse.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, which is hard to see at the time. If we tell our anger, 'Thank you, you've done a good job,' it doesn't have to get so angry then. You've let me know I'm angry, now I'm going to deal with it from here.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You'll have to help me with that a bit, I think.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, we will. We will.

video_details.title: 2011 Yale-NEABPD New Haven, CT
video_details.description:
This video features a role-play demonstration of Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) for Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD), focused on self-harm, suicidal urges, emotion dysregulation, and relationship distress.

In this session, Alan Fruzzetti, PhD demonstrates DBT with role player Andrea Gold, MS, at the 2011 Yale conference hosted by NEABPD, now known as BPD Alliance, in New Haven, Connecticut. Using a patient scenario involving self-harm, fear of abandonment, eating restriction, and inten

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: To orient you, in Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT), we have a treatment target hierarchy. Alice and I have collaboratively agreed upon targets like self-harm, eating habits, and relationships, which she monitors daily on a diary card. Patients also rate their current urges and connection to the therapist right before and after each session. Today, we're assuming we're in the fifth or sixth session, where the focus moves toward quality-of-life issues.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, Alice.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hi.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you okay? You look like you feel terrible.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thanks. That was really mean.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm sorry, I was too abrupt. I meant you look like you're in pain. Let's look at your week. It says you hurt yourself on Friday. Are you having trouble focusing right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You want to quit therapy because I cut myself.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Look at me, Alice. Your urges and misery are high, but I don't want to quit. Why do you think that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Because I cut myself on Friday. All my other therapists fired me for that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're stuck in your head and focused on past history. I'm right here, and we've just started. What if I'm not going to fire you? Could you be open to that possibility?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Being open to the chance of it not happening means I'm opening myself to the disappointment of it actually happening.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You've already decided it happened, which causes you suffering. Try to be open to the other possibility. I see you've had a terrible week, and you're worried I'll give up on you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You're judging how terrible I am. You're going to find out just like all the others did.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I don't want you to get stuck on something that isn't true right now. I'm not firing you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's hard to remember our plans; you talk so much. I didn't call for coaching because I already knew I was going to cut myself.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You don't get fired for failing to call or for having the problems that brought you into therapy. I want us to work on what's actually going on in your life.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Will you write down that you won't fire me on my diary card, please?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sure. I'll write 'I won't fire you, Alice' and sign it so you have it in writing. Does that make a difference for you right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, because I can hold on to it. Do you blame me for being so scared?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No, it makes complete sense given your history. But your job is to look at me and see that I'm not being critical. If you stay present, your shame will go down. I'm going to record the rest of our session so you can listen later when you're less upset.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Even for cutting myself? If I kill myself, then I fire you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That’s not a fair deal. We both have to stay alive for the year. Right now, your urges are at a six. If you feel like bolting, tell me, and I'll sit in front of the door.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: If it got that bad, I'd go to the hospital. Let's talk about Friday; I cut myself because I was feeling suicidal, but I promise I won't kill myself.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. How is your therapy group going? Did you learn any new skills?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I learned alternate rebellion. After group, I got in a fight with John. Instead of yelling, I peed in the shower because I knew he'd hate it, and it made me laugh.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's a fantastic example of using the skill. Now, let's go back to Friday night. You cut yourself around 10:00 PM after your roommate left?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. I hadn't eaten and felt sick. I was drinking on Thursday and didn't sleep much either.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you were physically vulnerable. John came over to watch a movie, and you were excited but also really scared.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was worried I would mess things up. I asked him to hold me, but he said he wanted to take things slow and just sit next to me. I wanted to disappear in him.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You were longing for closeness, and his refusal felt invalidating, like you shouldn't even want it. It's sensible to feel disappointed when you don't get what you need.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I felt a black hole of hurt. I tried to focus on my cat instead, but I was thinking about killing myself. I felt like I'd never have closeness and didn't deserve it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Instead of sinking into hopelessness, try to notice 'I don't deserve it' as a judgment. Can you practice noticing these judgments twice a day this week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. I'll set alarms for 10:00 AM and 7:00 PM. The message will be 'notice judgment and play with the cat'.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Perfect. Let's re-rate your urges. How are you feeling now at the end of the session?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My suicidal urges are down to a three. My misery is at a five, and I feel a seven in terms of being connected to you. I'll call if I get stuck.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's great, Alice. I'll see you at the same time next week.

video_details.title: Sue Johnson Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy (EFT) in Action Video
video_details.description:
Watch the full video at:  http://www.psychotherapy.net/video/johnson-emotionally-focused-therapy

Sue Johnson uses Emotionally Focused Therapy (EFT) to work with a couple having communication problems after the husband has returned from military duty.

​    #psychotherapy #therapist #couplestherapy 
@DrSueJohnson

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't even need a who's right. I don't need to always be right. I would just like to be heard.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm sorry. I hear that you feel that way, Ria. I don't mean it to be like that. I love you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That would be okay. I don't need to hear that everything I said is right. If you said, 'I don't really agree with you, Ria, but I hear what you're saying, and I love you, and I don't know what to do next, so I gotta go.'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you help me. You're saying something incredibly powerful to this man. What you're saying to him, if I'm hearing you right, is: 'Matt, I don't need you to be perfect. I don't need to be right.'

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't need you to fix it right this second.
