diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I don't need you to fix it. It's okay for me to be disappointed sometimes. I just need to know that I'm important to you and you can reach for me. That's all I need to know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What I'm doing here is reflecting her attachment needs and longings. Validating her and reflecting her feelings helps calm her down and stay with the present process. Something like, 'I care about how you feel. I care that you're hurt. I love you.' You need reassurance, yeah?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're saying to him, in those moments, 'I do love you.' Even though you're overwhelmed, what I need is to know that you're still struggling to be with me, that I matter to you, and that you love me.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Because I don't really know that he loves me right now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. I need reassurance. That's what you're telling him, yeah?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just don't know that he loves me, really.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you tell him that right now? This is the first time I create an enactment, which is a central part of EFT. I've tried to distill her emotions, focusing on the attachment meaning. It would help me not to spiral down into despair to know that I still matter to you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It would help me calm down. And it would help me stop trying to be right if you could just somehow reassure me and tell me that you love me or make some gesture.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Reach for me. Yeah?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Anything would be nice. To make me feel like you don't just have nothing for me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I hear what you're saying. I hear that. My immediate reaction is nobody's doing that for me and I'm putting forth one more effort. My finger is in the dam and the water is lapping over, and I've got to do one more thing?

video_details.title: Feminist Therapy

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Feminist family therapy grew out of the second wave of feminism in the 1960s and 70s. The model focuses on the personal as political, challenging sex-role stereotypes, and forming egalitarian relationships. In this video, Dr. Patricia Robertson works with an African American family, highlighting interventions where women's voices are valued and their experiences are de-pathologized and reframed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good morning. I'm interested in getting to know all of you and finding out why you're here. One of you called for an appointment, who did that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I did. I wanted to get some help for my mom who just ended a four-year relationship. She was really sad for a long time, and I just want her to be happy. I want to be happy too.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is your perception of your mother in that relationship, and how has him being out of your life been significant?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: She was happy for a long time, but I think she has a problem picking men. He needed too much of her time and attention, and I kind of lost her when he was around. I liked him okay, but I just want her to be happy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Lee, how does it feel for you to hear your daughters' perceptions that they lose you when men are in your life?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess I have a 'Mother Teresa syndrome' where I'm always bringing in wounded dogs. I start out giving and nurturing, but then I do all the work and get tired of it. I was attracted to Ralph because he was quiet, supportive, and wasn't insecure about me being a strong, educated black woman, but eventually I was the only one fulfilling his needs.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What I'm hearing is that you fell in love with someone respectful, but when things shifted, you had the courage to get out. Instead of a flawed picking mechanism, you chose someone who looked like a good partner and then had the strength to leave when they weren't.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I really want an equal partnership where I'm not always the one giving more. When I get my courage back, I feel like Wonder Woman again. I feel energized and like I've thrown off a shell. It feels good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How is it for the daughters to hear your mom say that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I remember when you were strong applying for the bank vice presidency. I was the best candidate, but colleagues said I was 'playing the race card.' It was hurtful because they knew my abilities, but I stayed quiet to maintain the work environment and did my best anyway.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In a non-dominant culture, messages often say you are 'less than.' We pathologize members instead of asking why there aren't more women of color in power. It shifts focus away from systemic issues to personal accusations like 'playing the race card.' Are there other similar experiences?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: In college and my career, I feel I must represent all black women. If I'm absent, everyone notices. If I fail, it's proof I don't belong; if I succeed, they assume I had extra help. It's a burden. My mom is strong, but I've decided to keep men at a distance for now because I like my own space and independence.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I worry my girls picked up on a flawed mechanism from me, maybe because my father died young and I had an unfulfilled need. Growing up, I just feel men are hopeless. Mom is a great role model; she puts her whole self into relationships, and getting hurt is just part of loving someone.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I want you to honor your mom's grieving and let her choose her own timeline. I'm interested in us having more conversations to bear witness to your perspectives, including issues with commitment and men.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: This has been very beneficial, and I see things in a different light now. Thanks for dragging me in here, girls. It was nice to meet you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Pat, thank you for the demonstration of feminist family therapy. What were your favorite parts of it?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I enjoyed the demonstration of egalitarianism and the chance to de-pathologize their experiences. Re-labeling the 'picking mechanism' as courage and reframing the systemic issues at work were key. It was about validating the women's experiences and collaborating in the therapeutic process.

video_details.title: Multicultural Counseling Part 1

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Good morning, Curtis. It's good seeing you again. Go ahead and have a seat. How are you doing today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm doing very well, how are you doing?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm doing good. So today is your first visit with me. Were you okay with traffic? Were you able to find this place?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was, I was. A little shaky but...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, did you find parking okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I did, I did. Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, I just wanted to interview you. I know you had some concerns, you called me, so we're going to go over that today. What I wanted to do first of all was ask you what brings you here today to my office.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I think I need like therapeutic help. You know, looking into some therapy classes or...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. What kind of classes are you looking for?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Drug and alcohol, perhaps?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, okay. Drug and alcohol. Are you experiencing right now today, are you using any drugs today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Very little. Not as much as I used to, honestly. I used to go out and party with my friends and use a lot, like almost on a daily basis, but I don't do it as much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. What is your number one drug of choice right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Weed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Weed. You smoke a lot of weed?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Now do you smoke it with friends, by yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Usually with friends, actually. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Do you find yourself doing that at home or do you go out?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I go out because my mom doesn't allow it. So I usually go out to the park or you know, after school or something like that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And do you feel that that's something that you need to help you function or is it something...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You know what, it's just a habit and it helps me relax, honestly. Like keeps me down, mellow, you know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. Now do you go smoke weed with other friends or by yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I usually go with my other friends because they're my influences to be around.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So I mean do you feel that it helps you function better or is it just something that you're just experimenting with?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It actually helps me function better. A lot better, actually. I know it's not the right choice or anything. That's why I'm kind of looking into therapy so I can find other ways to stay right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. Do you find yourself spending a lot of money on marijuana?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How much do you spend a week or what's your habit like right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: About $100 a week.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: $100 a week. Okay, so that's almost equivalent to about maybe $10 to $15 a day. What we want to do is help you create some steps to begin to phase out. I wanted to identify the problem, and that's the marijuana. Are there events in your life that trigger your use? What's your family structure like right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You know what, I get along with my family. I have a foster family because when I was born, I was kind of separated from my biological family so they put me in foster care. I lived with my two other siblings. That's about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So pretty much you've been raised by your foster parents and your biological parents are not in the picture?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not in the picture, actually.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Now in your family, how many siblings do you have?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Six, but I only lived with two.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what number are you? Are you the youngest?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm actually the oldest.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're the oldest of six siblings. So do you feel maybe there was added responsibility put on you, or did you guys live together?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was only two of us. Two of my sisters. We just lived together and I didn't have full responsibility on them, it was just kind of... yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. And so your other four siblings, where did they go?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You know what, I have no clue.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you've been separated since birth and you were raised by your foster parents. How do you feel about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I used to get made fun of when I was in school and it was a little hard on me, but I'm kind of getting over it now. I've tried to contact them but it's not working out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. Okay, so pretty much your biological parents are not here and your foster parents are the ones that raised you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I like to consider them my parents, yeah. That's my mom and dad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And then also as you were living together at home, how are you disciplined or who were you disciplined by?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My mom. Not so much of my dad, he was kind of laid back. My mom, she would discipline. It can go from being grounded to a whipping, or she'll take our equipment like PlayStations or phones.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So there was pretty much a consequence for your behavior. Would you say that mom was consistent? Did she pretty much discipline everybody the same?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah, she disciplined everybody the same.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, that's good. Growing up, do you feel the discipline helped you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I do. Other than this whole drug use, I think it helped me a lot. Kind of set some boundaries.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does your mother know that you smoke marijuana?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: She doesn't know that I do it at this exact moment because a while ago I kind of stopped and I told her that, so she doesn't really know that I'm doing it as much right now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The reason why I'm asking is because in order for us to help you, we want to develop a good support system. Tell me a little bit about yourself when you were growing up. Were you more of an introvert or an extrovert?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I was more outgoing. I like to be in the center, in the spot. Attention seeker, class clown, I was that type of person.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That kind of explains why this conversation is going well, you're pretty much open. Now, right now, how old are you, Curtis?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're 20 years old. Do you have a girlfriend?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I do, I have a girlfriend.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How old is your girlfriend?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: She's 17.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And when does she turn 18?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: She turns 18 in actually like three weeks.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, okay. How long have you known her and been together?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not that long. About two months. I've been off and on with girlfriends because of the whole drug use and they don't like to deal with it, so it's been not that good for me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So your past relationships pretty much have been blown due to your drug problem. Did your partners know that you were smoking marijuana? Were you upfront with them or did they find out?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They found out. Exactly what it was.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So some of your choices had consequences. We want to be able to identify your problem and what triggers you to go use marijuana. Growing up with six siblings, did you all go to the same school? Tell me about your school history.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I had a sister who is one year younger than me so we were on the same grade level. Me and her went to the same school for a while, then she got into this honors class and moved into an honors school. I was at school by myself then.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And this was a younger sister, so you were pretty close to her?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. During high school, I moved through seven different high schools.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Seven?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's been hard, but I got it together around two years ago and I got my high school diploma and graduated.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How did that affect you being moved around seven times? Did you move physically?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: When I was 13, I moved from my foster parents and went into a group home. So as I moved from group home to group home, it would be different areas and different schools.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So then you had to make a whole new set of friends and that was the challenge. What are some of the subjects that came easy to you, that you enjoyed?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Spelling, I like spelling, I was in every spelling bee. I like reading, that's about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So spelling and reading are your strong points. That kind of explains why you're pretty good as far as being vocal. What were some of the classes that you didn't really enjoy?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Math, science, PE... that's about it.

video_details.title: Multicultural Counseling Part 2

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. What was your relationship with your teachers and maybe some of the peers that you had at the school?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I didn't get along with the teachers, honestly. I was always the class clown, so I was usually getting kicked out or getting detention.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So overall today, do you want to further your education?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'm trying to go to college, actually.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Great. So you're looking into maybe like a four-year or junior college?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, a junior college for now, actually.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: During the time that you were in school, did you have a job? Have you worked?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was working at Paul's place, a restaurant through the school, as part of a job program.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How did that make you feel when you were working?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I liked it. It got boring at times and paychecks were small, but it was a start.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It taught you how to work at a young age. How old were you when you started working?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I was fifteen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you've known at a young age it's going to take hard work. What would be your dream job?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A pilot. I want to be a pilot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A pilot. Wow. And what's your reasoning behind that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I love airplanes. I just want to fly, be in the air, and go fast.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you looked into what it would take to become a pilot?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: The only struggle with that is math. I don't think it's going to work out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What would be your next dream job?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A cop. I'm trying to get back into a cadet program.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We can discuss helping you find a program close by. Regarding the marijuana, you know that being a cop, you'd have to let it go.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Let it go.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We want to help you develop a treatment plan. What about your medical history? Have you ever been in the hospital?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've had surgery on my arm because I was in a motorcycle race. I fell and had to get stitched up.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What about in your family, is there any history of illness or anyone who has been in therapy?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, none at all.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We want to look at your support system. Today you're using marijuana how many times a day?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Three or four times a day. In the morning, at noon, at 5:00 PM, and before bed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: A realistic goal is looking at your relationships. How many of your friends smoke marijuana?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably about six or seven of them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So a goal is to begin to see which friends to hang out with.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, my mom tells me if I keep this up, I'll end up with jail time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We also want to look at your idle time and maybe help you find a job. Before you smoke, is there a specific feeling you have?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'm usually depressed.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We can look at the depression. What other feelings do you have?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sad or angry. I'd like to have been born with my real parents. It still bothers me.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Specifically during holidays like Thanksgiving and Christmas.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We want to equip you with coping skills for those times. I'm glad you came into my office, Curtis. Do you have any other questions?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm just wondering how many times a week I'll be allowed to come to therapy?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'd like to meet twice a week. We'll work on a job and tapering down the marijuana use. It was a pleasure meeting you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Alright, thank you.

video_details.title: Psychiatric Interviews for Teaching: Somatisation
video_details.description:
In this film, you see a GP talking to a patient who has repeatedly presented to the surgery for abdominal problems for which no organic cause has been found. The GP asks the patients at length about her symptoms. The information is already in the GP notes, but the GP knows that if the patient is to trust the advice given, she must first feel that the history has been heard and understood by the new doctor. 
 
It is apparent that the symptoms are more problematic when the patient is lonely, and a

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Barbara Roberts?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, good afternoon.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello there. My name's Dr. Beddy, one of the new GPs in the practice. First of all, what would you like me to call you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, you can call me Barbara, that'll be fine. Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, that's fine. So Barbara, I'm seeing you today, but I think it's usually Dr. Brown that sees you, is that right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, Dr. Brown's my doctor.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. What is it that's brought you to see me today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I've come about my tummy problem. I've got terrible trouble with my stomach and Dr. Brown just doesn't seem to be able to get to the bottom of it. I thought perhaps I'd come and see you to see if you could help.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. Okay. Can you tell me a bit more about your tummy problems?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have this terrible discomfort nearly all the time. It very often feels bloated. I swing between being constipated and having diarrhea. I have cramping feelings sometimes and other times it stabs. I often have the urge to go to the toilet and I pass very smelly wind.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Quite a few symptoms there, and some of them sound quite troublesome to you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how long has this been going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've traced it back to a holiday I had in Egypt about four years ago. I had a horrible bout of sickness and diarrhea, and I don't think my stomach's ever been really right since then.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So you think it began about four years ago after this holiday?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what sort of treatments have you tried for this before?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Dr. Brown gave me some muscle relaxants at the beginning. But I've been to the health shop and they've given me lots of different tablets and medicines for different things. And Imodium, I have Imodium in my handbag all the time just in case.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So these different tablets from the herbal shop, how are you taking them?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Different tablets for different symptoms. I don't have the same problem every day, so I'll take certain tablets for certain symptoms.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So am I right in thinking you perhaps decide on a day-to-day basis what you're going to take depending on what your stomach's doing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what about tests? Have you had any tests for these problems?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: In the early days I had a gastroscopy and at the same time a barium enema, which was very uncomfortable. But I don't think he's tried enough tests because he's just not sent me for any more.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. Sounds as though you're not happy with that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think actually the NHS are running out of money and he's decided I've had enough tests. If you go on the internet, there's loads of tests he could have sent me for. If I had a bit more money, I'd go private. I just don't think he's got to the bottom of it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you feel as though actually enough hasn't been done in the way of tests?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, he's not. There's loads more he could do, I'm sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like you've had these problems for about four years, tried many remedies, and had some investigations, but you're not happy that you've been investigated thoroughly enough. Have I got the story right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd say so, yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how is all of this affecting you day-to-day? How is it affecting your life?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's had a big impact. I went from full-time to part-time at work, then stopped altogether. I miss the girls; we used to go out at least once a week. I used to go to an exercise class, too, but I was worried I'd be taken short, so I stopped that. My husband and I don't even go out for meals anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds as though your life has really changed quite a lot because of these symptoms. What do you spend your average day doing now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I potter around the house. I've got a bit hooked on daytime television, to be honest. I read a bit, but generally I'm just at home.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have there been any times over the last four years that you've noticed any significant changes? For example, times when things have been better?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Last year my son got married and I was in good form for that. For about three weeks in the summer getting ready for the wedding, I was in really good form.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how were your tummy symptoms then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I hardly noticed them. It seemed to clear up, which was good.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's interesting. And are there any times when your symptoms bother you more, seem particularly bad?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm having a bit of a bad patch at the moment. I notice it when my husband's away for work; it's very often not good then.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you notice it's worse when your husband's not around?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe I'm thinking about it a bit more when he's not there, I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I know you've been seeing Dr. Brown about this. What is it that he's said that he thinks might be wrong with you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He thinks it's all in my head. He says it's stress.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. Okay. And what do you think?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It can't all be in my head. I get too much physical pain for that. It's real pain.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And have you had any thoughts yourself about what might be causing it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sometimes I think it's IBS, sometimes an ulcer. On a really bad day, I think it might be cancer. My mother-in-law died of cancer last year. At night I feel and make sure there's nothing different going on; I worry about that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're actually prodding, having a feel at night to see if you can feel anything?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I just want to make sure there's nothing changing down there.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, you've tried many medications without much success, and feel you need more investigations. At times you worry it could be something serious like cancer. Is that right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I'd say so.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And Barbara, what was it that you were hoping that I'd do for you today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I thought with you being a new doctor, you might know about different tests that my doctor doesn't know about, that perhaps you could send me for.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So you were hoping that I'd send you for more tests.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I think there's got to be something that a test might reveal.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm not sure that sending you for more tests would be the most useful thing. You've had the main investigations and they've not shown anything. It's unlikely that more tests now would show anything different from what we already know.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So, do you think it's all in my head then? You're going to be like Dr. Brown?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No, I think that you clearly have pain that's causing you disability. I guess I'm wondering if there might be a link between what's going on in your life and how much your symptoms trouble you. Do you think that's a possibility?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can't see that my mind can be causing this amount of pain.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm not saying the pain's in your mind, but the way we feel can impact how we notice symptoms. I'm wondering whether it would be a good idea to try a different approach, looking at those areas of your life that have shrunk down.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I just can't do them anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I wonder if trying to bring back some of those pleasurable things might improve your quality of life. I'm also wondering if we should look at the tablets you're taking and really decide which are helping and which aren't.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What would you think about trying that slightly different approach for two or three months just to see whether it makes a difference?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Two or three months is a long time if there is something going on. That's what happened to my mother-in-law.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: If we worked together on this, I'd be seeing you regularly. We'd keep an eye on your symptoms and investigate if they change. How would that sound?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So... what are you saying then? That I should come back and see you?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think that would be a good idea. If you booked a double slot next week, we could think about this new approach. And perhaps if you could also bring your tablets or make a list of them, we can look at those. How would that sound?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, I'll make an appointment for next week and talk about it a bit more. I'll make a list of the tablets I'm taking.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I think that would be a good start. Shall I see you again next week?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'll make an appointment for next week, yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Thank you, Barbara. Bye-bye.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

video_details.title: Psychiatric Interviews for Teaching: Self-Harm
video_details.description:
In this film, you see a psychiatrist who works in the liaison psychiatry department seeing a patient who has recently been treated in the emergency department for wrist lacerations. The lacerations were self-inflicted after a relationship ended.

The patient describes an emotional response to the end of a relatively short-lived relationship. She also gives a history of cutting since her teenage years and she is aware that she uses cutting to manage difficult emotions. She describes very low self

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Jane Evans?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, my name's Dr. Betty. I'm one of the psychiatrists who works here in the Department of Psychological Medicine. And I'm seeing you today because you were referred up from A&E. I understand that you were there a couple of nights ago having cut your arms. Yeah? And I think that was you'd come in after after your relationship had ended. Is that right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Can I just check, have they bandaged you up and are things settling down there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. How have you been, Jane, since we last saw you in A&E?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Crap. I mean, I just can't... I just can't believe that he's gone.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. And this is your boyfriend, Mark, is that right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. How long had you two been together?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I mean, it was only a couple of weeks, but you know, things seemed to be going really, really well. I don't understand. I can't believe he's just gone.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. What was it that happened, Jane, to bring that relationship to an end?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it's like I said because it was going so well, you know, I asked... I asked him to move in. And he said that he didn't want to. And we ended up arguing and getting into a big fight and then he said he was going and you know, I begged him not to. But he still went anyway.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So was it after he had gone that you cut?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. And can you tell me a bit more about what happened when you cut?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He'd gone and I just felt so... I just couldn't bear the pain anymore. And like the voices were just incessant. And I just, you know, just wanted to get rid of all the pain, all the voices and so yeah, I just, you know, I just cut myself.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And did that help with the pain and the voices?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah. Yeah, I mean yeah. It took the pain away and I don't know, it's just something about seeing the blood really, it's... I don't know, just made it feel better.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So with the cutting, is this something that you've done before?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Been doing it since I was, I don't know, a teenager.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, okay. And it sounds like there are times when you do it when it helps.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it takes the pain off.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. And are there any downsides to the cutting?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well yeah, I mean there's been a few, but I suppose the main thing is sort of, I don't know, my arms and legs are a mess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, okay. And you mentioned, Jane, voices. And I know you've spoken to doctors about them before. But can I just ask you a few more questions about them, please, if that's okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Can you tell me how long is it that you've been hearing the voices?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: About since I was a teenager as well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, okay. And do you know, are there... how many voices are there or who they are?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, I know who they are. It's mainly my stepdad. And he, I don't know, just tells me how dirty I am and how horrible I am. And then I don't know, sometimes it's my mum as well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what kind of things does your mum say?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think mainly she just thinks I'm a liar.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, okay. And how often is it that you get these voices, Jane?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They're not there all the time, but you know, generally they're sort of like sitting there, but I don't know, they're sometimes louder than others and it's like the other night, they might as well have been in the room.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. And did you think they were in the room?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I mean I know that they're not there. But it's like they're just so loud in my head.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So can I just clarify that? Do the voices seem as though they're inside your head or is it like my voice coming through your ears?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, it's like inside. Inside your head.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And am I right in thinking that they trouble you more at times when you're stressed out?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Can I ask you a few more general questions about how you are in your mood? How would you say that you feel generally, kind of in yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I hate myself. Most of the time it's not... I just don't like being me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That sounds as though it can be very difficult sometimes. And it sounds like you've used cutting in the past to help. Are there any other things that you do to help when you feel really bad?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Drinking. I have... smoke a few spliffs now and then, you know. I don't do it so much now but in the past... I don't know, I just had a funny thing about food. You know, I'd sort of like binge and then just throw it all back up again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, okay. And that was in the past but not recently.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not done it recently, no.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And can I ask, Jane, it sounds like when you cut the other night you were doing it to kind of get rid of the pain. Can I just clarify, were you doing it to try and kill yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Have there ever been times in the past when you have tried to kill yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My late teens.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. What happened then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably around when I was 19. I don't know, it just got to a point where I didn't want to be anymore so I took some tablets.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, okay. So that was in your late teens and at the time you took the tablets because you wanted to be dead, is that right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. But you've not wanted to be dead since that time in your late teens?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can I ask you a few more general questions about your home situation? Who is it that... is there anyone at home with you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, not now, but my daughter used to live with me. But she's gone to live with her dad now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So she's gone to live with her dad. Was that quite a recent thing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: About a year ago.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. And what was that about?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: She just couldn't cope with the fact that I was cutting myself. I didn't do it in front of her, but she knew it was happening. And I suppose one of the big things as well was the relationships I had.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The relationships you had. Can you tell me a bit more about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's like the one I just had with Mark, you know, starts off being great and then I get really scared. I just get really scared that they're going to leave and then it turns into a big fight and they end up leaving anyway.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. And it sounds like your daughter struggled with that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I mean I suppose she didn't know whether she was coming or going really.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, okay. And were there a lot of relationships like that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You've seen, Jane, a few people in the past. You've seen a couple of psychiatrists and a couple of counselors. Has anything that anyone's done for you before been particularly helpful?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's been crap. I just feel like I'm being passed from pillar to post.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. So you've not found anything that people have done particularly helpful in helping you to manage your relationships and your cutting and the things that seem to go wrong for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well it's like... it's like nobody's listening to me. You know, I think you're the only person who's actually sat and listened to what I've got to say.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you think it would be worth, given that this has been such a long-standing problem and clearly does get in the way of quite a lot of aspects of your life... Do you think it would be worth us meeting again one more time and perhaps having a think together about how the service could best support you with this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: What do you mean one more time? Can't I see you, you know, sort of properly?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, the way that we work here in this department is that we see people once or twice and try and think with them about the best place for them to be and then refer them on to the most appropriate part of the service. So it wouldn't be usual for me to see you more than once or twice, Jane.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, but you're like I said, you're the only person that's listened to me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I know it's very difficult to open up to people and I know that you have opened up here today and it can feel quite hard that you're not going to continue to see me, but it is the way that we work here, is to pass you on to somebody who is perhaps a bit more appropriate for your needs, Jane.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So would it be okay if for me to book you in to come back and see me say next week for our second appointment and we can perhaps have a think of where to go from there? Would that be okay?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I suppose so.

video_details.title: Psychiatric Interviews for Teaching: Psychosis
video_details.description:
Please note that this video has been made by the University of Nottingham for teaching purposes. The psychiatrist is a real psychiatrist but the patient is played by an actor. No real names or personal details have been used. 

In this film, an on-call psychiatrist is assessing a young man who has been referred urgently by his GP. The psychiatrist takes a history in which she elicits persecutory delusions, third person auditory hallucinations, running commentary, thought insertion, and somatic h

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi Andy. Do you want to come on in and have a seat?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm Dr. Taylor, the on-call psychiatrist. I received a call about you having some distressing experiences and thought it might be helpful to talk. Would that be alright?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would it be alright if you told me a little bit about what's been going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My housemates are working for MI5 and they're doing stuff to my brain. They're out to get me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That must be very difficult. How long has this been going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: About two months.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How did you first realize this was happening?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I came home once and the TV had been moved. I just knew then they were working for MI5.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what was it that you knew at that moment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That they were for MI5.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it's been a couple of months?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, a new lecturer at uni works for MI5 and drafted my housemates and turned them against me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I've noticed you looking around. Could I ask what's happening at those times?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I can hear them talking about me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Who can you hear?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My housemates. I hear them all the time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How many voices?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Three of them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do they sound real, like my voice?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, but I hear them even when they aren't here, like they're in another room.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you hear what they're actually saying?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They're always talking about me and commenting on everything I'm doing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can you give me an example?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: If I'm packing my bag, they'll comment that I've left the house now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Anything else? Do they talk to each other about you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, they know I've twigged and they say I'm making trouble and they're going to sort me out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do they ever talk directly to you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you felt like thoughts are being put into your head that aren't your own?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, they're putting stuff in my brain. It's not me thinking it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Different thoughts?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, stupid stuff, like thinking about a Coronation Street character when I don't watch it. They aren't my thoughts.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you have any idea how that's happening?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's a chip MI5 put in my head. I can feel it all the time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What about others knowing what you're thinking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, they're just putting stuff in.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do your thoughts ever just stop altogether?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, if anything there's too much. I wish I could unplug it and get this thing out of my head.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me more about this chip.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's a tracking device. I can feel it moving around in my head.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That must be difficult. Do you know why they're doing this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know why. I've done nothing wrong.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any other sensations in your body?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I'm not ill, I just want this thing out of my head.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How are you coping with all this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't leave my room much. I wait until they go out to get food, but now they're poisoning it.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: They're poisoning it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you eating much?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you don't feel safe? Have you taken steps to protect yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've got a knife and a baseball bat in case they come in my room. I don't want to hurt anyone, but I have to protect myself.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you used either or taken them out with you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I don't want to get caught. It's just for my room.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Has it ever felt so bad you've wanted to hurt or kill yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I thought about getting pills to overdose, but I couldn't leave the house to get them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: In the past, have you had issues with temper or aggression?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I'm not that kind of person, but they're driving me to this.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you been in trouble with the police?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, never.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there anywhere you feel safe?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My parents' house.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you seen much of them recently?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I thought about going back, but I don't want to drag them into this or have MI5 know about them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you worried your parents might be involved?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I thought about it, but no.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Are you generally fit and well? Any medications?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm not ill, it's just this thing in my head. I don't take any pills.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What about alcohol or other drugs like cannabis?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't drink much. Is my mom going to know about this?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No, we wouldn't discuss this with your mom.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I smoke weed daily, about a ten-bag a day.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any other drugs, like speed?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've done speed with mates on weekends, most recently about a week ago.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: But it's not the drugs. This is constantly there regardless.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I was checking because certain drugs can make these experiences worse. Do you think this could be due to stress or being mentally unwell?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, because I'm not ill. It's them. I just want it to stop.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you think a psychiatrist, medication, or a short hospital stay would help?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. I'm only here because of my mom. She doesn't believe me... do you believe me?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I believe you're having a difficult time, but I'm not sure MI5 is the cause. We should bring your mom in and discuss getting you some support. Would that be alright?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'll go get her now.

video_details.title: Psychiatric Interviews for Teaching: Mania
video_details.description:
In this film, a psychiatrist assesses a man who has been referred by his GP. The patient demonstrates flight of ideas, pressure of speech, disinhibition, punning, grandiose delusions, and second person auditory hallucinations. His presentation is consistent with mania.

Please note that this video has been made by the University of Nottingham for teaching purposes. The psychiatrist is a real psychiatrist but the patient is played by an actor.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello there, Mr. Riley.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Hello, you alright? Yeah?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: My name's Dr. Bedi, and I'm the psychiatrist.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right, I've come to see you because my GP sent me to see you, didn't he? He said I should come and see a "trick-chiatrist", psychiatrist, yeah. Anyway, he said come and see you because you have time to listen to me. He's not had time to listen to me, you see, because he's a GP, he's a doctor, but I don't think he's very clever. He's not very clever because he's not let me get into this, you see, he won't let me talk about this. He listens to some things sometimes, but then sometimes he doesn't.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can I just clarify why you're here and why I'm here? I'm the psychiatrist in the emergency clinic today, and your GP's asked me to see you. Is that right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right, well, that's why I'm here. Because I've got to tell you about this. Yeah, and this, because this is important stuff. Really, really important stuff.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, before we start with that, can I just ask you what you'd like me to call you, Mr. Riley?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Names, names are a game, so don't bother with names, that's just stupid. Call me John.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: John, okay.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, okay. What's your name?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm Dr. Bedi.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, your proper name.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: My name is Dr. Bedi.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Your proper name, your proper name's not Doctor.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: At work, I am Dr. Bedi.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not doctor, Dr. Who, diddly-dang, woddly-dang, skip-de-dang. Do you watch that? That's fantastic, that programme.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Now, John, can I ask you how old you are?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: How old? Only as old as the woman you feel, aren't you? Hey? Right, okay. You know, wait, a man's heart is through his stomach. Oh yeah, fantastic.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how old would that make you, John?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Food for the soul, nice bit of soul, yeah? Hey? Bit of fish, fan- I'm hungry. You got any food? Any food round here? Any... Oi, down there, you got any food? I'm starving.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: They won't be able to get you any food. Let's perhaps, I'll tell you what, let's perhaps think about food in a minute.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, that's a good idea. Because this is important, this is why I'm here, to talk to you about this, tell you what's going on.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, well tell me a bit about this then.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, this is the work I've been doing, you know, this is really important, and it's my cure for cancer. That's what it is, you know, it's all written down here. Well, it's not written down, it's here, and it's at home in me books at home. What I get from the papers is I get sort of clues as to what I'm supposed to do and how I'm supposed to get the other clues so I can hone it down and come up with the final thing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how long, John, has all of this been going on for, would you say?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's been going on for ages now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How long would you say?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Ages now. Well, I've been up all week, mostly this week I've been working really hard at this. It's been going on longer than a week, but I've been working at it really hard for this week, because it's the numbers you have to find out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right. Am I right in thinking you normally do a different job?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I'm a mechanic. Car mechanic, yeah. "Manic mechanic," they call me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Manic mechanic?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it was my mate Dave. My mate Dave, I showed him this, and he told me it- he told me to go away because I was bonkers. He didn't say go away, he told me to fuck off. He said "fuck off, you're bonkers." Anyway, you see, he did that. And so I said, "Well, you know, I don't think he was clever enough, really." Not enough, you know, that's why I went to see the doctor about it. Because I thought, you know, show him, because he's a doctor, you know, he's been to university, he's done stuff. No, thick as shit. No. He really, he said he didn't have time. I thought, "How can you not have time to hear about the cure for cancer?" You know what I mean? Yeah. So that's why he's sent me to see you, because I'll tell you all about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, well tell me about it then. Tell me what's going on.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right, well, I've got my various bits and pieces here and I find things in the papers, like the football results, you see, they need adding together and then I have to find some other information on this page, there's some pages and page numbers there, I have to add those together and take it away from what's on there, yeah? So that's how I do that, and then you find other things...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what does that number tell you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That number corresponds to numbers I've got on my chart at home. I've got a big chart on my wall, and I find that number and then that adds up to something else. And it's- it's all there, I mean, that's- that's really good. I'm going to get one of those.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's- that's really good. That's- that's a phone that does the internet and everything. So I'll be able to find out more stuff that way when I'm out and about. But that's- and there's numbers, you see, I use those numbers there, they need adding up and taking away from something.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And John, when you've done all this with all the numbers and the chart, where will that leave you? What is it you're headed for?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it's the cure for cancer, isn't it? That's what it is, the cure for cancer.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How's that going to work then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: How it works is God tells me that I'm doing a really good job and how great I am and how fantastic I am working at this, you know, and I just keep going at it, you know, I don't stop. I don't stop.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can I just take you back a step? You said God tells you. Can you tell me a bit more about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, he tells me. He just tells- he just talks to me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: He talks?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He just talks to me, tells me I'm doing a really good job and I'm fantastic and really wonderful and I'm great, you know, I'm doing- and I have to show this to people. That's why I'm coming to show you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And John, when God talks to you, can I just clarify this with you, does he talk to you like I'm talking to you, with the voice coming through your ears, or does it feel more like...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Voice doesn't come through your ears, comes out your mouth. Voice comes out your mouth and goes in your ears. Yeah, I get straight- you should know that, because you know, you're a doctor as well, aren't you? So you should know these things.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And is that how the voice seems to you, John? You hear him in your ears.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I hear him in my ears, because that's what you use for hearing. And you know, and he talks to me with his mouth because, you know, he's a big bloke.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So the voice seems to come through your ears rather than inside your head.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's quite loud, because he's a big bloke.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is he a big bloke?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He's a big bloke, yeah. He's got a big beard.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's he like then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, he's a big bloke, big beard, yeah. I've called him beardy-beardy once, he didn't like that. He got right up, oh, crusty, he got right up when I called him beardy-beardy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I can imagine.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, so I just call him sir. He loves to be called sir, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what kind of things when he's talking to you, what kind of things does he say to you, John? No more monkeys, the organ grinder for me, I want to talk to the top man, top boss, top cat, that's what I want to talk to, top cat, top cat, top cat, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: He tells me I am fantastic and how great I am for doing this, getting stuck into this and keeping at it, and I should show it to people. And that's what I do, you know, I come out and I show it to people.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So who have you been showing it to?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, okay, who have I been showing it to? Well, I've sent copies of stuff to the Pope, and the Archbishop of Canterbury. None of them have written back. You'd think they would, you know, because they're close to God, they probably know him. You know, they've probably met him and stuff, you know. I mean, the Pope, he claims to have met him, I mean, you don't know, I would assume that the Pope knows God, you know, he's got his address and telephone number and everything like that. But, you know, the Archbishop of Canterbury, he's just rude, because he's not written back at all. And there's Tony Blair.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you've written to Tony Blair as well?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, he was in the wrong way for him, though.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what did he say?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: What? Nothing. I got a letter back- well, I didn't even get a letter back from him, I got it back from somebody else. Not him. It might have got lost in the post and somebody got it by mistake, but I just hope nobody's stolen my ideas, really, because that's what it is.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds, John, as though this has all been keeping you really busy.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Really busy, really busy.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you been sleeping at all?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, no time to sleep.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: No time to sleep. When was the last time you had a good night's sleep, would you say?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Don't need it. Don't need it. I've got all this enthusiasm from God, you know, it's there, it's all this energy inside me that's working. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you feel as though you've got lots of energy?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, tonnes of it, tonnes of it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how are your thoughts? Are they going fast? Are you thinking lots of different ideas?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, yeah, because I have to think really intensely. You look at stuff down here, I mean, you know, there's- I got that in the door the other day, you know, and there's lots of numbers on there that need adding up and taking away from other numbers...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And John, how are you feeling about yourself? Your self-esteem. How do you feel about yourself as a person at the moment?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Fantastic. I feel fantastic because, you know, God's telling me that I am, you know, I'm doing a really, really good job and it's all there and it's all happening.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And tell me this, John, because I couldn't get it from your GP letter, have you ever had anything like this before in your life where you felt full of energy and lots of bright ideas?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, but this has been going on for so long that I can't really remember anything else, you know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And have there ever been any times in your life where you've kind of been the opposite, John? Where you've been a bit down in the dumps, not much energy?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, nothing like that, no.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And what about any family history? Does anyone in your family have things like...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, it's just me, it's just me. It's really- well, they're not that really clever, you know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Not that clever?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, me family. You know, that's why I have to come and see doctors and places, hospitals and things like that because they're full of people- you're a clever person, that's what I want.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you feel as though you're more clever than perhaps other people?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, yeah, I'm certainly cleverer than those people at work, because they're a bit thick.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And John, I guess I'm just wondering what might have happened to start all this off for you. Have you any thoughts yourself what's brought this on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, God.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: God.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah. And he just came to me one day. One day he just came to me, you know. I started noticing connections with numbers and things. And it's- it's all there, you've just got to find it, just got to dig deep and look for it, you know what I mean?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I wonder, John, how have you been feeling physically in your physical health? Any problems there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Fine, fine. I'm fine, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And have you been taking any prescribed medication or even any drugs that aren't prescribed, any substances?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, nothing like that, it's just I've just got everything that's within me now. I don't need anything else.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you know how you were saying that your mate at work said that you were...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Who, Dave?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, he said rude things. I don't like repeating...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: He said rude things, you kind of suggested that you might not be very well at the moment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I told you what he said, didn't I? He said the F-word. I don't like that. No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But it sounded like he thought you weren't very well at the moment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I'm fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you think to that? Do you think that...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, look- can we look at this now? Because this is what I want to talk about. This is- I've come here to talk about this and you seem to be going off on something else and you're not really paying attention to me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you want to do that now? Can we look at it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Can we look a bit more of this now? Can we talk about it now, please?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I guess before we get back into that, I guess...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Why not? I don't want to get back into it, I want to talk to you about it now. Can we talk about it now, please?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I guess, John, what I'm wondering is whether this might be a sign that you're not very well at the moment.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I'm fine, I want to talk about this, you seem to want to change the subject, so I don't want to talk to you anymore. I've had enough of you and I've had enough of being in here, I want to talk to somebody else, I want to talk to the boss. Where's your boss? Where's your boss?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: John, I am the boss, I'm the consultant.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, you're a shit boss and I want to talk to somebody else, there must be somebody else I can talk to. I want to talk to the head man, I'm fed up with talking to all you rag, I want to talk to the engineer, no more monkeys, the organ grinder for me, I want to talk to the top man, top boss, top cat, that's what I want to talk to, top cat, top cat, top cat, yeah.

video_details.title: Psychiatric Interviews for Teaching: Anxiety
video_details.description:
In this film, the GP is seeing a patient who has presented several times before with complaints of palpitations and shortness of breath.

The patient describes the onset of her problems, which was a panic attack. She has then gone on to develop agoraphobia. The problem has affected a number of areas of her life.

The GP explores the patient's understanding of the problem and it is apparent that she has attributed this to a problem with her heart. The GP then goes on to give the patient an altern

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello, Julie Thomas?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, hi.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hello there. My name's Dr. Beddy. I'm one of the new GPs in the practice, and I'm seeing you today instead of Dr. Jones, who is your usual GP.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, he is. Yeah. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: First of all, what would you like me to call you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, Julie's fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, okay. Right, Julie. So what is it that's brought you to see me today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it's the same thing that I see Dr. Jones about. It's my heart.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, yeah, I understand that you've been in to see him a few times over the last few months. Would you mind if I ask you to go over again what the problem is, perhaps in your own words so that I get an understanding of it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, not at all. It's just I keep getting these situations where my heart starts to really, really race like boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom. I get chest pains. I can't catch my breath and it's making me feel funny talking to you about it. And so my heart starts to race, I can't get my breath and then I get chest pains and I'm get very afraid that I'm gonna have a heart attack.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, right. And you're feeling a little bit anxious just here with me?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm, yeah, just talking about it, I can feel it starting to come up. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, right. Take your time. Okay, thank you. So your heart starts to race, it really beats really fast and you feel like you can't catch your breath. Is that right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, that's exactly it. Yes. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How long has all this been going on for, Julie?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I think it's probably about six months basically. Yeah. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And can you remember what happened to start it all off?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, um, I think we've had some problems at work. Um, and um, I have felt more stressed about work than I normally do. And basically I was just trying to get into town one day on a day off and it was very hot, it was very, one of those funny hot days and it just happened, my heart just started to race and race and race and I couldn't get my breath. I was just like gasping for breath. Then I started to get chest pains and it was just awful and I managed to sit down and call my husband and he came out, he actually left work to come and get me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, so that sounds like quite an unpleasant experience for you, Julie.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It was awful. It was really, really frightening. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And when that was happening to you, Julie, when you're in the middle of town, what was it that you thought was going on?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I thought I was having a heart attack. I really did, yeah. And each time it happens, I'm so afraid that that's what's happening. So, you know, I've started to try to avoid situations where I might get like that basically.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, so what kind of things are you finding yourself avoiding?

diarization.speaker: Patient
