diarization.text: I can't get into town now without my husband taking me. So my husband has to take me to and from work. And then I also thought I shouldn't do anything to put any strain on my heart at all. So I don't do much exercise or anything at the moment. And other things as well.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And other things, what sort of other things are you not doing?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, just sort of personal things, really.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, I guess I'm wondering if you're talking about your sex life there?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I just feel, you know, that I shouldn't do anything like that because it just might put too much strain on me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, so you're avoiding sex in case that puts your heart rate up? Okay, okay. How's that affecting things between you and your husband, Julie?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's, I mean, yeah, my husband's getting really fed up with it to be honest, doctor. Um, he's been really, really kind and really supportive, but I think it's starting to affect his life quite a lot now. I mean, he wanted me to go to the pub last week and I absolutely promised that I would because I've begun to stop wanting to go out because I'm so afraid it's going to happen. And I promised and promised him I'd go to the pub and then when it came to it, I just couldn't, I just sat on the sofa and it started to happen again. And then I was worried that if I went to the pub I'd actually like get ill in the pub and then it'd be really embarrassing for everybody so I just said I couldn't go and I think he's getting a bit to the end of his tether now because it just seems to have come out of the blue and I've never suffered from anything like this before.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it sounds like he's getting to the end of his tether, but it also sounds like you're pretty fed up with the whole thing as well, Julie. Is that right?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I am actually, yeah. Yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so just so that I've got the story straight, it, this all began about six months ago. Before that, had you had anything like this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, not at all. I mean, I think that we had a new manager at work, I work in a bank actually, and then we had a new computer system put in and so it became much more stressful for all the staff, not just me. Um, and that's, I can sort of see that I was under a lot more pressure and that could be affecting me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So to make sure I've got the right, the right way round, it began six months ago, pressure at work, you went to town, you had the first of these attacks and then since then you've had some more of them. And now it's kind of got to the point that you don't want to go out, you don't go to town by yourself, you're not going to the pub, you're not socializing like you used to, and you're avoiding things like exercise and things like sex and that's having a bit of a, taking its toll on your relationship. Okay, okay. And looking at your, I know you've had an ECG that Dr. Jones organized for you a couple of months ago. What have you been told about the results of that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, Dr. Jones said that it was okay and there were no problems and you know, I did feel relieved you know because obviously there's been heart attacks in my family, my dad died of one you know at 72, so I'm thinking it must be my heart, there must be something wrong with it. And I did feel pleased when Dr. Jones said that, but on the other hand nothing's changed, you know, I'm still getting exactly the same problems, um, nothing, you know, I'm not getting any help with it. I just feel a bit like, well, so I haven't got a bad heart according to the experts but I'm still getting all the same symptoms you know worse and worse.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So even though the GP's told you there's nothing, there's nothing to worry about with your heart, do you still worry that there might be something wrong with your heart?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I do, I just I can't understand it and what do you think it is doctor?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well Julie, I think I'd agree with Dr. Jones. I don't think there is anything wrong with your heart. The reason I say that is that you've had an ECG which has come back perfectly normal and usually if there was a problem with the heart the ECG would pick something up. Also, you've got none of the risk factors really for heart disease because you don't smoke, your blood pressure from what I can gather from your notes has always been fine. Um, you're fairly young, before this you were pretty fit and active. And also, I know you worried about your dad having had a heart attack but actually he was a lot older than you are, um, and so you're not really in the same risk sort of bracket as he would have been. So I don't think that there is a problem with your heart. I guess what I'm wondering is whether actually what's going on is a little bit more what Dr. Jones thought, whether actually this might be the anxiety that's giving you a lot of these symptoms. Have you ever thought it might be that rather than a heart problem?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think I've been thinking more recently it could be because um, well my friend has like panic attacks and I've discussed it with her and she said to be honest it just sounds like that. But I, I've always thought it was my heart and what I can't understand is how my brain is making my heart start racing like it is.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, right. Okay. Has anyone explained to you about anxiety and panic attacks?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not really, no.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, well perhaps it would be helpful to sort of hear a little bit more about that. What we have on top of our kidneys is two little glands and they're called our adrenal glands. And they produce a hormone called adrenaline. Have you heard of that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, I have heard of that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, and what adrenaline does is it prepares us for situations of fight or flight. Is that a term you perhaps remember from biology at school?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I do, I do, yeah, I do remember that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you remember what, what we mean by fight or flight?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I think like if you're in a scary situation, you fight or you run away basically, your body sort of triggers that to do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, that's exactly it. And what's released to allow you to do the flight or fight response is the adrenaline. So when your body needs to, to get ready to do something, it surges out a load of adrenaline. And the adrenaline basically gets you ready for action. So it does things like it puts your heart rate up, it makes your breathing speed up so that you're ready to, to run. It can sometimes make people feel as though their mouth is dry, it can sometimes make people feel a bit lightheaded. Are those the kind of symptoms that you can get?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, definitely. Yeah, definitely. All of those, actually.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And what often happens with people with panic is that the first time that happens, the first adrenaline release occurs out of the blue, um, perhaps at times of stress, and you mentioned that there was stuff going on at work and you're feeling a bit stressed out and you're in town, it was a bit hot. And so that may have been what was behind that very first panic attack. What happens to people is that once they've had one panic attack, they go on to have more. And the reason for that is that once you've had something like that happen to you, you're kind of there thinking, 'Oh, will this happen again?' Is that something that you do?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, absolutely. I've started to really monitor my heart and when it starts to race, I start to get worried and then it starts getting faster and faster, so it does feel...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's, yeah, yes, yes. You, you're describing it exactly, Julie. That's what we call hyper-vigilance. So you're there kind of keeping a bit of an eye on your heart. And for most of us, our heart rate will go up and down all through the day, but most of us don't worry about it because we don't notice it. But because you've had a panic attack, you're there thinking, 'Oh, what's my heart doing?' And then the minute it starts to change, you clock it, you notice it, and then you start to get anxious thoughts. So you might...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: You start worrying. I really do. I keep thinking, 'Is it going to be now? You know, is my heart going to stop beating?'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, so you get those kind of anxious thoughts, and they're very frightening.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Very.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And because you're thinking, 'Oh my goodness me, could my heart stop?', that makes you even more anxious and that causes even more adrenaline to be released. And that makes the symptoms even more pronounced and then that makes you believe even more that there's something wrong with you. Does that make sense as to what might be happening?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It does, it does make sense, doctor.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: One of the things that you have been doing, which is something that a lot of people with anxiety do, is that you've started to avoid doing things that trigger it off.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I have, yeah. Yeah, yeah, like not walking into town or anything. I just won't do it anymore.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Exactly, exactly. And whilst in the short term that sort of alleviates your symptoms because you don't have to get panicky, what's happening is that the more you avoid doing things, the less likely you are to ever get round to finding out whether or not anything awful really happens.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. Yeah. Right.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does that make sense?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It does, it does make sense.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, if we are starting to tackle this as if it was an anxiety problem, there are a number of approaches. We can think about tablets and we can think about other kind of talking approaches. And there are pros and cons to those and side effects and things that we need to discuss. So I'm just slightly watchful of the time. We seem to be coming to the end of today's session for the appointment, but what I wonder is whether we should meet again, perhaps next week, and look again more carefully at some of the treatment options and think together about which might suit you best. How would that sound, Julie?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, that's fine. That's fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any other questions before we finish?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I'll make an appointment to see you next week.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's fine. And I'll see you next week.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Thank you, doctor.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That's pleasure. All right. Bye-bye.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Bye-bye.

video_details.title: How to do Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT): Role Play Session
video_details.uploader: Russ Curtis, Ph.D., Professor of Counseling
video_details.description: Russ Curtis, Ph.D., LCMHC is a professor of counseling at Western Carolina University. Prior to becoming a counselor educator, Russ worked in a clinical mental health center where he coordinated with medical providers to ensure optimal care for at-risk clients with co-morbid mental and physical illnesses. Dr. Curtis’s co-edited textbook, Integrated Care: Applying Theory to Practice (Curtis & Christian, 2012) was selected by The Council on Social Work Education in collaboration with SAMHSA as one

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Just from what you've told me so far, I'm drawing this map with four quadrants: feelings, thoughts about self, behaviors, and physiology.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Would panic be too strong of a word or just heightened anxiety?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Mhm, yeah, so high anxiety.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Any other feelings when you're driving in general that come up for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just being really anxious and feeling like I can't do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And the thoughts that you have about yourself when you feel that anxiety? One of them is 'I can't do this.' Any others?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I feel like I could possibly have an accident. Like, I could hit that car or I can kind of imagine hitting someone.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And that affects your behavior in what way?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: One time it made me stop what I was doing. It was on a merging lane and I just kind of stopped in the corner because it was running out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And now it's affecting you in what way? You had that one incident where you actually did stop.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: So now I just slow down and try to take notice of who is in which lane and make sure I get over in time.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So we've looked at feeling anxious, thinking 'I can't do this' or 'I could have an accident,' and the behavior of stopping or being hyper-cautious. What physiological reaction do you experience?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess my palms get like sweaty and I just feel kind of nauseous sometimes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sweaty palms and feeling nauseous. We're trying to encapsulate how this all works together. If you were to label this map, what would you call it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe like 'nervous driving.'

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Nervous driving. Now let's look at a goal map for where we want to be when we're done counseling. When you're driving, you'll be feeling what?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Calm, relaxed, confident.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'll put 'calmer,' increased confidence, and increased relaxation. If you're feeling that, what kind of thoughts about yourself would you have?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That I'm a better driver, that I'm able to merge over and to drive in lots of traffic without feeling so nervous.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So thoughts like, 'I am able to drive in excessive traffic and feel confident to perform.' How is that going to affect your behavior?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'll be able to keep driving regularly without it affecting me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So not quite as hyper-cautious. And how would that affect your physiology?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not having the nauseous feeling and just being more regular, I guess.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: More comfortable, with less sweaty palms and less nauseousness. What would be a small first step you could take towards this goal before next session?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just trying to change my thought patterns, I think.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What would be a first step with that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I think positive visualization would work well for me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Even while you're driving? Or before? Or maybe both?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, maybe both. Just visualizing myself doing those actions, like moving over in lanes and merging into traffic, and being successful at it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We could practice some visualization in session along with some quick relaxation techniques. Do you have any types of relaxation that work for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Deep breathing and praying.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Those are things we can look at. We can also talk about incidents like your close call. I'll make a copy of this map for you so we know where we're wanting to go.

video_details.title: 03.Medical Interview -Chief Concern (History of Present Illness)
video_details.description:
Complete Medical History. University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health.
Video 03/07

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, Mrs. Jones. I'm Jane Crone, I'm a medical student with the university here. I've been sent here by Dr. Smith as part of our training as a medical student to do an interview with you. Then I'll take that information back to Dr. Smith, and she will come back in and see you then after that. How may I address you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Nice to meet you. Mrs. Jones is fine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you. Is that okay with you today to talk?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes, that would be fine. Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I'm going to start out today by just talking a little bit with you about your chief complaint, what brings you here today.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: My left elbow's actually been bugging me a lot. Every once in a while I've been getting a little bit of pain extending my arm and going back to bending it. Really that's the primary reason I've come in. I've attempted to take a little bit of Tylenol to relieve the pain, but it's not really seemed to help much.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Before we talk a little bit more about that, is there anything else that you want to talk with either me or Dr. Smith today?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not that I can think of, no.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me more about this pain.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's just kind of a throbbing pain. It'll act up kind of randomly throughout the day. It's not specific to, you know, the morning or evening or even in the middle of the day or night. It just kind of randomly acts up. I would say excessively like when I'm doing work, like after the dishes. It'll start to act up if I lift one of my children up. So any sort of exertion is kind of where I've noticed a lot of the pain coming from.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And tell me, when did it start for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would say in the area of maybe a week and a half to two weeks ago.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you described the pain as throbbing. Is there anything else about the pain in terms of the quality of the pain that you want to describe for me?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, just really throbbing.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Started about a week to two weeks ago. And do you recall what you were doing at the time that it started?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've been helping my husband clean out the garage lately and we were lifting some boxes. And that's kind of, I didn't notice it at the moment but later in the evening it started to act up.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I would like to hear a little bit about the severity of it on a pain scale of one to ten, ten being the worst pain you've ever had, one or zero being no pain. At this, how bad is this pain?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would measure it probably about a six or seven. It's become more of a nuisance than an actual physical pain.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And is it a six or seven all the time?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Whenever it starts to act up, yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how often a day does that happen?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would say maybe two to three times per day.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Do you notice any pattern to that at all?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. And can you point exactly to where it is for me? The location of it exactly.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's kind of the area that just kind of wraps around the actual elbow that's really bothering me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And does that pain go up your arm or down your arm or anywhere else on your arm?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, it stays right in that area.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there anything else that goes on at the same time? Any other symptoms that happen? Anything else other than when the pain is happening there, anything else going on for you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not that I've noticed, no.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Is there anything that makes it feel better?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Nothing that completely gets rid of it. Tylenol will relieve it for a temporary period of time, but it hasn't gotten rid of it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how much Tylenol do you take?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Whatever it says on the bottle, usually one to two tablets.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And is that regular strength or extra strength?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Regular strength.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And you just take it across the counter, the normal directions on the bottle? Okay. And does anything make it worse?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like I mentioned, any sort of exertion, picking up a child, doing the dishes, pretty much daily kind of living activities.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So using it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Have you seen anybody else for this complaint? What else have you tried other than the Tylenol and anything else?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I've attempted to use a heating pad on it and I've also attempted ice. Neither were successful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds you've talked a little bit about how it's impacted you to be able to work in the garage or do the dishes or lift your child. Is there other impact on your life?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Like I mentioned, it's just more of a nuisance. There will be times in the middle of the night that it'll start to act up if I get up to go to the bathroom. I'll notice pain in my elbow.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Does it wake you at night?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It doesn't, but if I wake up in the middle of the night it will trouble me in falling back asleep.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you think it is?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm not quite sure. My best guess is maybe some sort of pulled muscle or something, but honestly I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What I'd like to do now is just kind of go through all the things that you've told me and summarize for you. This is information that I want to take back, but I want to make sure that I have it all correct. So if I've forgotten something or I've gotten something incorrect, please help me.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You came to the clinic today for a complaint of left elbow pain. And it's pain that you mostly noticed when you were bending it or using it in some capacity. It's a throbbing pain that happens randomly, but it does happen two to three times during the day. What you noticed about it is if you exert or you extend or flex your elbow at all, that's when it seems to be at its worst. It's gone on for about a week, maybe to two weeks when you think back on it. And it started out when you were helping your husband clean the garage and you were lifting lots of boxes. It's about a six to seven on a pain scale and you describe it over and over as being a nuisance, which tells me that it's getting kind of in the way of doing some things that you want to. You report that it happens probably two to three times a day and that the pain wraps around the joint completely. You've taken some Tylenol for it across the counter. You've taken that several times a day without much relief, that it hasn't helped much. You've also tried a heating pad, you've tried some ice, that hasn't really helped either too much. It sounds like again you kept referring to it as a nuisance, that it's just kind of getting in the way of your daily activities. It doesn't necessarily keep you up at night, but you do notice it at night when you wake up that it's still going on for you, so sleep doesn't seem to help. And that what you mostly think this could be is a pulled muscle of some type. Is there anything I've forgotten or that you wanted to tell me about this?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Not that I can think of, no.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Thank you for telling me about your chief concern. I'm going to take it back to Dr. Smith. Thank you very much.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

video_details.title: DBT for Eating Disorders
video_details.description: This video demonstrates how to implement techniques of Dialectical Behavior Therapy, particularly emotion regulation skills, when working with clients with eating disorders.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi, my name is Enie Hinos. I'm a graduate student at the University of Nevada, Reno. In this video, I'll be providing instruction on how to use techniques from Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) when working with a client with an eating disorder, specifically emotion regulation skills during a food exposure exercise.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's going on? What are you feeling right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm feeling disgust. I feel like I can't do this.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Tell me what that feeling of disgust is. What are you disgusted about?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Just my body. Eating that makes my body feel gross and uncomfortable.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It sounds like there are some judgments in there, like you're feeling fat, but you're describing it as feeling uncomfortable, which is great.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Eating that makes me feel icky.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I understand how you'd feel that way, but I think there's a primary emotion under the disgust. What might that be?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Looking at that cake makes me want to run out the door. I'm afraid of what will happen if I eat that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: That makes sense. I see you're worried and having a hard time approaching it. When was the last time you ate cheesecake?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I honestly can't remember. I used to like it, but it was a long time ago.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You've been avoiding this for so long that it makes sense you're feeling fear, especially since this is one of your hardest foods.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I just see it as a big blob of fat.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What is that thought, 'a big blob of fat'?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: A judgment.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Exactly. Let's try 'opposite action' to that fear. Instead of running away, we want you to approach the thing that scares you. Can we have the fear right now and still take a few more bites?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: All right. Let's do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So how was that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: It's difficult and uncomfortable, but I'm doing it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You did perfect opposite action. You felt uncomfortable, but you still did it. Do you feel a little bit proud of yourself?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, a little bit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: This shows me that you can do it. Let's take a breath and do more opposite action.

Produced by University of Florida Department of Psychiatry. Funded by Flight Attendant Medical Research Institute Grant #63504 (Co-Pls: Gold & Merlo). THANK YOU!

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so I've finished the exam. I have some good news and I have some not-so-good news. It looks like you don't have any cavities, so that's the good news.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's great!

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: However, I'm pretty concerned about something I'm noticing in your mouth. Actually, if we look up here, the roof of your mouth, I'm noticing a lot of irritation that's really consistent with tobacco use. And you had said on your form that you're not a tobacco user, so I'm just wondering what's going on.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't smoke cigarettes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, well, as I said, there's a lot of irritation, and particularly like I was mentioning up here in the roof of your mouth, it's turned really deathly white colored and there's little red spots. You're really damaging this tissue in your mouth, which can really cause some severe problems. It's called nicotinic stomatitis, and this is something we don't see in patients who don't use tobacco. So maybe you're not smoking cigarettes, are you smoking a pipe or cigars?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, the only thing, I've never smoked cigarettes ever, but when I go out with my friends, we like to go out to lounges and sometimes there are those nice young men that gift you different sorts of things and we got some of those mini cigars, Swisher Sweets. That's the only time that I've ever really used anything that's got tobacco in it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so I think that's a pretty common misconception because they're fruit flavored people think they're okay. Those are really bad for you. Did you know that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Really bad? But they're just little mini little cute little girly cigar things.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right, they're still cigars and they're still tobacco. And so they still cause lung cancer, oral cancer, emphysema, all those same kinds of things that you'd see with cigarettes. So it's really important—

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I only use 'em just to relax. I mean, it's not like it's something that I would smoke 20 or 30 cigarettes a day. I mean, I only do it when we go out.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, at least you're not doing that, so that's good. But it's still causing a lot of problems and as I said, I can see the evidence in the roof of your mouth. You're causing some serious damage and this needs to stop. Have you thought about quitting?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I didn't really know I'd started.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you mean?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I didn't really think that it was anything more than just like social drinking, just something that I do in a social setting when me and my friends go out to the bars.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you're gonna quit then?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, maybe.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What do you mean maybe? I just told you how bad it is for you. It's messing up your mouth, you're putting yourself at risk for all these other diseases. This is really important, you need to quit.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it's something that I'll have to think about.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What's there to think about? You said it's not something you do all that often. There's all these negative side effects, all these risks you're putting yourself in.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it's just something that I do to relax and I don't do it that often and so I probably could cut back.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, well that's a good start, but cutting back isn't gonna do it. If you actually quit the smoking, you can reverse all the damage you've done in your mouth and you can stop yourself from being at risk for these other diseases.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I don't believe that they're cigars and what I do believe is that it's a choice and it's my right and it's something that I choose to do. And so I will think about cutting back, but I'm not at a point where I'm ready to do that and I'm not really sure that I even believe that what you're telling me is real.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're choosing to really damage your mouth and actually it can cause problems with your teeth too. There are a lot of really negative things that go along with any tobacco use. You're really choosing to make yourself sick and potentially die.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it's something that I'll think about.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I appreciate you thinking about it. I hope you'll think about it really hard. You know, this is something that I'm going to continue to ask you about because it's something that really needs to change.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Can I help you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I just got off work and apparently they're going smoke-free so I thought I'd stop by the pharmacy here and see what my options are. Some of my friends have tried nicotine patches and they say they don't work very well. I don't really want to quit smoking, I just need something to get me through the day.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you want nicotine replacement but you don't want to quit smoking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Maybe like during the day nicotine replacement. Does that, I mean, do y'all have anything like that?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: We don't really recommend that. The idea is you would use the nicotine replacement to actually quit so then you wouldn't be smoking at work, but you also wouldn't be smoking the rest of the time either.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well I don't really want to quit. I mean, I like smoking. I go out after work to have a beer with my friends and I'll smoke cigarettes. I mean, it's not really a big deal. Cigarettes aren't that bad. I mean, I know that it's popular to say that smoking is bad for you, but you know, I like it so I'm going to keep doing it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, well smoking really is really bad for you. You know, it causes things like lung cancer, emphysema, heart disease, oral disease.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, okay. Well, what are my options? You know, assuming that I'm right, what are my options?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, to be honest with you, you mentioned the patch. I can't recommend a patch to you if you're going to continue smoking. That can actually be pretty dangerous for you. In order to advise you about this at all, I need you to tell me a little bit more about your smoking history and how much you're smoking now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I mean, I smoke barely a pack a day. I've probably smoked for five or six years now. It's not really a lot of cigarettes, but it's sort of hard to get through the day at work.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, well we actually consider 20 cigarettes a day to be a significant amount and in fact I would then recommend to you that you'd start on the highest dose of nicotine replacement.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sounds good to me, the more nicotine the better. Is it like gum or something? I could chew it like while I'm in the office. That sounds pretty great. I mean, do you have that?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, there are some products that you could use to take away some of your cravings, and probably the gum would be the best option for you. It's not something you would continue to use continuously throughout the day, however. The gum is something you use just when you have a craving.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, okay. Well, where's that?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, we have that here, but again, the idea would be for you to actually quit smoking.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I'm probably not going to buy anything today. I mean, I just came by to see what my options are. Thanks for the input. I mean, do you have anything else? Do you have any other advice for me?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Aside from the gum, you could try the nicotine lozenge, that would be another option for you. Again, that's not something you'd want to use continuously throughout the day. The nicotine patch is the best for continuous nicotine replacement, but again, that's not something you can use while you're continuing to smoke.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, well, okay. Well, thanks. I mean, I guess that helps a little bit. Maybe I'll be back later. Thanks.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so I wrote a prescription for an antibiotic for Aiden, that should help with the ear infection, but in looking through the chart, I mean, it seems like he's had six or seven of these just in the past year or so. That's really a big problem.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, it's... it's pretty stressful for both of us. I think it's really upsetting.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, one of the primary risk factors for multiple ear infections in kids is actually smoke exposure. Are you smoking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I... yeah, I do smoke, but I don't smoke around him. I try really hard not to smoke around him.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, the fact that he's having these ear infections is indicating to me that he is being exposed to smoke, and so what can you tell me about that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I... I don't know. I mean, I try really hard not to smoke around him. I don't smoke in the car. Um, when he's home, I go outside to smoke. I just... I mean, I know it's bad, and I know it's bad for him, so I don't want him to be around it, so I try really hard.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I really need you to quit smoking both for your health and for Aiden's. Did you know smoking around your child is associated not only with ear infections, it could get to the point where we have to put tubes in his ears pretty shortly here, but also things like Vitamin C deficiency, cavities, like dental cavities, behavior problems, asthma, other upper respiratory infections. It's really putting him at a lot of risk. In addition to that, kids of smokers end up smoking themselves. Do you want him to grow up to be a smoker?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, but I... I've thought about quitting, but it's just... it's really hard, so I just don't know how to do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, now's the time to quit. It's really gotten to the point where you can't keep smoking. Not only for him, like I said, but also for you. You're putting yourself at risk for lung cancer, for emphysema, for oral cancers, for heart disease, for all kinds of things.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I know, I know. I've heard... people have told me before, I've heard all that. I just... don't know how to do it. How am I supposed to quit? It's... it's so hard.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, there's all kinds of things you can use now. It's not as hard as it used to be. You can use nicotine replacement, there's patches, there's lozenges, there's gum, there's the inhaler, there's nasal spray. We can talk about medications, you can try Chantix, you can try Zyban. There's quit smoking groups you can go to, there's hotlines you can call. There's no reason why you shouldn't be able to quit. This is really important.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't have time for all that. I understand that. I know it is. I mean, everybody has problems, right? It's just... really, it's really, really hard.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, what can be more important to you than the health of your child?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I really need you to tell me that you're going to quit smoking. This is really important.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'll... I'll go look at all those things, and I'll find... I guess I'll try to find something, and I'll talk to my doctor about it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, well I think you really need to think about this seriously. Like I said, it's really putting yourself and your child in danger.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay. Whatever. Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, I wrote a prescription for antibiotics for Aiden. I did want to talk to you though, I'm a little bit concerned looking through his chart at how many ear infections he's had recently and I noticed that you had checked the box that someone smokes in the home. So I was wondering if you can tell me a little more about that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it's just me and him and I do smoke. I try really hard not to smoke around him. But I've been smoking for 10 years except when I was pregnant with him but everything's so stressful being a single mom and my having a full-time job and so it's just that's why I started smoking again.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You have a lot of things going on and smoking's kind of a way to relax and de-stress.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes. Yeah. Some people have a glass of wine, I have a cigarette.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sure. And it sounds like you're trying not to smoke around him. Why'd you make that decision?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I know it's not good for him. I mean I read those things about ear infections and asthma and stuff and but other kids have ear infections and their parents don't smoke.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So, on the one hand you're worried about how your smoking might be affecting him and on the other hand you're not so sure if it's really the smoking that's causing these problems.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right. Yeah. I mean he doesn't have asthma. I don't he hasn't had a lot of other problems that his other friends have so and I've thought about quitting before in the past but I just don't I just don't see how it's possible right now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: What made you decide to quit smoking when you were pregnant?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, he was inside me and we were sharing everything and I knew that he would get some of that and I just didn't think I could live with myself if something happened to him.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Right now though it feels almost too difficult to even manage or even to try.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, exactly.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How were you successful when you quit before?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. I think about it now I don't even know how I did it. I just I just did it. You know I just I just couldn't imagine like him not being born or going into labor early and and him having problems and stuff like that, all the stuff that they talk about with women who smoke. So I that was just enough to to say okay, you know what, I'm not gonna risk that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: The risks were so scary then that you were able to stop and they don't feel as scary to you now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I mean we're two separate people and like I said I don't I try really hard not to smoke around him. I'm pretty good about that. I don't let other people smoke around him. So I you know...

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're doing the best you can do.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. But it sounds to me too like part of you really does want to quit.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I I know that I need to and I you know I keep every new year I say okay this year I'm gonna quit smoking but then something happens and it just doesn't. And quitting just doesn't happen.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: It's on your to-do list, it's just not making it to the top. If you did decide to quit on a scale of 1 to 10 where 1 is not at all confident and you don't think you could do it and 10 is you feel pretty certain that you could, where do you think you fall right now?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Probably like a 5. Kind of in the unsure area, like I know I've done it before so I know I can do it but at the same time it just seems really hard and it's not the same situation.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well what made you say 5 rather than 2 or 3?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I know, I know all the ways it's bad for me and I don't want him to grow up thinking that it's okay to smoke. I don't want him to use any kind I don't want him to chew or or anything like that. Um so I know I need to especially before he gets old enough to understand what mommy's doing but I just don't know if I can do it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. So, it sounds like you have a lot of reasons why you'd like to quit. You have been successful quitting in the past and right now you're just feeling a little bit hesitant about your ability to do it. Where do you think we should go from here?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know. I'd like some help. I just don't know what kind of help I need.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sure. Well, if you'd be interested that's something I can definitely talk to you about. There are a lot of new options that can actually help people be way more successful in their attempt at quitting. There's different medications you can try...

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't like medicine.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. There's also a lot of support groups and classes that you can take where you have other people to go through it with you and sometimes just having that support can be a big part of it especially for people like you where smoking is such a stress reliever.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That sounds nice but I'm not sure if I have the time for all that.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sure. It feels like something that would take up a lot of time and maybe not fit into your life. I wonder if we could talk about some options that might fit into your life.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That would be really nice.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Well if you're willing then we could set up another appointment where you could come in and we could talk more about that.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I would like that. That would be great.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Great.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sure.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: How can I help you?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yeah, I hope so. My workplace has just gone smoke-free. I'm not very happy about it. I'm going to keep smoking, but I was wondering if there is anything that can help me get through the day so I can go get my beer and smoke a cigarette after work.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So your workplace just went smoke-free and you're not too pleased, huh?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No. I'm not going to quit smoking. I like it, it helps me relax. I don't see what the big deal is.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, tell me a little bit about how smoking fits into your day. It'll help with the consultation.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I smoke a little less than a pack a day. It's not too bad. I've probably smoked for the last five years. I could quit if I wanted to, but I don't really want to right now.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, so you feel like right now smoking is a pretty important part of your life. It's not something you're ready to change, but if the time came when you did decide to quit, you feel pretty confident you could go ahead and do that?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Sure, I could quit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, what makes you so confident?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I don't see why I couldn't. Although I have not ever tried to quit. It's just something that I do for fun on breaks at work, in the morning, and after work.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And so in terms of a readiness to actually go ahead and make a quit attempt, where do you think you fall on the scale of one to 10, where one is I'm not considering it at all and 10 is I'm definitely ready to quit?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm probably a two. I haven't even thought about quitting until this great announcement at work today. I am totally not going to quit smoking.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, what made you say two instead of one?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, anything is possible. I guess I could maybe be convinced. Is there anything I can try that would make me want to quit smoking?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, there are a lot of products available now that can actually help you curb that urge to smoke. We have products that can help to replace nicotine, which can help to decrease withdrawal symptoms you might experience when quitting or cutting down. And also some medications your doctor could prescribe for you that might take away even some of the desire to smoke.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, well that's good information. I'm not going to do anything today. I just need to know my options. But that's encouraging if I decided to quit smoking, I do have at least tools to help me quit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sure. And back to that scale you mentioned, you said you were a two. What do you think it would take to move you up to a four or a five?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I don't know, I guess if my friends, like if one of my friends decided to quit with me, that would probably help too. But all my friends love to smoke, so I don't see that happening in the near future.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Sure. I wonder if now that your workplace is going smoke-free if there'll be some people at work who are planning to quit.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: That's a good point, I hadn't really thought about that. That's a good idea, yeah.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, well it sounds like you're really here just for information today. I'm happy to help you pick out some of these products if and when you do decide that the time is right for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Okay, well thanks a lot.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, hard part's over. So the good news is no cavities.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh great.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yes, always happy to hear that. I do have some concerns though because I'm seeing some irritation in your mouth, in the palate, that's called nicotinic stomatitis.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, that sounds bad.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, it is. It's some damage to the roof of your mouth that happens from tobacco smoking. And so I'm wondering if you can tell me a little bit how tobacco fits in your life right now.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Tobacco? I mean, I don't smoke cigarettes. I've never smoked cigarettes. I do go out with my friends, um, you know, we go out to bars and, you know, we'll have a few drinks and smoke some of those little cigarillo type things. I mean, I don't even think of them as cigars and they're certainly not cigarettes. Um, and I'll have one or two of those in an evening with, with my friends, but certainly not 20 or 30 of them a day like you would with cigarettes. I mean, that's the only thing that could possibly have anything to do with tobacco.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you've made a decision in your life not to smoke cigarettes. That's something you didn't want to do. It sounds like you're kind of concerned about the health effects of cigarettes, but you have been smoking the little cigarillos at least one or two every time you go out.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Right, but that's, that's just like a social thing. That's something that my friends and I do. We, um, we, it's not a habit or something that I have to have. And, you know, we're talking about one or two when we go out for an evening, not packs of them.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, so you're not like those chain smokers. You're not smoking packs and packs a day. The amount you smoke is so minuscule you can't even imagine that it would cause any harm. And yet here it is damaging the roof of your mouth.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, well, you have a point there. Um, now that you mention it, um, I have started, um, having one or two at work, you know, when we have breaks, because I have a couple of friends at work that smoke. And so every time we have a break, you know, we all go out to the break place outside, um, and so I now I go with them and I have one of these Swisher Sweets. Um, I like the peach flavor the best. They're so cute. Um, but that's really only pretty recently.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So smoking's kind of become a big part of your social life now. When you go out you're smoking, and even during breaks at work you're smoking.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, yeah, yeah, you know, now that you say it like that, it's true. Um, I am smoking on a daily basis.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So aside from that social aspect, what are other things you like about it?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, it's relaxing and it's just nice to be with people. Um, and you know, when, you know, I like to go to Las Vegas. And so when we go to Vegas, it's really fun to go to the cigar bars. It's kind of sophisticated and fun. And so, you know, it's mostly a social thing. Okay. I wouldn't say I was a chain smoker.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. How about the other side? Have you noticed any not-so-good things about the smoking?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I was going to ask you about um, whitening my teeth, because I've noticed that they have more stains on them, um, than a few years ago. And so I imagine that has something to do with the smoking.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah, so we're noticing some pretty negative effects in terms of your oral health with the smoking. Are there any other things that you're concerned about?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, well, there's the expense, you know, what with the economy and all, um, I've had to be careful about my money. And so, um, there is the extra expense of, um, because I'm buying more of them than I used to. So the, the money aspect is also a concern.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Mhm. So there's your oral health, there's the financial aspect. And then earlier you brought up some concerns about smoking cigarettes and how that can be harmful for you. Were you aware of the fact that smoking these little cigarillos, the Swisher Sweets, can have some of the same negative health effects?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, absolutely not. I mean, I thought of it more as a, a fun thing to do with my friends. Certainly not a smoking habit or anything that would be harmful.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Mhm. So it's kind of surprising to you that something you've been doing and you've been doing more and more of it is actually pretty bad for you.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, yes. I, um, I checked the box on your form when you asked if I used tobacco. I checked no, because I never thought of myself as a smoker.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, what do you kind of make of that now that you realize that you're actually a tobacco user and that you might actually be causing some pretty serious health effects?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'm really concerned. I mean, I don't want to, um, develop cancer, lung cancer, or any of the awful things that happen from smoking. And you know, really until this conversation, I never really thought of myself as a smoker at all. So I'm very concerned.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, the good news is in terms of the nicotinic stomatitis, at the point in which you stop smoking, you can actually reverse all the negative effects that occurred. And you might also know that you can stop the progression of any other diseases that had started just by quitting smoking.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Really?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Yeah. Is that something you'd be interested in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, I would. I really would, because like I said, I'm a brand new smoker. I didn't know I was a smoker until I came to see you.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Mhm. Well, if you think about it on a scale of 1 to 10, where 1 is really don't think you could do it at all and 10 is really confident that you could quit if you tried, where do you think you fall?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, I think I'd probably be in 7 or 8. I, I'm, I'm pretty confident that I could stop doing this.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. What made you choose 7 or 8 as opposed to a 5?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Because it's not a part of my daily life. I don't have to have a, um, smoke when I get up in the morning. I don't smoke 20 or 30 of them a day. So it's not that much exposure and I feel pretty confident that I could stop.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So it sounds like just to kind of summarize, you've noticed some negative effects of the smoking. You have some concerns about health effects that could occur. There's the financial aspect. And yet you feel pretty confident that you could quit if you tried. So where do you think we should go from here?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Um, I'd really like some more information about quitting. I mean, I've heard there's some, some new medications, there's some new things that can be done to help people make quitting more comfortable. And I, I really want to quit.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Well, I'd be happy to talk to you more about that and give you some tips and advice and give you some suggestions about where you can get some support with quitting.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Oh, that'd be wonderful. I really appreciate you talking to me about this today. Thank you.

video_details.title: Motivational Interviewing: Evoking Commitment to Change
video_details.description: In this video clip, the Physician works together with the patient to develop a specific focus.  The provider does this by asking open-ended questions, providing affirmation, using reflective listening and summarizing for the patients (OARS).  He also helps the patient to scale the importance of the issue and the patients confidence level for change behavior.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Hi John, nice to see you again. So, tell me, how are things going?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, doc, I know you told me that I needed to lose weight, and even though the scale didn't show it today, I was able to lose about five pounds, but then I gained it right back.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Well, I appreciate you bringing your weight to the forefront. Do you mind if we explore this issue further?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, by all means, I know we have to discuss it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right. Well, it sounds like you've been struggling with your weight recently, and I understand how difficult it is to lose the weight and then have it come back again. So tell me what you did to lose that initial five pounds.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I started watching what I ate and I ate less. I've been eating more fruits and vegetables. I've also been walking more, I'm walking up to 20 minutes a day now. I saw the weight come slowly off and I felt better, but then when I watched it come back on again, I gave up.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But you did have some success. Tell me how you felt when you lost the weight.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I felt great, I felt really proud of myself. I thought that this was something that I could do.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay, well it sounds like you realize that when you lost the weight you felt better, and that it's going to affect your overall health. So tell me what you think changed that caused you to gain the weight back.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, I think it's because I've been eating more fruits and vegetables, that's it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: And how many servings of fruits and vegetables on average per day would you have?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: To be honest, I have four to six glasses of orange juice a day. I have fruit for lunch and breakfast. I have usually one to two servings of a vegetable like lettuce or broccoli with dinner.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: John, it's very important that you recognize that some fruits, but especially fruit juice, can contain a huge amount of calories. Did you know that a glass of orange juice has almost as many calories as a can of cola?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: No, I didn't know. But doesn't the food pyramid classify fruit juice as a serving?

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: You're absolutely right, but keep in mind that the food pyramid is to be used as a guideline only. When it comes to nutrition, we have to have a more personalized approach. So I have a hunch, and that is the excess fruit that you were consuming probably caused your weight rebound. What's your impression?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Well, this changes quite a bit. I mean, here I am thinking that my fruit intake is making me healthier and it's actually making me fatter.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Indeed. Let me ask you something. Knowing what you know now, how important is it to you to lose the weight by decreasing the amount of juice that you're currently taking in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Obviously I need to cut back on the fruit juice, but boy do I love that OJ.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Oh, I understand. Let me ask you this. On a scale from zero to ten, zero meaning that there's no way you can do it, and ten meaning that you're 100% confident that you can do it, how confident are you that you'll be able to reduce the amount of juice you're currently taking in?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Six or seven.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: All right, so you're not a zero. So that tells me that you've got some confidence that this is doable, this is something you certainly can do. Why are you not a zero?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I guess it's because I know that I need to do it to lose the weight.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: So you realize, again, that if you decrease the amount of juice you're taking in, you're going to decrease your weight, you're going to feel better, and you're going to impact your health positively.

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Yes.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: But you're also not a ten, and that tells me that there may be some obstacles to your success. What would it take for you to be a ten or even an eight or nine?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Getting the fruit juice out of the house, because I know if it's there I'll drink it. My wife does the shopping for us, so maybe if I ask her not to get the juice, that would solve it.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Okay. Now, if the juice was still there, can you think of anything else you could do?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I suppose I could replace it with a low-calorie drink or drink more water.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Excellent. John, I get the impression that you want to stay on course with weight reduction, and the best way to do this will be to decrease the amount of juice that you're currently taking in. So if I saw you in two weeks and I asked you how much juice you're drinking and how you did it, what would you tell me?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: I'd say I didn't have any and I substituted it with sugar-free drinks.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Excellent. Well, it sounds like you have a plan. Same scale, zero to ten, how confident are you that you can make this happen?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Ten.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: I agree. All right. Well, you know what? I'm not going to start any medications today. Your labs were a little bit off, but I think we can handle this from a purely lifestyle standpoint. What do you think?

diarization.speaker: Patient
diarization.text: Great. Sounds good to me.

diarization.speaker: Therapist
diarization.text: Excellent. I'll see you in two weeks.
